docs.title: The limit order book
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A limit order book (LOB) is the list of resting buy and sell limit orders on one venue, sorted by price and, within each price, by arrival time. Marketable orders consume it from the best price outward.
  • Price-time priority makes your place in the queue an asset. An early order gets more fills, and its fills are less adversely selected, than an identical order at the back.
  • Hidden and iceberg orders trade visibility for priority: they hide size but queue behind displayed orders at the same price.
  • What execution algos and market makers care about is depth (how much trades near the touch) and resilience (how fast the book refills after a sweep), not just the spread.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Intuition: a queue at every price
docs.text:
Picture a row of ticket windows, one per price, with buyers (or sellers) lined up at each in arrival order. A seller who wants to trade now goes to the highest bid window and serves the line from the front. The limit order book is exactly this, kept by each exchange's matching engine.

Three events change the book:

  • Add: a non-marketable limit order joins the back of the queue at its price.
  • Cancel: a resting order leaves. Most US equity orders are cancelled, not filled.
  • Execute: a marketable order matches against the front of the best opposite queue.

On US exchanges the minimum quoting increment (tick size) is $0.01 for stocks priced at $1 or more. The SEC's 2024 amendments add a $0.005 tick for stocks whose spread is pinned at one tick, but compliance has been pushed to the first business day of November 2027 [Verified]. See fees, rebates and ticks.

    Q1 -->|"no"| R1["Rest in book at its price,<br/>behind earlier orders"]
    Q1 -->|"yes"| M1["Match the best opposite level,<br/>oldest order first"]
    M1 --> Q2{"Quantity left?"}
    Q2 -->|"no"| F1["Fully filled"]
    Q2 -->|"yes"| Q3{"Next level still<br/>within the limit?"}
    Q3 -->|"yes"| M1
    Q3 -->|"no"| Q4{"Time in force"}
    Q4 -->|"IOC"| C1["Cancel the remainder"]
    Q4 -->|"Day or GTC"| R1

docs.title: Price-time priority
docs.text:
Matching follows price-time priority: better price first, then earlier arrival (FIFO) within a price. Most US equity venues use strict FIFO; some options markets allocate pro rata by size instead [Lore]. Priority is fragile: reducing size usually keeps your place, while changing price or increasing size sends you to the back with a new timestamp.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Resting: post limit order
    Resting --> Resting: size reduced, keeps priority
    Resting --> Requeued: price change or size increase
    Requeued --> Resting: new timestamp at back of queue
    Resting --> PartFilled: partial execution
    PartFilled --> Filled: remainder executes
    Resting --> Filled: full execution
    Resting --> Cancelled: cancel
    PartFilled --> Cancelled: cancel remainder
    Filled --> [*]
    Cancelled --> [*]

docs.title: Worked example: a market order walks the book
docs.text:
An illustrative book for stock XYZ on one exchange (sizes in shares, order IDs in brackets):

Bid size Bid Ask Ask size 600 [G 600] 100.00 100.01 400 [E 100, F 300] 800 99.99 100.02 500 [C 200, D 300] 1,500 99.98 100.03 300 [A 100, B 200]

The mid is 100.005 and the spread is one tick. A market buy for 1,000 shares arrives:

  • 400 at 100.01 (E first, then F, by time)
  • 500 at 100.02 (C, then D)
  • 100 at 100.03 (A; B is untouched)

Average price = (400 × 100.01 + 500 × 100.02 + 100 × 100.03) / 1,000 = 100.017. That is 1.2 cents, or about 1.2 bps, above the pre-trade mid: $12 of cost on a $100k order. The book after the trade shows 100.00 bid and 100.03 ask, a 3-cent spread. How fast market makers re-quote 100.01 and 100.02 is the book's resilience; in liquid names it is often milliseconds [Lore]. In practice a router would sweep several venues at once with ISOs rather than walk one book (see order types and auctions). Lab 01 implements a price-time matching engine you can replay this on.

docs.title: Queue value: why being early is worth money
docs.text:
Take a large-tick stock where the spread is almost always one cent and 10,000 shares sit on the best bid. Compare joining that bid as the first 500 shares in line with joining as the last 500.

  1. Fill probability. The front gets filled by ordinary small sell orders. The back is filled only if enough selling arrives to chew through 9,500 shares ahead of it.
  2. Adverse selection. When the back does get filled, it is usually because a large or informed seller is sweeping the level, and the price then ticks down. A back-of-queue fill is a signal that you just bought before a drop.

Illustrative numbers, per share, for a resting bid that gets filled. The markout is the mid's move against you shortly after the fill.

Front of queue Back of queue Half-spread earned vs mid +0.50¢ +0.50¢ Maker rebate +0.20¢ +0.20¢ Markout (adverse selection) −0.20¢ −0.90¢ Net if filled +0.50¢ −0.20¢ Fill probability over the next minute 90% 30% Expected value per share posted +0.45¢ −0.06¢

The front is worth about half a cent a share more than the back, roughly the half-spread, a common rule of thumb for large-tick names [Lore]. Most of the gap is adverse selection, not fill rate. That is why HFT market makers race to the front when a new price level opens, and why the queue-position card models the two together. Academic queue models include Cont, Stoikov and Talreja (2010) and Huang, Lehalle and Rosenbaum's queue-reactive model (2015).

Lab 01 measures the same effect in a simulated order book with informed and noise traders. It posts 14,004 probe orders at different depths in the queue. Orders in the front quartile filled within 10 s 86% of the time, against 47% for the back quartile. Their 10-second markouts were +0.28 vs −0.23 ticks. Comparing the front and back of the same queue puts priority at about $0.56 per 100 shares (synthetic lab result).

Lab 01, synthetic data. The more shares ahead of you, the less likely a fill within 10 seconds. The fills you do get at the back come disproportionately from informed sweeps.

docs.title: Hidden and iceberg orders
docs.text:
• Non-displayed (hidden) orders rest in the book but are not shown on market data. On most venues they rank behind displayed orders at the same price, so hiding costs priority. Midpoint pegs are usually non-displayed.
  • Iceberg (reserve) orders show a small tip, for example 100 shares, and refill from a hidden reserve. Each refill normally gets a new timestamp, so the visible part keeps going to the back of the line.
  • Detection. Prints larger than the visible size, or a level that keeps refilling after being hit, reveal hidden interest.

docs.title: Depth and resilience
docs.text:
Depth is how much you can trade within k ticks of the mid. It differs by stock type:

  • Large-tick stocks (low price, high volume) have a spread stuck at one tick and long queues. Cost is mostly waiting time and queue position.
  • Small-tick stocks (high price) have spreads of many ticks and thin levels. Cost is mostly walking the book.

Displayed depth understates true liquidity (hidden, off-exchange and reactive interest is missing) and overstates it (quotes vanish when price starts to move). Resilience is the speed at which spread and depth recover after a sweep. Part of a trade's price impact is transient (the book refills) and part is permanent (information). That split is the core of transaction cost and impact models. Kyle (1985) formalized depth as the price move per unit of order flow, Kyle's lambda.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• Market making is queue management. Equity market making and fee- and microstructure-driven strategies earn the spread and rebate only from positions near the front. See queue position and order placement, quoting and inventory control and adverse selection and markouts.
  • The book is a signal. Queue sizes at the touch feed the microprice and order-flow imbalance. Short-horizon forecasts in ML-driven short-horizon alpha start from these features.
  • Walking the book is a cost. The worked example is the micro version of what impact models estimate and what VWAP, TWAP and POV and smart order routing try to avoid.
  • Stale queues get picked off. Latency arbitrage races to hit resting orders before they are cancelled.

docs.title: Venues and retail flow
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • US stocks trade on 18 exchanges (as of October 2026), 33 NMS-stock ATSs and over 200 other off-exchange dealers. In 2025 off-exchange volume was 50.6% of the total, the first annual majority, and about four-fifths of it went through principal dealers such as wholesalers.
  • Wholesalers pay retail brokers for marketable orders (PFOF) because retail flow is "less toxic": it rarely predicts the next price move. They can give price improvement and still earn a spread.
  • Flow toxicity is measured by markouts: how far the price moves against the liquidity provider after the fill.
  • Of the SEC's four December 2022 proposals, two were adopted (Rule 605 disclosure; ticks, access fees and round lots) and two were withdrawn in June 2025 (the Order Competition Rule and Regulation Best Execution).

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

The market is this fragmented because Regulation NMS (2005) obliges every venue to respect the best protected quote anywhere. That makes a new exchange instantly reachable, and fee competition does the rest (see fees, rebates and ticks).

docs.title: Wholesalers and payment for order flow
docs.text:
When the SEC proposed its Order Competition Rule in December 2022, it found that brokers sent more than 90% of individual investors' marketable orders to six wholesalers [Verified]. Academic work using 2019–2022 data finds that two of them, Citadel Securities and Virtu, handled over 70% of US retail flow [Reported]. Wholesalers fill those orders as principal at or better than the NBBO, usually with price improvement, and pay the broker PFOF. Robinhood's 2025 Rule 606 reports show payments from tens of cents to about a dollar per 100 shares, depending on wholesaler, order type and stock group [Reported]. Citadel Securities paid about $341M for US retail equity and options flow in Q2 2025 alone [Reported].

A wholesaler's per-share income statement for a 100-share retail buy (illustrative: $50 stock, NBBO $49.99 × $50.01):

Line ¢ per share Sell at $50.006 (0.4¢ price improvement); spread captured vs mid $50.00 +0.60 Adverse selection: mid drifts 0.10¢ up over the next minute −0.10 PFOF to the broker −0.15 Hedging, exchange fees, clearing, technology −0.10 Net +0.25

Run the same fill against an informed taker whose one-minute markout is 1.5¢ and the result is −1.15¢. The whole business rests on being able to tell those two counterparties apart.

docs.title: Flow toxicity: why retail is "less toxic"
docs.text:
Flow toxicity is the probability-weighted damage a counterparty does to a liquidity provider. It is the expected price move against you after you trade with them. Glosten and Milgrom (1985) showed that a dealer facing some informed traders must widen the spread to everyone. VPIN (Easley, López de Prado and O'Hara, 2012) estimates toxicity from volume imbalance. Practitioners mostly measure it directly with markouts. The realized spread is the effective spread minus the subsequent price move.

Retail marketable orders are small, uncorrelated across accounts and rarely timed on information that matters over the next seconds to minutes, so their markouts are small. The key difference is segmentation. A wholesaler knows which broker sent the order, so it knows the flow is retail. An exchange sees anonymous orders and must price for the average counterparty. The two sides of the debate:

  • For the current model: retail gets better-than-NBBO fills and zero commissions, paid for by the low cost of serving uninformed flow.
  • Against: the SEC estimated a $1.5B-a-year "competitive shortfall" versus order-by-order auctions [Verified]. Critics also argue that taking benign flow off exchanges leaves lit quotes facing more toxic flow, so lit spreads are wider for everyone.

The evidence is mixed. This KB takes no side.

docs.title: Disclosure: Rules 605 and 606
docs.text:
• Rule 605 requires monthly execution-quality statistics: effective spreads, price improvement and speed. The March 6, 2024 amendments extend it to brokers with 100,000 or more customer accounts, add a summary report, and add realized spreads at several horizons from 50 ms to 5 minutes [Reported]. Compliance moved from December 14, 2025 to August 1, 2026 [Verified]. Short-horizon realized spreads are, in effect, standardized public markouts.
  • Rule 606 requires quarterly broker routing reports: where orders went and the PFOF received per 100 shares.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• Retail flow is a strategy. Retail flow internalization is the wholesaler business above. Its risk model is adverse selection and markouts, and its pricing engine is fair value and microprice.
  • Toxicity sets the quote. Equity market making and quoting and inventory control widen or skew quotes on toxicity estimates. Latency arbitrage is the most toxic flow there is.
  • Venue choice is an algorithm. Smart order routing ranks venues by fill rate and post-fill markout. Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos handle the dark pools. Transaction cost analysis audits the result.

docs.title: Strategies: the map
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • This module has 30 strategy dossiers in seven families (A–G), plus five cross-cutting pages (H). Every dossier follows one template, so any two compare directly.
  • Every strategy sits at a point on two axes: holding horizon (microseconds to months) and edge source (speed · liquidity provision · structural/regulatory · informational · behavioral · risk premium).
  • Short horizons are dominated by liquidity provision, speed and structure; long horizons by risk premia and behavioral effects. Informational edges sit in the middle.
  • Most "stat arb" is liquidity provision on a slower clock: you are paid for absorbing other people's price pressure.
  • Read every dossier's header table first. If you only remember one row, make it "Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it."

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Three lessons. First, horizon and edge are correlated, not identical: liquidity provision runs from microseconds (quoting) to weeks (pairs), because absorbing price pressure is paid at every horizon (Grossman and Miller; Nagel) [Verified]. Second, capacity rises with horizon while Sharpe falls; the comparison matrix puts numbers on it. Third, the middle is the most crowded: days-to-weeks informational and behavioral signals are where most quant funds and pods compete, and where published signals decay fastest (evaluation).

docs.title: How to read a dossier
docs.text:
Every dossier opens with this header table:

Field What it tells you How to read it Family Which of the seven groups (A–G) Families share data, infrastructure and failure modes Edge source Primary edge first, then secondary The six-way taxonomy is defined in How quants evaluate a strategy Holding period Typical life of a position Sets infrastructure, turnover and how fast you learn the strategy is broken Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it The economic victim or customer If nobody identifiable pays, assume the backtest is lying Universe & instruments What gets traded and hedged Wider universes add breadth; illiquid names add cost Data required Inputs, from direct feeds to filings to alt data Drives cost and point-in-time risk Core algorithms used The 2–6 central module 03 cards Feeds the strategy × algorithm matrix Infra intensity Latency sensitivity and compute Says whether a microsecond, or a GPU cluster, matters Capacity (rough $ range) Money one firm can run before costs eat the edge Always tagged, with reasoning; treat as an order of magnitude Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Risk-adjusted return before and after costs Look for period, source type and decay; an academic backtest is an upper bound Turnover How often the book trades Turnover × cost per dollar traded = cost drag Main risks / failure modes How it loses money Mechanisms plus dated episodes Crowding risk How many others hold the same positions Crowded trades fail together, fast Firm types that run it Types from the big picture Named firms only when sourced Lab A runnable synthetic-data lab, if any Toy markets; each lab lists what it misses

Confidence tags. [Verified] means a primary source (filing, regulator, paper, exchange document). [Reported] means credible press, survey or practitioner book. [Estimate] means our derivation, with the reasoning shown. [Lore] means widely repeated but unverified. Every Sharpe ratio, capacity or return figure states gross or net, the period, the source type (academic backtest, fund disclosure, practitioner estimate) and known post-publication decay.

The body always runs: intuition → economic rationale → the trade → worked example → algorithms and pseudocode → implementation → P&L decomposition → evidence → capacity and decay → failures → textbook vs practice → variants → diagram → practitioner talk → myths → questions to ask (🔒 = proprietary territory) → collapsible math.

docs.title: How quants evaluate a strategy
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Every strategy is a claim that someone will keep paying you. The first test is naming that payer and one of six edge sources: risk premium, behavioral, structural/regulatory, informational, liquidity provision, speed.
  • Judge the net Sharpe, not the gross. Breakeven cost is gross alpha ÷ turnover; at high turnover, a haircut to gross alpha becomes a much larger haircut to net alpha.
  • A new strategy improves a book only if its Sharpe exceeds ρ × the book's Sharpe. A mediocre, uncorrelated strategy often beats a brilliant clone.
  • Backtests shrink live: published anomalies lost 26% out-of-sample and 58% after publication in one large study [Verified]. Plan on a haircut.
  • Funding is staged (shadow, small capital, ramp) with kill criteria written down before the first trade. Months of live P&L cannot prove alpha; they can prove the implementation.

Level: Core · Read time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11

A strategy pitch is a business plan: a revenue source (the edge), a customer (the counterparty), a cost base, a market size (capacity) and a risk of sudden death. A PM or CIO interrogates it like an acquisition: is the revenue real, will it last, what does it cost, and what does it do to the rest of the portfolio?

docs.title: The six edge sources
docs.text:
Each edge source has its own reason to persist and its own way to die.

Edge source You are paid for Why it persists How it dies Examples Risk premium Holding a risk others want to shed (crashes, distress, illiquidity) The risk is real: it periodically hurts, so the premium is a fair price Rarely dies; compresses when capital floods in Factors, VRP, carry Behavioral Other investors' systematic errors: under-reaction, extrapolation, anchoring Biases are human; arbitrage is limited by risk and career risk Publication and crowding arbitrage it down Momentum, earnings drift, revisions Structural / regulatory Someone forced by a rule or mandate to trade at a bad price Lasts as long as the rule or the mandate Rule changes, or competitors bid the edge to zero Flow-driven, auctions, fee-driven Informational Knowing or processing something sooner or better Data is scarce or hard to process The data commoditizes: vendors sell it to everyone Alt data, NLP Liquidity provision Immediacy for impatient traders, plus bearing inventory risk and adverse selection Demand for immediacy never goes away Margins are competed down; only scale survives Market making, reversal Speed Reacting first to public information Latency differences always exist somewhere Winner-take-most arms race; everyone but the fastest is priced out Latency arbitrage, lead-lag

Our view [Estimate] (reasoning: the persistence column): edges where the counterparty has a lasting reason to pay (risk premia, liquidity provision, rules) are the most durable. Informational and behavioral signals at days-to-weeks horizons are the least durable, because they are the easiest to copy.

docs.title: The evaluation checklist
docs.text: # Question Red flag 1 Economic rationale: why should this make money? "The model found it" 2 Counterparty: who pays, and why do they accept it? No identifiable payer 3 Sharpe or IR, gross and net, with significance Only gross shown; short sample; hundreds of variants tried 4 Capacity: dollars before costs eat the edge Capacity quoted without an impact model 5 Turnover and cost sensitivity Breakeven cost within 2× of the modeled cost 6 Correlation to the existing book Fails the ρ × Sharpe hurdle 7 Tail risk Smooth returns from selling insurance 8 Decay No out-of-sample or post-publication period 9 Crowding Same positions as published factors or peers 10 Data and infrastructure cost Fixed costs larger than expected net alpha at realistic size

docs.title: Sharpe and IR: gross vs net, and why short horizons win
docs.text:
The Sharpe ratio is excess return over volatility; the information ratio applies it to active return. Only the net figure pays anyone.

Short-horizon strategies post higher Sharpe ratios because they make many small, nearly independent bets; annualized Sharpe scales with the square root of independent bets per year. A daily Sharpe of 0.2 annualizes to 0.2 × √252 ≈ 3.2. Virtu's 2014 IPO filing showed one losing day in 1,238 (2009–2013) [Reported]. If daily P&L were normal, that would imply a daily Sharpe near 3.2 and an annualized figure around 50 [Estimate] (illustrative; P&L has fat tails). The price of that Sharpe is capacity: such books cannot absorb billions.

Confidence grows slowly: the t-statistic is roughly Sharpe × √years, so a true Sharpe of 0.75 needs about seven years to reach t = 2. Lo (2002) shows serial correlation can distort annualized Sharpe ratios [Verified]. Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue a new factor needs t > 3, not 2, given how many have been tried [Verified]. The deflated Sharpe ratio of Bailey and López de Prado corrects for the number of trials and for non-normality [Verified] (see overfitting and multiple testing).

docs.title: Turnover, costs and breakeven
docs.text:
Let gross alpha be \(\alpha\) (per year, as a fraction of gross market value), turnover \(T\) (dollars traded per year ÷ GMV, both sides counted) and all-in cost \(c\) per dollar traded (spread, fees, market impact). Then:

\[ \alpha_{net} = \alpha - T\,c, \qquad c^{*} = \frac{\alpha}{T} \]

The sensitivity of net alpha to cost is \(-T\): every extra basis point of cost subtracts \(T\) basis points of return.

Illustrative strategy Gross α Turnover T Breakeven c* Modeled cost Net α +1 bp of cost costs you Monthly factor book 3% 6× 50 bp 10 bp 2.4% 0.06% a year Daily residual reversal 12% 60× 20 bp 8 bp 7.2% 0.6% a year Intraday stat arb 25% 500× 5 bp 3 bp 10% 5% a year

Novy-Marx and Velikov agree: most anomalies with under 50% monthly one-sided turnover survive costs; few higher-turnover ones do [Verified]. Cost models are covered in P5; measuring realized cost in E6.

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text: Capacity is the size at which marginal net alpha reaches zero, or net Sharpe hits the hurdle; impact rises roughly with the square root of participation. An AQR study using live execution data estimated break-even fund sizes for US long-short size, value and momentum factors of $103B, $83B and $52B [Verified] (2012 working paper; one manager's 1998–2011 costs; an upper bound, since rivals share the capacity). For latency-sensitive strategies, capacity is better counted in P&L than in capital: the edge per trade is a fraction of a tick, and the whole global latency-arbitrage pool in equities has been estimated at about $5B a year (Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill) [Verified].

docs.title: Correlation to the book: the marginal Sharpe test
docs.text:
Adding a small allocation to a new strategy raises the book's Sharpe only if

\[ SR_{new} > \rho \cdot SR_{book} \]

where \(\rho\) is the correlation between the new strategy and the existing book (derivation below; see also Benhamou and Guez). With an existing book at Sharpe 2.0:

Candidate Standalone Sharpe ρ to book Hurdle ρ × 2.0 Book Sharpe after optimal mix A: decent, mildly correlated 0.8 0.3 0.6 2.01 B: same, uncorrelated 0.8 0.0 0.0 2.15 C: weak, negatively correlated 0.6 −0.3 −0.6 2.36 D: strong clone 1.5 0.8 1.6 2.00 (optimal weight is zero)

Candidate C, the weakest standalone, adds the most; D, the best on paper, adds nothing. Caveats: correlations jump toward one in a crisis (in August 2007 many quant equity books unwound the same positions at once, per Khandani and Lo [Verified]); and a strategy that barely moves the book's Sharpe can still be worth funding if the book is at capacity.

docs.title: Tail risk, decay, crowding and cost of doing business
docs.text:
• Tail risk. Sharpe treats upside and downside alike. Insurance-selling strategies (short volatility, carry, much liquidity provision) show smooth returns and negative skew. Ask for the worst day, week and month; Khandani and Lo's simulated market maker lost heavily in the week of August 6, 2007 [Verified]. See the failure gallery.
  • Decay. Across 97 published predictors, returns were 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower after publication (McLean and Pontiff) [Verified]. Falck, Rej and Thesmar find out-of-sample performance around half of in-sample, with publication date the main predictor of alpha decay [Verified]. Monitor live decay with L2.
  • Crowding. Warning signs: P&L correlated with published factors or peers, falling alpha per unit of turnover, violent reversals on de-risking days (crowding).
  • Data and infrastructure. Investment managers spent roughly $2.8B on alternative data in 2025, up 17% [Reported]. Fixed costs set a minimum size: a $1M-a-year dataset needs $25M of GMV at 4% net alpha to pay for itself [Estimate]. For HFT, colocation, feeds and hardware make breakeven a dollar figure, not a basis-point one.

docs.title: How a PM or CIO decides to fund a strategy
docs.text:
Funding is staged so that each dollar buys information: research review (the checklist) → shadow trading (live signals, no capital) → small capital (enough to measure real costs and fills) → ramp in steps, re-estimating impact at each size → steady state and retirement, with kill criteria set in advance.

Pods use hard drawdown limits. Widely reported Millennium practice: a PM's capital is roughly halved at a 5% drawdown and the PM is usually out near 7.5% (some accounts say 10%) [Reported]; firms do not publish these rules.

flowchart TD
    A["New strategy idea"] --> B{"Named counterparty<br/>and edge source?"}
    B -->|"no"| K["Reject"]
    B -->|"yes"| C{"Net Sharpe after costs<br/>and trial haircut clears hurdle?"}
    C -->|"no"| R["Redesign: cut turnover,<br/>widen universe, combine"]
    R --> C
    C -->|"yes"| D{"Beats rho times<br/>book Sharpe?"}
    D -->|"no"| K
    D -->|"yes"| E{"Capacity pays for<br/>data and infrastructure?"}
    E -->|"no"| K
    E -->|"yes"| F["Shadow trading"]
    F --> G["Small capital"]
    G --> H{"Costs, fills and tracking<br/>match the model?"}
    H -->|"no"| R
    H -->|"yes"| I["Ramp in steps"]
    I --> J["Monitor decay and crowding"]
    J -->|"kill criteria hit"| Z["Cut or retire"]

docs.title: Worked example (illustrative numbers)
docs.text:
A researcher proposes a 1–3 day residual-reversal strategy on ~1,000 liquid US stocks. Backtest 2014–2025 (12 years); 200 parameter variants tried. Gross alpha 12% of GMV a year at 4% volatility (gross Sharpe 3.0); turnover 60×; modeled cost 8 bp per dollar traded, so net alpha 7.2% (net Sharpe 1.8). Correlation to the existing book is 0.3; the book runs at Sharpe 2.0.

  1. Is it noise? Over 12 years the standard error of an annual Sharpe is about 1/√12 ≈ 0.29, so the best of 200 independent zero-alpha variants would show about 2.75 × 0.29 ≈ 0.8 by luck. Net 1.8 clears that bar.
  2. Haircut gross, not net. Apply a 30–50% decay haircut (the range from the studies above) to gross alpha: 6.0–8.4%. Costs stay at 4.8% (60 × 8 bp), so net becomes 1.2–3.6%, Sharpe 0.3–0.9. A 50% haircut to gross is an 83% haircut to net.
  3. Marginal test. The hurdle is 0.3 × 2.0 = 0.6. The planning range of 0.3–0.9 straddles it. Not fundable as designed.
  4. Redesign. A no-trade band and trading toward the aim cut turnover to 35× while keeping, say, 80% of gross alpha (9.6%). Costs drop to 2.8%. After the same haircut: net 2.0–3.9%, Sharpe 0.5–1.0. The midpoint (0.75) clears 0.6; the low end does not, which is why it gets small capital rather than a full allocation.
  5. Funding plan. Shadow-trade for 2–3 months. Then $50M GMV at 4% volatility: about $2M of annual risk, about $126k daily. Ramp to $150M, then $300M, if realized costs stay within 25% of the model, re-fitting impact at each step.
  6. Kill criteria, written first. Hard stop at a drawdown of 1.5× the annual volatility budget ($3M at stage one); review if realized cost runs 50% above model for a month or live P&L stops tracking the backtest replayed on live dates.

Why judge implementation, not P&L, early? At a true Sharpe of 0.75, the chance of losing money over six months is about 30%, over a year about 23% [Estimate] (normal approximation). In simulation, the 1.5× stop trips within a year about 8% of the time at Sharpe 0.75 but only 23% of the time when alpha is zero [Estimate]. Stops limit damage; they are weak detectors of dead strategies. Cost, fill and tracking diagnostics carry the early decision (L1).

Math: the Fundamental Law of Active Management

Grinold's law: information ratio ≈ skill × √(independent bets per year):

\[ IR \approx IC \times \sqrt{BR} \]

where IC (the information coefficient) is the correlation between forecasts and realized returns and BR (breadth) is the number of independent forecasts per year. Clarke, de Silva and Thorley add the transfer coefficient TC, roughly the correlation between the risk-adjusted weights an unconstrained optimizer would hold and those actually held:

\[ IR \approx TC \times IC \times \sqrt{BR} \]

Long-only limits, turnover caps and neutrality constraints push TC below 1; their paper reports realized performance at about 0.3–0.8 of the unconstrained law's prediction [Verified].

Illustration: IC = 0.03 on 500 stocks rebalanced monthly gives BR = 6,000 if bets were independent, so IR ≈ 0.03 × 77 ≈ 2.3; with TC = 0.5, 1.2; if correlation also cuts effective breadth to 1,500, 0.58. Breadth counts independent bets, not trades.

Math: why the hurdle is ρ × SR_book

Scale both return streams to unit volatility. The maximum Sharpe of an optimal mix of a book with Sharpe \(S_b\) and a candidate with Sharpe \(S_n\) and correlation \(\rho\) is

\[ S^{*2} = \frac{S_b^2 + S_n^2 - 2\rho S_b S_n}{1-\rho^2} \]

and the optimal risk weight on the candidate is proportional to \(S_n - \rho S_b\). It is positive (the candidate belongs in the book) only when \(S_n > \rho S_b\).

docs.text:
• Basic: What is the edge source, and who is on the other side? Is that Sharpe gross or net, and over what period?
  • Informed: What is the breakeven cost versus realized cost? How correlated is this with the book and with published factors? How many variants did you try?
  • Sharp: What did it do in August 2007, March 2020 or your worst week? At what size does net Sharpe hit your hurdle? 🔒 (exact capacity is usually proprietary) Were the kill criteria written before launch?

docs.title: Auctions and closing liquidity
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • In the closing auction, index funds, ETFs and benchmarked managers trade at whatever price clears. When their orders don't balance, someone with balance sheet takes the other side.
  • Auction liquidity providers read the published imbalance, offer the other side and earn the price concession, which reverts "quickly and almost completely" on average (Bogousslavsky & Muravyev 2023) [Verified].
  • The close keeps growing: about 3.1% of dollar volume in 2010, a record 9.4% of notional in Q2 2024, about 20% on rebalance days [Reported]. Nasdaq's cross printed a record $334B on the June 2026 Russell reconstitution [Reported].
  • Edge per share is small; the risk is overnight inventory and informed imbalances. Trading to move the close is manipulation.

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family liquidity provision Edge source liquidity provision · structural/regulatory Holding period overnight to a few days Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Index funds, ETFs and benchmarked managers that must trade at the official close: tracking error costs them more than a few bps of price, so they concede price to whoever absorbs the imbalance. Universe & instruments US-listed stocks and ETFs, heaviest on index events; futures as hedges Data required real-time imbalance feeds; index event calendars; auction and next-day price history Core algorithms used E5 Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos · M4 Quoting and inventory control · M5 Adverse selection and markouts · P5 Transaction cost and impact models Infra intensity moderate: one-second imbalance updates, hard cutoffs, an overnight risk model Capacity (rough $ range) $50M to $500M of overnight inventory per large provider per day, more on event days [Estimate] (imbalances are a few percent of $50B+ of daily closing notional) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) no public figures; positive on most event days with a fat left tail from news after the cutoff [Lore] Turnover about 100% of inventory per day Main risks / failure modes overnight gaps, informed imbalances, crowded event days, manipulation exposure Crowding risk high on known index events: everyone sees the same feed Firm types that run it electronic market makers, NYSE designated market makers, bank facilitation desks, stat-arb funds trading index events Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: At 3:50 p.m. NYSE publishes: "XYZ, 300,000 shares to buy at the close, indicative $50.10." The buyers are mostly index funds that must own XYZ at the 4:00 print, whatever it is. Someone has to sell 300,000 shares they may not own and carry the short overnight. That someone sets the closing price, and is paid by selling a few cents above where XYZ will trade tomorrow morning.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Grossman and Miller (1988): liquidity providers earn a price concession for carrying inventory until the offsetting trader arrives. Closing demand is the cleanest case: mechanical, scheduled, price-insensitive. US equity index funds passed active funds in assets in August 2019 [Reported], and closing volume tracks indexing and ETFs, spiking on S&P 500 additions [Verified].

Leveraged ETFs add mechanical flow: they buy after up days and sell after down days near the close (math below).

The concession is small: closing prices typically match pre-close bid or ask prices [Verified]. Profit comes from scale and selection.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Forecast: estimate imbalances from index changes and passive assets before publication.
  2. Read: after the cutoff (NYSE 3:50, Nasdaq 3:55), track paired shares, imbalance and indicative price every second.
  3. Size and price: expected reversion against overnight risk; send Nasdaq imbalance-only or NYSE closing-offset orders, or LOC orders.
  4. Hedge the book's net beta and sectors with futures, which trade after 4:00 p.m.
  5. Unwind next morning or over days; record close-to-open markouts (M5).

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative, extending the example in order types and auctions. XYZ last $50.00; MOC buys 1.2M, MOC sells 0.9M; other sell limits: 100k at $50.02, 150k at $50.05, 200k at $50.10. Alone, the close would print $50.10. We add a 100k sell at limit $50.04.

Price Buys Sells Matched 50.04 1.20M 1.10M 1.10M 50.05 1.20M 1.25M 1.20M 50.10 1.20M 1.45M 1.20M

The close is $50.05 (maximum volume, smallest surplus); MOC buyers pay $60,000 less. Next morning we buy back at $50.015.

Line $ Gross: 100,000 × (50.05 − 50.015) +3,500 Auction and take fees −400 Borrow, one night −35 Futures hedge slippage −100 Expected net +2,965

One overnight standard deviation of residual risk (1% of $5M) is $50,000, seventeen times the expected profit: the trade works only across hundreds of hedged names.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
The concession forecast is an impact model; size comes from inventory control; order mechanics mirror the agency auction algos.

# How much of a published closing imbalance to absorb (simplified, one stock).
# d = +1 for a buy imbalance (we sell), -1 for a sell imbalance (we buy).
K_IMPACT = 0.8       # P5: square-root impact coefficient, in units of daily vol
REVERT = 0.6         # share of the concession expected to revert by the next open
GAMMA = 2e-6         # risk aversion per $^2 of overnight variance
MAX_PCT_IMB = 0.5    # never absorb more than half the imbalance

def size_auction_offer(msg, s):
    d, imb, px = msg.imb_side, msg.imbalance_shares, msg.ref_price
    concession = K_IMPACT * s.daily_vol[msg.sym] * np.sqrt(imb / s.adv[msg.sym])  # fraction
    edge = REVERT * concession * px - s.fees_per_share                              # $/share
    var = (s.overnight_resid_vol[msg.sym] * px) ** 2           # $^2/share after the beta hedge
    q = edge / (2 * GAMMA * var)                               # mean-variance optimal shares
    q = int(np.clip(q, 0, min(MAX_PCT_IMB * imb, s.risk_room(msg.sym))))   # M4/M9 limits
    limit = px * (1 + d * 0.5 * concession)                    # demand at least half the concession
    order_type = "IO" if msg.listing == "NASDAQ" else "CO"     # imbalance-only / closing offset
    return order_type, -d, q, round(limit, 2)

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Timing: early offsets get priority; late ones see a clearer imbalance. NYSE floor D orders are accepted until 3:59:50 [Verified].
  • Which events: Russell reconstitution, S&P and MSCI rebalances and expiries; continuation (permanent index effect) differs from reversion by event type [Lore].
  • Hedging: many names net against each other; futures hedge the rest.
  • Conduct: sizing must follow from forecast reversion, never from a desire to move the print.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Size of the close: about 3.1% of dollar volume (2010) → 7.5% (2018) → record 9.4% of notional in Q2 2024; 2025 monthly 5–10% of share volume [Reported].
  • Reversion: auction price deviations revert quickly and almost completely, on average (Bogousslavsky & Muravyev 2023, JFM) [Verified].
  • Events: Nasdaq's June 26, 2026 Russell cross executed 4.59B shares, $334.0B [Reported]. Russell went semi-annual in 2026; the next reconstitution takes effect after the close on 2026-12-11 [Verified].
  • Manipulation detection: Comerton-Forde & Putniņš (2011) build an index of closing-price manipulation from prosecuted cases [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Capacity scales with imbalances, so it grows with passive assets and peaks on a few event days a year, which is also when every provider is present and concessions shrink. Semi-annual Russell reconstitution adds an event but may split the flow.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Informed imbalance: news after the cutoff makes the concession permanent.
  • Crowded events: too many offsets flip the imbalance and the close prints against providers.
  • Manipulation: in 2009 Athena Capital Research traded so heavily in the last two seconds (over 70% of Nasdaq volume in the affected stocks) that it moved closing prices in favor of its imbalance orders; it settled with the SEC in October 2014 for $1M [Verified]. In 2015 the D.C. Circuit upheld marking-the-close findings against an adviser (Koch v. SEC) [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: an auction is a single uncross. Practice: the last ten minutes are a continuous game played on one-second imbalance updates (order types and auctions).
  • Textbook: price-insensitive demand earns providers big concessions. Practice: competition keeps closing prices near the pre-close quotes [Verified]; profit is thin per share.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "The imbalance is 4% of ADV and growing." → Big concession likely; size up.
  • "Russell day, everyone's in the cross." → Crowded; concessions shrink.
  • "That paired-off by 3:58." → Offsetting interest arrived; the trade vanished.
  • "We hold the residual overnight." → Idiosyncratic risk after the futures hedge.
  • "Close-to-open markouts were negative this week." → Imbalances were informed or continued.
  • "Never trade to the print." → Compliance's warning about marking the close.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: imbalance traders manipulate the close. Reality: offsetting imbalances moves the close toward fair value; trading to move it is illegal.
  • Myth: it's riskless because index flow is predictable. Reality: overnight gaps dwarf per-name edge.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: What share of your closing fills come on index event days?
  • Informed: How do you separate mechanical imbalances from informed ones?
  • Informed: What is your close-to-open markout by event type?
  • Sharp: How do you show compliance your late orders don't target the print?
  • Sharp: 🔒 Your imbalance forecast error before publication?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the uncross, optimal absorption, and leveraged-ETF rebalancing

Uncross. \(p^* = \arg\max_p \min\{B(p), S(p)\}\); ties go to the smallest surplus \(|B(p) - S(p)|\).

Absorption. Expected concession \(c = k\,\sigma_d\sqrt{Q/\text{ADV}}\); edge per share \(e = \rho\,c\,p - f\); residual overnight variance \(v = (\sigma_{on}\,p)^2\). Maximizing \(q e - \gamma q^2 v\) gives

\[ q^* = \frac{e}{2\gamma v}. \]

Leveraged ETFs. A fund with assets \(A\) holds \(LA\). After return \(r\) it holds \(LA(1+r)\) but needs \(LA(1+Lr)\), so it trades

\[ \Delta = A\,L\,(L-1)\,r . \]

Illustrative: $10B of 3× funds on a +2% day buy 10 × 3 × 2 × 0.02 = $1.2B into the close [Estimate].

docs.title: Equity market making
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Electronic market makers quote both sides of thousands of US stocks, earn the half-spread plus rebates, and pay adverse selection to informed traders. Net margin is about a tenth of a cent per share [Estimate].
  • Menkveld (2013): one HFT market maker earned €0.88 gross per trade, a €1.55 net spread less a €0.68 loss on positions; gross Sharpe 9.35 [Verified].
  • The edge is fair value, speed (cancelling stale quotes in time) and cost per share, more than the quoting formula. Lab 05 (synthetic): adverse selection cuts an optimal quoter from $95 to $42 an hour; cancelling half the stale quotes in time lifts it to $68.
  • It fails through adverse-selection spikes, technology errors (Knight Capital, over $460M in 45 minutes, 2012 [Verified]) and volatility events. The half-penny tick and 10-mil fee cap, delayed to November 2027 [Verified], would reprice it.

Level: Core · Read time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family liquidity provision Edge source liquidity provision · speed Holding period seconds to minutes; mostly flat or hedged overnight [Lore] Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Impatient liquidity demanders (execution algos, rebalancers, routed retail orders) pay the half-spread for immediacy, because waiting costs them more in drift and leakage. Informed traders and latency arbitrageurs also trade against the market maker and win; uninformed flow pays for them. Universe & instruments NMS stocks and ETFs on 18 exchanges [Reported]; index futures and ETFs as hedges Data required order-by-order feeds from every exchange and CME; own fills with hardware timestamps; fee tiers; borrow lists Core algorithms used M2 Fair value and microprice · M4 Quoting and inventory control · M5 Adverse selection and markouts · M6 Queue position and order placement · M7 Hedging algorithms · M9 Algorithmic risk controls Infra intensity extreme: New Jersey colocation, FPGAs or kernel-bypass software, microwave to Chicago Capacity (rough $ range) P&L-limited, not capital-limited: US equity market making nets roughly $1–3B a year industry-wide [Estimate] (17.6B shares/day × 50–70% with a market maker on one side × 0.05–0.10¢ net per share × 250 days) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Not meaningful on capital. Menkveld's market maker: gross 9.35 annualized on maximum capital, 5.88 charging a 6% premium (Dutch stocks 2007–2008, academic case study) [Verified]. Virtu's 2014 IPO filing: one losing day in 1,238 [Reported]. Net of technology lower; margins compressed since [Lore] Turnover extreme: Menkveld's market maker traded 1,397 times per stock per day [Verified] Main risks / failure modes adverse-selection spikes, technology failure, volatility events, factor exposure, tick and fee rules Crowding risk high: a few firms race for the same queue spots Firm types that run it principal trading firms and electronic market makers (Virtu, a listed company [Reported]); NYSE designated market makers; exchange-registered market makers; wholesalers off-exchange Lab Lab 05 · Lab 04

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A market maker is a shop that buys at the bid and sells at the offer all day, aiming to hold nothing for long. Most customers are in a hurry and know nothing special; a few know the price is about to move. The job is to earn more from the first group than you lose to the second. Today it runs across thousands of stocks and 18 exchanges in microseconds, and fees of a fraction of a cent decide whether a trade made money.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text: Three costs set the spread. Adverse selection: Glosten & Milgrom (1985) show a dealer facing some informed traders must quote wide enough that uninformed flow covers losses to the informed [Verified]. Inventory risk: a dealer who must hold positions demands compensation (Ho & Stoll 1981) [Verified]. Processing: technology, fees, clearing. With competition the spread settles at the marginal market maker's cost, so profit goes to the firms with the lowest costs: the best fair value (fewer pick-offs), the fastest cancels and the most scale. Speed improves HFT performance partly through better risk management, not just sniping (Baron et al. 2019) [Verified].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Fair value per stock: microprice plus signals from futures, ETFs and sector peers (M2, M3).
  2. Quotes: center at fair value minus an inventory skew; width at least expected markout plus fees (M4). Snap to the tick and choose venue and queue (M6).
  3. Risk gate (M9), then orders out.
  4. Fills: update inventory; log markouts at 1–300 seconds (M5).
  5. Hedge: net the book's beta and sector exposure and offset it with index futures or ETFs (M7).
  6. Inventory: stock-specific residuals are worked off through skew; by the close the book is flat or hedged, sometimes via the closing auction.
flowchart LR
  fd["Direct feeds<br/>stocks and futures"] --> fv["Fair value M2 M3"]
  fv --> qt["Quote and skew M4"]
  qt --> pl["Tick, venue, queue M6"]
  pl --> rk["Risk gate M9"]
  rk --> ex["18 exchanges"]
  ex -->|"fills"| inv["Inventory"]
  inv -->|"skew"| qt
  inv --> hd["Hedger M7<br/>futures and ETFs"]
  hd --> ex
  ex -->|"fills"| mk["Markouts M5"]
  mk -->|"spread floor"| qt

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: a $40 tick-constrained stock quoted $39.99 × $40.00 (mid $39.995), maker rebate 0.25¢, take fee 0.30¢. The market maker's 300-share bid is hit by a seller who knows something; the market drops two ticks to $39.97 × $39.98. It skews: pulls its bid, sells 200 shares passively at $39.98, then 100 aggressively at $39.97.

Line Calculation $ Spread capture 300 × 0.5¢ + 200 × 0.5¢ − 100 × 0.5¢ (each fill vs mid) +2.00 Rebates and fees (300 + 200) × 0.25¢ − 100 × 0.30¢ +0.95 Mid move on inventory 300 × (39.975 − 39.995) −6.00 Round trip cash −$4.00 plus fees $0.95 −3.05

A benign round trip (buy 300 at $39.99, sell 300 at $40.00, mid unchanged) earns $3.00 of spread plus $1.50 of rebates: +$4.50. If 40% of round trips are toxic like the first, the expectation is 0.6 × 4.50 − 0.4 × 3.05 = $1.48 per 600 shares, 0.25¢ a share before hedging, clearing and technology.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
The loop is M1. The requote below calls Lab 05's glft_quotes, floored by markouts as computed in Lab 04.

# One requote for one stock (simplified). Units as in Lab 05: cents/share, 100-share lots.
def requote(stock, s, p):
    fair = s.microprice(stock) + s.signals.predict_cents(stock)     # M2/M3: fair value, not the mid
    q = s.inventory[stock] - s.hedged_lots(stock)                    # M7: factor part already hedged
    d_bid, d_ask = glft_quotes(q, p.gamma, s.sigma[stock], p.A, p.k, p.q_max)   # M4, Lab 05
    floor = s.exp_markout[stock] + s.fee_net_of_rebate(stock)        # M5: e.g. 60 s markout, cents
    # (Lab 05 instead adds a fixed 'widen' to both distances; this max() floor is a simplification)
    bid = floor_to_tick(fair - max(d_bid, floor))                     # M6: 1-cent grid
    ask = ceil_to_tick(fair + max(d_ask, floor))
    if s.risk.ok(stock, bid, ask):                                    # M9: limits, collars, kill switch
        s.gateway.replace(stock, bid, ask, size=p.clip)

def on_fill(fill, s):
    s.inventory[fill.stock] += fill.signed_lots
    s.fills.append(fill)        # Lab 04 markouts(): side * (mid(t + h) - price) / price, h = 0..300 s
    s.hedger.update(s.inventory)                                      # M7: beta-weighted net -> futures

Lab 05, synthetic. GLFT and naive quoting have similar means but naive's outcomes are far wider; with informed traders (dashed) every rule earns about half.

Synthetic lab result: GLFT earns $95 an hour (sd $46) against naive's $94 (sd $217). With sniping, GLFT's spread capture rises to $120 while adverse selection costs $79, leaving $42; cancelling half of stale quotes lifts it to $68. With no rivals, fees or ticks, levels are meaningless; the ranking is the lesson.

Lab 04, synthetic. Informed fills turn negative after about 5 seconds and settle near −1.5 bps; uninformed fills stay positive, +1.5 to +2.2 bps.

In Lab 04 (synthetic lab result) liquidity providers capture $77,818 a day of spread, lose $49,723 to adverse selection at 60 seconds and keep 36%.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Tick regime. In one-tick names the game is queue position and rebates; in wide-spread names, price and fair value (fees, rebates and ticks).
  • Venue and fee tier. Maker-taker rebates against inverted venues' paid priority; tiers reward volume concentration.
  • Hedging granularity. Hedge the book's factors with futures; skew only residuals.
  • Markout horizon and segments. 1 second misses informed flow; 60 seconds catches it. Size is a toxicity proxy:

Lab 04, synthetic. 800+ share orders are 68% informed and mark out at −0.45 bps at 60 seconds; 100-share orders keep +1.64 bps.

  • Short sales. Bona fide market making is exempt from the Reg SHO locate requirement [Verified], which lets a market maker sell before it owns the stock (shorting and settlement).

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative mid-sized lit market maker: 300M shares a day (about 1.7% of 2025 volume), 250 days.

Line ¢/share $M/yr Spread capture (fill vs mid) +0.45 +337.5 Exchange rebates net of take fees +0.13 +97.5 Gross revenue +0.58 +435.0 Adverse selection (60-second markout) −0.33 −247.5 Gross trading margin +0.25 +187.5 Residual inventory P&L −0.02 −15.0 Hedging (futures, ETFs) −0.03 −22.5 Clearing, regulatory and CAT fees −0.02 −15.0 Technology, colocation, data, staff −0.08 −60.0 Net +0.10 +75.0

Adverse selection, the cost of goods sold, eats 57% of gross revenue. Rebates exceed the net margin, which is why the 10-mil access-fee cap matters.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Menkveld (2013): one HFT market maker in Dutch stocks, 2007–2008. Gross €0.88 per trade = €1.55 net spread − €0.68 positioning loss; positions under five seconds made €0.45, longer ones lost €1.13. About 78% of trades were passive; the passive exchange fee averaged −€0.31 (a rebate) on Chi-X but +€0.68 on Euronext [Verified].
  • Virtu FY2025: Market Making adjusted net trading income $1,666M, all asset classes and regions; total adjusted net trading income $2,145M, up 34% [Reported]. That is about $6.7M per trading day [Estimate].
  • Inventory bites: NYSE specialist spreads widened when specialists held large positions or lost money (Comerton-Forde et al. 2010) [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Capacity is set by volume and spread, not capital. 2025 US volume averaged a record 17.6B shares a day, up 44.6% [Reported]; Virtu's 2025 jump came with it. Fixed technology costs and fee tiers favor scale, so a few firms take most of the flow. A half-penny tick would halve the tick rent in the tightest names; the fees page works the per-share arithmetic.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Adverse-selection spikes. News or a large informed order turns the markout curve negative across the book; skew lags.
  • Technology failure. On 2012-08-01 Knight Capital's router turned retail orders into about 397M shares traded in 45 minutes, leaving $3.5B long and $3.15B short and a loss over $460M [Verified] (risk controls).
  • Volatility events. On 2010-05-06 many trades executed more than 60% from pre-decline prices, a significant share against stub quotes, and were broken [Verified]. On 2015-08-24 there were 1,278 LULD halts [Verified]. See the failure gallery.
  • Correlated inventory. In a sell-off every name fills on the bid at once; per-name limits look fine while the book is one large long.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: a monopolist specialist with obligations. Today: competing firms quote voluntarily. Exchange market makers must keep continuous two-sided quotes no further than 8% from the NBBO for S&P 500 and Russell 1000 stocks, 20% before 9:45 a.m. and after 3:35 p.m., 30% for others (rules approved in 2010, effective 2010-12-06) [Verified]. NYSE DMMs must hold a bid or offer at the NBBO for at least 10% (active stocks) or 15% of the day [Verified].
  • Textbook: the quoting formula is the strategy. Practice: fair value and speed decide P&L [Lore].
  • Textbook: single-stock inventory. Practice: book-level factor hedging [Lore]; Menkveld's firm offloaded positions on a second venue [Verified].
  • Rules that bind: the Market Access Rule (15c3-5) requires automated pre-trade limits [Verified]. The 2024 half-penny tick and 10-mil fee cap are delayed to the first business day of November 2027, and the SEC has proposed repealing the Rule 611 order-protection rule [Verified].

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text:
Role Obligation Page NYSE DMM NBBO presence, runs open and close auctions and closing liquidity Registered market maker two-sided quotes within bands this page Unregistered PTF none beyond market-access controls this page; fee-driven strategies Wholesaler best execution off-exchange retail flow internalization

Also ETF and options market making; the opposite side of the race is latency arbitrage.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're giving it back at 10 seconds." → markouts turn negative within 10 s of fills.
  • "We're the back of the queue on Arca." → late in line, so its fills are more often toxic.
  • "Rebates are our margin." → net P&L roughly equals rebates; spread minus markout is near zero.
  • "Pull everything on an ES move." → cancel quotes when futures jump, before snipers arrive.
  • "We're long the market through 400 names." → small per-name inventories add up to one factor bet.
  • "What's our p99 to cancel?" → tail latency of pulling quotes, the defense against pick-offs.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: HFT market makers front-run orders. Reality: they trade against public orders and lose to the informed ones; Menkveld's firm lost money on its positions [Verified].
  • Myth: market makers must provide liquidity in crises. Reality: obligations are loose bands, not a duty to buy [Verified].

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: What share of your volume is passive?
  • Basic: Do you carry inventory overnight?
  • Informed: At what horizon do you measure markouts, and by which segments?
  • Informed: How much of net P&L is rebates?
  • Informed: What would the half-penny tick do to your queue strategy?
  • Sharp: 🔒 How often do your cancels lose the race in your top 100 names?
  • Sharp: 🔒 What is your adverse selection as a share of spread capture?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: break-even spread and the market maker's P&L identity

If a fraction \(\pi\) of takers know the next move \(\pm\Delta\), a competitive quoter breaks even at

\[ \frac{s}{2} = \pi\,\Delta + c , \]

with \(c\) the processing cost per share. For fills at prices \(p_i\), signed \(d_i\) (+1 bought), with mid \(m\):

\[ \text{P\&L} = \underbrace{\sum_i d_i\,(m_{t_i} - p_i)}_{\text{spread capture}} + \text{rebates} + \underbrace{\int q_t\,dm_t}_{\text{inventory and adverse selection}} - \text{costs}, \]

the identity behind Lab 05's income statement and Menkveld's split.

docs.title: ETF market making
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • ETF market makers quote off their own fair value, built from the basket, futures and correlated ETFs: hedge cost plus a small margin.
  • Inventory is hedged at once and netted at the close by creation or redemption: spread capture minus hedge, creation and financing costs.
  • Margins are thin, scale concentrated: Flow Traders made €485.8M of net trading income on €1,940bn of ETP value traded in 2025, ~2.5 bps [Reported]; Jane Street reportedly did 24% of US ETF primary-market activity in 2024 [Reported].
  • When the basket is stale or shut (bond ETFs in 2020, Greece in 2015), the ETF becomes the price; the market maker prices the fund, not its NAV.
  • It fails when hedges cannot be priced: 24 August 2015 saw 1,058 LULD halts in 327 ETPs [Verified].

Level: Core · Read time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family liquidity provision Edge source liquidity provision · structural/regulatory Holding period seconds to hours (hedged at once); the net residual is created or redeemed at the close Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Investors wanting a basket in one ticket (advisers, retail, institutions, hedgers) and block traders buying immediate risk transfer: the spread is cheaper than trading hundreds of stocks or OTC bonds. Universe & instruments US-listed equity, bond and commodity ETFs and their baskets; ES, NQ, RTY and Treasury futures; peer ETFs; FX Data required daily basket files; constituent, futures and FX feeds; bond prices and TRACE Core algorithms used M2 Fair value and microprice · M4 Quoting and inventory control · M7 Hedging algorithms · P5 Transaction cost and impact models Infra intensity high: low-latency quoting on thousands of tickers, heavy reference data, RFQ systems Capacity (rough $ range) P&L-limited: hundreds of $M to ~$2B a year for a top US book [Estimate] (2.5 bps on Jane Street's reported ~$8.5T 2024 ETF volume, an upper bound) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) No strategy disclosure. Annualized gross Sharpe said to exceed 3 for diversified books [Lore]. Net, firm level: Flow Traders' 2025 EBITDA margin 41%, Q4 NTI −20% year on year [Reported]. Margins compressed, not gone. Turnover very high: inventory turns many times a day Main risks / failure modes unpriceable baskets (halts, closed markets), hedge basis breaks, informed flow, balance-sheet limits, basket-file errors Crowding risk high in the largest funds (one-tick spreads); lower in bond, international and niche ETFs Firm types that run it electronic market makers acting as lead market makers and APs; bank APs. Sourced: Flow Traders, Jane Street; Virtu, Citadel Securities, HRT gaining AP share [Reported] Lab Lab 07

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
At 10:30 a pension fund asks for a price on $20M of a small-cap ETF. No seller is needed. The market maker sells shares it doesn't own, a few basis points above fair value, and hedges within milliseconds with index futures, a correlated ETF or the stocks. By the close it holds the basket and creates the ETF shares it owes.

It is a wholesaler: it buys in bulk through the primary market and sells retail as ETF shares. Competition pushes the quote down to the cheapest hedge's cost.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Investors pay for immediacy and packaging. Each quote prices the hedge, expected adverse selection, inventory risk until hedged, and a margin. Creation and redemption cap the premium at the all-in cost of the primary market, the no-arbitrage band (ETF and index arbitrage). Market making happens inside that band.

The structural edge is access. Only an authorized participant (AP) can create and redeem. Exchanges pay lead market makers credits tied to quoting obligations; FINRA Rule 5250 generally bars issuers from paying market makers directly [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Pre-open: load basket files (shares per creation unit, cash, fees, cutoffs).
  2. Fair value: recompute from constituent microprices; roll stale, closed or OTC constituents forward with futures, peer ETFs and FX (M2).
  3. Quote: width = hedge cost + adverse selection; center skewed by inventory (M4). Answer RFQs.
  4. Hedge each fill in the cheapest instrument, given its basis risk (M7).
  5. Net and roll: offsetting flow cancels; futures hedges become basket in the closing auction.
  6. Primary market: create or redeem the net residual in whole units, or carry it hedged overnight.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Small-cap index ETF, fair value $80.00, creation unit 50,000 shares ($4M). A client buys 250,000 shares ($20M, five units) on an RFQ.

Step Calculation P&L Sell ETF at fair value + 8 bps 250,000 × ($80.064 − $80.000) +$16,000 Buy ~170 E-mini Russell 2000 futures at once ($120,000 each) 0.5 bp on $20M −$1,000 Buy the 2,000-stock basket into the close half-spreads + impact ≈ 4 bps on $20M −$8,000 Sell the futures back at the close 0.5 bp on $20M −$1,000 Create five units fixed fee, illustrative −$1,500 Net +$4,500 ≈ 2.25 bps

The quote was hedge cost (5.75 bps) plus 2.25 bps of margin. A 100,000-share seller at 14:00 would net two units internally and save their basket cost. SPY's fee is the lower of $3,000 or 10 bps of a unit, per participant per day [Verified].

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Fair value feeds quoting inside an HFT loop; hedging routes offsets, cost models price the band, markouts police flow and risk controls cap exposure.

import numpy as np
# nav() and the band follow Lab 07's CORE ALGORITHM (same names; +units = create).
# Stale-price roll-forward, quote width and skew are simplified additions.

def nav(prices, basket_shares, cash_per_unit, cu_size=50_000):
    return (np.asarray(prices) @ np.asarray(basket_shares) + cash_per_unit) / cu_size

def fair_value(last_px, basket_shares, cash, stale, proxy_ret, beta):
    # Roll stale or closed constituents forward by their proxy-implied move (futures, ETFs, FX)
    px = np.where(stale, last_px * (1.0 + beta * proxy_ret), last_px)
    return nav(px, basket_shares, cash)

def etf_quotes(fv, hedge_cost_bps, create_cost_bps, redeem_cost_bps, inv_units,
               adverse_bps=0.5, skew_bps_per_unit=0.4):
    half = hedge_cost_bps + adverse_bps             # cost of laying off the risk now
    center = -skew_bps_per_unit * inv_units         # short ETF -> lift both quotes
    bid_bps = max(center - half, -redeem_cost_bps)  # arbitrage bounds the quote: beyond
    ask_bps = min(center + half, create_cost_bps)   # the band an AP would undercut us
    return fv * (1 + bid_bps / 1e4), fv * (1 + ask_bps / 1e4)

def end_of_day_units(inv_units):
    # Net ETF inventory at the cutoff goes to the primary market in whole units
    return -int(np.round(inv_units))                # short 5 units -> create +5

Synthetic data. Without creations and redemptions (grey) the premium wanders by ±100 bps; arbitrage (blue) pins it to the band edges. The lab has only end-of-day arbitrage; intraday market makers pull real liquid ETFs well inside the band.

In Lab 07, arbitrage cuts the premium's standard deviation from 45.7 to 6.7 bps and its half-life from 10.8 to 0.7 days (synthetic lab result). Real liquid funds, with intraday market making, are tighter still.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
Fair value depends on what the basket is doing during US hours:

ETF type Basket during US hours Fair-value inputs Usual hedge US large-cap, sector live microprices, ES, NQ futures, SPY, basket US small-cap live, wide spreads RTY, correlated ETFs, basket futures, basket at close International closed (Asia), or closes 11:30 ET (Europe) futures, ADRs, FX, peer ETFs futures plus FX Corporate bond OTC, stale evaluated prices Treasury futures, TRACE, peer ETFs futures, peer ETFs
  • Hedge-cost-aware fair value. A desk hedging in futures marks the ETF partly to futures: fair value is where risk can be laid off, not NAV [Lore].
  • Carry or create. Carrying overnight costs financing and basis risk but may net against tomorrow's flow.
  • Custom baskets. SEC Rule 6c-11 (2019) allows negotiated baskets under written policies [Verified]. Bond ETFs use cash plus a subset of bonds to steer AP activity (Koont, Ma, Pástor & Zeng 2025) [Verified].

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative, in bps of ETF value traded, calibrated so the EBITDA margin matches Flow Traders' 41% [Estimate].

Line bps Spread capture (gross, vs fair value) +4.0 Exchange rebates and lead-market-maker credits +0.3 Adverse selection (markout losses) −1.0 Hedge execution (futures, basket, ETF) −0.8 Exchange and clearing fees −0.2 Financing, borrow, overnight carry −0.2 Creation and redemption fees −0.1 Net trading income +2.0 Staff, technology, market data −1.2 EBITDA +0.8

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Flow Traders, FY2025: net trading income €485.8M (+4%), EBITDA €198.9M (41% margin), net profit €133.6M; ETP value traded €1,940bn, up 26% [Reported]. NTI over value traded ≈ 2.5 bps [Estimate] (NTI includes non-ETP lines). The Americas were only €40.9M of €283.6M NTI in H1 2025 [Reported].
  • Jane Street: $527bn a month of ETF volume in 2023, about 14% of US and 20% of European ETF trading (FT, 2024) [Reported]; $707bn a month in 2024, with 24% of US primary and 16% of secondary activity (Global Trading, 2025) [Reported]; a self-estimated 41% of bond-ETF creations and redemptions [Reported].
  • Academic: across 1,813 ETFs (2007–2014) the average premium was 6 bps with 49 bps volatility, larger for international and illiquid holdings (Petajisto 2017) [Verified]; much apparent premium is stale NAV (Engle & Sarkar 2006) [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: US ETF assets hit a record $16.36T at the end of August 2026, with record year-to-date inflows of $1.41T [Reported]. The largest funds trade at one tick, so margin moves to bond, international, active and new funds and block RFQs. In November 2025 the SEC granted Dimensional relief for ETF share classes of mutual funds; the first launched in March 2026, with more than 50 managers applying [Reported]. Crowding shows up as concentration in a handful of firms.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
Always the same mechanism: fair value cannot be computed, or the hedge cannot be traded.

  • 24 August 2015. Many constituents opened late, so desks could not price baskets and widened or withdrew [Reported]. There were 1,278 LULD halts, 1,058 in 327 ETPs, though 80% of ETPs had none [Verified].
  • March 2020, bond ETFs. LQD closed at a 5.0% discount in the week to 20 March, after never closing beyond 1% in 2018–2019 [Reported]. After the Fed said on 23 March it could buy bond ETFs, LQD closed at a 3.2% premium that Thursday [Reported]. Issuers such as Invesco read the discount as stale bond NAV, with the ETF as the true price [Reported]; Haddad, Moreira & Muir (2021) see a real dislocation, larger for safer bonds, driven by forced selling and erased by the Fed [Verified].
  • Greece, 2015. While Athens was shut (late June to 3 August), GREK traded in New York and fell about 16.5%; Athens fell 16–23% on reopening [Reported].

More in the strategy failure gallery.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: APs arbitrage each mispricing. Practice: market makers hedge intraday and create or redeem the net at the close (ETF linkages) [Lore].
  • Textbook: quote around the public iNAV. Practice: iNAV is slow and Rule 6c-11 does not require it; desks build their own fair value [Verified].
  • Textbook: NAV is the truth. Practice: for bonds and closed markets the ETF price is often the better estimate (Engle & Sarkar 2006) [Verified].

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Block RFQ liquidity; bond and international ETFs; leveraged ETFs, whose rebalancing hits the close; options on ETFs. Neighbours: equity market making, ETF and index arbitrage (the band itself), lead-lag (fair-value inputs), flow-driven strategies.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Tokyo's shut, so the fair is futures plus FX." → Asia ETFs are priced off proxies in US hours.
  • "The basket is the hedge of last resort." → Futures and peer ETFs come first; the stocks are bought only to hold risk or to create.
  • "We're short three units; create at the cutoff." → Net inventory goes to the primary market.
  • "LQD is the price; the NAV is an opinion." → In stress, bond ETFs lead their stale NAVs.
  • "We live inside the band; it only bites at four." → Intraday quoting rarely touches the creation bound.
  • "Markouts on that block were ugly: informed sector flow." → The client knew something.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: an ETF is only as liquid as its own volume. Reality: through creation, the basket's liquidity sets the limit [Lore].
  • Myth: a discount means the ETF broke. Reality: in March 2020 it was partly stale bond NAV, partly a real bond-market dislocation [Reported].
  • Myth: APs must keep prices in line. Reality: an AP has a contract, not a duty, and steps away when balance sheet is scarce [Lore].

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this

• Basic: What do you hedge a small-cap ETF fill with first, and why?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: stale-basket fair value, hedge choice and the quote bounds

NAV is nav() in the code above. If constituent \(i\) last traded at \(t_i\), roll it forward with proxy returns (futures, peer ETFs, FX) and betas \(\beta_i\):

\[ \widehat{P}_{i,t} = P_{i,t_i}\left(1 + \beta_i^\top r^{\text{proxy}}_{t_i \to t}\right) \]

Hedge \(h\) costs \(c_h\) per dollar and leaves basis variance \(\sigma^2_{b,h}\) per unit time over holding time \(\tau_h\); with risk aversion \(\gamma\):

\[ h^* = \arg\min_h \; c_h |q| + \frac{\gamma}{2}\, q^2 \sigma^2_{b,h}\, \tau_h \]

Futures win short holds, the basket long ones. Quotes (bps around fair value, half-width \(\delta\), skew \(\kappa\)):

\[ \text{bid} = \max(-\kappa q - \delta, \, -c_{\text{redeem}}), \qquad \text{ask} = \min(-\kappa q + \delta, \, c_{\text{create}}) \]
