docs.title: Options market making
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Quote two-sided prices on thousands of series per underlying, all read off one fitted volatility surface; 4.87 million US option series traded in 2025 [Verified].
  • Revenue is edge (price minus theoretical value). Inventory is held as Greeks: delta hedged within seconds, gamma and vega warehoused and shaded away through quotes.
  • As an income statement: edge is revenue; theta minus gamma is realized-vs-implied volatility; vega is a mark; hedging, fees and payment for order flow are costs.
  • Retail drives the flow: over 60% of volume (Bryzgalova et al. 2023) [Verified], and options PFOF is two-thirds of all PFOF [Verified]. 0DTE was 66.2% of SPX volume in July 2026 [Verified]. All trades execute on 20 exchanges [Verified].
  • It fails on gaps and volatility spikes: one session can erase weeks of theta.

Level: Core · Read time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family liquidity provision Edge source liquidity provision · speed Holding period delta: milliseconds to minutes; options: hours (0DTE) to weeks Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Retail buyers of short-dated options pay wide percentage spreads for leverage (brokers are paid PFOF); institutions buying index puts and structured-product desks hedging notes pay for immediacy and size; covered-call and put-write funds sell volatility cheaply for income. Nobody else stands ready in millions of series. Universe & instruments US single-stock, ETF and index options (SPX, SPY, QQQ, VIX); hedges in stock, ETFs, E-mini futures Data required OPRA (median 131 billion messages a day, December 2025 [Verified]), underlying feeds, dividends, borrow, rates, earnings dates, own markouts Core algorithms used M8 Options pricing and vol surfaces · M4 Quoting and inventory control · M7 Hedging algorithms · M9 Algorithmic risk controls Infra intensity very high: microsecond requoting of millions of series, continuous surface refits Capacity (rough $ range) flow-limited: industry gross trading revenue $3B–$9B a year [Estimate] (15.2B contracts in 2025 [Verified] × ~60% market-maker share × $0.30–$1.00 net capture per contract); Optiver's 2025 net trading income, all products, was €4.556B [Verified] Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) no public figures; practitioner lore puts annualized net Sharpe at 3–10 for diversified flow books and 1–3 for books that warehouse vega [Lore], with edge thinning in index options Turnover options turn over in days; hundreds to thousands of hedge trades per underlying a day [Lore] Main risks / failure modes gaps on short gamma, vol and skew spikes, informed flow, pin and assignment, wing model error, runaway quoting Crowding risk moderate: top three firms pay up to ~90% of options PFOF [Verified]; dealers positioned alike Firm types that run it electronic market makers, wholesalers ("consolidators"), floor specialists; e.g. Citadel Securities, Susquehanna, Optiver, IMC, Jane Street, Wolverine [Reported] Lab Lab 06

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: An options market maker is a bookmaker and an insurer at once. It prices everything, keeps a small margin on each trade and hedges stock direction away within seconds. What it cannot lay off is volatility: how much the stock actually moves against what option prices assumed. Theta is premium earned daily, gamma losses are claims paid when the stock moves, and the quoted edge is the loading on top.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
1. Immediacy across a huge product set. Traded series rose more than sevenfold since 2012, to 4.87 million on 8,439 underliers in 2025 [Verified] (SEC staff). Only surface-based pricing can cover them all.
  2. Mostly uninformed flow. Retail favors cheap weekly options, pays an average bid-ask spread of 12.6% and loses money on average (Bryzgalova, Pavlova & Sikorskaya 2023) [Verified].
  3. Structural access. Listed options must execute on an exchange. Exchanges court flow with guaranteed allocations to "directed" market makers (for example 40%), entitlements to orders of five contracts or fewer, price-improvement auctions and "marketing fees" passed to brokers [Verified] (SEC staff, April 2026).
  4. A small, unreliable premium. End users are net long index options, so dealers are paid to warehouse them (Gârleanu, Pedersen & Poteshman 2009) [Verified]. Since about 2010, though, delta-hedged index options earn near-zero CAPM alpha and dealers' net SPX gamma is zero or positive (Dew-Becker & Giglio 2025) [Verified]. The money is mostly spread (premium: see the volatility risk premium dossier).

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Imply the forward from put-call parity; fit one smile per expiry into an arbitrage-free surface (M8).
  2. Compute theo and Greeks for every series.
  3. Quote theo ± a half-width that grows with vega × surface uncertainty, expected adverse selection (M5) and fees; lean both sides against book Greeks (M4).
  4. On a fill, book edge = (price − theo) × 100 × contracts.
  5. Hedge delta in stock, ETF or futures, at once or when net delta leaves a band (M7).
  6. Manage vega by expiry, gamma and skew; offload concentrations through quote skew, complex orders or other dealers.
  7. Enforce limits and kill switches (M9); manage pin risk and early assignment (calls before ex-dividend); explain P&L daily (L1).

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Stock at $100; a 21-trading-day at-the-money call has theo $2.88 at 25% implied vol. A retail order buys 20 calls at $2.93. Short 20 contracts, the book has delta −1,029 shares, gamma −110.5 shares per $1, vega −$230 per vol point and theta +$137 a day.

Line Calculation $ Edge at the fill (2.93 − 2.88) × 100 × 20 +100 Exchange fee (illustrative $0.30 a contract) 0.30 × 20 −6 PFOF (illustrative $0.40 a contract) 0.40 × 20 −8 Delta hedge: buy 1,029 shares, 1¢ half-spread 1,029 × 0.01 −10 Net at the fill +76 Quiet next day: stock +1%, IV flat theta +137, gamma ½ × (−110.5) × 1² = −55 +82 Breakeven move ½ × 110.5 × ΔS² = 137 gives ΔS = $1.57 = 25%/√252 0 Gap: stock +5%, IV +3 points gamma −1,381, vega −691, theta +137 −1,935 (−1,743 fully repriced)

One gap costs about 13 days of theta. The $192 between the Greek estimate and full repricing is what a P&L explain books as "unexplained".

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Surface: M8. Width and lean: M4, M5. Hedging: M7. Limits: M9. Daily explain: L1.

# One quoting-and-hedging cycle for one underlying (simplified). fit_smile, delta_hedge_pnl
# and greeks_attribution are Lab 06's CORE ALGORITHM functions; position Greeks are negative when short.
smiles = {T: fit_smile(np.log(K / F), iv_mid, T, method="svi")      # M8: one raw-SVI fit per expiry
          for T, (K, iv_mid) in chain_by_expiry.items()}
for opt in series:                                                  # thousands of strikes x expiries
    vol = smiles[opt.T](np.log(opt.K / F))
    theo, g = bs_price_and_greeks(F, opt.K, opt.T, vol)             # per share: delta, gamma, vega
    half = max(min_tick, vol_unc * g["vega"] + tox[opt] + fee)       # M5: wider where flow is toxic
    lean = -k_vega * book["vega"] * g["vega"]                        # M4: short vega -> raise both prices
    quote(opt, bid=theo - half + lean, ask=theo + half + lean)

# On a fill, premium > 0 if we sold; position value at theo is < 0 when short.
quoted_edge = premium + position_value_at_theo                      # = (fill - theo) x 100 x qty on a sale
# Lab 06 bands are per share of one straddle; a real book sets the band in shares or $ delta.
h = delta_hedge_pnl(spot_path, book_delta_path, band=delta_band, cost_bps=1.0)       # M7
pnl = greeks_attribution(book_value, spot_path, iv_path, book_greeks, h["shares"],   # L1
                         dt, premium, h["costs"])
# keys: quoted_edge, theta, gamma, vega, vanna, volga, delta_hedge_residual, hedging_costs, unexplained

Lab 06, synthetic data. Notice that the quoted edge is a sliver next to theta and gamma, that hedging more often cuts the variance of P&L but not its mean, and that trade P&L tracks dollar-gamma-weighted implied minus realized variance.

Synthetic lab results (398 short 30-day straddles sold at fitted vol + 0.5 points): mean edge $13.1 a straddle against theta +$262.6 and gamma −$210.8. Hedging every 15 minutes costs $14.9, more than the edge; a ±0.10 delta band matches hourly hedging's P&L standard deviation ($117 vs $114) with a quarter of the rebalances.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Surface model. SVI-type fits extrapolate sanely into the wings, where retail lottery tickets trade; in Lab 06 a quadratic missed the wings by 1.25 vol points, SVI by 0.12 (synthetic). Many desks use smile-adjusted deltas [Lore].
  • Where to quote tightly. Quoted spreads widened from 2012 to 2025 in nearly all but the top-10 underliers [Verified].
  • Flow. Consolidator or screen-only. Single-leg auctions gave retail marketable orders price improvement 22–89% of the time, the electronic book 0–13% [Verified].
  • Complex orders. Multi-leg orders were the second and fourth most common retail execution types in December 2025 [Verified].

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative income statement, mid-size book: 500,000 contracts a day, 126 million a year [Estimate].

Line (accounting analogue) $ per contract $M per year Revenue: edge vs theo at the fill +1.60 +201.6 Cost of revenue: adverse selection (5-minute markout) −0.55 −69.3 Inventory gain: theta minus gamma +0.10 +12.6 Fair-value marks: vega and skew 0 on average ±40 Hedging costs −0.15 −18.9 Exchange fees net of rebates −0.25 −31.5 PFOF paid to brokers −0.20 −25.2 Clearing and regulatory fees −0.04 −5.0 Technology, OPRA data, people −0.12 −15.1 Loss reserve: gap days, amortized −0.10 −12.6 Net +0.29 +36.5

Most gross edge leaks to informed flow, venues and brokers. The vega line does not move the mean, but it decides the quarter.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Growth. 15.2 billion contracts in 2025, +26%, a sixth straight record [Verified]. Q3 2026 averaged 70.6 million a day; 0DTE was ~36% of all volume [Verified] (Cboe).
  • PFOF. SEC staff (April 2026): consolidators handle virtually all retail options orders; options PFOF is two-thirds of all PFOF; the top three providers pay up to ~90% [Verified]. Options PFOF remains legal; the SEC withdrew its 2022 order-auction proposal in June 2025 [Reported]. Q3 2025 retail-flow payments rose 40% year on year, led by Citadel Securities and IMC [Reported].
  • Firms. Citadel Securities says it holds about 30% of US listed options [Reported] (self-reported). Rule 606 analyses name Dash/IMC, Susquehanna, Jane Street and Wolverine as major liquidity providers [Reported]; Optiver is hiring to compete in US single-stock options [Reported] (Bloomberg).
  • Spreads. Median effective spread 1.9% for equity options, 1.4% for ETF options, in 2025 [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Capacity is set by flow, so firms compete with PFOF, exchange incentives and tighter quotes. The business concentrated: from 2015 to 2021 the number of broker-dealers reporting options market-making revenue fell, mostly among small-capital firms [Verified]. Fragmentation raises fixed costs: 18 exchanges each held more than 1% in 2025, and two more launched in Q3 2026 [Verified]. Edge is thinnest in index and top-ETF options.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Gaps. Short gamma loses with the square of the move (worked example).
  • Vol and skew spikes. Short vega is marked down at once; put skew steepens as customers buy puts.
  • Informed flow before news; markouts catch it late (M5).
  • Pin and assignment. Unknown exercise near the strike can leave an unhedged position over a weekend.

Episodes: 2018-02-05, VIX +115.6% in a day [Verified] (failure gallery). 2024-08-05, bid-ask spreads on deep out-of-the-money puts exceeded 80% of mid before the open as market makers widened; the quote-based VIX touched ~66 [Verified] (BIS). 2025-04-03 to 04-09, the S&P 500 moved −4.8%, −6.0%, then +9.5%; the VIX closed at 52.33 on 8 April [Verified] (Cboe data), and options volume first topped 100 million contracts on 4 April [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: continuous hedging removes risk. Practice: discrete, band-based hedging, because costs scale with frequency (Leland 1985; Whalley & Wilmott 1997) [Verified].
  • Textbook: price each option with a model. Practice: price off a fitted surface and skew by inventory (Stoikov & Sağlam 2009) [Verified].
  • Textbook: spread from noise traders. Practice: flow bought via PFOF and exchange allocations [Verified].
  • Textbook: dealers earn a volatility premium. Practice: near zero since ~2010 (Dew-Becker & Giglio 2025) [Verified].

Practitioner references: Natenberg (2015) on pricing and Greeks; Sinclair (2013) on volatility trading.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're short gamma into the print." → Loses if earnings move the stock more than implied.
  • "Theta paid for the gamma this week." → Realized came in below implied.
  • "Lean the vega." → Skew quotes so customers take risk off the book.
  • "Markouts on that broker went negative." → The flow became informed.
  • "We hedge on a 10-delta band." → Rebalance only past a threshold.
  • "Model risk lives in the wings." → Far strikes are extrapolated.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: they bet on direction. Reality: delta is hedged in seconds; they bet on flow and realized vs implied vol.
  • Myth: PFOF obviously harms retail. Reality: contested: auctions improve prices far more than the book; one study links higher PFOF to less improvement, and critics dispute its method [Verified] (SEC staff summary).
  • Myth: 0DTE is a retail casino. Reality: market makers have the largest 0DTE footprint, above 190 million contracts a month [Verified].

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: How many underliers do you quote, and what do you hedge with?
  • Informed: How do you split P&L between edge, theta-gamma and vega?
  • Informed: How do markouts differ between auction and screen flow?
  • Sharp: How do your deltas account for the smile?
  • Sharp: Was 2025-04-04 a gamma or a vega loss?
  • Sharp: 🔒 Vega limits per expiry, and PFOF paid per contract?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: theta-gamma identity, hedging error and the Leland band

With \(r = 0\), \(\Theta = -\tfrac12 \Gamma S^2 \sigma_i^2\), so a delta-hedged short option earns per step

\[ dP = \tfrac12 \Gamma S^2 \left(\sigma_i^2\,dt - \left(\tfrac{dS}{S}\right)^2\right), \qquad P \approx \sum_t \tfrac12 \Gamma_t S_t^2 \left(\sigma_i^2 - \sigma_{r,t}^2\right) dt . \]

P&L is dollar-gamma-weighted implied minus realized variance, so it is path-dependent (Lab 06: R² 0.82). Hedging error falls roughly as \(1/\sqrt{N}\) in rebalances (Boyle & Emanuel 1980). Leland (1985): a writer hedging every \(\Delta t\) at round-trip cost \(k\) should price at

\[ \hat\sigma^2 = \sigma^2\left(1 + \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\pi}}\;\frac{k}{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}\right). \]

At \(\sigma = 20\%\) and \(k = 2\) bp, 15-minute hedging needs ~0.6 vol points of extra edge and daily hedging ~0.13. Lab 06 quoted 0.5, so at 15-minute hedging the costs ($14.9) exceeded the quoted edge ($13.1).

docs.title: Retail flow internalization
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Wholesalers pay brokers for retail marketable orders (PFOF), fill them as principal at or inside the NBBO and keep a fraction of a cent per share.
  • The edge is segmentation: an exchange prices for its average counterparty; a wholesaler knows the broker and prices that flow. Round-trip costs for identical orders ranged from 0.07% to 0.46% across six brokerage accounts [Verified].
  • Concentrated: six wholesalers received over 90% of individual investors' marketable orders [Verified]; Citadel Securities claims about 35% of US-listed retail volume [Reported].
  • It fails when retail turns correlated: GameStop's off-exchange share of dollar volume fell from 62.6% to 32.8% in a week of January 2021, consistent with wholesalers internalizing less [Verified].

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family liquidity provision Edge source liquidity provision · structural/regulatory Holding period seconds to minutes Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Retail investors via their brokers: they pay less than the quoted spread and no commission, and value convenience over a tenth of a cent; brokers are paid PFOF. Critics say lit quoters also pay, left with more toxic flow (contested). Universe & instruments all NMS stocks and ETFs; retail options flow is the sister business Data required direct feeds; markout history per broker segment; competitors' Rule 605 statistics Core algorithms used M5 Adverse selection and markouts · M2 Fair value and microprice · M4 Quoting and inventory control · M9 Algorithmic risk controls Infra intensity high: microsecond pricing of millions of orders a day, but no queue race Capacity (rough $ range) set by retail volume, not capital: industry gross capture several $B/yr [Estimate] (it must exceed the $4.9B+/yr of equity and options PFOF in 2025 Rule 606 data [Reported]) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) not meaningful on capital; thin margin, few losing days [Lore]. No segment disclosure; Virtu's FY2025 Market Making adjusted net trading income was $1,666M, all asset classes [Reported] Turnover shares held seconds to minutes [Lore] Main risks / failure modes correlated retail surges, mis-segmented flow, code errors, margin calls, PFOF bans Crowding risk moderate: competition is for broker routing, not queue position Firm types that run it wholesalers; Citadel Securities and Virtu had over 70% of retail flow in 2019–2022 data [Reported]; Susquehanna, HRT and Jane Street compete [Reported] Lab Lab 04

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A customer taps "buy 200 shares." The broker's router sends the order to a wholesaler, which sells from its own book at $40.0076 when the best offer is $40.01: a quarter-cent of price improvement. No queue, no race. The order arrived because of who sent it, and the only question is what that broker's flow is worth, judged by its markout.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Glosten and Milgrom (1985): a dealer facing some informed traders widens the spread for everyone. An exchange cannot tell retail from a latency arbitrageur, so its spread prices the mix. A wholesaler sees the broker, prices a segment with little adverse selection, and still beats the NBBO: internalization of benign flow.

Wholesalers may also fill in sub-pennies, which exchanges cannot for displayed orders (Rule 612) [Verified], and brokers may choose how the surplus splits between price improvement and PFOF [Verified]. Retail is benign only short-term: net retail buying predicts about 10 bps of outperformance over the next week (Boehmer et al. 2021) [Verified], irrelevant to a desk holding for seconds.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Order arrives with broker, type, size, symbol.
  2. Look up the segment's expected markout (M5).
  3. Price off fair value plus costs; share the remaining room as price improvement.
  4. Fill as principal, or route out if too big, toxic or near a halt.
  5. Net against opposite retail orders; hedge the residual (M4).
  6. Report: TRF prints, monthly Rule 605 statistics, brokers' Rule 606 PFOF disclosures.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: NBBO $39.99 × $40.01, microprice $40.002, client buys 200 shares.

Cost item $/share Expected 60-second markout 0.0012 PFOF ($0.10 per 100 shares) 0.0010 Hedge, fees, clearing 0.0005 Minimum margin 0.0005 Floor edge 0.0032

Lowest acceptable sale price: 40.002 + 0.0032 = $40.0052, leaving 0.48¢ to the offer. Giving the client half: fill at $40.0076, 0.24¢ improvement. Expected profit: 0.56 − 0.12 − 0.10 − 0.05 = 0.29¢/share; on 50M shares a day from this broker, about $145,000 a day. A segment marking out at 0.9¢ needs a $40.013 floor, above the offer, so it is routed to an exchange.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Fair value (M2), segment markouts (M5; Lab 04 measures them), inventory (M4), collars and auto-route rules (M9).

# Price one marketable retail order (simplified). d = +1 client buys, -1 client sells.
# Markout cost = expected move against the wholesaler, $/share (> 0 is bad for us).
MIN_MARGIN, HEDGE_COST = 0.0005, 0.0005   # $/share
MAX_AUTO_SHARES = 5_000                   # larger orders go to the street

def price_retail_order(order, book, stats, contract):
    d = +1 if order.side == "BUY" else -1
    nbbo_px = book.best_ask if d > 0 else book.best_bid       # what the client gets on exchange
    fair = book.microprice()                                   # M2: fair value from direct feeds
    seg = (order.broker, order.order_type, size_bucket(order.qty), symbol_bucket(order.symbol))
    exp_adverse = stats.shrunk_markout(seg, horizon_s=60)      # M5: shrunk toward the pooled estimate
    floor_edge = exp_adverse + contract.pfof_per_share(seg) + HEDGE_COST + MIN_MARGIN
    best_px = fair + d * floor_edge                            # most generous price that still pays
    if d * (best_px - nbbo_px) > 0 or order.qty > MAX_AUTO_SHARES or book.near_luld_band():
        return route_to_exchange(order)                        # cannot beat the NBBO profitably
    room = d * (nbbo_px - best_px)                             # $/share between our floor and the NBBO
    px = nbbo_px - d * contract.pi_share * room                # give the contracted share as improvement
    return fill_as_principal(order, round_subpenny(px, d))     # off-exchange, sub-penny allowed

Lab 04, synthetic. Uninformed fills keep about +2 bps at 60 seconds; informed fills lose about 1.5 bps. Broker segments proxy for this split.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Segments: finer ones price better but have noisy markouts; thin ones are shrunk toward pooled estimates [Lore].
  • Horizon: one second catches latency-driven flow, minutes catch informed retail. Amended Rule 605 publishes realized spreads from 50 ms to 5 minutes since August 2026 [Reported].
  • Improvement policy: brokers rank wholesalers on price improvement and effective-over-quoted (E/Q) spread [Reported].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• SEC (December 2022): over 90% of marketable individual-investor orders went to six wholesalers; auctions would save an estimated $1.5B a year [Verified]. The Order Competition Rule was withdrawn on 2025-06-12 [Verified].
  • Schwarz et al. (2025, JF): 85,000 simultaneous orders across six accounts; wholesalers priced the same trade differently by broker, and PFOF did not explain the gap [Verified].
  • Over $4.9B a year was paid for equity and options flow in 2025 [Reported]; Robinhood's Q4 2025 revenue included $314M from options and $94M from equities [Reported].
  • December 2020: Robinhood paid a $65M SEC penalty for misleading customers about PFOF and for execution that cost them $34.1M [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Fixed costs favor scale, hence concentration. Margins face amended Rule 605 comparisons, a $0.005 tick for tick-constrained stocks due by November 2027 [Verified], and the EU PFOF ban, whose national exemptions ended 30 June 2026 [Reported].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Correlated retail. Netting fails and hedges move prices. On 2021-01-27 NSCC called $6.9B of intraday margin from 36 members; brokers then restricted buying, and GameStop volume moved on-exchange [Verified].
  • Code errors. On 2012-08-01 Knight Capital, a leading wholesaler, deployed code for NYSE's Retail Liquidity Program; 212 small retail orders became 4 million executions in 45 minutes and a loss over $460M [Verified].
  • Mis-segmentation: professionals hiding in retail flow.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: PFOF harms clients. Practice: fills beat the NBBO, but how much depends on the broker (Schwarz et al. 2025) [Verified]; whether auctions would beat wholesalers is contested.
  • Textbook: retail is noise. Practice: noise over seconds, mildly informed over a week [Verified].
  • Textbook: hedge every fill. Practice: net opposite flow first [Lore].

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Lit equity market making; options market making (retail options must execute on exchange); exchange retail liquidity programs (fee-driven strategies).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "That broker marks out at a tenth of a cent." → Benign flow, worth paying for.
  • "We run 30% E/Q there." → Effective spread is 30% of quoted.
  • "Their flow got sharper." → Markouts worsened; reprice.
  • "Meme names go to the street today." → Correlated flow is routed out.
  • "PFOF is our COGS." → The cost of acquiring inventory.
  • "We lost share on the 606." → The broker moved flow to a rival.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: wholesalers front-run retail. Reality: they trade against the order as principal; trading ahead of customers is barred by FINRA Rule 5320.
  • Myth: retail flow is valuable because it is dumb. Reality: because it is uncorrelated; correlated retail is the dangerous kind.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: What share of retail flow do you internalize?
  • Informed: Which markout horizon do you price off?
  • Informed: What did amended Rule 605 change in broker scorecards?
  • Informed: How much capture would a half-penny tick remove?
  • Sharp: At what retail order-imbalance correlation do you stop internalizing?
  • Sharp: 🔒 Your markouts by broker, and the PFOF-versus-improvement split?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: segmentation in Glosten-Milgrom, and markout accounting

If a share \(\pi\) of takers know the next move \(\Delta\), an exchange quoter breaks even at \(s_{\text{ex}}/2 = \pi\,\mathbb{E}|\Delta|\). A wholesaler with informed share \(\pi_r \ll \pi\), PFOF \(f\) and costs \(c\) breaks even at

\[ \frac{s_r}{2} = \pi_r\,\mathbb{E}|\Delta| + f + c , \]

leaving up to \((s_{\text{ex}} - s_r)/2\) for price improvement. For a fill at \(p\), client side \(d\), mid \(m_t\):

\[ \text{PnL}_h = -d\,(m_t - p) - d\,(m_{t+h} - m_t), \]

capture minus adverse selection; Rule 605's realized spread is \(2\,\text{PnL}_h\).

docs.title: ETF and index arbitrage
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Three trades tie one index exposure together: ETF vs basket (creation and redemption), futures vs basket (carry), ETF vs constituents (statistical).
  • Each lives inside a no-arbitrage band, the cheapest arbitrageur's all-in cost: ±7.4 bps on average in Lab 07, up to 14.9 bps in stress (synthetic lab result). Trade inside your band and you lose.
  • Competition turned pure index arbitrage into a speed race and a financing market, with the basis quoted in bps [Verified].
  • It fails when the basket cannot be traded: halts, closed markets, capacity limits.

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family speed & structural Edge source structural/regulatory · speed Holding period milliseconds (ETF vs futures) to a day (creation); basis trades to expiry Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Hurried ETF buyers and sellers, and leveraged longs paying implied financing in futures: one ticket, leverage and no borrow are worth a few bps. Universe & instruments index and sector baskets; ES, NQ, RTY futures; SPY, IVV, QQQ, IWM, sector ETFs Data required basket files, constituent and futures feeds, dividends, financing and borrow rates Core algorithms used P5 Transaction cost and impact models · M2 Fair value and microprice · M7 Hedging algorithms · E5 Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos Infra intensity extreme for ETF vs futures; moderate, balance-sheet heavy otherwise Capacity (rough $ range) ~$0.3B–$2B a year of US industry P&L [Estimate]: perhaps $3–6T of gross primary flow (1.5–3× 2026's ~$2T annualized net inflow) at 1–3 bps Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) No disclosures. ETF premium strategies: ~7% abnormal return gross of costs (Petajisto 2017, 2007–2014 backtest) [Verified]. ES–SPY racing: high for the fastest only [Lore]. Turnover very high Main risks / failure modes leg risk, halts, illiquid baskets, borrow recalls, dividend surprises Crowding risk extreme in SPY and ES; moderate in niche, international and bond funds Firm types that run it ETF market makers and APs; bank delta-one desks; HFT firms Lab Lab 07

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: The S&P 500 exists as 500 stocks, SPY and the ES future (linkages). When one wrapper gets cheaper than the others by more than the cost of trading the gap, arbitrageurs buy it and sell the rest (ETF arbitrage). ETF market makers keep prices inside the gap; this page covers its edges.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text: The arbitrageur manufactures wrappers. When ETF demand outruns supply, it builds shares from the basket (creation and redemption); when futures buyers want leverage, it carries the basket against short futures, lending its balance sheet. Whoever demands the wrapper pays: the ETF buyer through the premium, the futures buyer through financing above the arbitrageur's funding. Competition squeezes the margin toward the marginal arbitrageur's cost.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Premium: ETF price vs your real-time NAV (M2).
  2. Create above the create cost (sell ETF, buy basket); redeem below the redeem cost (buy ETF, short and borrow the basket).
  3. Strike the basket at the close (MOC), the prices NAV uses.
  4. Basis: if futures are rich against \(S e^{(r-q)T}\) at your funding rate, sell them and hold the basket.
  5. Statistical: trade ETF vs constituents when the gap beats costs.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Creation (Lab 07 parameters, illustrative). Unit $2.5M; create cost: ETF half-spread 1.53 + basket half-spreads 1.77 + square-root impact 1.69 + $500 fee 2.00 = 7.0 bps. Closing premium 10 bps; each unit sold lowers it 2 bps.

Step Calculation Result Units floor((10 − 7) / 2 + 0.5) 2 Captured minus costs 2 × 10 − 2 × 2² / 2 − 2 × 7.0 2 bp-units Net 2 bps × $2.5M +$500

A third unit would average a 5 bp premium, below cost.

Index basis (illustrative). Index 6,000, 60 days, funding 4.00%, dividend yield 1.30%.

Step Calculation Result Fair futures; ES trades 6,030.0 6,000 × e^(0.027 × 60/365) 6,026.7; implied financing 4.33% Sell 100 ES, buy $30M basket 3.31 × $50 × 100 +$16,553 Basket in and out, futures fees 4 bps × $30M + $200 −$12,200 Net, 60 days ≈ +$4,350 (1.5 bps)

A desk funding at 4.33% earns nothing: the trade belongs to the cheapest balance sheet.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
The band is a cost model; NAV is fair value; legs use hedging and closing algos.

import numpy as np
# Lab 07 CORE ALGORITHM (labs/07-etf-nav-arbitrage/lab.py), same names and signs.

def no_arbitrage_band(weights, half_spread_bps, daily_vol, adv_usd, unit_value, n_units=1,
                      etf_half_spread_bps=1.5, fee_usd=500.0, borrow_bps_per_year=25.0,
                      settle_days=1, impact_coef=0.5):
    w = np.asarray(weights)
    order_usd = w * unit_value * n_units                                 # dollars traded per stock
    impact_bps = impact_coef * np.asarray(daily_vol) * np.sqrt(order_usd / np.asarray(adv_usd)) * 1e4
    basket_bps = np.sum(w * (np.asarray(half_spread_bps) + impact_bps))
    fee_bps = fee_usd / (unit_value * n_units) * 1e4                     # fixed fee per order
    create = etf_half_spread_bps + basket_bps + fee_bps
    borrow_bps = borrow_bps_per_year * settle_days / 360.0               # redeem: short basket until delivery
    return create, create + borrow_bps                                   # band = [-redeem, +create]

def arb_decision(premium_bps, create_cost_bps, redeem_cost_bps, impact_bps_per_unit,
                 max_units=10, buffer_bps=0.0):
    p = np.asarray(premium_bps, float)
    up = np.asarray(create_cost_bps) + buffer_bps                        # create trigger (ETF rich)
    dn = np.asarray(redeem_cost_bps) + buffer_bps                        # redeem trigger (ETF cheap)
    n_create = np.floor((p - up) / impact_bps_per_unit + 0.5)            # units whose AVERAGE premium
    n_redeem = np.floor((-p - dn) / impact_bps_per_unit + 0.5)           # still beats the trigger
    units = np.where(n_create > 0, n_create, np.where(n_redeem > 0, -n_redeem, 0.0))
    return np.clip(units, -max_units, max_units)                         # +create, -redeem, 0 = none

Synthetic data. P&L is negative for triggers inside the cost band, peaks near the average one-unit cost and flattens beyond the rivals' cost.

Synthetic lab result: a 0 bps trigger loses $0.53M a year, the best fixed trigger (7 bps) earns $0.18M and the cost-aware rule $0.21M, 2.8 bps per unit. Both legs strike at one closing price in the toy; real P&L is noisier.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Band width: spreads jump in stress; impact grows with √(order / ADV); the fixed fee amortizes over units (SPY: at most $3,000 per participant per day) [Verified]; borrow bites in hard-to-borrow names; funding and capital set the basis band.
  • Statistical leg: ETF minus live NAV mean-reverts within minutes; since the ETF usually leads, constituents do most of the catching up [Lore].
  • Custom baskets (Rule 6c-11, 2019) let APs drop illiquid or hard-to-borrow names [Verified].
  • Futures tools: BTIC trades futures at a spread to the index close; AIR total return futures quote the financing spread in bps [Verified].

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative, per creation unit, from Lab 07 averages (synthetic lab result).

Line bps of unit value Premium captured (average) +10.2 ETF half-spread −1.5 Basket half-spreads and impact −3.8 Creation or redemption fee −2.0 Borrow (redemptions) −0.1 Net per unit +2.8

Real books add leg slippage, financing and capital charges.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Basis: futures mispricing grows with maturity and is path-dependent (MacKinlay & Ramaswamy 1988) [Verified]; basis and liquidity Granger-cause each other (Roll, Schwartz & Subrahmanyam 2007) [Verified].
  • Speed: median ES–SPY windows fell from 97 ms (2005) to 7 ms (2011); profit per opportunity stayed flat (Budish, Cramton & Shim 2015) [Verified].
  • ETF vs ETF: SPY–IVV mispricings follow spread widening (Marshall, Nguyen & Visaltanachoti 2013) [Verified].
  • Spillover: arbitrage carries ETF flow shocks into stocks (Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi 2018) [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Pure index arbitrage is decades old and competed down to cost [Lore]; the race moved to speed, not lower profit per trade (Budish, Cramton & Shim 2015), and the basis became a financing market. Capacity is premium episodes times balance sheet, and it binds when flows peak (8 of 1,260 days in Lab 07, synthetic). Edge remains in niche baskets.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Illiquid basket: stress widens the band (up to 14.9 vs 7.4 bps on average in Lab 07).
  • Halts: 24 August 2015 brought 1,278 LULD halts, 1,058 in 327 ETPs [Verified].
  • Capacity: LQD closed at a 5.0% discount in the week to 20 March 2020 [Reported]; bond-ETF discounts disappeared once the Fed announced bond purchases (Haddad, Moreira & Muir 2021) [Verified].
  • Legs: borrow recalls, dividend surprises, financing spikes; a discount to stale NAV is no arbitrage.

See also the failure gallery.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: any gap from \(S e^{(r-q)T}\) is free money. Practice: funding differs by firm, so the basis trades as a financing rate (CME AIR futures) [Verified].
  • Textbook: APs create on any premium. Practice: only beyond the band; market makers hold prices inside it [Lore].
  • Textbook: stocks lead. Practice: futures and ETFs often lead (lead-lag) [Verified].

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: optimal creation units

With premium \(p\), unit cost \(c\) and impact \(\lambda\) per unit (bps), unit \(k\) sells at average premium \(p - \lambda(k - \tfrac12)\), so

\[ \Pi(n) = n p - \frac{\lambda n^2}{2} - n c . \]

The lab trades every unit whose average premium beats \(c\): \(n = \lfloor (p - c)/\lambda + \tfrac12 \rfloor\), capped by balance sheet.

docs.title: Fee- and microstructure-driven strategies
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Under maker-taker pricing, takers pay up to the 30-mil access-fee cap and makers earn a rebate; in one-cent-spread stocks the rebate can be most of a market maker's edge.
  • Inverted venues flip the signs: makers pay to jump the queue at the same displayed price. Routers rank net-of-fee prices.
  • Odd-lot, midpoint and order-type mechanics add smaller edges.
  • The SEC's 2024 10-mil cap and half-penny tick would compress this, but are delayed to the first business day of November 2027 [Verified]; price-tiered round lots are live since 2025-11-03 [Reported].
  • Fee and queue optimization is legal; spoofing, layering and wash trades are not.

Level: Core · Read time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family speed & structural Edge source structural/regulatory · liquidity provision Holding period seconds to minutes (rebate capture); milliseconds for order-type and odd-lot edges Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Takers paying access fees, and naive routers that rest at queue backs or chase rebates, filling mostly before adverse moves. They accept because the cost is a fraction of a cent per share, buried in commissions. Universe & instruments tick-constrained stocks; high-priced stocks that trade in odd lots; ETFs; all lit venues and midpoint ATSs Data required fee schedules and tier status; direct feeds with odd lots; queue estimates; venue-level markouts Core algorithms used E4 Smart order routing · M6 Queue position and order placement · M4 Quoting and inventory control · M5 Adverse selection and markouts Infra intensity medium-high: colocation and direct feeds to manage queues; microwave not required Capacity (rough $ range) $10–100M/yr net for a large market maker [Estimate] (roughly 4–8 mils, $0.0004–$0.0008, of net fee and queue edge per share on 100–500M shares/day × 250 days) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) rarely standalone; part of very stable market-making P&L [Lore]; net near zero for sub-scale players [Estimate]; no disclosures; would shrink under the 2027 rules Turnover very high; flat by the close Main risks / failure modes fee and tier changes; rule changes; adverse selection outrunning rebates; enforcement Crowding risk high: rebates are competed away through longer queues Firm types that run it electronic market makers and HFT prop firms; agency routers on the cost side Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A one-cent spread in a $10 stock is a hard floor: no exchange can display $10.005. Fee schedules let traders deal in fractions of a cent anyway: the same $10.00 bid nets a passive buyer less than $10.00 on a rebate-paying venue and more on an inverted one. The displayed price is not the price; the net-of-fee price is. Strategies live in that gap: earning rebates, buying priority, posting odd lots inside the spread, and exploiting order-type behavior (Fees, rebates and ticks).

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text: Reg NMS caps take fees at 30 mils ($0.0030) and fixes a one-cent tick above $1, but leaves rebates and tiers to exchanges. In tick-constrained names competition moves from spread to queue position and fees. Rebates attract displayed size, which attracts fee-paying takers. Firms that model net economics venue by venue collect what slower routers leave behind.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Net prices per venue and side (E4).
  2. Queues: estimate queue position and fill probability (M6).
  3. Post where expected value is highest, post-only to guarantee maker status.
  4. Skew inventory (M4); scratch out passively to collect a second rebate.
  5. Audit markouts by venue and order type (M5) and tier progress.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative schedules, close to Nasdaq's top tier and Cboe BYX's inverted schedule [Verified]: venue A charges takers 30 mils and pays makers 29; venue B charges makers 15 mils and pays takers 2. Stock quoted $10.00 × $10.01.

At the $10.00 bid Venue A Venue B Passive buyer's net price $9.9971 $10.0015 Taking seller's net price $9.9970 $10.0002 Shares queued ahead 80,000 3,000

Sellers hit B first (0.32¢ more), so 0.44¢ buys the front of the line.

Rebate capture: buy 1,000 shares passively at $10.00 on A ($ per 1,000 shares).

Outcome (probability) Today: 1¢ tick, 29-mil rebate Under 2024 rules: ½¢ tick, 9-mil rebate Sell passively one tick up (40%) 10.00 + 5.80 = +15.80 5.00 + 1.80 = +6.80 Scratch passively at $10.00 (35%) +5.80 +1.80 Stop out, take one tick down (25%) −10.00 + 2.90 − 3.00 = −10.10 −5.00 + 0.90 − 1.00 = −5.10 Expected value +5.83 +2.08

Without rebates today's EV is +0.75 (0.40 × 10 − 0.25 × 13): rebates supply ~87% of it.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
The router (E4) and queue model (M6) do the work; TCA shows the client side of the same economics.

# Where to post a passive buy at the NBBO bid (simplified; queue models in M6)
def passive_venue_value(v, half_spread, horizon_s, urgency_cost):
    p_fill = v.fill_prob(queue_ahead=v.queue_ahead, horizon=horizon_s)  # queue model
    markout = v.expected_markout_if_filled     # $/share, negative = adverse (M5)
    rebate = -v.maker_fee                      # > 0 on maker-taker, < 0 on inverted venues
    return p_fill * (half_spread + rebate + markout) - (1 - p_fill) * urgency_cost

def choose_post_venue(venues, half_spread=0.005, horizon_s=2.0, urgency_cost=0.002):
    scores = {v.name: passive_venue_value(v, half_spread, horizon_s, urgency_cost)
              for v in venues}
    return max(scores, key=scores.get), scores

def net_take_price(price, side, v):
    # Net-of-fee price a taker really pays or receives: what routers actually rank
    fee = v.take_fee     # > 0 on maker-taker (cap 30 mils today), < 0 (a rebate) on inverted
    return price + fee if side == "BUY" else price - fee

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Tiers. Near a monthly volume threshold the marginal share is worth far more than the average; trading with yourself to get there is illegal wash trading.
  • Odd lots. Odd-lot quotes inside the NBBO were invisible on the SIP; price-tiered round lots (2025-11-03) and the SIP odd-lot best quote (late April 2026) shrink that edge, with depth deferred to May 2028 [Reported].
  • Midpoint. Pegs save half the spread but get picked off before NBBO moves; IEX's crumbling-quote indicator guards against this [Verified].
  • Locked markets. Post-only orders that would lock are repriced; a pending June 2026 proposal would repeal that ban (Rule 610(e)) with Rule 611 [Verified].

docs.text:
Illustrative: 1,000 round trips like the "today" column (1M shares bought passively). Across a whole book, with worse setups, net edge falls to the few mils in the header.

Line $ Spread captured +4,000 Maker rebates +5,075 Stop-out losses −2,500 Take fees on stop-outs −750 Trading margin +5,825 (0.58¢/share) Clearing, regulatory and data costs −1,000 Net +4,825

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• SEC 2024 amendments (adopted 2024-09-18): $0.005 tick for tick-constrained stocks, 10-mil access-fee cap, price-tiered round lots and odd-lot data in the SIP [Verified]. Compliance moved from 2025-11-03 to 2026-11-02, then to the first business day of November 2027 (order of 2026-06-11), with staff told to review Rules 610(c) and 612 [Verified].
  • Industry: MEMX asked for a 15-mil cap in half-penny names; SIFMA sought delay pending the Rule 611 review [Reported].
  • Routing conflicts: Battalio, Corwin & Jennings (2016, JF) link rebate-maximizing limit-order routing to worse execution quality [Reported].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Fee schedules set the pool; queues lengthen until rebate ≈ adverse selection plus waiting cost. A 10-mil cap would cut the maximum rebate by about two-thirds [Estimate] (30 → 10 mils), and half-penny ticks would shorten queues, eroding inverted venues' priority premium.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Schedule risk: a missed tier reprices a whole month.
  • Adverse selection: a long queue fills you mainly when the level is about to break.
  • Rule risk: firms ready for 2025-11-03 faced two delays; the rules may yet change [Verified].
  • Enforcement: spoofing and layering are illegal. Regulators charged Navinder Sarao with E-mini spoofing in 2015 [Reported] and Avalon FA and Lek Securities with layering US stocks in 2017 (alleged profits ~$21M) [Verified]. See rules that shape strategies.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: a price is a price. Practice: routers rank net price times fill probability [Lore].
  • Textbook: rebates subsidize liquidity. Practice: in tick-constrained names they mostly lengthen queues, and inverted venues sell priority [Lore].
  • Legal line: high cancel rates are normal for market makers; spoofing turns on intent to cancel before execution [Reported].

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Rebate capture, queue jumping, odd-lot posting, midpoint pegs, retail liquidity programs. Neighbours: equity market making, retail flow internalization, latency arbitrage.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're scratching for rebates." → Exiting at the entry price; the rebate is the profit.
  • "Post on BYX to get to the front." → Pay the inverted venue's maker fee for priority [Lore].
  • "We're 2M shares short of the top tier." → Month-end volume decides the rebate rate.
  • "Back-of-queue fills are toxic." → Those fills come just before the price drops.
  • "Odd lots are the real inside in that name." → In a high-priced stock, the best prices sit in odd lots.
  • "Net capture is four mils after markouts." → Spread plus rebate minus adverse selection, per share.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: rebates are free money. Reality: they are competed into queue length and offset by adverse selection.
  • Myth: cancelling most orders is spoofing. Reality: intent to deceive is the line.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: net prices and the value of a passive order

Taker's net buy price: \(P + f\); maker's: \(P - r\) (\(f\), \(r\) negative on inverted venues). A resting order with fill probability \(p\), half-spread \(h\), markout \(m\) and waiting cost \(c\) is worth:

\[ V = p \,(h + r + m) - (1-p)\,c \]

docs.title: Latency arbitrage
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Latency arbitrage trades against quotes left stale for microseconds after public news (a futures tick, a sweep on another venue) moved fair value. Whoever reaches the matching engine first wins.
  • It is a race, not a forecast: in London Stock Exchange data the winner beat the first loser by a modal 5–10 µs, and races were about 20% of FTSE 100 volume [Verified].
  • Sniped quoters pay first and investors pay last, through wider spreads: a "tax" of roughly 0.5 bp of trading volume, about $5B a year globally [Verified].
  • The edge is rank, not capital. Speed bumps (IEX) blunt it on one venue only.

Level: Deep dive · Read time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family speed & structural Edge source speed · structural/regulatory Holding period microseconds to seconds Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Quoters whose cancels lose the race. They keep quoting because uninformed flow still pays on average, and pass the pick-off cost to investors as wider spreads. Universe & instruments liquid US stocks and ETFs quoted on many venues; ES/NQ futures as triggers Data required direct feeds from every venue and CME; synchronized hardware timestamps Core algorithms used M1 Anatomy of an HFT trading loop · M2 Fair value and microprice · M3 Order-book and trade-flow signals · M9 Algorithmic risk controls Infra intensity extreme: colocation, FPGA tick-to-trade, microwave or millimeter-wave links Capacity (rough $ range) P&L-limited, not capital-limited: US pool roughly $1–3B/yr, a top firm tens to low hundreds of $M [Estimate] (from ABO's ~$5B global figure and top-6 concentration) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Not meaningful on capital. Fastest firm: annualized gross Sharpe far above 5; runner-up near zero [Lore]. No fund disclosures. Profits track latency rank (Baron et al. 2019, academic) [Verified]; per-race profit held flat 2005–2011 (BCS) [Verified] Turnover extreme: about one race per minute per FTSE 100 stock [Verified] Main risks / failure modes rank loss, false triggers, hedge-leg slippage, rain fade, runaway code, venue redesign Crowding risk extreme: winner-take-most among a handful of firms Firm types that run it HFT prop firms and electronic market makers (unnamed in academic data) Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: E-mini S&P 500 futures (ES) trade in CME's data center in Aurora, Illinois; SPY trades in New Jersey. When ES ticks up, every SPY offer in New Jersey is suddenly too cheap, but New Jersey learns it only about 4 ms later, by microwave. Market makers' cancels and snipers' immediate-or-cancel buys then race; the exchange processes them one at a time, and if the buy lands first, the sniper buys below the new fair value. Nothing was predicted. The same race runs inside New Jersey when a sweep hits one venue, or when a direct feed shows an NBBO change before the SIP does (NBBO and market data).

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text: Budish, Cramton & Shim (2015) call it a design flaw. A continuous limit order book serializes messages, so each public jump is a race the quoter usually loses (with N equally fast firms, its cancel wins one time in N). Quoters widen spreads to cover it; speed spending raises the entry price, not the rent. Reg NMS fragmentation multiplies the triggers.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Trigger: an ES print, a sweep on one venue, or a direct-feed NBBO change.
  2. Reprice follower fair value; require edge above take fee plus exit cost.
  3. Fire IOCs at all stale venues at once, as intermarket sweep orders.
  4. Exit: hedge in the leader or pass inventory to the market-making book, behind hardware risk limits.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Index 6,000, SPY ≈ $600. ES ticks up 0.25 points (0.42 bp); SPY fair value rises ≈ $0.025, from a 599.995 mid to ≈ 600.02. Three venues still offer 600, 600 and 800 shares at 600.00.

Step Calculation $ Win the two 600-share venues 1,200 shares at 600.00 720,000 notional Stale-quote edge 1,200 × 0.02 +24.00 Take fee 1,200 × 0.0030 −3.60 Exit slippage 1,200 × 0.005 −6.00 Net +14.40 (≈ 0.2 bps)

The market maker who sold lost $24.00, less a ~$2.40 rebate. About a penny a share: only volume and win rate matter.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
A stripped-down HFT loop: triggers from order-book signals, a leader-implied fair value, risk controls in the path. Victims measure it with markouts.

# Event-driven stale-quote loop (simplified; production runs in FPGA/C++ in well under 1 µs)
TAKE_FEE = 0.0030        # $/share, today's Rule 610(c) access-fee cap (30 mils)
EDGE_TICKS = 0.6         # required edge after fees, in ticks (covers exit cost + false triggers)

def on_leader_update(leader_mid, st):
    # Follower fair value implied by the leader (beta-weighted move since last sync)
    fv = st.follower_anchor + st.beta * (leader_mid - st.leader_anchor)
    orders = []
    for venue, book in st.books.items():                  # one direct feed per venue
        if fv - book.best_ask - TAKE_FEE > EDGE_TICKS * st.tick:
            orders.append(("BUY", venue, book.best_ask, book.ask_size, "IOC_ISO"))
        elif book.best_bid - fv - TAKE_FEE > EDGE_TICKS * st.tick:
            orders.append(("SELL", venue, book.best_bid, book.bid_size, "IOC_ISO"))
    orders = st.risk.check(orders)                         # position, rate, notional caps
    st.gateway.send_all(orders)                            # all venues at once
    # Defensive half of the same race: pull our own quotes that fv just made stale
    st.gateway.cancel_if_stale(fv, st.my_quotes)

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Path. The 2013 CME–Nasdaq microwave service promised under 4.25 ms one way versus 6.65 ms for the fastest fiber [Reported]; a 2016 report cited 3.982 ms rack to rack [Reported].
  • Threshold. Winner's curse: you fill most easily when faster rivals knew the trigger was false.
  • Venues. IEX delays every inbound message 350 µs, and its D-Limit orders reprice when its crumbling-quote indicator fires [Verified].

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative: 8M shares/day of race fills, 250 days.

Line ¢/share $M/yr Stale-quote capture +1.20 +24.0 Take fees −0.30 −6.0 Exit and hedge slippage −0.40 −8.0 False triggers −0.15 −3.0 Trading margin +0.35 +7.0 Links, colocation, FPGA team −5.0 Net +2.0

Double the wins and net rises to $9M: rank is operating leverage.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Budish, Cramton & Shim (2015, QJE): the median ES–SPY opportunity shrank from 97 ms (2005) to 7 ms (2011), with profit per opportunity roughly flat [Verified].
  • Aquilina, Budish & O'Neill (2022, QJE): about 20% of FTSE 100 trading volume in races, a latency-arbitrage tax of roughly 0.5 bp of trading volume, top 6 firms in over 80% of race wins and losses; removing races would cut the cost of liquidity ~17% [Verified].
  • Wah (2016): over $3B of potential 2014 profit in S&P 500 stocks, an upper bound [Reported].
  • Shkilko & Sokolov (2020, JF): when rain disables microwave links, adverse selection falls and liquidity improves [Verified].
  • Counterpoint: Bartlett & McCrary (2016) find US SIP-based arbitrage too small to explain the arms race [Reported]; Menkveld (2013) and Baron et al. (2019) show speed also serving market making [Verified]. Net welfare is contested.

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: The pool scales with public price jumps times stale size, not capital. Per BCS the rent moved into towers and FPGA engineers rather than vanishing. Microwave now sits within ~2% of the light-speed bound [Estimate], so the contest is over the last microseconds.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Rank loss: a shorter rival path turns a winner into a payer overnight (Baron et al.) [Verified].
  • False triggers and leg risk: a flickering ES quote or failed hedge leaves bad inventory.
  • Episodes: from April 2010 to August 2012 one-way Chicago–New York times fell ~3 ms (Laughlin, Aguirre & Grundfest 2014), stranding firms on old routes [Verified]; IEX launched D-Limit (October 2020) to shield quotes from this trade [Verified]. For runaway code, see Knight Capital in the failure gallery.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: identical snipers. Practice: racers are mostly market makers too, sniping one name while cancelling in another [Lore].
  • Textbook: frequent batch auctions end the race. Practice: no US equity exchange runs them; the SEC accepted IEX's symmetric delay in 2016 [Reported] but in February 2020 rejected Cboe EDGA's asymmetric 4 ms delay as unfairly discriminatory [Reported]. Infrastructure: colocation and the speed of light.

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Same-stock cross-venue races; futures to cash (lead-lag); ETF vs basket (ETF arbitrage); the defensive cancel in equity market making; stale option quotes.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We got picked off on the ES tick." → A faster firm hit our stale quote.
  • "We're third on the Chicago link." → Third earns close to nothing.
  • "Rain fade killed our hit rate." → Microwave was down.
  • "Our cancel lost by two micros." → The rival's take arrived 2 µs earlier.
  • "The SIP is a lagging indicator." → We trade on direct feeds.
  • "That's a pick-off venue." → We quote thinner there.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: it is front-running. Reality: it reacts to public prints, not client orders, though quoters and investors still pay.
  • Myth: it is risk-free. Reality: false triggers and rank loss produce losing days.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: What triggers most races: futures, other venues or the SIP?
  • Basic: When you lose, is it a missed fill or a cancel-back?
  • Informed: How do you separate pick-off losses from ordinary adverse selection in markouts?
  • Informed: How does your win rate move on rainy days?
  • Sharp: Under one-second batch auctions, which P&L lines vanish?
  • Sharp: 🔒 What is your tick-to-trade, and your rank on each route?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the BCS race and the speed-of-light bound

BCS zero-profit spread. Investors arrive at rate \(\lambda_I\), public jumps \(J\) at rate \(\lambda_J\); the quoter loses each race with probability \((N-1)/N\):

\[ \lambda_I \frac{s}{2} = \lambda_J \Pr(J > \tfrac{s}{2}) \, \mathbb{E}[J - \tfrac{s}{2} \mid J > \tfrac{s}{2}] \, \frac{N-1}{N} \]

Faster technology for all leaves the right side unchanged.

Light-speed bound [Estimate]. Route ≈ 1,175 km (730 miles): vacuum \(1175/299792 \approx 3.92\) ms; straight fiber (index ≈ 1.47) ≈ 5.76 ms. The 3.982 ms microwave figure is ~1.6% above the vacuum bound.

docs.title: Lead-lag and cross-asset arbitrage
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Prices are discovered first in the cheapest, most levered instrument (for US large caps, E-mini futures) and propagate to ETFs, constituents and ADRs (Hasbrouck 2003) [Verified].
  • The trade: price each follower from beta-weighted leader moves, take stale quotes or skew your own, and hedge in the leader.
  • The fast end is latency arbitrage over a Chicago–New Jersey path within ~2% of light speed [Estimate]; at seconds to minutes it is a statistical forecast with more capacity.
  • Slow quoters and resting orders in the follower pay. Windows shrank from ~100 ms (2005) to single-digit ms (2011) [Verified].

Level: Core · Read time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family speed & structural Edge source speed · informational Holding period milliseconds (futures to ETF) to minutes (ETF to constituents); hours for ADRs across time zones Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Stale quoters and resting limit orders in the follower. Market makers accept because spread income covers the misses; passive institutional orders accept pick-offs in exchange for not paying the spread. Universe & instruments ES, NQ and RTY futures; SPY, QQQ, IWM and sector ETFs; large-cap constituents; ADRs vs home-market shares Data required CME and equity direct feeds with synchronized clocks; ETF holdings; FX for ADRs Core algorithms used M2 Fair value and microprice · F1 Linear models and regularization · M3 Order-book and trade-flow signals · M7 Hedging algorithms Infra intensity extreme for sub-ms futures to cash; moderate at seconds; low for ADRs Capacity (rough $ range) fast end: tens of $M/yr P&L for a top firm; slow end: a few hundred $M of gross intraday positions [Estimate] (fast end shares the latency-arbitrage pool; slow end is capped by follower liquidity) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) fast end: very high for the fastest, near zero for the rest [Lore]; seconds-to-minutes books: gross 2–4, net 1–2 [Estimate] (practitioner estimate: many small bets, low R²); no disclosures; fast windows decayed 2005–2011 Turnover very high; inventory flattened intraday Main risks / failure modes beta breaks on stock news, leader noise, coarse hedges, rank loss, halts Crowding risk high at the fast end; moderate at the statistical end Firm types that run it HFT prop firms, electronic and ETF market makers; stat-arb funds at the slower end Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: When news hits the S&P 500, the cheapest way to act is one E-mini contract: high leverage, tiny fees, no short-sale friction. So futures move first, in Aurora, Illinois. SPY, sector ETFs and stocks in New Jersey follow once the news arrives and their market makers react. Knowing how much each follower moves per point of ES lets you price it before its own book does. The same logic links an ETF to its holdings, a sector ETF to its members, and an ADR to its home-market share (ETF, futures and options linkages).

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text: Informed traders concentrate in the leader, so it carries most of the information share. Followers lag by transmission plus reaction time, and stale quotes in that window fund the trade. The fast end is pure speed; at seconds to minutes it is slow diffusion of factor news into thinly watched names, a genuine forecast of fair value.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Estimate offline: each follower's betas and lag profile by regularized regression (F1).
  2. Reprice live: on every leader update, shift the follower's fair value by the beta-weighted leader return (M2).
  3. Combine: blend with the follower's own microprice and order flow (M3).
  4. Act: usually skew quotes; take only when edge beats fees.
  5. Hedge and unwind: offset in the leader, then flatten when the follower catches up (M7).

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Speed [Estimate]: Aurora to New Jersey is ~1,175 km, 3.92 ms at vacuum light speed; microwave reached 3.982 ms (2016) and the best fiber took 6.65 ms (2013) [Reported]. Fiber users arrive ~2.7 ms after the race ends.

Fair value (illustrative): ES at 6,000 jumps 2.5 points (10 ticks) on a headline; a $200 stock has 100 ms beta 1.3, shrunk by 0.5.

Step Calculation Result Leader return 2.5 / 6,000 +4.17 bps Implied follower move 0.5 × 1.3 × 4.17 bps × $200 +$0.054 New fair value mid 199.99 + 0.054 200.044 Edge on stale 200.00 ask after 0.3¢ fee 4.4¢ − 0.3¢ 4.1¢/share Expected P&L, 500 shares 500 × $0.041 +$20.50 Hedge 500 × $200 × 1.3 ÷ $30,000 per Micro E-mini sell ≈ 4 contracts

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Betas come from regularized linear models; the live fair value runs inside the HFT trading loop; offsets use hedging algorithms.

import numpy as np

def fit_betas(X_lead, y_follow, lam=1e-3):
    # Offline ridge: X_lead (n_events, k) leader log-returns over the last L ms,
    # y_follow (n_events,) follower log-return over the next H ms, in event time
    k = X_lead.shape[1]
    return np.linalg.solve(X_lead.T @ X_lead + lam * np.eye(k), X_lead.T @ y_follow)

def lead_lag_fair_value(follower_micro, leader_ret_since_sync, betas, shrink=0.5):
    # Shrink toward zero: out-of-sample R^2 at ms horizons is low
    implied_ret = shrink * float(np.dot(betas, leader_ret_since_sync))
    return follower_micro * (1.0 + implied_ret)

def decide(fv, best_bid, best_ask, take_fee=0.003, edge_ticks=0.5, tick=0.01):
    if fv - best_ask - take_fee > edge_ticks * tick:
        return "TAKE_ASK"        # lift the stale offer, then hedge in the leader
    if best_bid - fv - take_fee > edge_ticks * tick:
        return "HIT_BID"
    return "SKEW_QUOTES"         # usual case: move our own quotes toward fv

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Event time, not clock time. Asynchronous trading depresses measured correlation at short horizons (the Epps effect); sample on leader updates.
  • Timestamps. Estimate lags with exchange timestamps, not your receive times.
  • Leader set. ES, NQ, the sector ETF and top holdings; ridge keeps them from fighting.
  • Hedge size. ES is $50 × index; Micro E-minis ($5 × index) hedge finer at higher cost.

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative seconds-scale taking book, 3M shares/day.

Line ¢/share $k/day Predicted move captured +0.80 +24.0 Take fees −0.30 −9.0 Hedge slippage and futures fees −0.15 −4.5 Misses on stock-specific news −0.15 −4.5 Trading margin +0.20 +6.0

The bigger payoff is often defensive: less adverse selection on market-making quotes [Lore].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Hasbrouck (2003, JF): E-mini futures dominate price discovery for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100; for the S&P 400, without an E-mini, discovery is shared between regular futures and the ETF [Verified]. Method: information shares (Hasbrouck 1995).
  • Ates & Wang (2005): since September 1998, E-minis out-contribute floor-traded futures [Verified].
  • Budish, Cramton & Shim (2015): ES–SPY correlation collapses at millisecond horizons; median arbitrage windows fell from 97 ms (2005) to 7 ms (2011) [Verified].
  • Laughlin, Aguirre & Grundfest (2014): one-way Chicago–New York time fell ~3 ms between 2010 and 2012 [Verified].
  • Cross-market HFT: Menkveld (2013) and Baron et al. (2019) show speed paying off across markets [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Physics saturates the futures-to-cash leg, so edge migrated to better models (more leaders, intraday betas) and slower horizons with more capacity but lower R² [Estimate]. As ETF trading grows, the ETF can lead its own constituents [Lore].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Beta breaks: on single-stock news the follower leads, and leader-based fair value is badly wrong.
  • Leader noise and halts: a flickering ES quote triggers trades that reverse; a halted follower cannot be traded.
  • Episodes: on 6 May 2010, per the CFTC-SEC report, E-mini selling was transmitted to equities through cross-market arbitrage [Reported]; on 24 August 2015 many stocks opened late and ETFs traded far from their constituents (see ETF and index arbitrage) [Reported].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: a cointegrated futures-cash VECM in clock time (Hasbrouck) [Verified]. Practice: event-time models keyed to leader updates, re-estimated intraday and shrunk [Lore].
  • Textbook: ADR parity arbitrage. Practice: conversion fees, FX, borrow and non-overlapping hours make it a statistical trade during the overlap [Lore].
  • Textbook: a standalone strategy. Practice: mostly an input to equity and ETF market making [Lore].

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Futures to ETFs; ETF to constituents; sector ETF to members; ADRs; options-implied prices to stock; Treasury futures to rate-sensitive stocks. Neighbours: latency arbitrage (mechanical end), ETF and index arbitrage (creation-anchored), pairs trading (days-scale cousin).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Shrink the beta, the R² is garbage at 50 ms." → Use partial adjustments at short horizons.
  • "The stock decoupled on the headline." → Single-stock news broke the beta.
  • "It's in our fair value, not a strategy." → Lead-lag is an input to quoting.
  • "NQ led on that print, not ES." → Tech news hit Nasdaq futures first.
  • "We're flat deltas, long the lag." → Hedged in futures, waiting for the follower.
  • "ADRs are dead until London opens." → No overlap means no hedge.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: futures always lead. Reality: information shares vary; on single-stock news the cash market leads.
  • Myth: cointegration means riskless arbitrage. Reality: conversion costs, borrow and halts limit enforcement.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: Which instruments lead your names, and how do you know?
  • Basic: Do you mostly take on these signals or quote on them?
  • Informed: Do you estimate lags in event time or clock time?
  • Informed: How fast do betas recover after a single-stock headline?
  • Sharp: What share of your lead-lag value shows up as lower adverse selection rather than taking P&L?
  • Sharp: 🔒 How many leaders feed each fair value, and how do you shrink them?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: information share and lag estimation

Prices of one asset in \(n\) markets follow a VECM with error covariance \(\Omega\) and efficient-price innovation \(\psi e_t\). With \(F\) the Cholesky factor of \(\Omega\), market \(j\)'s information share is

\[ IS_j = \frac{([\psi F]_j)^2}{\psi \Omega \psi'} \]

Ordering changes \(F\), so studies report bounds. A simple lag estimate:

\[ \ell^* = \arg\max_{\ell} \operatorname{corr}\left(r^{\text{lead}}_t, \, r^{\text{follow}}_{t+\ell}\right) \]

docs.title: Factor-residual mean reversion
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Strip each stock's return of what its factors (market, sector, statistical components) explain. The leftover residual tends to reverse over days: buy stocks whose cumulative residual is unusually low, short the unusually high, hedge the factors.
  • Avellaneda & Lee (2010): 15 PCA eigenportfolios, residuals fitted as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, trade at |s| > 1.25. Net of 10 bps round-trip costs: Sharpe 1.44 over 1997–2007 but 0.9 in 2003–07; sector-ETF version 1.1 [Verified].
  • You are paid for absorbing price-insensitive flows; typical NYSE pricing errors have a 3.2-point standard deviation and a 6.2-week half-life [Verified].
  • It is a turnover machine. Lab 09 turns its gross book 57× a year: gross Sharpe 3.0 becomes 0.63 net at $10M and −2.20 at $100M, with a break-even cost of 9.7 bps per dollar traded (synthetic lab result).
  • It is crowded: in August 2007 Avellaneda–Lee backtests lost 5% (PCA) and 10% (ETF) in days, then recovered [Verified].

Level: Core · Read time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family stat arb Edge source liquidity provision · behavioral Holding period 1–15 days (A&L: average expected reversion ~7 days [Verified]; Lab 09: 9.3 days) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Price-insensitive liquidity demanders: funds rebalancing or meeting redemptions, index and ETF flows, liquidations. Their motive is a mandate or a deadline, so a few bps of slippage is acceptable. Traders who overreact to moves without news also pay. docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
If a chipmaker falls 3% on a day semiconductors fall 3%, there is nothing to trade. If it falls 3% while its sector rises 1% and there is no news, its residual is −4%, and on average part of that comes back.

Pairs trading hedges with one twin. Here every stock gets a synthetic twin built from factors: 15 statistical components, a sector ETF, or a commercial risk model. That gives a residual for every name, not only the few with a natural partner, so the book holds hundreds of small bets.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
1. Liquidity provision. The same fee that pays short-term reversal: it rises with the VIX (Nagel 2012) [Verified], and moves on heavy volume reverse more (Campbell, Grossman & Wang 1993) [Reported], which is why A&L also scale returns by volume ("trading time").
  2. Measured pricing errors. In a structural model of NYSE inventories and retail flow, the typical stock's pricing error has a standard deviation of 3.2 percentage points and a 6.2-week half-life, 9.4% of daily idiosyncratic variance (Hendershott, Menkveld, Praz & Seasholes 2022) [Verified].
  3. Overreaction, but only to non-news. Residuals not explained by cash-flow news reverse more; removing news quadruples the risk-adjusted reversal return. Liquidity shocks drive the long side, sentiment the short side (Da, Liu & Schaumburg 2014) [Verified]. News-driven residuals drift instead (earnings).

    F["Price-insensitive flow<br/>redemption, index trade"] --> P["Residual pushed<br/>away from peers"]
    P --> S["s-score crosses band"]
    S --> L["Stat-arb book absorbs<br/>the other side"]
    L --> R["Pressure fades<br/>residual reverts"]

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Factors. Take the 252-day correlation matrix (Lab 09 refits it weekly) and its top 15 eigenvectors; eigenportfolio weights are \(Q_{ij} = v_{ij}/\sigma_i\) (PCA). Or use sector ETFs.
  2. Residuals. Regress each stock's last 60 daily returns (about one earnings cycle) on the factor returns, with an intercept.
  3. OU fit. Fit the cumulative residual as an AR(1); keep stocks whose mean-reversion time is under 30 days.
  4. s-score = distance from equilibrium in equilibrium standard deviations, with equilibrium levels centered across stocks.
  5. Bands (A&L). Open long below −1.25, short above +1.25; close longs above −0.50, shorts below +0.75.
  6. Hedge. A&L hedge each $1 of stock with β dollars of its ETF (SPY for the PCA book); Lab 09 hedges net dollars with an equal-weight basket.

docs.text:
Illustrative stock XYZ, $10M book, 1% per position.

Quantity Calculation Value AR(1) fit on 60 days X[t+1] = a + b X[t] + ζ b = 0.90, sd(ζ) = 1.2% Mean-reversion time 1 / (−ln 0.90) 9.5 days (under 30: tradeable) Equilibrium sd 1.2% / √(1 − 0.81) 2.75% s-score: X today is 0 (the intercept makes residuals sum to zero); centered m = +4.0% (0 − 4.0%) / 2.75% −1.45 → buy $100k, hedge factors OU-implied gain in 7 days 4.0% × (1 − 0.9⁷) 2.1%, $2,100 Lab 09 realized gross per round trip $1.07M ÷ ~5,000 round trips ~$210 (21 bps) [Estimate] Costs per round trip $0.81M ÷ ~5,000 ~$160 (16 bps)

The model expects 210 bps; the market pays about a tenth of that, because a 60-day OU fit mostly fits noise (the s-score's IC is 0.013). Costs then eat three-quarters of what is left.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Factors come from P1 and P2; the s-score is a D3 transform. Production books feed −s into an optimizer (P3, P6) with a cost model (P5).

# Mirrors Lab 09's core (labs/09-pca-residual-stat-arb/lab.py); days x stocks, last row = today.
def pca_residuals(returns, n_factors=15, resid_window=60):     # returns: last 252 days
    sigma = returns.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
    Y = (returns - returns.mean(axis=0)) / sigma
    eigval, U = np.linalg.eigh(Y @ Y.T)                        # days x days Gram trick
    top = np.argsort(eigval)[::-1][:n_factors]
    Q = (Y.T @ U[:, top] / np.sqrt(eigval[top])) / sigma[:, None]   # eigenportfolios v / sigma
    R = returns[-resid_window:]
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(resid_window), R @ Q])        # drift + factor returns
    return R - X @ np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ R)           # residuals

def ou_sscore(residuals, max_reversion_days=30.0):
    X = np.cumsum(residuals, axis=0)                           # cumulative residual: OU level
    x0, x1 = X[:-1], X[1:]
    d0, d1 = x0 - x0.mean(0), x1 - x1.mean(0)
    b = (d0 * d1).sum(0) / (d0 ** 2).sum(0);  a = x1.mean(0) - b * x0.mean(0)  # AR(1) per stock
    m = a / (1 - b);  m = m - m.mean()                         # equilibrium, centered across stocks
    sigma_eq = np.sqrt((x1 - a - b * x0).var(0, ddof=1) / (1 - b**2))
    ok = (b > 0) & (b < 1) & (-1 / np.log(b) < max_reversion_days)  # 1/kappa in days
    return np.where(ok, (X[-1] - m) / sigma_eq, np.nan)        # (lab guards invalid b first)

def sscore_positions(s, prev, s_open=1.25, s_close_long=0.50, s_close_short=0.75):
    pos = prev.copy()
    pos[(prev == 0) & (s < -s_open)] = 1;  pos[(prev == 0) & (s > s_open)] = -1
    pos[((prev == 1) & (s > -s_close_long)) | ((prev == -1) & (s < s_close_short))] = 0
    pos[np.isnan(s)] = 0                                       # no valid fit: close
    return pos

Lab 09 runs this on 500 synthetic stocks with a planted 5-day residual reversal (daily IC 0.04, strong and stationary by design), and compares PCA, sector-ETF and oracle residuals.

One stock's s-score over a year with the ±1.25 entry bands. Notice how many band crossings there are: each is a round trip that pays costs. Synthetic data.

Left: gross (dashed) vs net (solid) P&L, $10M book; costs take most of the gross. Right: net Sharpe falls below zero between $10M and $30M for PCA. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab result: PCA residuals correlate 0.86 with the true specific returns, but the s-score recovers an IC of only 0.013 of the planted 0.04. Gross Sharpe 2.98, net 0.63 at $10M. With a flat cost per dollar traded, net Sharpe is 2.89 at 0 bps, 1.40 at 5 bps and −0.10 at 10 bps. These Sharpes are far above A&L's real 0.9–1.44 because the planted effect is clean and constant.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Factor set. In Lab 09 the oracle fundamental model beats PCA and ETF on every seed, while PCA vs ETF flips by seed. A&L found 15-PCA beat actual ETFs after 2002, but volume-scaled ETF signals did best in 2003–07 [Verified].
  • Number of factors. Too many overfits the 60-day regression: Lab 09 net Sharpe −0.38 with 30 factors vs 0.63 with 15. A&L also tried a variable count explaining 55% of variance [Verified].
  • News filters. Skip residuals on earnings and news days (Da et al. logic).
  • From bands to optimizer. Treat −s as an alpha, net it against other signals, and trade toward the target with a turnover penalty [Lore].
  • Execution. Break-even near 10 bps per dollar traded means all-in costs of a few bps: passive orders, the close, internal crossing (execution algorithms).

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Avellaneda & Lee (2010). Stocks above $1B market cap; 60-day window; 5 bps per trade; 2+2 leverage targeting about 10% volatility. Typical residuals had about 300 bps of equilibrium volatility and 7-day reversion. Best PCA years (Sharpe above 2) were 2000–2002 and 2004 [Verified].
  • Decay. A simple contrarian rule fell from 1.38% a day (1995) to 0.13% (2007) (Khandani & Lo) [Verified].
  • ML residuals. Deep-learning residual portfolios reach Sharpe above 4 before costs (Guijarro-Ordonez, Pelger & Zanotti 2026, academic backtest) [Verified].

docs.text:
Lab 09 net Sharpe by capital (1% of capital per position, synthetic):

Capital $3M $10M $30M $100M $1B PCA, 15 factors 1.22 0.63 −0.32 −2.20 −11.09 Sector ETF 1.30 0.96 0.40 −0.70 −6.00

The toy executes every position in one day against about $56M of ADV, so real capacity is far larger; the shape is the lesson. Square-root impact makes cost per dollar rise with size while alpha per dollar is fixed. Crowding is structural: shared factor models produce the same residuals, hence the same trades.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Crowded unwind, August 2007. All of A&L's mean-reversion strategies fell sharply in early August and recovered in about 10 days: −5% for PCA, −10% for ETF, at 2+2 leverage. Technology and consumer discretionary moved more than financials, consistent with forced unwinding [Verified]. See the failure gallery.
  • Correlation spikes. In summer 2007 the top 15 eigenvectors explained more variance (A&L) [Verified]; when one factor dominates, residuals carry market risk.
  • News residuals drift against the position.
  • Cost overrun. In Lab 09, 10 bps per dollar instead of 5 turns net Sharpe 1.40 into −0.10.
