docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Fifteen PCs, sixty days, 1.25 in, a half out." → The A&L recipe.
  • "We turn the book fifty times a year; execution is the strategy." → Break-even sits near 10 bps.
  • "Don't fade earnings residuals." → News residuals drift.
  • "The first eigenvector ate half the variance that week." → Correlation spike; residuals carry market risk.
  • "We're the other side of the redemption flow." → Liquidity provision.
  • "Our residual alpha is mostly crossed against the momentum book." → Internal netting saves the spread.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: a gross Sharpe of 3 means a great strategy. Reality: at 57× turnover, 10 bps per dollar erases it.
  • Myth: more factors give cleaner residuals. Reality: they overfit short windows (Lab 09).
  • Myth: every residual reverts. Reality: news-driven residuals drift.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: eigenportfolios, the OU fit and the s-score

Factors. With standardized returns \(Y\), take the top eigenvectors \(v_j\) of the correlation matrix. Eigenportfolio \(j\) holds \(Q_{ij} = v_{ij}/\sigma_i\), so \(F_{jt} = \sum_i Q_{ij} R_{it}\). Residuals come from

\[ R_{it} = \beta_{i0} + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_{ij} F_{jt} + \epsilon_{it} . \]

OU fit. The cumulative residual \(X_i(t) = \sum_{s \le t} \epsilon_{is}\) follows \(dX = \kappa(m - X)\,dt + \sigma\,dW\). Daily, \(X_{t+1} = a + b X_t + \zeta\) with \(b = e^{-\kappa/252}\) and \(a = m(1-b)\), so

\[ \kappa = -252 \ln b, \qquad m = \frac{a}{1-b}, \qquad \sigma_{eq} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\kappa}} = \sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\zeta)}{1-b^2}}, \qquad s = \frac{X - m}{\sigma_{eq}} . \]

A&L require \(\kappa > 252/30 \approx 8.4\). Because the regression has an intercept, the residuals sum to zero over the window, so \(X_{60} = 0\) and \(s = -m/\sigma_{eq}\): a stock is cheap when its fitted equilibrium sits above today's level. A&L (and Lab 09) subtract the cross-sectional mean of \(m\). With a residual drift \(\alpha\), they define \(s_{mod} = s - \alpha/(\kappa\,\sigma_{eq})\) and found it changed little.

Break-even cost. Gross return \(g\) per year and dollars traded \(T\) per dollar of capital give break-even cost \(c^* \approx g/T\). Lab 09: \(10.7\% / 107 \approx 10\) bps.

docs.title: Intraday patterns and seasonality
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Activity is U-shaped: volume and volatility peak at the open and close; spreads are widest at the open. The closing auction alone prints roughly 5–10% of volume (2025) [Reported].
  • Market intraday momentum: the day's return to 3:30 p.m. predicts the last half-hour in 60+ futures markets (1974–2020), tied to dealers' and leveraged ETFs' gamma hedging.
  • Returns split into night and day: momentum and reversal profits accrue overnight, other strategies' intraday ("tug of war", Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019).
  • Calendar effects (turn of month, same-month seasonality, pre-FOMC drift) are small, and some have faded.
  • Firms mostly monetize these patterns as execution timing and ML features, not standalone bets.

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
Overnight news is priced at the open; midday is quiet; at the close, index funds, option hedgers and everyone benchmarked to the close trade. These flows are predictable in timing, sometimes in direction, and whoever takes the other side earns a small premium.

timeline
    title A US equity trading day, Eastern time
    Before the open : Overnight news : Thin pre-market trading
    Open auction : Widest spreads : Highest volatility
    Midday : Volume trough : Tightest continuous spreads
    Afternoon : Macro releases and FOMC days
    Last half-hour : Gamma and leveraged-ETF hedging
    Closing auction : Index and fund flows : Official close for NAVs

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Clustering. Discretionary traders bunch to cut costs and informed traders follow: U-shapes (Admati & Pfleiderer 1988) [Verified].
  • Hedging demand. A dealer short gamma must buy after rises and sell after falls, pushing prices the same way into the close [Verified].
  • Periodic institutions. Funds trade at the same time daily, so half-hour returns repeat on later days (Heston, Korajczyk & Sadka 2010) [Verified].
  • Clienteles and cash. Different investors dominate night and day [Verified]; month-end payment needs move prices (Etula et al. 2020) [Verified].

Illustrative E-mini S&P 500 trade ($50 per index point, 0.25-point tick):

Step Value Prior close → 15:30 5,000.00 → 5,060.00: +1.20% Base forecast, β = 0.04 +0.048% = 2.4 points Dealers estimated short gamma: scale × 1.5 +0.072% = 3.6 points Position Buy 100 contracts = 100 × $50 × 5,060 = $25.3M Expected gain 3.6 × $50 × 100 = $18,000 Costs: 1 tick round trip ($1,250) + fees ~$4 per contract round trip ($400) −$1,650 Net expected $16,350

Last-half-hour volatility of ~0.25% ($63,000) gives one day a mean-to-risk ratio near 0.26: the edge needs hundreds of days and a stable regime.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Time-of-day normalization and calendar features: D2. Trading the close and reading imbalances: E5, M3. Volume curves: VWAP, TWAP and POV. Calendar snooping and timestamps: V3, V4. Gamma regimes: F6.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def intraday_momentum_forecast(bars, prev_close, dealer_gamma, beta=0.04, boost=0.5):
    """bars: 1-minute futures bars for today, indexed by Eastern time, column 'close'.
    dealer_gamma: estimated net dealer gamma ($ per 1% move); negative = short gamma.
    Returns the predicted 15:30-16:00 return (decimal)."""
    px_1530 = bars.loc[bars.index.time <= pd.Timestamp("15:30").time(), "close"].iloc[-1]
    r_rest = px_1530 / prev_close - 1                 # prior 16:00 close -> 15:30
    scale = 1 + boost * (dealer_gamma < 0)            # hedgers chase moves when short gamma
    return beta * scale * r_rest

def contracts(pred, price, multiplier=50, risk_notional=25e6, min_edge=1.5e-4):
    if abs(pred) < min_edge:                          # skip below ~1.5 bps: costs dominate
        return 0
    return int(np.sign(pred) * risk_notional / (price * multiplier))
    # exit at 16:00 via trade-at-settlement (futures) or market-on-close (ETF)

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Clocks. Store Eastern time; handle daylight saving and 13:00 half-day closes.
  • Open and close prices. Use auction prints, not the first or last trade (order types and auctions).
  • Events and gamma. Model FOMC days, expiries and month-ends separately; open-interest guesses at dealer positioning are noisy [Lore].
  • Execution. MOC entry stops at 15:50 (NYSE) and 15:55 (Nasdaq) [Verified]; later trades must offset the imbalance.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Spreads: minute-by-minute NYSE spreads trace a reverse J, high at the open (McInish & Wood 1992) [Verified].
  • Periodicity: half-hour returns continue at daily multiples for 40+ days; timing saves about the effective spread (Heston et al. 2010) [Verified].
  • Intraday momentum: SPY 1993–2013, stronger on volatile and macro-news days (Gao, Han, Li & Zhou 2018) [Verified], R² about 1–2% [Reported]; in 60+ futures, 1974–2020, it reverts over later days and tracks gamma hedging (Baltussen et al. 2021) [Verified].
  • Night and day: reversal and momentum profits accrue overnight, others intraday (Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019) [Verified].
  • Seasonality: same-calendar-month outperformance repeats for up to 20 years, 1963–2002 (Heston & Sadka 2008) [Reported].
  • FOMC: +49 bps in the 24 hours before announcements, 1994–2011 (Lucca & Moench 2015) [Reported]; weaker since January 2016 (Kurov, Wolfe & Gilbert 2021) [Reported].
  • Expiry: optionable stocks cluster at strike prices on expiration days (Ni, Pearson & Poteshman 2005) [Reported].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: The close is crowded: auction share rose from ~3% of dollar volume in 2010 to a record ~9.4% of notional in Q2 2024 [Reported]. Zero-day options reached ~66% of SPX volume in July 2026 [Reported], moving dealer gamma inside the day. Planned 23-hour weekday trading (target launch December 6, 2026) [Reported] will blur the night-and-day split.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Regime flips. Long-gamma dealers dampen moves; mislabel the regime and the bet reverses [Estimate].
  • Broken opens (August 24, 2015). 1,278 limit-up/limit-down halts (1,058 in 327 ETPs) and many late NYSE openings made "open" prices meaningless that day [Verified].
  • Data snooping. Calendar effects are easy to mine and hard to kill (V4); several faded after publication.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: gamma-driven hedge flow and the intraday momentum regression

A dealer with net gamma \(\Gamma_D\) (shares per $1) who stays delta-hedged trades

\[ dq = -\Gamma_D \, dS , \]

so a short-gamma dealer buys after rises. Regression:

\[ r_{last,t} = \alpha + \beta\, r_{rest,t} + \gamma\, r_{rest,t}\,\mathbf 1\{\Gamma_{D,t} < 0\} + \varepsilon_t , \qquad \gamma > 0 . \]

Periodicity (Heston–Korajczyk–Sadka): for half-hour slot \(k\), \(\operatorname{corr}(r_{t,k}, r_{t-d,k}) > 0\) at daily lags \(d\) up to about 40.

docs.title: ML-driven short-horizon alpha
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Large teams forecast residual returns 5 minutes to 1 day ahead for thousands of stocks from hundreds to thousands of features, with boosted trees and neural nets; a cost-aware optimizer turns forecasts into trades.
  • Each prediction barely beats a coin flip (rank IC 0.01–0.05). Breadth makes the money; costs take most of it, so they belong in the objective.
  • The hard parts are labels, purged validation, retraining and resisting overfitting, more than model choice.
  • Academic ML stat arb on the S&P 500 earned over 0.45% a day before costs (1992–2015), shrinking over time. Industry runs on large GPU clusters.
  • Capacity is capped by market impact. Failures come from regime breaks, crowded unwinds (August 2007) and backtests that learned noise.

Level: Deep dive · Read time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family stat arb Edge source informational · liquidity provision Holding period Minutes to 1–2 days; forecast half-lives of 30 minutes to a day Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Institutions whose executions leave footprints, late reactors to sector moves, impatient traders paying for immediacy: on their longer horizons a few bps of slippage is small Universe & instruments 2,000–5,000 liquid US stocks; ETFs and futures as hedges and features Data required Years of tick and depth-of-book history, cross-asset prices, corporate events, borrow Core algorithms used F2 Tree ensembles · F3 Neural nets and sequence models · F5 Alpha combination and ensembling · V1 Time-series cross-validation · P5 Transaction cost and impact models · D2 Feature engineering Infra intensity High: GPU and CPU research clusters, intraday feature pipelines, fast in-house execution Capacity (rough $ range) $200M–$2B GMV per book [Estimate] (participation capped at ~1–3% of ADV across ~3,000 names; edges of 2–5 bps per trade; square-root impact) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Academic daily ML stat arb, S&P 500: >0.45% a day before costs, 1992–2015, shrinking later [Reported]; an LSTM variant, same period: Sharpe 5.8 gross [Reported]. Practitioner net: 2–6 for small intraday books, 1–2 at scale [Lore] Turnover 50–200% of GMV a day [Estimate] Main risks / failure modes Overfitting, leakage, regime breaks, crowded deleveraging, cost-model error, outages Crowding risk High: similar features on the same data lead to correlated de-risking Firm types that run it Quant hedge funds, multi-manager quant pods, proprietary trading firms Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: Instead of one theory ("losers bounce back"), a model learns from thousands of weak regularities which stocks will beat their peers over the next hour. Like credit scoring: millions of decisions, each barely better than chance, profitable in aggregate, with trading costs as loss given default.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Predictable flows. Large orders are sliced over hours, so their pressure persists and shows in volume and imbalance (execution algorithms).
  • Liquidity provision. Temporary price moves revert, paying whoever absorbs them (short-term reversal).
  • Slow diffusion. News spreads across related stocks with lags: LASSO on the whole cross-section of 1-minute returns found sparse, short-lived, news-linked predictors (Chinco, Clark-Joseph & Ye 2019) [Verified].
  • Breadth. Information ratio ≈ IC × √(independent bets), so a tiny IC across thousands of names compounds.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Every 1–5 minutes, compute features: residual returns at many lags, volume and volatility versus time-of-day norms, book imbalance, futures and sector-ETF moves, events.
  2. Targets: forward residual returns at several horizons (5, 30, 60 minutes, to close, next day), ranked or clipped.
  3. Train GBDT, MLP and ridge models on rolling windows with purged validation.
  4. Combine models and horizons into one expected-return curve per stock.
  5. The optimizer trades toward a target net of impact, risk and borrow (trading toward the aim).
  6. Execute with in-house algos; attribute P&L back to signals.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Forecasts are z-scored; expected residual return = IC × σ × z, and the top quintile averages z ≈ 1.4.

30-minute horizon 1-day horizon Rank IC 0.03 0.02 Cross-sectional σ of residual return 0.40% 1.50% Expected return per leg: IC × σ × 1.4 1.7 bps 4.2 bps Round-trip cost, aggressive (2 × (1.5 spread + 1.0 impact + 0.2 fees)) 5.4 bps 5.4 bps Round-trip cost, passive fills and crossing 2.5 bps 2.5 bps Net per leg, best case −0.8 bps +1.7 bps

The faster forecast is more accurate but loses alone; it earns its keep by timing slower forecasts' trades. A $500M GMV book at 100% daily turnover nets $500M × 1.7 bps = $85,000 a day, $21.4M a year (4.3%). At ~4% volatility, Sharpe ≈ 1.1 [Estimate].

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Features: D2, M3. Models: F2, F3, F1. Blending: F5. Validation: V1, V4. Costs: P5. Decay: L2.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def make_target(resid_index, h):
    """resid_index: cumulative residual-return index (bars x stocks) after removing
    market and sector moves. Target: forward h-bar residual return, ranked per bar."""
    fwd = resid_index.shift(-h) / resid_index - 1
    return fwd.rank(axis=1, pct=True) - 0.5            # ranks tame fat tails

def walk_forward(X, y, day, fit, train_days=250, test_days=20, embargo_days=1):
    """Purged walk-forward: labels look h bars ahead, so drop training days whose
    labels could overlap the test block (an embargo of whole days)."""
    days, preds = np.unique(day), []
    for s in range(train_days, len(days) - test_days + 1, test_days):
        tr = np.isin(day, days[s - train_days:s - embargo_days])
        te = np.isin(day, days[s:s + test_days])
        model = fit(X[tr], y[tr])                      # e.g. LightGBM plus an MLP seed ensemble
        preds.append(pd.Series(model.predict(X[te]), index=np.flatnonzero(te)))
    return pd.concat(preds)

def cost_gated_trades(alpha_bps, cost_bps, w_now, w_target):
    """Move toward the target only where expected alpha beats the round-trip cost."""
    worth_it = alpha_bps.abs() > 2 * cost_bps          # round trip ~ 2 x one-way cost
    return (w_target - w_now).where(worth_it, 0.0)

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Labels. Overlapping forward returns make neighbouring rows near-duplicates: purge, embargo, weight by uniqueness (López de Prado 2018).
  • Normalization. Scale volume and volatility by time-of-day norms (intraday patterns); residualize returns first.
  • Retraining and costs. Daily refits on rolling 1–3 years [Lore]; penalize turnover in the optimizer, or train on net-of-cost targets.
  • Teams. Signal researchers feed a combination team, then the optimizer and execution [Lore].
  • Compute. XTX Markets reports over 25,000 GPUs for research; Hudson River Trading calls ML on GPU clusters central to its research and signed a multi-year cloud deal for NVIDIA Vera Rubin systems in 2026 [Verified]. Live Sharpe and capacity are undisclosed.

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative $1B GMV book, % of GMV a year:

Line % Gross alpha capture +14.0 Passive fills and rebates +1.0 Spread paid −4.5 Market impact −3.5 Fees and clearing −0.8 Borrow and financing −0.7 Compute and data (fixed) −0.5 Net +5.0

At 3% volatility, net Sharpe ≈ 1.7 [Estimate]. Costs consume about two-thirds of gross alpha, so a 10% cost-model error moves net P&L by about 20%.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Monthly ML: in Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020), trees and neural nets more than doubled the monthly out-of-sample R² of a three-characteristic linear model; details in F2 [Verified].
  • Daily ML stat arb: Krauss, Do & Huck (2017): a DNN, boosted-tree and random-forest ensemble on lagged S&P 500 returns earned >0.45% a day before costs, 1992–2015, declining in later years [Reported]. Fischer & Krauss (2018): LSTM, 0.46% a day and Sharpe 5.8 before costs [Reported].
  • Minute-level: that LASSO improved out-of-sample fit and forecast-implied Sharpe ratios (Chinco et al. 2019) [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Impact grows with the square root of size (P5) while edges are a few bps, so doubling capital cuts net bps sharply. Shared data and features make forecasts correlate across firms; ICs decay within months without retraining [Lore].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Crowded unwind (August 2007). A simple contrarian strategy lost sharply over a few days, consistent with forced liquidation of similar quant books (Khandani & Lo 2011) [Reported].
  • Regime break (2020). New pandemic-era drivers broke relationships learned on calmer data; Man FRM called 2020 a "blow to the head" for factor-based quant equity funds, and said even ML approaches felt "somewhat impotent" [Reported].
  • Overfitting and leakage. Thousands of settings guarantee an in-sample winner (V4); one feature using not-yet-public data makes it perfect (V3).

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: fundamental law, cost hurdle, purging

Expected residual return given a z-scored forecast, and the fundamental law:

\[ E[r_i \mid z_i] = IC \cdot \sigma \cdot z_i, \qquad IR \approx IC \cdot \sqrt{N_{\text{eff}}} . \]

Trade only when the edge clears the round trip, with square-root impact:

\[ |E[r_i]| > 2\left(\tfrac{s_i}{2} + f_i + Y\sigma_i\sqrt{q_i/V_i}\right) . \]

Purging drops training rows whose label window \([t_j, t_j + h]\) overlaps the test block.

docs.title: Pairs trading and cointegration
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Buy the laggard, short the leader of two stocks whose prices move together, and bet the gap closes: the two-stock case of statistical arbitrage, paid for absorbing temporary price pressure.
  • Pairs are chosen by distance (Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst 2006) or by cointegration tests (Engle–Granger, Johansen). GGR found up to 11% a year before costs over 1962–2002, with top-20 returns falling from 118 to 38 bps a month after 1988 [Verified].
  • After realistic costs the simple version has been largely unprofitable since 2002 [Verified].
  • Selection is the hard part: of the same-sector pairs passing a 5% cointegration test, about 94% are false; Benjamini–Hochberg keeps none (Lab 08, synthetic lab result).
  • A broken relationship costs about a period's profit. Stops are insurance, not alpha.

Level: Core · Read time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family stat arb Edge source liquidity provision · behavioral Holding period days to weeks (Lab 08: 16–22 days per round trip) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Investors trading one stock for reasons unrelated to its twin (a liquidation, an index deletion, a block sale) who want execution, not relative value. When the gap is news, the counterparty is informed and the pairs trader pays. Universe & instruments liquid same-sub-industry US stocks; share classes, dual listings; stock vs sector ETF Data required total-return prices, corporate actions, industry codes, borrow, earnings and M&A calendars Core algorithms used D3 Signal transforms · V4 Overfitting and multiple testing · F6 Regime detection · P5 Transaction cost and impact models Infra intensity low: overnight batch; intraday pairs need simultaneous leg execution Capacity (rough $ range) $50M–$500M gross per firm [Estimate] (tens of pairs, legs near 1% of ADV in $100M–$1B ADV names); Lab 08 net Sharpe 0.61 at $1M per leg, −0.93 at $16M (synthetic) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) GGR top 20, one-day wait, before costs: ≈ 2.0 over 1962–2002, ≈ 1.3 after 1988 (academic backtest) [Estimate] (from their tables); after costs 30–38 bps a month, largely gone after 2002 [Verified]; standalone practitioner net 0–1 [Lore] Turnover committed capital traded ~7× a year (Lab 08) Main risks / failure modes false discoveries, breaks, short squeezes, leg risk, crowded unwinds Crowding risk medium to high: public screens pick the same pairs Firm types that run it historically bank proprietary desks (Morgan Stanley, 1980s) [Reported]; today mostly inside multi-name stat-arb books [Lore] Lab Lab 08

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
Two regional banks share a deposit base and a regulator. A large holder dumps one; it falls 4% while its twin is flat, with no news. Buy the laggard, short the leader in a ratio that cancels their shared driver, and wait.

The key word is tethered. In Murray's image of a drunk walking her dog, each wanders, but the leash stops them drifting apart. Correlated daily returns are not a leash: two stocks can correlate at 0.9 and diverge forever. Cointegration means a weighted difference of the log prices, the spread, is stationary and keeps returning to its mean (mean reversion).

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
1. Liquidity provision. Uninformed flow pushes one of two close substitutes away from the law of one price; the pairs trader is paid as the pressure fades. GGR tie profits to temporary mispricing and a latent common factor [Verified].
  2. Limits to arbitrage. Even Royal Dutch and Shell, twins with pooled cash flows, drifted with their home markets for years (Froot & Dabora 1999) [Verified]. Persistence is why the trade pays and why it hurts.
  3. Arbitrage risk. Do & Faff (2010) attribute much of the decline to rising fundamental, noise-trader and synchronization risk, not only efficiency [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Formation (GGR: 12 months). Rank pairs by the sum of squared differences (SSD) of normalized prices, or test same-industry pairs for cointegration.
  2. Hedge ratio. Regress log P_A on log P_B: spread = log P_A − α − β log P_B (hedge ratio β). Distance pairs hold $1 long, $1 short.
  3. Signal. In the trading window (GGR: 6 months), z-score the spread using formation mean and standard deviation.
  4. Rules (Lab 08). Enter at |z| > 2, exit at |z| < 0.5, stop at |z| > 4 and sit out the period. GGR close when prices cross.
  5. Other exits: a time stop at 2–3 half-lives, or news [Lore].

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Legs of $1M; formation spread standard deviation 2.5%; hedge ratio 1.

Step Calculation P&L Entry: A lags B by 5.5% z = −5.5 / 2.5 = −2.2 → buy $1M A, short $1M B Exit 12 days later at a 1.0% gap z = −0.4 +$45,000 Trading costs 4 trades × $1M × 15 bps (Lab 08's cost per $ traded) −$6,000 Borrow on the short $1M × 0.35% × 12/252 −$167 Winning trade, net +$38,833 Losing trade: gap runs to 10% stop at z = −4: −4.5% of a leg, plus costs −$51,000

Break-even win rate = 51,000 / (38,833 + 51,000) ≈ 57%. For a spread with no leash (a random walk), the chance of reaching z = −0.5 before z = −4, starting from −2.2, is (4 − 2.2) / (4 − 0.5) ≈ 51% [Estimate] (gambler's-ruin odds). A false pair is a coin flip that pays less than it costs.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Cards: z-score (D3), OLS or minimum-variance hedge ratio (F1, M7), multiple testing (V4), breaks (F6), costs (P5).

# Mirrors Lab 08's core (labs/08-pairs-cointegration/lab.py). Prices are days x stocks.
def ssd_distance(norm_prices):                     # GGR distance; each column starts at 1
    sq = (norm_prices ** 2).sum(axis=0)
    ssd = sq[:, None] + sq[None, :] - 2.0 * norm_prices.T @ norm_prices
    np.fill_diagonal(ssd, np.inf)
    return ssd                                     # trade the 20 smallest entries

def hedge_ratio(log_a, log_b):                     # Engle-Granger step 1: OLS of A on B
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(log_b), log_b])
    (alpha, beta), *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, log_a, rcond=None)
    return beta, alpha, log_a - alpha - beta * log_b   # step 2: unit-root test on this spread

def zscore_signals(z, entry=2.0, exit=0.5, stop=4.0):  # +1 long spread (long A), -1 short, 0 flat
    pos, state, stopped = np.zeros(len(z), int), 0, False
    for t, zt in enumerate(z):                     # z uses formation mean and sd
        if state == 0 and not stopped and entry < abs(zt) < stop:
            state = -1 if zt > 0 else 1            # bet on convergence
        elif state != 0 and abs(zt) >= stop:
            state, stopped = 0, True               # stop-loss: sit out the rest of the period
        elif (state == 1 and zt > -exit) or (state == -1 and zt < exit):
            state = 0                              # converged: take profit
        pos[t] = state
    pos[-1] = 0                                    # flat at period end
    return pos

Lab 08 plants 8 cointegrated pairs (4 later break) among 200 synthetic stocks and compares five selection methods.

A planted pair (half-life 4.9 days). Notice the clean convergence trades, then the break (red line): the spread runs through the stop at |z| = 4 and the pair is never selected again. Synthetic data.

Left: net P&L by method; only the oracle (true pairs) is clearly profitable. Right: pairs passing Engle–Granger at p < 0.05 each period, mostly false. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab result (seed 7): each period 48.8 of 1,719 same-sector pairs pass p < 0.05, only 3.1 of them real. Net Sharpe is 0.61 (distance) and 0.56 (cointegration top 20), against 2.68 for the oracle. Seed 7 is lucky: across 8 seeds the median net Sharpe is about −0.1 and −0.4, while the oracle ranges from +1.0 to +2.7. Caveat: the toy has no natural cointegration, so distance looks worse than in GGR's data.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Candidate set. Testing all 19,900 pairs guarantees false positives; restrict by economics (sub-industry, share classes, supply chains). SSD-then-test double-dips: Lab 08's SSD top 100 pass at 29%, yet about 3 are real.
  • Power. A year of daily data detects only half of Lab 08's true pairs.
  • Hedge ratio. OLS of A on B is not the inverse of B on A; total least squares or Johansen are symmetric. Desks update betas with rolling or Kalman-filter estimates (Elliott, van der Hoek & Malcolm 2005; Chan 2013) [Verified].
  • Thresholds. Fit an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process; set entry from costs and exit after 2–3 half-lives [Lore]. Flatten before earnings; drop pairs with pending M&A.
  • Execution. Trade both legs together; borrow and recalls bind on the short leg (shorting and financing).

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• GGR (2006). Distance pairs, 1962–2002: top 20 earned 1.44% a month fully invested (0.81% on committed capital), 0.90% when trading a day late. The gap implies ~162 bps round-trip cost per pair, leaving 113–225 bps net per six months. A 1999–2002 holdout earned 10.4% a year at 3.8% volatility. After 1988, returns fell from 118 to 38 bps a month; risk-adjusted, from 67 to 42 [Verified].
  • Do & Faff (2010). Decline continued to 2009, but pairs did well in prolonged turbulence, such as 2007–09 [Verified].
  • Do & Faff (2012). Net of commissions, impact and short fees: about 30 bps a month risk-adjusted, largely unprofitable after 2002 [Verified].
  • Rad, Low & Faff (2016). 1962–2014: distance, cointegration and copula earned 91, 85 and 43 bps a month before costs, 38, 33 and 5 after; opportunities thinned after 2009 [Verified].

$ per leg $0.25M $1M $4M $16M Distance 0.86 0.61 0.09 −0.93 Cointegration, top 20 0.75 0.56 0.17 −0.60

The toy trades each leg in one day against $63M of ADV; real desks work orders in larger names, so capacity is higher [Estimate], but capped by the few good pairs and the smaller leg's liquidity.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• The pair never existed (most screened pairs; see above).
  • The relationship breaks. Lab 08's four breaks cost −2.2%, −4.0%, −0.5% and −7.2% of a leg, against +6.5% for an intact pair-period; without the stop, −11.3%, +20.8%, −0.4% and −7.2% (synthetic lab result). The stop capped the worst loss and cut a winner.
  • Crowded unwind, August 2007. A model contrarian strategy lost 6.85% over 7–9 August, then regained 5.92% on 10 August (Khandani & Lo) [Verified]; see the failure gallery.
  • Squeeze, October 2008. After Porsche's 26 October disclosure, VW ordinaries went from €211 to above €1,005 on 28 October; shorts of the "overvalued" ordinaries lost an estimated €20B+ (Allen et al. 2021) [Reported].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: rank all pairs by distance. Practice: economically linked candidates, multiple-testing control, out-of-sample survival [Lore].
  • Textbook: static OLS beta. Practice: Kalman or rolling betas (Elliott et al. 2005; Chan 2013) [Verified].
  • Textbook: fixed 2-sigma entry. Practice: half-life- and cost-based thresholds, time stops [Lore].
  • Textbook: a standalone book. Practice: one input to a factor-neutral residual book (stat-arb overview) [Lore].

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text:
• Baskets: Johansen handles several stocks; cointegrated triplets earned less than pairs (Do & Faff 2016) [Verified].
  • Stock vs ETF: the single-partner form of factor-residual mean reversion.
  • Copulas: model the joint distribution, not a linear spread (Rad et al. 2016).
  • Contractual leashes: share classes, dual listings, ETF and index arbitrage, merger arbitrage (event-driven).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Half-life is eight days; if it hasn't come in by week three, we're out." → A time stop.
  • "It passed at 1%, but so did 40 others out of 2,000." → Multiple testing.
  • "The beta went from 0.9 to 1.3 after the acquisition." → A structural break.
  • "It stopped out at four sigma and came back the next week." → Stops are insurance; insurance costs premium.
  • "Distance pairs are half a reversal factor." → GGR's pre-1989 pairs loaded on short-term reversal, yet earned alpha beyond it [Verified].

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: high correlation makes a good pair. Reality: correlated returns do not tie prices together.
  • Myth: passing a 5% test proves the relationship. Reality: 1,719 tests yield dozens of chance passes.
  • Myth: market neutral means safe. Reality: breaks, squeezes and crowding.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: How many candidate pairs do you test, and how are they chosen?
  • Informed: How do you correct for multiple testing, and how many pairs survive out of sample?
  • Informed: OLS, total least squares or Kalman for the hedge ratio?
  • Sharp: What share of losses come from pairs that broke versus pairs that never were?
  • Sharp: How correlated is pairs P&L with the reversal factor?
  • Sharp: 🔒 Which pair families still pay after costs, and at what size?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: cointegration tests, the OU spread, and false discoveries

Cointegration. Log prices \(p_A, p_B\) are each I(1). They are cointegrated if some \(\beta\) makes \(s_t = p_{A,t} - \alpha - \beta\, p_{B,t}\) stationary. Engle–Granger: estimate \(\alpha, \beta\) by OLS, then run an ADF regression

\[ \Delta s_t = \gamma\, s_{t-1} + \sum_i \phi_i\, \Delta s_{t-i} + e_t \]

and reject a unit root if \(\gamma\) is significantly negative; critical values are more negative than standard ADF tables because \(\beta\) was fitted. Johansen tests the rank of \(\Pi\) in \(\Delta Y_t = \Pi Y_{t-1} + \sum_i \Gamma_i \Delta Y_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t\) (the number of cointegrating vectors).

OU spread. \(ds = \theta(\mu - s)\,dt + \sigma\,dW\); as a daily AR(1), \(s_{t+1} = a + b\,s_t + \zeta\) with \(b = e^{-\theta}\):

\[ \text{half-life} = -\frac{\ln 2}{\ln b}, \qquad \sigma_{eq} = \sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\zeta)}{1-b^2}} . \]

A 10-day half-life gives \(b \approx 0.933\): hard to tell from 1 with a year of data.

False discoveries. Benjamini–Hochberg sorts p-values \(p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}\) and rejects the \(k\) smallest, with \(k\) the largest index satisfying

\[ p_{(k)} \le \frac{k}{m}\, q . \]

At \(m = 1{,}719\), \(q = 0.05\), any discovery needs a p-value below \(2.9 \times 10^{-5}\).

docs.title: Short-term cross-sectional reversal
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Last week's losers beat last week's winners next week (Lehmann 1990; Jegadeesh 1990; Lo & MacKinlay 1990).
  • It is a fee for absorbing temporary price pressure; expected returns rise with the VIX (Nagel 2012).
  • Highest gross Sharpe of the classic anomalies, thinnest net: 50–100× annual turnover means costs decide everything.
  • The plain version has decayed to about zero (Sharpe 0.92 in 1963–1991, 0.01 in 2010–2026; −18% in 2025). It survives residualized, news-filtered and inside multi-signal books.
  • It fails when liquidity providers all need liquidity at once: August 2007, March 2020.

Level: Core · Read time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family stat arb Edge source liquidity provision · behavioral Holding period 1 day to 1 month (classically 1 week) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Impatient traders (large institutional orders, redemptions, margin calls, chasers of last week's winners) who pay a temporary concession because finishing now matters more than a few bps Universe & instruments 500–3,000 liquid US stocks, cash or swaps; ETF and futures hedges Data required Point-in-time returns, volume, spreads; risk model; news flags; borrow Core algorithms used D3 Signal transforms · P1 Risk models · P5 Transaction cost and impact models · P6 Multi-period optimization and trading toward the aim Infra intensity Moderate: daily or intraday rebalancing; execution matters more than latency Capacity (rough $ range) Break-even $9B US, $13B global (1998–2011 cost data, AQR-affiliated authors) [Verified]; profitable standalone books $100M–$1B [Estimate] (profit peaks near 4/9 of break-even; see Go deeper) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) French 1-month reversal factor, gross: 0.92 (1963–1991), 0.15 (1992–2026), 0.01 (2010–2026) [Verified] (our computation); standalone net ≤ 0 [Estimate]; residual versions about 2× in backtests [Verified] Turnover 50–100× gross a year, weekly rebalancing (Lab 10: 90×) [Estimate] Main risks / failure modes Cost-model error, news moves, liquidity crises, momentum regimes Crowding risk High: nearly every stat-arb book holds some version Firm types that run it Stat-arb funds, pods, principal desks; Morgan Stanley in the 1980s (history) [Reported] Lab Lab 10

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A fund dumps 3% of a mid-cap's float; the price falls 4% on no news and drifts back next week. The buyer was a one-week wholesaler. Short-term reversal does this across 1,000 names, long losers and short winners, earning a few bps per trade while replacing most of the book weekly.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Liquidity provision. Market makers are paid by the reversal of non-informational selling (Campbell, Grossman & Wang 1993) [Reported]; reversal returns proxy that payment and are predictable with the VIX (Nagel 2012) [Verified]. Intra-industry reversals follow order imbalances and strengthen after market declines (Hameed & Mian 2015) [Verified].
  • Overreaction. Lehmann (1990) read weekly reversals as fads [Verified]; Da, Liu & Schaumburg (2014) tie the short side to sentiment plus short-sale constraints [Verified].
  • Noise. Bid-ask bounce and cross-stock lead-lag (Lo & MacKinlay 1990) [Verified] inflate backtests but cannot be harvested.

The edge exists only where the move carried no information.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Universe: liquid names, minus those with earnings or major news.
  2. Signal: minus the past 5-day market-relative return (Lab 10), or better the residual return (P1).
  3. Transform (D3): winsorize, z-score within industry.
  4. Portfolio: cost-aware optimizer (P5) with no-trade buffers (P6), factor-neutral.
  5. Execute through the day and at the close (E2, E5); hold about a week.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: $500M gross, 400 names, $100M ADV and 2% daily volatility each, square-root market impact coefficient 0.5.

Step Calculation Per week Gross alpha, naive rebalance $500M × 20 bps +$1.00M Traded 1.5 × $500M (about $1.9M per name) $750M Cost per $ traded 2.5 bps half-spread + 0.5 × 200 bps × √(1.9/100) 16.3 bps Trading cost $750M × 16.3 bps −$1.22M Net, naive −$0.22M Buffered: keep 70% of alpha 0.7 × $1.00M +$0.70M Trade 0.8×, patiently, at 9 bps $400M × 9 bps −$0.36M Net, buffered +$0.34M

That is $17.7M a year; with weekly volatility of $2.5M (0.5% of gross), Sharpe ≈ 0.34 / 2.5 × √52 ≈ 0.98. Only the trading changed.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Signals are scored by information coefficient (D4); costs follow the square-root law (P5).

# Mirrors the CORE ALGORITHM of Lab 10 (labs/10-reversal-momentum-costs/lab.py).
# Weights are fractions of the gross book; signals use returns known at the close of day t.
def reversal_signal(returns, lookback=5):
    """Positive score = past-week loser vs the equal-weighted market = BUY (Lo-MacKinlay)."""
    past = returns.rolling(lookback).sum()
    return -past.sub(past.mean(axis=1), axis=0)

def residual_reversal_signal(resid_returns, lookback=5):
    """Practitioner variant, not in the lab: the same rule on factor-model residuals (P1),
    so the book stops betting against industry and style moves."""
    past = resid_returns.rolling(lookback).sum()
    return -past.sub(past.mean(axis=1), axis=0).div(past.std(axis=1), axis=0)

def apply_costs(weights, returns, book_usd, spread_bps, adv_usd, daily_vol,
                impact_coef=0.5, borrow_bps_per_year=35.0):
    traded = weights.diff().abs()                       # fraction of the book traded at t
    cost_rate = spread_bps / 2e4 + impact_coef * daily_vol * np.sqrt(traded * book_usd / adv_usd)
    trading_cost = (traded * cost_rate).sum(axis=1)     # half-spread + square-root impact
    borrow = weights.shift(1).clip(upper=0).abs().sum(axis=1) * borrow_bps_per_year / 1e4 / 252
    gross = (weights.shift(1) * returns).sum(axis=1)    # weights set at t-1 earn day t
    return gross - trading_cost - borrow                # the lab returns every column

Left panel: reversal's gross P&L (dashed) climbs while net (solid) falls, at $100M. Synthetic data.

Reversal (blue) turns negative above 12.7 bps per dollar traded, and between a $10M and a $30M book. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab result: the weekly decile book's Sharpe is 2.37 gross and −1.43 net, with 90× turnover and costs of 19.5% of the book a year; daily rebalancing gives 3.84 gross, −5.30 net. The planted IC of 0.03 is clean, stationary and uncontested; the real frictionless daily factor has managed 0.26–0.67 gross since 2010 [Verified].

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Residualize. Residual reversal doubles the risk-adjusted return and survives costs in post-1990 large caps (Blitz et al. 2013) [Verified]. The plain version has "vanished entirely in most regions"; hedging out industry and factor short-term momentum revives it (Blitz, van der Grient & Honarvar 2023) [Verified].
  • Filter informed moves. Removing moves explained by analyst revisions quadruples the risk-adjusted return (Da et al. 2014) [Verified]. High-turnover stocks show short-term momentum; reversal lives in low-turnover ones (Medhat & Schmeling 2022) [Verified].
  • Universe and construction. Large caps plus lower turnover give 30–50 bps a week net (de Groot, Huij & Zhou 2012) [Verified]; in illiquid names profits trail likely costs (Avramov, Chordia & Goyal 2006) [Verified].
  • Combine. Rarely run alone: one input to an alpha combination [Lore], as Blitz et al. (2023) recommend [Verified].

docs.text:
Gross Sharpe ratios of the Fama-French reversal factors, our computation [Verified]:

Period 1-month reversal, monthly 20-day reversal, rebalanced daily 1963–1989 1.05 3.62 1990–1999 0.16 4.57 2000–2009 0.25 0.90 2010–2019 0.42 0.67 2020–2026-09 −0.39 0.26

The daily column is frictionless and, before 2001's decimal ticks, partly bid-ask bounce. Khandani & Lo's daily contrarian rule fell from 1.38% a day (1995) to 0.13% (2007) [Verified]. The monthly factor fell 40% from January 2020 to May 2026, including −18.0% in 2025 (monthly returns compounded) [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz (2012) put the US break-even at $9B versus $52B for momentum; optimized global reversal reaches only $17B [Verified]. Decay came from competition, decimalization and cheaper execution (evolution); since most stat-arb books hold reversal, crowding is the tail risk.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Information, not pressure. News moves keep going; the book is adversely selected, like a market maker.
  • August 2007. A crowded unwind; the daily factor lost 3.5% from 1 to 9 August, then made 4.58% on 10 August [Verified] (failure gallery).
  • March 2020. The daily factor lost 18.4% from 20 February to 23 March, then made 31.7% to 30 April [Verified] (our computation). Nagel's high expected return came only after the drawdown.
  • Momentum regimes. In 2024–2026 recent winners kept winning (the factor losses above).

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Deciles on raw 1-week returns (Lehmann 1990) [Verified] Residual, news-filtered scores (Blitz et al. 2013; Da et al. 2014) [Verified] A standalone anomaly One ML feature among many (ML short-horizon alpha) [Lore] Trade at the close Intraday execution, internal crossing [Lore]

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Reversal is a cost trade." → Net P&L depends on execution.
  • "We only fade residuals." → Reversal on factor-model residuals.
  • "Strip the news days." → Exclude earnings and revisions.
  • "High-turnover names momentum." → Medhat–Schmeling.
  • "VIX at 40 is when reversal pays." → Nagel's result.
  • "Our break-even is 12 bps." → Cost at which net alpha is zero.

docs.text: Myth Reality Highest gross Sharpe wins Lab 10: gross 2.37, net −1.43 (synthetic) Reversal is dead The plain version is; residual versions survive in backtests It is arbitrage It warehouses risk that crashes in liquidity crises

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: break-even cost and optimal size

Break-even one-way cost per dollar traded:

\[ c^{*} = \frac{\mu_{\text{gross}}}{\text{turnover}} . \]

Lab 10's weekly book: 11.4% after borrow / 90 ≈ 12.7 bps.

With square-root impact, cost grows as \(S^{3/2}\) in book size \(S\): \(\pi(S) = aS - kS^{3/2}\), break-even \(S_{be} = (a/k)^2\), and profit peaks at

\[ S^{*} = \left(\frac{2a}{3k}\right)^2 = \tfrac{4}{9}\, S_{be} . \]

docs.title: Stat arb: overview and history
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Statistical arbitrage holds thousands of small long and short bets on short-horizon relative mispricings, neutral to market, sectors and styles. Mostly it is paid for absorbing other investors' temporary price pressure.
  • It began at Morgan Stanley in the early-to-mid 1980s (Gerry Bamberger's industry-group reversal system, scaled by Nunzio Tartaglia's group) and at Princeton-Newport Partners; D. E. Shaw, founded in 1988, carried it into the hedge-fund era [Reported].
  • The academic record (Lehmann 1990 to Avellaneda & Lee 2010) shows real but decaying profits [Verified].
  • Crowding is the signature risk: a simple contrarian strategy's average daily return fell from 1.38% (1995) to 0.13% (2007), so it needed about 9:1 leverage to match 1998 returns, and it lost 6.85% unlevered in three days of August 2007 [Verified].
  • Today: 1,000–3,000 names, factor-neutral, 1–10 day holds, many signals, cost-aware optimizers.

Level: Core · Read time: ~10 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family stat arb Edge source liquidity provision · behavioral Holding period hours to about 10 days (classically 1–5 days) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Liquidity demanders who push prices away from relative value: institutions working large orders, index flows, herding retail, forced sellers. Finishing the trade matters more to them than a few bps. Universe & instruments 1,000–3,000 liquid US stocks, in cash or swaps; futures and ETFs as hedges Data required point-in-time prices, volumes, corporate actions; sector codes; a factor risk model; borrow rates Core algorithms used D3 Signal transforms · F5 Alpha combination and ensembling · P1 Risk models · P3 Mean-variance optimization · P5 Transaction cost and impact models Infra intensity moderate: daily to intraday rebalances, optimizer solves in seconds; not microsecond-sensitive Capacity (rough $ range) $0.5B to $5B gross market value per book [Estimate] (with square-root impact, costs overtake alpha within a few multiples of optimal size; see below) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) academic: PCA residual strategy 1.44 net of 10 bps round-trip costs, 1997–2007, falling to 0.9 in 2003–2007 [Verified]; practitioner: diversified books net 1–3 [Lore]; simple reversal decayed sharply after 1995 [Verified] Turnover 20–60% of gross market value per day [Lore] (roughly one over the holding period) Main risks / failure modes crowded deleveraging, factor leakage, cost-model error, alpha decay, short squeezes Crowding risk high: shared signals, data and commercial risk models Firm types that run it quant hedge funds, multi-manager pods, market makers' and banks' principal desks; historically Morgan Stanley, Princeton-Newport and D. E. Shaw [Reported] Lab Lab 09

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
A pension fund sells two million shares of a regional bank in a morning. The bank drops 3% while peers are flat; nothing changed in the business, and the gap tends to close within days. Buy the bank, short its peers, wait.

Do that daily across 2,000 stocks, stripping out market, sector and style moves so each position bets on one stock's residual. Each bet wins perhaps 51–53% of the time; the law of large numbers does the rest. Stat arb is a market maker on a slower clock, quoting through an optimizer.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
1. Liquidity provision. Uninformed demand moves prices temporarily; the provider is paid to warehouse it. Nagel (2012) shows short-term reversal returns behave like returns to liquidity provision, predictable with VIX and highest in turmoil [Verified]. Khandani and Lo note that most quant market-neutral strategies have a significant market-making component [Verified].
  2. Overreaction. Lehmann (1990) read weekly reversals as fads [Verified].
  3. Lead-lag. Lo and MacKinlay (1990) found that much of contrarian profit comes from cross-stock lead-lag, not overreaction [Verified].

The first explanation dominates practitioner thinking [Lore], and it predicts the failure mode: when providers all need liquidity at once, the trade reverses violently.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Universe: liquid names with borrow; drop stocks with pending corporate events.
  2. Signals: residual reversal (s-scores) plus volume, flow, earnings and analyst features.
  3. Transform (D3): winsorize, z-score, neutralize by sector.
  4. Combine (F5): weighted by IC, or an ML model, into a 1–5 day forecast.
  5. Risk (P1): factor covariance plus specific risk.
  6. Optimize (P3) with costs: alpha minus risk minus impact, subject to neutrality and position caps.
  7. Execute with VWAP or IS algos, some at the close; attribute P&L next morning.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative book: $1B gross market value (GMV), 2,000 names, 30% traded per day, 5 bps one-way cost per dollar traded, annual volatility 3% of GMV.

Item Calculation Per day Gross alpha $1B × 3 bps +$300,000 Trading cost $300M × 5 bps −$150,000 Net +$150,000 P&L volatility $1B × 3% / √250 $1.90M

Net: $37.5M a year, 3.75% on GMV before borrow, financing and fees. Annualized Sharpe = 150,000 / 1,900,000 × √250 ≈ 1.25. At 5× leverage (GMV over equity) that is about 19% on $200M of capital.

The Fundamental Law shows why breadth is everything: an IC of 0.01 across 2,000 names and about 50 independent rebalances a year gives IR ≈ 0.01 × √100,000 ≈ 3.2 before costs and constraints. The example's gross Sharpe is 2.5 (300,000 / 1,900,000 × √250), implying a transfer coefficient (the share of the forecast that survives constraints) near 0.8; costs then halve it to 1.25.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
The classic residual signal follows Avellaneda and Lee (2010): 15 PCA eigenportfolios from a 252-day correlation matrix as factors, 60-day residuals modeled as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, entries at |s| > 1.25. Lab 09 runs this recipe on 500 synthetic stocks with a planted residual reversal: gross Sharpe 2.98, but 0.63 net for a $10M book, with break-even near 10 bps per dollar traded (synthetic lab result; the clean, constant planted effect flatters it, against A&L's real 0.9–1.44 net). Factor-residual mean reversion walks through it. Production books feed such scores into F5 and an optimizer rather than trading them directly.

# PCA-residual s-scores and trading rule, condensed from Lab 09 (pca_residuals, ou_sscore).
CORR_WINDOW, RESID_WINDOW, N_FACTORS = 252, 60, 15        # correlation days, residual days, factors
S_OPEN, S_CLOSE_LONG, S_CLOSE_SHORT = 1.25, 0.50, 0.75    # bands from the paper
MAX_REVERSION_DAYS = 30             # trade only if 1/kappa < 30 days (about half the window)

def s_scores(R):                    # R: CORR_WINDOW x N daily returns, last row = today
    _, eigvec = np.linalg.eigh(np.corrcoef(R, rowvar=False))
    Q = eigvec[:, -N_FACTORS:] / R.std(0)[:, None]       # eigenportfolio weights v / sigma
    r = R[-RESID_WINDOW:]
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(RESID_WINDOW), r @ Q])  # drift + factor returns
    cum = np.cumsum(r - X @ np.linalg.lstsq(X, r, rcond=None)[0], axis=0)  # OU level
    a, b, var_zeta = ar1_fit(cum)                        # cum[t+1] = a + b cum[t] + zeta
    m = a / (1 - b);  m = m - m.mean()                   # equilibrium, centered across stocks
    s = (cum[-1] - m) / np.sqrt(var_zeta / (1 - b**2))   # cum[-1] = 0, so s = -m / sigma_eq
    ok = (b > 0) & (b < 1) & (-1 / np.log(b) < MAX_REVERSION_DAYS)
    return np.where(ok, s, np.nan)

def target_side(s, current):        # one stock: +1 long, -1 short, 0 flat (factors hedged)
    if np.isnan(s): return 0
    if current == 0: return +1 if s < -S_OPEN else (-1 if s > S_OPEN else 0)
    if (current == +1 and s > -S_CLOSE_LONG) or (current == -1 and s < S_CLOSE_SHORT):
        return 0                    # converged: close
    return current

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Neutrality: dollar-neutral is not enough; books neutralize beta, sectors and styles (size, value, momentum) with a risk model [Lore].
  • Horizon versus cost: a signal with a 2-day half-life can afford about half the cost per trade of a 4-day one; the optimizer's cost term decides how much alpha to chase.
  • Execution: participation caps of a few percent of ADV; internal crossing between signals saves spread [Lore].
  • Shorts: hard-to-borrow names carry fees and recall risk; many books exclude them.
  • Leverage: 4–8× GMV over equity is typical for market-neutral books [Lore].

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative, $1B GMV, one year:

Line $M % of GMV Gross alpha +75.0 +7.5 Spread and impact −37.5 −3.75 Commissions and exchange fees −2.5 −0.25 Borrow fees −5.0 −0.5 Financing spread −4.0 −0.4 Net, before management and performance fees +26.0 +2.6

On $200M of equity, 13% before fees. Costs take about two-thirds of gross alpha: stat arb is an execution business.

docs.title: Where it came from
docs.text:
• 1979–80: Ed Thorp's Princeton-Newport "indicators project" found short-term reversal, then shelved it [Reported].
  • 1982–85: Gerry Bamberger at Morgan Stanley traded reversal live from about 1983, dollar-neutral within industry groups of 2–13 stocks; by 1985 it was a significant profit center. His boss Nunzio Tartaglia expanded it, and Bamberger left, joining Princeton-Newport in 1985 (Thorp's account) [Reported]. Princeton-Newport later replaced industry groups with factor analysis, and BARRA found its returns essentially factor-neutral [Reported].
  • 1987–89: Tartaglia's group reportedly made $50M in 1987 and disbanded in 1989 after bad years (Gatev et al., citing a 1989 Institutional Investor article) [Reported]. Thorp relays a rumor of a 1988 expansion to about $900M a side and losses of 6–12% [Lore].
  • 1988: David E. Shaw, described by Gatev et al. as an early Tartaglia protégé, left Morgan Stanley [Reported] and founded D. E. Shaw with six employees and $28M [Verified].
  • 1992: Peter Muller started Morgan Stanley's Process Driven Trading, which made most of its money from stat arb, former employees say [Reported].

docs.title: What the papers show
docs.text:
• Lehmann (1990, QJE): one week's winners and losers reverse the next week, with apparent arbitrage profits after spreads and plausible costs [Verified].
  • Jegadeesh (1990, JF): predictable monthly return reversals [Verified].
  • Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst (2006, RFS): pairs trading on 1962–2002 data earned up to 11% a year on self-financing portfolios, above conservative cost estimates [Verified].
  • Avellaneda & Lee (2010): the Sharpe ratios in the table above; ETF-factor version 1.1 [Verified].
  • Krauss, Do & Huck (2017): an ensemble of a deep net, boosted trees and a random forest earned over 0.45% a day before costs on S&P 500 stocks (1992–2015), declining in later years [Verified].
  • Guijarro-Ordonez, Pelger & Zanotti (2026, Management Science): deep-learning residual portfolios with an annual Sharpe above 4 before costs (academic backtest) [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text:
Khandani and Lo applied the Lo-MacKinlay contrarian rule to US stocks: average daily return fell from 1.38% (1995) to 0.44% (2000) and 0.13% (2007), so almost 9:1 leverage was needed in 2007 to match 1998 expected returns [Verified]. They cite competition, market structure, technology, more assets and lower volatility; 1995 figures are not achievable (eighth-dollar ticks) [Verified].

Capacity, with the example's costs scaling as the square root of size [Estimate]:

GMV Traded per day Cost per $ Net per day $1B $300M 5.0 bps +$150k $2B $600M 7.1 bps +$176k $4B $1.2B 10.0 bps $0

Doubling capital adds 17% to P&L; quadrupling erases it. As daily reversal decayed, firms moved to intraday horizons, more signals and ML combination [Lore].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Crowded unwind: on 2007-08-07/08/09 the contrarian rule lost 1.16%, 2.83% and 2.86% (12 daily standard deviations), then gained 5.92% on August 10; at 8:1 leverage the three days cost over 25% [Verified]. Losses reported by the Wall Street Journal (quoted by Khandani and Lo): Goldman Sachs Global Equity Opportunities over 30% in a week; Highbridge Statistical Opportunities 18% in the first eight days of August [Reported]. Khandani and Lo blame a forced liquidation of similar portfolios.
  • Liquidity spirals: losses force deleveraging, which moves prices against everyone holding the same book (Brunnermeier & Pedersen 2009) [Verified].
  • Factor leakage: an unhedged style bet (momentum, crowded shorts) dominates P&L on a factor reversal.

See the failure gallery and quant winters.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: find cointegrated pairs. Practice: one optimizer across thousands of residuals; Bamberger already used industry groups, and Princeton-Newport moved to factor analysis [Reported]. Pairs are a special case.
  • Textbook: one reversal signal. Practice: dozens to hundreds of signals combined, often with ML (Krauss et al.; Guijarro-Ordonez et al.) [Lore].
  • Textbook: close-to-close daily trading. Practice: intraday rebalancing and execution-aware alpha [Lore].
  • Textbook: arbitrage. Practice: risky liquidity provision whose Sharpe depends on everyone else's leverage.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're paid to warehouse other people's urgency." → Stat arb as liquidity provision.
  • "Residual reversal is a crowded factor now." → Many books hold it; unwinds correlate.
  • "Half our gross goes to impact." → Costs are the binding constraint.
  • "We're flat beta, sector and the Barra styles." → The P&L should be idiosyncratic.
  • "Our half-life is two days." → Hold short; trade often.
  • "August '07 was a liquidity event, not a model failure." → Khandani-Lo's unwind story.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: stat arb is riskless arbitrage. Reality: it is statistical: positive expectation, fat-tailed crowding risk.
  • Myth: stat arb means pairs trading. Reality: pairs are the textbook special case.
  • Myth: market neutral means low risk. Reality: August 2007 hit market-neutral books hardest.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: What is your typical holding period and daily turnover?
  • Basic: Which factors do you neutralize?
  • Informed: How much of gross alpha do costs consume?
  • Informed: How do you detect crowding in your own signals?
  • Sharp: How did your book behave in August 2007 or March 2020, and what changed?
  • Sharp: 🔒 Your capacity curve, and where alpha decay shows first?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: residuals, s-scores, contrarian profits and the Fundamental Law

Factor residual and OU. \(r_{i,t} = \sum_k \beta_{ik} F_{k,t} + \epsilon_{i,t}\); cumulative residual \(X_i\) follows \(dX = \kappa(m - X)\,dt + \sigma\,dW\), half-life \(\ln 2/\kappa\), equilibrium sigma \(\sigma_{eq} = \sigma/\sqrt{2\kappa}\), and

\[ s_i = \frac{X_i - m_i}{\sigma_{eq,i}} . \]

Lo-MacKinlay contrarian profit. With weights \(w_{i,t} = -\tfrac{1}{N}(r_{i,t-1} - \bar r_{t-1})\) and lag-1 autocovariance matrix \(\Gamma\) (elements \(\gamma_{ij}\)):

\[ \mathbb{E}[\pi_t] = -\frac{N-1}{N^2}\sum_i \gamma_{ii} + \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{i\ne j}\gamma_{ij} - \sigma^2(\mu), \]

so negative own-autocovariance (overreaction) and positive cross-autocovariance (lead-lag) both pay; \(\sigma^2(\mu)\) is the cross-sectional variance of mean returns.

Fundamental Law. \(\text{IR} \approx \text{TC} \cdot \text{IC} \cdot \sqrt{\text{BR}}\).

docs.title: Alternative data
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Alternative data (card transactions, app and web traffic, satellite and location counts, job postings, supply-chain links, scraped prices, text) estimates a company's numbers before it reports: mostly a revenue nowcast ahead of earnings.
  • The edge is in the plumbing: panel-bias correction, ticker mapping, as-delivered history, backfill detection.
  • Evidence is real but narrow: satellite parking-lot counts earned ~4–5% in the three days around retailer earnings (2011–2017) [Reported]. Edges shrink as vendors add clients.
  • Legal review binds first: MNPI and provenance (App Annie's $10M SEC penalty, 2021), scraping law, privacy.
  • Most buyers spend $0.5–2.5M a year on data [Reported], a fixed cost against small capacity, so each dataset has a break-even size.

Level: Core · Read time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: Revenue is reported quarterly, weeks after quarter end, but its evidence appears daily: card swipes, app sessions, cars in lots. Sample it and scale it up, and you know the quarter before the print. It is a statistical channel check: diligence teams check one target's sell-through; a quant does it for 400 companies and compares each with consensus.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Costly information. If prices fully reflected costly information, nobody would buy it (Grossman–Stiglitz); alternative data returns pay for processing it.
  • Unequal access. Satellite coverage of retailers brought more informed short selling and lower liquidity around reports (Katona et al.) [Verified], and such data cut insider-trading profits (Zhu 2019) [Reported].
  • Inattention. Prices react slowly to news about a firm's main customers: over 150 bps a month long-short (Cohen & Frazzini 2008) [Verified].
  • Short horizon. Analysts exposed to alt data forecast the near term better and the long term worse (Dessaint, Foucault & Frésard 2024) [Verified].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Trial and diligence: compliance reviews provenance and terms before researchers see data.
  2. Map entities: merchant string ("SQ *JOES COFFEE 1123") → brand → parent → ticker, point-in-time through M&A.
  3. De-bias: normalize for panel growth, churn and demographics.
  4. Nowcast: regress past reported growth on panel growth.
  5. Surprise: nowcast minus consensus, in standard errors.
  6. Position 2–10 days before the report, sector-hedged; exit after the print.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative card-panel nowcast for retailer XYZ:

Step Value Panel spend, quarter to date, vs last year $41.6M vs $38.0M → +9.5% Panel active cardholders (a new bank joined) +3.0% Per-user growth: 1.095 / 1.030 − 1 +6.3% Calibration (16 quarters): 0.5% + 0.85 × 6.3% +5.9% → revenue $10.59B on last year's $10.00B Consensus $10.40B (+4.0%) Surprise; model s.e. 1.2% +1.9% → z ≈ +1.6

Without the per-user step: +8.6%, as panel growth masquerades as sales.

Trade. History says a 1% surprise moves the stock ~1.5% over three days; halve that because rivals own the panel. Expected return = 1.9 × 1.5 × 0.5 ≈ 1.4%, or $71,000 on a $5M hedged long, minus ~16 bps round-trip costs ($8,000): ~$63,000. Earnings-day volatility of 6% ($300,000) makes each trade a tilted coin flip; breadth across names does the work. A $750,000 license needs ~12 such trades a year to break even.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Timestamps and backfill: D1. Panel features: D2. Hit rate and decay by days-to-earnings: D4. Pooling short datasets: F2 or ridge. Text: F4.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def data_surprise(panel, fit, consensus_g, asof):
    """panel: [ticker, period, spend, active_users, delivered_at], one row per ticker and
    quarter-to-date window (this year and the same window last year). fit: per-ticker
    alpha, beta, resid_sd from past quarters. consensus_g: consensus growth known at asof."""
    p = panel[panel.delivered_at <= asof]                    # as delivered only: no backfill
    p = p.sort_values("period")
    per_user = p.spend / p.active_users                      # strip panel growth and churn
    g = per_user.groupby(p.ticker).agg(lambda s: s.iloc[-1] / s.iloc[-2] - 1)
    nowcast = fit.alpha + fit.beta * g                       # panel growth -> reported growth
    z = (nowcast - consensus_g) / fit.resid_sd               # surprise in standard errors
    return z.clip(-3, 3).dropna()

def earnings_window_book(z, days_to_report, gross=50e6, lo=2, hi=10):
    live = z[(days_to_report >= lo) & (days_to_report <= hi)]
    w = live - live.mean()                                   # dollar-neutral across live names
    return gross * w / w.abs().sum()                         # sector hedges added by the optimizer

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Panel bias: card panels skew by bank, region and income; reweight, and model online versus in-store.
  • History: demand data as delivered, not restated. Pre-launch history is backfill; pruned dead series add survivorship bias.
  • Short samples: five years is 20 quarters per stock; pool across stocks and shrink.
  • Calendars: 4-4-5 fiscal quarters, Easter shifts, leap days.
  • Procurement: exclusivity costs a premium [Lore]; ask how many funds hold the data.

docs.text:

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text:
Coverage clusters in consumer names and the edge before earnings, so capacity per dataset is small. As a vendor adds clients, the data leaks into whisper numbers and sell-side estimates, and the surprise folds into consensus (alpha decay).

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Provenance (September 2021). App Annie and its founder paid $10M and $300,000 to settle SEC fraud charges: it had used confidential app data in its estimates despite promising not to. No buying fund was charged [Reported].
  • Scraping (December 2022). hiQ v. LinkedIn narrowed computer-fraud claims over public data, but LinkedIn's anti-scraping terms were held enforceable; hiQ accepted a $500,000 consent judgment and deleted its data [Reported].
  • Panel drift. A bank partner leaves, an SDK changes, a privacy rule cuts location data, and the series breaks [Lore].

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: panel de-biasing, surprise, break-even cost

Post-stratify: weight panel cell \(c\) (region × income × channel) by population share \(\pi_c\) over panel share \(p_{c,t}\), with spend \(S\) and active users \(U\):

\[ \hat S_t = \sum_c \frac{\pi_c}{p_{c,t}} \, \frac{S_{c,t}}{U_{c,t}} , \qquad z_i = \frac{\alpha_i + \beta_i \, \Delta \log \hat S_{i} - g_i^{cons}}{\hat\sigma_{\varepsilon,i}} . \]

With license \(L\), engineering cost \(C\) and net alpha \(\alpha_{net}\), the minimum capacity worth buying is

\[ K_{min} = \frac{L + C}{\alpha_{net}} , \]

so $1.2M of costs at 2% net alpha needs $60M of GMV.

docs.title: Analyst revisions and sentiment
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Analysts update slowly and in herds, so consensus estimate revisions are serially correlated and prices drift after them: revision momentum is one of the most durable mid-frequency alphas.
  • Recommendation changes move prices on the day and drift afterwards, especially downgrades, but trading on them is costly.
  • Short interest and days-to-cover read the footprints of informed short sellers; the same crowded shorts are the squeeze candidates.
  • News scores, social-media sentiment and options-implied signals (skew, put-call parity deviations) add fast, crowded information that decays in days.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source informational · behavioral Holding period Days (news, options) to 1–3 months (revisions, short interest) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Investors anchored on stale estimates; attention-driven buyers of heavily discussed names; stock traders slower than informed option buyers. They are not watching continuously, or trade for other reasons. Universe & instruments US stocks with at least three estimates; listed options for implied signals; borrowable names for shorts Data required Point-in-time estimates and recommendations (for example I/B/E/S), short interest, lending utilization and fees, scored news, option implied volatilities Core algorithms used D2 Feature engineering · D3 Signal transforms · D4 Evaluating signals · F5 Alpha combination and ensembling · F4 LLMs and foundation models in quant Infra intensity Overnight batch; real-time feeds for news Capacity (rough $ range) Revisions and short interest: $1B–$5B as a component [Estimate]; news and options signals: $100M–$1B [Estimate] (decay within days forces high turnover) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Recommendation long-short: >4% a year gross, 1986–1996, not reliably positive after costs [Verified]; option-skew long-short: ~10.9% a year risk-adjusted, gross of costs, 1996–2005 [Verified]; both academic backtests, decayed since. Inside a composite: +0.2–0.5 net Sharpe contribution [Lore] Turnover Revisions 100–400% a year; news sleeves 20–50% a day [Lore] Main risks / failure modes Short squeezes, vendor-signal crowding, back-filled data, regime shifts in analyst behaviour Crowding risk High: revisions and short interest are standard in commercial factor libraries; vendor sentiment is sold to many clients Firm types that run it Quant hedge funds, systematic asset managers, multi-manager quant pods Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
Analysts are slow, careful and social: when news arrives, each moves part of the way and watches peers, so one upward revision predicts more. Prices under-react too, following the revision trail for weeks.

Other signals read who is already acting on information: short sellers are, on average, informed, as are option traders buying puts before bad news. News and social tone is sometimes information and sometimes noise that reverses.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Partial adjustment and herding. Gradual analyst updating makes earnings revisions autocorrelated, and prices drift after them (Givoly & Lakonishok 1979; Stickel 1991) [Reported].
  • Informed footprints. Stocks with the heaviest short-selling flow underperform the lightest by 1.16% over the next 20 trading days, risk-adjusted (NYSE order data, 2000–2004; Boehmer, Jones & Zhang 2008) [Verified]. Informed traders favour options, so skew leads stock prices (Xing, Zhang & Zhao 2010) [Verified].
  • Noise versus news. Tetlock (2007) found media pessimism pushes prices down and then reverses (noise); Tetlock, Saar-Tsechansky & Macskassy (2008) found negative words in firm news predict earnings and returns (information) [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
Signal Construction Horizon Origin Revision momentum (up − down revisions) / analysts, 1–3 months; or Δconsensus / price 1–3 months Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok (1996) Recommendation changes Upgrades, downgrades, initiations Days to months Womack (1996) Days-to-cover Short interest / average daily volume 1–3 months Asquith, Pathak & Ritter (2005) News sentiment Vendor score × relevance × novelty 1–5 days Heston & Sinha (2017) Social sentiment Tone of investor posts and articles Days to months Chen, De, Hu & Hwang (2014) Option skew OTM put IV − ATM call IV 1–4 weeks Xing, Zhang & Zhao (2010); Cremers & Weinbaum (2010)

Then z-score within sector, orthogonalize to surprise and momentum, IC-weight, neutralize and pass to the optimizer.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Revisions (illustrative). Twelve analysts; over 60 days seven raised next-year EPS and one cut. Net revision ratio = (7 − 1) / 12 = 0.50. Consensus moved $4.00 → $4.20 on an $80 stock: revision-to-price = 0.20 / 80 = 0.25%. Within sector these z-score to +1.6 and +1.2; average +1.4.

The short-side trap (illustrative). Days-to-cover = 6M shares short / 0.5M ADV = 12 days, top decile; the model wants to short $2M. Expected underperformance 1.0% a month = +$20,000. Borrow fee 25% a year = 2.1% a month = −$41,700. Net ≈ −$21,700 a month before squeeze risk: fee-adjusted alpha is what matters.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Feature design: D2; transforms: D3; decay and IC by horizon: D4; blending with other alphas: F5; LLM news scoring: F4; point-in-time estimates: D1.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def revision_signal(est, asof, window_days=60, min_analysts=3):
    """est: detail estimates (ticker, analyst, eps, announce_date), used only if
    announced by `asof` (point-in-time). Returns net up-minus-down share."""
    e = est[(est.announce_date <= asof) &
            (est.announce_date > asof - pd.Timedelta(days=window_days))]
    e = e.sort_values("announce_date")
    e["chg"] = e.groupby(["ticker", "analyst"]).eps.diff()  # simplified: ignores pre-window
    g = e.dropna(subset=["chg"]).groupby("ticker").chg
    net = g.apply(lambda c: (c > 0).sum() - (c < 0).sum()) / g.count()
    return net[g.count() >= min_analysts]

def sentiment_composite(rev, dtc, news, skew, sector):
    """Inputs: Series by ticker. Signs: revisions +, days-to-cover -, news +, skew -."""
    raw = pd.DataFrame({"rev": rev, "dtc": -np.log1p(dtc), "news": news, "skew": -skew})
    z = raw.groupby(sector).transform(lambda c: ((c - c.mean()) / c.std()).clip(-3, 3))
    return z.mean(axis=1, skipna=True)          # equal weight; F5 would IC-weight

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Point-in-time estimates. Ljungqvist, Malloy & Marston (2009) showed historical I/B/E/S recommendation records were altered after the fact [Reported]; use archived snapshots and announcement dates.
  • Hygiene. Drop estimates older than about 90–120 days and strip the post-earnings revision wave that echoes the surprise (earnings).
  • Short-interest timing. Exchange short interest is reported twice monthly with a lag; key it to publication date, not settlement date (shorting).
  • Borrow. Score alpha net of lending fees; cap utilization.
  • News. Deduplicate, require relevance and novelty, trade fast (NLP and LLM signals).

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok (1996): revisions and earnings surprises predict returns, and price momentum partly reflects earnings momentum [Reported].
  • Womack (1996): new sell ratings drift −9.1% over six months; new buys +2.4%, briefly [Verified]. Barber et al. (2001): consensus-recommendation strategies earned >4% a year gross, not reliably positive net [Verified].
  • Asquith, Pathak & Ritter (2005): high short interest plus low institutional ownership predicts underperformance [Reported].
  • Chen et al. (2014): Seeking Alpha opinions predict returns and earnings surprises [Reported].
  • Xing, Zhang & Zhao (2010): steepest-smirk stocks underperform by about 10.9% a year, risk-adjusted (1996–2005) [Verified].
  • McLean & Pontiff (2016): published predictors lose 58% post-publication [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Revisions and short interest sit in every commercial factor library, so standalone returns have shrunk and drawdowns are shared. Vendor news scores reach many clients at once and decay within hours to days [Lore]; edge has moved to proprietary parsing and LLM scoring.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Short squeezes. In January 2021, GameStop and other heavily shorted stocks rose many-fold as retail buying, call options and short covering fed each other [Verified] (SEC staff report, 2021).
  • Rule changes. Regulation FD (effective October 2000) ended selective disclosure to analysts, changing what revisions contain [Verified].
  • Crowding and back-filled data inflate backtests (backtest pitfalls).

docs.text:
• "Revisions are still working, but only analyst-level." → Consensus revisions are crowded; individual-analyst detail adds edge.
  • "Strip the post-earnings wave." → Remove revisions that merely echo the surprise.
  • "Days-to-cover beats the raw short ratio." → Scaling by volume measures how hard covering is.
  • "It's a good short, but not at that fee." → Borrow cost exceeds expected alpha.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: why revisions are autocorrelated, and signal definitions

Partial adjustment: if each analyst moves a fraction \(\kappa \in (0,1)\) toward the full-information forecast \(E_t\),

\[ F_t = F_{t-1} + \kappa \left(E_t - F_{t-1}\right) , \]

then after a one-time shock to \(E\), revisions \(F_t - F_{t-1}\) shrink geometrically by \((1-\kappa)\) but keep the same sign: today's revision predicts tomorrow's.

Days-to-cover and option skew:

\[ DTC_i = \frac{\text{shares short}_i}{\text{ADV}_i}, \qquad SKEW_i = IV^{put}_{OTM,i} - IV^{call}_{ATM,i} . \]
