docs.title: Cross-sectional alpha and neutralization
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • The canonical mid-frequency quant equity book ranks 1,000–3,000 US stocks against each other every day on many weak signals ("alphas") and holds the top against the bottom for days to weeks, with near-zero market exposure.
  • The pipeline: raw alphas → transforms (winsorize, rank or z-score) → neutralization (regress out beta, industries, styles) → combination → risk model → optimizer with a cost model → trades.
  • The Fundamental Law (IR ≈ TC · IC · √breadth) explains the design: each alpha is barely better than a coin flip (daily IC roughly 0.005–0.05), so the edge comes from many nearly independent bets.
  • It fails through costs (turnover of 10–40% of the book per day), crowding (August 2007) and decay of known signals.

Level: Core · Read time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source behavioral · informational (plus liquidity provision for reversal-type alphas) Holding period 1–20 trading days Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Benchmarked funds rebalancing to an index, institutions paying for immediacy on large orders, investors who under-react to news. They accept a few bps of leakage per trade because their objective (tracking, liquidity, a multi-year thesis) dominates. Universe & instruments US common stocks above a liquidity floor, long and short in cash or swaps; index futures to hedge residual beta Data required Point-in-time prices, corporate actions, fundamentals, estimates; industry codes; a factor risk model; spread, ADV and volatility for costs; borrow fees Core algorithms used D3 Signal transforms · D4 Evaluating signals · F5 Alpha combination and ensembling · P1 Risk models · P3 Mean-variance optimization · P5 Transaction cost and impact models Infra intensity Low latency sensitivity; heavy batch research compute; seconds per optimizer solve Capacity (rough $ range) $1B–$10B gross market value (GMV) per book [Estimate] (square-root impact: total cost grows like size^1.5, alpha like size) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Diversified multi-alpha book: gross 1.5–3, net 1–2 [Lore] (practitioner estimates, 2010s–2020s; no audited disclosure). Single published anomalies are weaker and lose ~58% of in-sample return after publication [Verified] (McLean & Pontiff 2016) Turnover 10–40% of GMV per day [Lore] (about 25–100× per year) Main risks / failure modes Crowded deleveraging, cost-model error, factor leakage, alpha decay, look-ahead, short squeezes Crowding risk High: shared data (Compustat, I/B/E/S), similar transforms and commercial risk models Firm types that run it Quant hedge funds, multi-manager quant pods, alpha-research platforms; WorldQuant stated that 80 of the 101 alphas in Kakushadze (2016) were in production when published [Verified] Lab Lab 11

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text:
A cross-sectional book never asks "will the market go up?" It asks "which of these 2,000 stocks will beat the others over the next week?" If every stock falls 3% tomorrow, a well-built book should barely notice.

Each alpha is a weak opinion: "analysts just raised estimates", "fell hard last week", "low accruals". Each is right perhaps 51–52% of the time. Hold hundreds of names per side and the coin flips average out.

Neutralization makes sure each flip is about what you think. If your "cheap stocks" list is 60% banks, you are betting on banks, not cheapness. Neutralization removes the bank bet (and the market and small-cap bets), leaving the stock-specific part the alpha was meant to capture.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
1. Behavioral under-reaction. Investors digest earnings news, revisions and accounting quality slowly; prices drift toward the news (see earnings and revisions).
  2. Liquidity provision. Reversal alphas are paid for absorbing temporary order imbalances (see short-term reversal).
  3. Residual risk premia. Some signals earn pay for risks your model omits; neutralization deliberately removes most known premia.

Arbitrage stays limited because shorting is costly, capital is finite and every dollar of alpha must clear a cost hurdle.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Universe: point-in-time membership and a liquidity floor (D1).
  2. Raw alphas: one number per stock per day (D2).
  3. Transform: winsorize, then rank or z-score across stocks each date.
  4. Neutralize: regress on beta, industry dummies and style exposures; keep the residual.
  5. Evaluate and combine: information coefficient, decay, turnover; blend into one forecast.
  6. Scale: alpha = IC × residual volatility × score (Grinold).
  7. Optimize with risk, cost and constraints; trade part of the way to target.
  8. Execute (VWAP/IS, closing auction) and attribute P&L next morning.
flowchart LR
    U["Universe<br/>(PIT, liquid)"] --> A["Raw alphas"]
    A --> T["Transforms<br/>winsorize, rank"]
    T --> N["Neutralize<br/>beta, industry, style"]
    N --> C["Combine<br/>IC-weighted, ridge, ML"]
    C --> R["Risk and<br/>cost models"]
    R --> O["Optimizer"]
    O --> X["Execution"]
    X --> P["P&L attribution"]
    P -.->|"decay, IC drift"| A

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
A. Neutralization (illustrative). Four stocks, two sectors, one raw z-scored signal:

Stock Sector Beta Raw z Sector mean Sector-neutral A Semis 1.4 +1.5 +1.0 +0.5 B Semis 1.3 +0.5 +1.0 −0.5 C Banks 1.1 −0.3 −1.0 +0.7 D Banks 0.9 −1.7 −1.0 −0.7

The raw signal is mostly "long semis, short banks". Sector-neutral, the book is long A and C, short B and D. At $100M GMV ($41.7M per unit of score): A +$20.8M, C +$29.2M, B −$20.8M, D −$29.2M. Net beta dollars: 20.8×1.4 + 29.2×1.1 − 20.8×1.3 − 29.2×0.9 = +$7.9M, so a 2% market drop costs ~$158k. Sector-neutral is not beta-neutral: add beta to the regression or hedge with ~$7.9M of index futures.

B. Dollar- vs beta-neutral (illustrative). $500M long at beta 0.8 against $500M short at beta 1.2 is dollar-neutral but carries −$200M of beta: a +1% market day loses ~$2M.

C. Fundamental Law (illustrative). IC 0.03, 2,000 stocks, 5-day horizon (≈ 50 periods a year): nominal breadth 100,000, √ ≈ 316, IR ≈ 9.5; with a transfer coefficient of 0.4, 3.8. If correlated residuals and overlapping holds leave 10% of bets truly independent, √10,000 = 100 and IR ≈ 0.03 × 100 × 0.4 = 1.2, where real books live.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Transforms and IC: D3, D4. Combination: F5. Risk model: P1, P2. Optimizer and costs: P3, P5, P6. Lab 11 implements the transforms and IC diagnostics on synthetic data.

import numpy as np

def winsorize(x, pct=0.01):
    """Clip raw values at the date's 1st/99th percentiles (bad prints, outliers)."""
    lo, hi = np.nanquantile(x, [pct, 1 - pct])
    return np.clip(x, lo, hi)

def zscore(x, clip=3.0):
    """Cross-sectional z-score on one date, then clipped at +/- clip sd."""
    z = (x - np.nanmean(x)) / np.nanstd(x)
    return np.clip(z, -clip, clip)

def neutralize(signal, exposures):
    """Residual after least-squares regression of the signal on exposures.
    exposures: N x K (beta column, industry dummies, style z-scores)."""
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(exposures, signal, rcond=None)
    return signal - exposures @ coef        # orthogonal to every exposure column

def daily_forecast(raw_alphas, exposures, ic, resid_vol, ic_combo=0.04):
    """raw_alphas: {name: N-vector}; ic: {name: trailing rank IC}; returns daily alpha."""
    combo = np.zeros(len(resid_vol))
    for name, x in raw_alphas.items():
        s = neutralize(zscore(winsorize(x)), exposures)
        combo += max(ic[name], 0.0) * s / np.std(s)   # IC-weighted; ignores alpha correlations
    score = neutralize(zscore(combo), exposures)      # re-neutralize after clipping
    return ic_combo * resid_vol * score              # Grinold: alpha = IC * vol * score
# Names follow Lab 11 (winsorize, zscore, neutralize); simplified: no NaN handling, unweighted regression.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Rank vs z-score. Ranks resist outliers but discard magnitude; z-scores keep it but need winsorizing.
  • What to neutralize. Beta and industries always; styles (size, value, momentum, volatility) usually. Over-neutralizing deletes alpha correlated with a factor.
  • Signal vs optimizer. If the alpha has parts the risk model cannot "see", the optimizer over-loads on them (Ceria, Saxena & Stubbs 2012, "factor alignment").
  • Weighted regression (for example by √market cap) stops tiny names dominating.
  • Trade toward the aim: move a fraction of the way to target daily (Gârleanu & Pedersen 2013).
  • Execution and borrow: participation caps of 1–5% of ADV [Lore]; hard-to-borrow names penalized (shorting and financing).

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative: $1B GMV, turnover 15% per day ($37.8B traded per year).

Line $M per year % of GMV Residual alpha captured +80.0 +8.0% Factor P&L (leakage) ≈ 0 expected, ±10 realized ≈ 0 Half-spread (3 bps traded) −11.3 −1.1% Market impact (4 bps) −15.1 −1.5% Commissions and fees (1 bp) −3.8 −0.4% Borrow (0.4% on $500M short) −2.0 −0.2% Financing spread, net −3.0 −0.3% Net +44.8 +4.5%

At 4% annualized volatility on GMV, gross Sharpe ≈ 2.0 and net ≈ 1.1: costs take 44% of gross alpha [Estimate].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Kakushadze (2016) published 101 real-life trading alphas with average holding periods of about 0.6–6.4 days and average pairwise correlation of 15.9% [Verified]; low correlation is what makes breadth across alphas valuable.
  • McLean & Pontiff (2016): across 97 predictors, returns are 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower post-publication [Verified].
  • Grinold (1989) derived IR ≈ IC·√breadth; Clarke, de Silva & Thorley (2002) added the transfer coefficient and showed constraints shrink realized IR [Verified].
  • Daily rank ICs of roughly 0.005–0.03 per alpha are the practitioner norm (0.05 is exceptional); above 0.1 on a large universe usually means a bug [Lore].
  • Tulchinsky et al. (Finding Alphas) and Isichenko (2021) describe this pipeline at industrial scale [Reported].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text:
Capacity. Under square-root impact, doubling the book raises impact per dollar ~41%. In the table, a $4B book pays ~8 bps impact and ~12 bps all-in, about 4.5% of GMV a year, unless it slows down and drops its fastest alphas [Estimate].

Crowding. Shared vendors, academic signals and risk models make residual books overlap; one forced seller hurts all (see the diagram).

Decay. Known alphas lose about half their return (McLean & Pontiff); research must keep replacing them (L2).

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• August 2007. Over 7–9 August many quant equity funds lost heavily at once, then partly rebounded on 10 August; Khandani & Lo (2007, 2011) attribute it to the rapid unwind of large market-neutral portfolios [Verified].
  • Factor leakage. Imperfect neutralization leaves hidden style bets, exposed in the 2018–2020 value drawdown (see quant winters).
  • Short squeezes. In January 2021, heavily shorted stocks spiked on retail buying and short covering [Verified] (SEC staff report, 2021).
  • Backtest bias and underestimated impact (V3).

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today One alpha into mean-variance Hundreds to thousands of alphas, combined by regularized regression or ML (Kakushadze 2016; Tulchinsky et al.) [Reported] IR = IC·√N, independent bets Effective breadth far below nominal, backed out from realized IR [Lore] One commercial risk model Proprietary or statistical models to trade, commercial ones for limits [Lore] Rebalance fully Partial, cost-aware trading toward an aim (Gârleanu & Pedersen 2013) [Verified]

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text:
• Factor-residual mean reversion: the residual's reversion is the alpha.
  • Fundamental quant signals, earnings, revisions and sentiment: alpha families that feed this book.
  • Factor investing: the long-only, un-neutralized, low-turnover cousin.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
The crowding loop behind August 2007:

flowchart TD
    S["Large fund de-risks"] --> L["Sells longs, covers shorts"]
    L --> M["Common longs fall,<br/>common shorts rise"]
    M --> Q["Overlapping quant books lose"]
    Q --> V["Risk limits breached"]
    V --> D["They de-lever too"]
    D --> L
    M --> F["Index barely moves:<br/>the damage is residual"]

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Neutralize to industry and the Barra styles before you look at the IC." → Otherwise the IC partly measures factor returns.
  • "That alpha is short-vol in disguise." → It loads on low volatility; neutralized, little remains.
  • "Our effective breadth is a few hundred bets a year." → Correlated bets shrink the √N.
  • "The TC on that book is terrible." → Constraints stop holdings reflecting the forecast.
  • "IC is 2%, but it's a 1-day signal and costs eat it." → Real but unusable at that turnover.
  • "We trade a third of the way to target each day." → Partial adjustment: the trade rate balances transaction costs against risk aversion, while fast-decaying alphas are discounted inside the aim portfolio (Gârleanu–Pedersen).

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text: Myth Reality Market-neutral means riskless It removes beta, not factor, crowding or squeeze risk Higher IC is always better IC 0.05 at 80% daily turnover can lose to IC 0.02 at 5% after costs More neutralization is safer It can delete real alpha and create exposures the model cannot see

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
Basic

  • Do you neutralize at the signal level, in the optimizer, or both?
  • Dollar-neutral, beta-neutral or both?

Informed

  • How far is effective breadth from nominal?
  • Which constraint costs the most transfer coefficient?
  • How do you set the trade-toward-target rate per alpha half-life?

Sharp

  • How did the book behave on 7–9 August 2007, and what changed afterwards?
  • How much residual return does your statistical risk model explain that the commercial one misses? 🔒
  • What is the IC half-life of a newly added alpha in production? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: residualization, the Fundamental Law and alpha scaling

Neutralization as projection. Signal \(s\), exposures \(X\) (\(N \times K\)), weights \(W\):

\[ s_\perp = \left(I - X (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W\right) s, \qquad X^\top W s_\perp = 0 . \]

Sector-demeaning is the case where \(X\) holds only industry dummies and \(W = I\). Beta-neutral holdings satisfy \(\beta^\top h = 0\); dollar-neutral, \(\mathbf{1}^\top h = 0\).

Fundamental Law (Grinold 1989; Clarke, de Silva & Thorley 2002), with \(BR\) the number of independent forecasts per year:

\[ IR \approx TC \cdot IC \cdot \sqrt{BR} . \]

Alpha scaling (Grinold and Kahn), score \(z_i\), residual volatility \(\omega_i\):

\[ \alpha_i = IC \cdot \omega_i \cdot z_i . \]

With \(IC = 0.03\), \(\omega = 30\%\) and \(z = 2\): 1.8% a year, which is why costs dominate.

docs.title: Earnings and event-driven
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Earnings releases are a stock's biggest scheduled information events; the classic quant trade is post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD): buy positive surprises, short negative ones, hold for weeks.
  • Bernard & Thomas (1989): about 4.2% over 60 trading days for top-minus-bottom surprise deciles (1974–1985). Martineau (2022): gone in non-microcaps since 2006. 2025 papers dispute it; the question is open.
  • Neighbouring event alphas: the earnings-announcement premium, pre-announcement liquidity reversal, guidance changes, and merger arbitrage (a short put on deal completion).
  • Execution is the hard part: gaps and event-day spreads eat much of a thin edge.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source behavioral · liquidity provision (plus a risk premium in merger arbitrage) Holding period 1–60 trading days after the event; merger arbitrage holds until deal close (months) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Inattentive investors who under-react on busy days and Fridays; impatient traders needing liquidity before announcements; target holders who sell rather than bear deal-break risk Universe & instruments US stocks with scheduled earnings; merger targets and acquirers; options for event-volatility variants Data required Point-in-time release timestamps, actuals and consensus (for example I/B/E/S), guidance, intraday prices; deal terms Core algorithms used D1 Point-in-time data and cleaning · D2 Feature engineering · D4 Evaluating signals · V3 Backtest pitfalls · E5 Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos Infra intensity Moderate: minutes matter for the reaction, days for drift Capacity (rough $ range) $100M–$2B for standalone PEAD [Estimate] (drift is concentrated in small, illiquid names and entries cluster on high-cost days) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) PEAD: ~4.2% per 60 days top-minus-bottom decile, gross, 1974–1985 academic backtest [Reported]; near zero in non-microcaps since 2006 [Verified] (Martineau 2022), contested. Merger arbitrage: ~4% a year excess, net of transaction costs, 1963–1998 academic study [Verified] Turnover High and lumpy: positions open after each event and roll off within weeks Main risks / failure modes Overnight gaps, guidance shocks, stale consensus, timestamp errors, deal breaks Crowding risk High: everyone has the same consensus feed and the same SUE formula Firm types that run it Quant hedge funds, event-driven pods at multi-manager firms, merger-arbitrage funds Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: Earnings are a quarterly exam. The market grades it within seconds but historically took weeks to finish: beats kept drifting up, misses kept drifting down. A quant needs not why a company beat but by how much, relative to how noisy its surprises usually are, and a way to trade after the first reaction without paying it all away in spreads.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Limited attention. Responses are weaker and drift stronger for Friday announcements (DellaVigna & Pollet 2009) and on days crowded with other announcements (Hirshleifer, Lim & Teoh 2009) [Reported].
  • Misread persistence. Bernard & Thomas (1990): prices act as if earnings were a random walk although seasonal changes are autocorrelated, so much of the drift lands at the next announcements [Reported].
  • Liquidity provision. Short-term reversals are much larger just before announcements, when liquidity providers demand more (So & Wang 2014) [Reported].
  • Risk. Announcement months earn higher returns, read as systematic risk (Savor & Wilson 2016) or attention-driven buying (Frazzini & Lamont 2007) [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Keep a point-in-time calendar of confirmed dates and times.
  2. At release, compute standardized unexpected earnings (SUE): surprise scaled by the stock's usual surprise size; add revenue surprise.
  3. Rank against other recent announcers within sector.
  4. Enter after the gap over one to three sessions (VWAP, closing auction).
  5. Hold 20–60 days with decaying weight; neutralize beta and industry.
  6. Decide whether to hold through the next announcement.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
PEAD (illustrative). EPS $1.20 against consensus $1.05; past surprises have a standard deviation of $0.10, so SUE = 0.15 / 0.10 = 1.5 (top decile). The stock gaps +6% at the open. Buy $5M over two days.

Line If drift exists If it does not Drift capture (+2% of $5M) +$100,000 $0 Entry: 10 bps spread + 15 bps impact on event days −$12,500 −$12,500 Exit: 10 bps −$5,000 −$5,000 Net +$82,500 −$17,500

The 2% is one leg's half of the historical 4.2% spread; whether it survives in large caps decides the trade.

Merger arbitrage (illustrative). Cash offer $50; target trades at $47.50; expected close in six months; estimated break price $38. Spread = 2.50 / 47.50 = 5.3% (≈ 10.8% annualized). Market-implied completion probability, ignoring discounting: (47.50 − 38) / (50 − 38) = 79%. Payoff: +5.3% if it closes, −20% if it breaks, the shape of a short put.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Timestamps come from D1; surprise features from D2; drift curves and IC by horizon from D4; timing look-ahead from V3; event-day execution from E5.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def sue(actual_eps, consensus_eps, past_surprises, min_hist=4):
    """Standardized unexpected earnings (analyst-consensus version)."""
    if len(past_surprises) < min_hist:
        return np.nan
    scale = max(np.std(past_surprises), 0.01)       # floor avoids dividing by ~0
    return (actual_eps - consensus_eps) / scale

def pead_weights(events, today, hold_days=40, entry_lag=1, half_life=20):
    """events: DataFrame(ticker, ann_ts, sue, sector); ages in calendar days.
    Enter only on the first full session after the release (never the pre-release close)."""
    age = (today - events.ann_ts).dt.days
    live = events[(age >= entry_lag) & (age <= hold_days)].set_index("ticker")
    score = live.groupby("sector").sue.rank(pct=True) - 0.5       # sector-relative
    w = score * 0.5 ** ((today - live.ann_ts).dt.days / half_life)  # decay with age
    return (w - w.mean()) / (w - w.mean()).abs().sum()            # dollar-neutral, gross 1

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Timestamps. An after-close release cannot trade at that day's close.
  • Consensus hygiene. Stale estimates and GAAP versus "street" EPS change SUE; analyst-based SUE drifts more than time-series SUE (Livnat & Mendenhall 2006) [Reported].
  • More than EPS. Revenue surprises and guidance add information (Jegadeesh & Livnat 2006) [Reported].
  • Liquidity. Event-day spreads are wide [Lore]; spreading entry over days and using the close cuts costs.
  • Index events follow the same logic with flows: see flow-driven strategies.

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative large-cap PEAD book, $500M GMV, ~30-day holds ($8.4B traded per year):

Line % of GMV per year Drift capture +3.0% Announcement-premium tilt +0.5% Spread and impact at event liquidity (12 bps) −2.0% Borrow and financing −0.5% Net +1.0%

At 4% volatility, net Sharpe ≈ 0.25 [Estimate]: thin, which is why most firms run SUE as one input to a multi-alpha book rather than standalone.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Ball & Brown (1968) first documented drift; Bernard & Thomas (1989): ~4.2% top-minus-bottom over 60 days, positive in 41 of 48 quarters, 1974–1985 [Reported].
  • Chordia et al. (2009): drift concentrates in illiquid stocks; costs absorb most paper profits [Reported].
  • Martineau (2022): no drift in large stocks since 2006, recently none in microcaps; prices now absorb surprises on the day [Verified].
  • Subrahmanyam (2025) notes two 2025 papers reporting strong PEAD (t-statistics above 14) and attributes the disagreement to research design [Reported]. Evidence is mixed; no verdict here.
  • Mitchell & Pulvino (2001): 4,750 mergers, 1963–1998: ~4% a year excess after transaction costs; returns track the market only in sharp declines, like a short index put [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Drift lives where costs are highest, so capacity is small. Decay is central: the reaction moved into the first minutes, shifting edge to whoever parses releases and calls fastest (NLP and LLM signals).

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Gap risk. On 3 February 2022 Meta fell 26% in one session after earnings, erasing over $230B of market value [Reported].
  • Deal breaks. In October 2014 AbbVie abandoned its $55B Shire deal after new US anti-inversion rules; merger-arbitrage funds lost and de-risked other deals [Reported].
  • Timing bugs. Misdated releases create fictitious backtest drift.

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Time-series SUE, quarterly deciles (Bernard & Thomas 1989) [Reported] Consensus SUE plus revenue, guidance and call text, sector-neutral [Lore] Hold 60 days Hold until the measured drift decays, often shorter in large caps (Martineau 2022) [Verified] Trade at the announcement close Enter after the gap with auction and VWAP algos [Lore]

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Merger arbitrage, flow-driven index events, guidance and negative pre-announcements, post-release analyst revisions, options event volatility (volatility risk premium).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We don't trade the print, we trade the day after." → Enter after the gap to avoid event-day costs.
  • "SUE alone is a commodity." → Everyone has it; edge comes from extra features or speed.
  • "PEAD's a small-cap story now." → Drift survives, if anywhere, where it is costly to trade.
  • "The arb spread is pricing about an 80% close." → Market-implied deal probability.
  • "Don't hold through the next print without a view." → Gap risk resets each quarter.
  • "Watch the late reporters." → Unexpected delays to a release date often precede bad news.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text: Myth Reality PEAD is a free lunch Largely gone in large caps since 2006, and costly where it remains Merger arbitrage is low risk It is a short put: steady small gains, rare large losses Faster is always better For drift, waiting a day often beats event-day spreads

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
Basic

  • Do you use consensus or time-series surprises?
  • When do you enter relative to the release?

Informed

  • How has your measured drift by size bucket changed since 2006?

Sharp

  • Do you hold through the next announcement, and what does that add? 🔒
  • What share of event P&L arrives in the first hour versus the drift window? 🔒
  • How do you size merger arbitrage against correlated deal breaks?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: SUE and implied deal probability

Standardized unexpected earnings, with consensus \(F_{t}\) and the standard deviation of the last \(k\) surprises:

\[ SUE_{t} = \frac{EPS_{t} - F_{t}}{\sigma\left(EPS_{t-j} - F_{t-j}\right)_{j=1..k}} . \]

Implied completion probability with discount rate \(r\) and time to close \(T\):

\[ P_0 = \frac{p \, O + (1-p) \, B}{(1+r)^{T}} \;\Rightarrow\; p = \frac{P_0 (1+r)^{T} - B}{O - B} . \]

docs.title: Flow-driven strategies
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Some investors must trade on a rule or calendar whatever the price: index funds, pensions, funds facing redemptions, hedging dealers. Flow traders position early and take the other side.
  • The classic case: S&P 500 additions averaged +7.4% in the 1990s but under 1% in the 2010s (Greenwood & Sammon 2025) [Verified].
  • Index funds pay at least 21–28 bp a year (S&P 500) and 38–77 bp (Russell 2000), 1990–2005 (Petajisto) [Verified].
  • Rules are public, so crowding shrinks the effect and pulls it earlier.
  • Russell now reconstitutes twice a year; the December 2026 changes take effect after the close on 11 December [Verified].

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-frequency alpha (event and flow) Edge source liquidity provision · structural/regulatory Holding period days to weeks (index events); hours to days (calendar and hedging flows) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Index funds that must trade at the effective-day close and value tracking error over price; pensions on calendar rules; funds meeting redemptions; dealers hedging mechanically. Universe & instruments US stocks near index cutoffs (Russell, S&P, MSCI, Nasdaq-100); index futures as hedges Data required Point-in-time index rules and membership, float, passive ownership, fund flows, auction imbalances Core algorithms used D1 Point-in-time data and cleaning · D4 Evaluating signals · P5 Transaction cost and impact models · E5 Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos Infra intensity Low to moderate: daily batch plus closing-auction execution Capacity (rough $ range) $100M–$1B per firm [Estimate] (index demand of tens of billions a year, shared by all arbitrageurs) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) No public live figures. docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: In an index reconstitution, index funds announce what they will buy, how much and on which closing print, and promise not to care about price: a tender offer with a deadline. The flow trader buys early, carries the risk for weeks, and sells into the deadline.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Demand curves slope down. After 1976, S&P 500 additions earned abnormal returns tied to index-fund buying, lasting beyond ten days (Shleifer 1986) [Verified].
  • Price pressure. Added stocks rose more than 3% on announcement, nearly all reversed within two weeks (Harris & Gurel 1986) [Verified].
  • Limits to arbitrage. Capital, borrow and list uncertainty limit who pre-positions, so a concession survives.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Predict the list from the rules: Russell rank day, S&P committee criteria, MSCI reviews (D1).
  2. Size the demand: passive ownership × float, in days of volume.
  3. Enter before or at the announcement; hedge beta and sector.
  4. Exit into the effective-day close with market-on-close orders (E5).
  5. Repeat for month-end, pension, option-expiry and leveraged-ETF flows.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: XYZ (cap $12B, float 90%) joins an index whose passive funds own 20% of every member's float: demand = 0.2 × $10.8B = $2.16B, 14 days of its $150M daily volume. It rises 4.0% from the announcement close to the effective close.

Line Arbitrageur, $50M long, beta-hedged Gain to the effective close 4.0% × $50M = +$2,000,000 Entry spread and impact (15 bp) −$75,000 Exit in the closing auction (5 bp) −$25,000 Futures hedge (1 bp) −$5,000 Net over 20 trading days +$1,895,000 (3.8%) If held 10 more days through a 2% reversal −$1,000,000

Index funds pay about 4% × $2.16B = $86M more than at the announcement close: Petajisto's "index turnover cost".

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Cards: D1 membership history; D4 testing; P5 impact; E5 exit; M7 beta hedge. The event study, as in Lab 20:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def abnormal_returns(returns, market, events, window=(-20, 40), est_window=(-270, -21), intercept=False):
    """Market-model ARs per event; day 0 = announcement A. Default drops alpha (mostly past luck)."""
    rel, est = np.arange(window[0], window[1] + 1), np.arange(est_window[0], est_window[1] + 1)
    ar, ar_est = [], []
    for stock, d0 in zip(events["stock"], events["day0"]):
        r_e, m_e = returns[d0 + est, stock], market[d0 + est]
        beta = np.cov(r_e, m_e)[0, 1] / np.var(m_e, ddof=1)
        alpha = (r_e.mean() - beta * m_e.mean()) if intercept else 0.0
        ar.append(returns[d0 + rel, stock] - alpha - beta * market[d0 + rel])
        ar_est.append(r_e - alpha - beta * m_e)
    return np.array(ar), np.array(ar_est)

def event_study(ar, ar_est, window=(-20, 40)):
    """Mean CAR and 95% band (lab also returns both standard errors; omitted here)."""
    n = ar.shape[0]
    car_i = np.cumsum(np.c_[np.zeros(n), ar[:, 1:]], axis=1)           # each event's CAR
    se_cross = car_i.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)                   # assumes independent events
    se_dep = ar_est.mean(axis=0).std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(np.arange(ar.shape[1]))  # Brown-Warner
    se, car = np.maximum(se_cross, se_dep), car_i.mean(axis=0)
    return pd.DataFrame({"car": car, "lo": car - 1.96 * se, "hi": car + 1.96 * se},
                        index=np.arange(window[0], window[1] + 1))

Adds rise into the effective day, then give much back; volume spikes in the effective-day close. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab result: long adds and short deletes from the announcement close to the effective close earn 197 bp gross, 177 bp net per trade (63% winners); holding 20 more days gives −50 bp. The planted 5% effect is far above today's real S&P effect (under 1%); read the mechanics, not the level.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Predict early. More arbitrage capital moves more of the effect before the announcement (Lab 20).
  • Index family. S&P: short, committee-chosen lists; Russell: long, rules-based ones.
  • Adds vs deletes. Adds rise permanently, deletes do not fall permanently (Chen, Noronha & Singal 2004) [Verified]; deletes are often hard to borrow.
  • Exit. The effective-day closing auction is where the fund's size meets yours.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Index premium, 1990–2005 (announcement to effective day): S&P 500 adds +8.8%, deletes −15.1%; Russell 2000 +4.7%, −4.6% (Petajisto) [Verified]. By the 2010s: S&P adds under 1%, deletes 0.1%, other families similar (Greenwood & Sammon) [Verified].
  • Fire sales: funds with extreme outflows depress shared holdings, and liquidity providers profit (Coval & Stafford 2007) [Verified]; predicted flow-induced trading forecasts returns for a year, then reverses (Lou 2012) [Verified].
  • Calendar flows: month-end cash needs move prices (Etula et al. 2020) [Verified]; rebalancing out of overweight equities lowers next-day equity returns 17 bp and costs investors about $16B a year (Harvey et al., working paper) [Verified].
  • Hedging flows: dealer rebalancing moves stock volatility (Ni et al. 2021) [Verified]; short-gamma hedging drives last-30-minute momentum in 60+ futures (Baltussen et al. 2021) [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text:
More arbitrage capital per dollar of index demand: return per trade falls toward zero; total arbitrage profit is hump-shaped. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab result: net return per trade falls from 407 bp with no competitors to 39 bp when arbitrage capital equals index demand. Nasdaq's close printed a record $334.0B on the June 2026 reconstitution [Reported]; December 2026 dates are in the diagram [Verified].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Decay. The effect fades decade by decade (Greenwood & Sammon) [Verified].
  • Tesla, December 2020. The largest-ever S&P 500 addition, announced 16 November: about +12% after hours; over $150B traded on 18 December; about −4.5% before the open on its first index day [Reported]. Everyone exits in the same auction.
  • Volmageddon, 5 February 2018. Inverse VIX products had to buy futures at the close; traders bought first, and 115,862 contracts traded in one minute (BIS) [Verified] (failure gallery).

docs.text: Textbook Practice today Buy at announcement, sell at effective day Trade predicted lists before the announcement [Lore] Pure price pressure Mixed: reversal (Harris–Gurel) vs persistence (Shleifer) [Verified] Only index events A calendar of forced flows [Verified]

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Recon is a liquidity event, not an alpha event." → The profit is a fee for absorbing flow.
  • "We're positioned off rank day." → Bought predicted adds before the lists.
  • "The add is priced; the trade is the close." → Only the auction is left.
  • "Watch the month-end pension bid." → Calendar rebalancing.
  • "Dealers are short gamma; expect a late push." → Hedging chases the day's move.
  • "Deletes are hard to borrow." → The short leg is costly.

docs.text: Myth Reality Index inclusion is a free 5–8% Under 1% in the 2010s [Verified] Passive buying only pushes prices up Flows reverse; rebalancing sells winners Trading index changes is front-running Lists are public; front-running misuses a client's confidential order [Lore]

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: abnormal returns, the Brown–Warner band, hump-shaped arbitrage profit

Market model per event \(i\), fitted over trading days −270 to −21 relative to the announcement (as in Lab 20):

\[ AR_{i,t} = r_{i,t} - \hat\beta_i\, r_{m,t}, \qquad CAR(k) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{t=\tau_0+1}^{k} AR_{i,t}. \]

Events share dates, so the Brown–Warner error is \(SE(k) = s\sqrt{k - \tau_0}\), with \(s\) the daily standard deviation of the average estimation-window AR.

With arbitrage capital \(c\) (share of index demand \(D\)), capturable move \(g(c)\) and cost \(\kappa\):

\[ \Pi(c) = c\, D\, \big(g(c) - \kappa\big), \]

zero at \(c = 0\), negative once \(g(c) < \kappa\), peaking in between.

docs.title: Fundamental quant signals
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Fundamental quant turns financial-statement judgments (is it cheap? are earnings backed by cash? is management over-investing?) into ratios computed identically for 3,000 stocks and ranked within sector.
  • The core families: value (B/M, E/P, EV/EBITDA), profitability (gross profits / assets), accruals, asset growth, and earnings-quality composites.
  • The hard part is the data, not the ratio: point-in-time availability, reporting lags and restatements decide whether a backtest is honest.
  • Slow, cheap to trade and high capacity, but crowded and decayed: accruals largely faded, and published predictors lose about half their return.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source risk premium · behavioral Holding period 1–12 months (inputs update quarterly) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Investors who extrapolate growth and fixate on headline earnings rather than their cash content; insofar as value and investment are risk premia, anyone avoiding that risk Universe & instruments US stocks with statement coverage; financials and utilities often excluded or scored separately Data required Point-in-time fundamentals with filing dates (vendor PIT archives or SEC XBRL), prices, estimates, industry codes Core algorithms used D1 Point-in-time data and cleaning · D2 Feature engineering · D3 Signal transforms · D4 Evaluating signals · P1 Risk models Infra intensity Negligible latency sensitivity; data engineering is the main cost Capacity (rough $ range) $1B–$20B+ per strategy [Estimate] (turnover ~1–3× a year versus 25–100× for daily books, so impact per dollar of alpha is an order of magnitude lower) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Single academic long-short factors (value, profitability, investment): gross roughly 0.3–0.5 over 1963–2020s, weaker post-publication [Estimate]; diversified sector-neutral composite: net 0.5–1.0 [Lore] Turnover 100–300% of GMV per year [Lore] Main risks / failure modes Long value drawdowns, junk rallies, look-ahead in data, sector concentration Crowding risk High: same Compustat fields and the same papers everywhere Firm types that run it Systematic asset managers, quant hedge funds, "quantamental" teams, smart-beta index providers (long-only versions) Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A fundamental analyst reads one 10-K deeply; a fundamental quant reads 3,000 shallowly but identically. Each diligence judgment (cheap versus peers? earnings converting to cash? balance sheet bloating through acquisitions?) becomes a ratio ranked within its industry daily, and breadth does the rest.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Two explanations compete, and both have evidence:

  • Risk. The clean-surplus valuation identity says that, at a given price-to-book, higher expected profitability implies a higher expected return and higher expected investment a lower one; Fama & French (2015) built their profitability (RMW) and investment (CMA) factors on this logic [Verified].
  • Mispricing. Sloan (1996) argued investors fixate on reported earnings and miss that accrual-heavy earnings persist less than cash earnings [Reported]. Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008) read the asset-growth effect as over-extrapolation of growth [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Build a point-in-time panel: every value stamped with the date it became public.
  2. Compute ratios from trailing-twelve-month flows and latest balances.
  3. Winsorize and z-score within industry; banks' book-to-market is not comparable to software's.
  4. Combine into a composite; neutralize to beta, industry and size.
  5. Feed it to the cross-sectional book as a slow alpha, or rebalance standalone monthly.
Signal Construction Sign Origin Value Book equity / market cap; earnings / price; EBITDA / EV + Fama & French (1992); Loughran & Wellman (2011) Profitability (Revenue − COGS) / total assets + Novy-Marx (2013) Accruals (Net income − operating cash flow) / average assets − Sloan (1996) Asset growth Year-over-year change in total assets − Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008) Quality composites Piotroski F-score, quality-minus-junk + Piotroski (2000); Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2019)

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: two semiconductor-equipment firms, same market capitalization and same trailing earnings of $100M.

Item ($M) Firm X Firm Y Net income 100 100 Operating cash flow 40 130 Total assets, now vs a year ago 1,000 vs 800 1,000 vs 950 Accruals / average assets (100 − 40)/900 = +6.7% (100 − 130)/975 = −3.1% Revenue − COGS 320 300 Gross profitability (÷ current assets) 32% 30% Asset growth +25% +5.3%

Same E/P, different quality. Suppose within-sector z-scores are X: value 0, profitability +0.3, accruals −1.2 (sign flipped), asset growth −1.5; Y: 0, +0.1, +0.6, +0.2. Equal-weight composites: X = −0.60, Y = +0.23. With a monthly IC of 0.03, residual volatility of 7% a month and Grinold's alpha = IC × vol × score, the forecast spread is 0.03 × 7% × 0.83 ≈ 17 bps per month: tiny per name, which is why it needs breadth.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Point-in-time handling is D1; ratio design D2; sector-relative transforms D3; IC and decay D4; factor exposures P1.

import pandas as pd

def pit_snapshot(filings, asof, lag_days=1):
    """filings: DataFrame(ticker, item, value, filed_date) with values AS FIRST REPORTED.
    Returns the latest value per (ticker, item) that was public on date `asof`."""
    public = filings[filings.filed_date + pd.Timedelta(days=lag_days) <= asof]
    return (public.sort_values("filed_date")
                  .groupby(["ticker", "item"]).value.last().unstack("item"))

def sector_z(col):
    col = col.clip(col.quantile(0.01), col.quantile(0.99))   # winsorize 1%/99%
    return (col - col.mean()) / col.std()

def fundamental_composite(s, mcap, sector):
    """s: pit_snapshot output (TTM flows, latest balances); higher score = buy."""
    raw = pd.DataFrame({
        "value":   s.book_equity / mcap,                          # B/M
        "gp":      (s.revenue - s.cogs) / s.total_assets,           # Novy-Marx
        "accrual": -(s.net_income - s.cfo) / ((s.total_assets + s.total_assets_lag) / 2),  # Sloan, flipped
        "invest":  -(s.total_assets / s.total_assets_lag - 1),      # asset growth, flipped
    })
    return raw.groupby(sector).transform(sector_z).mean(axis=1)  # then neutralize (D3)

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Reporting lags. 10-Ks are due 60, 75 or 90 days after fiscal year-end and 10-Qs 40 or 45 days after quarter-end, depending on filer size [Verified]. Academic tests often assume a six-month lag; practitioners use the actual filing or announcement timestamp.
  • Announcement vs filing. The release carries income-statement items; the cash-flow statement needed for accruals often arrives only with the 10-Q [Lore]. Timestamp items separately.
  • Restatements. "As-restated" databases overwrite originals with numbers nobody knew then; use values as first reported.
  • Survivorship. Keep delisted firms and delisting returns.
  • Sector-relative and sign-safe. Use E/P, not P/E, so losses rank smoothly; use sector-specific metrics (tangible book for banks).

docs.text:

Line $M per year % of GMV Residual alpha captured +40.0 +4.0% Factor P&L (value, quality tilt not neutralized) ±15 realized ≈ 0 expected Trading costs (15 bps × $2B) −3.0 −0.3% Borrow (0.4% on $500M short) −2.0 −0.2% Financing spread, net −3.0 −0.3% Net +32.0 +3.2%

At 4% volatility, gross Sharpe ≈ 1.0, net ≈ 0.8; factor drawdowns, not costs, are the big risk [Estimate].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Novy-Marx (2013): gross profits-to-assets predicts returns about as well as book-to-market and improves value strategies [Verified].
  • Sloan (1996): low-minus-high accrual hedge earned 10.4% size-adjusted in the following year, 1962–1991 [Reported]; Green, Hand & Soliman (2011): the anomaly decayed until no longer reliably positive, plausibly due to hedge-fund capital [Verified].
  • Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008): low-minus-high asset growth earned about 20% a year in their sample, smaller value-weighted [Reported].
  • McLean & Pontiff (2016): 97 predictors lose 26% out-of-sample and 58% post-publication [Verified].
  • Hou, Xue & Zhang (2020): most of 452 anomalies fail once microcaps are controlled for [Reported].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Low turnover gives large capacity, but everyone sees the same Compustat fields, so value, quality and investment are among the most crowded quant trades. Decay is steepest for simple published ratios; composites, sector-specific metrics and XBRL parsed at filing time hold up better [Lore].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Value drawdowns. Value lost badly in 2018–2020 (see quant winters).
  • Junk rallies. Rebounds in unprofitable growth stocks punish quality and investment shorts.
  • Look-ahead. As-restated data or period-end dating can manufacture a Sharpe (V3).

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Annual June sorts, six-month lag (Fama & French 1992) [Reported] Daily updates keyed to actual filing timestamps [Lore] Decile long-short, one ratio Sector-relative composites inside a multi-alpha optimizer [Lore] Book equity as given Adjustments for intangibles, buybacks and industry accounting [Lore]

docs.text: Value, quality and low volatility (long-only premia), earnings and event-driven (statements traded around release), NLP and LLM signals (reading footnotes), F-score and M-score screens.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Is that point-in-time or as-restated?" → Were values known on the trade date?
  • "We score it within GICS industry." → Ratios are compared only to peers.
  • "Accruals is dead as a standalone." → Decayed, but still useful inside a composite.
  • "Our value leg is really a junk-avoidance leg now." → Returns come more from shorting poor quality than from buying cheap.
  • "Profitability rescued our value sleeve." → Pairing cheap with profitable (Novy-Marx 2013).
  • "Lag everything to the filing timestamp plus a day." → Conservative timing to avoid look-ahead.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text: Myth Reality Quants ignore fundamentals Statement data is a core input to most equity quant books A great backtest on value proves it works Without PIT data and delisting returns, it may be look-ahead Published anomalies stay profitable They lose roughly half their return (McLean & Pontiff 2016)

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
Basic

  • Do you use as-first-reported data, and how do you timestamp items?
  • Do you score within sector or neutralize afterwards?

Informed

  • How did your composite behave in the 2018–2020 value drawdown?
  • Do you adjust book equity for intangibles?

Sharp

  • What share of your fundamental alpha survives full factor neutralization? 🔒
  • Which accounting items do you parse from XBRL before vendors update? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the valuation identity behind profitability and investment

Dividend discount with clean-surplus accounting (\(D_t = Y_t - \Delta B_t\), earnings \(Y\), book equity \(B\)):

\[ \frac{M_t}{B_t} = \frac{\sum_{\tau \ge 1} \mathbb{E}\left[Y_{t+\tau} - \Delta B_{t+\tau}\right] / (1+r)^{\tau}}{B_t} . \]

At fixed \(M/B\), higher expected earnings imply higher \(r\); higher expected investment \(\Delta B\), lower \(r\) (Fama & French 2015).

Cash-flow-statement accruals scaled by average total assets \(A\):

\[ \text{Accruals}_t = \frac{NI_t - CFO_t}{(A_t + A_{t-1})/2} . \]

docs.title: NLP and LLM signals
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Text becomes numbers via word lists (Loughran & McDonald 2011), supervised word weights, transformer classifiers and LLM prompts or embeddings. Each reads context better; none removes point-in-time discipline.
  • Three clocks: machine-readable news (seconds to days), earnings-call tone (days to weeks), filing changes (months; "Lazy Prices" earned up to 188 bps a month, 1995–2014).
  • LLM headline scores predict next-day returns, and the edge shrinks as adoption rises (Lopez-Lira & Tang, JFE 2026).
  • Pretraining look-ahead is the signature backtest trap; time-stamped models suggest it is modest but real.
  • Fast news is a latency race with little capacity; slow text has capacity but is crowded, and firms now write for machine readers.

Level: Core · Read time: ~8 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family mid-freq alpha Edge source informational · behavioral Holding period Seconds to minutes (machine-readable news); 1–5 days (news, call tone); 1–6 months (filing changes) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Holders who never diff this 10-K against last year's, and traders who react to news late: reading everything costs them more than it would earn Universe & instruments US stocks with news and EDGAR coverage (~3,000–4,000 names) Data required Timestamped machine-readable news, EDGAR filings with acceptance times, call transcripts and audio, point-in-time entity mapping Core algorithms used F4 LLMs and foundation models in quant · D2 Feature engineering · D3 Signal transforms · D4 Evaluating signals Infra intensity News: millisecond feed handling and fast execution. Filings and calls: overnight batch, GPU inference Capacity (rough $ range) News sleeves $50M–$500M [Estimate] (30–100% daily turnover); filing and call signals $1B–$5B as composite components [Estimate] (monthly rebalancing, large caps) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Lazy Prices: up to 188 bps a month alpha, gross, 1995–2014 academic backtest [Verified]. Look-ahead-free LLM headline signal: Sharpe 3.20 gross, before costs, on 61,000 firm-day headlines from 2013–2024 (DatedGPT, 2026 preprint) [Verified]. In a composite: +0.2–0.5 net [Lore] Turnover News 30–100% of GMV a day; filing signals 100–300% a year [Estimate] Main risks / failure modes Pretraining look-ahead, bad timestamps, silent model updates, fake news, boilerplate drift Crowding risk High for vendor scores and public-LLM headline scoring; moderate for proprietary document models Firm types that run it Quant hedge funds, multi-manager pods; HFT firms for machine-readable news Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: Information appears in words before numbers. Humans read selectively; machines read everything. The job: a per-stock score at the moment you could have acted. A headline is priced in seconds, a call's tone over days, a quietly rewritten risk-factor section over months.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Limited attention. Lazy Prices found no announcement effect when 10-K language changed; returns came only when the news surfaced later [Verified].
  • Processing cost. LLMs cut the cost of reading, and LLM strategy returns decline as adoption rises (Lopez-Lira & Tang) [Verified].
  • Speed. News analytics speed price responses, and high-frequency traders trade on them (von Beschwitz, Keim & Massa 2020) [Verified].
  • Noise. Some tone is sentiment that reverses (Tetlock; see analyst revisions).

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
Family Signal Horizon Origin Filing changes Similarity to the same filing a year earlier; low → short 1–6 months Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen (2020) Filing tone Share of finance-specific negative or uncertain words Weeks Loughran & McDonald (2011) Call tone Tone of remarks and Q&A; vocal cues Days to weeks Price et al. (2012); Mayew & Venkatachalam (2012) News sentiment Score × relevance × novelty, mapped to the next session Hours to days Ke, Kelly & Xiu (2019) LLM scores or embeddings Prompted score, or embedding → ridge 1–5 days Lopez-Lira & Tang (2026)

Then standardize daily, test incremental IC over earnings surprise, and blend (F5).

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Filing similarity (illustrative). Last year's risk section counts "risk" 10, "supplier" 4, "litigation" 1; this year 11, 4, 6.

\[ \cos = \frac{10\cdot 11 + 4\cdot 4 + 1\cdot 6}{\sqrt{117}\,\sqrt{173}} = \frac{132}{10.82 \times 13.15} = 0.928 . \]

Against a universe median of 0.97, this is a bottom-decile "changer": a short candidate.

Latency ladder (illustrative). After a correctly read positive headline, abnormal return reaches +0.3% at 1 second, +0.8% at 1 minute, +1.0% at 1 hour and +1.2% by the next close.

Act at Captured to next close Round-trip cost Net 1 second 0.9% 0.15% 0.75% 1 minute 0.4% 0.10% 0.30% 1 hour 0.2% 0.08% 0.12%

The same reading is worth six times more in the first second than at one hour. Slow traders need slow information.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Prompts versus embeddings and compute costs: F4. Features: D2; decay weighting: D3; IC by hour since publication: D4; embedding models: ridge, neural nets; timestamps: D1.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

LM_NEG = {"loss", "impairment", "litigation", "restated", "adverse", "decline"}  # excerpt only

def tone(text):
    words = text.lower().split()
    return -sum(w in LM_NEG for w in words) / max(len(words), 1)   # minus negative-word share

def cosine(a, b):
    va = pd.Series(a.lower().split()).value_counts()
    vb = pd.Series(b.lower().split()).value_counts()
    va, vb = va.align(vb, fill_value=0)
    return float(va @ vb / np.sqrt((va @ va) * (vb @ vb)))

def lazy_prices_signal(filings, asof):
    """filings: [ticker, period, accepted_at, text], 10-Ks and 10-Qs in period order.
    Compare each with the filing four periods back (same quarter, prior year)."""
    f = filings[filings.accepted_at <= asof].sort_values("period")   # EDGAR acceptance time
    f["prev"] = f.groupby("ticker").text.shift(4)
    f = f.dropna(subset=["prev"]).groupby("ticker").tail(1)          # latest filing per firm
    sim = pd.Series([cosine(a, b) for a, b in zip(f.text, f.prev)], index=f.ticker)
    return sim.rank(pct=True) - 0.5          # long non-changers, short changers

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Timestamps: vendor receive time and EDGAR acceptance time; after-close text maps to the next open.
  • Relevance and novelty: link entities; drop reprints. Parse risk factors (Item 1A) and MD&A separately.
  • Governance: pin model versions, store outputs, anonymize pre-cutoff text (F4).
  • Incrementality: text often re-encodes the earnings surprise; orthogonalize first.

Line % Filing-change sleeve +1.5 Call-tone sleeve +0.8 News sentiment (1–5 days) +3.0 Trading costs (mostly the news sleeve) −2.2 News and transcript licenses −0.3 Borrow and financing −0.3 GPU and LLM inference −0.05 Net +2.45

At 4% volatility, net Sharpe ≈ 0.6 [Estimate].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Dictionaries: about three-quarters of Harvard-dictionary "negative" words are not negative in 10-Ks (1994–2008) (Loughran & McDonald 2011) [Verified].
  • Filing changes: up to 188 bps a month, 1995–2014; executive, litigation and risk-factor changes matter most (Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen 2020) [Verified].
  • Calls: tone adds to the earnings surprise in explaining reaction and drift (Price et al. 2012); vocal affect predicts performance (Mayew & Venkatachalam 2012) [Reported].
  • News: return-trained sentiment on Dow Jones Newswires beats generic scores (Ke, Kelly & Xiu 2019); LLM news embeddings in 16 markets beat older text methods (Chen, Kelly & Xiu, working paper) [Reported].
  • LLMs: portfolios sorted on GPT-4 headline scores match the direction of the same-day, non-tradable reaction on about 90% of days, a portfolio-day hit rate, not per-headline accuracy; predictability of the later drift is much weaker and concentrated in small stocks and bad news (Lopez-Lira & Tang 2026) [Verified]. Models trained only on past text do nearly as well (He et al. 2025); DatedGPT (Yan et al. 2026) puts the look-ahead premium at 26.4 bps per standard deviation of signal [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text:
Fast news is capped by depth in the first seconds and contested by HFT firms. Slow text has capacity but is public; published predictors lose about 58% after publication (McLean & Pontiff 2016) [Verified]. After Loughran & McDonald, firms with heavy machine readership avoided its negative words (Cao et al. 2023) [Verified]. The signal changed its own input.

flowchart LR
    A["Researchers publish<br/>a word list or model"] --> B["Funds trade on it"]
    B --> C["Firms learn machines read filings"]
    C --> D["Wording avoids<br/>flagged terms"]
    D --> E["Old signal decays"]
    E --> F["New models read<br/>context, audio, diffs"]

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Fake news (April 23, 2013). A hacked AP account tweeted explosions at the White House; the Dow fell about 143 points and the S&P 500 briefly lost ~$136B of value, recovering within minutes [Reported]. Speed amplifies misreads.
  • Look-ahead. A model that has read the future flatters every pre-cutoff backtest (backtest pitfalls).
  • Silent drift. Boilerplate, vendor re-scoring or hosted-model updates change the series without notice [Lore].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Negative-word counts in 10-Ks [Verified] Sentence-level transformer scores and embeddings feeding ridge or GBDT [Lore] "ChatGPT predicts stocks" Modest post-cutoff predictability that shrinks with adoption [Verified]; mostly features and research tooling [Lore] Vendor sentiment scores In-house parsing with novelty and relevance filters [Lore] Backtest from 2000 with today's model Time-stamped models or anonymization [Verified]

docs.text:
Math: tone, similarity and decay weighting

Tone and similarity (term-count vectors \(v\); filing four periods back):

\[ \text{tone}_d = -\frac{\#\{w \in d : w \in \text{NEG}\}}{|d|}, \qquad \text{sim}_{i,t} = \frac{v_{i,t}\cdot v_{i,t-4}}{\lVert v_{i,t}\rVert\,\lVert v_{i,t-4}\rVert} . \]

Decay-weighted news signal with half-life \(h\):

\[ s_{i,t} = \sum_{d:\ t_d \le t} \text{score}_d \, 2^{-(t - t_d)/h} . \]

docs.title: Factor investing fundamentals
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A factor is a long-short rule (cheap minus expensive, winners minus losers) whose return many stocks share. It pays as a risk premium, a persistent mispricing, or a structural constraint on others.
  • Lineage: CAPM → Fama–French 3 (1993) → Carhart 4 (1997) → Fama–French 5 and the q-factor model (2015). Each step re-labels yesterday's "alpha" as beta.
  • Construction choices (breakpoints, weighting, price lag) move results almost as much as the signal.
  • The "factor zoo": one camp says most of 400+ anomalies fail honest tests, another that most replicate. Both find published returns shrink by about half.
  • Single US factors earned gross Sharpe 0.2–0.5 over 1963–2026, far less since 2007; diversification across factors is where the Sharpe comes from.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family risk premia / factors Edge source risk premium · behavioral (structural for low-risk factors) Holding period months (monthly to annual rebalance) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Investors unwilling to hold the factor's bad-times risk, extrapolators who overpay for glamour, and leverage- or benchmark-constrained managers who overpay for high beta Universe & instruments Top 1,000–3,000 US (or global) stocks; long-short via prime broker or swaps, or long-only tilts Data required Point-in-time fundamentals, prices with delisting returns, industry codes; public factor libraries as benchmarks Core algorithms used D3 Signal transforms · P1 Risk models · P3 Mean-variance optimization · P4 Alternatives to MVO · P7 Position sizing and risk budgeting Infra intensity No latency sensitivity; monthly batch Capacity (rough $ range) $5B–$50B gross per long-short manager, far more as long-only tilts [Estimate] (low turnover in large caps; Novy-Marx & Velikov 2016) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Gross academic long-short, 1963-07 to 2026-09 (our computation, French library): HML 0.34, momentum 0.50, RMW 0.37; equal-risk mix 0.71, only 0.23 over 2007–2026 [Verified]. Live multi-asset style fund (AQR Style Premia Alternative): net 0.54 since 2013 (fund disclosure) [Verified]. Post-publication decay ~58% [Verified] Turnover 20–100% a year for value and quality; several times that for momentum [Estimate] Main risks / failure modes Multi-year drawdowns, momentum crashes, crowded deleveraging Crowding risk High: same papers, data and breakpoints Firm types that run it Systematic asset managers, style-premia funds, smart-beta index providers; pods treat factors as risk to neutralize Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: Sort 3,000 stocks on one characteristic, buy the top slice, short the bottom: that spread portfolio is a factor, a common driver of returns like an industry. In M&A terms, CAPM alpha is adjusted EBITDA; a factor model is the reconciliation showing how much is cheap, recurring exposure rather than skill.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Story Logic Examples Predicts Risk premium Loses in bad times, so holders demand pay value, carry persists Mispricing Extrapolation or under-reaction plus limits to arbitrage momentum, value decays as capital arrives Structural Leverage limits or benchmarks force overpaying low beta lasts while the constraint binds

For most factors the evidence is mixed; see value, quality and low-vol.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Characteristic, point-in-time (D1): Fama–French use fiscal-year t−1 book equity over December t−1 market equity.
  2. Breakpoints: NYSE median for size; NYSE 30th and 70th percentiles for the characteristic.
  3. Portfolios: six value-weighted; HML = ½(small value + big value) − ½(small growth + big growth) [Verified] (French library).
  4. Rebalance: each June for value, profitability and investment; monthly for momentum.
  5. Implement: long-short, or a long-only smart beta tilt with a 2–4% tracking error budget [Estimate].
  6. Attribute: regress returns on the factors; the residual mean is alpha.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: a manager earns 9.0% a year over cash with market beta 0.9. Our computed 1963–2026 premia: market 7.2%, HML 3.5%, RMW 3.0%, momentum 7.3%.

Step Calculation Result CAPM alpha 9.0 − 0.9 × 7.2 +2.5% Value exposure loading 0.3 × 3.5 1.05% Profitability exposure 0.4 × 3.0 1.20% Momentum exposure 0.2 × 7.3 1.46% Multi-factor alpha 2.5 − 1.05 − 1.20 − 1.46 −1.2%

The "alpha" was factor beta, available from a style-premia fund for a fraction of the fee; allocators run exactly this regression.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Ranks and z-scores come from D3; factor covariances from P1; combining factors uses P3 or risk parity (P4); volatility targeting is P7.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def ff_factor(df):
    """Fama-French-style 2x3 factor for one formation date (end of June).
    df: one row per stock with me (market equity), char (e.g. book-to-market,
    point-in-time), is_nyse (bool), ret_next (returns for the next 12 months)."""
    nyse = df[df.is_nyse]
    size_bp = nyse.me.median()                          # NYSE size breakpoint
    lo, hi = nyse.char.quantile([0.3, 0.7])             # NYSE 30th / 70th percentiles
    df = df.assign(size=np.where(df.me <= size_bp, "S", "B"),
                   style=np.select([df.char <= lo, df.char >= hi], ["L", "H"], "M"))

    def vw(g):                                          # value-weighted portfolio return
        return (g.ret_next * g.me).sum() / g.me.sum()
    port = df.groupby(["size", "style"]).apply(vw)
    # HML = 1/2 (small high + big high) - 1/2 (small low + big low)
    return 0.5 * (port["S", "H"] + port["B", "H"]) - 0.5 * (port["S", "L"] + port["B", "L"])

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Breakpoints and weights. All-stock breakpoints with equal weights let microcaps dominate; NYSE breakpoints and value weights are what make most anomalies insignificant in Hou, Xue & Zhang (2020) [Verified].
  • Price lag. Fama–French hold December prices up to 18 months; using the current price improves value, especially alongside momentum (Asness & Frazzini 2013, AQR's "HML Devil") [Reported].
  • Long-only. Smart beta drops the short leg: cheaper, more capacity, but mostly market risk [Lore].
  • Costs. Anomalies with under 50% monthly turnover mostly survive costs with a buy/hold buffer; few faster ones do (Novy-Marx & Velikov 2016) [Verified].

docs.title: P&L decomposition
docs.text:
Illustrative: $1B NAV, $1B long and $1B short, equal-risk value + profitability + momentum, 8% volatility target.

Line % of NAV a year Factor premia, gross (Sharpe 0.5 × 8%) +4.0 Trading costs (150% turnover × $2B × 10 bps) −0.3 Borrow on $1B short (0.3%) −0.3 Financing spread, net −0.2 Management fee −1.0 Net to investor +2.2 (Sharpe ≈ 0.28)

Fees, not trading costs, are the biggest leak.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Our computation of gross Sharpe ratios from the French library (monthly, no costs) [Verified]:

Factor 1963–1991 1992–2026 2007–2026 Market 0.31 0.60 0.65 HML (value) 0.52 0.23 −0.12 Momentum (UMD) 0.84 0.30 0.10 RMW (profitability) 0.46 0.35 0.38 CMA (investment) 0.52 0.33 0.01 Equal-risk HML + UMD + RMW 1.30 0.49 0.23
  • Fama & French (2015): with profitability and investment added, HML is redundant in their sample [Verified]. Hou, Xue & Zhang (2015): about half of ~80 anomalies are insignificant; the q-factor model matches or beats Fama–French and Carhart on the rest [Verified].
  • Skeptics. Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2016): after hundreds of tests a new factor needs t > 3.0 [Verified]. Hou, Xue & Zhang (2020): 65% of 452 anomalies fail |t| ≥ 1.96; 82% fail 2.78 [Verified].
  • Defenders. Chen & Zimmermann (2022): of 161 clearly significant originals, 98% still show t > 1.96 [Verified]. Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen (2023): 153 factors form 13 themes, and most replicate across 93 countries [Verified].
  • Decay. McLean & Pontiff (2016): 97 predictors lose 26% out of sample and 58% after publication [Verified].

Both camps agree magnitudes shrink; they disagree on whether the factor zoo is mostly false or mostly redundant.

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Low turnover in large caps gives the most capacity of any equity quant style; the price is crowding and correlated exits (see factor timing and crowding).

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• August 2007: crowded books unwound together (Khandani & Lo 2011) [Verified].
  • Spring 2009: momentum lost about 49% over March–May (our computation) [Verified]; see momentum.
  • Value winter: HML fell 58% from December 2006 to September 2020 [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today One characteristic, 2×3 sorts, annual rebalance (Fama & French 1993) [Verified] Multi-measure composites per theme, rebalanced monthly or daily with buffers [Lore] Factors as the expected-return model Risk to hedge in pods; cheap beta in style funds [Lore] Static weights Risk budgets (P7), sometimes timed (F6) [Lore]

docs.text:

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: factor regressions, t-statistics and the t > 3 hurdle

Time-series regression of an excess return on \(K\) factors:

\[ r_t - r_f = \alpha + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_k f_{k,t} + \varepsilon_t . \]

With annualized Sharpe \(SR\) over \(T\) years, the t-statistic of the mean is

\[ t \approx SR \sqrt{T} . \]

Over 50 years, \(t > 3\) needs \(SR > 3/\sqrt{50} \approx 0.42\); \(t > 2\) needs only \(0.28\).

Combining \(N\) equal-risk factors with Sharpe \(\overline{SR}\) and average correlation \(\bar\rho\):

\[ SR_{\text{combo}} = \overline{SR} \sqrt{\frac{N}{1 + (N-1)\bar\rho}} . \]

With \(N = 3\), \(\overline{SR} = 0.40\), \(\bar\rho \approx 0\): \(0.40\sqrt{3} \approx 0.69\), near the 0.71 computed above.

docs.title: Factor timing, crowding and quant winters
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Factor books suffer two kinds of pain: fast crowded unwinds (August 2007, days) and slow premium droughts (the 2018–2020 "quant winter", years). They need different defenses.
  • Timing factors with value spreads or factor momentum works in some academic tests and disappoints in others; value-spread timing is largely more value.
  • Crowding is measured indirectly: short interest, comomentum, valuation spreads, prime-broker positioning data.
  • Leverage turns a crowded trade into a spiral, and selling at the bottom locks in losses the unlevered trade later recovers.
  • The usual response is diversification, volatility targeting, bounded tilts and less-crowded signal variants, not heroic timing.

Level: Deep dive · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family risk premia / factors (overlay and risk management) Edge source risk premium; timing tries to add a behavioral edge Holding period timing tilts: months to years; crowding responses: days to weeks Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it If timing works, investors who chase factor returns or capitulate at the bottom; in an unwind, forced sellers pay whoever has balance sheet Universe & instruments The factor book itself: equity long-short factors, cross-asset styles Data required Daily factor returns, leg valuations, short interest, holdings, prime-broker crowding reports, residual returns Core algorithms used F6 Regime detection · L2 Alpha decay detection · P7 Position sizing and risk budgeting · P1 Risk models Infra intensity Low; daily risk batch, intraday monitoring in stress Capacity (rough $ range) An overlay on the factor book, so capacity is the book's; providing liquidity in unwinds is limited by balance sheet [Estimate] Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Not standalone; bounded timing overlays plausibly add 0–0.2 gross [Estimate]. Academic results range from little gain (Asness et al. 2017) to substantial (Haddad, Kozak & Santosh 2020) [Verified] Turnover Low for spread timing; monthly for factor momentum Main risks / failure modes Cheap factors getting cheaper; de-grossing at the bottom; noisy crowding gauges Crowding risk The subject of this page Firm types that run it Every factor and quant equity manager; prime brokers publish crowding analytics [Reported] Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A premium drought is a long recession in one industry: nothing is forced, the business just earns too little for years. A crowded unwind is a bank run: leveraged funds share positions, one is forced to sell, prices move against all, and the next must sell. Timing tries to dodge droughts; crowding monitors try to dodge runs.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Why timing could work. Expected factor returns should rise when the long leg is cheap relative to the short leg (a wide value spread). Factors are also autocorrelated: the average factor earned 6 bps a month after a losing year and 51 bps after a winning one (Ehsani & Linnainmaa 2022) [Verified].

Why it is hard. Few independent episodes, and value-spread timing is mostly more value exposure (Asness, Chandra, Ilmanen & Israel 2017) [Verified].

Why crowding matters. Capital in value and momentum grew from the late 1980s and lowered their returns (Hanson & Sunderam 2014) [Verified]; crowded momentum trading can push prices past fundamentals (Lou & Polk 2022) [Verified].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Value spread per factor: log book-to-market of the long leg minus the short leg, z-scored against history.
  2. Factor momentum: sign of the factor's trailing 12-month return.
  3. Crowding: excess residual correlation inside each leg, short interest in the short leg, overlap with peers' holdings.
  4. Tilt: bounded multipliers, for example 0.5× to 1.5× of the strategic weight, changed slowly.
  5. Risk overlay: volatility targeting (P7), factor covariances (P1), stress regimes (F6).
  6. Decay review (L2): separate a drought from a dead signal.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative deleveraging spiral: $1,000M NAV, gross 8× ($4,000M long, $4,000M short), prime-broker cap 8×.

Day Spread move P&L ($M) NAV ($M) Gross allowed ($M) Forced trading ($M) 1 −3% −4,000 × 3% = −120 880 7,040 960 2 −2% −3,520 × 2% = −70 810 6,477 563 3 +5% (reversal) +3,238 × 5% = +162 972 — — Costs 30 bps on 1,523 traded −5 967

An investor who held without trading would be flat (−120 − 80 + 200 = 0); the de-levered fund is down 3.3%. Khandani & Lo (2011) estimate an 8:1 levered book-to-market portfolio lost 24% from 1 August to the close of 7 August 2007, before prices reverted on 10 August [Verified].

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def value_spread_z(bm_long, bm_short, hist):
    """Log book-to-market of the long leg minus the short leg, z-scored vs its history."""
    spread = np.log(np.median(bm_long)) - np.log(np.median(bm_short))
    return (spread - np.mean(hist)) / np.std(hist)

def comomentum(resid_long):
    """Lou-Polk-style gauge (simplified): mean pairwise correlation of weekly
    factor-model residuals among long-leg stocks over the past 52 weeks."""
    c = np.corrcoef(resid_long.T)
    n = c.shape[0]
    return (c.sum() - n) / (n * (n - 1))

def factor_weight(base_w, spread_z, ret_12m, crowd_z, vol, target_vol=0.05,
                  k=0.15, lo=0.5, hi=1.5):
    tilt = 1 + k * spread_z + k * np.sign(ret_12m) - k * crowd_z  # cheap, trending, uncrowded
    tilt = np.clip(tilt, lo, hi)              # bounded: timing never dominates the book
    return base_w * tilt * target_vol / vol   # P7 volatility targeting

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Bounded and slow. Tilts of ±50%, changed monthly, keep timing errors survivable [Lore].
  • Spread definition. Industry-neutral spreads avoid reading a sector bubble as factor cheapness [Lore].
  • Crowding data. Short interest is twice-monthly, holdings quarterly and stale; prime-broker reports are timelier but cover only that broker's clients [Reported].
  • Pre-agreed de-grossing. Rules set in calm markets beat judgment in a run, at the cost shown above [Lore].
  • De-crowding. Proprietary variants, other universes and faster signals reduce overlap [Lore].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Timing works. Haddad, Kozak & Santosh (2020): market-neutral equity factors are strongly predictable, and exploiting this substantially improves on static factor investing [Verified].
  • Timing disappoints. Asness et al. (2017): value-spread timing inside a portfolio that already holds value adds little over a strategic value allocation [Verified].
  • Spreads can widen for years. Our computation from French data: value-over-growth book-to-market at June formation ranked at the 10th percentile of 1951–2026 in 2007, the 86th in 2017, the 99th in 2022 and the widest on record in June 2026 [Verified]; intangibles may inflate book-based spreads. Value lost 51% from January 2017 to September 2020.
  • Quant winter, firm level. AQR's Style Premia Alternative Fund returned −12.4%, −8.2% and −22.0% in 2018–2020, then +24.8% and +30.6% in 2021–2022 (fund fact sheet) [Verified]. AQR's regulatory assets (SEC-reported, including leverage) fell from $248.9B in 2019 to $164.4B in 2020 (Institutional Investor) [Reported]. AQR argues the losses came from value spreads widening, not crowded unwinds [Verified] (firm white paper, 2026).

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Crowding depends on capital, leverage and overlap, not the idea. A crowded factor earns less and has fatter left tails; the same gauges feed L2 decay reviews.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• August 2007. The sustained unwind started at the open on 6 August; market makers withdrew from 8 August (Khandani & Lo 2011) [Verified]. Goldman and outside investors put $3B into its Global Equity Opportunities fund on 13 August [Verified].
  • 2020. HML lost 13.8% in March; momentum lost 12.6% in November's vaccine rotation (our computation) [Verified].
  • 2025–2026. Systematic equity funds, on pace for a record monthly loss in a junk rally, finished July 2025 down about 2%; a June–July 2026 AI-stock reversal cut their year-to-date return from 14.4% to 10.8% (Goldman prime-brokerage data via press) [Reported].

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: why leverage squares forced selling

Equity \(E\), leverage cap \(\lambda\), gross \(G = \lambda E\) split equally long and short. A spread move \(s\) against the book loses

\[ \Delta E = -\frac{G}{2} s = -\frac{\lambda E s}{2} . \]

Restoring \(G = \lambda (E + \Delta E)\) forces trades of

\[ \Delta G = \lambda \Delta E = -\frac{\lambda^2 E s}{2} . \]

Forced selling scales with \(\lambda^2\): doubling leverage quadruples it. Comomentum for long-leg stocks \(i, j\) with residuals \(\varepsilon\):

\[ \text{CoMom}_t = \frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} \text{corr}(\varepsilon_{i}, \varepsilon_{j}) . \]
