docs.title: Momentum
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Buy the past year's winners, short its losers, skip the latest month ("12-1"). About 1% a month over 1965–1989 (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993), and it outlived publication.
  • It appears across industries, countries and asset classes, negatively correlated with value, its natural partner (Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen 2013).
  • US long-run gross Sharpe is about 0.5 but only 0.14 since 2000, with the worst crashes of any major factor (−74% in July–August 1932, −49% in March–May 2009) when high-beta losers rebound.
  • Crashes are partly predictable: volatility scaling roughly doubles the Sharpe (0.45 → 0.87 on the same 1927–2026 months, our replication).
  • Low turnover (Lab 10: 6.5× a year against reversal's 90×) gives large capacity, with break-even estimates of $52B in the US. Crowding is the price.

Level: Core · Read time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family risk premia / factors Edge source behavioral · risk premium (contested) Holding period Monthly rebalance; positions last about 4 months [Estimate] (Lab 10 turnover) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Under-reacting investors who anchor on old prices, sell winners early, cling to losers and update slowly; if the risk story is right, also investors unwilling to carry momentum's crash exposure Universe & instruments Top 1,000–3,000 US stocks (also global stocks, industries, futures); long-short, or long-only indexes Data required Point-in-time total returns including delisted stocks; market caps; industry codes; factor residuals; daily returns; borrow Core algorithms used D3 Signal transforms · P1 Risk models · P7 Position sizing and risk budgeting · P5 Transaction cost and impact models Infra intensity Low: monthly batch; trades worked over days Capacity (rough $ range) Break-even $52B US, $89B global, $122B global optimized (Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz 2012; AQR-affiliated, 1998–2011 costs) [Verified]; $5B+ liquidity-weighted at 1999 caps (Korajczyk & Sadka 2004) [Verified]. Per manager $1B–$20B [Estimate] (profit peaks near 4/9 of break-even; many managers share it) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Fama-French momentum factor (UMD), gross: 0.46 (1927–2026), 0.84 (1963–1991), 0.30 (1992–2026), 0.14 (2000–2026); volatility-scaled 0.87 and 0.41 (1927– and 2000–2026) [Verified] (our computation, French library). Net: subtract 0.05–0.15 for costs at moderate size [Estimate] Turnover 5–8× the gross book a year for a monthly decile book (Lab 10: 6.5×) [Estimate] Main risks / failure modes Crashes in rebounds after bear markets; junk rallies; abrupt leadership rotations; crowding Crowding risk High: standard in risk models, smart beta and quant books [Lore]; see comomentum Firm types that run it Systematic asset managers, style-premia funds, smart-beta providers, quant hedge funds; pods hedge it as risk Lab Lab 10

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: News reaches prices in steps: an earnings beat, a guidance raise, analysts lifting estimates for months. A stock that has beaten the market for a year tends to keep beating it for a few months. Momentum buys that persistence across thousands of stocks and shorts its mirror image, skipping the latest month because one-month moves reverse (short-term reversal). The market prices a turnaround the way a board backs one: partially, then fully once several quarters confirm it.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Story Mechanism Supporting evidence Under-reaction Information diffuses gradually; trend-chasers overshoot (Hong & Stein 1999) [Verified] Part of the first-year profit later reverses (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993, 2001) [Verified] Overconfidence Biased self-attribution creates short-lag momentum and long-lag reversal (Daniel, Hirshleifer & Subrahmanyam 1998) [Verified] The same later reversal Rational risk Time-varying expected growth rates produce momentum (Johnson 2002) [Verified] A common factor across eight markets and asset classes, partly funding liquidity risk (Asness et al. 2013) [Verified] Crash premium In panics, losers' option-like payoffs carry a high premium (Daniel & Moskowitz 2016) [Verified] UMD skewness −3.0 since 1927 (our computation) [Verified]

The later reversal is what behavioral models predict, though Jegadeesh and Titman temper their support with caution [Verified]. Yet momentum co-moves across asset classes with very different investors, which one bias explains poorly. The evidence is mixed.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Universe: point-in-time at month-end, including later-delisted names (D1).
  2. Score: return from 12 months ago to 1 month ago ("12-1").
  3. Clean (D3): winsorize; optionally rank within industry or on factor-model residuals (P1).
  4. Portfolio: long the top decile or 30%, short the bottom; hedge beta and industries.
  5. Size (P7): scale to a volatility target; cut further after bear markets (F6).
  6. Rebalance monthly with buffers (P6); trade over days (E2), netting against value.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative crash mechanics: $1B long winners, $1B short losers, entering a rebound after a 30% market fall.

Step Calculation Result Long winners, beta 0.6 $1B × 0.6 +$0.6B market exposure Short losers, beta 1.8 −$1B × 1.8 −$1.8B Net market exposure 0.6 − 1.8 −$1.2B Market rebounds 15% in a month −$1.2B × 15% −$180M A normal month's expected premium $1B × 0.6% +$6M Months of premium lost 180 / 6 30 Beta hedge: buy $1.2B of index futures market term → 0 industry and style tilts remain

These betas are mild: after major declines Daniel and Moskowitz find loser betas above 3 and winner betas below 0.5 [Verified]. The 0.6% monthly premium matches UMD's long-run 7.3% a year.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Residual momentum and the beta hedge need P1; volatility targeting is P7; costs come from P5.

# Mirrors Lab 10 (labs/10-reversal-momentum-costs/lab.py); vol scaling is an addition.
def momentum_signal(returns, lookback=252, skip=21):
    """12-1 momentum (Jegadeesh-Titman 1993): log return over days t-251 .. t-21."""
    log_ret = np.log1p(returns)
    return log_ret.rolling(lookback - skip).sum().shift(skip)   # skip the reversal month

def decile_weights(signal, q=0.1):
    """Long top decile, short bottom decile, equal weight, +0.5 / -0.5 (gross 1)."""
    rank = signal.rank(axis=1, pct=True)
    top, bottom = rank > 1 - q, rank <= q
    return top.div(top.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 0.5 - bottom.div(bottom.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 0.5

def beta_hedge(weights, beta):
    """Add an equal-weighted universe basket so the book's beta sum(w * beta) is zero."""
    hedge = -weights.mul(beta, axis=1).sum(axis=1) / beta.mean()
    return weights + np.outer(hedge, np.full(len(beta), 1.0 / len(beta)))

def vol_scale(book_daily_returns, target_vol=0.12, window=126):
    """Not in the lab: Barroso & Santa-Clara (2015) leverage, known before each month."""
    realized = book_daily_returns.rolling(window).std() * np.sqrt(252)
    return (target_vol / realized).shift(1)
# The lab rebalances the decile book every 21 trading days and charges apply_costs().

Right panel: momentum's net P&L (solid) stays close to gross (dashed); the arrow marks its worst month. Synthetic data.

Momentum (orange) stays positive up to 52.5 bps per dollar traded and to just under a $1B book. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab result: at $100M the decile book's Sharpe is 0.81 gross and 0.47 net, with 6.5× turnover and costs of 1.3% of the book a year (reversal: 19.5%). Its worst month lost 3.7% as the market rose 5.5% after a −28% year; 2.6 points came from sector and style tilts, so the beta-hedged book still lost 3.2%. The constant planted IC and gentle simulated rebounds flatter the toy: real UMD has a Sharpe of 0.14 since 2000 and a −34% month.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Lookback. 12-1 is standard. Novy-Marx (2012) finds returns from 12 to 7 months ago do most of the work [Reported].
  • Residual momentum. Ranking on factor-model residuals about doubles the risk-adjusted profit (Blitz, Huij & Martens 2011) [Verified]: Sharpe 0.90 against 0.45, 1926–2009 [Reported].
  • Industry. Industry momentum accounts for much of stock momentum (Moskowitz & Grinblatt 1999) [Verified]; industry-neutral books give it up to avoid sector concentration.
  • Crash management. Scaling to constant risk virtually eliminates crashes and nearly doubles the Sharpe (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015) [Verified], as do Daniel and Moskowitz's dynamic weights [Verified].
  • Buffers and netting. Buy at the top decile but sell only below the top 20–30% [Lore]. Netting momentum's trades against value's raises the pair's US break-even to $100B (Frazzini et al. 2012) [Verified].
  • Shorts. Losers are more often hard to borrow; long-only indexes avoid this but are mostly market beta [Lore].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Our computation from the French library (monthly, gross, no costs; volatility-scaled to 12% using the prior 126 days) [Verified]:

Period UMD Sharpe Volatility-scaled Worst month 1927–1962 0.41 0.82 −52.6% (August 1932) 1963-07 to 1991 0.84 1.12 −13.8% (January 1975) 1992 to 2026-09 0.30 0.66 −34.4% (April 2009) 2010 to 2026-09 0.26 0.46 −16.2% (January 2023)
  • Original result. Over 1965–1989, 6-month formation earned about 1% a month and 12-month/3-month 1.31%, despite losing about 7% each January (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993) [Verified].
  • After publication. Profits continued in the 1990s (Jegadeesh & Titman 2001) [Verified]; UMD's 1990–1999 Sharpe was 1.21.
  • Everywhere. Value and momentum premia in eight markets and asset classes, negatively correlated (Asness et al. 2013) [Verified]. UMD–HML correlation is −0.41 since 1927 (−0.19 since 1963); a 50/50 risk mix has a Sharpe of 0.73 against 0.46 and 0.34 alone [Verified].
  • Bear-market state. In the 235 months after the market's monthly excess returns summed to a negative number over the prior 24 months, UMD averaged −0.27% a month, against +0.83% otherwise [Verified].
  • Costs. Lesmond, Schill & Zhou (2004) call the profits illusory [Reported]; live execution data put costs below a tenth of earlier estimates (Frazzini et al. 2012) [Verified].
  • Recent years (monthly returns compounded). UMD: +20.2% (2022), −20.5% (2023, −16.2% in January), +18.5% (2024), −2.2% (2025), +11.0% (2026 to September) [Verified].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Momentum's break-even ($52B US) is almost six times reversal's ($9B) because it trades far less (a fourteenth as much in Lab 10). Decay is real: the Sharpe fell from 0.84 before 1992 to 0.30 after, about the average post-publication loss across anomalies (factor fundamentals). Crowded momentum trading can push prices past fundamentals, and comomentum detects it (Lou & Polk 2022) [Verified]. See factor timing and crowding.

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Rebound crashes. In July–August 1932 past losers returned 232% against winners' 32%; in March–May 2009, 163% against 8% (Daniel & Moskowitz, 1927–2013 sample) [Verified]. UMD lost 74% and 49% in those windows [Verified].
  • Rotations and junk rallies. January 2001 −25.4%; 9 November 2020 −14.4% in one day on vaccine news; January 2023 −16.2% [Verified].
  • Leadership reversal, 2026. UMD lost 17.9% from 22 June to 3 September 2026 (July −12.2%) [Verified] as crowded AI winners reversed [Reported].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Equal-weighted 12-1 deciles, monthly (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993) [Verified] Risk-weighted, residual or industry-adjusted, buffered, optimized [Lore] Static exposure Volatility-scaled or crash-managed (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015; Daniel & Moskowitz 2016) [Verified]; how widely firms do this is [Lore] A standalone factor Paired with value (Asness et al. 2013) [Verified]; pods neutralize it as risk [Lore]

  • Related signals: industry and residual momentum; factor momentum (factor timing); earnings drift; analyst revisions; short-term momentum in high-turnover stocks (Medhat & Schmeling 2022) [Verified].

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the 12-1 score, crash beta and volatility scaling

12-1 score for holding month \(t\) (French: months \(t-12\) to \(t-2\); Lab 10: days \(t-251\) to \(t-21\)):

\[ \text{MOM}_{i,t} = \sum_{k=2}^{12} \ln\left(1 + r_{i,t-k}\right). \]

The book's beta is the difference of its legs' betas:

\[ \beta_{WML,t} = \beta_{W,t} - \beta_{L,t} . \]

After a decline, \(\beta_{L,t}\) can exceed 3 and \(\beta_{W,t}\) fall below 0.5, so a rebound \(R_m\) costs about \(|\beta_{WML,t}| R_m\) with \(|\beta_{WML,t}| > 2\).

Volatility scaling with target \(\sigma^{*}\) and 126 prior daily returns:

\[ w_t = \frac{\sigma^{*}}{\hat\sigma_t}, \qquad \hat\sigma_t^2 = \frac{252}{126} \sum_{j=1}^{126} r_{t-j}^2 . \]

Volatility spikes before crashes, so \(w_t\) falls first: in our replication leverage was 0.3× in spring 2009, and the loss was 16% instead of 49%.

docs.title: Value, quality and low volatility
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Three questions per stock: is it cheap (value), a good business (quality), boring (low beta or volatility)? Buy the yeses, short the noes.
  • They pay for different reasons (distress and extrapolation; underpriced profitability; leverage constraints) and are weakly correlated with each other and with momentum, so the combination carries the Sharpe.
  • Value's worst run on record: HML −58% from December 2006 to September 2020, then +68% to December 2022. Whether intangibles broke book value is still debated.
  • Long-run gross Sharpe: value 0.34, profitability 0.37, quality-minus-junk 0.48, betting-against-beta 0.70. Capacity is large; crowding and long drawdowns are the risks.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family risk premia / factors Edge source risk premium · behavioral (structural for low beta) Holding period 3–12 months Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Extrapolators overpaying for glamour; investors shunning distress; lottery-seekers buying unprofitable "junk"; leverage-constrained or benchmarked managers buying high beta instead of borrowing Universe & instruments US and global large and mid caps; long-short, or long-only value, quality and minimum-volatility products Data required Point-in-time book, gross profit, earnings, leverage, accruals; 1–5 years of daily returns for betas and volatility Core algorithms used D3 Signal transforms · P1 Risk models · P3 Mean-variance optimization · P4 Alternatives to MVO Infra intensity No latency sensitivity; monthly batch Capacity (rough $ range) $10B+ per long-short manager; long-only far larger [Estimate] (slow large-cap rebalancing; high capacity per Novy-Marx & Velikov 2016) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Gross academic long-short (our computation from French and AQR data): HML 0.34 and RMW 0.37 (1963–2026), QMJ 0.48 (1957–2026), BAB 0.70 (1930–2026); since 2010: HML −0.06, RMW 0.22, QMJ 0.25, BAB 0.76 [Verified]. Net of costs and fees, subtract roughly 0.1–0.3 [Estimate] Turnover 30–80% a year for value and quality; more for beta sorts [Estimate] Main risks / failure modes Growth bubbles, junk rallies, rate shocks for low-vol, funding squeezes for levered low beta Crowding risk High, especially in long-only quality and minimum-volatility products Firm types that run it Systematic asset managers, style-premia funds, smart-beta index providers Lab —

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A disciplined fundamental investor buys cheap, good, unexciting companies. These three styles do the same mechanically across 3,000 stocks. Each alone has decade-long losing streaks; together they hedge one another, because cheap stocks are often low quality and quality stocks are rarely cheap.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text: Style Risk story Behavioral or structural story Value Cheap firms are distressed and do worst in bad times Investors extrapolate growth and overpay for glamour Quality / profitability Weak: profitable firms are less distressed (Novy-Marx 2013) [Verified] Quality is only modestly priced, and analysts err systematically on it (Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen 2019) [Verified] Low beta and low volatility High-beta stocks pay off in good times Leverage-constrained investors buy high beta instead of borrowing (Frazzini & Pedersen 2014) [Verified]; benchmarked managers avoid low-beta stocks (Baker, Bradley & Wurgler 2011) [Verified]

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Value: book-to-market at the current price, plus earnings and cash-flow yields.
  2. Quality: gross profits to assets, ROE, low accruals, low leverage, stable earnings.
  3. Low beta: betas from daily returns, shrunk toward 1.
  4. Rank within sector (D3); combine scores or run sleeves.
  5. Size sleeves to equal risk with a factor covariance (P1, P4), or optimize (P3).
  6. For betting against beta, scale each leg to beta 1.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative betting-against-beta (BAB) leg sizing. Low-beta portfolio β = 0.7, high-beta β = 1.4, market premium 6%.

Step Calculation Result Long low-beta, scaled to β = 1 $1 / 0.7 $1.43 Short high-beta, scaled to β = 1 $1 / 1.4 $0.71 CAPM excess returns 0.7 × 6% and 1.4 × 6% 4.2% and 8.4% BAB return if CAPM holds 1.43 × 4.2 − 0.71 × 8.4 ≈ 0% "Flat" market line: low-beta earns 6%, high-beta 7% 1.43 × 6 − 0.71 × 7 +3.6% Funding spread on $0.71 net long at 0.5% 0.71 × 0.5 −0.36%

The trade earns exactly the flatness of the security market line, which Frazzini & Pedersen attribute to leverage-constrained buyers of high beta.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def defensive_value_scores(f, sector):
    """f: point-in-time DataFrame per stock. Returns sector-relative ranks in [-0.5, 0.5]."""
    raw = pd.DataFrame({
        "value":   f.book_equity / f.mcap_today,             # current price, not lagged
        "quality": f.gross_profit / f.total_assets,          # Novy-Marx (2013)
        "lowbeta": -(0.6 * f.beta_ts + 0.4 * 1.0),           # shrunk beta, sign flipped
    })
    return raw.groupby(sector).rank(pct=True) - 0.5          # D3: within-sector ranks

def bab_weights(beta, n_tail=0.3):
    """Long low-beta, short high-beta; each leg scaled to beta 1 (Frazzini-Pedersen)."""
    z = beta.rank(pct=True)
    lo, hi = z <= n_tail, z >= 1 - n_tail
    w_lo = pd.Series(np.where(lo, 1.0, 0.0), beta.index); w_lo /= w_lo.sum()
    w_hi = pd.Series(np.where(hi, 1.0, 0.0), beta.index); w_hi /= w_hi.sum()
    beta_lo, beta_hi = (w_lo * beta).sum(), (w_hi * beta).sum()
    return w_lo / beta_lo - w_hi / beta_hi                   # net long when beta_lo < beta_hi

Simplified: Frazzini & Pedersen rank-weight within legs; this sketch equal-weights the tails.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Which value. Plain B/M penalizes firms whose assets are expensed R&D and brands; capitalizing intangibles changes what looks cheap (Eisfeldt, Kim & Papanikolaou 2022) [Reported].
  • Which quality. One ratio (gross profitability) or a composite of profitability, growth and safety (QMJ); composites are steadier [Lore].
  • Sector control. Unconstrained low-vol loads on utilities and staples, a bond-rate bet [Lore].
  • BAB construction. Its results rest on choices that effectively equal-weight, putting $1.05 per $1 into the smallest 1% of stocks (Novy-Marx & Velikov 2022) [Verified].
  • Integrate or stack. One composite avoids buying a stock in one sleeve while selling it in another [Lore].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Our computation, gross annualized Sharpe ratios (HML, RMW from French; QMJ, BAB from AQR) [Verified]:

Factor Full history 1963–1991 1992–2026 2010–2026 HML value 0.34 (1926–) 0.52 0.23 −0.06 RMW profitability 0.37 (1963–) 0.46 0.35 0.22 QMJ quality 0.48 (1957–) 0.68 0.40 0.25 BAB low beta 0.70 (1930–) 1.06 0.67 0.76

Correlations of monthly returns, 1963–2026: HML with momentum −0.19, HML with RMW 0.10, HML with BAB 0.31, RMW with QMJ 0.70 [Verified]. Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013) find value and momentum negatively correlated across asset classes [Reported].

The value debate. Arnott, Harvey, Kalesnik & Linnainmaa (2021) measure a 55% HML drawdown to mid-2020, attribute all of it to value getting cheaper relative to growth rather than to failing fundamentals, and find intangibles-adjusted value did far better [Verified]. Lev & Srivastava (2022) argue book value mis-measures intangible-heavy firms [Reported]; Israel, Laursen & Richardson (2021) argue systematic value is not dead [Reported]. The other side: a dying premium would also show widening spreads and a negative Sharpe since 2007.

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Slow large-cap trading makes these the highest-capacity equity factors. Decay is uneven: value faded after 2007, profitability less, BAB held up in AQR's data. Crowding shows in valuation spreads (see factor timing and crowding).

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Growth bubbles. HML fell 51% from January 2017 to September 2020, including −13.8% in March 2020 alone (our computation) [Verified].
  • Junk rallies. QMJ lost 36% from October 2023 to June 2026, including −11% in 2025, as unprofitable and speculative stocks surged [Verified] (AQR data, our computation).
  • Beta manias and funding squeezes. BAB fell 55% from May 1998 to February 2000, the tech bubble [Verified]; Frazzini & Pedersen predict BAB does badly when funding tightens [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today HML on December prices (Fama & French 1993) [Verified] Current prices, several value measures, intangibles adjustments [Lore] One profitability ratio (Novy-Marx 2013) [Verified] Multi-metric quality composites [Lore] Rank-weighted BAB with small caps (Frazzini & Pedersen 2014) [Verified] Sector-constrained low-beta inside an optimizer [Lore]

docs.text: Momentum (the natural hedge for value), fundamental quant signals (the same ratios as alpha), minimum-variance portfolios (P4), and cross-asset value and carry.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Value is a trade on growth's multiple." → Returns depend on the valuation spread.
  • "Our value is intangibles-adjusted." → Book equity includes capitalized R&D and SG&A.
  • "That's a junk rally." → Low-quality, high-beta stocks are outperforming.
  • "Low-vol is a bond proxy." → Defensive stocks trade on interest rates.
  • "BAB is mostly a small-cap trade." → The Novy-Marx & Velikov critique.
  • "Quality pays for value's tail." → Quality hedges value's distress risk.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text: Myth Reality Value is dead Down 58% to 2020, then up 68% to 2022; contested, not settled Low risk means low return Low-beta stocks have had similar returns to high-beta ones, hence BAB Quality is always defensive QMJ fell 36% in 2023–2026

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
Basic

  • Do you adjust book value for intangibles?
  • Is your low-vol sleeve sector-constrained?

Informed

  • How do you weight value against momentum, and was that changed after 2020?
  • How much of your BAB return survives value weighting?

Sharp

  • What was your quality sleeve's drawdown in 2025 versus QMJ? 🔒
  • Do you integrate scores or stack sleeves, and what turnover does that save? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the betting-against-beta factor

Frazzini & Pedersen shrink time-series betas toward 1 [Reported]:

\[ \hat\beta_i = 0.6\, \hat\beta_i^{TS} + 0.4 \times 1 . \]

With low- and high-beta portfolio returns \(r_L, r_H\) and betas \(\beta_L, \beta_H\):

\[ r_{BAB} = \frac{r_L - r_f}{\beta_L} - \frac{r_H - r_f}{\beta_H} . \]

The factor has beta zero by construction. If the security market line has intercept \(\gamma_0\) above \(r_f\) and slope \(\gamma_1\), then

\[ \mathbb{E}[r_{BAB}] = \gamma_0 \left(\frac{1}{\beta_L} - \frac{1}{\beta_H}\right) > 0 , \]

which is zero under the CAPM (\(\gamma_0 = 0\)).

docs.title: Dispersion and correlation trading
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Index variance is roughly average stock variance times average correlation. Selling index volatility and buying constituent volatility is therefore a bet that stocks will move together less than options imply: short implied correlation.
  • Implied correlation has on average exceeded realized: 39.5% versus 32.5% for the S&P 500 in 1996–2012, with the gap shrinking after 2001 [Verified]. Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov (2009) show the risk is priced but hard to harvest after frictions [Verified].
  • It is short a crisis: Cboe's 3-month implied correlation index (COR3M) read 90 on 2020-03-16 and hit a record low of 7.2 on 2026-07-10 [Verified].
  • In 2024–2026 the trade was crowded and very profitable; some funds have flipped to "reverse dispersion" [Reported].

Level: Deep dive · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family vol & derivatives Edge source risk premium · structural Holding period weeks to months (1- to 3-month options or variance swaps) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Buyers of index puts (pensions, insurers, hedgers) pay up because index protection pays exactly when diversification fails; covered-call sellers supply single-stock vol cheaply for income. Universe & instruments S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 options and variance swaps versus options on the top 30–50 constituents; OTC correlation swaps Data required index and single-stock vol surfaces, index weights, realized correlations, earnings dates, dividends Core algorithms used M8 Options pricing and vol surfaces · M7 Hedging algorithms · P2 Covariance estimation and shrinkage · M9 Algorithmic risk controls Infra intensity moderate: daily surface fits for 50+ names, daily delta hedges; not latency-sensitive Capacity (rough $ range) a few $M of index vega per firm [Estimate] (single-stock option bid-ask on 30–50 legs per roll caps size) Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) academic: high pre-friction alpha, not exploitable after realistic frictions (DMV 2009) [Verified]; practitioner: net 0.3–0.8 over a cycle, crisis losses included [Lore] Turnover rolled monthly or quarterly; legs delta-hedged daily Main risks / failure modes correlation spikes, index gaps, single-name illiquidity, residual vega, earnings Crowding risk high in 2024–2026 [Reported] Firm types that run it bank exotics desks, volatility hedge funds, options market makers Lab Lab 06

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: If 50 stocks each have 30% implied volatility and moved in lockstep, their index would also have 30% volatility. The index option market says 16%, because stocks diversify each other. That 16% implies how much they will co-move: an implied correlation of about 0.27. If you think realized co-movement will be lower, or that implied correlation is systematically too high, sell the index's volatility and buy the members'.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
Investors fear correlation spikes because diversification fails exactly when it is needed, so they overpay for index protection, the asset that hedges it. Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov (2009) find correlation risk carries a large negative price and explains the cross-section of index and single-stock option returns [Verified]. Their later work finds single-stock variance risk premia mostly insignificant in 1996–2001 while index premia were large [Verified]. Covered-call writing adds single-stock vol supply [Lore].

Outside the US, supply runs the other way: retail autocallables in Korea, Japan and Europe leave dealers long index vega, concentrated in long-dated Nikkei, HSCEI and Euro Stoxx vol [Reported]. Dealers selling that vol back cheapens index vol there [Lore]. Korean worst-of notes also leave dealers with correlation exposure [Reported].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Pick the index and the 30–50 names covering most of its variance.
  2. Compute implied correlation; compare with a realized-correlation forecast (P2).
  3. Size legs (vega-neutral, theta-neutral or correlation-weighted).
  4. Sell index straddles or variance; buy single-stock straddles or variance.
  5. Delta-hedge every leg daily (M7).
  6. Cap correlation vega and buy tail protection (M9); roll or close at expiry.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: 50 equal-weight stocks (2% each), each at 30% implied; index at 16%. Implied correlation = (0.0256 − 0.0018) / 0.0882 = 0.27. Short an index variance swap with $1M vega (variance notional $1M / (2 × 16) = $31,250 per vol² point); long 50 stock variance swaps with $20,000 vega each, or $333 per vol² point.

Realized outcome Index vol Index leg Stock legs Net Calm: stocks 30%, correlation 0.20 13.9% +$1.93M $0 +$1.93M Vol up: stocks 35%, correlation 0.27 18.7% −$2.89M +$5.42M +$2.52M Crash: stocks 45%, correlation 0.70 37.8% −$36.7M +$18.75M −$17.9M

Calm row: 31,250 × (16² − 13.9²) = $1.93M. Equal vega leaves the book net long volatility (row 2) yet still loses heavily when correlation jumps (row 3). A 2.5× strike cap, common in practice [Lore], would not bind here (40 vol on the index).

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Surfaces and Greeks come from M8; Lab 06 shows delta-hedging P&L for one leg; this book runs 51 legs.

# Dispersion signal and leg sizing (simplified). Vols are annualized decimals.
def implied_correlation(sig_idx, w, sig):
    own = np.sum(w**2 * sig**2)                         # diagonal part of index variance
    cross = np.sum(w * sig) ** 2 - own                  # sum over i != j of w_i w_j s_i s_j
    return (sig_idx**2 - own) / cross

def dispersion_trade(sig_idx, w, sig, cov_fcst, index_vega=1_000_000, weighting="corr"):
    rho_imp = implied_correlation(sig_idx, w, sig)
    vol_f = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov_fcst))                  # P2: shrunk covariance forecast
    rho_fcst = implied_correlation(np.sqrt(w @ cov_fcst @ w), w, vol_f)
    if rho_imp - rho_fcst < 0.05:                       # demand a 5-point correlation cushion
        return None
    # 'vega': equal vega, net long vol. 'corr': scale by sqrt(rho_imp) so a parallel
    # vol move nets out and the book is closer to pure correlation.
    scale = 1.0 if weighting == "vega" else np.sqrt(rho_imp)
    stock_vega = scale * index_vega * (w * sig) / np.sum(w * sig)
    return {"index": -index_vega, "stocks": stock_vega}  # delta-hedge every leg daily (M7)

Lab 06, one short straddle, synthetic data. Bottom right: hedged P&L tracks dollar-gamma-weighted implied minus realized variance (R² 0.82); the rest is path noise. An options-based dispersion book carries that noise on all 51 legs.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Instrument: options need delta hedging and their P&L depends on the path; variance swaps are cleaner but capped; correlation swaps are OTC.
  • Weighting: equal vega is net long vol; correlation weighting (stock vega ≈ √ρ × index vega) isolates correlation.
  • Tenor: the implied-realized gap grows with maturity [Verified].
  • Timing: earnings seasons raise single-stock dispersion; tail hedges cost carry.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• DMV (2009, JF): S&P 100 index options versus options on all members; correlation risk is priced, but the premium "cannot be exploited with realistic trading frictions" [Verified].
  • DMV (2013 working paper): S&P 500, 30-day implied minus realized correlation was 12.5 points in 1996–2001, 3.2 in 2002–2007 and 4.5 in 2008–2012 [Verified].
  • Public gauges: COR3M (launched July 2021; top 50 S&P 500 stocks) [Verified] closed at 11.8 on 2026-11-11, against a 2006–2026 median of 41 [Verified]. The Cboe S&P 500 Dispersion Index (DSPX, launched September 2023) read 38.1 that day [Verified].
  • 2026: a bank trader called dispersion returns "phenomenal" [Reported].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: The shrinking gap after 2001 fits more arbitrage capital. Crowding showed in 2024 [Reported]: COR3M fell to 7.6 on 3 July, then jumped from 14.0 on 31 July to 35.7 on 5 August [Verified]. In 2026 it set new lows, and some managers called the trade crowded and bought reverse dispersion [Reported].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Mechanism: in a selloff stocks move together, index gamma losses explode, single-name options gap and widen, and margin calls force exits.
  • Episodes (Cboe data; values before the 2021 launch are back-calculated): 1-month implied correlation 96.6 on 2008-10-24; COR3M 90.8 on 2011-12-08 and 90.3 on 2020-03-16, when VIX closed at 82.7; 1-month correlation from 2.9 (2024-07-12) to 39.6 (2024-08-05) [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: trade correlation directly with correlation swaps. Practice: most books use options or variance swaps and carry residual vol exposure [Lore].
  • Textbook: a correlation premium is free alpha. Practice: frictions absorb much of it and losses cluster in crises (DMV 2009) [Verified].

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Implied corr is 12; we're barely paid to be short it." → The premium is thin.
  • "We run it correlation-weighted, not vega-flat." → Pure correlation, not long vol.
  • "Earnings season is when dispersion pays." → Single-name moves diverge.
  • "The index leg is our tail." → Losses come from short index gamma.
  • "Reverse dispersion is cheap convexity here." → Buying correlation near record lows.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: dispersion is market-neutral. Reality: short correlation is short crashes.
  • Myth: low implied correlation means the trade is over. Reality: realized can be lower still, as in 2026.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: implied correlation and dispersion P&L

Index variance with weights \(w_i\), vols \(\sigma_i\) and average correlation \( ho\):

\[ \sigma_I^2 = \sum_i w_i^2\sigma_i^2 + ho \sum_{i e j} w_i w_j \sigma_i \sigma_j \quad\Rightarrow\quad ho_{ ext{imp}} = rac{\sigma_I^2 - \sum_i w_i^2\sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i e j} w_i w_j \sigma_i\sigma_j}. \]

If stocks realize their implied vols, short index variance with notional \(N\) earns

\[ N\,( ho_{ ext{imp}} - ho_{ ext{real}}) \sum_{i e j} w_i w_j \sigma_i\sigma_j . \]

For many names \(\sigma_I \approx ar\sigma\sqrt{ ho}\), so \(\partial\sigma_I/\partial ar\sigma \approx \sqrt{ ho}\): stock vega of \(\sqrt{ ho}\) times index vega neutralizes parallel vol moves.

docs.title: Volatility risk premium and vol arb
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Index options usually price more volatility than arrives: in 1990–2026 the VIX averaged 19.4 against 15.3 realized over the next 21 trading days, and exceeded it on 86% of days [Verified] (our computation from Cboe data).
  • Sellers harvest it via short variance swaps, hedged straddles, put writing or short VIX futures: many small gains, rare huge losses (monthly skewness near −6 [Verified], our computation).
  • It is crash insurance and pays like it: 2008, February 2018, March 2020, April 2025.
  • It persists because hedgers must buy protection and sellers face margin limits, but its CAPM alpha has shrunk toward zero since about 2010 [Verified].

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family vol & derivatives Edge source risk premium · structural Holding period one week to three months; delta hedged daily Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Pensions, insurers, structured-product dealers and risk-targeting funds buy index puts and variance: protection pays when their losses and margin calls peak. Retail buys short-dated options as lottery tickets. Universe & instruments SPX, SPY, QQQ options; OTC variance swaps; VIX futures and options; single stocks (smaller premium) Data required vol surfaces, intraday realized vol, VIX futures curve, event calendar Core algorithms used M8 Options pricing and vol surfaces · M7 Hedging algorithms · P7 Position sizing and risk budgeting Infra intensity low latency sensitivity; daily surface fits and hedges Capacity (rough $ range) large: option-overlay and defined-outcome ETFs exceed $300B (mid-2026) [Reported]; $0.1B–$5B notional per manager before bid-ask and crowding bite [Estimate] Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) short one-month S&P 500 variance at the VIX, gross, 1990–2026: ~1.2 (1.35 with a 2.5× cap); capped, 1.6 before 2010 and 1.1 after [Estimate] (our computation); net of costs and tail hedges 0.3–0.8 [Lore] Turnover monthly roll; daily delta hedges Main risks / failure modes crashes, volatility spikes, margin calls, vanishing liquidity Crowding risk high: income ETFs, overwriters and VIX products sell the same risk Firm types that run it vol hedge funds and pods, bank volatility-premia indices, option-income ETFs; options market makers warehouse the other side Lab Lab 06

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: Selling index options is selling insurance on the stock market. Most months premiums exceed claims; occasionally every claim arrives at once, in a crash. The variance risk premium is the loading for that catastrophe exposure.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
1. Insurance demand. End users are net long index options, especially puts; dealers absorbing that demand charge for it, lifting prices and skew (Gârleanu, Pedersen & Poteshman 2009) [Verified].
  2. Variance hedges the market. It spikes when stocks fall, so buyers accept a negative return; market beta explains only a small part (Carr & Wu 2009) [Verified].
  3. Limits to arbitrage. Selling needs margin that rises in crises. Dew-Becker & Giglio (2025) argue the premium mainly reflected intermediary frictions: options synthesized from stock show no negative alpha in a century of data [Verified].

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Measure implied variance: the variance swap rate from the whole strip, as the VIX does (M8).
  2. Forecast realized volatility to expiry (for example a HAR model on daily, weekly and monthly realized vol).
  3. Trade when implied² exceeds forecast² by a margin; stand aside when the VIX curve is inverted.
  4. Size to a stress loss such as a VIX doubling (P7).
  5. Sell variance, straddles or puts and delta-hedge (M7); buy far tail protection; roll monthly.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Short a one-month S&P 500 variance swap: $100,000 vega notional, strike 18. Variance notional = 100,000 / (2 × 18) = $2,778 per variance point; P&L = 2,778 × (18² − realized²).

Realized vol Calculation P&L 14 (calm) 2,778 × (324 − 196) +$356K 30 (spike) 2,778 × (324 − 900) −$1.60M 45 or more (crash; a 2.5× cap, common in practice [Lore], binds) 2,778 × (324 − 2,025) −$4.73M 80 (uncapped) 2,778 × (324 − 6,400) −$16.9M

One capped crash month erases 13 calm months.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Surfaces: M8; hedging: M7; sizing: P7; vol regimes: F6.

# Harvest the VRP with a delta-hedged short straddle (simplified; names follow Lab 06).
iv_atm = fit_smile(np.log(K / F), iv_mid, T, method="svi")(0.0)   # M8: fitted ATM vol (Lab 06 atm_quote_vols)
rv_fcst = har_forecast(rv_daily, rv_weekly, rv_monthly)          # realized-vol forecast to expiry
vrp = iv_atm**2 - rv_fcst**2                                     # signal in variance units
if vrp > min_vrp and vix < vix3m:                                # skip when the VIX curve is inverted
    n = stress_budget / stress_loss(vix_shock=2.0)               # P7: size to the crash, not to vol
    premium = straddle_price(F, K=F, T=T, vol=iv_atm + EDGE_VOL) # Lab 06 sells at fitted vol + 0.5 pts
    h = delta_hedge_pnl(spot_path, -straddle_delta_path, band=0.10)   # M7; per straddle share, x n x 100
# Before costs, P&L ~ dollar-gamma-weighted implied minus realized variance (Lab 06's "classic" check);
# gamma_sale = straddle gamma at the sale vol iv0 along the path, dt = years per hedge step.
ret2 = (np.diff(S) / S[:-1]) ** 2
classic = (0.5 * gamma_sale[:-1] * S[:-1]**2 * (iv0**2 * dt - ret2)).sum() * n * 100

Lab 06, synthetic data with a planted premium. Notice that implied usually sits above realized, but the red overshoots are large: the histogram has a fat left tail.

Synthetic lab results: mean 30-day ATM implied vol 20.3% against 18.4% subsequently realized (+1.9 vol points), implied above realized on 65% of days; the variance-swap rate was 1.26× realized variance (1.25 planted).

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Instrument. Variance swaps are clean but OTC and capped; straddle P&L is path-dependent (Lab 06). Unhedged put writing is mostly equity beta: the Cboe PUT index's daily beta to the S&P 500 was 0.63 in 2007–2026 [Verified] (our computation).
  • VIX futures. The VIX sat below the 3-month VIX on 92% of days in 2009–2026 [Verified] (our computation), so shorts usually earn roll; the basis predicts futures returns, not spot VIX (Simon & Campasano 2014) [Verified].
  • Tenor. Investors pay mostly to hedge near-term realized variance; forward variance earns little (Dew-Becker et al. 2017) [Verified].

docs.text:
Per year, $100,000 monthly vega notional, VIX as strike, 2.5× cap; gross lines from 1990–2026 data (our computation), costs illustrative [Estimate].

Line $M per year Carry in months where implied beat realized (85%) +4.84 Losses in months where realized beat implied −1.51 Bid-ask, 12 rolls at 0.5 vol points −0.60 Tail hedges −0.73 Margin financing −0.10 Net +1.90

The worst month, struck 2008-09-04, lost $5.2M: more than two years of net carry.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Carr & Wu (2009): 1996–2003; strongly negative for the S&P 500, S&P 100 and Dow, smaller for single stocks; unexplained by CAPM or Fama-French factors [Verified].
  • Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou (2009): the premium predicts quarterly stock returns after 1990 [Verified].
  • Coval & Shumway (2001): zero-beta ATM straddles lost ~3% a week [Verified]; Bakshi & Kapadia (2003): delta-hedged gains negative [Verified].
  • Our computation: VIX minus realized averaged 5.4, 3.4, 3.7 and 3.8 vol points in the 1990s, 2000s, 2010s and 2020–2026 [Verified].
  • PUT index, 2010–2026: 8.2% a year at 12.0% volatility against 12.0% at 17.2% for S&P 500 price returns (dividends excluded): return per unit of risk 0.69 vs 0.70 [Verified] (our computation).

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Dew-Becker & Giglio (2025) find a break around 2010: traded-option CAPM alphas converge to zero and dealers' net SPX gamma moves from negative to zero or positive [Verified]. In February 2018, inverse and leveraged VIX products, about $4B of assets at end-2017, had to buy futures into a spike [Verified] (BIS). Whether systematic selling suppresses realized volatility is contested (linkages).

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
Losses, wider quotes and margin calls coincide.

  • 2008-10: the PUT index fell 17.7% in a month [Verified] (our computation).
  • 2018-02-05: VIX +115.6% to 37.32 [Verified]; XIV's indicative value fell about 96% (BIS: 84%) and the note was terminated [Reported] (failure gallery).
  • 2020-03-16: record VIX close 82.69; a swap struck 2020-02-10 at 15.0 realized 50.9 [Verified] (our computation).
  • 2024-08-05: VIX near 66 before the open [Verified] (BIS). 2025-04-08: close of 52.33 [Verified] (Cboe).

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text:
• Textbook: a free insurance premium. Practice: implied still beats realized (85% of days in 2020–2026), but the remainder is largely pay for crash beta (Dew-Becker & Giglio 2025) [Verified].
  • Textbook: a delta-hedged straddle isolates volatility. Practice: P&L is path-dependent (Lab 06).

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text: Volatility arbitrage is the relative-value cousin: sell rich implied against a realized forecast, steep skew against ATM, or a rich expiry against a cheap one, each delta-hedged. Also: the mirror image, long-vol gamma scalping and tail hedging; dispersion; carry.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're short the wings." → Sold out-of-the-money options.
  • "Curve's inverted, we're flat." → Backwardation signals stress.
  • "Size it to the gap, not the vol." → Assume a VIX doubling.
  • "The carry pays for the tail." → Part of the premium funds hedges.
  • "Realized is running hot." → The hedged short is losing on gamma.
  • "Vol of vol is bid." → VIX options are expensive; a spike is feared.

docs.title: Myths vs reality
docs.text:
• Myth: option selling is income. Reality: it is insurance with fat-tailed claims.
  • Myth: put writing beats the market risk-adjusted. Reality: not since 2010 (PUT index above).
  • Myth: delta hedging removes crash risk. Reality: it removes direction, not gaps.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:

  • Basic: How do you forecast realized volatility?
  • Informed: What stress do you size to, and how much carry goes to tail hedges?
  • Informed: What did February 2018 and April 2025 cost you?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: variance swap replication and the premium

With \(r = 0\), the fair variance strike is a static strip of out-of-the-money options (Demeterfi et al. 1999):

\[ K_{\text{var}} = \frac{2}{T}\left(\int_0^{F} \frac{P(K)}{K^2}\,dK + \int_{F}^{\infty} \frac{C(K)}{K^2}\,dK\right), \qquad \text{VRP}_t = \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}_t[\sigma_R^2] - \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}_t[\sigma_R^2] > 0 . \]

The \(1/K^2\) weights favor low strikes, so negative skew lifts \(K_{\text{var}}\) above ATM variance (Lab 06: 1.26 vs 1.19).

docs.title: Carry and cross-asset risk premia
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Carry is what a position earns if prices and curves do not move: rate differentials in FX, roll yield in commodities, yield plus roll-down in bonds, dividends minus financing in equity futures. One formula covers all: (spot − futures) / futures.
  • Long high-carry, short low-carry works in every asset class studied: gross Sharpe about 0.7 per class and 1.1 diversified, 1972–2012 (Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen & Vrugt).
  • It pays largely for crash risk: carry loses in every class at once in global recessions; AUD/JPY fell 46% in three months of 2008.
  • For a US equity quant, carry is a cross-asset hedge, a risk-on/risk-off regime input and a hidden correlation in multi-strategy books (the August 2024 yen unwind hit equities too).

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A bond bought at par pays its coupon unless the price falls: that is carry. Every futures contract embeds a similar "coupon" in its gap to spot. Carry strategies collect the fattest coupons, funded by shorting the thinnest, until the rare day when high-coupon assets all fall at once.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Crash compensation. High-yield currencies lose when global FX volatility jumps; a volatility factor explains over 90% of carry portfolios' cross-sectional returns (Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling & Schrimpf 2012) [Verified]. Brunnermeier, Nagel & Pedersen (2008) tie currency crashes to funding-liquidity unwinds [Reported].
  • Hedging pressure. Producers short futures and pay speculators to take the other side [Lore]; roll returns drive commodity futures returns (Erb & Harvey 2006; Gorton & Rouwenhorst 2006) [Reported].
  • Recession risk. The three worst global carry drawdowns (1972–75, 1980–82, 2008–09) coincide with global recessions (Koijen et al.) [Verified].
  • Leverage aversion. Investors under-own low-risk assets that need leverage (Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen 2012) [Verified], the logic of risk parity.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Measure carry per instrument as (spot − futures) / futures, annualized.
  2. Rank within each asset class: long high carry, short low carry, weights proportional to rank.
  3. Scale by inverse volatility (P7).
  4. Combine classes at equal risk (P4) with a cross-asset covariance (P1).
  5. Crash control: cut gross when volatility regimes shift (F6).
  6. Execute with forwards and futures; roll before expiry.

Asset Inputs Carry Long AUD vs JPY AUD rate 4.35%, JPY rate 0.25% 4.35 − 0.25 = +4.1% Long crude, backwardated front $80.00, next month $78.50 (80.00 − 78.50) / 78.50 × 12 = +22.9% Long 10-year bond future (roll-down) yield 4.20%, repo 4.00%, 9-year yield 4.10%, duration 8 (4.20 − 4.00) + 8 × 0.10 = +1.0% Long S&P 500 future dividend yield 1.3%, financing 4.0% 1.3 − 4.0 = −2.7%

The price of the AUD/JPY coupon: from 21 July to 27 October 2008 AUD/JPY fell 46% (our computation from Federal Reserve rates) [Verified], about 11 years of carry in three months.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def carry(a):
    """Annualized carry: return if spot and curve stay unchanged, (S - F) / F style."""
    if a.cls == "fx":           # forward discount = interest differential (covered parity)
        return (a.spot - a.fwd_1m) / a.fwd_1m * 12
    if a.cls == "commodity":    # roll yield between the first two contracts
        return (a.f1 - a.f2) / a.f2 * 12 / a.months_between
    if a.cls == "bond":         # yield over financing plus roll-down along the curve
        return (a.y - a.repo) + a.dur * (a.y - a.y_shorter)
    if a.cls == "equity":       # expected dividend yield minus financing
        return (a.spot - a.fut) / a.fut * 12 / a.months_to_expiry

def carry_portfolio(assets, vol, target_vol=0.10):
    c = pd.Series({a.name: carry(a) for a in assets})
    cls = pd.Series({a.name: a.cls for a in assets})
    rank = c.groupby(cls).rank(pct=True)                    # rank within asset class only
    w = (rank - rank.groupby(cls).transform("mean")) / vol  # P7: demeaned, inverse-vol
    sleeve_vol = (w * vol).pow(2).groupby(cls).sum().pow(0.5)  # ignores correlations
    w = w / cls.map(sleeve_vol)                              # P4: equal risk per class
    return w * target_vol / np.sqrt(cls.nunique())           # if sleeves are uncorrelated

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Seasonality. Compare natural gas and grain contracts a year apart so seasonality is not read as carry [Lore].
  • G10 vs EM. Emerging-market forwards add carry plus convertibility and jump risk [Lore].
  • Slope vs level. 10-year minus 2-year carry is a separate, duration-light strategy (Koijen et al.) [Verified].
  • Other styles. Carry aligns with value in equities and momentum in bonds and commodities (Koijen et al.) [Verified], so combine with a covariance.
  • Crash hedges. Out-of-the-money options on high-yielders cut the tail but eat much of the carry [Lore].

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: FX carry crowds into one funding currency: in 2024 the yen, about ¥40 trillion by BIS estimate [Verified]. G10 carry earned little in the zero-rate decade after 2008 [Lore].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• 2008. AUD/JPY −46% from July to October [Verified]; Koijen et al. date the global carry drawdown to August 2008 – February 2009 [Verified].
  • August 2024. USD/JPY fell from 161.7 (10 July) to 144.0 (5 August); that day the Nikkei 225 fell 12.4% and the VIX closed at 38.6 (our computation, FRED) [Verified]. The BIS says leveraged unwinds in equities and currencies amplified the move [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today Currency carry only (Lustig et al. 2011) [Reported] All classes, ranked within class, risk-balanced (Koijen et al.) [Verified] Static risk parity (Asness et al. 2012) [Verified] Volatility-targeted with regime overlays [Lore] Standalone carry fund One of four styles (value, momentum, carry, defensive) in multi-asset premia funds such as QSPIX [Reported] (prospectus)

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text:
Trend following (often paired with carry), the volatility risk premium (option carry), cross-asset value, and risk parity (Bridgewater's All Weather, launched 1996) [Verified].

For an equity quant. Index carry tracks dividend yield, so it overlaps value. FX carry and credit spreads feed regime detection. Long yen or Treasuries can hedge equity crash risk. In multi-strategy platforms, carry, short-volatility and equity beta lose together in crises.

• "Carry is short vol in disguise." → Steady income, crash exposure.
  • "We're funded in yen." → Short a low-rate currency to finance longs.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: carry as (S − F)/F, and its four special cases

A collateralized futures position returns \((F_{t+1} - F_t)/F_t\); if spot stays at \(S_t\) the futures converges to it, so

\[ C_t = \frac{S_t - F_t}{F_t}, \qquad \mathbb{E}_t[r_{t+1}] = C_t + \mathbb{E}_t\!\left[\frac{S_{t+1} - S_t}{F_t}\right]. \]

FX, covered parity \(F_t = S_t (1 + r_t)/(1 + r_t^*)\), foreign rate \(r^*\):

\[ C_t = \frac{r_t^* - r_t}{1 + r_t} \approx r_t^* - r_t . \]

Equity index, dividend yield \(\delta\): \(C_t \approx \delta - r_t\). Bond, maturity \(\tau\), duration \(D\):

\[ C_t \approx (y_t^{\tau} - r_t) + D\left(y_t^{\tau} - y_t^{\tau - 1}\right). \]

docs.title: Trend following and CTAs
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Time-series momentum: long futures that have risen, short those that have fallen, across 50–150 markets at equal risk.
  • Long evidence: persistence in all 58 futures Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen tested, and positive returns in every decade since 1880 [Verified].
  • Convex payoff: bleeds in chop, earns in long moves ("crisis alpha"), loses on V-shaped reversals.
  • Live returns trail backtests: the SG Trend Index made +27.4% in 2022, −4.2% in 2023, +2.4% in 2024 and 2025, +15.8% in 2026 to September [Reported].
  • For an equity quant: a diversifier, a source of index-futures flow, and the textbook case of volatility targeting.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Family futures and macro context Edge source behavioral · risk premium (hedging pressure) Holding period weeks to months (1–12-month lookbacks) Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it Hedgers laying off price risk, who lose to trend-following speculators (Moskowitz et al.) [Verified]; central banks; investors who under-react, then chase. None trade on the trend itself. Universe & instruments Equity-index, bond, short-rate, currency and commodity futures; FX forwards Data required Daily settlements, roll calendars, margin rates Core algorithms used P7 Position sizing and risk budgeting · D3 Signal transforms · P1 Risk models · P6 Multi-period optimization and trading toward the aim Infra intensity Low latency sensitivity; daily batch; roll and execution algorithms at size Capacity (rough $ range) Tens of billions per manager [Estimate]; industry $354B (Q2 2026, BarclayHedge) [Reported]; at $280B in 2014, trend followers held about 0.2% of equity and 6% of commodity market size [Verified] Typical Sharpe (gross vs net) Backtests: above 1.0 gross, 1985–2009 [Verified]; 0.77 net of costs and fees, 1880–2013, 0.62 in 2000–2013 [Verified]. Live SG Trend Index since 2000: 5.75% a year, maximum drawdown 20.6% [Reported]. Realistic net 0.3–0.6 [Estimate] Turnover Notional 50–150× NAV a year in rate-heavy books [Estimate] (Lab 19: 141×) Main risks / failure modes Whipsaw, V-shaped reversals, hidden correlation, roll costs Crowding risk Moderate: large managers run similar models (correlation 0.95 with a ~50-program peer index) [Reported] Firm types that run it CTAs, multi-asset quant managers, multi-strategy platforms; SG Trend Index constituents in 2025–2026 have included Winton, Systematica and PIMCO [Reported] Lab Lab 19

docs.title: Intuition (the story in plain English)
docs.text: A CTA running trend following never asks why oil is rising. It assumes that what has moved for months keeps moving, because the people moving it adjust slowly. Each market is a slightly biased coin; sixty of them, sized so none dominates, behave like cheap options on big moves.

docs.title: Economic rationale: why should this make money at all?
docs.text:
• Under-reaction, then over-reaction. Returns persist for 1–12 months and partially reverse later (Moskowitz et al.) [Verified].
  • Hedging pressure. In CFTC data, speculators ride time-series momentum and hedgers take the other side [Verified]; Hurst et al. add central banks and other non-profit-seeking traders [Verified].
  • Not a crash premium. Returns peak when equity markets are most extreme, either way, like a lookback straddle (Fung & Hsieh 2001) [Verified]; a strategy that pays in crises is hard to call risk compensation.

docs.title: The trade, step by step
docs.text:
1. Data: back-adjusted contracts.
  2. Signal (D3): average sign of each market's own 1-, 3- and 12-month return.
  3. Risk (P1): exponentially weighted volatilities and correlations.
  4. Size (P7): equal risk per asset class, inverse volatility within it, a 10% volatility target for the book.
  5. Trade (P6) only outside a no-trade buffer; roll before expiry; keep collateral in Treasury bills.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: $1B book, each market sized to about 2.5% of NAV standalone volatility.

Market Ex-ante vol Signal Position (notional / NAV) Notional 2-year Treasury future 2% −1 −2.5 / 2 = −125% −$1.25B 10-year Treasury future 6% −1 −2.5 / 6 = −42% −$417M S&P 500 future 16% +1/3 +1/3 × 2.5 / 16 = +5.2% +$52M

A trending quarter. Bond prices fall 1.5% (2-year) and 4% (10-year); equities fall 10%. P&L: 1.25 × 1.5% + 0.417 × 4% − 0.052 × 10% = +3.0% of NAV (+$30M); the weak equity signal cost little.

A reversal day. Bonds rally 1.0% and 1.5%: 1.25 × 1.0% + 0.417 × 1.5% = −1.9% of NAV in a day. Low-volatility rate futures carry the most notional.

docs.title: Signals and algorithms under the hood
docs.text:
Cards: D3 signal; P1 and P2 risk; P7 and P4 sizing; P6 buffer; P5 costs. Code as in Lab 19:

import numpy as np

def tsmom_signal(returns, lookbacks=(21, 63, 252)):
    """Average sign of each market's OWN past 1-, 3-, 12-month return: -1, -1/3, +1/3 or +1."""
    votes = [np.sign(returns.rolling(L).sum()) for L in lookbacks]
    return sum(votes) / len(lookbacks)                 # known at the close of day t

def vol_target_positions(signal, ann_vol, corr, asset_class, target_vol=0.10, asset_cap=0.40):
    """Notional / NAV per market: equal risk per class, inverse vol inside it, book at target vol."""
    classes, counts = np.unique(asset_class, return_counts=True)
    n_in_class = dict(zip(classes, counts))
    budget = np.array([1.0 / (len(classes) * n_in_class[c]) for c in asset_class])
    w = signal * budget / ann_vol                      # a 2%-vol bond gets 20x a 40%-vol gas future
    port_vol = np.sqrt(w @ (corr * np.outer(ann_vol, ann_vol)) @ w)
    if port_vol > 0:
        w = w * target_vol / port_vol                  # scale the whole book to 10% ex-ante vol
    cap = asset_cap * target_vol / ann_vol             # no market above 4% of NAV standalone vol
    return np.clip(w, -cap, cap)

def trade_with_buffer(target, current, band):
    gap = target - current                             # trade only if the target leaves the band,
    return np.where(np.abs(gap) > band, target - np.sign(gap) * band, current)  # to its edge

Same forecast, three sizing schemes, 24 synthetic futures: the vol-targeted book holds risk near 10%; equal notional swings from 5% to 17%. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab result: net Sharpe 0.72 (0.84 gross) at 9.8% realized volatility; the buffer cuts turnover from 252× to 141× NAV and lifts net Sharpe from 0.59. That sits near academic backtests and above the realistic 0.3–0.6 net: the toy has no fees, crises or capacity limits.

docs.title: Implementation choices that matter
docs.text:
• Speed. Fast signals lose more to costs: synthetic lab result 0.52 gross to 0.36 net at 1 month, 0.88 to 0.82 at 12. Managers blend speeds because trend lengths are unknown.
  • Risk budgets. Under equal notional, commodities and equities carry 92% of risk (synthetic lab result).
  • Contracts. Short-rate futures need huge notional; position limits bind in small commodities [Lore].

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012): time-series momentum in all 58 futures; diversified Sharpe above 1, about 2.5× the equity market's, before costs [Verified].
  • Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen: 1880–2013, 14.9% a year gross, 11.2% after 2-and-20 fees, 9.7% volatility, correlation to US equities 0.00; positive in 8 of the 10 worst 60/40 drawdowns [Verified].
  • Live: the SG Trend Index tracks the ten largest trend CTAs, net of fees (figures in the TL;DR) [Reported].

Quarterly trend returns against equity returns form a smile: gains in both tails. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab result: curvature +1.23 (t = 2.6); in the worst 10% of equity quarters (mean −13.4%) the book made +0.8%.

docs.title: Capacity, crowding and decay
docs.text: Futures markets are deep, so capacity rarely binds; decay does. The backtest earned 11% net a year; the live index compounds at about 6% including cash interest. From 2008 to 2014, "risk-on/risk-off" correlation left fewer independent trends [Verified].

docs.title: How it fails
docs.text:
• Choppy years. 2016: −6.19%, the index's first losing year since 2012 [Reported].
  • V-shaped reversals. March 2023: −7.69%; 10 and 13 March, when the regional-bank crisis squeezed short bond positions, were two of the index's worst days ever (AlphaSimplex) [Verified]. April 2025: −4.89%, −9.33% year to date [Reported].
  • Fast crashes. A 1987-style crash arrives before signals flip (Hurst et al.) [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook vs how it's done today
docs.text: Textbook Practice today 12-month sign, monthly, 40% volatility per market [Verified] Blended speeds, daily rebalancing with buffers [Lore] Equal risk per market Class budgets, correlation-aware scaling [Lore] ~60 markets 100–300+, including "alternative" markets [Lore] Pure trend, 2-and-20 Trend plus carry, lower fees [Lore]

docs.title: Variants and neighbours
docs.text:
Cross-sectional momentum ranks assets against each other; carry is the usual partner; short-term CTAs hold for days.

Why an equity quant should care. Trend diversifies equity books; vol-targeted trend books sell index futures into falling, volatile markets, a flow sell-side desks estimate daily [Lore]; and the sizing machinery is reused in equity factor books.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: time-series momentum return, diversification and the smile

For market \(i\) with signal \(s_{i,t} \in [-1, 1]\), ex-ante volatility \(\sigma_{i,t}\) and target \(\sigma^*\):

\[ r^{\text{TSMOM}}_{i,t+1} = s_{i,t}\,\frac{\sigma^*}{\sigma_{i,t}}\, r_{i,t+1}. \]

With \(N\) markets at equal risk, single-market Sharpe \(S\) and average correlation \(\rho\):

\[ S_{\text{book}} = S\sqrt{\frac{N}{1 + (N-1)\rho}}, \qquad S = 0.2,\; N = 60,\; \rho = 0.1 \;\Rightarrow\; S_{\text{book}} \approx 0.59 . \]

The smile: regress quarterly trend returns on equity returns and their square; the square's coefficient \(c\) is positive.

docs.title: Evolution of quant strategies
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Most quant edges follow one life cycle: discovery → early profits → publication and diffusion → crowding → decay (or a crowded crash) → migration to a faster horizon, new data, new markets or a more complex combination.
  • Decay is measured, not folklore: 97 published predictors lost 26% out of sample and 58% after publication; anomaly returns roughly halved after decimalization; a simple daily reversal rule fell from 1.38% a day (1995) to 0.13% (2007) [Verified].
  • Crowded edges do not just fade. Funds lever up to keep their returns, which turns a slow decline into a fast unwind (August 2007).
  • Speed edges did not shrink per opportunity; the window did (97 ms to 7 ms), and the profit pool concentrated in the fastest few firms.
  • Treat a signal as an amortizing intangible: research is maintenance capex, and a book that stops replacing alpha shrinks every year.

Level: Deep dive · Read time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11

A strategy is an intangible asset with a finite and uncertain useful life. Nobody can patent a trading rule, so every profitable idea leaks: through papers, through staff who change firms, through vendors selling the same data to everyone, and through prices themselves, which reveal the trade to anyone who looks.

docs.title: The life cycle in one picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D["Discovery<br/>paper or desk insight"] --> P["Early profits<br/>few users, high Sharpe"]
    P --> U["Publication and diffusion<br/>papers, staff moves, vendors"]
    U --> C["Crowding<br/>more capital, more leverage"]
    C --> K["Decay<br/>alpha arbitraged away"]
    C --> X["Crowded unwind<br/>fast, correlated losses"]
    X --> K
    K --> M["Migration<br/>faster, new data,<br/>new markets, combinations"]
    M --> D

docs.title: Stage by stage
docs.text:
Discovery. Ideas come from two places, and practitioners usually get there first. Gerry Bamberger was trading industry-group reversal at Morgan Stanley around 1983 [Reported], seven years before Lehmann (1990) published weekly reversals (see the stat arb history). Academic papers then turn a desk secret into a public recipe.

Early profits. With few users, the edge is limited only by costs and the strategy's natural capacity. Backtests from this phase look like free money. Khandani and Lo's contrarian rule earned a gross, frictionless 1.38% a day in 1995 [Verified]. Nobody could have captured that with eighth-dollar ticks, but it is a fair picture of how much price pressure went unabsorbed.

Publication and diffusion. McLean and Pontiff (2016) studied 97 published return predictors. Returns were 26% lower out of sample but before publication (an upper bound on data mining) and 58% lower after publication, so about 32 points of the decline is investors trading on the paper [Verified]. Two details matter for practitioners: the best in-sample predictors lost the most, and after publication each predictor's returns became more correlated with other published predictors [Verified]. Publication does not just shrink an edge; it pulls the edge into the common, crowded book. Falck, Rej and Thesmar (2022) find out-of-sample performance around half of in-sample, with publication date the main predictor of alpha decay [Verified].

Crowding. Capital follows returns. Hanson and Sunderam (2014) infer from short interest that money devoted to value and momentum grew substantially from the late 1980s and lowered their returns [Verified]. Chordia, Subrahmanyam and Tong (2014) find most prominent anomalies attenuated, and a portfolio of them earned roughly half as much after decimalization in 2001; hedge fund assets, short interest and share turnover explain the decline [Verified]. Cheaper trading lets more statistical arbitrage capital reach each mispricing.

Decay, or a crowded crash. A crowded edge dies in one of two ways. The slow way is a drought: the premium is competed down and returns fall below the cost of capital. The fast way is an unwind. As returns compress, funds add leverage to hit their targets: Khandani and Lo estimate the contrarian rule needed about 2:1 leverage in 1998 and nearly 9:1 in 2007 to deliver the same expected return, while long/short equity and market-neutral hedge fund assets in their database topped $160B at the start of 2007 [Verified]. One forced seller then hurts everyone holding the same positions: the quant quake of August 2007 (details in quant winters and the failure gallery).

A subtle trap sits inside the decay phase. When an anomaly becomes widely known, buying pressure reprices it, and that repricing shows up as positive realized return. Pénasse (2022) estimates this biases measured alpha by about 1.4% a year for commonly studied anomalies [Verified]. A strategy can look healthiest in the very years its future alpha is being competed away.

Migration. Surviving teams move in one of four directions: faster (the same liquidity-provision edge on a shorter clock), new data (information not yet in prices), new markets (less competed asset classes and regions) or more complex combinations (many weak signals, nonlinear models, better execution). Each direction restarts the cycle.

docs.title: Stat arb: from daily reversal to intraday and machine learning
docs.text:
Khandani and Lo's contrarian rule fell from 1.38% a day in 1995 to 0.44% in 2000 and 0.13% in the first eight months of 2007, all gross and frictionless [Verified]; they cite competition, decimalization, lower volatility and more assets. Avellaneda and Lee's PCA-residual strategy earned an after-cost Sharpe of 1.44 over 1997–2007, much stronger before 2003 and only 0.9 in 2003–2007 (academic backtest) [Verified]. Their fix is a textbook migration: measuring signals in volume-based "trading time" lifted the ETF-residual variant to a Sharpe of 1.51 in 2003–2007 [Verified]. Do and Faff (2010) confirm a continuing decline in simple pairs trading profits, with strong performance only in prolonged turbulence [Verified].

Industry moved toward intraday horizons, hundreds of combined signals and ML forecasts [Lore] (see ML-driven short-horizon alpha). The edge source did not change: it is still mostly payment for absorbing other traders' price pressure. What changed is that the payment is now collected faster, in smaller pieces, by teams with better cost models.

docs.title: HFT: boom, arms race, compression, consolidation
docs.text:
High-frequency trading boomed after Reg NMS (adopted 2005) fragmented US equities [Reported]. Tabb Group estimated US-equity HFT revenue at $7.2B in 2009 and expected it to fall below $1B in 2017, as reported by the Financial Times [Reported]. The causes were ordinary economics: low volatility and volumes, rising market-data and connectivity costs, and speed parity among competitors [Reported].

The latency arbitrage data show what competition does at the top speed tier. Budish, Cramton and Shim found the median ES–SPY arbitrage window shrank from 97 ms in 2005 to 7 ms in 2011 while profit per opportunity stayed roughly flat [Verified]: competition raised the speed required, not the price paid. Baron, Brogaard, Hagströmer and Kirilenko (2019) show that relative latency rank drives HFT trading performance [Verified], a recipe for winner-take-most. Consolidation followed: Virtu bought KCG for $1.4B, DRW bought Chopper Trading and RGM Advisors, and Teza sold its HFT business to Quantlab [Reported].

The pool then migrated rather than died. For 2025 the largest liquidity providers were reported to earn record revenues, global and multi-asset: Jane Street about $39.6B of net trading revenue (helped by gains on private stakes), Hudson River Trading about $12.3B and Citadel Securities about $12.2B [Reported]. OCC-cleared volume set a sixth straight annual record in 2025 at 15.26B contracts, 15.21B of them options [Verified]. The rent moved to options, ETFs, bonds and other markets, and onto the balance sheets of a handful of firms (see equity market making and options market making).

docs.title: Data edges: alternative data, then LLMs
docs.text:
Alternative data restarted the cycle for informational edges. Katona, Painter, Patatoukas and Zeng find that once satellite coverage of retailers' parking lots appeared (sample 2011–2017), investors with access traded profitably, especially ahead of bad-news quarters, and liquidity around reports fell [Verified]. Managers spent roughly $2.8B on alternative data in 2025 [Reported], so most datasets now have many buyers; as vendors add clients, the edge folds into consensus (alternative data).

Text shows the cycle compressing. After Loughran and McDonald published finance-specific word lists (2011), firms whose filings were heavily machine-read avoided the flagged words (Cao et al. 2023) [Verified]: the signal changed its own input. Lopez-Lira and Tang find GPT-4 headline scores predict the subsequent drift, especially in small stocks and on bad news, and that strategy returns decline as LLM adoption rises [Verified]. Our view [Estimate]: LLMs shorten the time from "new data type" to "commodity", because the scarce input used to be the ability to process text, and that is now cheap (see NLP and LLM signals and F4).

docs.title: What survives
docs.text: Not everything decays at the same rate. Momentum kept working through the 1990s after its 1993 publication (Jegadeesh and Titman 2001) [Verified], and liquidity provision re-expanded after 2017 instead of vanishing. The pattern matches the edge-source taxonomy in how quants evaluate a strategy. Our view [Estimate]: edges that pay for a service or a risk (immediacy, inventory, crash exposure) compress toward a fair price but persist, because someone keeps needing the service. Edges that pay for knowing something first (informational and many behavioral signals) decay toward zero, because knowledge spreads. Speed edges persist as a pool but concentrate in the fastest few.

docs.title: Planning for decay
docs.text:
Firms treat decay as a cost line, not a surprise.

  • Haircut every backtest. 30–60% of gross alpha is a common planning range [Lore], bracketing McLean and Pontiff's 26% out-of-sample and 58% post-publication declines (L2).
  • Budget research as maintenance capex. Illustrative: if a signal's alpha halves every three years, it loses 1 − 0.5^(1/3) ≈ 21% a year. A book needs that much new alpha every year just to stand still; with a two-year half-life, 29%.
  • Monitor crowding, not just P&L: rising correlation with peers and published factors, falling alpha per unit of turnover, violent reversals on de-risking days.
  • Refuse to lever a decaying edge to defend a return target. That choice turned 2007 from a drought into a crash.
  • Diversify across life-cycle stages so that not every signal is crowded at once (how firms combine strategies).

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: Where did this signal come from: a paper, a vendor or your own research? When was it published?
  • Informed: How has live Sharpe compared with the backtest, year by year? Has its correlation with published factors risen?
  • Sharp: What share of this year's research output replaced decayed alpha, and what share was net new? 🔒 Where did your last retired strategy's capital and people go?

docs.title: How firms combine strategies
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A multi-strategy book earns its Sharpe mostly from low correlation, not from precise weights. Three strategies at Sharpe 1.0, 1.5 and 0.8 combine to about 1.57 at equal risk and 1.64 at optimal weights (illustrative).
  • Two architectures: pod shops combine P&L streams from independent teams under central risk limits; centralized quant funds combine signals into one forecast and one optimizer ("one book"). One book nets trades and constraints before they cost money; pods buy talent, accountability and fast failure detection.
  • Correlation sets a ceiling: pods with Sharpe \(S\) and average pairwise correlation \(\rho\) can never combine to more than \(S/\sqrt{\rho}\). Crowding across pods raises \(\rho\).
  • Capital moves with drawdowns: Millennium reportedly halves a PM's capital at a 5% loss and is likely to part ways near 7.5% [Reported]. Such stops cap damage but detect skill poorly.
  • Multi-manager pass-through expenses typically run 3–10% of net assets [Reported], and the platform pays winning pods even in a flat year.

Level: Core · Read time: ~12 min · Last verified: 2026-11

A firm with several strategies faces a corporate-finance problem: allocate scarce capital and risk to business units with different returns, capacities and correlations, then decide how much to centralize. A pod shop is a conglomerate with divisional P&Ls, a central treasury and a tough capital-allocation committee. A centralized quant fund is one integrated factory: research teams supply signals (inputs) to one production line.

docs.text:

        direction TB
        p1["Pod 1<br/>own signals, own optimizer"] --> net1["Optional internal crossing"]
        p2["Pod 2<br/>own signals, own optimizer"] --> net1
        p3["Pod N<br/>own signals, own optimizer"] --> net1
        net1 --> mkt1["Market"]

        cr -.-> p3
    end
    subgraph ONE["One book: combine signals"]

        s2["Signal team B"] --> comb
