    end
Pod shop One book Unit combined P&L streams Forecasts (alpha combination) Who sets positions Each PM One optimizer Constraints Each pod neutral to market and factors Applied once, to the total Opposing trades Both executed unless crossed Netted before trading Accountability Clear: each PM owns a P&L Diffuse: credit split by attribution Examples Citadel, Millennium, Point72, Balyasny, ExodusPoint run multi-strategy funds with pass-through fees [Reported] Renaissance's Medallion was built as one unified trading model [Reported]

Most quant firms sit in between: a few books, each combining signals internally, with capital allocated across books [Lore].

docs.title: The portfolio math
docs.text:
Measure each strategy's allocation \(x_i\) in dollars of annual P&L volatility. With Sharpe ratios \(S_i\) and correlation matrix \(R\), expected P&L is \(\sum_i x_i S_i\) and risk is \(\sqrt{x^\top R x}\), so the book's Sharpe ratio is their ratio. The max-Sharpe weights are proportional to \(R^{-1}S\).

Worked example (illustrative). A firm targets $20M of annual P&L volatility across three strategies: A, residual stat arb (Sharpe 1.0); B, intraday ML alpha (1.5); C, slower fundamental signals (0.8). Correlations: A–B 0.4, A–C 0.1, B–C 0.2.

Allocation Risk to A / B / C ($M vol) Expected P&L Book Sharpe Best single strategy (B only) 0 / 20 / 0 $30.0M 1.50 Equal risk 9.5 / 9.5 / 9.5 9.53 × 3.3 = $31.5M 31.5 / 20 = 1.57 Max-Sharpe 5.7 / 14.8 / 6.2 $32.8M 1.64 Max-Sharpe, but B degrades to Sharpe 1.0 at that size 5.7 / 14.8 / 6.2 $25.4M 1.27 B capped at its capacity of $8M vol 9.9 / 8.0 / 10.9 $30.6M 1.53

Equal risk: each strategy runs at $9.53M because \(9.53 \times \sqrt{3 + 2(0.4+0.1+0.2)} = 9.53 \times 2.10 = 20\). Three lessons:

  1. Diversification does most of the work. Equal risk already beats the best single strategy, while depending less on any one edge.
  2. Optimizing weights adds little and is fragile. The optimizer gains 0.07 of Sharpe, less than the error in any Sharpe estimate; DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (2009) find naive 1/N weights hard to beat out of sample [Verified]. Firms start near equal risk (risk parity across strategies) and tilt.
  3. Allocate by marginal net Sharpe after impact, not standalone Sharpe. The optimizer piles into B, but B's capacity is limited; if its Sharpe falls to 1.0 at $14.8M of risk, the "optimal" book earns 1.27. Capping B and refilling A and C gives 1.53. Capacity-weighted allocation means each strategy gets risk until its marginal contribution, net of market impact, equals everyone else's.

Correlations are not constant. Crowded quant books lost together in August 2007 [Verified]. If all three correlations jump to 0.8 (illustrative), the equal-risk book's volatility becomes \(9.53 \times \sqrt{3 + 6 \times 0.8} = \$26.6M\), 33% over budget before returns change.

docs.title: Correlation sets the ceiling
docs.text:
For \(N\) pods with equal risk, Sharpe \(S\) each and average pairwise correlation \(\rho\):

\[ S_{book} = S\sqrt{\frac{N}{1+(N-1)\rho}} \;\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}\; \frac{S}{\sqrt{\rho}} \] Pods (\(S\) = 0.8 each, gross, illustrative) ρ = 0.02 ρ = 0.05 ρ = 0.10 ρ = 0.20 10 2.33 2.10 1.84 1.51 50 4.02 3.05 2.33 1.72 300 5.24 3.47 2.49 1.78 Ceiling, \(S/\sqrt{\rho}\) 5.66 3.58 2.53 1.79

Hiring more pods helps only while their average correlation stays low. That makes crowding the platform's central risk: pods hire from the same talent pool, buy the same data and hedge the same factors. Citadel's Ken Griffin has said he worries about "the correlation of holdings between the firms" [Reported], and an investor-marketing executive warned that such strategies could suffer much bigger drawdowns than their track records suggest [Reported]. Central risk teams watch holdings overlap across pods, residual-return correlations, aggregate position size as a share of daily volume, and prime brokers' crowding reports [Lore] (quant winters).

docs.title: Risk budgeting and drawdown cuts
docs.text:
Each pod gets capital and a risk budget: a volatility target, gross and net limits, and tight limits on market, sector and style exposure, so that the platform's return is mostly idiosyncratic (pod). The stop rules are reported, not published: a Millennium PM who loses 5% of allocated capital typically has it halved, and at a 7.5% total loss is likely fired, with occasional exceptions (Business Insider, citing the Wall Street Journal) [Reported]. Other accounts put the exit near 10% [Lore].

flowchart LR
    A["Allocate capital<br/>and risk budget"] --> B["Pods trade"]
    B --> C["Daily P and L, exposures,<br/>drawdown vs allocation"]
    C --> D{"Drawdown<br/>threshold hit?"}
    D -->|"5 pct"| E["Cut capital by half"]
    D -->|"7.5 pct"| F["Stop pod,<br/>review or exit"]
    D -->|"no"| G["Review Sharpe, capacity,<br/>correlation to other pods"]
    G -->|"strong, uncorrelated"| H["Add capital"]
    G -->|"crowded or decaying"| I["Trim capital"]
    E --> A
    F --> J["Recycle capital to<br/>new hires or winners"]
    J --> A
    H --> A
    I --> A

How good a filter is a 5% stop? In a simulation (normal daily P&L, one year, no cut after the first threshold) at 4% annual volatility, the chance of a 5% peak-to-trough drawdown within a year is about 37% for a zero-skill pod, 13% at Sharpe 1 and 3% at Sharpe 2 [Estimate]. At 6% volatility the zero-skill figure rises to 72% and Sharpe 1 to 43% [Estimate]. Measured as a loss from the starting allocation, as in the reported Millennium rule, the stop fires less often: about 20%, 4% and 0.5% at 4% volatility, and 38% and 13% (zero skill, Sharpe 1) at 6% [Estimate]. Two consequences: stops cull bad pods faster than good ones but still fire on many skilled ones, and they push PMs to run low volatility on allocated capital, with the platform adding leverage on top. Grossman and Zhou (1993) show that under a drawdown floor the optimal risky position is proportional to the cushion above the floor [Verified]; the 5%/7.5% ladder is a crude, discrete version of that rule.

import numpy as np

def allocate_risk(sharpe_hat, haircut, corr, capacity_vol, budget_vol, dd, prev_vol,
                  cut_dd=0.05, stop_dd=0.075):
    """Split a firm-wide risk budget ($ of annual P&L vol) across strategies or pods.
    haircut is per strategy: e.g. 0.5 if backtest-only, 0.2 with years of live history."""
    s = (1 - np.asarray(haircut)) * np.asarray(sharpe_hat, float)   # plan on decayed, net Sharpe
    w = np.clip(np.linalg.solve(corr, s), 0, None)           # max-Sharpe risk weights; no negative pods
    # Drawdown ladder (reported pod practice; thresholds differ by firm):
    cap = np.where(dd >= cut_dd, 0.5 * prev_vol, capacity_vol)   # >= 5%: half the old allocation
    cap = np.where(dd >= stop_dd, 0.0, cap)                       # >= 7.5%: switched off
    w = np.where(cap > 0, w, 0.0)
    x = np.minimum(w * budget_vol / max(np.sqrt(w @ corr @ w), 1e-12), cap)  # to $ units, then cap
    for _ in range(100):                                     # rescale to the budget without breaching caps
        vol = np.sqrt(x @ corr @ x)
        if vol == 0:
            break
        scale = budget_vol / vol
        grow = (x < cap) & (x > 0)
        if abs(scale - 1) < 1e-9 or (scale > 1 and not grow.any()):
            break                                            # on budget, or every pod capped: keep dry powder
        x = x * scale if scale < 1 else np.where(grow, np.minimum(x * scale, cap), x)
    return x                                                 # capital_i = x_i / vol_i (vol as a fraction)

With the example's inputs, no haircut and B capped at $8M, this returns $9.9M / $8.0M / $10.9M (the last table row). If C then sits in a 5.5% drawdown, C is cut to $5.4M and A grows to $13.7M; book Sharpe falls from 1.53 to 1.50 [Estimate].

docs.title: Signals first or P&L first?
docs.text:
The case for one book. The transfer coefficient measures how much of a forecast survives into positions; Clarke, de Silva and Thorley (2002) report realized performance at about 0.3–0.8 of the unconstrained prediction [Verified]. Forcing every pod to be separately market-, sector- and factor-neutral spends that budget N times; one optimizer spends it once. Opposite views also cancel: if signal A says +1 and signal B says −1 on a stock, two pods hold +X and −X, paying spread, borrow and margin for a net position of zero; one book holds nothing. Sharpe (1981) framed the cost of splitting a portfolio among independent managers; van Binsbergen, Brandt and Koijen (2008) show it loses diversification and misaligns risk appetite, costs a CIO can only partly fix with benchmarks [Verified]. Zuckerman reports that Medallion was built as one model absorbing several, which made new signals easier to add [Reported].

The case for pods. Independent people with independent methods produce less correlated returns, which the ceiling table rewards. Each P&L is observable, so failure is detected and cut quickly, and the structure scales by hiring.

The evidence is mixed. For long-only factor portfolios, Ghayur, Heaney and Platt (2018) find blending portfolios gives higher information ratios at low-to-moderate tracking error and blending signals wins at high tracking error [Verified]; AQR researchers argue that for long-only style portfolios, integrating signals beats mixing portfolios [Reported]. No study settles pods versus one book for market-neutral platforms.

docs.title: Internal netting: a worked example
docs.text:
Illustrative: a momentum pod wants to buy 200,000 shares of XYZ at $50, or $10M, while a reversal pod sells 150,000 shares, or $7.5M. Cost model: 2 bp half-spread plus impact of 6 bp at $10M, scaling with the square root of size.

Trades Cost Separately Buy $10M at 2 + 6 = 8 bp; sell $7.5M at 2 + 6 × √0.75 = 7.2 bp $8,000 + $5,400 = $13,400 Netted Cross $7.5M internally at the midpoint; buy the net $2.5M at 2 + 6 × √0.25 = 5 bp $1,250

Saving: $12,150, or 91%. Firm level [Estimate]: a $5B book turning over 50× a year trades $250B; if 15% crosses internally at an average 7 bp avoided, that is about $26M a year, roughly 0.5% of gross capital. Practice points [Lore]: cross at the midpoint or arrival price so neither pod is favored; hold orders briefly in a crossing engine because opposite orders rarely arrive together; keep information barriers so pods cannot read each other's flow. Crossing between two separate funds is a regulated cross trade, not bookkeeping; for registered funds the rule is Investment Company Act rule 17a-7, which the SEC proposed to modernize (91 FR 65622, published 2026-10-15; comments due 2026-12-14) [Verified].

docs.title: The economics
docs.text:
Multi-managers typically pass operating costs, mostly PM pay, through to investors: pass-through fees typically run 3–10% of net assets [Reported], against a typical hedge fund management fee of about 1.35% [Reported]. Balyasny's flagship fund (Atlas Enhanced) reportedly earned 15.2% gross in 2023 but 2.8% net, with $768M of pass-through expenses, 87% of it compensation [Reported]. Man Group added pass-through fees for its multi-strategy fund in 2024 [Reported]. Investor appetite cooled: Goldman Sachs data showed the sector's first net outflows in seven years, more than $30B in the 12 months to June 2024 [Reported].

The hidden cost is netting risk. Illustrative: PMs keep 20% of their own positive P&L [Lore]. Winning pods make $300M and losing pods lose $200M; the fund nets $100M but pays 20% × $300M = $60M, 60% of net P&L. Each payout is a call option on one pod's P&L, and a sum of calls is worth more than a call on the sum. That is why platforms cut losers fast and fight correlation: losses are borne in full, gains are shared.

Math: combined Sharpe and optimal risk weights

With risk allocations \(x\) (dollars of volatility), Sharpe vector \(S\) and correlation matrix \(R\):

\[ S_{book}(x) = \frac{x^\top S}{\sqrt{x^\top R x}}, \qquad x^{*} \propto R^{-1} S, \qquad S_{book}(x^{*}) = \sqrt{S^\top R^{-1} S} \]

For the example, \(S^\top R^{-1} S = 2.69\), so the maximum is \(\sqrt{2.69} = 1.64\). Adding a strategy at a small weight helps only if its Sharpe exceeds \(\rho \times S_{book}\) (derivation). The \(N\)-pod formula follows from setting all \(S_i = S\) and all off-diagonal correlations to \(\rho\).

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
• Basic: Do you combine signals or P&L streams? How is risk budgeted across books?
  • Informed: What share of your gross trading is netted internally? What average pairwise correlation do your pods run at?
  • Sharp: How much of the platform's Sharpe comes from diversification versus pod skill? 🔒 What are your drawdown thresholds, and how often do they fire on PMs who later prove skilled?

docs.title: Strategy comparison matrix
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • One row per dossier, condensed from its header table, with the confidence tags carried over. Treat every number as an order of magnitude and click through for the reasoning.
  • Capacity and Sharpe trade off. Market-making and speed books show Sharpe ratios above 3 where the number means anything, on profit pools of a few $B a year for the whole industry; risk-premia books run tens of billions at net Sharpe 0.3–0.7.
  • Evidence quality runs the other way: slow strategies' Sharpe ratios are [Verified] from decades of public data, fast strategies' are mostly [Lore].
  • Strategies cluster by failure mode: crowded deleveraging (stat arb, mid-frequency alpha, factors), short convexity (volatility selling, dispersion, carry, options market making), and technology or rule changes (speed and market making). Diversify across clusters, not across rows.

Level: Core · Read time: ~11 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Every dossier opens with the same header table, so the 30 strategies compare directly. This page lines them up. Cells are compressed to a few words; the dossier holds the period, source type and reasoning behind each figure.

docs.title: How to read this table
docs.text:
Capacity comes in three units, and they do not compare. For portfolio strategies (families C–G) it is the gross market value or notional one firm can run before costs eat the edge. For market making and speed (A–B) capital is not what binds; the flow available to intermediate is, so the dossiers quote an annual profit pool, usually for the whole industry. Dispersion quotes vega. "$1–3B a year of P&L" and "$1–10B of GMV" describe different things.

The Sharpe column mixes sources on purpose. An arrow separates gross from net when the dossier gives both; otherwise the cell says which. Academic gross backtests are upper bounds, measured over different decades, and published anomalies lose about 58% of their in-sample return after publication (McLean and Pontiff 2016) [Verified]. For a market maker, Sharpe ratio on capital is "n/m": the capital at risk is small, and technology, data and staff costs, not volatility, decide whether the business pays.

Turnover times cost is the drag. A book trading 50× its GMV a year at 5 bps per dollar traded pays 2.5% of GMV a year before any alpha (illustrative). That is why the short-horizon rows live or die by their transaction cost models.

Positions are approximate and illustrative, read off the table above. Market-making Sharpe is measured on the small capital those books use.

The upper-right quadrant is nearly empty. The reason is market impact: under the square-root law, cost per dollar traded rises with the square root of trade size, so total cost grows like size^1.5 while gross alpha grows like size. Profit peaks at 4/9 of the break-even size (derivation in the reversal dossier). Fast strategies hit that wall early because they trade their book 50–250 times a year; factor and trend books trade it a few times a year and run tens of billions.

docs.title: 2. Short horizons show higher Sharpe
docs.text: The fundamental law of active management says the information ratio is roughly skill per bet times the square root of independent bets per year, the breadth (Grinold 1989) [Verified]. Illustrative: a daily residual book with an IC of 0.01 and ~200 independent bets a day has breadth of about 50,000, so IR ≈ 0.01 × 224 ≈ 2.2. A monthly factor book with IC 0.05 but only ~20 independent bets a month has breadth 240 and IR ≈ 0.8. A market maker's day is thousands of nearly independent small bets, which is how Virtu's IPO filing could show one losing day in 1,238 [Reported]. The catch is the previous section: breadth bought with turnover runs into capacity.

docs.title: 3. The best numbers have the weakest evidence
docs.text: The [Verified] Sharpe ratios cluster in families E–G, computed from public data spanning four decades or more. Nearly every market-making and speed figure is [Lore] or a single academic case study, because those firms do not publish strategy returns. The most reliable numbers in the table are the lowest ones.

"High" crowding appears in most rows; what matters is who is crowded with whom. In August 2007 stat-arb and factor books lost together, consistent with a rapid unwind of overlapping positions (Khandani and Lo 2011) [Verified]. The short-convexity rows lose in the same volatility spike. The speed rows fail one firm at a time, through code or lost latency rank, or all at once through rule changes such as the half-penny tick and 10-mil access-fee cap, now delayed to November 2027 [Verified]. Episodes are in the failure gallery.

docs.title: 5. Complements for a multi-strategy book
docs.text: Rows from different clusters diversify each other; rows from the same cluster do not. Trend following had about zero correlation to US equities over 1880–2013 and made money in 8 of the 10 worst 60/40 drawdowns (Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen) [Verified], the opposite profile to volatility selling and carry. Value and momentum correlated −0.19 month to month over 1963–2026 [Verified] (our computation, French data). Short-term reversal's expected return rises with the VIX (Nagel 2012) [Verified], but only after the drawdown: in March 2020 the daily factor lost 18.4% before gaining 31.7% [Verified]. Capacity complements too: small, high-Sharpe books add return per unit of risk, while large, low-Sharpe books absorb capital. How firms combine strategies gives the arithmetic, including the \(S/\sqrt{\rho}\) ceiling that crowding imposes.

docs.title: Strategy failure gallery
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Nine documented episodes, three kinds of failure. Most were crowded, levered positions unwinding into thin liquidity (1998, 2007, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024). Two were machines doing exactly what they were told (2010, 2012). One was a slow drought rather than a crash (value, 2017–2020).
  • The common engine is a feedback loop. Losses force selling, the selling moves prices, and the new prices force more selling. Leverage sets how fast the loop runs; liquidity sets how far prices go.
  • Many of these losses reversed for anyone who could keep holding. Khandani and Lo's model stat-arb strategy lost 6.85% over 7–9 August 2007 and made back 5.92% on 10 August [Verified]. Survival depended on leverage and on rules agreed in advance, not on the signal.
  • Much of today's US equity rulebook was written after these days: LULD bands and new circuit breakers (after 2010), the first big market access rule case (Knight, 2013), T+1 settlement (after 2021).
  • The practical lessons repeat. Size positions by stress loss, not volatility. Measure crowding. Keep risk checks independent of strategy code. Never let a calm-period hedge ratio or a pre-market quote-based index drive automatic de-risking.

Level: Core · Read time: ~22 min · Last verified: 2026-11

Every strategy has a way it dies, and that is part of its specification. The cases below follow one format: the strategy involved, the loss mechanism step by step with the numbers, who was on the other side, what changed afterwards, and lessons for quants. Each links to the dossiers and algorithm cards that cover the machinery. Fund-level loss figures come from press reports and are tagged [Reported]. Mechanism figures come from regulators' reports, papers or our own computations on public data.

docs.title: 1. LTCM and the convergence trade (August–September 1998)
docs.text:
Strategy: convergence arbitrage, a close neighbour of statistical arbitrage. Buy the cheaper of two near-identical claims, short the dearer one, and lever the small spread. About 80% of LTCM's securities were G-7 government bonds [Verified] (CRS 1999).

Loss mechanism, step by step

  1. Scale. In spring 1998 LTCM had about $3.5B of investor equity. It held about $100B of securities through repo and short sales, about $500B of futures and about $750B of OTC derivatives notional. On securities alone that is roughly 30:1 leverage [Verified] (CRS). At the end of 1997 it had returned $2.75B of capital to investors without cutting its positions, which raised leverage [Verified] (Greenspan; McDonough).
  2. Fragility. Illustrative: at 30:1, a spread worth 0.2% of the gross book earns 6% on equity when it converges, and a 0.2% move against the book costs 6% of equity. A 1.7% adverse move halves equity (0.5 ÷ 30) [Estimate]. The edge belongs only to a holder who can sit through the marks.
  3. Shock. After Russia's August default, investors fled to the most liquid Treasuries. The spreads LTCM was paid to own widened instead of narrowing [Verified] (CRS).
  4. Correlation. Positions chosen to be independent moved together, because the same flight to liquidity drove all of them [Verified] (CRS).
  5. Loss. On 2 September LTCM told investors it was down 52% for the year through 31 August [Verified] (McDonough). The VIX had closed at 44.3 on 31 August [Verified] (FRED).

Who was on the other side. Investors paying up for liquidity and safety, and dealers who knew LTCM's positions and could trade ahead of a forced seller [Lore]. LTCM had more than 75 counterparties. A disorderly close-out of hundreds of billions of dollars of positions could have cost some of them several billion dollars [Verified] (McDonough).

What changed. On 23 September, 14 banks and securities firms, convened by the New York Fed, injected about $3.6B for roughly 90% of the fund, heavily diluting the original investors [Verified] (McDonough; CRS; Greenspan). The President's Working Group report of April 1999 named excessive leverage as the core policy problem and called for better counterparty risk management and more disclosure [Verified] (CRS). Greenspan said creditors had not stress-tested their exposures [Verified].

Lessons for quants

  • A convergence trade is short liquidity. It loses at exactly the moment liquidity is scarce.
  • Correlations estimated in calm markets understate correlations in a crisis (P2).
  • If competitors know your positions, they become part of your risk model.
  • Convergence is certain only at maturity, if at all. The marks before then decide whether you are still there to collect it.

Go deeper: stat arb overview · pairs trading · P1 risk models · P7 position sizing.

docs.title: 2. The August 2007 quant quake
docs.text:
Strategy: equity market-neutral stat arb and multi-factor long-short books, run at high leverage by many firms with overlapping signals. This is the canonical quant quake.

Loss mechanism, step by step (Khandani & Lo 2007, 2011)

  1. Alpha decay, then leverage. A simple daily contrarian strategy (short-term reversal) earned a mean of 1.38% a day in 1995, falling to 0.13% in 2007 to August. Matching 1998's expected return would have needed almost 9:1 leverage in 2007 [Verified].
  2. Trigger (hypothesis). In July, losses elsewhere led at least one large multi-strategy fund or bank desk to liquidate a quant equity book quickly. The authors call this a speculative hypothesis built on indirect evidence [Verified]. Using transactions data, their 2011 paper dates the sustained unwind to the open on 6 August, after deleveraging through July [Verified].
  3. Unwind. On 7, 8 and 9 August the base strategy (2:1 gross-to-capital, the Reg T convention the authors use) lost 1.16%, 2.83% and 2.86%. The total, −6.85%, was 12 daily standard deviations at its 2006 volatility [Verified].
  4. Leverage. At 8:1, four times the base, the same days read −4.64%, −11.33% and −11.43%, a quarter of capital in three days [Verified]. Market makers pulled back from 8 August, and other funds' stop-losses and de-grossing added to the selling on 8–9 August [Verified].
  5. Reversal. On 10 August the strategy made 5.92% (11.4 standard deviations). Its return for the whole week was −0.43% [Verified].

Reported fund results: one Renaissance fund −8.7% so far in August (WSJ, 10 August); Highbridge Statistical Opportunities −18% to 8 August; Goldman's Global Equity Opportunities fund down more than 30% in a week (WSJ, cited by Khandani & Lo) [Reported]. Goldman's CFO described "25-standard deviation moves, several days in a row" [Reported].

Who was on the other side. Whoever had balance sheet and nerve. On 13 August Goldman and outside investors put $3B into the Global Equity Opportunities fund, in effect buying the unwind [Verified]. Market makers who stayed in charged wide spreads; those who withdrew on 8 August made every forced sale move prices further. Funds that de-grossed at the bottom handed the 10 August rebound to whoever bought from them.

What changed. Crowding became a risk factor that firms measure: peer overlap, prime-broker crowding reports, residual co-movement (comomentum) [Reported]. Leverage on these books came down, and de-grossing rules began to be written in advance [Lore].

Lessons for quants

  • Your risk model sees your factors, not your neighbours' portfolios. Crowding is a hidden common factor.
  • A 12-sigma day means the return distribution was wrong, not that you were unlucky.
  • Selling into an unwind turns a temporary mark-to-market loss into a realized one. The worked deleveraging example in the factor-timing dossier shows the arithmetic.

Go deeper: factor timing, crowding and quant winters · short-term reversal · factor-residual mean reversion · F6 regime detection · P7 position sizing.

docs.title: 3. The Flash Crash (6 May 2010)
docs.text:
Strategies: an execution algorithm hedging a $4.1B equity position; HFT intermediaries in the E-mini; cross-market index arbitrage; equity market makers and retail internalizers.

Loss mechanism, step by step (CFTC-SEC staff report, 2010-09-30)

  1. Fragile start. Markets were already down over 4% on European debt news. E-mini buy-side depth had fallen 55%, from nearly $6B to $2.65B [Verified].
  2. The sell program. At 2:32 p.m. a mutual fund complex began selling 75,000 E-minis (about $4.1B) to hedge an equity position. Its algorithm targeted 9% of the previous minute's volume, "without regard to price or time". A similar program had earlier taken more than five hours [Verified].
  3. Volume is not liquidity. HFTs bought, then resold to cut inventory. The extra volume made the algorithm sell faster. From 2:41 to 2:44 the E-mini fell about 3%, and arbitrageurs who bought it sold SPY and stock baskets [Verified].
  4. Hot potato. Between 2:45:13 and 2:45:27, HFTs traded over 27,000 contracts, 49% of volume, but added only about 200 contracts net. Buy-side depth fell to about $58M, under 1% of the morning level. In 4.5 minutes the E-mini fell more than 5% and SPY more than 6% [Verified].
  5. Pause. CME's Stop Logic halted the E-mini for five seconds at 2:45:28, and prices recovered [Verified].
  6. Stocks. Liquidity providers' automatic pauses fired together. Internalizers routed retail orders, including stop-losses, to exchanges. Over 20,000 trades in more than 300 securities executed 60% or more away from 2:40 prices, some at stub quotes of a penny or $100,000, and were broken [Verified].
sequenceDiagram
    participant FS as Fundamental seller algo
    participant EM as E-mini book
    participant HF as HFT intermediaries
    participant AR as Index arbitrageurs
    participant EQ as SPY and stocks
    FS->>EM: Sell 9 percent of last minute volume, no price limit
    HF->>EM: Buy, then resell to cut inventory
    EM-->>FS: Volume rises, so the algo sells faster
    AR->>EM: Buy E-mini
    AR->>EQ: Sell SPY and stock baskets
    HF->>HF: Hot potato, 27,000 contracts traded, about 200 net
    Note over EM: CME Stop Logic pauses trading for five seconds
    EM-->>EQ: Futures recover first, then SPY
    Note over EQ: Market makers pause, market orders hit stub quotes

Who was on the other side. In the 13 minutes from 2:32, fundamental buyers absorbed about 50,000 contracts against 80,000 sold [Verified]. Kirilenko et al. (2017) find the most active HFTs did not change their trading pattern as prices fell [Verified]. They kept intermediating but did not absorb the imbalance.

What changed. A single-stock circuit breaker pilot started in June 2010 (a 5-minute pause after a 10% move in 5 minutes) [Verified]. Stub quotes were banned from 6 December 2010: market makers' quotes must sit within 8% of the NBBO for large stocks [Verified]. The market access rule followed in November 2010, then large-trader reporting (2011) and the consolidated audit trail (2012) [Verified]. LULD and market-wide circuit breakers at 7/13/20% of the S&P 500 were approved on 2012-05-31 and phased in from 2013 [Reported]. LULD's big test came on 24 August 2015: 1,278 halts, 1,058 of them in 327 ETPs [Verified].

Lessons for quants

  • A participation-rate algorithm needs a price limit (E2).
  • Market makers' kill switches are correlated. Everyone's fires at the same time (M9).
  • Arbitrage links between futures, ETFs and stocks carry a shock from one market to the next.

Go deeper: equity market making · latency arbitrage · ETF and index arbitrage · E1 execution algorithms.

docs.title: 4. Knight Capital (1 August 2012)
docs.text:
Strategy: retail market making. Knight was a leading wholesaler, and its router was being updated for NYSE's new Retail Liquidity Program.

Loss mechanism, step by step (SEC order, 2013-10-16)

  1. Deployment. New code was installed on eight servers but missed one. A repurposed flag woke long-dead order logic on that server [Verified].
  2. Runaway loop. The dead code sent child orders without counting fills. In about 45 minutes, 212 small retail parent orders produced over 4 million executions in 154 stocks, about 397 million shares [Verified].
  3. Position. Knight ended with about $3.5B of unintended longs and $3.15B of shorts [Verified]. That is $6.65B gross in 2,700 seconds, about $2.5M a second. A $50M firm-wide gross cap would have tripped after about 20 seconds [Estimate] (worked in the M9 card).
  4. Missed warnings. Before the open, 97 automated emails flagged an error. They were not designed as alerts and nobody acted on them [Verified].
  5. Missing controls. No check compared orders leaving the router with orders entering it, and no automated firm-wide limit was linked to the account [Verified].
  6. Loss. Over $460M [Verified], about $1.16 per share traded [Estimate].

Who was on the other side. Everyone who traded with the algorithm. It repeatedly bought at the offer and sold at the bid, paying the spread on hundreds of millions of shares to market makers and other traders. Its own buying and selling also moved prices against it [Estimate].

What changed. On 6 August a Jefferies-led group bought $400M of convertible preferred, leaving investors with roughly 73% of Knight [Reported]. In December 2012 Knight agreed to merge with GETCO; the merged firm, KCG Holdings, formed in 2013 [Reported]. The SEC's first market access rule case followed, with a $12M penalty [Verified]. The rule requires pre-trade credit and capital limits, checks for erroneous orders, the broker's direct and exclusive control of those checks, and an annual CEO certification [Verified] (M9 card). Firms also moved toward staged deployments, automatic post-release reconciliation and risk gateways separate from the strategy [Lore]. Regulation SCI (adopted 2014) set systems-integrity requirements for exchanges and other key market systems, though not for broker-dealers like Knight [Verified].

Lessons for quants

  • Risk checks must sit outside the strategy code and compare intent with outcome: orders with fills, position with limit (M9).
  • An alert nobody reads is just a log (L1).
  • Detection time has a price. At $2.5M of new gross exposure a second, a kill switch that needs a human to notice is far too slow.
  • Retire dead code the way you retire dead models (L2).

Go deeper: retail flow internalization · equity market making · M1 anatomy of an HFT loop.

docs.title: 5. The value "quant winter" (December 2016 – September 2020)
docs.text:
Strategy: value tilts inside multi-factor quant equity books and style-premia funds, long and long-short.

Loss mechanism, step by step

  1. No single shock. The Fama-French value factor (HML) peaked in December 2016, then lost 51% to September 2020, compounding monthly returns. From its December 2006 high the drawdown reached 58% [Verified] (our computation, French data).
  2. Cheap got cheaper. The value spread, the valuation gap between cheap and expensive stocks, was at the 86th percentile of its 1951–2026 history in 2017 and kept widening [Verified] (factor-timing dossier). Prices of expensive stocks rose faster than their fundamentals, so the gap widened even as value lost. A long-short value book earns roughly its carry plus the change in the spread. A widening spread is a mark-to-market loss today that raises expected returns tomorrow, which is why managers called the factor cheap while clients called it broken.
  3. Leverage and clients. Style funds run at several times gross leverage felt the drought fully. AQR's Style Premia Alternative Fund lost 22.0% in 2020 (fund fact sheet), and AQR's regulatory assets fell from $248.9B (2019) to $164.4B (2020) [Reported].
  4. Final leg. HML lost 13.8% in March 2020 alone [Verified] (our computation).
  5. Rebound. On 9 November 2020, vaccine news lifted HML 6.7% while momentum lost 14.4% in one day. From October 2020 to December 2022, HML gained 68% [Verified] (our computation). The same AQR fund returned about 25% in 2021 and 31% in 2022 [Reported]. HML was still 18% below its December 2016 level at the end of 2022 and fell again in 2023–2024 [Verified] (our computation).

Who was on the other side. No forced buyer: holders of expensive growth stocks, chiefly large-cap technology, earned what value lost [Estimate]. Clients who redeemed near the bottom left the rebound to those who stayed.

What changed. Managers diluted pure book-to-market, using several value measures, intangible-adjusted book and more residual and alternative signals [Lore]. The causes are still debated. AQR attributes the losses to spreads widening, not crowded unwinds [Verified] (AQR, 2026). Arnott, Harvey, Kalesnik and Linnainmaa (2021) find the change in the valuation spread explains the entire drawdown. They also argue that book-to-price misses intangible assets, and that capitalizing R&D and part of SG&A gives a better value measure [Reported]. Factor timing remains contested (dossier).

Lessons for quants

  • How long a drawdown lasts can kill a fund faster than how deep it goes, because clients redeem.
  • Separate "the signal died" from "the premium got wider": a decay test (L2) plus the value spread.
  • One factor's drought is survivable only inside a diversified book (how firms combine strategies).

Go deeper: value, quality and low volatility · factor investing fundamentals · F6 regime detection · AQR profile.

docs.title: 6. "Volmageddon": the short-volatility unwind (5 February 2018)
docs.text:
Strategy: harvesting the variance risk premium by being short VIX futures, packaged as daily-reset inverse exchange-traded products (XIV, SVXY) and held by investors betting that volatility stays low.

Loss mechanism, step by step

  1. Growth. VIX futures open interest rose from about 180,000 contracts a day on average in 2011 to 590,000 in 2017. Leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs reached about $4B of assets [Verified] (BIS).
  2. Daily reset. A product with multiple \(L\) must trade \(L(L-1) \times \text{NAV} \times r\) of futures at the close after an index return \(r\). For a 2× long fund and a −1× inverse fund alike, that means buying after volatility rises. Both rebalance just before 4:15 p.m. [Verified] (BIS).
  3. Shock. The S&P 500 fell about 4%. The VIX closed at 37.32 against 17.31, up 115.6%, the largest one-day percentage rise in the 1990–2026 daily series [Verified] (FRED, our computation).
  4. Front-running. Traders bid up VIX futures from about 3:30 p.m. In the single minute at 4:08 p.m., 115,862 contracts traded, roughly a quarter of the market [Verified] (BIS).
  5. Wipe-out. XIV's closing indicative value fell from $108.37 to about $4.22, −96% [Reported]; the BIS gives −84%. An intraday value at or below 20% of the prior close was an acceleration event, so Credit Suisse terminated the note, with final valuation on 15 February [Verified].

Illustrative sizing: an inverse product with $2B of NAV facing a +96% index day must buy $3.84B of VIX futures. At a futures price near 30 ($30,000 a contract), that is about 128,000 contracts, the same order as the 4:08 p.m. print [Estimate].

def etp_rebalance(nav, lev, r):
    """Futures notional a daily-reset ETP must buy (+) or sell (-) at the close.
    nav: assets before the move ($); lev: +2 (2x long), -1 (inverse); r: index return."""
    exposure_after_move = lev * nav * (1 + r)   # futures position, marked to market
    nav_after = nav * (1 + lev * r)             # fund NAV after the day
    target = lev * nav_after                    # restore the target multiple
    return target - exposure_after_move         # = lev * (lev - 1) * nav * r

# 5 Feb 2018, illustrative sizes; index +96% close to close (implied by XIV's -96%)
etp_rebalance(2.0e9, -1.0, 0.96)   # inverse: buy ~$3.84B of VIX futures
etp_rebalance(1.5e9,  2.0, 0.96)   # 2x long: buy ~$2.88B
etp_rebalance(2.0e9, -0.5, 0.96)   # after the -0.5x redesign: buy ~$1.44B

Who was on the other side. Long-volatility holders, traders who anticipated the rebalance, and VIX futures dealers. The dealers hedged their sales to the ETPs by shorting E-minis, pushing equities lower [Verified] (BIS).

What changed. XIV was terminated. ProShares cut SVXY from −1× to −0.5× and UVXY from 2× to 1.5× from the close of 2018-02-27 [Verified]. For the inverse product, that cuts the rebalancing factor \(L(L-1)\) from 2 to 0.75 [Estimate]. In 2020 the SEC's fund derivatives rule (Rule 18f-4) set value-at-risk limits on fund leverage [Verified].

Lessons for quants

  • Mechanical rebalancers are predictable, and others will trade ahead of them.
  • A short-volatility book should be sized for a VIX that doubles in a day, which is now in the data (P7).
  • Losses on short volatility are convex. XIV could lose at most 100%, but anything levered on it could lose more.

Go deeper: volatility risk premium and vol arb · options market making · M7 hedging algorithms.

Math: why leveraged and inverse ETPs both trade with the market

A fund with NAV \(A\) and target multiple \(L\) holds exposure \(LA\). After an index return \(r\), exposure is \(LA(1+r)\) and NAV is \(A(1+Lr)\). Restoring the multiple needs a trade

\[ \Delta = L A (1 + L r) - L A (1 + r) = L (L - 1)\, A\, r . \]

\(L(L-1) > 0\) whenever \(L > 1\) or \(L < 0\). Leveraged long and inverse funds therefore both buy after the index rises and sell after it falls: they are momentum traders by construction. Only a multiple between 0 and 1 trades against the move. Cutting an inverse fund from \(L = -1\) to \(L = -0.5\) cuts \(L(L-1)\) from 2 to 0.75.

docs.title: 7. March 2020: deleveraging and liquidity spirals
docs.text:
Strategies: quant equity market-neutral, volatility targeting and risk parity, and fixed-income relative value. All shared one constraint: margin.

Loss mechanism, step by step

  1. Volatility shock. The VIX went from 14.38 on 19 February to a record close of 82.69 on 16 March [Verified] (FRED). Market-wide circuit breakers fired four times in March [Verified].
  2. Mechanical selling. Volatility targeting sets exposure to target volatility divided by realized volatility. Illustrative: a fund targeting 10% volatility holds 1.0× exposure while realized volatility is 10%. At 40% realized volatility the rule says 0.25×, so the fund sells three-quarters of its book after the fall that raised volatility [Estimate] (P7). Every fund with the same rule sells in the same week.
  3. Margin and broken hedges. Most of the rise in initial margin on cleared derivatives came between 6 and 13 March. In the "dash for cash", investors sold even Treasuries, so stocks and government bonds fell together instead of offsetting. US equity and Treasury market depth fell to levels last seen in the worst of 2008 [Verified] (FSB).
  4. Spirals. Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2009) describe two loops. In the loss spiral, losses force sales that depress prices. In the margin spiral, higher volatility raises margins, which force more sales [Verified].
  5. Factors. HML lost 4.75% on 9 March and 4.74% on 18 March, and 13.8% for the month [Verified] (our computation).
  6. Hedges misfire. Renaissance's RIEF fell about 14% in the first quarter and 19% in 2020. RIDA lost 32% and RIDGE 31%, while the insiders' Medallion fund gained 76% [Reported]. Investor letters reportedly blamed under-hedging in March and over-hedging from April to June [Reported].
flowchart LR
    shock["Initial loss or<br/>volatility spike"] --> margin["Margins, VaR and<br/>vol targets tighten"]
    margin --> sell["Forced selling<br/>of shared positions"]
    sell --> price["Prices move against<br/>everyone holding them"]
    price --> loss["Mark-to-market losses<br/>cut equity"]
    loss --> margin
    price --> mm["Market makers widen<br/>quotes or withdraw"]
    mm --> price
    sell --> stop{"Selling stops?<br/>pause, rescue capital,<br/>central bank"}
    stop --> revert["Prices revert: holders<br/>recover, sellers do not"]

Who was on the other side. Liquidity providers who charged wide spreads (the FSB documents wider bid-ask spreads in US equities), unlevered investors with cash and, in the end, central banks. The FSB notes that the dash for cash lasted until central banks intervened [Verified]. Funds that had to sell supplied the discount; whoever could buy and hold collected it.

What changed. The FSB's November 2020 review launched work on margin practices and on non-bank leverage and liquidity [Verified]. Inside firms, the lesson was about estimation windows. Betas and hedge ratios fitted to calm data were wrong in stress, and slow, capped volatility targeting replaced fast rules at some firms [Lore].

Lessons for quants

  • Market-neutral is not liquidity-neutral.
  • Your sizing rule is someone else's order flow. Volatility targeters sell together.
  • Estimate hedge ratios under stress as well as in calm markets, and watch them during regime breaks (F6).

Go deeper: factor timing and crowding · trend following and CTAs · P1 risk models · Renaissance profile.

docs.title: 8. The meme-stock squeezes (January 2021)
docs.text:
Strategies: fundamental short selling, quant books holding the same crowded shorts, retail-flow internalization, and options market making.

Loss mechanism, step by step

  1. Crowded short. GameStop was the only stock SEC staff observed with short interest above its shares outstanding in January 2021 [Reported] (summaries of the SEC staff report).
  2. Buying wave. Retail investors coordinating on social media bought shares and call options. GameStop rose from about $18 in early January to a record close of $347.51 on 27 January and an intraday peak of $483 [Reported] (prices before the 2022 split).
  3. Convex short loss. Illustrative: a 1M-share short opened at $20 loses $327.5M at $347.51, 16 times the position's starting value. A broker's margin demand on a short rises with the price, and borrow can be recalled [Estimate].
  4. Not mainly a squeeze. Staff found that buying to cover was a small fraction of buy volume and that the price stayed high after covering ended. They found no evidence of a "gamma squeeze" driven by option dealers' hedging [Reported] (SEC staff report, as summarized).
  5. Plumbing. On 27 January NSCC called $6.9B of intraday margin from 36 members, and some brokers restricted buying. Wholesalers routed the stock out: its off-exchange share fell from 62.6% to 32.8% within a week [Verified] (retail-flow dossier). The VIX rose 62% that day, from 23.02 to 37.21 [Verified] (FRED).
  6. Fund loss. Melvin Capital lost 53% in January and took $2.75B from Citadel ($2B) and Point72 ($750M). It announced its wind-down in May 2022 [Reported].

Who was on the other side. Retail buyers of shares and calls, the option market makers who delta-hedged those calls, and early sellers who took profits from late buyers. Quant books with crowding or short-interest signals held the same shorts, so de-grossing spread across the market [Lore].

What changed. SEC staff published a report in October 2021. T+1 settlement was adopted in 2023 and has been live since 2024-05-28 [Verified]. New short-position reporting (Form SHO) and securities-lending reporting were adopted but have been deferred to 2028 [Reported]. Payment for order flow drew scrutiny. The SEC's 2022 order-competition and best-execution proposals were withdrawn on 2025-06-12, while amended Rule 605 execution-quality disclosures became mandatory on 2026-08-01 [Reported].

Lessons for quants

  • Losses on a short are unbounded. Cap short size by a stress price several times today's, not by volatility.
  • Short crowding is visible: short interest, borrow fees, days-to-cover. Treat it as a risk factor.
  • Clearing-margin plumbing can cut off your counterparties' order flow in the middle of an event.

Go deeper: retail flow internalization · shorting, financing and settlement · options market making · M9 risk controls.

docs.title: 9. The yen-carry unwind and VIX spike (2–5 August 2024)
docs.text:
Strategies: yen-funded FX carry, short volatility and dispersion, trend following, and volatility-targeted equity.

Loss mechanism, step by step (BIS Bulletins 90 and 95)

  1. Fragility. From early July the yen's depreciation reversed. On 24 July AI and technology stocks with strong momentum lost about $1 trillion of value. The Bank of Japan's rate rise was seen as hawkish [Verified].
  2. Trigger. A disappointing US jobs report on 2 August took the S&P 500 down 1.8% [Verified].
  3. Unwind. On 5 August the TOPIX lost 12% in a day and the S&P 500 a further 3.0% [Verified]. The BIS puts yen loans to non-banks outside Japan at about ¥40 trillion ($250B). Speculators' short yen futures of about ¥2 trillion were unwound, and trend followers that had flipped long yen in July amplified the move [Verified].
  4. Margin. Japan's clearing house raised initial margin on long equity-index positions by 60–80% [Verified].
  5. Quote-driven VIX. Before the US open the VIX rose 180% to almost 66, its biggest one-day spike. Bid-ask spreads on deep out-of-the-money puts exceeded 80% of the mid-price, and those puts drove about 86% of the rise. The VIX is computed from quote midpoints, not trades [Verified] (BIS 95). It closed at 38.57, up from 23.39 [Verified] (FRED). Illustrative: a rule that halves gross exposure when the VIX passes 40 would have fired before the open and sold near the low [Estimate].
  6. Correlation. One-month implied correlation went from 2.9 on 12 July to 39.6 on 5 August, hurting dispersion books [Verified] (dispersion dossier).
  7. Fast reversal. By Friday 9 August the S&P 500 had recovered all its losses since Monday [Verified], and the VIX closed at 20.37 [Verified] (FRED).

Who was on the other side. Option market makers, who widened quotes to avoid lopsided books, and buyers who stepped in on 5 August [Verified] (BIS 95). The BIS finds that VIX products and dispersion unwinds were unlikely to be the main driver [Verified].

What changed. No new rules. The BIS and Cboe argued publicly over VIX construction [Reported], and the BIS flagged margin procyclicality for policymakers [Verified]. Later shocks hit systematic equity in July 2025 and June–July 2026 (factor-timing dossier) [Reported].

Lessons for quants

  • Never trigger de-risking from a quote-based index outside regular hours (M9).
  • Crowding crosses asset classes. A Tokyo FX trade can de-gross a US equity book.
  • A spike that reverses within a week punishes fast de-risking rules. Slower, capped rules ride through it, at the cost of more loss if the spike persists.

Go deeper: carry and cross-asset risk premia · dispersion and correlation trading · volatility risk premium · F6 regime detection.

docs.title: Strategy × algorithm matrix
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Rows are the 30 strategy dossiers; columns are the 39 algorithm cards. ● = core, ○ = supporting, · = not used. A script builds the table from the dossier and card headers, so it cannot drift from them.
  • 357 of 1,170 cells are filled (131 core, 226 supporting). The workhorses are the cost model (P5, 18 strategies), signal transforms (D3, 15), risk models (P1, 14) and signal evaluation (D4, 14).
  • Two clusters barely overlap. Market-making and speed strategies fill 69% of the market-making columns and 8% of the rest; stat-arb, mid-frequency and factor strategies fill 48% of the other columns and 4% of the market-making ones.
  • Execution and validation cards are rarely core but support almost every portfolio strategy: no strategy is "about" VWAP or purged cross-validation, yet a bad one sinks many.
  • Specialists: options pricing (M8) appears in 3 rows, all core; LLM methods (F4) appear only in mid-frequency alpha.

Level: Core · Read time: ~9 min · Last verified: 2026-11

A trading strategy is not one algorithm but a pipeline of them (there is no single algorithm). This page shows which pipeline components each strategy depends on. Read a row to see which cards to study for a strategy. Read a column to see which strategies suffer when one component is wrong: a mis-specified cost model touches 18 of the 30.

docs.title: How to read the matrix
docs.text:
• Rows are the dossiers, grouped by family folder (A liquidity provision through G futures and macro) and sorted alphabetically within each.
  • Columns are card IDs. The letter is the card group: D data and signals, F forecasting models, V validation and backtesting, P portfolio construction, E execution, M market making and HFT, L live trading. The legend maps each ID to its card.
  • ● core: the dossier links the card in its "Core algorithms used" field, one of the 3–6 components without which the strategy would not exist.
  • ○ supporting: the card lists the dossier in its "Used by strategies" field, but the dossier does not call it core. The strategy uses the method materially; the edge does not live there.
  • · not used: neither page links the other. That does not mean a firm running the strategy never touches the method, only that it is not material to the strategy as this knowledge base describes it.

The table is generated by python scripts/check_matrix.py --write and checked by python scripts/check_matrix.py; it is never edited by hand. Counts on this page were computed from the table as generated in November 2026; if they disagree with the table, the table wins.

x = number of dossiers using the card (● or ○), scaled so 20 dossiers is the right edge; y = share of those uses that are core. Selected cards; positions computed from the table.

Backbone (many rows, mostly core). Three cards carry the portfolio strategies: P5 cost and impact models (18 dossiers, 11 core), D3 signal transforms (15, 12 core) and P1 risk models (14, 11 core). P5 is the only card that reaches six of the seven families; only the two volatility dossiers do without it. Anything that trades enough to move prices needs a cost forecast, from an ETF market maker's hedge to a factor book's rebalance. The textbook decomposition of a quant system into alpha, risk and transaction-cost models feeding portfolio construction and execution (Narang 2024) [Verified] shows up in exactly these columns.

Shared plumbing (many rows, rarely core). Ten cards (E1, E2, E3 and E6 for execution and cost measurement; V1–V4 for validation; L1 and L2 for live monitoring and decay) fill 99 cells between them, only 5 of them core. They are where a strategy leaks money rather than where it earns it: a mid-frequency book's edge lives in its signals, but slippage and overfitting decide how much survives. That is why backtest pitfalls and implementation shortfall matter to strategies that never mention them in their headline.

Specialist engines (few rows, mostly core). M4 quoting and inventory control is core in all 6 rows that use it; it defines market making. M8 options pricing appears in only 3 rows (options market making, dispersion, volatility risk premium), all core. F4 LLM methods appear in 5 rows, all in mid-frequency alpha. L3 reinforcement learning is never core, consistent with its card's finding that reported production use is mainly bank execution.

The HFT and market-making cluster (families A–B, 9 dossiers) fills 56 of 81 cells (69%) in the M columns and 21 of 270 (8%) elsewhere. Its pipeline is the HFT trading loop: fair value (M2), order-flow signals (M3), quoting and inventory (M4), markouts (M5), queue placement (M6), hedging (M7) and risk controls (M9). In these books the "forecast" is a fair value seconds ahead, "portfolio construction" is inventory skew plus hedging, and "validation" is markout analysis of live fills more than a cross-validated backtest.

The mid-frequency cluster (families C–E, 17 dossiers) is the mirror image: 246 of 510 cells (48%) outside the M columns and 6 of 153 (4%) inside them. Its rows walk the pipeline left to right (data, signal, forecast, validation, portfolio, execution), as in the mid-frequency stat-arb walkthrough.

Statistical arbitrage (family C) is the bridge: the only family that touches all seven card groups. Intraday patterns and ML short-horizon alpha borrow order-book signals (M3) and queue placement (M6) from market making while using the full forecasting and validation stack. Bridge cards run the other way too: P5 cost models, E4 smart order routing (families A–D), E5 auction and close algos (A–E), M7 hedging and M9 risk controls (both A–C and F).

docs.title: Thin rows
docs.text: Families F and G fill 28 of 156 cells (18%). Dispersion and the volatility risk premium use 4 cards each, carry 5: the card set is built around US equities, and these strategies run on derivatives pricing, hedging and risk budgeting more than on signal research. Trend following (15 cells) is the exception because it reuses the factor book's machinery: transforms, risk models, sizing and execution. At the other end, cross-sectional alpha (27 cells), ML short-horizon alpha (23) and fundamental quant signals (21) use most of the mid-frequency stack.

docs.title: Algorithms: overview
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • This module covers the concrete methods inside a quant firm's pipeline: 39 algorithm cards in seven sections (A–G), three overview pages and four end-to-end walkthroughs (H).
  • Start with There is no single algorithm, then use the algorithm map to find any card by its ID.
  • Every card has the same shape: a header table you can skim in 30 seconds, then intuition, pseudocode of 40 lines or fewer, a worked example, practitioner tweaks, failure modes and questions to ask.
  • Twenty runnable Python labs on synthetic data back the cards. The walkthroughs stitch the cards together using the labs' numbers.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: What this module covers
docs.text:
Strategies explains what quant firms trade and why it pays. This module explains how they do it. Each card covers one method (a risk model, a VWAP algorithm, a quoting rule) in enough depth that you can follow a quant's description of it, read its pseudocode, and ask where it breaks. Cards link to the strategies that use them, and the strategy x algorithm matrix shows the full mapping.

docs.title: The eight sections
docs.text: Section Cards The question it answers A. Data and signals D1–D4 Is the data honest, and does this signal predict anything? B. Forecasting models F1–F6 How do many signals become one expected return per stock? C. Validation and backtesting V1–V4 Is the backtest telling the truth? D. Portfolio construction P1–P7 Given forecasts, risk and costs, what should we hold? E. Execution algorithms E1–E6 How do we get there without moving the price? F. Market making and HFT M1–M9 Where should we quote, and how do we avoid being picked off? G. Live trading L1–L3 Is it still working, and when do we retire it? H. End-to-end walkthroughs 4 walkthroughs How do the cards fit together on real numbers?

docs.title: How to read an algorithm card
docs.text:
The line under the title gives three labels. Level is Core (on the main reading path) or Deep dive (optional). Pipeline stage is one of data, signal, forecast, validation, portfolio, execution, market making or live. Last verified is the month of the last fact check. Next comes the header table:

Field What it tells you Purpose (the question it answers) Why the method exists. If you remember one line, remember this one. Inputs → Outputs What it consumes and produces, which is how it plugs into its neighbours on the map. Used by strategies Dossiers that rely on it materially. The matrix is generated from these links. Latency / compute regime Nanoseconds, microseconds, milliseconds, seconds or overnight batch. This sets the kind of engineering it needs. Key parameters The knobs and their typical ranges, so you can tell a sensible setting from a strange one. Main failure modes How it breaks in production. Usually the best thing to talk about. Lab The runnable lab, or "—".

The body always runs in the same order. It starts with intuition and a diagram that highlights the card's place in the pipeline. Then come the algorithm itself (plain steps, then commented pseudocode matching the lab code), a worked example with numbers, and how practitioners tune the parameters. The "textbook vs practice" section sources or tags every claim. After that: how to tell whether the method is working, its failure modes, sample practitioner sentences with glosses, and questions to ask, ordered basic to sharp, with 🔒 marking proprietary territory. Math sits in a collapsed block at the end. Confidence tags ([Verified], [Reported], [Estimate], [Lore]) are explained on the home page.

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
Each lab is a short, deterministic Python script on synthetic data, so it shows mechanisms rather than real alpha, and its Sharpe ratios run far above real-world levels. The pseudocode in the cards uses the same names and parameters as the lab. "Cards it supports" lists the cards that name the lab in their header; "Also supports" lists dossiers and cards that quote its results.

docs.title: End-to-end walkthroughs
docs.text:
The capstones. Each follows one business through a full cycle with numbers taken from the labs:

  • A mid-frequency stat-arb book: universe → three alphas → IC-weighted combination → risk model → optimizer with costs → VWAP/IS execution → next-day attribution.
  • A day at an ETF market maker: fair value from basket and futures, quoting, inventory, creation/redemption, hedging, markouts, end-of-day P&L.
  • An options market maker: vol surface → theoretical values → quotes leaned against book vega → delta hedging on a band → Greeks P&L attribution.
  • Executing a $500M buy order: schedule choice, child orders, venues, the close, and the TCA report.

docs.title: Algorithm map
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • All 39 algorithm cards on one diagram: five research-to-trading stages (data and signals → forecasting → validation → portfolio construction → execution), a parallel market-making/HFT lane, and live trading as the loop that feeds results back.
  • Every card has a stable ID (D1…L3). The ID's letter tells you the stage; the five canonical pipelines are different paths through the same map.
  • Latency regimes run from nanosecond risk gates to research jobs that take hours. A card's regime tells you what kind of engineering it needs.
  • The map is not a one-way conveyor. Three feedback loops matter: TCA recalibrates the cost model, live monitoring retires decaying alphas, and markouts retune quoting.

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: How to read the map
docs.text: Solid arrows show what feeds what on a normal trading day; dotted arrows show research gates and feedback. Validation cards (V) never touch live orders; they decide whether a forecast reaches production. The market-making lane (M) is a separate, much faster loop that shares venues, risk controls and monitoring with the main pipeline. M9 Algorithmic risk controls sits in that lane, but every live order in every pipeline passes a pre-trade risk check.

docs.text:
Solid arrows explain one day; dotted arrows explain why a pipeline gets better or worse over months.

flowchart LR
  fills["Fills and child orders"] --> E6["E6 TCA"]
  E6 -->|"realized impact"| P5["P5 Cost model"]
  P5 -->|"trade more or less"| P3["P3 Optimizer"]
  P5 -->|"faster or slower"| E3["E3 Schedule"]
  pnl["Daily PnL"] --> L1["L1 Attribution"]
  L1 -->|"PnL by signal"| L2["L2 Decay tests"]
  L2 -->|"retire or down-weight"| F5["F5 Alpha combination"]

  1. Execution cost loop. TCA feeds realized market impact into the cost model. If impact runs above forecast, the optimizer trades less and schedules slow down. Without it, capacity estimates are guesses.
  2. Alpha lifecycle loop. Attribution splits P&L by signal; decay tests decide when live IC has fallen far enough below the backtest to cut a signal's weight, freeing risk budget for new research.
  3. Adverse-selection loop. Markouts expose adverse selection by venue and counterparty; quoting widens or skews and the fair-value model is refit.
