docs.title: There is no single algorithm
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • "What is their algorithm?" has no one-line answer. A quant firm runs a pipeline: dozens of algorithms, each answering one narrow question. What is the fair price right now? What will this stock do relative to its peers? How much risk is this? How do I buy it without moving the price?
  • The horizon sets the pipeline's shape. A market maker's loop closes in microseconds; a factor fund's closes once a month. A different tempo means a different bottleneck and a different place where money is made or lost.
  • Five canonical pipelines cover most US equity quant trading: the HFT market-making loop, short-horizon stat arb, mid-frequency cross-sectional equity, the systematic factor manager, and agency execution.
  • The edge rarely lives in one clever model. It lives in the joints between stages (forecast and cost model, fair value and quoting) and in unglamorous plumbing: point-in-time data, risk controls, feedback from fills.
  • A better question than "what's your algorithm?" is "which stage of your pipeline is the binding constraint?"

Level: Core · Read time: ~16 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: The short answer
docs.text:
Ask a quant "what's your algorithm?" and you will get a polite non-answer. Secrecy is part of the reason, but mostly the question is malformed. A systematic trading business is a production line of many algorithms, owned by different people, each solving a narrow problem, chained so that one stage's output is the next stage's input. Clean data becomes features; features become forecasts; forecasts become target positions; targets become orders; orders become fills; fills become P&L, which is attributed back to the forecasts that caused it.

A semiconductor fab is the right analogy. Nobody asks a foundry for "its process". They ask about lithography, etch, deposition, metrology and yield, because the product comes out of hundreds of steps and yield is multiplicative. Trading pipelines behave the same way. A forecast with real predictive power can be destroyed by a stale risk model, an optimizer that over-trades, or an execution algo that leaks intent. If each of five stages keeps 85% of what the previous stage delivered, only 44% of the original alpha reaches the P&L (0.85⁵ ≈ 0.44; illustrative).

flowchart LR
  A["Data<br/>D1"] --> B["Signals<br/>D2 D3 D4"]
  B --> C["Forecasts<br/>F1 to F6"]
  C --> D["Portfolio<br/>P1 to P7"]
  D --> E["Orders and fills<br/>E1 to E6, M1 to M9"]
  E --> F["PnL and monitoring<br/>L1 L2 L3"]
  V["Validation<br/>V1 to V4"] -.->|"gates"| C
  F -.->|"feedback"| B

Every pipeline in this KB maps onto these stages, and each stage has its own section of algorithm cards (A to G). The algorithm map puts all 39 cards on one diagram. Businesses differ in tempo and in which stage dominates. Below are the five canonical pipelines for US equities. Each gets a diagram, annotated pseudocode, its latency and compute regime, what dominates its P&L, and the cards used at each stage. The pseudocode is deliberately simplified: one function name stands in for a whole subsystem, and every number in it is illustrative.

docs.title: 1. The HFT / electronic market-maker loop
docs.text:
An electronic market maker continuously posts bids and offers in thousands of symbols. It earns the spread from impatient traders while trying not to be run over by informed ones. Strategies that run this loop: equity market making, ETF market making and options market making. The card-level version of this section is M1 Anatomy of an HFT trading loop.

flowchart LR
  md["Exchange feeds"] --> bb["Book build"]
  bb --> fv["Fair value<br/>M2 M3"]
  fv --> qs["Quote and skew<br/>M4 M6"]
  qs --> rk["Pre-trade risk<br/>M9"]
  rk --> ord["Order to venue"]
  ord --> fil["Fill"]
  fil --> hdg["Hedge<br/>M7"]
  fil --> inv["Inventory update"]
  hdg --> inv
  inv -->|"skew next quote"| qs
  fil -.->|"markouts M5"| fv
Stage What happens Cards Market data → book build Decode each exchange's direct feed; rebuild every venue's book; merge into one view M1 Fair value Mid-price tilted by queue imbalance (microprice), plus order-flow and futures/ETF lead-lag signals M2, M3 Quote and skew Center quotes on a reservation price shifted against inventory; keep or give up queue position M4, M6, M8 for options Pre-trade risk Position, notional, price-collar and message-rate checks before anything leaves M9 Order → fill New / replace / cancel; fills arrive asynchronously E4 for venue choice Hedge Offset unwanted risk in a correlated instrument (futures, ETF, basket, underlying) M7 Inventory and review Update position; measure markouts to detect adverse selection M5, L1 
# Event loop of an electronic market maker for ONE symbol (real systems run thousands in parallel).
# Simplified: production code is C++ or FPGA logic, lock-free and allocation-free. Numbers illustrative.
def on_market_data(msg, s):                        # s = per-symbol state, held in memory
    book = s.book.apply(msg)                       # 1. book build: add / cancel / execute at a level
    fv = microprice(book)                          # 2. fair value: mid tilted toward the thin side (M2)
    fv += s.signals.predict_ticks(book, msg) * s.tick   # + order-flow and futures lead-lag (M3)
    q = s.inventory                                # signed shares
    r = fv - q * s.gamma * s.sigma**2 * s.horizon  # 3. reservation price: long -> shade quotes down (M4)
    half = max(s.min_half_spread, s.half_spread(book, s.toxicity))  # widen when flow is toxic (M5)
    bid = floor_to_tick(r - half, s.tick)
    ask = ceil_to_tick(r + half, s.tick)
    for side, px in (("buy", bid), ("sell", ask)):
        if s.live[side] is not None and s.live[side].px == px:
            continue                               # unchanged price: keep the order and its queue spot (M6)
        o = Order(side, px, size=s.clip_for(side, q))   # smaller size on the side that adds inventory
        if pre_trade_ok(o, s.limits):              # 4. position, notional, collar, rate checks (M9)
            s.gateway.replace(s.live[side], o)     # 5. order out; fills come back asynchronously

def on_fill(fill, s):
    s.inventory += fill.signed_qty                 # 6. inventory update
    s.markouts.track(fill, horizons_s=[0.1, 1, 10])     # adverse-selection monitor (M5)
    h = s.hedger.order_for(fill, s.inventory)      # 7. e.g. offset an ETF fill with futures (M7)
    if h is not None and pre_trade_ok(h, s.limits):
        s.gateway.send(h)

Latency and compute regime. This is the only pipeline where the speed of light and the chip matter. The loop runs in memory on colocated servers. The critical path from an incoming market-data packet to an outgoing order (tick-to-trade) takes microseconds in optimized software and nanoseconds in FPGA hardware. For scale, an FPGA reference design reached a minimum of 13.9 ns in a STAC-T0 benchmark announced in June 2024 [Verified]. That benchmark was vendor-commissioned and measures network I/O only, with no strategy logic. Speed matters because of races. On London Stock Exchange message data, Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill find that the winner of the modal latency-arbitrage race beats the first loser by only 5–10 microseconds, and that about a fifth of FTSE 100 trading volume happens in such races [Verified]. Model fitting (fair-value weights, fill probabilities) happens offline. The live loop evaluates simple, precomputed models because there is no time budget for anything else.

What dominates P&L. Read a market maker's day as an income statement. Revenue is spread capture plus exchange rebates. Cost of goods sold is adverse selection: losses to counterparties who knew more. Below that come inventory gains and losses, then fees and technology. Menkveld's case study of one large HFT market maker in European stocks found gross profit of about €0.88 per trade: €1.55 of spread capture net of fees, less a €0.68 loss on positions [Verified] (working-paper figures). The business runs on the law of large numbers, with a tiny edge per trade and an enormous number of trades. Virtu's 2014 IPO filing reported one losing day in 1,238 [Reported]. Fair-value accuracy, meaning not getting picked off, matters more than cleverness in the quoting formula. The other big lever is cost per message and per fill.

docs.title: 2. Short-horizon stat arb (minutes to days)
docs.text:
A book of hundreds to a few thousand liquid names, usually market- and sector-neutral, rebalanced intraday on forecasts with horizons from about 30 minutes to a few days. Strategies: ML-driven short-horizon alpha, factor-residual mean reversion, short-term reversal and intraday patterns.

flowchart LR
  ft["Features<br/>D1 D2 D3"] --> ml["ML forecasts<br/>F1 F2 F3"]
  ml --> cb["Combination<br/>F5"]
  cb --> op["Optimizer with cost model<br/>P1 P3 P5 P6"]
  op --> ex["Execution<br/>E1 E4 M6"]
  ex --> pos["Positions and PnL<br/>L1"]
  pos -->|"current holdings"| op
  cv["Purged CV and overfitting tests<br/>V1 V4"] -.-> ml
  pos -.->|"realized costs"| op
Stage What happens Cards Features Residual returns, order-flow imbalance, volume surprises, time-of-day effects; identical code in backtest and live D1, D2, D3 ML forecast One model per horizon; regularized linear models and boosted trees are the workhorses F1, F2, F3 Validation Purged, embargoed cross-validation; deflate for the number of trials V1, V4 Combination Blend horizons and models into one expected return per name F5 Optimizer with cost model Trade only where expected alpha beats expected cost; trade partway toward target P1, P3, P5, P6 Execution Passive first, cross the spread when alpha is decaying fast E1, E4, M6 
# Intraday stat-arb rebalance, every 5 minutes over ~2,000 liquid US names (illustrative values)
def rebalance(now, w_now, models, risk, cost, nav):
    X = build_features(now)                     # D2: residual returns, imbalance, volume surprise,
                                                #     time of day; same code path as the backtest
    X = X.apply(winsorize, k=4).apply(zscore)   # D3: cross-sectional scaling, outliers clipped
    preds = {h: m.predict(X) for h, m in models.items()}   # F1/F2: one model per horizon (30m, 2h, 1d)
    alpha = sum(wt * preds[h] for h, wt in HORIZON_WEIGHTS.items())  # F5: weights fit out of sample (V1)
    alpha = neutralize(alpha, risk.exposures)   # strip market, sector and style tilts; units: bps

    # P3 + P5 + P6: maximize alpha'w - risk_aversion * risk(w) - cost(w - w_now)
    w_tgt = optimize(alpha_bps=alpha, risk=risk, w0=w_now,
                     cost=lambda dw: cost.half_spread(dw) + cost.impact(dw),  # square-root impact
                     risk_aversion=5.0, max_name=0.004, max_gross=4.0,
                     dollar_neutral=True)
    trades = (w_tgt - w_now) * nav              # dollars per name
    trades[trades.abs() < 5_000] = 0            # no-trade band: small trades cost more than they earn
    for sym, usd in trades.items():
        urgency = alpha_halflife(sym)           # fast-decaying alpha -> cross the spread sooner
        send_to_execution(sym, usd, urgency)    # E1/E4/M6: passive first, take liquidity if urgent
    return w_tgt

Latency and compute regime. Decisions come every few minutes to an hour, and features update continuously. The optimizer must solve a 1,000–3,000-name problem in seconds. Models retrain offline, nightly or weekly, on CPU or GPU clusters [Estimate] (reasoning: a forecast horizon of 30 minutes or more leaves seconds of slack per decision, not microseconds). Latency matters in the execution leg, because passive orders need decent queue position. It does not matter for the forecast.

What dominates P&L. A tug-of-war between gross alpha and trading costs. At these horizons a good forecast is worth a few basis points per trade, the same order of magnitude as the half-spread plus market impact. An illustrative case: a forecast of +6 bps over two hours on a large-cap with 150 bps daily volatility. The square-root law puts impact at about Y·σ·√(Q/V) [Verified] (Tóth et al.). With Y = 0.7 (illustrative), trading 0.1% of daily volume costs about 3.3 bps of impact; trading 1% costs about 10.5 bps. The same signal makes money in small size and loses money in large size. That is why the cost model and the trade-toward-target logic sit at the center of this pipeline. Turnover is high: an average holding period of one to two days means trading roughly 50–100% of the gross book every day [Estimate] (turnover ≈ 1 / holding period). Signals of this kind also decay. In Avellaneda and Lee's academic backtest, net of their cost assumption, the PCA-residual strategy earned an average Sharpe of 1.44 over 1997–2007, but only 0.9 over 2003–2007 [Verified].

docs.title: 3. Mid-frequency cross-sectional equity (days to weeks)
docs.text:
This is classic quant equity market-neutral. Dozens to hundreds of signals (value, quality, analyst revisions, sentiment, short-term reversal, alternative data) are combined into one forecast per stock. A risk model and an optimizer then turn those forecasts into a neutral book, rebalanced daily. Strategies: cross-sectional alpha and neutralization, fundamental quant signals, analyst revisions and sentiment and alternative data. The mid-frequency walkthrough runs this pipeline end to end with numbers.

flowchart TD
  d["Point-in-time data<br/>D1"] --> a["Alphas<br/>D2 F4"]
  a --> t["Transforms and evaluation<br/>D3 D4"]
  t --> c["Combination<br/>F5 F1"]
  c --> o["Optimizer<br/>P3 P4 P7"]
  rm["Risk model<br/>P1 P2"] --> o
  tc["Cost model<br/>P5"] --> o
  o --> tl["Trade list<br/>P6"]
  tl --> ex["Execution algos<br/>E2 E3 E5"]
  ex --> at["Attribution<br/>L1 E6"]
  at -.->|"retire or reweight"| c
  at -.->|"recalibrate"| tc
Stage What happens Cards Data As-of-date fundamentals, prices, estimates; delisted names kept D1 Alphas Raw signals from prices, fundamentals, text D2, F4 Transforms Winsorize, z-score, industry-neutralize; track information coefficient (IC) and decay D3, D4 Combination IC-weighted or regression blend, shrunk toward equal weights F5, F1 Risk model Factor exposures, factor covariance, specific risk P1, P2 Optimizer → trade list Max alpha minus risk minus cost, subject to neutrality and caps P3, P4, P5, P6, P7 Execution algos VWAP for most names, IS for urgent ones, part at the close E2, E3, E5 Attribution Split P&L into factor, specific, cost and unexplained L1, E6, L2 
# Nightly batch for a market-neutral US equity book (~3,000 names); trades go out tomorrow
def nightly_run(d, positions):
    data = load_point_in_time(d)                 # D1: values as known on date d; delisted names kept
    raw = {k: f(data) for k, f in ALPHAS.items()}     # D2/F4: value, quality, revisions, reversal, text
    sig = {k: neutralize(zscore(winsorize(v, 3.0)), data.industry)   # D3: comparable, industry-neutral
           for k, v in raw.items()}
    ic = {k: rolling_ic(sig[k], data.fwd_ret, window=252) for k in sig}   # D4: live track record
    z = combine(sig, weights=ic_weights(ic, shrink=0.5))   # F5: IC-weighted, shrunk toward equal weight
    alpha = IC_COMBINED * data.resid_vol * z     # Grinold's rule: forecast = IC x volatility x score

    B, F, D = risk_model(data)                   # P1/P2: exposures, factor covariance, specific variance
    w = optimize(alpha, B, F, D, w0=positions,
                 risk_aversion=10.0,
                 tcost=impact_model(data.adv, data.vol),            # P5
                 constraints=[beta_neutral(), industry_net(0.01),   # P3/P7: neutral and capped
                              name_cap(0.01), gross_leverage(4.0)])
    trades = shares(w - positions, data.close)
    trades = trades[trades.abs() >= 100]         # drop trades too small to be worth a ticket
    algos = assign_algos(trades, default="VWAP",              # E2: most of the list
                         urgent="IS", close_frac=0.25)        # E3 for fast alpha, E5 for the close
    return trades, algos

def morning_attribution(d):                      # L1/E6: where did yesterday's P&L come from?
    return decompose_pnl(d, parts=["factor", "specific", "trading_cost", "unexplained"])

Latency and compute regime. Overnight batch. Data land after the close, the pipeline runs in a few hours, and trading happens the next day through VWAP and IS schedules or the closing auction. The heavy compute is in research: thousands of backtests over decades of point-in-time data. Production is light. The optimizer for about 3,000 names with a factor risk model solves in seconds [Estimate]. Reasoning: it is a convex quadratic program with about 3,000 variables, and the covariance is factor-structured rather than a dense 3,000 × 3,000 matrix. MSCI's Barra USE4 model, for example, uses 60 industry factors, 12 style factors and one country factor [Verified].

What dominates P&L. Breadth of many weak signals. The fundamental law of active management (Grinold and Kahn) says the information ratio is roughly IC × √breadth. Take an IC of 0.02 on 2,000 names re-forecast monthly (illustrative). Breadth is 24,000, and the theoretical IR is 0.02 × 155 ≈ 3.1. Three things then cut it down. Bets are correlated. Constraints dilute the signal: the transfer coefficient is often 0.3–0.7 [Estimate]. Costs take a further share. A realized net IR of 1–2 is considered strong [Lore]. In accounting terms, P&L = unintended factor exposure (should be near zero) + stock-specific alpha − trading costs − financing. The risk model's job is to shrink the first term.

docs.title: 4. Systematic factor manager (monthly)
docs.text:
Long-only or long/short portfolios tilted toward documented factors (value, momentum, quality, low volatility), often managed against a benchmark. There are few signals, they are transparent, and capacity is large. Strategies: factor investing fundamentals, momentum, value, quality and low volatility and factor timing and crowding.

flowchart LR
  fs["Factor scores<br/>value, momentum, quality, low vol"] --> pc["Constrained construction<br/>P1 P3 P4 P7"]
  bm["Benchmark and constraints"] --> pc
  pc --> rb["Monthly rebalance<br/>P5 P6"]
  rb --> ex["VWAP or closing auction<br/>E2 E5"]
  ex --> mon["Monitoring<br/>L1 F6"]
  mon -.->|"next month"| fs
  bt["Backtests and overfitting tests<br/>V2 V3 V4"] -.-> fs
Stage What happens Cards Factor scores Point-in-time composites per factor, winsorized and z-scored D1, D3 Research gate Long backtests, multiple-testing discipline V2, V3, V4 Constrained construction Maximize factor exposure within a tracking error budget and position limits P1, P3, P4, P7 Rebalance Turnover caps and no-trade bands; simple cost model P5, P6 Execution and monitoring Multi-day VWAP or the close; regime and exposure monitoring E2, E5, L1, F6 
# Monthly rebalance of a long-only multi-factor fund vs a large-cap benchmark (illustrative values)
def monthly_rebalance(d, holdings, bench):
    univ = universe(d, min_mcap=2e9, min_adv_usd=20e6)          # D1: point-in-time, liquid names only
    s = pd.DataFrame({
        "value":    zscore(book_to_price(univ) + earnings_yield(univ)),
        "momentum": zscore(total_return(univ, months=12, skip=1)),   # 12-1 month momentum
        "quality":  zscore(gross_profitability(univ) - accruals(univ)),
        "low_vol":  zscore(-volatility(univ, days=252)),
    }).clip(-3, 3)                                              # D3: winsorized composites
    score = s.mean(axis=1)                                      # equal weights: hard to overfit
    w = optimize_vs_benchmark(                                  # P3/P4: most exposure per unit of risk
        score, bench=bench, w0=holdings,
        tracking_error=0.03,                                    # ~3% active risk budget
        max_active_name=0.015, max_active_sector=0.03,
        turnover_cap=0.20,                                      # P6: one-way monthly turnover limit
        tcost=linear_cost(bps=8))                               # P5: a simple cost model suffices here
    trades = w - holdings
    trades[trades.abs() < 0.0005] = 0                           # no-trade band: skip < 5 bp changes
    return schedule(trades, algo="VWAP", days=2, close_frac=0.3)    # E2/E5

Latency and compute regime. Rebalancing is monthly or quarterly, often with a no-trade band so that many names go untouched. Production compute is trivial; a single workstation could run it [Estimate]. Academic reference portfolios show the cadence: Fama–French size and value portfolios are re-formed once a year at the end of June, and momentum monthly [Verified]. The engineering effort goes into data history and into trading large rebalances cheaply.

What dominates P&L. The factor premia themselves, which arrive in lumps over years, minus implementation drag: turnover, costs and the dilution forced by tracking-error limits. Multi-year drawdowns come with the territory. Value suffered a deep drawdown in the late 2010s that ended only in late 2020: the HML factor lost about 51% from its December 2016 peak to September 2020 [Verified] (our computation from the French Data Library); see the failure gallery. Research discipline is the real edge. Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue that so many factors have been tested that a new one should clear a t-statistic of about 3.0, not the usual 2.0 [Verified].

docs.title: 5. Agency execution
docs.text:
A broker's algorithms execute a client's parent order by slicing it into many child orders over time and across venues. Every institutional investor uses this pipeline, and it forms the execution leg of the other four. The institutional execution walkthrough follows a $500M order through it. Related strategy: auctions and closing liquidity.

flowchart LR
  po["Parent order<br/>buy 2M shares"] --> pre["Pre-trade estimate<br/>P5"]
  pre --> sch["Schedule<br/>E2 VWAP or POV, E3 IS"]
  sch --> ch["Child orders<br/>M6 E5"]
  ch --> sor["Smart order router<br/>E4"]
  sor --> lit["Lit exchanges"]
  sor --> drk["Dark pools"]
  sor --> auc["Open or close auction"]
  lit --> tca["TCA<br/>E6"]
  drk --> tca
  auc --> tca
  tca -.->|"recalibrate impact"| pre
Stage What happens Cards Parent order and pre-trade estimate Expected cost and risk for the size, given volume and volatility P5, E1 Schedule Implementation shortfall (front-loaded), VWAP (volume curve) or POV (fixed participation) E2, E3 Child orders Size, price and post-vs-take for each slice; auction and dark tactics M6, E5 Smart order routing Pick venues and order types using fees, fill odds and toxicity E4 TCA Compare fills with arrival, interval VWAP and close; feed the cost model E6 
# Agency execution of one parent order, e.g. BUY 2,000,000 shares by today's close (illustrative)
def execute_parent(order, mkt, cost_model):
    est = cost_model.pretrade(order.qty, adv=mkt.adv, vol=mkt.vol)   # P5: expected impact and risk
    if order.algo == "IS":                                  # E3: Almgren-Chriss, front-loaded
        target = ac_schedule(order.qty, horizon=order.horizon, eta=est.eta,
                             sigma=mkt.vol, risk_aversion=order.urgency)
    elif order.algo == "VWAP":                              # E2: follow the expected volume curve
        target = lambda t: order.qty * mkt.volume_profile.cum(t)
    filled = 0
    for t in mkt.clock(step_seconds=15):
        if order.algo == "POV":                             # E2: fixed share of printed volume
            want = order.rate * mkt.volume_since(order.start)   # e.g. rate = 0.10
        else:
            want = target(t)
        need = min(want, order.qty) - filled
        if need <= 0:
            continue
        if order.limit is not None and mkt.ask(t) > order.limit:
            continue                                        # price guard: never chase blindly
        child = make_child(need, passive_frac=0.6,          # M6: post most, take the rest
                           max_show=mkt.median_trade_size)  # small, unremarkable slices
        for venue, qty, px in smart_route(child, mkt.books(t), fees=mkt.fees):  # E4/E5: lit, dark
            filled += send(venue, qty, px)
    return tca(order, filled, benchmarks=["arrival", "interval_vwap", "close"])  # E6

Latency and compute regime. Mixed. The schedule is computed when the order arrives and re-optimized every few seconds to minutes. The smart order router decides in microseconds to milliseconds. TCA runs after the trade, usually overnight [Estimate].

What dominates P&L. For the client, P&L is cost. Implementation shortfall, in Perold's 1988 definition, is the gap between a paper portfolio traded instantly at the decision price and the real one. It breaks into spread, impact, timing drift and the opportunity cost of shares never filled. Almgren and Chriss framed scheduling as a trade-off: trade slowly to cut impact, or fast to cut exposure to price moves. The result is an efficient frontier of schedules [Verified]. For the broker, revenue is commission, and algo desks compete on TCA league tables. The edge is less impact and less information leakage than rival algos. The cautionary tale is 6 May 2010. A large seller used an algorithm set to 9% of the previous minute's volume, without regard to price or time, to sell 75,000 E-mini futures contracts (about $4.1B). As volume exploded during the crash, the algorithm sold faster [Verified]. In equities, the same failure is a POV order with no limit price.

docs.title: The five pipelines side by side
docs.text:
Pipeline Horizon Decision frequency Where the edge is Hardest engineering problem Typical failure HFT / market-making loop Seconds to minutes of inventory; near flat by the close Every market-data event; microsecond reaction Fair-value accuracy, speed, queue position, cost per message Deterministic low latency across thousands of symbols, with risk checks inline Picked off on stale quotes; runaway order logic (Knight 2012) Short-horizon stat arb 30 minutes to a few days Every few minutes to hourly Many weak, short-lived signals netted against precise cost estimates Identical features in research and production; an accurate cost model Costs overtake decaying alpha; crowded unwinds (August 2007) Mid-frequency cross-sectional Days to weeks Daily, overnight batch Breadth: many signals combined, plus a good risk model and optimizer Point-in-time data and research tooling that resists overfitting Factor crowding, look-ahead bias, unmodeled risk such as short squeezes Systematic factor Months to years Monthly or quarterly Cheap, disciplined harvesting of documented premia at large capacity Trading large rebalances cheaply; turnover control Multi-year factor drawdowns ("quant winter"); crowding Agency execution Minutes to days per order Seconds for the schedule; µs–ms for routing Lower impact and less leakage than rival algos Impact and fill-probability models; venue analysis Price-insensitive schedules in thin markets (May 2010); leakage

Horizons and decision frequencies are typical orders of magnitude, not firm-specific facts [Estimate]. Two failures in the table are documented by regulators. On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital's router generated more than 4 million executions in 154 stocks within 45 minutes, and the firm lost over $460 million [Verified]. Khandani and Lo trace the August 2007 quant losses to rapid unwinding of similar long/short equity portfolios [Verified].

The five pipelines share a spine. Each has a forecast: even an agency algo forecasts volume and short-term price moves. Each has a cost model, a risk limit and a feedback loop from fills back to research. Each also fails in the same quiet way when the research version of a stage drifts from the live version. Since 2011, US broker-dealers with market access must run automated pre-trade risk controls under SEC Rule 15c3-5 [Verified]. That is why a risk gate appears in every live pipeline, not only the fast one.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: "Which stage of your pipeline takes most of your research time?" The answer tells you where they believe their edge is.
  2. Basic: "What's the horizon of your main forecasts, and how often do you rebalance?" This places them among the five pipelines in one sentence.
  3. Informed: "How do you guarantee that features in the backtest are computed exactly as in production?" Research-to-live drift is the most common silent killer.
  4. Informed: "Is your cost model calibrated on your own fills, and how often is it refit?" This tests whether the TCA → cost model feedback loop actually exists.
  5. Informed: "When the optimizer refuses to trade a strong signal, how do you tell whether the risk model or the cost model is responsible?" This shows whether they debug at the joints between stages.
  6. Sharp: "What fraction of gross alpha survives to net P&L, and which stage leaks the most?" 🔒
  7. Sharp: "What's your transfer coefficient after constraints?" 🔒
  8. Sharp, market making: "How do one-second markouts differ by venue and counterparty type, and what does the quoting logic do when they deteriorate?" 🔒
  9. Sharp: "What test retires a signal, and how many did you retire last year?" 🔒

docs.title: Evaluating signals
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • The core metric is the information coefficient (IC): each day's cross-sectional correlation of the signal with subsequent residual returns.
  • Real single signals have daily ICs of about 0.005–0.03; stability, decay, turnover and cost separate them.
  • Mean IC ÷ its sd, annualized, approximates the pre-cost Sharpe: the Fundamental Law in disguise.
  • Overlapping returns inflate t-stats (Lab 11: naive 45 vs Newey–West 25, synthetic lab result).
  • A new signal earns a positive weight only if its IR exceeds its correlation with the book times the book's IR.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: signal · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Does the signal predict residual returns, at what horizon, how reliably, net of costs and of the existing book? Inputs → Outputs Signal, forward residual returns, costs, production composite → IC, t-stat, decay, quantile spreads, turnover, net spread, marginal value Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Fundamental signals · Revisions · Earnings · Alt data · NLP · ML short-horizon · Reversal · Factor-residual · Stat arb · Factor investing · Value and quality · Momentum Latency / compute regime Research batch: seconds for 3,000 stocks × 20 years × 20 horizons [Estimate] Key parameters Horizons 1–20 days; Newey–West lags h − 1; 5–10 quantiles; t-hurdle 3.0; 3–5+ years Main failure modes Factor bets in total-return IC; overlap-inflated t-stats; look-ahead; microcap IC; multiple testing Lab Lab 11

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Like a credit-scoring model, a signal is judged across thousands of names, not one trade. The IC scores each day: the cross-sectional correlation between today's signal and the returns that follow. With 500 stocks a day's IC carries noise of about 0.045, so the signal lives in the multi-year average.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Align the signal at the close of t with residual returns over t+1…t+h.
  2. IC series: Pearson IC and rank IC per date.
  3. t-stat = mean IC ÷ (sd ÷ √T); Newey–West with h − 1 lags for overlapping windows.
  4. Decay: IC against day t+k's return, k = 1…20; fit a·d^k; half-life = ln 0.5 ÷ ln d.
  5. Quantiles: monotonic returns and the top-minus-bottom spread.
  6. Turnover and cost: autocorrelation ρ; turnover grows with √(1 − ρ); net = gross − cost.
  7. Marginal value and trial count (V4).
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# ic_series and ic_tstat follow Lab 11's lab.py. signal, resid_ret: T x N DataFrames (dates x
# stocks); the signal is known at the close of t. Simplified: no universe filters or weights.

def ic_series(signal, fwd_ret, method="pearson"):
    s, r = signal.align(fwd_ret, join="inner")
    s, r = s.where(r.notna()), r.where(s.notna())             # same names on both sides
    if method == "spearman":                                  # rank IC
        s, r = s.rank(axis=1), r.rank(axis=1)
    s, r = s.sub(s.mean(axis=1), axis=0), r.sub(r.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    return (s * r).sum(axis=1) / np.sqrt((s * s).sum(axis=1) * (r * r).sum(axis=1))

def ic_tstat(ic, lags=0):
    """t-stat of the mean IC; Newey-West with lags = h - 1 when h-day windows overlap."""
    x = ic.dropna().to_numpy()
    n, e = x.size, x - x.mean()
    var = e @ e / n
    for k in range(1, lags + 1):
        var += 2 * (1 - k / (lags + 1)) * (e[k:] @ e[:-k]) / n    # Bartlett weights
    return x.mean() / np.sqrt(var / n)

def evaluate(signal, resid_ret, cost_bps=8.0, max_h=20):
    fwd1 = resid_ret.shift(-1)                                 # day t+1 return, aligned at t
    ic1 = ic_series(signal, fwd1)
    decay = np.array([ic_series(signal, resid_ret.shift(-(1 + k))).mean() for k in range(max_h)])
    k, ok = np.arange(max_h), decay > 0.25 * decay[0]          # fit only lags clear of noise
    d = np.exp(np.polyfit(k[ok], np.log(decay[ok]), 1)[0])     # IC_k = a * d**k (lab: curve_fit)
    rho = ic_series(signal, signal.shift(1)).mean()            # day-over-day autocorrelation
    q = np.ceil(signal.rank(axis=1, pct=True) * 5)             # quintile labels 1..5
    q_ret = [1e4 * fwd1.where(q == j).stack().mean() for j in range(1, 6)]   # bps per day
    spread = q_ret[4] - q_ret[0]                               # $1 long Q5, $1 short Q1
    turnover = 1.1 * np.sqrt(2 * (1 - rho))                    # sd of daily score change; 1.1 fits Lab 11
    return dict(ic=ic1.mean(), rank_ic=ic_series(signal, fwd1, "spearman").mean(),
                t_stat=ic_tstat(ic1), ic_ratio_annual=ic1.mean() / ic1.std() * np.sqrt(252),
                half_life=np.log(0.5) / np.log(d), autocorr=rho, quintile_bps=q_ret,
                monotone=bool(np.all(np.diff(q_ret) > 0)), spread_gross=spread,
                spread_net=spread - 2 * turnover * cost_bps)   # cost_bps: per $ traded, one way

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
A. One date's IC (illustrative). Scores −1.5, −0.5, 0, +0.5, +1.5 for stocks A–E; next-day residual returns −20, +30, −10, 0, +50 bps.

  • Pearson: deviations from the +10 mean return are −30, +20, −20, −10, +40. Σ score × deviation = 90, Σ score² = 5, Σ deviation² = 3,400, so IC = 90 ÷ √17,000 = 0.69.
  • Rank: return ranks 1, 4, 2, 3, 5; squared rank gaps sum to 6; 1 − 36 ÷ 120 = 0.70.
  • One takeover: A (score −1.5) jumps +500 bps: Pearson IC −0.71, rank IC −0.30. Five names are noise anyway (sd ≈ 0.45).

B. From a series to a verdict. Lab 11's alpha_med: daily IC 0.030, sd 0.0443 (near 1/√500 = 0.0447), 1,259 days (synthetic lab result). Standard error 0.0443 ÷ √1,259 = 0.00125, t ≈ 24. Annualized IC ratio 0.030 ÷ 0.0443 × √252 ≈ 10.7, the Fundamental Law's 0.03 × √(500 × 252) = 10.6. Realistic (illustrative): IC 0.01, sd 0.10 gives 1.6 a year; t reaches 3.0 after 3.6 years.

C. Overlap. alpha_med's 5-day IC is 0.057. Sampled daily, adjacent windows share four days: naive t 45.1, Newey–West (4 lags) 25.2 (synthetic lab result).

D. Quintiles. alpha_med's quintile returns rise monotonically from −6.6 to +6.4 bps/day; Q5 − Q1 is 13.1 gross and 6.3 net at 41% daily turnover (synthetic lab result).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Pearson vs rank: report both; rank IC shrugs off takeovers and bad prints [Lore].
  • Quantiles: 5 for 500 names, 10 for 3,000 [Lore].
  • Hurdle: t > 3.0 for a new factor (Harvey, Liu & Zhu 2016) [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Fundamental Law: IR ≈ IC × √breadth (Grinold 1989), times a transfer coefficient (Clarke, de Silva & Thorley 2002) [Verified].
  • IC volatility: Qian & Hua (2004) estimate IR as mean IC ÷ sd of IC, since IC varies over time [Reported]. Daily IC 0.01 at Sharpe 1.5 implies IC sd ≈ 0.11, five times the sampling noise of 2,000 names [Estimate].
  • Real alphas: of 4,000 WorldQuant US-equity alphas (holding 0.7–19 days), the positive-Sharpe ones had a median Sharpe of 1.49 before costs; cents per share scaled as 1/turnover (Kakushadze & Tulchinsky 2016) [Verified].
  • Costs: anomalies with monthly turnover under 50% mostly survive costs; faster ones mostly do not (Novy-Marx & Velikov 2016) [Verified].
  • Tooling: Alphalens reports rank IC, quantile returns, turnover and rank autocorrelation [Verified]. Patton & Timmermann (2010) test monotonicity formally [Verified].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Recover a planted truth: Lab 11 measures ICs 0.041/0.030/0.020 vs planted 0.04/0.03/0.02, and half-lives 2.2/11.5/60.0 vs 2/10/60 days (synthetic lab result).
  • Noise looks like noise: one of 20 noise signals has |t| > 2 (synthetic lab result); within-date shuffled returns should give IC ≈ 0.
  • Calibrate the Sharpe. Lab 11's quintile books show gross Sharpe 6.3–12.6, net 2.6–4.4 (synthetic lab result): stylized, since clean ICs of 0.02–0.04 across 500 stocks give about 10 before costs. Real single signals net roughly 0.3–1.5 [Estimate] (the WorldQuant gross median, less costs and decay). Trust the ordering: alpha_fast loses 80% of its spread to costs, alpha_slow 30%.

Lab 11, synthetic data. Left: IC with day t+h's return, measured (±2 se) vs planted. Right: IC with the cumulative t+1…t+h return; the fast alpha peaks near 4 days, the slow one still rises at 20.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Total-return IC: factor noise; Lab 11's dirty signal had IC sd 0.075, 0.040 neutralized (D3).
  • Overlap without Newey–West; look-ahead in return windows.
  • Microcap IC: check by size bucket.
  • Multiple testing and decay: published predictors lose ~58% of their return (McLean & Pontiff 2016) [Verified].

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "What's the rank IC on residuals?" → Skill net of factor moves.
  • "Great IC, brutal decay." → It works for a day; costs eat it.
  • "Newey–West that t-stat." → Your windows overlap.
  • "It's 0.7 correlated with our reversal composite." → Little marginal value.
  • "What's the ICIR?" → Mean IC over its volatility: consistency, not size.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Rank or Pearson IC, on residual returns, at what horizon? (basic)
  2. How fast does your IC decay? (basic)
  3. How do you handle overlapping horizons? (informed)
  4. How do you measure marginal contribution to the book? (informed)
  5. How many variants did you try, and what hurdle applies? (sharp)
  6. How much backtest IC survives live? 🔒 (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: IC as a slope, breadth, Newey–West, marginal value

IC as a Fama–MacBeth slope: on a z-scored signal, slope \(= IC_t \cdot \mathrm{sd}(r_t)\).

Breadth: with no skill, \(\mathrm{sd}(IC) \approx 1/\sqrt{N}\), so \(t \approx IC\sqrt{NT}\) and the annualized IC ratio is \(IC\sqrt{252N}\): Grinold's law with breadth \(252N\).

Newey–West with \(L = h-1\) lags and IC autocovariances \(\hat\gamma_j\):

\[ \hat\sigma^2_{NW} = \hat\gamma_0 + 2\sum_{j=1}^{L}\Big(1 - \frac{j}{L+1}\Big)\hat\gamma_j . \]

Marginal value of two optimally weighted streams with correlation \(\rho\):

\[ IR_{12}^2 = \frac{IR_1^2 + IR_2^2 - 2\rho\, IR_1 IR_2}{1-\rho^2}, \]

which gives stream 2 a positive weight only if \(IR_2 > \rho\, IR_1\) (below that, only as a short hedge). Illustrative: 1.5 and 1.0 give 1.505 at \(\rho = 0.6\), 1.80 at \(\rho = 0\).

docs.title: Feature engineering
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A feature is one number per stock per timestamp, built only from data public before the decision, that might predict the target return.
  • A few families carry most of the signal: past returns over several windows, volatility, liquidity and trading activity, fundamental ratios, and expectations data. Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) found momentum, liquidity and volatility dominant.
  • The craft is making features scale-free, correctly lagged, relative to peers and robust to outliers.
  • Libraries run from 101 formulaic alphas to 300+ academic characteristics. More features mostly add leakage risk and multiple testing, not alpha.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: signal · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which numbers, computable at decision time, carry information about future residual returns? Inputs → Outputs Point-in-time panel (prices, volumes, fundamentals, estimates, book snapshots, alt data) → lagged, normalized feature matrix X[date, stock, feature] Used by strategies ML short-horizon alpha · Cross-sectional alpha · Fundamental signals · Earnings and events · Analyst revisions · Alternative data · NLP signals · Intraday patterns · Factor-residual reversion Latency / compute regime Overnight batch: 500 features × 3,000 stocks × 20 years ≈ 7.5 billion cells, minutes to hours on a cluster [Estimate]; order-book features update per message in µs Key parameters Windows 1–252 days; momentum skip 21 days; vol half-life 20–60 days; clip at ±3 robust z; one-session information lag; 20–2,000 features Main failure modes Leakage; nonstationary raw levels; redundant substitutes; feature-search overfitting; microcap-driven features Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
A raw price of $412 says nothing; "fell 8% in five days while its sector fell 2%, on twice its usual volume" says a lot. Feature engineering is the analyst's normalization of comps: EV/EBITDA instead of raw EBITDA, adjusted for one-offs, on a common calendar. Each feature should be comparable across stocks and decades, known at decision time, and tied to an economic story.

Family Examples Typical windows Returns reversal, 12–1 momentum, distance to 52-week high 1–252 days Risk realized vol, beta, idiosyncratic vol 20–252 days Liquidity turnover, log ADV, Amihud illiquidity, spread 5–63 days Fundamentals E/P, gross profitability, accruals, asset growth latest filing Expectations revisions, earnings surprise, days to earnings event-driven Microstructure order-flow imbalance, book imbalance ms to minutes Relative sector-relative return, ETF flow varies

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Fix the target first (say, 5-day residual return); lag rules follow from it.
  2. Compute raw features per family over explicit trailing windows.
  3. Lag by the gap between data cutoff and trade. With features through close t−1, the book can trade anytime on day t, including the close.
  4. Make features scale-free: returns, ratios, logs of skewed quantities.
  5. Make them relative: subtract the date's sector median (neutralization).
  6. Robustify per date: median/MAD z-scores, clipped. Statistics come from the same date only, never the full sample.
  7. Add a few interactions with an economic story.
  8. Store with definitions versioned and knowledge timestamps attached.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def xs_robust_z(x, clip=3.0):
    """Per-date cross-sectional z-score with median/MAD, clipped (more in D3)."""
    med = x.median(axis=1)
    mad = x.sub(med, axis=0).abs().median(axis=1) * 1.4826
    return x.sub(med, axis=0).div(mad, axis=0).clip(-clip, clip)

def sector_relative(x, sector):
    """Subtract each date's sector median. sector: Series stock -> sector code."""
    return x - x.T.groupby(sector).transform("median").T

def make_features(px, dollar_vol, sector, lag=1):
    """px, dollar_vol: [date x stock] adjusted close and $ volume from the PIT panel.
    After shift(lag), row t uses data through close t-1 only."""
    r = px.pct_change(fill_method=None)                       # never fill across gaps
    raw = {
        "rev_5d":   -(px / px.shift(5) - 1),                  # short-term reversal
        "mom_12_1": px.shift(21) / px.shift(252) - 1,         # skip the latest month
        "vol_63d":  r.rolling(63, min_periods=40).std() * np.sqrt(252),
        "turn_chg": np.log(dollar_vol.rolling(5).mean() / dollar_vol.rolling(63).mean()),
        "amihud":   np.log((r.abs() / dollar_vol).rolling(21, min_periods=15).mean() * 1e6),
    }
    feats = {}
    for name, x in raw.items():
        x = x.shift(lag)                                      # the information lag
        if name in ("rev_5d", "mom_12_1"):
            x = sector_relative(x, sector)
        feats[name] = xs_robust_z(x)                          # same-date stats only
    feats["rev_x_illiq"] = feats["rev_5d"] * feats["amihud"]  # one motivated interaction
    return pd.concat(feats, axis=1)                           # columns: (feature, stock)

def make_target(px, horizon=5):
    # close t -> close t+horizon; features end at close t-1, so no overlap
    return px.shift(-horizon) / px - 1

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
One stock, four days (illustrative): returns +2.0%, −1.0%, −3.0%, +1.0% on dollar volumes $40M, $25M, $60M, $20M.

Amihud (|return| ÷ dollar volume × 10⁶, averaged): 0.02/40 = 0.00050; 0.01/25 = 0.00040; 0.03/60 = 0.00050; 0.01/20 = 0.00050. Mean 0.000475: about 4.75 bps of price move per $1M traded. A mega-cap moving 1% on $10B gives 0.000001, a ratio of 475×. That is why the code takes logs: ln 0.000475 = −7.65 versus ln 0.000001 = −13.8.

Reversal: cumulative return = 1.02 × 0.99 × 0.97 × 1.01 − 1 = −1.07%, so raw reversal is +1.07% (buy). The sector median fell 2.5%, so the stock outperformed by 1.43% and the sector-relative reversal is −1.43% (sell). If the sector-relative feature's cross-sectional median is about zero and its MAD-scaled spread 3%, the z-score is −0.48. Normalization flipped the trade.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Windows spaced roughly geometrically (5, 21, 63, 252 days) so they are not near-duplicates.
  • Momentum skip: the 12–1 convention drops the latest month, which tends to reverse (momentum) [Reported].
  • Minimum history: about two-thirds of the window. Note that 252-day features exclude recent IPOs.
  • Missing values: fill with the date's median plus a "missing" flag, since missingness is often informative [Lore].
  • Count: fewer than the model can support. Each feature added in a search is another trial (multiple testing).

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Academic zoo: GKX 2020 used 94 characteristics [Verified]. Chen & Zimmermann reproduce 319; 98% of the 161 originally clear predictors give t > 1.96 [Verified].
  • Formulaic alphas: Kakushadze (2016) published 101 price-volume formulas with average holding periods of 0.6–6.4 days and 15.9% average pairwise correlation [Verified]. Microsoft's open-source Qlib ships Alpha158 and Alpha360 feature sets [Verified].
  • Order-book features: Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov (2014) found price changes linear in OFI with slope inversely proportional to depth [Verified], so OFI is normalized by depth.
  • Stationarity: fractional differentiation keeps memory while removing trends (López de Prado 2018, ch. 5) [Verified]; most desks use returns, ratios and ranks [Lore].
  • Practice: versioned feature stores with thousands of features; edge comes more from data and careful variants than new formulas [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Univariate rank IC and its decay by horizon (evaluating signals).
  • Coverage, autocorrelation (turnover cost) and correlation clusters across features.
  • Drop-column importance under purged CV (time-series CV).
  • Null test: shuffle the target within each date; IC must fall to about 0.
  • Stable IC across size buckets and years.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Leakage: centered windows, full-sample normalization, backfilled vendor fields, label windows overlapping feature windows.
  • Nonstationary levels: raw price, raw dollar volume or market cap drift for decades; use logs, ratios, ranks.
  • Substitutes: turnover, ADV and spread overlap; importance splits among them.
  • Microcap features: IC driven by stocks you cannot trade at size.
  • Same-close trading: a feature built from today's close cannot trade today's close.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Is that lagged a day?" → Could you have known it when you traded?
  • "Normalize it sector-relative." → Remove the common sector move.
  • "That's just size in disguise." → The feature mostly proxies market cap.
  • "Rank it per date." → Use cross-sectional ranks so outliers and drift stop mattering.
  • "Shuffle the target and rerun." → Leakage check.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Which feature families carry most of your IC? (basic)
  2. How do you lag features relative to execution? (informed)
  3. Raw, sector-relative or residualized features? (informed)
  4. How many features does the production model use, and how many did you try? 🔒 (sharp)
  5. How do you catch a vendor backfill before it enters a feature? (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: Amihud, momentum, OFI, fractional differencing

Amihud illiquidity over \(D\) days with return \(r_d\) and dollar volume \(V_d\):

\[ \text{ILLIQ} = \frac{1}{D} \sum_{d=1}^{D} \frac{|r_d|}{V_d} \]

Momentum 12–1: \(P_{t-21}/P_{t-252} - 1\). Annualized realized vol: \(\sqrt{252}\,\mathrm{sd}(r_{t-62..t})\).

OFI sums signed changes in best bid and ask queues; Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov fit \(\Delta P = \beta\,\text{OFI} + \varepsilon\) with \(\beta \propto 1/\text{depth}\).

Fractional difference of order \(d\): \(\tilde x_t = \sum_k w_k x_{t-k}\) with \(w_0 = 1\), \(w_k = -w_{k-1}(d-k+1)/k\).

Cost: rolling features are \(O(TN)\) per feature with cumulative sums.

docs.title: Point-in-time data and cleaning
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Every value needs two dates: the period it describes and the moment it became public. Backtests must key on the second.
  • Most fake alpha comes from four errors: as-restated fundamentals, missing dead stocks, unadjusted corporate actions and broken identifier maps.
  • The core tool is an as-of join: for each stock and decision time, take the latest record public strictly before the decision, plus a safety lag.
  • Missing delisting returns are large and negative. Standard imputation: −30% (NYSE/Amex, Shumway 1997), −55% (Nasdaq, Shumway & Warther 1999). With the fix, the Nasdaq size effect vanishes.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: data · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) What did the market know, about which security, when the decision was made? Inputs → Outputs Vendor prices, corporate actions, timestamped filings, estimates, identifiers, index membership → clean panel keyed by permanent ID and knowledge time; universe per date Used by strategies Fundamental signals · Earnings and events · Cross-sectional alpha · Analyst revisions · Value, quality, low vol · Momentum · Reversal · Flow-driven · Alternative data · NLP signals Latency / compute regime Overnight batch: as-of joins over ~10⁸ stock-days take minutes on a columnar store [Estimate]; tick filters run per message Key parameters Lag after public timestamp (minutes to one session); delisting imputation −30% / −55%; bad-tick limits (spread > 50× daily median); price ≥ $5, ADV ≥ $1–10M Main failure modes Restated or period-end-dated data; survivorship; split errors; reused tickers; time-zone slips; silent vendor revisions Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
A database says "FY2024 EPS = $1.60." A backtest needs what the market believed FY2024 EPS was at 3:45 p.m. on 2025-03-31. To an accountant: the fiscal period is not the filing date, and a restatement overwrites the number investors actually traded on.

Point-in-time data keeps both clocks, valid time and knowledge time, and appends every revision instead of overwriting. Cleaning is the other half: prices comparable across splits, one identity per security, and dead stocks kept with their final losses (no survivorship bias).

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Security master: map every vendor identifier to one permanent ID with validity dates. CRSP's PERMNO is permanent [Verified]; a FIGI is never reused [Verified]; tickers and CUSIPs change.
  2. Stamp knowledge time (EDGAR acceptance, press-release or vendor-receipt time, in UTC); else apply a conservative lag.
  3. Append, never overwrite restatements and revisions.
  4. Adjust for corporate actions via total returns; keep raw prices for price screens.
  5. Filter bad ticks; keep the dead, imputing missing delisting returns.
  6. Universe from prior-day price, trailing ADV and historical index membership; then as-of join everything onto decision times.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def asof_join(decisions, records, key="permno", lag=pd.Timedelta(days=1)):
    """decisions: [permno, decision_time]; records: one row per VERSION of a fact,
    with known_at = EDGAR acceptance / vendor receipt time (UTC). Restatements are
    extra rows, never overwrites. Returns the latest version usable at each decision."""
    recs = records.assign(usable_at=records["known_at"] + lag).sort_values("usable_at")
    dec = decisions.sort_values("decision_time")
    return pd.merge_asof(dec, recs, left_on="decision_time", right_on="usable_at",
                         by=key, direction="backward",     # only the past
                         allow_exact_matches=False)        # a tie is not yet known

def total_return(px, prev_px, div=0.0, split=1.0, dlret=np.nan,
                 delisted=False, perf_delist=False, exch="NYSE"):
    """split = new shares per old share (2.0 for 2-for-1); div per old share."""
    r = (px * split + div) / prev_px - 1 if px == px else 0.0  # px NaN on delist day
    if delisted:
        if np.isnan(dlret) and perf_delist:              # Shumway imputation
            dlret = -0.55 if exch == "NASDAQ" else -0.30
        r = (1 + r) * (1 + np.nan_to_num(dlret)) - 1     # compound, don't drop
    return r

def universe(snap, min_price=5.0, min_adv_usd=5e6, top_n=3000):
    """snap: one row per permno with PRIOR-day raw close, trailing ADV and cap."""
    ok = (snap["prev_close_raw"] >= min_price) & (snap["adv20_usd"] >= min_adv_usd)
    return snap[ok].nlargest(top_n, "mcap_prev")["permno"]

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Company figures are illustrative. A firm's 10-K is accepted Wednesday 2025-02-26 at 18:05 ET. Filings started after 5:30 p.m. are dated the next business day [Verified], so EDGAR shows 2025-02-27. EPS is $2.00; in August 2025 it is restated to $1.60.

Data treatment First decision that sees FY2024 EPS EPS in March 2025 E/P at $40 Period-end dating 2024-12-31 (59 days early) $2.00 5.0% As-restated 2024-12-31 $1.60 4.0% PIT, 1-day lag Fri 2025-02-28 close $2.00 5.0%

Against a median E/P of 4.5%, the stock is cheap on PIT data and expensive on restated data. A restated-data value backtest skips or shorts it from March and banks any August drop on the news, which nothing public predicted.

Delisting: 100 equal-weighted Nasdaq small caps; 97 survivors average +1.2%; 3 performance delistings lack returns. Dropping them reports +1.2%. Imputing −55%: (97 × 1.2% + 3 × −55%) / 100 = 1.164% − 1.65% = −0.486%.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Lag. 10-Ks are due 60, 75 or 90 days after year-end by filer size [Verified]; academic sorts often assume six months [Reported]. Practitioners use acceptance time plus a buffer, from minutes to a session [Lore]. Forms 4 and 13D filed until 10 p.m. keep same-day dates [Verified], so the filing date misleads.
  • Bad ticks. Barndorff-Nielsen et al. (2009) rules drop quotes with spreads above 50× the day's median, mids beyond 10 median absolute deviations of a 50-quote centered median, and trades over one spread outside the quote [Verified].
  • Screens. A $5 floor removes penny stocks; NYSE size breakpoints and value weights stop microcaps dominating (Hou, Xue & Zhang) [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Academic default: CRSP/Compustat via WRDS, conservative lags, Shumway imputation [Verified].
  • History is versioned. CRSP's legacy SIZ format had its last release in January 2025. CIZ reinvests dividends on the ex-date, rewriting 9.62% of monthly returns by over 1 bp (Schwarz, Walter & Weiss 2026) [Verified]. CIZ does not impute −30% for missing delisting returns [Verified].
  • Careful code still leaks. The Chen-Zimmermann replication fixed a look-ahead bug in one signal in October 2024 [Verified].
  • Practice: in-house bitemporal stores, snapshots of every vendor delivery, pinned vintages per backtest [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Index returns rebuilt from your panel track the published index within a few bps a month [Lore].
  • Every daily |return| above 40% matches a split, merger or news event.
  • Delistings per year are non-zero and stable across vendor changes.
  • One extra day of lag barely moves Sharpe; a collapse means edge-timing or a leak.
  • Last year's panel rebuilt today matches the archived snapshot.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Today's index members define the past universe: pure survivorship.
  • Backward fill copies the future into the past; only forward fill is safe.
  • Time zones: a fixed ET-to-UTC offset is wrong for part of the year (DST).
  • Closing price: NYSE MOC orders must be in by 3:50 p.m. [Verified], so a signal using the 4:00 p.m. close cannot trade it.
  • Vendor backfill: history added later was never available live.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "First-reported or as-restated?" → Were these the numbers investors saw that day?
  • "Key it on acceptance time." → Use the moment the data became public.
  • "Did you keep the dead?" → Are delisted stocks and their delisting returns included?
  • "Join as-of, strictly before." → A record stamped at the decision time does not count.
  • "Pin the vintage." → Record which data snapshot produced the result.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: as-of join, adjustment factors, delisting compounding

As-of join for security \(i\), decision time \(\tau\), lag \(\ell\), versions \(v\) known at \(k_v\):

\[ x_{i,\tau} = x_{i,v^*}, \qquad v^* = \arg\max_{v} \{\, k_v : k_v + \ell < \tau \,\} \]

A sorted merge costs \(O((N+M)\log(N+M))\).

Total return with split ratio \(s_t\) and dividend \(D_t\); past prices are divided by later cumulative splits:

\[ r_t = \frac{s_t P_t + D_t}{P_{t-1}} - 1, \qquad \tilde P_u = P_u \Big/ \prod_{u < w \le T} s_w \]

Delisting month: \(1 + r^{\text{adj}} = (1 + r)(1 + r^{\text{dl}})\).

docs.title: Signal transforms
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Transforms turn a raw, dirty signal into a clean cross-sectional score: winsorize, z-score or rank, neutralize, smooth, scale.
  • Winsorize before z-scoring, or one bad print sets everyone's scale.
  • Neutralization is a per-date regression on beta, industries and styles; keep the residual. In Lab 11 it lifts a winsorized signal's IC from 0.019 to 0.025 (synthetic lab result).
  • Smoothing trades a little IC for much less turnover.
  • Optimizers need expected returns: alpha = IC × volatility × score (Grinold 1994).

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: signal · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How do I make a raw number per stock comparable, outlier-proof and free of unintended bets? Inputs → Outputs Raw signal [date × stock], exposures, residual volatilities → per-date score (mean 0, sd 1) → alpha Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Fundamental signals · Revisions · Earnings · Alt data · NLP · ML short-horizon · Reversal · Factor-residual · Stat arb · Factor investing · Value and quality · Momentum Latency / compute regime Overnight batch: one least-squares solve per date, about a millisecond for 3,000 names × 80 exposures [Estimate] Key parameters Winsorize at 1st/99th percentile or ±3–5 MAD; z clip ±3; beta + 60–70 industries + 5–12 styles; EWMA half-life ≈ the signal's half-life Main failure modes Z-scoring before winsorizing; over-neutralizing; stale exposures; look-ahead in statistics Lab Lab 11

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Before ranking EV/EBITDA you strip one-offs and compare within an industry; transforms do the same for signals. A raw revision signal arrives in dollars per share, one stale share count makes a value 100× normal, and a good month for semis makes it secretly long semis:

Step Removes Price paid Winsorize bad prints, tiny denominators some genuine extremes Z-score or rank units, scale drift ranks discard magnitude Neutralize market, sector, style bets alpha that lives in those factors Smooth noise, turnover timeliness (some IC)

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Per date, point in time: that date's universe and data only (PIT data); never full-sample statistics.
  2. Winsorize at the 1st/99th percentiles or median ± 5 MAD (median absolute deviation).
  3. Normalize: a z-score keeps magnitude, a rank only order; Gaussianized ranks (rank, then normal quantile) sit between.
  4. Neutralize: least squares on exposures, keep the residual. Sector demeaning is the dummies-only case; adding beta removes the market tilt it leaves.
  5. Smooth with an EWMA, then re-neutralize.
  6. Re-standardize, combine horizons (F5) and scale to alpha for the optimizer.
import numpy as np

# Signals are T x N arrays (dates x stocks) known at the close of t; one row = one date.
# winsorize, zscore, rank_score and neutralize follow Lab 11's lab.py; ewma and to_alpha are
# not in the lab. Simplified: no NaNs, no ties, exposures fixed over time.

def winsorize(x, pct=0.01):
    lo = np.nanquantile(x, pct, axis=-1, keepdims=True)       # per-date 1st percentile
    hi = np.nanquantile(x, 1 - pct, axis=-1, keepdims=True)   # per-date 99th percentile
    return np.clip(x, lo, hi)

def zscore(x, clip=3.0):
    mu = np.nanmean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    sd = np.nanstd(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return np.clip((x - mu) / sd, -clip, clip)                # clipping here does NOT replace winsorizing

def rank_score(x):
    r = np.argsort(np.argsort(x, axis=-1), axis=-1)           # ranks 0..N-1 per date
    return r / (x.shape[-1] - 1) - 0.5                        # uniform on [-0.5, 0.5]

def neutralize(signal, exposures):
    """exposures: N x K, e.g. [beta, sector dummies]. Residual is orthogonal to every column."""
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(exposures, signal.T, rcond=None)   # K x T factor tilts
    return signal - (exposures @ coef).T

def ewma(x, halflife=2.0):
    lam = 0.5 ** (1 / halflife)                               # weight on yesterday's smoothed score
    out = x.copy()
    for t in range(1, len(x)):
        out[t] = lam * out[t - 1] + (1 - lam) * x[t]
    return out

def transform(raw, beta, sector_dummies, halflife=None):
    exposures = np.column_stack([beta, sector_dummies])       # dummies already span the intercept
    s = neutralize(zscore(winsorize(raw, 0.01)), exposures)   # Lab 11's best step
    if halflife:
        s = neutralize(ewma(s, halflife), exposures)          # smoothing re-imports old exposures
    return zscore(s, clip=3.0)                                # re-standardize: mean 0, sd 1

def to_alpha(score, ic=0.02, resid_vol_daily=0.015):
    return ic * resid_vol_daily * score                       # Grinold: alpha = IC x vol x score

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
A. One date, five stocks (illustrative). Raw signal −2, −1, 0, +1, +20; E's +20 is a bad print. Median 0, MAD 1, so winsorize at ±5.

Stock Sector Raw z, raw Winsorized z Sector-demeaned A Banks −2 −0.68 −2 −1.08 −0.21 B Banks −1 −0.56 −1 −0.66 +0.21 C Tech 0 −0.44 0 −0.25 −0.83 D Tech +1 −0.31 +1 +0.17 −0.41 E Tech +20 +1.99 +5 +1.82 +1.24
  • Raw z (mean 3.6, sd 8.26): D, above the median, is a short because E dragged the mean up. A ±3 clip is useless: E's z is 1.99.
  • Winsorized (mean 0.6, sd 2.42): D is long. Ranks get the order right regardless but cannot see that E is extreme.
  • Sector-demeaned (Tech +0.58, Banks −0.87): B becomes the long bank, D the short Tech laggard.

B. Smoothing a fast signal. Lab 11's alpha_fast (IC 0.041, half-life 2 days) earns 17.8 bps/day gross but 3.6 net after 14.1 bps of costs (synthetic lab result). A 2-day EWMA (λ = 0.707) keeps 82% of the IC and cuts daily turnover from 86% to about 38% (Go deeper): 14.5 gross − 6.2 cost ≈ 8.3 net [Estimate]. Our rerun of the lab's simulator with the EWMA (not in results.json) gives 7.9 net.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Winsorization: 1st/99th percentile or ±3–5 MAD [Lore].
  • Z vs rank: ranks for fat-tailed inputs (text, alt data), z-scores where magnitude matters. Rank IC ignores monotone transforms (Lab 11: 0.020 for raw, z-scored and winsorized; synthetic lab result).
  • Exposures: MSCI's Barra USE4 has 60 industries and 12 styles [Verified]; groups need ~10+ names [Lore].
  • Half-life: start at the signal's IC half-life (D4); tune net of costs.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Scaling: Grinold (1994) sets alpha = volatility × IC × score [Verified].
  • Industrial primitives: WorldQuant's 101 alphas (Kakushadze 2016) use the same operators: cross-sectional rank, scale, decay_linear and indneutralize (demean within industry groups) [Verified].
  • Partial neutralization: Numerai's open-source scoring ranks, Gaussianizes and neutralizes by least squares with a proportion from 0 to 1 [Verified]; partial neutralization is common [Lore].
  • Where: in the signal and again in the optimizer [Lore], which over-loads alpha its risk model cannot see (Ceria, Saxena & Stubbs 2012) [Reported].
  • Smoothing vs slow trading: Gârleanu & Pedersen (2013) trade partway toward an aim that weights persistent signals more [Verified]; heavy smoothing on top double-counts [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• IC up, IC volatility down. Lab 11 (synthetic lab result): raw IC 0.012 (t 5.8); winsorized z 0.019 (t 6.8); beta- and sector-neutral 0.025 (t 22.2), near the clean signal's 0.027. IC daily sd fell from 0.075 to 0.040, correlation with beta from 0.28 to 0.00.
  • These t-stats are stylized: the simulator plants IC 0.03 across 500 stocks. Real single signals show daily ICs of ~0.005–0.03 [Lore] and t-stats of ~2–5 over five years [Estimate].
  • Residual factor exposures near zero; lower turnover after smoothing.

Lab 11, synthetic data (500 stocks × 1,260 days). Left: IC t-stat of each transform step against next-day total and residual returns. Right: quintile returns of the planted alphas and a noise signal.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Clip instead of winsorize (example A).
  • Over-neutralizing: a value signal neutralized to value is gone.
  • Look-ahead: full-sample means or percentiles.
  • Stale exposures, tiny groups: old betas leave factor bets; a two-name industry turns its names into opposites.
  • Smoothing without re-neutralizing.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Did you winsorize before you z-scored?" → One bad print sets everyone's scale.
  • "Neutralize to subindustry." → Compare each stock with its closest peers.
  • "That signal is mostly beta." → Its IC vanishes once beta is regressed out.
  • "Gauss-rank it." → Rank, then map to normal quantiles.
  • "Put a three-day decay on it." → Smooth to cut turnover.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Ranks, z-scores or Gaussianized ranks, and why? (basic)
  2. Do you neutralize in the signal, the optimizer, or both? (basic)
  3. How often are your neutralization exposures re-estimated? (informed)
  4. Do you smooth each signal or only the combined forecast? (informed)
  5. How much IC does full style neutralization cost you? 🔒 (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: projection and the EWMA trade-off

Neutralization as projection. Signal \(s\), exposures \(X\) (\(N \times K\)):

\[ s_\perp = \left(I - X (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top\right) s, \qquad X^\top s_\perp = 0 . \]

Dummies only: group demeaning. Cost \(O(NK^2)\) per date.

EWMA of an AR(1) signal with autocorrelation \(\varphi\) and IC with day \(t+1+k\) equal to \(IC\cdot\varphi^k\) (as in Lab 11), smoothed as \(e_t = \lambda e_{t-1} + (1-\lambda)s_t\):

\[ \frac{IC_e}{IC} = \sqrt{\frac{1-\lambda^2}{1-\lambda^2\varphi^2}}, \qquad \rho_e = \lambda + \frac{\varphi(1-\lambda^2)}{1+\lambda\varphi} . \]

Turnover scales with \(\sqrt{1-\rho}\). With \(\lambda = \varphi = 0.707\): IC ratio 0.82, \(\rho_e = 0.943\), turnover ratio \(\sqrt{0.057/0.293} = 0.44\).

docs.title: Alpha combination and ensembling
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • The combiner turns 10–1,000 alphas into one forecast per stock, weighted by skill net of overlap, with weights stable enough to survive estimation error.
  • The ladder: equal weight → IC weighting → ridge or mean-variance on the alpha covariance → nonlinear meta-models. Each rung estimates more parameters.
  • Ridge sits between mean-variance (λ → 0) and IC weighting (λ → ∞) and pulls near-duplicates toward a shared weight. In Lab 12 it matched the oracle (out-of-sample IC 0.085 vs 0.087); equal weight, diluted by noise signals, scored 0.050 (synthetic lab result).
  • IC weighting double-counts correlated signals. Weight fast-decaying signals by the alpha that survives costs, not by raw IC.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: forecast · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which single forecast per stock, built from K overlapping signals, gives the best out-of-sample IC after costs? Inputs → Outputs Per-date ranked signals (date × stock × K) and forward residual returns or IC histories → weights (or a meta-model) and one composite forecast per stock Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Stat arb overview · ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Analyst revisions and sentiment · Fundamental quant signals · NLP and LLM signals · Alternative data · Factor-residual mean reversion · Short-term reversal · Factor investing · Value, quality, low vol · Momentum · Trend following Latency / compute regime Overnight batch: a 100-signal ridge solve takes under a millisecond, a GBDT meta-model minutes; refit daily to monthly Key parameters IC lookback 1–3 years (half-life 6–24 months); ridge λ by purged CV; covariance shrinkage 30–70%; per-signal cap 10–25%; entry IC t-stat 2–3 [Lore] Main failure modes Double-counting near-duplicates; weights chasing recent IC; meta-models fit on in-sample base forecasts; ignoring decay and turnover Lab Lab 12

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Think of an investment committee: one vote per analyst; votes weighted by track record; track record discounted for analysts who echo a colleague; or a meta-analyst who learns whom to trust. Those are the four rungs of alpha combination.

The third rung is consolidation: eliminate intercompany balances before adding up subsidiaries. Two reversal signals from two researchers are mostly one bet; add their information coefficients (IC) as if independent and you book the same revenue twice.

The tension is estimation error. In the forecast combination puzzle, simple averages beat "optimal" weights because estimation error swamps skill differences (Smith & Wallis 2009) [Verified]. But equal weight fails once the library holds dead or duplicated signals.
