docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Prepare: rank or z-score and neutralize each signal per date (signal transforms); target = per-date rank of the forward residual return.
  2. Estimate on training dates only (purged, see time-series CV): each signal's mean daily IC and, for mean-variance, its IC series.
  3. Combine: equal weight, IC-weighted (negative ICs floored at zero), pooled ridge, max-IR on the IC covariance, or a GBDT meta-model.
  4. Forecast the next block with frozen weights; score out-of-sample rank IC, turnover and net P&L.
  5. Roll forward: refit monthly, cap any one signal's weight, re-neutralize, and log every variant tried (overfitting).
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
# rank_target, combine_ic_weighted, fit_ridge: Lab 12 core functions (same names and logic).
# combine_mv and the loop are sketches added here. Rows = (date, stock).
# X: rows x K signals z-scored per date; dates: date index of each row.

def rank_target(ret, dates):
    # per-date percentile rank of the forward residual return, mapped to [-0.5, 0.5]
    g = pd.Series(ret).groupby(dates)
    return ((g.rank() - 1) / (g.transform("count") - 1) - 0.5).to_numpy()

def combine_ic_weighted(X, ic):
    # w ~ max(training IC, 0), summing to 1. Ignores overlap: a near-copy gets double weight
    w = np.clip(np.asarray(ic, dtype=float), 0.0, None)
    w = w / w.sum() if w.sum() > 0 else np.full(len(w), 1.0 / len(w))
    return X @ w, w

def fit_ridge(X, y, lam):
    # beta = (X'X + lam I)^-1 X'y. lam -> 0: OLS, uses overlap; lam -> inf: beta ~ X'y ~ IC weights
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * np.eye(X.shape[1]), X.T @ y)

def combine_mv(ic_hist, shrink=0.5):
    # NOT in Lab 12. Max-IR weights from the alphas' daily IC series (T x K):
    # w ~ inv(IC covariance) @ mean IC, with the covariance shrunk toward its diagonal
    S = np.cov(ic_hist, rowvar=False)
    S = (1 - shrink) * S + shrink * np.diag(np.diag(S))
    w = np.linalg.solve(S, ic_hist.mean(axis=0))
    return w / np.abs(w).sum()

# Lab 12 setting: 5-day horizon, lam = 0.1 x training rows (about 10% shrinkage)
# y = rank_target(fwd_resid_ret_5d, dates)
# for train_d, test_d in walk_forward_splits(n_dates, n_folds=5, horizon=5):
#     tr, te = rows_of(train_d), rows_of(test_d)
#     beta = fit_ridge(X[tr], y[tr], lam=0.1 * len(tr))
#     forecast[te] = X[te] @ beta            # weights frozen over the test block

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Signal A has IC 0.040; A′ is a noisy copy (correlation 0.85, IC 0.85 × 0.040 = 0.034); B has IC 0.030 and is uncorrelated with both. Composite IC is \(w^\top c / \sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}\) (\(c\): ICs, \(\Sigma\): correlations).

Method Weights A / A′ / B Composite IC OLS = mean-variance, Σ⁻¹c 57% / 0% / 43% 0.0500 Ridge, λ = 1 (correlation units) 38% / 25% / 37% 0.0489 Equal weight 33% / 33% / 33% 0.0480 IC-weighted 38% / 33% / 29% 0.0473 Equal weight plus 10 pure-noise signals 7.7% each 0.0271

By hand: the inverse of the A/A′ correlation block is 1/(1 − 0.85²) = 3.60 times [[1, −0.85], [−0.85, 1]]. So β_A = 3.60 × (0.040 − 0.85 × 0.034) = 0.040, β_A′ = 3.60 × (0.034 − 0.85 × 0.040) = 0, and β_B = 0.030. Composite IC = √(0.040² + 0.030²) = 0.050.

A′ adds nothing A lacks; OLS sees this, IC weighting gives the A cluster 71%. The top four rows differ by under 6%; noise costs 46% of the IC, the Lab 12 story.

Why ridge ≈ shrinking toward equal weight. Strictly, ridge shrinks toward zero, and as λ grows its weights approach the ICs. But the penalty bites hardest on the small-eigenvalue direction, "A minus A′", so within a correlated cluster weights move toward equality: A : A′ goes from ∞ (OLS) to 1.5 (λ = 1) to 1.2 (λ = 10). Stock & Watson (2004) shrink explicitly toward 1/K instead [Verified].

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Window: 1–3 years of daily ICs, or a 6–24-month exponential half-life [Lore].
  • λ and covariance shrinkage: chosen on purged walk-forward folds by rank IC. Lab 12's λ = 0.1 × rows is about 10% shrinkage, since X′X ≈ rows × Σ.
  • Caps and floors: 10–25% per signal; negative-IC signals floored at zero, not flipped (a flip is a fresh data-mined bet) [Lore].
  • Decay-aware weights: if positions move a fraction κ per day toward target and alpha decays at δ = ln 2 / half-life, the book captures κ/(κ + δ) of gross alpha. At κ = 0.2, a 1-day half-life keeps 22%, a 20-day half-life 85% [Estimate] (derivation below). Hence Gârleanu & Pedersen (2013) weight slow signals more in the aim portfolio [Verified].
  • Horizon blending: rescale signals to the optimizer's horizon by decay profile, or feed several horizons to a multi-period optimizer [Lore].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: Grinold & Kahn's refined forecast is volatility × IC × score; with several signals it becomes the regression Cov(r, g)·Var(g)⁻¹·g, the mean-variance combination (Grinold & Kahn 2000) [Verified]. Qian, Hua & Sorensen (2007) maximize the composite's mean IC / sd IC instead: w ∝ Σ_IC⁻¹ · mean IC [Reported].
  • Simple often beats optimal: in Stock & Watson the best combinations, like the mean, ignore recent performance [Verified]; Smith & Wallis support ignoring forecast-error covariances [Verified]. That helps when covariances are noisy, and hurts when a true near-copy is present.
  • Practice: slowly refit, shrunk linear weights dominate mid-frequency books; nonlinear meta-models appear mostly in short-horizon ML books [Lore]. For thousands of alphas, Kakushadze & Yu (2017) give an algorithm linear in their number [Verified]. Stacking must use out-of-fold base forecasts, as in Breiman (1996) [Reported].
  • Signal-level vs portfolio-level (contested): blending signals nets opposing trades before they reach the market (how firms combine strategies). AQR researchers find integrating beats mixing for long-only style portfolios (Fitzgibbons et al. 2017) [Verified]; Ghayur, Heaney & Platt (2018) find portfolio blending wins except at high factor exposure [Reported].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Composite out-of-sample rank IC beats the best single signal on identical purged folds; drop-one tests flag duplicates (near-zero marginal IC).
  • Weights keep their signs across refits; turnover is reported next to IC.

Lab 12 (150 stocks × 1,260 days; 3 planted alphas, 1 near-duplicate, 10 noise signals; 1,045 walk-forward test dates), synthetic lab result: mean daily out-of-sample rank IC of 0.050 for equal weight, 0.082 IC-weighted, 0.085 ridge and 0.066 GBDT; oracle 0.087, best single signal 0.051. Ridge's in-sample IC (0.084) matched its out-of-sample IC; GBDT's was 0.238. The planted truth is linear, so trees add only variance here (tree ensembles).

Lab 12, synthetic data: cumulative out-of-sample P&L (before costs) of each combiner under walk-forward validation; dashed line, what naive shuffled K-fold promised for GBDT.

P&L follows IC: Sharpe 9.6 gross and 5.6 net for ridge, 5.7 and 1.5 for equal weight (synthetic lab result). These levels are stylized: clean, stable planted alphas, free factor hedging and simple costs, and the fundamental law turns a daily IC of 0.03 across 500 stocks into an IR near 0.03 × √(500 × 252) ≈ 10 [Estimate]. Real diversified multi-alpha equity books run about 1.5–3 gross and 1–2 net [Lore]; the PCA stat arb of Avellaneda & Lee (2010) earned 1.44 net over 1997–2007, an academic backtest that weakened later [Verified]. Compare rows, not levels.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Double-counting: in Lab 12's last fold, IC weighting gave the original signal and its near-copy 43% of the weight; ridge gave the copy 6% of its absolute weight against 22% for the original (synthetic lab result).
  • Chasing IC: short lookbacks whipsaw weights; handle alpha decay with decay monitoring.
  • Stacking leak: a meta-model fit on in-sample base forecasts overweights the most overfit base model.
  • Shared signals: popular alphas sit in many firms' composites and unwind together (crowding).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "That new alpha is 0.8 correlated with the book, so its marginal IC is basically zero." → It duplicates existing signals.
  • "We ridge the combo and cap anything above 20%." → Shrunk regression weights with concentration limits.
  • "Fast stuff looks great on IC and dies on costs." → Weight by alpha that survives trading speed.
  • "Blend at the signal level so the optimizer nets the trades." → Signal-level combination saves costs.
  • "Stack on out-of-fold predictions only." → Meta-models must not see base models' training data.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Do you combine forecasts before the optimizer or positions after it? (basic)
  2. How do you weight alphas: equal, IC, regression or something nonlinear? (basic)
  3. How do you adjust weights for decay and turnover? (informed)
  4. What marginal IC must a new signal show to enter the combination? 🔒 (sharp)
  5. How much IC does your combiner add over equal weight, out of sample? 🔒 (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: composite IC, ridge along principal components, max-IR weights, decay capture

Signal correlation \(\Sigma\), IC vector \(c\):

\[ \text{IC}(w) = \frac{w^\top c}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}}, \qquad \arg\max_w \text{IC}(w) \propto \Sigma^{-1} c . \]

Ridge, with \(\Sigma = \sum_j d_j u_j u_j^\top\):

\[ \hat\beta(\lambda) = \sum_j \frac{u_j^\top c}{d_j + \lambda}\, u_j , \]

so contrasts between near-duplicates (\(d_j \approx 1-\rho\)) shrink most, and \(\hat\beta \to c/\lambda\) (IC weighting) as \(\lambda \to \infty\).

Max-IR weights: \(w \propto \Sigma_{IC}^{-1}\,\overline{\text{IC}}\), with \(\Sigma_{IC}\) the covariance of daily ICs.

Decay capture with signal \(s_0 e^{-\delta t}\) and position \(\dot x = \kappa(s - x)\), \(x_0 = 0\):

\[ \frac{\int_0^\infty x(t)\,s(t)\,dt}{\int_0^\infty s(t)^2\,dt} = \frac{\kappa}{\kappa + \delta}. \]

Cost: ridge \(O(nK^2 + K^3)\); IC covariance \(O(TK^2)\).

docs.title: Linear models and regularization
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • The workhorse equity forecaster is still linear: regress forward residual returns on standardized signals, then shrink the coefficients (ridge, lasso, elastic net).
  • Returns are mostly noise: the best monthly stock-level out-of-sample R² in Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) was 0.40%; daily, 0.05–0.25% is good [Estimate]. At that signal-to-noise ratio, estimation variance dominates, so shrunk coefficients beat OLS.
  • Pooled and per-date (Fama–MacBeth) regressions differ mainly in how they weight dates.
  • The penalty is chosen by purged walk-forward cross-validation on rank IC, never by random K-fold.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: forecast · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) What is the best linear forecast of next-period return from 10–300 standardized signals, and how much should each be trusted? Inputs → Outputs Signal panel (date × stock × K, ranked or z-scored per date) and forward residual returns → coefficients β and per-stock forecasts in bps Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Fundamental quant signals · Analyst revisions and sentiment · Factor-residual mean reversion · Short-term reversal · ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Factor investing · Equity market making Latency / compute regime Overnight batch: ridge on 2,000 stocks × 750 days × 100 signals takes seconds. Inference is a dot product (µs even in HFT fair-value models) Key parameters Penalty λ (by CV); elastic-net L1 share 0.1–0.5; window 1–3 years rolling or expanding; horizon 1–20 days; refit daily to monthly; winsorize at ±3σ Main failure modes Small λ with many signals; leakage from overlapping labels; sign-flipping coefficients under collinearity; stale β after regime shifts; microcap outliers Lab Lab 12

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Treat each signal as a witness about tomorrow's return; a regression decides how much to trust each one given the others. Over 99% of return variance is unpredictable, so some witnesses look reliable by luck, and OLS puts large, offsetting weights on correlated ones.

Regularization is a haircut on every estimate, like a reserve against numbers you cannot fully audit. Ridge shrinks all coefficients and spreads weight across correlated signals; lasso sets weak ones to zero; elastic net mixes both. You accept a little bias for a large cut in variance, the error that dominates at this signal-to-noise ratio. Linear forecasts also decompose by signal for attribution and change little day to day, which keeps turnover down.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Features: per date, rank or z-score each signal, winsorize, fill missing with 0 (the mean). Standardizing matters because the penalty is scale-dependent.
  2. Target: forward residual return over the holding horizon h, winsorized or ranked.
  3. Scheme: pooled (stack all dates) or per-date (Fama–MacBeth: one cross-sectional regression per date, average the slopes).
  4. Shrink and choose λ: walk-forward folds, training only on dates whose h-day labels end before each validation block; score mean daily rank IC.
  5. Refit on a rolling or expanding window; forecast = signals × β.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
# rank_target, fit_ridge, walk_forward_splits: Lab 12 core functions (same names and logic).
# zscore_xs, fama_macbeth, rank_ic and choose_lambda are sketches added here.

def zscore_xs(X):                          # X: (n_stocks, k) signals for ONE date
    X = (X - np.nanmean(X, 0)) / np.nanstd(X, 0)
    return np.nan_to_num(np.clip(X, -3, 3))     # winsorize at 3 sd; missing -> 0 (the mean)

def rank_target(ret, dates):               # per-date percentile rank of forward return, in [-0.5, 0.5]
    g = pd.Series(ret).groupby(dates)
    return ((g.rank() - 1) / (g.transform("count") - 1) - 0.5).to_numpy()

def fit_ridge(X, y, lam):                  # no intercept: X z-scored, y ranked per date (mean 0)
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * np.eye(X.shape[1]), X.T @ y)

def walk_forward_splits(n_dates, n_folds=5, horizon=5):
    blocks = np.array_split(np.arange(n_dates), n_folds + 1)
    for test in blocks[1:]:                # train only on dates whose label ends before the test block
        yield np.arange(0, test[0] - horizon + 1), test

def fama_macbeth(Xs, ys):
    # one OLS per date; the slopes' time series is each signal's daily "factor return"
    B = np.array([np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0] for X, y in zip(Xs, ys)])
    return B.mean(0), B.mean(0) / (B.std(0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(B)))   # mean slope, t-stat

def rank_ic(pred, y):
    return np.corrcoef(pred.argsort().argsort(), y.argsort().argsort())[0, 1]

def choose_lambda(Xs, ys, lams, n_folds=5, horizon=5):
    # Xs[t]: (n_stocks, k) z-scored signals; ys[t]: rank_target of date t's forward residual return
    score = {lam: [] for lam in lams}
    for tr, te in walk_forward_splits(len(Xs), n_folds, horizon):
        Xtr, ytr = np.vstack([Xs[t] for t in tr]), np.concatenate([ys[t] for t in tr])
        for lam in lams:                   # Lab 12 fixes lam = 0.1 x training rows instead
            b = fit_ridge(Xtr, ytr, lam)
            score[lam] += [rank_ic(Xs[t] @ b, ys[t]) for t in te]
    return max(lams, key=lambda lam: np.mean(score[lam]))   # best mean daily rank IC

# Daily step on date t (expanding window; labels known for dates <= t - horizon):
# beta = fit_ridge(np.vstack(Xs[:t - horizon + 1]), np.concatenate(ys[:t - horizon + 1]), lam_star)
# forecast_t = zscore_xs(raw_signals_t) @ beta

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Two standardized reversal signals with correlation 0.8 and ICs of 0.030 and 0.026.

OLS: Σ⁻¹ = (1/0.36)·[[1, −0.8], [−0.8, 1]] = 2.78·[[1, −0.8], [−0.8, 1]]. β₁ = 2.78 × (0.030 − 0.8 × 0.026) = 0.0256; β₂ = 2.78 × (0.026 − 0.8 × 0.030) = 0.0056. In-sample R² = 0.030 × 0.0256 + 0.026 × 0.0056 = 0.091%, versus 0.030² = 0.090% for the first signal alone.

Noise: with ~10,000 effectively independent observations, each IC has standard error ≈ 0.010, so each OLS coefficient has ≈ √2.78 × 0.010 = 0.0167, larger than β₂ itself.

Ridge, λ = 1 (correlation units): (Σ + I)⁻¹ = (1/3.36)·[[2, −0.8], [−0.8, 2]]. β₁ = (2 × 0.030 − 0.8 × 0.026)/3.36 = 0.0117; β₂ = (2 × 0.026 − 0.8 × 0.030)/3.36 = 0.0083. Standard error = √0.184 × 0.010 = 0.0043, four times smaller: a sliver of in-sample fit buys stable coefficients.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• λ: grid over 4–6 orders of magnitude; take the best validation rank IC or the largest λ within one standard error of it (the ESL rule).
  • Ridge vs lasso: many weak, correlated signals favor ridge; many candidates with few real ones favor lasso [Lore].
  • Window: rolling 1–3 years (or 6–24-month half-lives) for short-horizon books, expanding for slow fundamental signals [Lore]; GKX refit annually on an expanding window [Verified].
  • Weights: √(market cap) or inverse residual variance, so microcaps don't dominate [Lore].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Fama–MacBeth as a diagnostic: built to test asset pricing models (Fama & MacBeth 1973). In practice each day's slope is the return of a unit-exposure portfolio in that signal, i.e. the signal's P&L series; Barra-style risk models run the same regressions [Verified] (MSCI USE4).
  • Shrinkage matters: in GKX 2020, OLS on ~900 predictors had negative out-of-sample R². Penalized and reduced-rank linear models recovered roughly 0.1–0.3% per month, versus 0.16% for a three-characteristic OLS and 0.33–0.40% for trees and nets [Verified].
  • Lasso at high frequency: Chinco, Clark-Joseph & Ye (2019) ran lasso on lagged one-minute returns of all NYSE stocks and found sparse, short-lived predictors that improved out-of-sample fit [Verified].
  • Contested: Kelly, Malamud & Zhou (2024) argue heavily over-parameterized ridge models improve market timing; the claim is debated.
  • Many books still combine alphas linearly, with nonlinear models in short-horizon sleeves [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Out-of-sample rank IC (mean, t-stat, by year) beats the best single signal on folds the λ search never touched.
  • Out-of-sample R² against a zero forecast (the GKX convention), not the historical mean.
  • IC vs log λ is hump-shaped; coefficients keep their signs across refits.
  • Out-of-sample IC below half of in-sample IC signals overfitting [Lore]. In Lab 12, ridge kept all of it; GBDT kept 28% (synthetic lab result).

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Overlapping labels: consecutive 5-day forward returns share 4 days, so random K-fold leaks (time-series CV).
  • Full-sample standardization is look-ahead bias.
  • Outliers: one +300% microcap day can set an OLS coefficient.
  • Stale coefficients after regime breaks (regime detection).
  • Tuning on the test set: a λ × window × horizon grid is a multiple-testing problem.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We ridge everything; OLS weights on correlated alphas are noise." → Unshrunk collinear coefficients are unstable.
  • "The FM t-stat is 2.1, but half of it is 2009." → Significance comes from one period.
  • "Pick lambda on rank IC, not R²." → Rank IC resists outliers and matches how forecasts are used.
  • "Lasso keeps swapping the two value signals." → L1 picks arbitrarily among near-duplicates, adding turnover.
  • "Twenty bps of daily R² is a good model, not a bad one." → Tiny per-stock fit; the Sharpe comes from breadth.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Pooled or per-date, and how do you weight observations? (basic)
  2. Raw, residual or ranked target, over what horizon? (basic)
  3. How do you choose the penalty, and on what metric? (informed)
  4. Do you smooth coefficients across refits? (informed)
  5. How much IC does the combination add over the best single signal? (sharp)
  6. When did a nonlinear model last beat your linear one after costs? 🔒 (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: ridge, lasso, Fama–MacBeth, out-of-sample R²

Ridge (Gaussian prior on β):

\[ \hat\beta_{\text{ridge}} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y \]

Lasso with orthonormal \(X\) soft-thresholds OLS: \(\hat\beta_j = \operatorname{sign}(b_j)(\lvert b_j\rvert - \lambda/2)_+\).

Fama–MacBeth: \(\hat\gamma_t = (X_t^\top X_t)^{-1} X_t^\top r_{t+1}\), \(\bar\gamma = \tfrac{1}{T}\sum_t \hat\gamma_t\), \(\text{se} = \text{sd}(\hat\gamma_t)/\sqrt{T}\) (Newey–West if horizons overlap).

\(R^2_{oos} = 1 - \sum (r - \hat r)^2 / \sum r^2\). For one standardized predictor \(R^2 \approx \text{IC}^2\): daily ICs of 0.02–0.05 mean R² of 0.04–0.25% [Estimate].

Cost: \(O(nk^2 + k^3)\); one eigendecomposition serves the whole λ grid.

docs.title: LLMs and foundation models in quant
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • In production quant, LLMs mainly turn text (news, filings, call transcripts) into features for ordinary forecasting models, and serve as coding and research tools.
  • Lopez-Lira & Tang (JFE, 2026): GPT headline scores predict next-day returns; portfolios sorted on GPT-4 scores get the (non-tradable) same-day reaction right on about 90% of days.
  • Look-ahead leakage is the central problem: a model trained on text through year Y has read what happened next. Only post-cutoff backtests are clean.
  • Time-series foundation models (Chronos, TimesFM) forecast generic series well zero-shot; off the shelf they trail boosted trees on daily stock returns.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: forecast · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How do you turn unstructured text (and, speculatively, price series) into point-in-time forecasting features? Inputs → Outputs Timestamped text (headlines, 8-Ks and 10-Ks, transcripts) mapped to tickers → per stock-day scores (−1, 0, +1; event labels) or embedding vectors reduced to 16–128 dimensions Used by strategies NLP and LLM signals · Analyst revisions and sentiment · Earnings and event-driven · Alternative data · Fundamental quant signals Latency / compute regime Hosted LLM call 0.2–5 s per document; local embedding model ms per document on a GPU [Estimate]. Overnight batch or event-driven within seconds; never in the µs path Key parameters Pinned model version; prompt and answer format; temperature 0; news-to-session mapping (after 16:00 ET → next open); anonymization; embedding dimension after PCA Main failure modes Look-ahead from pretraining; bad timestamps; silent model updates; prompt overfitting; crowding on public models and public text; hallucinated extractions Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Text signals predate LLMs: dictionaries count negative words in filings (Loughran & McDonald 2011). An LLM reads in context ("beat estimates but cut guidance" is bad news): a better reader, not a price oracle.

Two ways to use one: prompt it ("good or bad for the stock?") for a score, or embed the text as a vector and let your own ridge or tree model learn which directions predict returns. Embedding keeps learning inside your validated, point-in-time pipeline; prompting outsources it to a model whose training data you cannot audit.

Time-series foundation models are pretrained on huge collections of series (web traffic, energy, retail) to forecast new ones zero-shot. They transfer seasonality and trend, which daily returns barely have.

flowchart LR

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Store each document with its vendor receive time and a point-in-time ticker mapping.
  2. Assign it to a session: after the 16:00 ET close (or before the open) means the next open.
  3. Backtest only on post-cutoff text; anonymize firm names for earlier periods.
  4. Score with a pinned model at temperature 0, or embed and reduce.
  5. Aggregate to stock-day, standardize, and test incremental IC over existing signals.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
# Headline scoring in the spirit of Lopez-Lira & Tang; anonymization per Glasserman & Lin.
# llm(prompt) and embed(text) stand for a pinned hosted model and a local embedding model.

def score_headline(llm, headline, company_name, anonymize=True):
    text = headline.replace(company_name, "Company X") if anonymize else headline
    prompt = ("Is this headline good, bad or unclear news for Company X's stock over the "
              "next trading day? Answer GOOD, BAD or UNKNOWN.\n" + text)
    answer = llm(prompt, temperature=0)            # store raw output, model id and version
    return {"GOOD": 1, "BAD": -1}.get(answer.strip().upper(), 0)

def daily_llm_signal(news, llm, model_cutoff):
    # news: DataFrame [ts (vendor receive time, ET), ticker, company_name, headline]
    news = news[news.ts > model_cutoff].copy()     # only post-cutoff text is a clean test
    day = news.ts.dt.normalize()                   # after the 16:00 close -> next business day
    news["trade_date"] = day.where(news.ts.dt.hour < 16, day + pd.offsets.BDay(1))
    # (simplified: pre-open news maps to the same day; exchange holidays ignored)
    news["s"] = [score_headline(llm, h, c) for h, c in zip(news.headline, news.company_name)]
    sig = news.groupby(["trade_date", "ticker"])["s"].mean().unstack()
    return sig.sub(sig.mean(axis=1), axis=0)       # demean per day -> long-short tilt

def embedding_features(docs, embed, pca_mean, pca_components):
    # alternative: text -> vector -> PCA -> features for ridge or GBDT
    E = np.vstack([embed(d) for d in docs])         # e.g. 768-4,096 dims per document
    return (E - pca_mean) @ pca_components          # 16-128 dims; mean and PCA fit on PAST docs only

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Compute cost ([Estimate]). 20,000 headlines a day × ~200 tokens (prompt plus headline) = 4 million tokens a day, ~1 billion a year. At $0.10–$3 per million input tokens (small to mid-size models; prices vary and keep falling), that is $100–$3,000 a year. Earnings calls: 3,000 firms × 4 calls × 12,000 tokens = 144 million tokens, $14–$430. Inference is cheap next to the news-feed license.

Does it survive costs? (illustrative) A $100M long-short book ($50M a side) whose longs beat its shorts by 10 bps a day earns $50M × 0.10% = $50,000 a day. Full daily turnover trades $100M; at 5 bps per dollar, costs are $50,000 a day. Net ≈ 0: a daily-turnover headline signal needs slower holding, cheaper execution, or a place in a combined forecast.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Scoring vs embeddings: scores are interpretable and need little data; embeddings capture more but need history to fit a model on [Lore].
  • Model version: pin it and store raw outputs; a silently updated hosted model rewrites the backtest.
  • Aggregation: mean or sum per stock-day, novelty filters for repeats, decay half-life of hours to days.
  • Prompt: fix it before seeing backtest results; every variant tried is a trial.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Return predictability: Lopez-Lira & Tang (2026) find ChatGPT headline scores predict next-day returns, especially in small stocks and after bad news, and that strategy returns fall as LLM adoption rises [Verified].
  • Leakage: Glasserman & Lin (2023) tested GPT-3.5 (training data to September 2021). Anonymizing firm names improved in-sample results: company knowledge distracted the model more than look-ahead helped [Verified].
  • Older baselines matter: FinBERT beat dictionaries on finance sentiment (Huang, Wang & Yang 2023); year-over-year 10-K text changes predicted returns (Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen 2020) [Verified].
  • Foundation models: Chronos (Amazon) quantizes scaled values into tokens for T5-family models of 20M–710M parameters; TimesFM (Google) is a 200M-parameter decoder trained on ~100 billion points, mostly Google Trends and Wikipedia pageviews. Both rival dataset-specific models zero-shot on general benchmarks [Verified]. On daily excess returns, zero-shot and fine-tuned versions trailed CatBoost and LightGBM; versions pre-trained from scratch on financial data came close on long-short Sharpe, gross of costs, but not on R² (Rahimikia, Ni & Wang 2025) [Verified].
  • Practice: Man Group built ManGPT, an internal portal to OpenAI's models (2023), and says its AlphaGPT agent drafts, codes and backtests signal ideas, several dozen approved for live trading after human review [Reported]. Claims that LLMs generate standalone alpha at scale are [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• IC on a post-cutoff window only, by hour since publication (news effects concentrate early [Lore]).
  • Incremental IC after controlling for earnings surprise, analyst revisions and news volume.
  • Agreement between anonymized and named scores, and across paraphrased prompts.
  • Cost-adjusted returns at realistic turnover, not gross decile spreads.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
timeline
    title Where an LLM backtest is clean
    Before training cutoff : Model may have read the outcome : Anonymize, treat as in-sample
    Training cutoff : e.g. September 2021 for GPT-3.5
    After cutoff : Clean out-of-sample window : Only period that counts as evidence
  • Pretraining look-ahead: the model may "remember" a stock's later move (look-ahead bias; point-in-time data).
  • Timestamps: publication time, vendor time and the time you could act differ by seconds to hours.
  • Prompt search on the backtest is multiple testing.
  • Crowding: public models reading public headlines produce correlated signals that decay fast (alpha decay) [Lore].
  • Hallucinated extraction: numbers "read" from a filing that aren't in it.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "What's the model's knowledge cutoff versus your backtest?" → Is any of this out of sample?
  • "We embed and let ridge decide." → Keep learning inside the validated pipeline.
  • "Same-day reaction is priced; show me tomorrow." → Only post-publication drift is tradable.
  • "The vendor updated the model and our history changed." → Pin versions, store raw outputs.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. LLMs for signals, productivity, or both? (basic)
  2. How do you handle the training-cutoff problem in backtests? (informed)
  3. Do you prompt for scores or embed and learn your own mapping? (informed)
  4. How much incremental IC does text add over earnings and revisions signals? 🔒 (sharp)
  5. How fast does the edge decay now that everyone has the same models? (sharp)

docs.text:
Math: leakage decomposition, embedding regression, cost scaling

Glasserman–Lin framing of an in-sample backtest return:

\[ R_{\text{observed}} = R_{\text{true}} + B_{\text{look-ahead}} + B_{\text{distraction}}, \qquad B_{\text{look-ahead}} \ge 0 \]

Comparing named and anonymized runs bounds the two biases.

Embedding signal: with document vectors \(e_{i,t}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) reduced by past-only PCA to \(u_{i,t}=P^\top e_{i,t}\), fit ridge \(\hat r_{i,t+1} = u_{i,t}^\top \beta\).

Annual cost ≈ documents/day × tokens/document × 250 × price per token.

docs.title: Neural nets and sequence models
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Two distinct uses: feed-forward nets (MLPs) on stock characteristics, and sequence models (CNN, LSTM, transformer) on limit-order-book data for seconds-ahead moves.
  • In Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) a three-layer net had the best monthly out-of-sample R² (0.40%). DeepLOB (Zhang, Zohren & Roberts 2019) is the reference order-book model.
  • Low signal-to-noise, nonstationary data punish flexible models; single nets vary by random seed, so seed ensembles are standard.
  • Training runs on GPUs overnight; HFT inference must fit a µs budget, so hot-path models are tiny, quantized or distilled.

Level: Deep dive · Pipeline stage: forecast · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Can a flexible function approximator find nonlinear or temporal structure (characteristic interactions, order-book dynamics) that linear models and trees miss? Inputs → Outputs Characteristics → expected return; or the last 50–100 book snapshots (10 levels × price, size × 2 sides = 40 features) → probability of an up, flat or down mid-price move Used by strategies ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Cross-sectional alpha · Equity market making · NLP and LLM signals · Alternative data Latency / compute regime Training: GPU hours to days, overnight or weekly. Inference: ms for a whole universe; in HFT roughly 1 µs or less of the tick-to-trade budget [Estimate] Key parameters 1–3 hidden layers (32-16-8 units in GKX); Adam learning rate 1e-4 to 1e-3; L1/dropout; early-stopping patience 5–20 epochs; 5–10 seeds; LOB lookback 50–100 events, horizon 10–100 events Main failure modes Seed variance; nonstationarity; leakage through normalization or labels; accuracy that doesn't survive the spread; latency overruns; opacity Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
A feed-forward net (MLP) stacks regressions with a kink (ReLU) between them, so it learns interactions ("momentum matters only in illiquid names") unprompted. A CNN reads the book's spatial layout (levels near the touch versus deeper); an LSTM or transformer remembers recent events.

Why deep learning dominates less here than in vision: a cat in a 2010 photo is still a cat in 2025, and labels are clean. Stock returns have R² below 1%, and patterns change once others trade them (nonstationarity); many parameters plus weak signal means high variance. Nets do best where data is plentiful and mechanics stable: microstructure, with millions of book events per stock per day.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Standardize inputs per date, or with trailing statistics only (order book).
  2. Split by time: train, purge gap, validation, test.
  3. Train a small penalized net; stop when validation loss stops falling.
  4. Repeat for 5–10 random seeds; average the forecasts.
  5. Standardize the averaged forecast and pass it to the combiner, or distill it into a smaller model for low-latency use.
import numpy as np
# GKX-style "NN1": one hidden layer, L1 penalty, early stopping, seed ensemble.
# Simplified: plain mini-batch SGD instead of Adam, no batch normalization.

def train_mlp(X_tr, y_tr, X_va, y_va, hidden=32, lr=1e-3, l1=1e-5,
              epochs=100, batch=10_000, patience=5, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)                     # seed drives init and batch order
    k = X_tr.shape[1]
    W1, b1 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / k), (k, hidden)), np.zeros(hidden)
    w2, b2 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(1 / hidden), hidden), 0.0
    best, best_loss, bad = None, np.inf, 0
    for ep in range(epochs):
        for idx in np.array_split(rng.permutation(len(y_tr)), max(1, len(y_tr) // batch)):
            X, y = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]
            H = np.maximum(X @ W1 + b1, 0)                # ReLU hidden layer
            err = H @ w2 + b2 - y                         # MSE gradient pieces
            gH = np.outer(err, w2) * (H > 0)
            w2 -= lr * (H.T @ err / len(y) + l1 * np.sign(w2)); b2 -= lr * err.mean()
            W1 -= lr * (X.T @ gH / len(y) + l1 * np.sign(W1)); b1 -= lr * gH.mean(0)
        pred_va = np.maximum(X_va @ W1 + b1, 0) @ w2 + b2
        loss = np.mean((pred_va - y_va) ** 2)             # time-ordered validation block
        if loss < best_loss:
            best, best_loss, bad = (W1.copy(), b1.copy(), w2.copy(), b2), loss, 0
        else:
            bad += 1
            if bad >= patience:                           # early stopping
                break
    W1, b1, w2, b2 = best
    return lambda X: np.maximum(X @ W1 + b1, 0) @ w2 + b2

def seed_ensemble(X_tr, y_tr, X_va, y_va, X_live, n_seeds=10):
    # single nets disagree at low SNR; averaging seeds removes the seed-specific part
    preds = [train_mlp(X_tr, y_tr, X_va, y_va, seed=s)(X_live) for s in range(n_seeds)]
    p = np.mean(preds, axis=0)
    return (p - p.mean()) / p.std()                       # cross-sectional z-score for the combiner

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Seed ensembling (illustrative). Each seed's forecast = common signal + seed-specific noise. Single-seed IC = 0.020; correlation between seeds' forecasts ρ = 0.5. Averaging M seeds divides the noise variance by M:

IC_ens = IC × √(1 / (ρ + (1 − ρ)/M)) = 0.020 × √(1 / (0.5 + 0.05)) = 0.020 × 1.35 = 0.027 for M = 10.

The infinite-seed ceiling is 0.020 × √2 = 0.028. With breadth and costs fixed, 35% more IC is roughly 35% more Sharpe.

HFT latency budget ([Estimate]). An MLP with 40 inputs, layers of 64 and 32, and one output needs 40 × 64 + 64 × 32 + 32 = 4,640 multiply-adds. At ~5 billion useful multiply-adds per second on one core, that is ≈ 0.9 µs. A CNN-LSTM over 100 snapshots × 40 features needs ~3 million, ≈ 600 µs: fine for a seconds-horizon signal, far too slow for quoting. A GPU adds microseconds of transfer and launch overhead. Hence tiny or distilled models on CPU, or fixed-point nets on FPGAs.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Depth and width: GKX used a pyramid (32, 16, 8, ...); three layers was best [Verified]. Add depth only if validation IC rises across seeds.
  • Regularization: GKX used an L1 weight penalty, early stopping, batch normalization and seed ensembles [Verified]; dropout is a common alternative.
  • Seeds: 5–10; seed-to-seed forecast correlation below ~0.5 means mostly noise [Lore].
  • LOB labels: smooth future mid-prices over k events and use a threshold to define "flat", or the model learns bid-ask bounce.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Cross-sectional MLPs: in GKX 2020, monthly stock-level R² rose from 0.33% (one layer) to 0.40% (three), against 0.16% for OLS-3; the value-weighted long-short decile Sharpe was 1.35 gross, 1987–2016 [Verified].
  • Order books: DeepLOB (convolutions, an Inception module, an LSTM) beat earlier models on the FI-2010 benchmark and a year of London Stock Exchange data, and transferred to unseen instruments [Verified]. Sirignano & Cont (2019) found a "universal" model pooled across many US stocks beat stock-specific ones [Verified]. Both report accuracy, not P&L after costs.
  • Autoencoder factor models: Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2021) let betas be a neural function of characteristics, with latent factors and a no-arbitrage restriction, and report much smaller out-of-sample pricing errors than leading factor models [Verified].
  • Practice: market makers train sizable nets on GPU clusters (XTX Markets says it has over 25,000 GPUs [Reported]) but run small, distilled versions in the latency-critical path [Lore]; mid-frequency books use nets as one ensemble input [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• The seed-ensemble IC beats GBDT and ridge on identical purged folds.
  • For order-book models, convert accuracy into markouts net of spread and fees.
  • IC by month since training shows decay and sets the retrain schedule.
  • p99 inference latency on production hardware stays inside budget.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Leakage through normalization: z-scoring with statistics that include the test window.
  • Overlapping or smoothed labels that peek ahead and inflate accuracy (time-series CV).
  • Architecture search: fifty architectures on one test set is multiple testing.
  • Regime breaks: a net trained in calm markets has never seen March 2020 (regime detection).
  • Opacity: in a drawdown it is hard to tell a broken model from bad luck.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Single-seed results are anecdotes." → Report the seed ensemble and the spread across seeds.
  • "Seventy percent accuracy on mid moves, minus the spread, is zero." → Direction accuracy is not edge after costs.
  • "We distill the big model into something that fits in a microsecond." → Train large offline, deploy small.
  • "Three layers was plenty." → Deeper nets add variance at this signal-to-noise ratio.
  • "Retrain weekly; it decays." → Nonstationarity makes stale weights lose edge.

  2. How many seeds do you average, and how correlated are they? (informed)
  3. How do you normalize order-book inputs without leaking the future? (informed)
  4. How do you turn classification accuracy into expected P&L after costs? (sharp)
  5. What runs in the hot path versus offline, and what latency does the model get? 🔒 (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: MLP, autoencoder asset pricing, attention cost

MLP: \(h^{(l)} = \text{ReLU}(W^{(l)} h^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)})\), \(\hat r = w^\top h^{(L)}\), loss \(\sum (r-\hat r)^2 + \lambda \lVert W\rVert_1\).

Conditional autoencoder (GKX 2021):

\[ r_{i,t} = \beta(z_{i,t-1})^\top f_t + \varepsilon_{i,t}, \qquad f_t = W\, (Z_{t-1}^\top Z_{t-1})^{-1} Z_{t-1}^\top r_t \]

Betas come from a net on characteristics; factors are linear combinations of characteristic-managed portfolios.

Self-attention over \(L\) events of width \(d\) costs \(O(L^2 d)\), one reason lookbacks stay short when latency binds.

docs.title: Regime detection
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A regime is a persistent market state, such as calm or stressed. Detection estimates each day the probability of each state, using only data available that day.
  • The toolkit: Markov-switching models and Gaussian hidden Markov models, change-point detectors, simple volatility filters and clustering.
  • Firms mostly use regimes defensively, to scale risk or gate strategies, rarely to forecast returns.
  • The trap is hindsight: smoothed probabilities and official recession dates use future data. Evidence that regime timing pays is contested.

Level: Deep dive · Pipeline stage: forecast · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which state is the market in now, and did it just change? Inputs → Outputs returns, realized vol, VIX, credit spreads → state probabilities, change alarms, a risk multiplier or on/off flag Used by strategies Momentum · Factor timing and crowding · Trend following · Volatility risk premium · Carry · Factor-residual mean reversion Latency / compute regime daily batch; a filter update takes microseconds, a refit seconds [Estimate] Key parameters 2–3 states; daily stay probability 0.95–0.99 (average spells of 20–100 days); vol lookback 20–63 days; VIX trigger 25–30; hysteresis band Main failure modes hindsight labels; detection lag; whipsaw; states changing meaning on refit; too many states Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: A credit analyst underwrites the same balance sheet differently in a boom and a bust. Markets are similar, and wild days cluster. From 1990 to November 2026 the VIX closed above 30 on 7.9% of days, and after such a close it stayed above 30 the next day 87% of the time (computed from FRED data) [Verified]. A regime model turns that persistence into a probability. The aim is not to call the crash but to notice quickly that the world changed, and resize.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
A two-state Gaussian HMM, filtered with the forward algorithm (Hamilton's filter):

  1. Model. A hidden state, calm or stressed, sets the mean and volatility of a normal daily return. A transition matrix with a large diagonal makes states persistent.
  2. Fit by expectation-maximization on past data only, walk-forward (V1).
  3. Predict: yesterday's probabilities times the transition matrix give today's prior.
  4. Update: multiply by the likelihood of today's return in each state, then normalize.
  5. Act: map the filtered probability, with hysteresis, to tomorrow's risk multiplier (P7).

The simplest alternative skips the model: scale by target vol ÷ 20-day realized vol, or halve risk above VIX 30.

import numpy as np

def normal_pdf(x, mu, sd):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sd) ** 2) / (sd * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))

def hmm_filter_step(p_prev, r_t, P, mu, sd):
    """One forward-algorithm step of a 2-state Gaussian HMM (state 0 calm, 1 stressed).
    p_prev: P(state | returns to t-1); P[i, j] = P(state j today | state i yesterday)."""
    prior = P.T @ p_prev                       # predict: where could we be today?
    post = prior * normal_pdf(r_t, mu, sd)     # update: how likely is today's return per state?
    return post / post.sum()                   # filtered: uses data up to t only

def regime_risk_multiplier(returns, P, mu, sd, enter=0.7, exit=0.3,
                           target_vol=10.0, max_mult=1.5, stressed_cut=0.5):
    """Tomorrow's risk multiplier per day. Returns in % per day, vols in % per year.
    P, mu, sd must be fit on data BEFORE the first return here (walk-forward)."""
    p, stressed, out = np.array([0.95, 0.05]), False, []
    for r in returns:                          # today's close-to-close return
        p = hmm_filter_step(p, r, P, mu, sd)
        if not stressed and p[1] > enter:      # hysteresis: switching needs strong evidence
            stressed = True
        elif stressed and p[1] < exit:
            stressed = False
        p_next = P.T @ p                       # state probabilities for tomorrow
        var = p_next @ (sd**2 + mu**2) - (p_next @ mu) ** 2   # variance of the mixture
        mult = min(max_mult, target_vol / (np.sqrt(var) * np.sqrt(252)))
        if stressed:
            mult *= stressed_cut               # optional gate on top of vol scaling
        out.append((p[1], stressed, mult))     # applied to TOMORROW's positions
    return out

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: calm days have mean +0.05% and volatility 0.7%; stressed days −0.10% and 2.0%. Stay probabilities 0.98 and 0.95 give average spells of 50 and 20 days and a long-run stressed share of 0.02 ÷ 0.07 = 29%. Start at P(stressed) = 0.05.

One −3.0% day.

  • Prior stressed = 0.95 × 0.02 + 0.05 × 0.95 = 0.0665; calm = 0.9335.
  • Likelihoods: calm z = (−3.0 − 0.05) ÷ 0.7 = −4.36, density 0.000043; stressed z = (−3.0 + 0.10) ÷ 2.0 = −1.45, density 0.0697.
  • Posterior stressed = (0.0665 × 0.0697) ÷ (0.0665 × 0.0697 + 0.9335 × 0.000043) = 0.00464 ÷ 0.00468 = 0.991.

Tomorrow's mixture volatility jumps from 13.5% to 30.9% a year, so with a 10% target the multiplier falls from 0.74 to 0.32; the gate halves it to 0.16.

Three −1.5% days instead. P(stressed) goes 0.18, 0.43, 0.70: a slow grind takes three days just to approach the 0.7 trigger; one shock flips the model at once.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• States: two is standard; a third crash state rests on few observations. Choose by out-of-sample likelihood [Lore].
  • Persistence: stay probability p means spells of 1 ÷ (1 − p) days on average; higher p gives fewer whipsaws but slower detection.
  • Inputs: realized vol, the VIX or credit spreads sharpen a returns-only model [Lore].
  • Thresholds: since 1990 the VIX closed above 25 on 17% of days [Verified]; realized-vol filters often trigger at the 80th–90th percentile [Lore].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Origins: Hamilton (1989) modeled US output growth as switching between two unobserved states, with the filter above [Verified]; Hamilton & Susmel (1994) added switching ARCH [Verified]; Ang & Bekaert (2002) found a high-volatility, high-correlation bear regime in international equities [Verified].
  • Change points: CUSUM (Page 1954) accumulates evidence of a shift [Verified]; Adams & MacKay's (2007) Bayesian online change-point detection tracks a posterior over the time since the last break [Verified]. Both flag one-off breaks, not recurring states (L2).
  • Clustering: Two Sigma fit a Gaussian mixture to 17 factors and named four conditions: Crisis, Steady State, Inflation and Walking on Ice [Verified].
  • Practice: HMMs fill allocation research (Kritzman, Page & Turkington 2012; Nystrup et al. 2015) [Verified]; production mostly uses plain volatility targeting [Lore].
  • Evidence for: cutting exposure when volatility is high raised Sharpe ratios for the market and many factors (Moreira & Muir 2017) [Verified]. Vol targeting raised Sharpe for equities and credit, not bonds, currencies or commodities, and thinned left tails (Harvey et al. 2018) [Verified]. Momentum crashes cluster in panic states; a dynamic version roughly doubled momentum's Sharpe (Daniel & Moskowitz 2016) [Verified].
  • Evidence against: across 103 equity strategies, managed versions had the higher Sharpe in only 53 cases, and real-time combinations of managed and original earned lower certainty-equivalent returns than the original alone in 72 (Cederburg et al. 2020) [Verified]. Both sides have strong evidence; the debate is open.

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Walk-forward backtests on filtered probabilities only, against inverse 20-day realized vol. If the model does not beat it after costs, ship the simple one [Lore].
  • Detection delay at known breaks versus false alarms and switches per year.
  • After a refit, "stressed" still means stressed.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Hindsight labels. Smoothed probabilities use future returns. Official dates are worse: the NBER dated the December 2007 peak on 1 December 2008 and the June 2009 trough on 20 September 2010 [Verified].
  • Lag. Filters confirm stress after the first big loss and exit after the rebound, when momentum crashes.
  • Whipsaw near thresholds becomes turnover.
  • Overfitting: extra states and features fit history (V4).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're in the high-vol regime; risk is at 60%." → the multiplier is 0.6.
  • "That chart is smoothed, not filtered." → it used future data.
  • "The HMM flipped on one day." → one large return dominated.
  • "Vol targeting did the work; the HMM added nothing." → it failed the benchmark test.
  • "Momentum's in a panic state." → high volatility after a fall; crash risk on the rebound.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: When regimes shift, do you change risk or change the model?
  2. Informed: Are backtests run on filtered or smoothed probabilities?
  3. Informed: Does the regime model beat inverse-vol scaling after costs?
  4. Sharp: How many days did your detector lag in March 2020, and what did that cost? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Forward filter, durations and change-point recursion

Forward recursion with transition matrix \(P\) and state densities \(f_j\):

\[ \alpha_t(j) = \Big[\sum_i \hat p_{t-1}(i)\, P_{ij}\Big] f_j(r_t), \qquad \hat p_t(j) = \frac{\alpha_t(j)}{\sum_k \alpha_t(k)}. \]

The long-run share of state 1 is \(P_{01}/(P_{01}+P_{10})\). Smoothed probabilities \(P(s_t \mid r_{1:T})\) add a backward pass over future data. Online change-point detection tracks run length \(\ell_t\), which grows by one with probability \(1-H\) or resets to 0.

docs.title: Tree ensembles
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM, XGBoost) are the default nonlinear model for tabular stock data, finding thresholds and interactions automatically.
  • In Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020), trees and neural nets reached monthly out-of-sample R² of 0.33–0.40% versus 0.16% for a three-characteristic OLS; the gains came from nonlinear interactions.
  • Winning settings are deliberately weak: shallow trees, learning rates of 0.01–0.05, big leaves, subsampling, early stopping on time-ordered validation.
  • Gain-based importance misleads; SHAP still splits credit among substitutes. Target engineering (residualized, ranked returns) often matters more than hyperparameters.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: forecast · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) What is each stock's expected (residual) return given many features, allowing nonlinear effects and interactions? Inputs → Outputs Panel of 20–500 ranked features per stock-date and a forward-return target → 200–5,000 small trees; per-stock scores Used by strategies ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Cross-sectional alpha · Alternative data · Fundamental quant signals · Earnings and event-driven · Intraday patterns Latency / compute regime Overnight batch: minutes on a multi-core CPU for ~5M rows × 100 features [Estimate]. Inference: 1,000 trees × depth 6 ≈ 6,000 comparisons, µs per stock [Estimate] Key parameters num_leaves 15–63 (depth 3–6); learning rate 0.01–0.05; 300–3,000 rounds via early stopping (patience 100–200); min_data_in_leaf 500–5,000; feature and bagging fraction 0.5–0.8; L2 1–100 Main failure modes Fitting noise or leaky features; early stopping on a random split; misread importances; no extrapolation; jumpy forecasts raising turnover Lab Lab 12

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
A decision tree asks yes/no questions ("5-day return below −2%? turnover in the top third?") and outputs the average return of the bucket it lands in. A depth-2 tree is a two-way interaction that a linear model gets only from a hand-crafted product term. One deep tree memorizes noise; ensembles fix that:

  • Random forest: average hundreds of trees fit to bootstrap samples and random feature subsets; averaging cuts variance.
  • Gradient boosting: add small trees one at a time, each fit to what the ensemble still gets wrong, scaled down by a learning rate. When R² is a fraction of a percent, boosting must be throttled hard and stopped early, before it fits noise.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Rank features per date so a split means the same thing in 1999 and 2025.
  2. Target: residual forward return, ranked per date (or clipped, with Huber loss).
  3. Split by time: train, a purge gap of one label horizon, 6–12 months of validation.
  4. Boost: fit a small tree to residuals on subsampled rows and columns, add it times the learning rate; stop after patience rounds without validation improvement.
  5. Refit on train plus validation, average 3–10 seeds, predict.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
# Boosting for L2 loss written out to show the mechanics; production uses LightGBM/XGBoost.
# Lab 12 fits LightGBM (sklearn fallback) with deliberately loose settings (31 leaves,
# 50 rows per leaf, lr 0.05, 150 rounds, no early stopping) to show overfitting.
# fit_tree(X, r, max_depth, min_leaf, lam): any CART regressor whose leaf value is
#   sum(residuals in leaf) / (n_leaf + lam)   <- ridge-like shrinkage of each leaf mean

def rank_target(ret, dates):               # Lab 12 core function (same logic)
    # per-date percentile rank in [-0.5, 0.5]: removes outliers and the day's market move
    g = pd.Series(ret).groupby(dates)
    return ((g.rank() - 1) / (g.transform("count") - 1) - 0.5).to_numpy()

def boost(X_tr, y_tr, X_va, y_va, lr=0.02, n_rounds=5000, patience=200,
          max_depth=5, min_leaf=2000, lam=10.0, row_frac=0.7, col_frac=0.7, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pred_tr, pred_va = np.zeros(len(y_tr)), np.zeros(len(y_va))
    trees, best, best_loss, since_best = [], 0, np.inf, 0
    for m in range(n_rounds):
        rows = rng.random(len(y_tr)) < row_frac                   # bagging
        cols = rng.choice(X_tr.shape[1], int(col_frac * X_tr.shape[1]), replace=False)
        resid = y_tr - pred_tr                                    # negative gradient of L2 loss
        tree = fit_tree(X_tr[rows][:, cols], resid[rows], max_depth, min_leaf, lam)
        pred_tr += lr * tree.predict(X_tr[:, cols])               # shrink every step by lr
        pred_va += lr * tree.predict(X_va[:, cols])
        trees.append((tree, cols))
        loss = np.mean((y_va - pred_va) ** 2)                     # or minus validation rank IC
        if loss < best_loss:
            best, best_loss, since_best = m + 1, loss, 0
        else:
            since_best += 1
        if since_best >= patience:                                # early stopping
            break
    return trees[:best]

def predict(trees, X, lr=0.02):
    return lr * sum(t.predict(X[:, c]) for t, c in trees)

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative mean next-day residual returns (bps) in four equal-sized buckets:

High turnover Low turnover 5-day loser +6 +1 5-day winner −5 −1

Linear fit (rev = +1 for losers, liq = +1 for high turnover, no interaction): intercept = (6 + 1 − 5 − 1)/4 = 0.25; rev slope = (6 + 1 + 5 + 1)/4 = 3.25; liq slope = (6 − 1 − 5 + 1)/4 = 0.25. Predictions +3.75, +3.25, −2.75, −3.25: every bucket is off by 2.25 bps, the missing interaction (6 − 1 + 5 − 1)/4.

Depth-2 tree: split on rev, then liq; leaves are exactly +6, +1, −5, −1. The liquid-name spread is 11 bps, not 6.5.

Boosting at learning rate 0.1 on noise-free data reaches 1 − 0.9ᵐ of the truth after m rounds: 65% after 10, 88% after 20. With noisy data, validation loss stops improving much earlier, and early stopping halts there.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Depth: 3–6 (up to 6-way interactions); deeper fits noise [Lore].
  • Learning rate × rounds: halve the rate, double the rounds. Stopping before ~50 rounds at 0.02 means weak signal [Lore].
  • min_data_in_leaf: the key regularizer; each leaf should average thousands of returns [Lore].
  • Subsampling: 0.5–0.8 of rows and features decorrelates trees; sampling whole dates respects cross-sectional correlation.
  • Monotone constraints (LightGBM, XGBoost) encode economic priors on a feature's direction.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Foundations: Breiman (2001) and Friedman (2001); XGBoost added a regularized second-order objective, LightGBM histogram binning and leaf-wise growth [Verified].
  • Academic evidence: in GKX 2020 (US stocks 1957–2016, tested 1987–2016, 94 characteristics), random forests and boosted trees with Huber loss sat near the top with neural nets, and all methods agreed on momentum, liquidity and volatility as the dominant predictors [Verified]. Neural-net long-short deciles reached a value-weighted Sharpe of 1.35 gross over 1987–2016, against 0.61 for a three-characteristic OLS [Verified].
  • Recent benchmark: on daily excess returns, CatBoost and LightGBM beat off-the-shelf time-series foundation models; versions pre-trained on financial data narrowed the gap (Rahimikia, Ni & Wang 2025, gross of costs) [Verified]; see LLMs and foundation models.
  • Practice: boosted trees are common in short-horizon books with hundreds of features, usually blended with linear and neural models [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Out-of-sample rank IC beats a ridge baseline on identical purged folds, net of added turnover.
  • Null test: retrain on per-date shuffled targets. IC should collapse to ~0; if not, a feature leaks.
  • IC by size bucket: microcap-only gains won't survive costs.
  • SHAP dependence plots look economically sane. In Lab 12, loose GBDT topped shuffled CV but trailed ridge under purged CV (synthetic lab result).

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Importance illusions: gain and split counts favor high-cardinality, noisy features (Strobl et al. 2007); substitutes split credit, so each looks unimportant while the pair matters (López de Prado 2018, ch. 8). Cluster correlated features first. SHAP measures attribution, not P&L.
  • Raw-return targets: squared error is dominated by volatile stocks, so splits go to predicting volatility. Rank the target.
  • Leaky or nonstationary features: IDs, dates, raw prices.
  • No extrapolation: beyond the training range (March 2020 volatility), trees predict a constant.
  • Early stopping on a random split leaks the future (time-series CV).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Bump min leaf to 5k; it's fitting noise." → Force each leaf to average more returns.
  • "It stopped at round 40." → Too little signal or too high a learning rate.
  • "Turnover's top SHAP feature, but it's a substitute for spread." → Correlated features share attribution.
  • "Ranked target, otherwise it's a vol model." → Raw squared error over-weights volatile names.
  • "Blend it with the ridge, don't replace it." → Trees add interactions; linear adds stability.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Trees or linear for your main forecast, and why? (basic)
  2. Where does your early-stopping block sit relative to the test period? (informed)
  3. What target do you train on: raw, residual, ranked? (informed)
  4. How much of the tree model's edge over ridge survives costs? 🔒 (sharp)
  5. How do you stop forecasts jumping between retrains? (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: boosting update, XGBoost split gain, SHAP

Boosting: \(F_m = F_{m-1} + \nu h_m\). XGBoost leaf weight and split gain (gradient sums \(G\), Hessian sums \(H\)):

\[ w^* = -\frac{G}{H+\lambda}, \qquad \text{Gain} = \tfrac12\Big[\tfrac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda} + \tfrac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda} - \tfrac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}\Big] - \gamma \]

For L2 loss \(H\) equals the leaf count, so \(w^*\) is the residual sum over \((n+\lambda)\): a ridge-shrunk mean.

SHAP values are Shapley values (average marginal contribution over feature subsets), exact in polynomial time for trees.

docs.title: Backtest pitfalls
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Nearly every backtest bias pushes the same way: up. The audit asks by how much, and why.
  • Data and timing errors invent returns; cost, borrow and capacity errors inflate real ones; statistical errors inflate confidence.
  • Predictor returns fall 26% out of sample and 58% after publication (McLean & Pontiff 2016). Across 888 Quantopian algorithms, backtest Sharpe explained under 2.5% of out-of-sample Sharpe.
  • Harvey & Liu (2015) haircut Sharpe ratios for the number of strategies tried. The haircut is nonlinear: a flat 50% is too lenient for marginal Sharpe ratios and too harsh for strong ones (table below).

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: validation · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Why does this backtest look better than live trading will be, and by how much? Inputs → Outputs Backtest P&L, weights, trade log, data lineage, a log of variants tried → flags with severity, haircut Sharpe, go/no-go for paper trading Used by strategies Earnings and events · Fundamental signals · Cross-sectional alpha · Momentum · Value, quality, low vol · Factor investing · Reversal · Alternative data · ML short-horizon alpha · Factor timing Latency / compute regime Offline audit: seconds to minutes per strategy, before capital and after every material change Key parameters Honest trial count N; t-hurdle 3.0; cost stress 2×; +1 day lag stress; position cap 1–5% of ADV; Newey–West lags = horizon − 1 Main failure modes Uncounted trials; box-ticking; interacting biases; fixing bugs only when results disappoint Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
A backtest is a model of the past built by someone who knows how it ended. Like management's adjusted EBITDA, each adjustment is defensible alone and all point the same way; diligence reverses them one at a time.

Pitfall How it inflates Fix Look-ahead restated, period-end-dated or same-bar data as-of joins (D1) Survivorship drops dead stocks and their final losses full history plus delisting returns Untradable close signal and fill on one print; bid-ask bounce next bar, or MOC before cutoff Costs flat bps ignore impact spread + fees + impact (P5) Short constraints free borrow, always locatable borrow fees, locate data Capacity profit sits in untradably small names ADV caps, impact at target AUM Data snooping best of many variants count trials, haircut (V4) Overlapping returns daily-sampled h-day returns treated as independent Newey–West errors Regime dependence one crisis carries the P&L subperiod Sharpe Parameter p-hacking lookbacks tuned to the sample choose plateaus, not peaks

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Lineage: point-in-time data, delisting returns, pinned vintage.
  2. Timing: compare same-day and forward IC; rerun with one extra day of lag.
  3. Costs: break-even cost per unit turnover; rerun at 2× costs.
  4. Shorts: hard-to-borrow share and fees.
  5. Capacity: position sizes as % of ADV at target AUM.
  6. Regimes: P&L by year; concentration in the best period.
  7. Statistics: overlap-corrected t-stats, then a multiple-testing haircut with an honest trial count.
  8. Decide: unresolved red flags block paper trading.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def sanity_check(bt, n_trials, horizon=5, cost_bps=10.0, aum=5e8, ann=252):
    """bt: backtester output (V2), daily rows; frames are [date x stock].
    norm_sf / norm_isf: standard normal tail and its inverse (e.g. scipy.stats.norm)."""
    flags = []
    sig, w, pnl_g, pnl_n = bt["signal"], bt["weights"], bt["pnl_gross"], bt["pnl_net"]
    ic = sig.corrwith(bt["fwd_ret_h"], axis=1, method="spearman")    # h-day forward
    ic_now = sig.corrwith(bt["ret_same_day"], axis=1, method="spearman").mean()
    if abs(ic_now) > 2 * abs(ic.mean()):                    # 1 look-ahead
        flags.append(("look-ahead?", f"same-day IC {ic_now:.3f} vs fwd {ic.mean():.3f}"))
    if bt["n_delisted_names_held"] == 0:                    # 2 survivorship
        flags.append(("survivorship?", "never held a stock that later delisted"))
    turnover = w.diff().abs().sum(axis=1).mean()            # 3 costs (one-way, daily)
    breakeven = 1e4 * pnl_g.mean() / turnover
    if breakeven < 2 * cost_bps:
        flags.append(("cost-fragile", f"break-even {breakeven:.1f} bps"))
    shorts = w.clip(upper=0).abs()                          # 4 borrow (fee > 5%/yr)
    htb = (shorts[bt["borrow_fee"] > 0.05].sum(axis=1) / shorts.sum(axis=1)).mean()
    if htb > 0.05:
        flags.append(("borrow", f"{htb:.0%} of the short book is hard to borrow"))
    part = (w.abs() * aum / bt["adv_usd"]).max(axis=1).quantile(0.95)   # 5 capacity
    if part > 0.05:
        flags.append(("capacity", f"largest positions reach {part:.0%} of ADV"))
    yearly = pnl_n.groupby(pnl_n.index.year).sum()          # 6 regime dependence
    if yearly.max() > 0.5 * yearly.sum():
        flags.append(("regime", "one year carries over half of the P&L"))
    t_ic = ic.mean() / ic.std() * np.sqrt(len(ic)) / np.sqrt(horizon)  # 7 overlap
    if t_ic < 3.0:
        flags.append(("weak IC", f"overlap-adjusted t = {t_ic:.1f}"))
    sr, years = pnl_n.mean() / pnl_n.std() * np.sqrt(ann), len(pnl_n) / ann
    p_multi = min(1.0, n_trials * 2 * norm_sf(abs(sr) * np.sqrt(years)))   # 8 Bonferroni
    sr_hc = norm_isf(p_multi / 2) / np.sqrt(years) if p_multi < 1 else 0.0
    flags.append(("haircut", f"Sharpe {sr:.2f} -> {sr_hc:.2f} after {n_trials} trials"))
    return flags

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Haircut by hand (Bonferroni, the bluntest of Harvey & Liu's three adjustments), 10 years of data:

Backtest Sharpe t = SR·√10 Trials N p × N Haircut t Haircut Sharpe Haircut 1.0 3.16 10 0.016 2.42 0.76 24% 1.0 3.16 100 0.157 1.42 0.45 55% 0.4 1.26 10 1.0 (capped) 0 0 100% 2.0 6.32 100 ≈ 0 5.57 1.76 12%

Harvey & Liu's own example: Sharpe 1.0 over 120 months, 100 tests and 0.4 average correlation becomes 0.44 under their BHY method, a 52% haircut from the autocorrelation-corrected 0.91 [Verified].

Overlap (illustrative): daily IC on 21-day forward returns with a naive t of 6.0 is really about 6.0 / √21 ≈ 1.3.

Bid-ask bounce (illustrative): a small cap with a 20 bp spread closes at the bid, looking 10 bps weak; a next close at mid gives a reversal backtest +10 bps of fake alpha [Estimate].

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• N trials: count every variant, abandoned ones included. Harvey, Liu & Zhu counted at least 316 published factors and set a t-hurdle of 3.0 [Verified].
  • Cost stress: with cost-aware design, most anomalies under 50% monthly turnover survive costs; few above do (Novy-Marx & Velikov 2016) [Verified].
  • Lag stress: add one day; a large drop means the edge lives in timing you may not get.
  • Capacity cap: positions at about 1–5% of ADV at target AUM [Lore].
  • Overlap: autocorrelation-robust errors with h − 1 lags for h-period returns (Hansen & Hodrick 1980; Newey & West 1987) [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Decay: McLean & Pontiff (2016): 97 predictors, 26% lower out of sample, 58% lower post-publication [Verified].
  • Replication: Hou, Xue & Zhang (2020): with microcaps controlled, 65% of 452 anomalies fail t ≥ 1.96, and 82% fail t ≥ 2.78 [Verified].
  • Survivorship: correcting Nasdaq delisting returns removes any evidence of a Nasdaq size effect (Shumway & Warther 1999) [Verified].
  • Backtests vs live: across 888 Quantopian algorithms, backtest Sharpe had R² < 0.025 for out-of-sample Sharpe, and more backtesting meant a bigger gap (Wiecki et al. 2016) [Verified].
  • Practice: a flat 50% haircut is a common rule of thumb (Harvey & Liu) [Verified]. Allocators typically want months of paper or small-capital live trading first [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
The audit works when live results land inside the backtest's confidence band. Checklist:

  • Point-in-time data, delisting returns, pinned vintage
  • Fill price attainable after the signal time
  • Profitable at 2× modeled costs at target AUM
  • Borrow fees and hard-to-borrow share modeled
  • Largest positions within the ADV cap
  • Positive in most years; no year above half the P&L
  • Overlap-corrected t ≥ 3 and haircut Sharpe reported with honest N
  • Parameters on a plateau

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Asymmetric debugging: bugs get hunted when results disappoint, so surviving bugs flatter [Lore].
  • Interacting biases: survivorship, microcaps and light costs compound in the same small, illiquid names.
  • The audit is a degree of freedom too: relax a flag, rerun, repeat.
  • Pre-publication samples: backtests of published factors include years before the crowd arrived (factor timing).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "What's the haircut Sharpe?" → Sharpe after adjusting for strategies tried.
  • "How many backtests did it take?" → The honest trial count.
  • "Break-even cost?" → Cost per unit turnover that zeroes the alpha.
  • "Is it all 2008?" → Is P&L concentrated in one regime?
  • "That's bounce, not reversal." → Profit comes from closing prints at bid or ask.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. How do you count trials across a research team? (basic)
  2. What fill price does your daily backtest assume? (informed)
  3. How much of the short-side P&L is in hard-to-borrow names? (informed)
  4. What's your typical backtest-to-live Sharpe ratio? 🔒 (sharp)
  5. Which flag most often kills a strategy at your shop? 🔒 (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: haircut Sharpe, overlap inflation, Newey–West

With \(T\) years, \(t = \widehat{SR}\sqrt{T}\), two-sided \(p_S = 2\,\Phi(-|t|)\). Bonferroni: \(p_M = \min(N p_S, 1)\); Holm and BHY are less severe. Haircut Sharpe and haircut:

\[ \widehat{SR}_{hc} = \frac{\Phi^{-1}(1 - p_M/2)}{\sqrt{T}}, \qquad hc = 1 - \widehat{SR}_{hc}/\widehat{SR} \]

Overlap: for i.i.d. daily returns, \(h\)-day sums sampled daily make the naive standard error too small by about \(\sqrt{h}\).

Newey–West with \(L = h-1\) lags and autocovariances \(\hat\gamma_j\):

\[ \hat\sigma^2_{NW} = \hat\gamma_0 + 2\sum_{j=1}^{L}\Big(1 - \frac{j}{L+1}\Big)\hat\gamma_j \]

docs.title: Backtesting engines
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A backtester simulates a P&L: it replays history, lets the strategy decide on past data only, models fills and keeps the books.
  • Vectorized engines run decades in seconds and suit daily cross-sectional research. Event-driven engines process one event at a time on production's code path; intraday and passive strategies need them.
  • Realism lives in the fill and cost model: spread, fees and rebates, impact, partial fills, queue position, latency, borrow, financing and corporate actions.
  • HFT uses market-replay simulators that rebuild the book and estimate queue position. Replay cannot show others reacting to you; live trading is the final test.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: validation · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) What would this strategy's P&L, costs and risk have been, trading as production would, on data it could have seen? Inputs → Outputs PIT data, strategy code, fill and cost model, borrow and financing rates → fill log, positions, daily P&L split into alpha, costs and financing Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Short-term reversal · Factor-residual reversion · Pairs trading · ML short-horizon alpha · Intraday patterns · Equity market making · Trend following Latency / compute regime Vectorized daily, 3,000 stocks × 20 years: seconds [Estimate]. Event-driven daily: minutes. Full-depth tick replay: hours per stock-year [Estimate] Key parameters Fill price (next open, VWAP, MOC); latency (1 bar daily; 10 µs–5 ms HFT); participation cap 5–20% of volume; cost model (half-spread + fees + k·σ·√(Q/ADV)); borrow 0.25% to 50%+ a year Main failure modes Unattainable fill prices; free passive fills; zero latency; infinite liquidity; no borrow; divergent research code; irreproducible runs Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Think of a backtester as a sub-ledger with a simulated counterparty. The strategy sends orders; an exchange model decides what fills, when and at what price; the ledger books cash, positions, fees, dividends, borrow and interest. Like a pro-forma P&L, it is only as good as its assumptions, and the ones that matter most sit in the fill model.

Vectorized Event-driven Unit of work whole weight matrix × return matrix one bar, quote, trade or fill at a time Speed seconds for decades 10–1,000× slower [Estimate] Fits daily and weekly cross-sectional books, parameter sweeps intraday, limit orders, path-dependent rules Look-ahead risk high: one wrong shift lower: data arrives in order
