docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Merge bars or ticks, corporate actions and financing into one time-ordered event stream.
  2. Apply corporate actions to positions before trading. Shorts pay dividends.
  3. Let the simulated exchange fill earlier orders against the new event. Respect latency, the participation cap and, for passive orders, queue position.
  4. Charge costs on each fill: half-spread, fees or rebates, impact.
  5. Show the event to the strategy, which sees only the past, and queue its new orders.
  6. Accrue borrow on shorts and interest on cash, mark to market and log.
import numpy as np

class CostModel:
    """Per-fill cost in $: half-spread + fees + square-root impact (see P5).
    Defaults are illustrative; firms calibrate k and fees on their own fills (E6)."""
    def __init__(self, fee_per_share=0.003, k=0.7, max_part=0.10, borrow_rate=0.003):
        self.fee, self.k, self.max_part, self.borrow = fee_per_share, k, max_part, borrow_rate

    def cost(self, qty, px, spread, sigma, adv):
        q = abs(qty)
        impact = self.k * sigma * np.sqrt(q / adv) * q * px      # square-root law
        return 0.5 * spread * q + self.fee * q + impact

def run_backtest(bars, strategy, cm, cash=1e7, latency_bars=1):
    """bars: time-ordered, one per (day t, sym): open, close, volume, adv, spread,
    sigma, split, div. An order sent on bar t fills no earlier than t + latency_bars."""
    pos, pending, ledger = {}, [], []
    for b in bars:
        q = pos.get(b.sym, 0.0) * b.split                    # corporate actions first
        cash += q * b.div                                    # shorts pay the dividend
        pos[b.sym] = q
        still = []
        for (t0, sym, qty) in pending:                       # the simulated exchange
            if sym != b.sym or b.t < t0 + latency_bars:
                still.append((t0, sym, qty))
                continue
            fill = np.sign(qty) * min(abs(qty), cm.max_part * b.volume)  # partial fill
            c = cm.cost(fill, b.open, b.spread, b.sigma, b.adv)
            cash -= fill * b.open + c                        # a LATER bar's open
            pos[sym] += fill
            ledger.append((b.t, sym, fill, b.open, c))
            if qty != fill:
                still.append((t0, sym, qty - fill))          # remainder keeps working
        pending = still
        if pos[b.sym] < 0:                                   # daily borrow on shorts
            cash -= cm.borrow / 252 * abs(pos[b.sym]) * b.close
        for sym, qty in strategy.on_bar(b, dict(pos)).items():   # sees only the past
            pending.append((b.t, sym, qty))
    return ledger, pos, cash          # simplified: no cash interest, no locates

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative: buy 50,000 shares of a $40 stock with a 2¢ spread, 2% daily volatility, 1M shares ADV, a $0.003 per-share take fee and k = 0.7.

Component Calculation $ bps Half-spread $0.01 × 50,000 500 2.5 Fees $0.003 × 50,000 150 0.75 Impact 0.7 × 0.02 × √(50,000 / 1,000,000) × $2,000,000 6,261 31.3 Total 6,911 34.6

A flat 5 bps charge books $1,000, about 7× too little. Against 30 bps of expected alpha, the flat model reports +25 bps net; the realistic one, −4.6 bps. With a 10% participation cap, a 150,000-share order on a 1M-share day fills 100,000 today and 50,000 tomorrow while the alpha decays.

Passive fills: you join a 10,000-share bid with 500 shares. Then 3,000 trade at your price and 2,000 cancel. A fill-on-touch engine fills you. A risk-averse queue model puts the cancels behind you, leaving 7,000 ahead. A probabilistic model leaves 5,000–7,000 ahead.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Fill price: next open or next-interval VWAP for daily books. The close is usable only if the decision came before the MOC cutoff (3:50 p.m. on NYSE) [Verified] (order types and auctions).
  • Impact coefficient: order 1 in the square-root law literature (Tóth et al. 2011) [Reported]. Firms refit it on their own fills via TCA [Lore].
  • Latency: HFT engines sample measured distributions, not constants [Lore].
  • Borrow: general collateral about 0.25–0.50% a year, hard-to-borrow 5–50%+ [Lore] (shorting).
  • Fees: take fees are capped at $0.0030 per share (Rule 610(c)); the cut to $0.0010 for stocks priced at $1 or more is delayed to November 2027 [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Zipline-reloaded: event-driven; Quantopian's engine, maintained by Stefan Jansen since Quantopian closed in late 2020; v3.2.1 in October 2026 [Verified].
  • backtrader: event-driven; last PyPI release April 2023 [Verified].
  • vectorbt: array-based research at scale; open-source edition of VectorBT PRO [Verified].
  • NautilusTrader: Rust-native, deterministic, event-driven; the same strategy code runs in backtest and live [Verified].
  • LEAN (QuantConnect): open-source event-driven engine in C# with Python support [Verified].
  • hftbacktest: L2/L3 replay with feed and order latency and queue models; its docs warn replay cannot model your impact [Verified].
  • ABIDES: agent-based discrete-event simulation, so other agents can react to yours (Byrd et al. 2019) [Verified].
  • In-house: large firms build simulators that share production code and are calibrated on live fills [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Unit tests: buy-and-hold reproduces the total-return series; no trades means zero P&L; split days show no jump.
  • Live reconciliation: replay the live period against realized P&L; the residual is unmodeled slippage.
  • Determinism: same data vintage, code and seed give identical output.
  • Sensitivity: P&L degrades smoothly at 2× costs and 2× latency.
  • Fill realism: simulated passive fill rates match live ones.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Same-bar fills: trading at the close that generated the signal.
  • Free passive fills: a limit order filled whenever price touches it ignores the queue and adverse selection.
  • Infinite liquidity: no participation cap.
  • No short frictions: no locates, recalls or borrow fees.
  • Two code paths: research logic drifts from production. More in backtest pitfalls.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Are you filling on the signal bar?" → Is there same-bar look-ahead?
  • "Touch fills are fantasy." → Passive orders need a queue model.
  • "What's the sim-to-live slippage?" → Gap between simulated and realized P&L.
  • "Same code path as prod?" → Does the backtest run production logic?
  • "Pin the vintage." → Record the exact data snapshot.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Vectorized or event-driven, and why? (basic)
  2. What fill price do you assume for daily rebalances? (informed)
  3. How do you model queue position for passive orders? (informed)
  4. How big is your sim-to-live gap, and is it stable? 🔒 (sharp)
  5. Is your impact model fitted on your own fills? (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: P&L identity, cost model, queue probability

Daily P&L with positions \(q_{i,t-1}\), dividends \(D\), fills \(f\), borrow rate \(b\) and cash rate \(r^c\):

\[ \Pi_t = \sum_i q_{i,t-1}(P_{i,t} - P_{i,t-1} + D_{i,t}) - \sum_{\text{fills}} c(f) - \sum_{i:q<0} \tfrac{b_i}{252}|q_i|P_i + \tfrac{r^c}{252}\,\text{cash} \]

Cost per fill: \(c(f) = \tfrac12 s|f| + \phi|f| + k\,\sigma\sqrt{|f|/\text{ADV}}\;|f|P\).

Queue models (hftbacktest): a cancel of size \(C\) is ahead of you with probability \(f(x)/(f(x)+f(1-x))\), where \(x\) is the queue fraction ahead, with \(f(x)=x^n\) or \(\log(1+x)\).

docs.title: Overfitting and multiple testing
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Try enough strategies and the best backtest looks good by luck: the best Sharpe of N zero-skill trials grows like √(2 ln N) standard errors.
  • The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) is the probability that the true Sharpe beats that luck hurdle; the Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) is how often the in-sample winner ends up below the out-of-sample median.
  • Lab 13: the best of 500 noise strategies went from Sharpe 2.18 in-sample to −0.90 out of sample; DSR 0.34 vs 0.94 for a planted alpha; PBO 0.64 vs 0.22 (synthetic lab result).
  • Every correction needs an honest trial count, research graveyard included.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: validation · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Given everything we tried, is the best backtest evidence of skill or of luck? Inputs → Outputs Returns of the chosen strategy and all N variants tried → SR0, DSR, PBO, adjusted p-values Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Factor investing · Momentum · Value, quality, low vol · Alternative data · NLP and LLM signals · Fundamental quant signals · Trend following · Pairs trading Latency / compute regime Offline, seconds: Lab 13 runs 12,870 CSCV splits on 500 strategies in 6 s Key parameters Effective N; DSR pass mark 0.95; CSCV blocks S = 16; t-hurdle 3.0; false discovery rate 5% [Lore] Main failure modes Undercounting trials; miscounting correlated variants; trusting one noisy estimate; overfitting these statistics cannot see Lab Lab 13

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Twenty invoices picked by management prove nothing; an auditor needs the population. A backtest shown after 500 tries is a maximum, and maxima of noise are large.

Five years of daily data pin down an annualized Sharpe ratio only to about ±0.45, so the best of 100 zero-skill strategies is expected to show 1.13. Multiple testing corrections raise the hurdle to match the search.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Log every trial (configuration, returns, date); abandoned ideas count.
  2. Estimate effective N by clustering correlated variants, and the spread of their Sharpe ratios.
  3. Hurdle: SR0 = expected maximum Sharpe of N zero-skill trials.
  4. DSR: probabilistic Sharpe against SR0, adjusted for length, skew and kurtosis.
  5. PBO by CSCV: over all half-and-half splits of S time blocks, the share where the in-sample winner ranks at or below the out-of-sample median.
  6. Cross-check with adjusted p-values (backtest pitfalls); proceed if DSR ≥ 0.95 and PBO is low [Lore].
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations
from scipy.stats import norm
# Lab 13 core functions (same names and formulas). Sharpe ratios are PER PERIOD (daily).
EULER_GAMMA = 0.5772156649

def expected_max_sharpe(n_trials, sr_std):
    # E[max Sharpe] of n_trials zero-skill strategies; sr_std = sd of their Sharpe estimates
    if n_trials <= 1:
        return 0.0
    g = EULER_GAMMA
    return sr_std * ((1 - g) * norm.ppf(1 - 1 / n_trials) + g * norm.ppf(1 - 1 / (n_trials * np.e)))

def deflated_sharpe(returns, n_trials, sr_std_trials):
    r = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    n, sr = r.size, r.mean() / r.std(ddof=1)
    z = (r - r.mean()) / r.std()
    skew, kurt = np.mean(z ** 3), np.mean(z ** 4)             # kurt = 3 for a normal
    sr0 = expected_max_sharpe(n_trials, sr_std_trials)        # the luck hurdle
    stat = (sr - sr0) * np.sqrt(n - 1) / np.sqrt(1 - skew * sr + (kurt - 1) / 4 * sr ** 2)
    return norm.cdf(stat), sr0                                # DSR = P[true Sharpe > SR0]

def pbo_cscv(R, n_blocks=16):
    # R: T x N returns of all N variants tried. Loop version of Lab 13's vectorized code.
    T, N = R.shape
    blocks = np.array_split(np.arange(T), n_blocks)
    logits = []
    for is_ids in combinations(range(n_blocks), n_blocks // 2):    # C(16, 8) = 12,870
        is_rows = np.concatenate([blocks[b] for b in is_ids])
        oos_rows = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(T), is_rows)
        sr_is = R[is_rows].mean(0) / R[is_rows].std(0)
        sr_oos = R[oos_rows].mean(0) / R[oos_rows].std(0)
        rank = (sr_oos < sr_oos[sr_is.argmax()]).sum() + 1     # IS winner's OOS rank, 1 = worst
        w = rank / (N + 1.0)
        logits.append(np.log(w / (1 - w)))
    return float(np.mean(np.array(logits) <= 0))              # PBO

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Luck hurdle by hand. Five years of daily data; a zero-skill strategy's annualized Sharpe has standard error ≈ 1/√5 = 0.447. For N = 100, with γ = 0.5772:

z = (1 − γ)·Φ⁻¹(1 − 1/100) + γ·Φ⁻¹(1 − 1/(100e)) = 0.4228 × 2.326 + 0.5772 × 2.680 = 2.53,

so SR0 = 0.447 × 2.53 = 1.13. For N = 45, SR0 = 1.00 [Estimate]: five years of data absorb only about 45 independent trials, the Minimum Backtest Length idea of Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2014) [Verified].

DSR, the paper's example. Sharpe 2.5 over 5 years of daily data, after 100 trials with Sharpe variance 0.5; skew −3, kurtosis 10. SR0 = 1.79 and DSR = 0.90, below the 95% bar; after 46 trials DSR would be 0.95 (Bailey & López de Prado 2014) [Verified], reproduced with deflated_sharpe above.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• N: count configurations, then cluster near-identical variants into a few effective trials [Reported] (López de Prado).
  • Pass marks: DSR ≥ 0.95; PBO below about 0.2–0.3 [Lore]; t > 3.0 for a new factor, the hurdle Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2016) set after counting at least 316 published factors [Verified].
  • CSCV blocks: S = 16 (12,870 splits) is the PBO authors' suggested default [Verified].
  • Error rate: Bonferroni and Holm control the chance of any false discovery; BHY controls the false discovery rate under dependence (Benjamini & Yekutieli 2001) [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Factor zoo (contested): Harvey, Liu & Zhu argue most claimed findings are likely false [Verified]; in the Bayesian model of Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen (2023), most factors replicate, across 93 countries [Verified].
  • Haircuts: Harvey & Liu cut a 10-year Sharpe of 1.0 found among 100 tests to 0.44 under BHY [Verified] (backtest pitfalls); the DSR authors call their hurdle complementary [Verified]. White's (2000) Reality Check is a bootstrap alternative [Verified].
  • Practice: López de Prado urges recording every backtest and reporting the trial count (2018) [Reported].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
Lab 13, synthetic data: first- vs second-half Sharpe of 500 noise strategies (gray), the in-sample winner (orange, 2.18 → −0.90) and a planted alpha (star, 2.40 → 1.96).

Synthetic lab result (100 stocks × 1,260 days, gross): corr(IS, OOS Sharpe) across noise strategies = +0.015; for N = 500 the hurdle was 2.03 (closed form) vs 1.98 (simulated); luck matches the planted alpha near N = 860. The best noise strategy's PSR was 0.998, its DSR 0.34. PBO was 0.64 for the noise-only search and 0.22 with the planted alpha included.

Lab 13, synthetic data: the best in-sample Sharpe of N noise strategies rises with N; the winner's out-of-sample Sharpe stays near zero.

The setting is generous: the planted alpha's true Sharpe is near 2, cost-free. Single academic factors earned gross Sharpe ratios of about 0.2–0.5 in the US over 1963–2026 (size 0.21, value 0.34, momentum 0.50; French data library) [Verified] and lose about 58% of their return after publication (McLean & Pontiff 2016) [Verified]; t = 2 takes about seven years at Sharpe 0.75 and 25 at 0.4 [Estimate].

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Miscounting: colleagues' attempts and the papers behind the idea are trials; overcounting correlated variants kills real alphas.
  • Noisy statistics: across four Lab 13 seeds the planted alpha's DSR at N = 500 ranged 0.56–0.95, its PBO 0.20–0.58 (synthetic lab result).
  • Invisible channels: look-ahead and survivorship inflate Sharpe without showing up in N (backtest pitfalls).
  • Decay is not overfitting: real alphas also die (alpha decay).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "What's the DSR at your real N?" → Is it significant after the search?
  • "Best of 400 lookbacks: that's a maximum, not an estimate." → Selection bias.
  • "PBO is 0.6; the in-sample winner is a coin flip." → Rankings do not persist.
  • "Show me the graveyard." → Disclose the failed variants.
  • "It clears t = 3 after BHY." → It survives a factor-zoo hurdle.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. How do you count trials across a research team? (basic)
  2. Do you compute deflated Sharpe or PBO before allocating? (informed)
  3. How do you estimate the effective number of trials? (informed)
  4. What share of strategies passing your hurdle hold up live? 🔒 (sharp)
  5. Have you funded a strategy that failed DSR? 🔒 (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: expected maximum, DSR, PBO, Minimum Backtest Length

Expected maximum of \(N\) zero-skill Sharpe estimates with dispersion \(\sigma_{SR}\):

\[ SR_0 = \sigma_{SR}\Big[(1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\!\big(1 - \tfrac{1}{N}\big) + \gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\big(1 - \tfrac{1}{Ne}\big)\Big] \]

The bracket grows roughly like \(\sqrt{2\ln N}\).

Deflated Sharpe (per-period \(\widehat{SR}\), \(T\) observations, skew \(\hat\gamma_3\), kurtosis \(\hat\gamma_4\)):

\[ DSR = \Phi\!\left[\frac{(\widehat{SR} - SR_0)\sqrt{T-1}}{\sqrt{1 - \hat\gamma_3\widehat{SR} + \tfrac{\hat\gamma_4 - 1}{4}\widehat{SR}^2}}\right] \]

PBO: with \(w_c\) the in-sample winner's relative out-of-sample rank in split \(c\), \(\lambda_c = \ln\frac{w_c}{1-w_c}\) and \(PBO = \Pr[\lambda \le 0]\), about 0.5 for pure noise.

Minimum Backtest Length (years) keeping \(E[\max] \le \bar{SR}\): \((z_N / \bar{SR})^2\), \(z_N\) the bracket above. CSCV cost: \(\binom{S}{S/2}\) splits × \(N\) Sharpes.

docs.title: Time-series cross-validation
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Shuffled K-fold assumes independent rows. Financial labels overlap (a daily-sampled 5-day return shares 4 days with its neighbor) and features persist, so shuffling leaks near-copies of test rows into training.
  • The fixes: walk-forward, purging training dates whose labels overlap test labels, and an embargo after each test block (López de Prado 2018). Combinatorial purged CV (CPCV) yields many backtest paths instead of one.
  • The leak scales with model flexibility. In Lab 12, GBDT's out-of-sample IC was 0.127 under shuffled K-fold, 0.066 walk-forward and 0.076 purged; ridge leaked 0.002 (synthetic lab result).
  • Tune hyperparameters in inner folds (nested CV). Separating two models whose ICs differ by 0.005 can take about three years of test data (illustrative).

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: validation · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How well will this model forecast unseen data, and which configuration should we pick, without leaking the future into training? Inputs → Outputs Date-indexed feature and label panel, label horizon h, a fitting routine → train/test date splits, out-of-sample forecasts, per-fold rank IC, a chosen configuration Used by strategies ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Cross-sectional alpha · Stat arb overview · Factor-residual mean reversion · Short-term reversal · Intraday patterns · Alternative data · NLP and LLM signals · Fundamental quant signals · Earnings and event-driven · Pairs trading Latency / compute regime Offline batch, one fit per fold: Lab 12's 12 scheme-model pairs take about 30 s; production grids take cluster-hours [Estimate] Key parameters Purge = label horizon h (1–20 days); embargo ≈ 1% of the sample, at least the feature memory; 5–10 folds; test blocks 3–12 months; training window 1–5 years rolling or expanding; CPCV with 6–10 groups and 2 test groups Main failure modes Shuffled rows; splitting by stock; full-sample preprocessing; tuning on the test fold; too few test dates Lab Lab 12

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Cross-validation hides part of the sample, fits on the rest and scores the hidden part. It is honest only if the hidden part is truly unseen.

In finance it usually is not. Monday's 5-day label covers Tuesday to the next Monday; Tuesday's covers Wednesday to the next Tuesday. They share four days (correlation about 0.8), and a 60-day momentum feature barely changes overnight. Shuffle rows and the model trains on Monday, is tested on Tuesday, and effectively sees the answer. A flexible model memorizes these near-copies; a dozen linear coefficients cannot.

Auditors test cut-off because transactions near period end leak between periods. Purging is cut-off testing for labels; the embargo is a margin for slow-moving features.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Split by date, not row: stocks on one day share the market's move. The label of date t is the return over t+1 … t+h.
  2. Walk-forward (walk-forward analysis): each fold trains on dates whose labels end before the test block; expanding or rolling.
  3. Purged K-fold: contiguous test blocks; drop training dates whose labels overlap a test label, plus an embargo after the block. Keeping dates after the test block assumes stationarity.
  4. CPCV (CPCV): N groups, test on every choice of k, giving (k/N)·C(N, k) complete backtest paths and a distribution of Sharpe ratios.
  5. Nest: tune hyperparameters with an inner purged split inside each outer training set; score each outer test block once.
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations
# purged_kfold_splits and walk_forward_splits: Lab 12 core functions (same names and logic).
# Splits are over DATES (all stocks on a date move together). Label of t = return t+1..t+horizon.

def purged_kfold_splits(n_dates, n_folds=5, horizon=5, embargo=10):
    dates = np.arange(n_dates)
    for test in np.array_split(dates, n_folds):           # contiguous test blocks
        first, last = test[0], test[-1]
        # keep a training date only if its label ends before the test block starts,
        # or it starts after the test labels end plus the embargo (serial correlation)
        keep = (dates + horizon <= first) | (dates >= last + horizon + embargo)
        yield dates[keep], test

def walk_forward_splits(n_dates, n_folds=5, horizon=5):
    blocks = np.array_split(np.arange(n_dates), n_folds + 1)
    for test in blocks[1:]:                               # expanding window, past only
        yield np.arange(0, test[0] - horizon + 1), test

def cpcv_splits(n_dates, n_groups=6, k_test=2, horizon=5, embargo=10):
    # NOT in Lab 12: combinatorial purged CV (Lopez de Prado 2018, ch. 12).
    # C(6, 2) = 15 splits; each group is tested 5 times -> 5 complete backtest paths
    dates = np.arange(n_dates)
    groups = np.array_split(dates, n_groups)
    for combo in combinations(range(n_groups), k_test):
        keep = np.ones(n_dates, dtype=bool)
        for g in combo:                                   # purge and embargo around each test group
            keep &= (dates + horizon <= groups[g][0]) | (dates >= groups[g][-1] + horizon + embargo)
        yield dates[keep], np.concatenate([groups[g] for g in combo])

# Nested use: tune on inner purged folds INSIDE each outer training set, score outer test once.
# for tr, te in walk_forward_splits(n_dates, 5, horizon=5):
#     lam = choose_lambda(...)          # inner walk-forward on dates in tr only (F1 card)
#     beta = fit_ridge(X[rows(tr)], y[rows(tr)], lam)
#     oos_ic.append(daily_rank_ic(X[rows(te)] @ beta, y[rows(te)]))

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Purge arithmetic (Lab 12 defaults, 1,000 dates). Test fold 3 is dates 400–599, whose labels span days 401–604. Date 395's label (days 396–400) ends before day 401, so it stays; date 396's label (397–401) overlaps and is purged. After the block, date 603's label (604–608) overlaps the last test label (600–604); date 604 is the first clean date, and the 10-day embargo moves the restart to 614. Training keeps 396 + 386 = 782 dates: 18 of 800 dropped, 2.25% of the training data.

Leak size. Two h-day returns sharing k days have correlation k/h for i.i.d. daily returns: 4/5 = 0.8 for neighbors, 0.2 for dates four apart [Estimate].

How much test data? Illustrative. Two models' daily rank ICs differ by a true 0.005, and the daily difference has a standard deviation of 0.03. With 5-day labels, consecutive daily ICs overlap, so roughly n/5 observations are independent. For t = 2 you need n/5 = (2 × 0.03 / 0.005)² = 144, so n ≈ 720 trading days, almost three years of out-of-sample data [Estimate]. Small IC gaps between models are usually noise.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Purge length: the longest label horizon used anywhere in training; purging 5 days with 20-day labels still leaks.
  • Embargo: covers feature autocorrelation; about 1% of the sample is commonly cited from López de Prado [Reported]. Lab 12 uses 10 of 1,255 dates.
  • Expanding vs rolling: expanding for slow, stable signals; rolling 1–3 years where alphas decay [Lore]. Step at the production refit cadence.
  • Folds and block length: 5–10 folds; test blocks of 3–12 months so each spans more than one market regime [Lore].
  • CPCV size: N = 6, k = 2 gives 15 fits and 5 paths; N = 10, k = 2 gives 45 fits and 9 paths.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• When plain K-fold is fine: Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo (2018) show it is valid for purely autoregressive models with uncorrelated errors [Verified]. Overlapping labels break that condition, though Lab 12's ridge shows the leak needs a flexible model to bite.
  • Purging, embargo, CPCV: from López de Prado's Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), ch. 7 and ch. 12 [Verified]; he argues walk-forward tests a single path and is easy to overfit [Reported].
  • Walk-forward vs CPCV is contested. Walk-forward never trains on the future, so it best mimics live trading. One synthetic study (Arian, Norouzi Mobarekeh & Seco 2024) finds CPCV gives lower probability of backtest overfitting and better deflated Sharpe ratios [Reported].
  • Academic ML in asset pricing: Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) did not cross-validate: training expanded from 18 years, a 12-year validation window rolled forward, models were refit yearly and tested on 1987–2016 [Verified].
  • Nested CV: tuning and scoring on the same folds is optimistic, shown on null data by Varma & Simon (2006); Cawley & Talbot (2010) call it overfitting the selection criterion [Verified].
  • Practice: purged schemes for model selection, a final walk-forward over the most recent 1–2 years touched once, then paper trading as the last fold [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Shuffled vs purged side by side: a large gap means a leakage-sensitive model. Also check the in-sample gap and fold-to-fold IC dispersion.
  • Null test: shuffle labels within each date; out-of-sample IC should fall to about zero.
  • Live check: paper or live results land inside the cross-validated range.

Lab 12, synthetic data: mean daily out-of-sample rank IC for four combiners under three validation schemes; dashed line, oracle weights using the planted ICs.

Synthetic lab result (150 stocks × 1,260 days, same 1,045 test dates): shuffled K-fold gave GBDT 0.127 and ranked it first; walk-forward (0.066) and purged K-fold (0.076) ranked it last of the fitted combiners; its in-sample IC was 0.238. Ridge: 0.087 shuffled vs 0.085 walk-forward. Purged K-fold scores GBDT higher than walk-forward because its folds train on about 80% of the sample, not 17–83%. Shuffled CV promised GBDT a gross Sharpe of 12.1; walk-forward delivered 7.0. Both are stylized (clean planted alphas, frictionless market); realistic net Sharpe for ML short-horizon books is about 1–2 at scale [Lore] (ML-driven short-horizon alpha).

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Early stopping on a random split leaks even when the final test is clean (tree ensembles).
  • Splitting by stock: the same dates in train and test share market and sector moves.
  • Preprocessing leaks: full-sample z-scores, a risk model or PCA fit on all dates, feature selection on all data (look-ahead bias).
  • Test-set reuse: every rerun after peeking is another trial (overfitting and multiple testing).
  • Regime folds: one fold holding 2008 can dominate the average; report per-fold results.
  • Training on the future: purged K-fold assumes stationarity and flatters decaying alphas; walk-forward is the safer final test.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Did you purge? Your labels are 20-day." → Training labels overlap the test period.
  • "Shuffled CV says 0.12, walk-forward says 0.07; I believe the 0.07." → The gap is leakage.
  • "The early-stopping set was random rows, so the whole thing leaks." → Validation inside training must also respect time.
  • "That's one path; show me the CPCV distribution." → One walk-forward Sharpe is a single draw.
  • "We burned the 2024 hold-out; it's in-sample now." → A test set looked at repeatedly is no longer out of sample.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Walk-forward, purged K-fold or CPCV, and why? (basic)
  2. Do you split by date, and how long are your test blocks? (basic)
  3. How do you set the purge and embargo for your label horizon? (informed)
  4. Where do hyperparameters get tuned relative to the test period? (informed)
  5. How many times has your final hold-out been looked at? (sharp)
  6. How does your cross-validated IC compare with live IC on the same models? 🔒 (sharp)

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: overlap correlation, effective sample size, CPCV paths, cost

Overlapping labels: for i.i.d. daily returns, two \(h\)-day returns sharing \(k\) days have

\[ \rho = \frac{k}{h}. \]

A daily-sampled series of \(h\)-day quantities has a variance inflation factor of about \(1 + 2\sum_{j=1}^{h-1}(1 - j/h) = h\), so \(n_{\text{eff}} \approx n/h\) (the logic behind Hansen–Hodrick and Newey–West errors with \(h-1\) lags).

Data needed to detect an IC gap \(\Delta\) with daily difference volatility \(\sigma_d\) at t-stat \(z\):

\[ n \approx h \left(\frac{z\,\sigma_d}{\Delta}\right)^2 . \]

CPCV with \(N\) groups and \(k\) test groups: \(\binom{N}{k}\) splits, each training on about \((N-k)/N\) of the data before purging; every group is tested \(\binom{N-1}{k-1}\) times, giving

\[ \varphi[N, k] = \frac{k}{N}\binom{N}{k} \]

complete backtest paths. Cost: one fit per split (45 for \(N = 10\), \(k = 2\)).

docs.title: Alternatives to MVO
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Plain mean-variance optimization (MVO) "maximizes error": it piles into assets with overestimated returns and underestimated risk (Michaud 1989).
  • Risk-based rules drop return forecasts: 1/N, inverse volatility, equal risk contribution (risk parity), minimum variance, hierarchical risk parity (HRP).
  • Other fixes keep MVO but tame its inputs: Black–Litterman starts from market-implied returns, robust optimization penalizes estimation error, constraints act as shrinkage.
  • Factor managers often skip the optimizer: rank- or signal-weighted long-short books, with risk controls bolted on.
  • Choose by how much you trust your return forecasts; the 1/N debate is unresolved.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: portfolio · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How should I weight positions when mean-variance inputs are too noisy to trust? Inputs → Outputs covariance matrix; optionally signals, market weights, views → portfolio weights Used by strategies Factor investing · Value, quality, low vol · Momentum · Factor timing and crowding · Trend following · Carry and cross-asset premia · Cross-sectional alpha Latency / compute regime monthly or overnight batch; milliseconds for 50-asset risk parity, seconds for HRP on 3,000 names Key parameters covariance lookback 1–3 years (or EWMA half-life 60–250 days); risk budgets; volatility target ~10% for levered risk parity; Black–Litterman τ 0.01–0.05; rebalance monthly Main failure modes ignoring returns (bond-heavy, levered books); correlation regime shifts; unstable clusters; overconfident views Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
MVO weights are proportional to Σ⁻¹μ: a noisy covariance matrix, inverted, times noisy expected returns. The optimizer hunts for the most flattering estimates, so its biggest bets sit where errors are largest. The alternatives trade a precise-looking, fragile answer for a biased, stable one: budgeting by headcount when the ROI forecasts are worthless.

Three routes: drop μ (risk-based rules), shrink inputs toward a prior (Black–Litterman, covariance shrinkage), or constrain the answer.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. 1/N: equal weights. Inverse volatility: w ∝ 1/σᵢ (ignores correlations).
  2. Equal risk contribution (ERC): choose w so each asset's share of variance, wᵢ(Σw)ᵢ / w′Σw, is equal. With two assets this equals inverse volatility.
  3. Minimum variance: w ∝ Σ⁻¹1, usually long-only with caps.
  4. HRP: cluster on correlation distance √(½(1−ρ)), order similar assets together, then split the list in halves recursively, giving the lower-variance half more weight.
  5. Black–Litterman: back out market-implied returns π = δΣw_mkt, blend with views by confidence, then run MVO.
  6. Rank weights: wᵢ ∝ rank(signalᵢ) − average rank, scaled to $1 long and $1 short (Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen).
import numpy as np

def erc_weights(cov, budget=None, n_iter=500, tol=1e-10):
    """Equal risk contribution (risk parity): each asset's share of portfolio
    variance, w_i (cov @ w)_i / w'cov w, equals its budget b_i (1/N by default)."""
    n = len(cov)
    b = np.full(n, 1.0 / n) if budget is None else np.asarray(budget)
    w = 1.0 / np.sqrt(np.diag(cov)); w /= w.sum()        # start at inverse vol
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        sigma = np.sqrt(w @ cov @ w)
        target = b * sigma / (cov @ w)                     # w_i that would give RC_i = b_i
        target /= target.sum()
        if np.abs(target - w).max() < tol:
            break
        w = 0.5 * w + 0.5 * target                         # damped fixed-point step
    return w

def hrp_weights(cov, order):
    """HRP stage 3, recursive bisection (Lopez de Prado 2016). order: indices from
    hierarchical clustering on sqrt(0.5 * (1 - corr)), read off the dendrogram."""
    w = np.ones(len(cov))
    clusters = [list(order)]
    while clusters:
        clusters = [c[s] for c in clusters if len(c) > 1
                    for s in (slice(0, len(c) // 2), slice(len(c) // 2, None))]
        for left, right in zip(clusters[0::2], clusters[1::2]):
            v_l, v_r = cluster_var(cov, left), cluster_var(cov, right)
            alpha = 1.0 - v_l / (v_l + v_r)                 # less risky half gets more
            w[left] *= alpha
            w[right] *= 1.0 - alpha
    return w / w.sum()

def cluster_var(cov, idx):
    """Variance of the inverse-variance portfolio inside one cluster."""
    sub = cov[np.ix_(idx, idx)]
    ivp = 1.0 / np.diag(sub); ivp /= ivp.sum()
    return ivp @ sub @ ivp

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Equities (vol 15%), bonds (5%), commodities (18%); correlations equity–bond −0.2, equity–commodity 0.3, bond–commodity 0.

Check 1/N by hand: variance = (1/9)(0.0225 + 0.0025 + 0.0324 − 0.0030 + 0.0162) = 0.00784, so vol 8.86%. (Σw)₁ = (0.0225 − 0.0015 + 0.0081)/3 = 0.0097, so equity's risk share = (0.0097/3) ÷ 0.00784 = 41%.

Method Weights E / B / C Vol Risk shares E / B / C Leverage for 10% vol 1/N 33 / 33 / 33% 8.9% 41 / 1 / 57% 1.1× Inverse vol 21 / 62 / 17% 5.6% 34 / 25 / 41% 1.8× ERC 20 / 66 / 14% 5.2% 33 / 33 / 33% 1.9× HRP 7 / 87 / 5% 4.5% 3 / 91 / 6% 2.2× Minimum variance 13 / 84 / 3% 4.4% 13 / 84 / 3% 2.3×

Equal dollars are not equal risk: under 1/N, bonds carry 1% of it. Every risk-based answer is bond-heavy, so a 10% volatility target needs about 2× leverage. HRP lands near minimum variance: clustering splits bonds from equities and commodities first, and inverse variance favors bonds.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Covariance window: 1–3 years daily or an exponentially weighted half-life; shrink it (P2).
  • Risk budgets: unequal budgets (e.g. 50% equity risk) turn ERC into general risk budgeting.
  • Volatility target and leverage: risk-parity books are levered to a target, often around 10% [Lore].
  • Black–Litterman: δ (market risk aversion) ≈ 2–3, τ 0.01–0.05, and view confidence [Lore].
  • Rank vs raw signal: ranks blunt outliers; Asness et al. found raw signals similar or slightly better [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• The critique: Michaud (1989) called mean-variance optimizers "estimation-error maximizers" [Reported].
  • 1/N's case: across 14 models and 7 datasets, none consistently beat 1/N; beating it would take about 3,000 months of data for 25 assets [Verified] (DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal 2009).
  • The rebuttal: on 13 datasets, Kritzman, Page and Turkington blame rolling short-sample return estimates, not optimization; sensible inputs beat 1/N [Reported]. The evidence is mixed.
  • Constraints as shrinkage: long-only limits cut risk even when "wrong"; with them, the sample covariance does as well as factor or shrinkage estimators [Verified] (Jagannathan & Ma 2003).
  • Minimum variance: since 1968, long-only minimum variance had about three-quarters of the cap-weighted market's risk with higher average return [Reported] (Clarke, de Silva & Thorley 2006).
  • ERC volatility lies between minimum variance and 1/N [Verified] (Maillard, Roncalli & Teïletche 2010).
  • HRP: in López de Prado's Monte Carlo (10 assets, 10,000 runs), the minimum-variance optimizer had 72% more out-of-sample variance than HRP, inverse variance 38% more [Verified]: the author's simulation, not live data.
  • Practice: factor managers mostly rank- or z-score signals and run a risk-model optimizer with caps; multi-asset and CTA books lean on inverse-volatility and risk parity [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Realized volatility near target; risk shares near budget between rebalances.
  • Out-of-sample Sharpe and drawdown versus a 1/N baseline: the honest benchmark.
  • Stable weights and HRP clusters month to month.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• No return view: risk parity owns what is least volatile, often long-duration bonds; positive stock–bond correlation (2022) hurts levered books [Lore].
  • Correlations jump in crises, so diversification fails when needed.
  • HRP's halving: the original code splits the sorted list in halves, not at dendrogram branches.
  • Black–Litterman views are only as good as their confidence settings.
  • Rank books carry hidden bets: without neutralization, value ranks are sector bets.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Equal weight is the benchmark to beat." → the DeMiguel test.
  • "It's risk-balanced, levered to ten vol." → ERC scaled to a volatility target.
  • "The optimizer found our estimation errors." → MVO went to extremes.
  • "We rank, then neutralize." → rank weights plus a risk-model step.
  • "Our prior is the market." → Black–Litterman's starting point.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Do you trust your expected returns enough to optimize on them?
  2. What does 1/N do on your universe over the same period?
  3. How much leverage does your risk-parity sleeve need?
  4. How stable are your HRP clusters month to month?
  5. 🔒 How do you set view confidence in Black–Litterman?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: risk contributions, Black–Litterman, robust MVO

Risk contributions sum to portfolio volatility:

\[ \sigma(w) = \sqrt{w^\top\Sigma w}, \qquad RC_i = \frac{w_i(\Sigma w)_i}{\sigma(w)}, \qquad \sum_i RC_i = \sigma(w). \]

ERC solves \(RC_i = \sigma/N\); Maillard et al. show \(\sigma_{MV} \le \sigma_{ERC} \le \sigma_{1/N}\). Long-only ERC is unique and solves a convex problem: minimize \(\tfrac12 w^\top\Sigma w - c\sum_i \log w_i\), then rescale.

Black–Litterman posterior mean, views \(P\mu = Q + \varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon \sim N(0,\Omega)\):

\[ \mu_{BL} = \big[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top\Omega^{-1}P\big]^{-1}\big[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1}\pi + P^\top\Omega^{-1}Q\big], \qquad \pi = \delta\Sigma w_{mkt}. \]

Robust MVO with an ellipsoidal uncertainty set on μ (covariance of the estimate \(\Omega_\mu\)):

\[ \max_w\; \hat\mu^\top w - \kappa\sqrt{w^\top\Omega_\mu w} - \lambda\, w^\top\Sigma w , \]

a second-order cone program (Ceria & Stubbs 2006).

docs.title: Covariance estimation and shrinkage
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • The sample covariance of N stocks from T days is singular when N > T (Lab 14: 500 stocks, 252 days, rank 251); near N = T its small eigenvalues are too small and large ones too large.
  • Random-matrix theory sizes the noise: pure-noise eigenvalues spread over (1 ± √(N/T))². For S&P 500 stocks, 94% of correlation eigenvalues sit inside that band.
  • Fixes: linear shrinkage toward a target (Ledoit–Wolf), factor models, eigenvalue clipping, nonlinear shrinkage.
  • EWMA weighting helps, but its effective sample (about 2.9 half-lives) must stay well above N; volatilities get short half-lives, correlations long ones.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: portfolio · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How do I get an invertible covariance that does not mislead an optimizer when assets rival observations? Inputs → Outputs T×N returns or residuals, weights, shrinkage target → N×N covariance Used by strategies Dispersion and correlation · Factor-residual · Stat arb · Cross-sectional alpha · Value, quality, low vol · Factor investing · Trend following · Carry and cross-asset premia Latency / compute regime overnight batch; an eigendecomposition of a 3,000 × 3,000 matrix takes seconds [Estimate] Key parameters shrinkage intensity δ (data-chosen; 0.08 in Lab 14); half-life 42–252 days (volatility), 200–756 (correlation); RiskMetrics λ = 0.94 Main failure modes singular matrix; optimizer loading on noise; half-life too short for N; poor target Lab Lab 14

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
A covariance matrix is a list of portfolios (eigenvectors) and their variances (eigenvalues). Estimation noise spreads the eigenvalues: some portfolios look far safer than they are. An optimizer is a bargain hunter and buys exactly those.

Shrinkage pulls extreme eigenvalues toward the middle: a deliberately biased, much less noisy estimate, like blending an outlier analyst forecast with consensus. Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage picks the blend from the data; a factor model imposes structure instead.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Data: clean daily returns with aligned closes, or residuals after a factor model.
  2. Weighting: an equal-weight window or EWMA. Check the effective sample, T_eff = (1 + λ)/(1 − λ) ≈ 2.9 × half-life, against N.
  3. Estimate the sample covariance S.
  4. Regularize: linear shrinkage (1 − δ)S + δ·target with δ from Ledoit–Wolf, clipping at the Marchenko–Pastur edge, nonlinear shrinkage, or a factor model.
  5. Split horizons: short half-life for volatilities, long for correlations; recombine.
  6. Validate on optimized portfolios, not random ones.
import numpy as np

def ledoit_wolf_cov(returns):
    """Ledoit-Wolf (2004) shrinkage toward mu * I: the estimator sklearn's LedoitWolf
    computes for Lab 14, written out so each step is visible."""
    X = returns - returns.mean(axis=0)
    T, N = X.shape
    S = X.T @ X / T                                    # sample covariance (MLE scaling)
    mu = np.trace(S) / N                               # target: average variance times I
    d2 = ((S - mu * np.eye(N)) ** 2).sum() / N         # distance of S from the target
    b2 = ((X ** 2).sum(axis=1) ** 2).sum() / T - (S ** 2).sum()
    b2 = min(b2 / (N * T), d2)                         # sampling noise in S
    delta = b2 / d2                                    # shrinkage intensity in [0, 1]
    return (1 - delta) * S + delta * mu * np.eye(N), delta

def ewma_cov(returns, half_life=84):
    """Exponentially weighted covariance, newest row last; effective sample ~2.9 half-lives."""
    lam = 0.5 ** (1 / half_life)
    wts = lam ** np.arange(len(returns))[::-1]
    wts /= wts.sum()
    X = returns - wts @ returns
    return (X * wts[:, None]).T @ X

def clip_eigenvalues(returns):
    """RMT cleaning (Laloux et al. 1999): flatten correlation eigenvalues in the noise band."""
    T, N = returns.shape
    sd = returns.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
    C = np.corrcoef(returns, rowvar=False)
    ev, V = np.linalg.eigh(C)
    noise = ev < (1 + np.sqrt(N / T)) ** 2             # Marchenko-Pastur upper edge
    ev[noise] = ev[noise].mean()                       # keep the trace, drop the noise structure
    C = V @ np.diag(ev) @ V.T
    d = np.sqrt(np.diag(C))
    return C / np.outer(d, d) * np.outer(sd, sd)       # unit diagonal, then back to covariance

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. 500 stocks whose true correlation matrix is the identity (every eigenvalue 1).

  • T = 252 days: S has rank 251, leaving 249 zero-variance directions: "riskless" long-short books that carry ordinary risk.
  • T = 1,000 days: N/T = 0.5, so noise eigenvalues spread from (1 − √0.5)² = 0.086 to (1 + √0.5)² = 2.91. The safest-looking portfolio's volatility is understated by 1/√0.086 = 3.4×. In our simulation the minimum-variance portfolio's true volatility was 2.1× its estimate, near the theoretical 1/(1 − N/T) = 2 [Estimate].
  • Shrink with δ = 0.33 toward the identity: 0.67 × 0.086 + 0.33 = 0.39, and 2.91 becomes 2.28. The eigenvalue range falls from 34:1 to 6:1.
  • EWMA: RiskMetrics' λ = 0.94 gives an effective sample of 1.94/0.06 ≈ 32 days: fine for five assets, singular for 100 stocks.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Target: Ledoit and Wolf proposed a single-index target (2003), then constant correlation, "comparable" and simpler [Verified]. On pure noise their δ ≈ 1 (the identity is the truth); on stocks with a strong market factor the identity is far off, so Lab 14's δ averaged 0.08 and the fix was partial.
  • Half-lives: MSCI's US models use 42–252 days for volatilities, 200–756 for correlations [Verified]; RiskMetrics used λ = 0.94 daily, 0.97 monthly [Verified].
  • Sample size: even N/T = 0.1 spreads noise eigenvalues from 0.47 to 1.73.
  • Tuning: minimize out-of-sample minimum-variance volatility or the optimized-portfolio bias statistic.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Against the sample matrix: on the largest US stocks, 1983–2002, constant-correlation shrinkage raised an active manager's realized information ratio by about 50% [Verified] (Ledoit & Wolf 2004).
  • Random-matrix evidence: for 406 S&P 500 stocks over 1,309 days, 94% of eigenvalues fell in the noise band; the informative 6% carried 26% of total volatility [Verified] (Laloux et al. 1999).
  • Nonlinear shrinkage adjusts each eigenvalue separately (Ledoit & Wolf 2012, 2017); the 2020 analytical version is about 1,000× faster and handles 10,000+ assets, including N > T [Verified].
  • In equities the factor model is the main regularizer; shrinkage goes into its pieces, as in USE4's eigenfactor adjustment and Bayesian specific-risk shrinkage [Verified]. Futures books of 50–200 contracts often use shrunk EWMA matrices directly [Lore].
  • Constraints shrink too: long-only limits act like covariance shrinkage [Verified] (Jagannathan & Ma 2003; see alternatives to MVO).

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Condition number (largest ÷ smallest eigenvalue) finite and stable; out-of-sample minimum-variance volatility below the sample matrix's; bias statistic of optimized portfolios near 1 (risk models).

Lab 14: dashed = risk each estimator predicts, solid = true risk of the same portfolios (synthetic data).

Synthetic lab result: at risk aversion 50, true ÷ predicted volatility was 3.17 (sample), 2.25 (Ledoit–Wolf), 1.28 (PCA), 1.00 (oracle); alpha per unit of true risk was 2.03, 2.09, 2.48, 2.58. A poor covariance cost about 20% of the achievable information ratio, with alpha known exactly. Real data shows the same mechanism: on weekly returns of the largest 100 US stocks, a 10-week EWMA half-life gave a minimum-volatility portfolio 550% long, 450% short, turning over 200%+ a week [Verified] (Menchero 2017).

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Ragged panels: pairwise-complete estimates can show negative variance; repair to the nearest valid matrix.
  • Asynchronous closes bias daily correlations toward zero; use multi-day returns or Newey–West.
  • Half-life too short makes the matrix near-singular; too long makes it stale in a regime shift.
  • Clipping real structure: share classes of one company (GOOG and GOOGL) have a genuinely tiny spread variance that cleaning erases.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Five hundred names on a year of data? It's singular." → N > T.
  • "Shrink toward constant correlation." → the Ledoit–Wolf 2004 target.
  • "Most of those eigenvalues are noise." → They sit inside the Marchenko–Pastur band.
  • "What's the effective sample on that half-life?" → About 2.9 half-lives, versus N.
  • "The optimizer is long the smallest eigenvector." → It is exploiting estimation error.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Do you estimate a full covariance or only a factor covariance?
  2. What shrinkage target do you use, and how is δ chosen?
  3. What is your effective sample size relative to the number of assets?
  4. 🔒 Where in production do you use nonlinear shrinkage or RMT cleaning?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: Ledoit–Wolf intensity, Marchenko–Pastur, EWMA sample size

Ledoit–Wolf intensity for \(\hat\Sigma = (1-\delta)S + \delta\mu I\) (minimizes expected Frobenius loss):

\[ \delta^* = \frac{b^2}{d^2}, \quad d^2 = \tfrac1N\lVert S - \mu I\rVert_F^2, \quad b^2 = \min\Big(d^2,\ \tfrac{1}{NT^2}\sum_{t}\lVert x_t x_t^\top - S\rVert_F^2\Big). \]

Marchenko–Pastur density for i.i.d. unit-variance data, \(q = N/T \le 1\):

\[ \rho(\lambda) = \frac{\sqrt{(\lambda_+ - \lambda)(\lambda - \lambda_-)}}{2\pi q \lambda}, \qquad \lambda_\pm = (1 \pm \sqrt q)^2 . \]

EWMA weights \(w_t \propto \lambda^{T-t}\): effective sample \((\sum w)^2/\sum w^2 = (1+\lambda)/(1-\lambda) \approx 2.885 \times\) half-life.

Pure noise, minimum variance: in-sample variance \(\approx (1-q)\times\) the true optimum, out-of-sample \(\approx\) optimum\(/(1-q)\) [Estimate]. Cost: \(O(TN^2)\) to form \(S\), \(O(N^3)\) to diagonalize.

docs.title: Mean-variance optimization
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • MVO picks weights to maximize α′w − λ·w′Σw − cost(w − w₀) subject to constraints: dollar, beta and sector neutrality, name caps, gross leverage, % of ADV, turnover. The problem is convex, so 3,000 names solve in seconds.
  • Unconstrained, w* = Σ⁻¹α/(2λ): a noisy inverse times noisy forecasts. The optimizer bets hardest where estimates are most wrong, which Michaud called error maximization.
  • Inputs matter more than the solver: scale alphas as IC × volatility × score (Grinold), use a factor risk model, charge realistic costs.
  • Constraints eat forecast: realized performance runs at 0.3–0.8 of the unconstrained Fundamental Law (the transfer coefficient).
  • Risk and cost aversion are tuned by backtest. In Lab 14 a cost aversion of 0.25 kept more net alpha than 0 or 1 (synthetic lab result).

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: portfolio · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Given forecasts, risk and costs, which portfolio should I hold tomorrow? Inputs → Outputs alphas, risk model (X, F, Δ), current holdings, cost model, constraints (beta, sectors, ADV, borrow) → target weights and a trade list Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Stat arb · Factor-residual · Reversal · ML short-horizon · Fundamental signals · Revisions · Alternative data · Factor investing · Momentum · Value, quality, low vol · Factor timing and crowding Latency / compute regime overnight or intraday batch: seconds per solve for 3,000 names with a factor risk model [Estimate]; Lab 14's 500 names solve in under a second Key parameters risk aversion λ 5–50 (annual decimal units); cost aversion 0.25–3; name cap 0.5–3% of capital; gross 200–600%; trades ≤ 5–10% of ADV Main failure modes error maximization; alpha–risk misalignment; overtrading; infeasible constraint sets; piling into caps Lab Lab 14

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Think of capital budgeting with correlated projects: fund each by the return it adds per unit of risk it adds to the whole portfolio, not of its own risk. Mean-variance optimization formalizes this: at the optimum, each position's alpha equals λ times its marginal contribution to variance.

Correlation is where the power and the danger live. Given two highly correlated stocks with different alphas, the optimizer goes long one and short the other: the spread is low-risk, so it can be sized up. If the correlation was overestimated, the hedge is weaker than believed and the book is bigger and riskier than intended. Each input error turns into a confident bet.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Scale forecasts to expected returns over the holding horizon: α_i = IC × σ_i × z_i, with σ_i residual volatility and z_i a z-score.
  2. Match horizons: α and Σ must cover the same period. Lab 14 uses 21 days for both, which makes λ horizon-free.
  3. Objective: α′w − λ·w′Σw − Σ cᵢ|wᵢ − w₀ᵢ|, with risk in factor form (w′XFX′w + w′Δw) so the problem stays small.
  4. Constraints: Σw = 0 (dollar neutral), β′w = 0 (beta neutral), sector sums zero, |wᵢ| ≤ cap, Σ|wᵢ| ≤ gross, trades within a share of ADV, turnover within budget.
  5. Solve with a convex solver, then round to shares, drop tiny trades and hand the list to execution.
import numpy as np
import cvxpy as cp   # convex modeling layer, as in Lab 14

def optimize_portfolio(alpha, cov, w_prev=None, risk_aversion=50.0, cost=None, beta=None,
                       sectors=None, max_weight=0.01, max_gross=2.0,
                       max_trade=None, max_turnover=None):
    """maximize alpha'w - risk_aversion * w'Sigma w - sum_i cost_i |w_i - w_prev_i|.
    Weights are fractions of capital; alpha and Sigma cover the same horizon.
    cov is factor form, Sigma = L'L + diag(specific_var) (Lab 14's FactorCov)."""
    n = len(alpha)
    w_prev = np.zeros(n) if w_prev is None else w_prev
    w = cp.Variable(n)
    y = cp.Variable(cov.L.shape[0])                       # factor exposures y = L w
    risk = cp.sum_squares(y) + cp.sum_squares(cp.multiply(np.sqrt(cov.specific_var), w))
    objective = alpha @ w - risk_aversion * risk
    if cost is not None:                                  # half-spread + impact per unit traded
        objective -= cost @ cp.abs(w - w_prev)
    cons = [y == cov.L @ w,
            cp.sum(w) == 0,                               # dollar neutral
            cp.abs(w) <= max_weight,                      # name cap
            cp.norm1(w) <= max_gross]                     # gross leverage
    if beta is not None:
        cons.append(beta @ w == 0)                        # beta neutral
    if sectors is not None:
        cons.append(sectors.T @ w == 0)                   # each sector nets to zero
    if max_trade is not None:                             # not in Lab 14: per-name trade cap,
        cons.append(cp.abs(w - w_prev) <= max_trade)      # e.g. 5% of ADV over capital
    if max_turnover is not None:                          # not in Lab 14: one-way turnover budget
        cons.append(cp.norm1(w - w_prev) / 2 <= max_turnover)
    prob = cp.Problem(cp.Maximize(objective), cons)
    prob.solve()      # Lab 14: SCS with a CLARABEL fallback; desks often license MOSEK or Gurobi
    return np.asarray(w.value).ravel()

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Two stocks in one industry, each with 20% residual volatility and correlation 0.8. With an IC of 0.05 and a score of +2, A's alpha is 0.05 × 20% × 2 = 2.0% a year; B scores 0, so its alpha is 0. Risk aversion λ = 5.

The unconstrained answer is w_A = α_A / (2λσ²(1 − ρ²)) and w_B = −ρ·w_A. With ρ = 0.8: w_A = 0.02 / (2 × 5 × 0.04 × 0.36) = 13.9% and w_B = −11.1%. The optimizer shorts 0.8 of B per unit of A to hedge the shared industry move, cutting A's 20% risk to the spread's 20% × √0.36 = 12%. Expected alpha is 0.28% with 1.67% volatility.

Now suppose the estimated correlation is too high (truth stays 0.8):

Estimated ρ w_A w_B Gross Predicted vol True vol True ÷ predicted 0.80 13.9% −11.1% 25% 1.67% 1.67% 1.00 0.90 26.3% −23.7% 50% 2.29% 3.20% 1.40 0.95 51.3% −48.7% 100% 3.20% 6.34% 1.98

Gross exposure scales with 1/(1 − ρ̂), so each step doubles the bet. The true information ratio barely moves (0.167, 0.164, 0.162; it is low because this is one pair, not 1,000), but risk runs up to twice the forecast. Lab 14 shows the same signature at scale: bias 2.78 with about 20% of the information ratio lost.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Risk aversion λ: unconstrained, ex-ante volatility equals IR/(2λ), so λ = IR ÷ (2 × target volatility). An ex-ante IR of 2 at a 5% volatility target gives λ = 20 [Estimate]. Desks usually set λ to hit a risk target, then verify realized risk [Lore].
  • Cost aversion κ multiplies the cost term. A trade's cost should be spread over the position's life, so κ ≈ rebalance interval ÷ holding period, times any overconfidence markup. In Lab 14 that is 10 days ÷ about 29 days (the mean life of a 20-day half-life signal) ≈ 0.35 [Estimate], near the winning 0.25. The 1–3× multiplier on the cost model card is a separate markup for overconfident alphas, applied to correctly amortized costs [Estimate].
  • Caps: 0.5–3% of capital per name; trades ≤ 5–10% of ADV and positions ≤ a few days of ADV [Lore].
  • Gross: 200% in Lab 14; market-neutral books often run 400–600% [Lore].
  • Turnover: a penalty rather than a hard budget, because hard budgets bind arbitrarily [Lore].
  • Tuning: walk-forward grid over λ and κ, maximizing net Sharpe, with overfitting controls.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Origin: Markowitz (1952) framed portfolio choice as mean versus variance [Verified].
  • Error maximization: Michaud (1989) showed optimizers overweight assets with overestimated returns and underestimated risk [Verified]. Errors in means did over 10× the damage of errors in variances and over 20× that of errors in covariances (Chopra & Ziemba 1993) [Reported], so alphas need the most shrinkage.
  • Alpha scaling: Grinold's (1994) rule α = IC × volatility × score turns z-scores into return forecasts [Verified]; raw scores give arbitrary position sizes.
  • Transfer coefficient: Clarke, de Silva and Thorley (2002) generalize the Fundamental Law to IR ≈ TC × IC × √breadth; realized performance runs at 0.3–0.8 of the unconstrained prediction [Verified]. A 50% annual turnover cap alone gives TC 0.73; adding long-only and market-cap neutrality cuts it to 0.3 [Reported].
  • Solvers: cvxpy is the common open-source modeling layer [Verified] (Diamond & Boyd 2016); MOSEK and Gurobi publish portfolio-optimization guides [Verified]. Which solver a given fund runs is rarely public [Lore].
  • Constraints as regularizers: caps and long-only limits act like shrinkage [Verified] (Jagannathan & Ma 2003). Robust, resampled and Black–Litterman variants are on alternatives to MVO.
  • Cost-aware and multi-period: Boyd et al. (2017) cast multi-period trading as a sequence of convex problems [Verified]; P6 covers trading partway toward a target.

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Optimized-book bias statistic near 1 (risk models).
  • Transfer coefficient: correlation between risk-adjusted alphas and risk-adjusted weights; track it as constraints change.
  • Shadow prices: which constraint costs the most objective per unit relaxed.
  • Realized vs planned turnover and costs.

Lab 14: the dashed frontiers are what the optimizer promises with each covariance; solid lines show the true risk of the same portfolios (synthetic data).

Synthetic lab result: at λ = 50, true risk was 3.17× predicted with the sample covariance and 1.28× with PCA. The biweekly cost test (PCA risk model, two years):

Cost aversion Turnover (× capital per year) Costs (bps/yr) Expected net alpha (bps/yr) Realized net Sharpe 0 19.4 316 493 2.42 0.25 15.0 244 549 2.63 1 7.4 119 541 2.43

The Sharpe ratios are far above real books because the alpha is known exactly and never decays; the standard error is about ±0.7. Diversified market-neutral books are put at net Sharpe 1–2 [Lore] (cross-sectional alpha). The gap between 0.25 and 1 is small; the robust lesson is that ignoring costs overtrades.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Error maximization: offsetting long-short pairs, positions pinned at caps, weights that flip daily.
  • Alpha–risk misalignment: alpha the risk model cannot see becomes a hidden factor bet (risk models).
  • Infeasibility: beta neutrality plus tight caps plus a turnover budget may have no solution; make soft constraints penalties.
  • Horizon mismatch: a daily Σ with monthly α makes λ meaningless.
  • Crowding: similar signals, risk models and optimizers produce similar trades (August 2007; failure gallery).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "The optimizer is levering up our estimation error." → Error maximization.
  • "TC on that book is 0.4." → Constraints let only 40% of the forecast reach positions.
  • "We're pinned against the beta constraint." → It binds and has a high shadow price.
  • "Scale it to IC times vol before it goes in." → Grinold's alpha scaling.
  • "Run cost aversion at a third on a biweekly rebalance." → Costs amortized over the holding period.
  • "Half the names sit at the cap." → Caps, not forecasts, are sizing the book.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Do you set risk aversion to a volatility target or by backtest?
  2. How do you make alpha and risk horizons consistent?
  3. Which constraint binds most often, and what does it cost in transfer coefficient?
  4. How does your cost aversion relate to your signals' half-lives?
  5. How often does the problem go infeasible, and what gives way?
  6. 🔒 How much do you shrink alphas before the optimizer sees them?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the unconstrained solution, risk aversion, transfer coefficient, costs

Maximizing \(\alpha^\top w - \lambda w^\top\Sigma w\) gives

\[ w^* = \frac{1}{2\lambda}\Sigma^{-1}\alpha, \qquad \sigma(w^*) = \frac{\sqrt{\alpha^\top\Sigma^{-1}\alpha}}{2\lambda} = \frac{IR^*}{2\lambda}. \]

Errors in \(\hat\Sigma\) enter through \(\hat\Sigma^{-1}\), which amplifies the smallest eigenvalues, where estimation error is largest.

Transfer coefficient (Clarke et al.), with \(\sigma_i\) the residual volatilities:

\[ TC = \operatorname{corr}\!\left(\frac{\alpha_i}{\sigma_i},\; w_i\sigma_i\right), \qquad IR \approx TC \cdot IC \cdot \sqrt{BR}. \]

A linear cost \(c_i\lvert w_i - w_{0,i}\rvert\) creates a no-trade band: position \(i\) moves only if its marginal utility \(\alpha_i - 2\lambda(\Sigma w)_i\) exceeds \(c_i\) in absolute value. A 3/2-power impact term stays convex (second-order cone).

Complexity: with factor-form risk the problem has \(N + K\) variables and \(O(NK)\) nonzeros; interior-point solvers handle \(N = 3{,}000\), \(K \approx 75\) in seconds [Estimate].

docs.title: Multi-period optimization and trading toward the aim
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • With costs, rebalancing to today's Markowitz portfolio is a trap. Gârleanu and Pedersen (2013): aim in front of the target, trade partially toward the aim.
  • The aim shrinks fast-decaying signals: in Lab 15 a 60-day-half-life signal keeps 96% of its weight, a 1-day signal 35%.
  • The trade rate depends on costs and risk aversion, not alpha decay; Lab 15's grid search recovers the closed-form 0.213 within about 2% (synthetic).
  • Full daily rebalancing of a 1-day signal nets a Sharpe of −17.5 (synthetic).
  • Linear costs add no-trade bands and constraints break the closed form, so desks solve multi-period convex problems.

Level: Deep dive · Pipeline stage: portfolio · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Toward what, and how far, should I trade today when signals decay and costs grow with size? Inputs → Outputs positions, alpha and decay per signal, risk model, cost model, risk aversion γ, constraints → aim, trade rate, trade list Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Stat arb · Factor-residual · ML short-horizon · Reversal · Momentum · Factor investing · Fundamental signals · Revisions · Trend following Latency / compute regime overnight batch; closed form microseconds per name, constrained multi-period solve seconds to minutes [Estimate] Key parameters trade rate 0.05–0.6 per day (Lab 15: 0.058–0.605 over a 256× cost range); half-lives 1–250 days; γ; cost scale λ; band; horizon 2–20 periods [Lore] Main failure modes full rebalancing; myopic optimizer; overstated persistence; non-quadratic costs; binding constraints Lab Lab 15

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Mean-variance optimization says where you would be if trading were free. With costs you cannot get there at once, and the target keeps moving, most for fast signals.

Treat a trade as capital expenditure and alpha as its revenue: a fast signal is a project whose revenue stops before the spend is recovered. Gârleanu and Pedersen (GP) give a closed-form rule for trading toward the aim. The aim averages today's Markowitz portfolio with those expected on future dates, so it leans toward persistent signals. Each day you trade a fixed fraction of the way to it.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Per signal k: expected return α_k and daily decay φ_k = 1 − 0.5^(1/half-life), from IC decay curves.
  2. Pick γ; fit λ for the cost ½·λ·Δx′ΣΔx.
  3. Rate a/λ: costs and risk aversion only.
  4. Aim: each signal's Markowitz portfolio, shrunk by 1/(1 + aφ_k/γ), summed.
  5. Trade: x_new = x + rate × (aim − x); then bands and caps (not in the lab).
import numpy as np

# Lab 15 core (Garleanu-Pedersen 2013). Positions x in $, factor-hedged book, diagonal Sigma.
# Quadratic trading cost: 1/2 * dx' Lambda dx with Lambda = lam * Sigma.
def gp_trade_rate(gamma, lam, rho=0.0):
    """Fraction of the gap to the aim closed each period: a / lam. No signal decay in here."""
    g = gamma * (1 - rho) + lam * rho
    a = (-g + np.sqrt(g ** 2 + 4 * gamma * lam * (1 - rho) ** 2)) / (2 * (1 - rho))
    return a / lam

def aim_portfolio(signal_alphas, decay_rates, sigma2, gamma, lam, rho=0.0):
    """Each signal's Markowitz portfolio shrunk by 1 / (1 + a * phi_k / gamma).
    phi_k = 1 - 0.5 ** (1 / half_life): fast signals are shrunk the most."""
    a = gp_trade_rate(gamma, lam, rho) * lam
    aim = 0.0
    for alpha_k, phi_k in zip(signal_alphas, decay_rates):
        markowitz_k = alpha_k / (gamma * sigma2)            # (gamma Sigma)^-1 alpha_k
        aim = aim + markowitz_k / (1 + a * phi_k / gamma)
    return aim

def trade_toward_aim(current, aim, rate):
    """rate = 1 is full rebalancing; GP's optimum is gp_trade_rate(gamma, lam)."""
    return current + rate * (aim - current)

# Not in the lab: overlays most desks add because real costs are not purely quadratic.
def todays_positions(current, signal_alphas, half_lives, sigma2, gamma, lam,
                     band_usd=50_000, cap_usd=None):
    phis = [1 - 0.5 ** (1 / h) for h in half_lives]
    aim = aim_portfolio(signal_alphas, phis, sigma2, gamma, lam)
    trade = trade_toward_aim(current, aim, gp_trade_rate(gamma, lam)) - current
    trade[np.abs(trade) < band_usd] = 0.0                   # crude no-trade band (spread, fees)
    if cap_usd is not None:
        trade = np.clip(trade, -cap_usd, cap_usd)           # e.g. a %ADV cap per name
    return current + trade

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative, Lab 15 parameters. Specific volatility 1.7% a day, γ = 2×10⁻⁷ and λ = 3.46×10⁻⁶ per $, so λσ² = 10⁻⁹ ($1M traded moves the price 10 bps).

  1. Rate. a = (−γ + √(γ² + 4γλ))/2 = 7.38×10⁻⁷; a/λ = 0.213 per day (myopic: γ/(γ + λ) = 0.055).
  2. Aim. a/γ = 3.69. Two signals each imply a $10M Markowitz position:
Signal half-life φ Shrink 1/(1 + 3.69φ) Aim contribution 5 days 0.129 0.677 $6.77M 60 days 0.0115 0.959 $9.59M Total $16.36M (Markowitz: $20M)
  1. Trade. From $5M: 0.213 × (16.36 − 5) = $2.42M; new position $7.42M.
  2. Cost. ½ × 10⁻⁹ × (2.42×10⁶)² = $2,930, 12 bps of the trade.
  3. Full rebalance: $15M costs ½ × 10⁻⁹ × (1.5×10⁷)² = $112,500: 6.2× the trade, 38× the cost.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Rate: derive it; don't hand-tune it. For small γ/λ, a/λ ≈ √(γ/λ): 16× the costs cut Lab 15's rate from 0.213 to 0.058.
  • Half-lives: from IC decay by horizon. When unsure, understate persistence: overstating it brings back overtrading.
  • λ: from your impact model (P5); GP's simple form assumes cost proportional to variance, so rescale by liquidity per name.
  • Band: skip trades whose alpha does not cover half-spread plus fees [Lore].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Theory: closed form for many assets and signals [Verified] (GP 2013); continuous time in GP (2016) [Verified].
  • Real data: commodity futures, 5-day, 12-month and 5-year signals (half-lives 3, 205, 701 days): net Sharpe 0.54 for GP, 0.44 for the best static policy, −18 for frictionless rebalancing (low-cost case, in-sample regressions) [Verified] (2009 working paper).
  • Linear costs create a no-trade region instead of partial trading [Verified] (Constantinides 1986; Davis and Norman 1990).
  • Model-predictive control: plan trades over a horizon, execute the first, repeat; any convex cost or constraint fits [Verified] (Boyd et al. 2017; library cvxportfolio).
  • Common shortcut: single-period optimization with horizon-blended alphas, amortized costs and turnover limits [Lore]. Real impact is nearer 3/2-power in dollars (P5): no closed form.

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Backtest net utility vs rate peaks near a/λ, on a flat top.
  • Costs ÷ gross alpha and turnover match plan; fast signals net positive in P&L attribution.

Lab 15, synthetic: toward the GP aim (left) every half-life peaks near the same rate; toward Markowitz (right) the best rate falls as signals get faster.

Synthetic lab result (200 stocks, planted IC 0.01, known decay): best rates 0.209–0.212 for every half-life. Toward Markowitz the best rate falls from 0.20 to 0.06 as signals speed up, losing up to 35% of utility. Full rebalancing turns the 1-day signal's gross 2.30 into net −17.5, like GP's −18 on commodities. For a 5 + 60-day mix: GP 2.93, myopic 2.74, full rebalancing −0.71 (costs $67.4M a year vs $2.9M). Live signals are far noisier: diversified books run net 1–2 [Lore].

Lab 15, synthetic: the GP position smooths a jumpy target (left); best rates follow the closed form (right).

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Myopia: a one-period optimizer charges the whole cost against one day of alpha, trading 4× too slowly (0.055 vs 0.213).
  • Markowitz as target: the best rate shifts with the signal mix.
  • Misestimated decay gives the wrong aim.
  • Constraints, crowding, transient impact: none are in the closed form.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We close about a fifth of the gap each day." → trade rate ≈ 0.2.
  • "Reversal rides on the slow book." → the shrunk fast signal mostly tweaks trades made anyway.
  • "Don't chase the target." → never rebalance fully to Markowitz.
  • "We amortize costs over the holding period." → single-period proxy for multi-period.
  • "It's inside the band, leave it." → no-trade region from linear costs.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Do you rebalance fully, partially, or within bands?
  2. Is the trade rate derived or tuned?
  3. Do fast signals get less target weight than slow ones of equal IC?
  4. How stable are your half-life estimates?
  5. Multi-period solve, or single-period with amortized costs?
  6. 🔒 What share of gross alpha goes to costs?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the GP solution, the myopic rate and no-trade bands

With \(r_{t+1} = B f_t + u_{t+1}\) and \(\Delta f_{t+1} = -\Phi f_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}\), maximize

\[ \mathbb{E}\sum_t \Big[x_t^\top B f_t - \tfrac{\gamma}{2} x_t^\top \Sigma x_t - \tfrac12 \Delta x_t^\top \Lambda \Delta x_t\Big], \qquad \Lambda = \lambda\Sigma . \]

With \(\rho = 0\) (see the paper for discounting):

\[ x_t = \Big(1 - \frac{a}{\lambda}\Big) x_{t-1} + \frac{a}{\lambda}\,\text{aim}_t, \qquad a = \frac{-\gamma + \sqrt{\gamma^2 + 4\gamma\lambda}}{2}, \] \[ \text{aim}_t = (\gamma\Sigma)^{-1} \sum_k \frac{B_k f_t^k}{1 + \phi_k a/\gamma} . \]

For \(\gamma \ll \lambda\), \(a/\lambda \approx \sqrt{\gamma/\lambda}\). One period alone gives a rate of \(\gamma/(\gamma+\lambda)\). A linear cost \(\kappa|\Delta x|\) adds a no-trade region where the marginal gain is below \(\kappa\).

docs.title: Position sizing and risk budgeting
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Sizing turns a forecast into a position; it decides drawdowns and survival more than Sharpe.
  • Volatility targeting scales each bet by 1/σ so it carries a set risk; risk budgeting splits the total across markets, strategies or pods.
  • The Kelly criterion maximizes growth at leverage μ/σ², given the true Sharpe. At twice true Kelly growth is zero, so practitioners run a quarter to half Kelly or less.
  • Stop-losses help when returns trend and cost money under a random walk (Kaminski & Lo 2014) [Verified].
  • Synthetic lab result (Lab 19): vol targeting held rolling volatility at 7.0–12.3% (5th–95th percentile) against 4.9–16.7% for equal notional.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: portfolio · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How big should each position, strategy and the book be? Inputs → Outputs Signals, ex-ante volatilities and correlations, risk budgets, drawdown, leverage limits → target notional per position (fraction of NAV) Used by strategies Trend following · Carry and cross-asset premia · Factor investing · Factor timing and crowding · Momentum · Value, quality, low vol · Volatility risk premium · Cross-sectional alpha · Stat arb overview Latency / compute regime Daily batch: milliseconds for 50 futures, seconds for 3,000 stocks; intraday limits live in M9 Key parameters Volatility target 8–15%, 10% common [Lore]; EWMA center of mass 20–60 days; Kelly fraction 0.25–0.5; drawdown triggers 5–10%; gross cap 3–6× NAV (futures); buffer 10–30% of a typical position Main failure modes Lagging volatility estimates, correlation spikes, Kelly on an overstated Sharpe, procyclical selling Lab Lab 19

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Budget by risk, not revenue: a 2%-volatility bond future and a 40%-volatility gas future get the same risk, so the bond gets 20× the notional. The forecast says which way; sizing says how much, and how much less after a bad month. Over-sizing a good forecast ruins a fund as surely as a bad one.
