docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Estimate each position's ex-ante volatility (EWMA, 60-day center of mass) and the correlation matrix (P1, P2).
  2. Assign risk budgets: equal per asset class or strategy (risk parity, P4), or tilted by conviction.
  3. Size inversely to volatility: weight = signal × budget / σ.
  4. Scale the book so its ex-ante volatility equals the target.
  5. Apply caps: per position, gross leverage, margin.
  6. Multiply by a drawdown scaler.
  7. Trade only when the target leaves a no-trade band (P6).
import numpy as np

def vol_target_positions(signal, ann_vol, corr, asset_class, target_vol=0.10, asset_cap=0.40):
    """As in Lab 19: notional / NAV per market. Equal risk per class, inverse vol inside it."""
    classes, counts = np.unique(asset_class, return_counts=True)
    n_in_class = dict(zip(classes, counts))
    budget = np.array([1.0 / (len(classes) * n_in_class[c]) for c in asset_class])
    w = signal * budget / ann_vol
    port_vol = np.sqrt(w @ (corr * np.outer(ann_vol, ann_vol)) @ w)
    if port_vol > 0:
        w = w * target_vol / port_vol                 # whole book at the target ex-ante vol
    cap = asset_cap * target_vol / ann_vol            # max standalone vol per market
    return np.clip(w, -cap, cap)

def trade_with_buffer(target, current, band):
    """As in Lab 19: move only when the target leaves the band, and only to its edge."""
    gap = target - current
    return np.where(np.abs(gap) > band, target - np.sign(gap) * band, current)

# --- Illustrative extensions, not in Lab 19 ---
def kelly_leverage(mu, sigma, fraction=0.5):
    """Growth-optimal leverage mu / sigma^2 (continuous time), scaled down."""
    return fraction * mu / sigma ** 2

def drawdown_scaler(nav, cut_dd=0.05, stop_dd=0.10, min_scale=0.5):
    """1.0 until a 5% drawdown, linear to 0.5 at 10%, then flat (stop and review)."""
    dd = 1.0 - nav[-1] / np.max(nav)
    if dd >= stop_dd:
        return 0.0
    if dd <= cut_dd:
        return 1.0
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - min_scale) * (dd - cut_dd) / (stop_dd - cut_dd)

def size_book(signal, ann_vol, corr, asset_class, nav, current, typical, max_gross=6.0):
    target = vol_target_positions(signal, ann_vol, corr, asset_class) * drawdown_scaler(nav)
    gross = np.abs(target).sum()
    if gross > max_gross:                             # leverage limit, notional / NAV
        target = target * max_gross / gross
    return trade_with_buffer(target, current, 0.25 * typical)

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Excess return μ = 7%, volatility σ = 10% at 1× (Sharpe 0.7). Kelly leverage is μ/σ² = 0.07 / 0.01 = 7×. Log growth at leverage f is fμ − f²σ²/2; the chance of ever losing half is 0.5^(2/c − 1) at Kelly fraction c.

Leverage Kelly fraction Volatility Growth: fμ − f²σ²/2 P(ever −50%) 1× 1/7 10% 0.07 − 0.005 = 6.5% 0.01% 1.75× 1/4 17.5% 0.1225 − 0.0153 = 10.7% 0.8% 3.5× 1/2 35% 0.245 − 0.0613 = 18.4% 12.5% 7× 1 70% 0.49 − 0.245 = 24.5% 50% 14× 2 140% 0.98 − 0.98 = 0% 100%

Half Kelly keeps 75% of the growth at half the volatility. If the true Sharpe is 0.35 (a routine haircut), "full Kelly" 7× is twice true Kelly: zero growth, certain halving. A 10% target here is 1/7 Kelly.

Volatility rescale. Ex-ante volatility jumps from 10% to 14%: scale 10/14 = 0.71, gross leverage 3.8× → 2.7× NAV.

Drawdown cut. NAV 93 against a peak of 100: scale = 1 − 0.5 × (7 − 5)/(10 − 5) = 0.8.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Target volatility. 10% in Hurst et al.'s trend simulations [Verified]; pods often run lower [Lore].
  • Estimator. Moskowitz et al. use a 60-day center of mass [Verified]; shorter windows churn; floors cap notional in quiet markets [Lore].
  • Kelly fraction. A quarter to a half [Lore], less for backtest-only Sharpes.
  • Across strategies or pods. Start near equal risk, tilt toward capacity-adjusted Sharpe, and cut on drawdowns: one multi-manager reportedly halves capital at a 5% loss and exits near 7.5% [Reported] (how firms combine strategies).

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Kelly. Kelly (1956) derived the growth-optimal bet [Verified]; Thorp used fractional Kelly in practice [Reported]; full Kelly's short-run drawdowns are large (MacLean, Thorp & Ziemba) [Reported].
  • Volatility timing. Volatility-managed factors earn large alphas (Moreira & Muir 2017) [Verified], but across 103 equity strategies real-time versions do not systematically win (Cederburg et al. 2020) [Verified]. Across 60+ assets since 1926, Sharpe rises for equities and credit only, and left tails shrink (Harvey et al. 2018) [Verified]. Risk-managed momentum nearly doubles its Sharpe (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015) [Verified]. Mixed for returns; consistent for risk control.
  • Stop-losses lower expected return under a random walk and can add value under momentum (Kaminski & Lo 2014) [Verified].
  • Drawdown control. Risk proportional to the cushion above a floor is optimal (Grossman & Zhou 1993) [Verified]; pod ladders are discrete versions.

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Realized/target volatility near 1 in a narrow band; realized risk shares near budgets; little turnover from rescaling.

Right panel: rolling volatility of the vol-targeted book hugs the dotted 10% target; equal notional swings far more. Synthetic data.

Synthetic lab results: realized volatility 9.8% against 10%; risk shares equity 36%, rates 25%, commodities 20%, FX 19% (equities exceed 25%: the budget ignores within-class correlation), against 92% for commodities plus equities under equal notional; the buffer cuts turnover from 252× to 141× NAV. Real volatility jumps, so real bands are wider.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Calm before the storm. Low trailing volatility means maximum leverage before a shock [Lore].
  • Correlation breaks. Stocks and bonds fell together in 2022 [Lore].
  • Procyclical selling. Vol-targeters de-gross into the same spike [Lore]; the BIS says procyclical deleveraging amplified the August 2024 sell-off [Verified].
  • Low-volatility instruments get huge notional and gap risk.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We run ten vol." → Annualized volatility target 10%.
  • "Half Kelly at most." → Leverage at half the growth-optimal level.
  • "Risk-budget the sleeves equally." → Equal risk per strategy.
  • "Vol spiked, so we de-grossed." → Rescaled to the target.
  • "She's at her soft stop." → Drawdown threshold that cuts capital.
  • "The buffer halves our turnover." → No-trade band.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: What volatility target do you run?
  2. Basic: Standalone volatility or risk contribution?
  3. Informed: Do you floor your volatility estimate?
  4. Informed: What Kelly fraction does your leverage imply?
  5. Sharp: How did your de-grossing rules behave in August 2024? 🔒
  6. Sharp: When do you re-risk after a drawdown cut? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: Kelly growth, ruin probability, risk contributions

With leverage \(f\), excess drift \(\mu\) and volatility \(\sigma\), log wealth drifts at \(g(f) = f\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}f^2\sigma^2\), maximized at \(f^* = \mu/\sigma^2\) with \(g^* = \tfrac{1}{2}(\mu/\sigma)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}SR^2\). At \(f = c f^*\):

\[ g(cf^*) = (2c - c^2)\, g^*, \qquad P(\text{wealth ever falls to } x) = x^{2/c - 1}. \]

Log wealth is Brownian with drift \(m\) and variance \(v\), hitting \(\ln x < 0\) with probability \(e^{2m\ln x / v}\), and \(2m/v = 2/c - 1\).

Euler risk contributions for weights \(w\) and covariance \(\Sigma\):

\[ RC_i = \frac{w_i (\Sigma w)_i}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}}, \qquad \sum_i RC_i = \sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}. \]

Scaling to target \(\sigma^*\) uses \(k = \sigma^* / \sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}\), \(O(N^2)\) per day.

docs.title: Risk models
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A risk model forecasts the covariance of 1,000–3,000 stocks from a few dozen factors plus one specific variance per stock: Σ = XFX′ + Δ. Millions of unknowns shrink to thousands.
  • Three families: fundamental (BARRA-style industries and styles, factor returns from a daily cross-sectional regression), statistical (principal components) and hybrids.
  • The craft is in the time series: half-lives (shorter for volatilities than correlations), Newey–West, a volatility-regime adjustment, shrunk specific risk.
  • Grade it with the bias statistic (std of return ÷ forecast risk; 1 = unbiased) on optimized portfolios. In Lab 14 the sample covariance scored 1.00 on random portfolios and 2.78 on optimized ones (synthetic lab result).
  • Alpha the model cannot see looks diversifiable, so the optimizer overloads it: the alignment problem.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: portfolio · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How risky is this portfolio, and how much of the risk is factor bets versus stock-specific bets? Inputs → Outputs returns, industry codes, style descriptors, market caps → exposures X (N×K), factor covariance F, specific variances Δ; risk and its decomposition for any portfolio Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Stat arb · Factor-residual · Reversal · ML short-horizon · Fundamental signals · Revisions · Alternative data · Factor investing · Momentum · Value, quality, low vol · Factor timing and crowding · Carry and cross-asset premia · Trend following Latency / compute regime overnight batch (vendor files land before the open); one portfolio's risk takes well under a millisecond [Estimate] (one N×K product) Key parameters K: 10–20 statistical, ~70–100 fundamental factors; half-lives 42–252 days (volatility), 200–756 (correlation); Newey–West lags 0–10 Main failure modes underpredicting optimized portfolios; lagging regime shifts; alpha factors missing from the model; stale exposures Lab Lab 14

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
The covariance matrix of 3,000 stocks has 4,501,500 distinct entries; a year of daily returns supplies 756,000 numbers. The covariance card shows what goes wrong if you estimate it directly.

A factor model assumes stocks co-move only through shared exposures to a few drivers: market, industry, size, momentum, value. With 75 factors, exposures are observed, the factor covariance has 2,850 entries and specific risk adds 3,000. The model is a chart of accounts for risk: each unit of variance is booked to a factor line or the specific line, and P&L attribution later reconciles against the same ledger.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Exposures X (N×K): industry dummies, style z-scores standardized across stocks each day, and a market or country column.
  2. Factor returns: each day, regress stock returns on X by weighted least squares, giving K factor returns and N specific (residual) returns.
  3. Factor covariance F: exponentially weighted (EWMA), with a shorter half-life for volatilities than correlations, plus Newey–West terms and a volatility-regime multiplier.
  4. Specific risk Δ: EWMA of squared residuals, shrunk toward the average of similar stocks.
  5. Statistical alternative: the top k principal components of trailing returns are the factors; leftover variance is specific (Lab 14's pca_factor_cov).
  6. Use: portfolio variance h′XFX′h + h′Δh; validate with the bias statistic.
flowchart TD
  ex["Exposures X<br/>industries, styles, market"] --> reg["Cross-sectional WLS<br/>one regression per day"]
  r["Stock returns"] --> reg
  reg --> f["Factor returns"]
  reg --> u["Specific returns"]
  f --> F["Factor covariance F<br/>EWMA, Newey-West,<br/>regime adjustment"]
  u --> D["Specific risk Delta<br/>EWMA, Bayesian shrinkage"]
  F --> S["Sigma = X F XT + Delta"]
  D --> S
  ex --> S
import numpy as np

def factor_returns_wls(r, X, mcap):
    """One day of a BARRA-style model (sketch; Lab 14 has no fundamental model).
    r: (N,) returns, X: (N x K) exposures. sqrt(cap) weights proxy 1 / specific variance."""
    w = np.sqrt(mcap)
    XtW = X.T * w                                    # K x N
    f = np.linalg.solve(XtW @ X, XtW @ r)            # today's factor returns (K,)
    return f, r - X @ f                              # ...and specific returns (N,)

def ewma_cov(F, hl_vol=84, hl_corr=504):
    """K x K covariance from T x K daily factor returns, oldest row first.
    Short half-life for volatilities, long one for correlations (USE4S: 84 / 504 days)."""
    def ew(hl):
        wts = 0.5 ** (np.arange(len(F))[::-1] / hl)  # newest day gets weight 1
        return (F * (wts / wts.sum())[:, None]).T @ F
    V, C = ew(hl_vol), ew(hl_corr)
    corr = C / np.sqrt(np.outer(np.diag(C), np.diag(C)))
    vol = np.sqrt(np.diag(V))
    return corr * np.outer(vol, vol)                 # Newey-West and regime scaling omitted

def pca_factor_cov(returns, n_factors=16, min_specific_var=1e-6):
    """Statistical model as in Lab 14: Sigma = L'L + diag(specific_var)."""
    X = returns - returns.mean(axis=0)
    S = X.T @ X / (len(X) - 1)                       # sample covariance (N x N)
    eigval, eigvec = np.linalg.eigh(S)
    top = np.argsort(eigval)[::-1][:n_factors]
    L = (eigvec[:, top] * np.sqrt(eigval[top])).T    # (k, N) loadings times factor vol
    specific = np.maximum(np.diag(S) - (L ** 2).sum(axis=0), min_specific_var)
    return L, specific                               # the lab wraps these in FactorCov

def portfolio_variance(w, L, specific_var):
    return ((L @ w) ** 2).sum() + (w ** 2) @ specific_var   # factor part + specific part

def bias_statistic(realized_returns, predicted_vol):
    """Std of r / sigma_pred. 1 = unbiased; > 1 = risk underpredicted."""
    z = np.asarray(realized_returns) / np.asarray(predicted_vol)
    return float(np.std(z, ddof=1))

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. A dollar-neutral book holds 400 names at 0.5% of capital each (gross 200%). Exposures: market beta 0.02, momentum 0.15, tech 0.05. Annual factor volatilities: market 16%, momentum 10%, tech 12%; momentum–tech correlation 0.3, others 0. Specific volatility is 30% for every stock.

Line Calculation Variance (×10⁻⁴) Share Market (0.02 × 0.16)² 0.10 0.8% Momentum (0.15 × 0.10)² 2.25 18.4% Tech (0.05 × 0.12)² 0.36 2.9% Momentum × tech 2 × 0.3 × 0.015 × 0.006 0.54 4.4% Specific 400 × 0.005² × 0.30² 9.00 73.5% Total 12.25 100%

Forecast volatility is √0.001225 = 3.50% a year, 0.22% a day. Specific risk dominates, as intended, but a modest momentum tilt carries almost a fifth of the variance.

If daily P&L over the next 252 days has a standard deviation of 0.29%, the bias statistic is 0.29 ÷ 0.22 = 1.32, outside the 1 ± √(2/252) = 1 ± 0.09 band: realized risk ran about a third above forecast.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
MSCI's published USE4 settings, by horizon [Verified]:

Setting USE4S (short) USE4L (long) USE4D (daily) Factor volatility half-life 84 days 252 42 Factor correlation half-life 504 days 504 200 Newey–West lags, volatility / correlation 5 / 2 5 / 2 0 / 0 Volatility-regime half-life 42 days 168 4 Specific-risk Bayesian shrinkage 0.1 0.1 0.05

Shorter horizons get shorter half-lives and no Newey–West, since a one-day forecast adds up no autocorrelated days. Correlations get longer half-lives: thousands of factor pairs need more effective data (an EWMA's effective sample is about 2.9 half-lives) or F turns singular.

  • Statistical factors: 10–20 [Lore]; Avellaneda and Lee used 15 eigenportfolios [Verified]. Lab 14's 16 matches its simulator; real data has no true k.
  • Regression weights: √(market cap), used by USE4 as a proxy for inverse specific variance [Verified].
  • Tuning: pick half-lives by bias statistics across portfolio types, calm and stressed years; match the model's horizon to the holding period.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Lineage: Barra models descend from Rosenberg (1974), who modeled covariance through company descriptors [Verified].
  • Fundamental vs statistical vs macro: on 779 US stocks (monthly, 1985–1993) they explained 42.6%, 39.0% and 10.9% of return variance; macro factors added nothing to the fundamental model [Verified] (Connor 1995). Statistical factors are unlabeled and rotate, but catch transient themes (a crowded trade) fast. A hybrid adds a few statistical factors estimated on a fundamental model's residuals [Lore].
  • Commercial models: MSCI's Barra USE4 (2011) has 60 GICS-based industries, 12 styles and a country factor, regresses on √cap weights and lets a firm sit in up to five industries [Verified]. MSCI's newer US Total Market suite adds a long-term model (16 styles, 2014) and a trading model (24 styles including sentiment, short interest and one-day reversal, plus option-implied volatility, 2015) [Verified]; we found no public "USE5". Axioma, sold by SimCorp, offers fundamental, statistical and macroeconomic variants at trading, short and medium horizons, plus custom models [Verified]. Bloomberg also sells factor models [Verified].
  • Custom vs vendor: large quant funds tend to trade on in-house models and keep a vendor model for limits, investor reporting and talking to prime brokers [Lore]. A shared vendor model means shared neutralization, which feeds crowding [Lore].
  • Optimization bias: USE4 includes an "Optimization Bias Adjustment" for under-forecast optimized portfolios [Verified]. Menchero, Wang and Orr (2012) find the lowest-volatility eigenportfolios carry the largest underprediction and correct them by simulation [Verified].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
The bias statistic is the standard deviation of realized return ÷ forecast volatility. Over T observations, 1 ± √(2/T) is consistent with an unbiased forecast [Estimate] (a standard deviation's sampling error is about 1/√(2T)); noisy but unbiased forecasts score about 1.03 [Verified] (Menchero 2017). Test random, factor-mimicking and optimized portfolios and the live book.

Lab 14: grey dots are random dollar-neutral portfolios, colored dots the optimizer's portfolios; the dashed line is a perfect forecast (synthetic data).

Synthetic lab result: on random long-short portfolios all four estimators score 0.99–1.00; on optimized portfolios, sample covariance 2.78, Ledoit–Wolf 1.92, 16-factor PCA 1.00, true covariance 0.92. Random portfolios cannot tell good from bad; optimized ones can. The lab flatters PCA: exposures never drift and the true factor count is known. Real models need explicit fixes such as MSCI's.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Error maximization: the optimizer seeks directions with underestimated risk, so a model fine "on average" fails for the one portfolio you hold.
  • Alpha–risk misalignment: an alpha factor absent from the model looks like diversifiable specific risk, so the optimizer builds a hidden factor bet; an alpha that is a risk factor gets penalized: "risk factors eat alphas" [Reported] (Lee & Stefek 2008). Fixes include an alpha alignment factor (Saxena & Stubbs 2013) and custom factors [Reported] (Ceria, Saxena & Stubbs 2012).
  • Regime shifts: long half-lives lag a volatility spike. In August 2007 the shared risk was a crowded unwind no factor described (failure gallery).
  • Horizon mismatch: a daily model for a monthly book understates risk when returns are autocorrelated.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're flat the Barra styles." → Exposures to the vendor's style factors are near zero.
  • "Bias stat on the optimized book is 1.4." → Realized risk ran 40% above forecast for the portfolio that matters.
  • "That's a stat factor, it'll rotate." → A PCA factor with no stable label.
  • "The optimizer found a factor we don't model." → A hidden common bet drove returns.
  • "Vol half-life is too long for this tape." → Forecasts lag the current regime.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Do you trade on a vendor model, your own, or both?
  2. What share of your risk is factor versus specific?
  3. What is your bias statistic on optimized portfolios, not just the live book?
  4. How do you handle alpha factors that are not in the risk model?
  5. 🔒 Which statistical factors do you add on top of the fundamental ones?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the factor model, the regression, Newey–West and the bias band

With \(r_t = X_t f_t + u_t\), \(\operatorname{cov}(f) = F\) and diagonal \(\operatorname{cov}(u) = \Delta\):

\[ \Sigma = X F X^\top + \Delta, \qquad \sigma^2(h) = (X^\top h)^\top F (X^\top h) + \textstyle\sum_i h_i^2 \Delta_{ii}. \]

Daily weighted least squares with \(W = \operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\text{cap}_i})\):

\[ \hat f_t = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W r_t . \]

A country factor plus all industry dummies makes X collinear; USE4 constrains cap-weighted industry returns to sum to zero [Reported].

H-day variance from autocorrelated daily returns (Newey–West, L lags):

\[ \sigma_H^2 = H\Big[\gamma_0 + 2\sum_{l=1}^{L}\Big(1 - \tfrac{l}{L+1}\Big)\gamma_l\Big]. \]

Volatility-regime adjustment, roughly: EWMA-average the daily cross-sectional bias \(B_t^2 = \tfrac1K\sum_k (f_{k,t}/\sigma_{k,t})^2\) and scale all factor volatilities by its square root [Reported].

Bias band: for i.i.d. standard normal \(z_t\), the sample standard deviation has standard error \(\approx 1/\sqrt{2T}\), so 95% lies in \(1 \pm \sqrt{2/T}\); fat tails widen it.

Cost: a dense covariance needs \(O(N^2)\) memory and \(O(N^3)\) to invert; the factor form needs \(O(NK)\) and inverts in \(O(NK^2)\) (Woodbury).

docs.title: Transaction cost and impact models
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A cost model prices a trade in advance: fees + half-spread + market impact, plus borrow and the opportunity cost of skipped trades. The optimizer nets it against alpha.
  • Impact is concave. The square-root law, impact ≈ Y·σ·√(Q/V) with Y of order 1, holds across markets and decades. Double the order: +41% cost per share, 2.8× the dollars.
  • Trading 5% of daily volume in a 2%-volatility stock costs roughly 15–30 bps of impact, plus a few bps of spread and commission.
  • Optimizers use a 3/2-power penalty (square-root law) or a quadratic one (linear impact: simpler, wrong at the extremes). Calibrate on your own fills: AQR's live trades cost an order of magnitude less than academic estimates.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: portfolio · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) What will this trade cost, and how does cost grow with size and speed? Inputs → Outputs size Q, daily volume V, daily volatility σ, spread, fees, borrow → cost per name (bps, $) and a convex optimizer penalty Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Factor-residual · Reversal · ML short-horizon · Stat arb · Pairs · Intraday patterns · Momentum · Factor investing · Value, quality, low vol · Fundamental signals · Revisions · Event-driven · Flow-driven · Trend following Latency / compute regime overnight batch calibration; microseconds per name inside a seconds-long optimizer solve Key parameters Y 0.5–1; exponent δ 0.4–0.7; ADV and σ windows 20–60 days; optimizer cost multiplier 1–3×; commission 0.5–2¢/share Main failure modes alpha leaking into calibration; stale ADV on event days; crowding; linear models at large size Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Costs are the cost of goods sold for alpha. Explicit costs (commissions, fees) are known in advance. The half-spread is paid each time you cross the quote. Market impact is the hidden line: your demand moves the price. Part is temporary (consumed liquidity that partly returns), part permanent (what the market infers from your flow). Add borrow fees on shorts and opportunity cost: alpha lost on trades skipped or finished late.

Impact is concave because liquidity is latent. Most sellers are not in the visible book; they arrive as price moves. Tóth et al. (2011) derive the square-root law from this.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Nightly, per name: ADV V (20–60-day median), daily σ, average quoted spread, price, borrow fee.
  2. Cost in bps = commission ÷ price + half-spread + Y·σ·(Q/V)^δ, for an order worked over about a day.
  3. Give the optimizer a convex penalty per name: linear (spread, fees) plus 3/2-power (impact).
  4. Monthly, refit Y and check δ on your own parent orders, binned by participation.
import numpy as np

def expected_cost_bps(q_shares, adv_shares, sigma_daily, spread_bps, price,
                      Y=0.7, delta=0.5, commission_per_share=0.005):
    """Pre-trade cost of a parent order worked over about one day, bps of notional.
    Y here is fitted to average fill slippage (about 2/3 of the peak impact)."""
    participation = q_shares / adv_shares
    commission = 1e4 * commission_per_share / price        # explicit, known in advance
    half_spread = 0.5 * spread_bps                          # paid when crossing
    impact = 1e4 * Y * sigma_daily * participation**delta   # concave in size
    return commission + half_spread + impact

def optimizer_cost(dw, nav, price, adv_shares, sigma_daily, spread_bps, Y=0.7):
    """$ cost of trading dw (fraction of NAV) per name: linear + 3/2-power terms.
    Both are convex, so a conic solver handles them (cvxpy: cp.power(cp.abs(dw), 1.5))."""
    a = 0.5 * spread_bps / 1e4                              # $ per $ traded
    b = Y * sigma_daily * np.sqrt(nav / (adv_shares * price))
    return nav * (a * np.abs(dw) + b * np.abs(dw) ** 1.5)   # summed over names

def calibrate_Y(slip_bps, spread_bps, sigma_daily, participation, n_bins=10):
    """Fit Y from your parent orders (slippage vs arrival, + = cost).
    Bin by participation and use medians: one order is mostly price noise."""
    y = (slip_bps - 0.5 * spread_bps) / (1e4 * sigma_daily)    # impact in units of sigma
    x = np.sqrt(participation)
    edges = np.quantile(x, np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1))
    xb = np.array([np.median(x[(x >= lo) & (x <= hi)]) for lo, hi in zip(edges, edges[1:])])
    yb = np.array([np.median(y[(x >= lo) & (x <= hi)]) for lo, hi in zip(edges, edges[1:])])
    Y_hat = (xb @ yb) / (xb @ xb)                           # least squares through the origin
    delta_hat = np.polyfit(np.log(xb**2), np.log(np.maximum(yb, 1e-6)), 1)[0]
    return Y_hat, delta_hat                                 # expect delta_hat near 0.5

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. $50 stock, ADV 4M shares ($200M), σ = 2% a day (200 bps), spread 4 bps, commission 0.5¢. Buy 5% of ADV: 200,000 shares, $10M.

  • √0.05 = 0.2236. Peak impact = Y × 200 × 0.2236 = 22.4 bps (Y = 0.5) to 44.7 bps (Y = 1).
  • At a steady rate the average fill pays 2/3 of the peak (Go deeper): 14.9–29.8 bps.
  • Half-spread 2 bps if every fill crosses; commission 1 bp.
  • Total ≈ 18–33 bps: $18,000–$33,000.

Scaling (peak impact, Y = 0.5) vs a linear model matched at 5%:

% of ADV Square-root Linear Square-root $ 1% ($2M) 10.0 bps 4.5 bps $2,000 5% ($10M) 22.4 bps 22.4 bps $22,400 20% ($40M) 44.7 bps 89.4 bps $178,900

Four times the size: twice the cost per share, eight times the dollars. The linear model halves small-trade costs and doubles large ones.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Y: "of order unity" (Tóth et al.) [Verified]; desks quote 0.5–1 [Lore]. Peak-impact and average-slippage fits differ by a third.
  • δ: published 0.4–0.7 [Verified]; keep 0.5 unless your bins disagree.
  • Duration: slower is cheaper; Bacry et al. find a 1/T^0.25 duration factor [Verified]. On earnings and rebalance days use event forecasts of V and σ.
  • Cost multiplier: 1–3×, tuned to maximize backtested net Sharpe, since forecast alpha is overconfident [Lore].
  • Borrow: annual fee × days ÷ 252; general collateral 0.25–0.5%, hard-to-borrow 5–50%+ [Lore] (shorting and financing).

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: linear temporary and permanent impact, so quadratic costs (Almgren & Chriss 2000). That gives Gârleanu and Pedersen's closed-form partial trading rule [Verified] (P6).
  • Measured impact is concave: exponent ≈ 0.6 on about 700,000 Citigroup US orders (Almgren et al. 2005); 0.5–0.6 on nearly 500,000 CFM futures trades [Verified] (both per Tóth et al.). About 400,000 European metaorders confirm the square root [Verified] (Bacry et al.).
  • Contested at the edges: a logarithm fits almost five orders of magnitude of size, the square root about two [Verified] (Zarinelli et al.); tiny orders look linear [Verified] (Bucci et al.).
  • Academic estimates are too high: on $1.7 trillion of AQR live trades (21 markets, 19 years), costs were an order of magnitude below earlier studies; a calibrated model beat the literature out of sample [Verified]. AQR trades patiently with limit orders, so this may not transfer [Reported].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Realized ÷ predicted ≈ 1.0 per bucket (participation, volatility, sector) over hundreds of orders; a trend across participation buckets means a wrong exponent.
  • Model error at speed: in Lab 16 the fastest schedule costs 241.8 bps under linear impact, 83.9 bps under matched square-root impact (synthetic lab result). Lab 15 uses a simple cost model in a trade-toward-target rule.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Alpha in the calibration: you buy expected winners, so slippage includes alpha and fitted impact runs high. Subtract expected alpha or market-adjust.
  • Crowding: others on your side (August 2007) push impact past the model.
  • Accumulation: daily trading in one name stacks impact; on average it relaxes to only 2/3 of peak [Verified] (Zarinelli et al.).
  • Optimizer exploits errors: underestimated names get traded most.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "What's impact at 10% of ADV?" → cost of a standard-size order.
  • "We run costs at 1.5×." → deliberate overcharge against overconfident alpha.
  • "Impact is three-halves in dollars." → total cost ∝ size^1.5.
  • "Y came in at 0.6." → refit square-root coefficient.
  • "Half that slippage was our alpha." → the price moved because the signal was right.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Is Y fitted to peak impact or average slippage?
  2. How do you strip your own alpha out of the calibration?
  3. 3/2-power or quadratic penalty in the optimizer, and why?
  4. Where does realized cost diverge from the model?
  5. 🔒 What cost multiplier do you run?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: average fill cost and the optimal trade size

Peak impact \(I(Q) = Y\sigma\sqrt{Q/V}\). At a constant rate, the fill after fraction \(x\) pays \(I(xQ)\), so on average

\[ \int_0^1 Y\sigma\sqrt{xQ/V}\,dx = \tfrac{2}{3}\,I(Q), \qquad \text{dollars} \propto Q^{3/2}. \]

Fair-pricing theory predicts permanent impact of about \(\tfrac{2}{3}I(Q)\) (Farmer et al. 2013).

One trade, gain \(\alpha\) per dollar, cost \(b\,q^{3/2}\):

\[ q^* = \left(\frac{2\alpha}{3b}\right)^2, \qquad \text{cost}(q^*) = \tfrac{2}{3}\,\alpha q^* . \]

At the optimum impact eats two-thirds of gross alpha (half under quadratic costs). A linear term \(a|q|\) adds a no-trade band: trade only if \(|\alpha| > a\). Summed over names, these are second-order cone terms in the MVO objective.

docs.title: Auction, close and dark-liquidity algos
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • The close is about 9% of US notional, about 20% on rebalance days. Close algos size MOC/LOC orders before the cutoff (NYSE 3:50 p.m., Nasdaq 3:55 p.m.), then react to the imbalance.
  • After the cutoff you may only add on the side that offsets the imbalance, which is exactly when the auction pays a price concession.
  • Dark algos rest midpoint pegs and conditional orders across dark pools and block venues, using minimum fill sizes against probing.
  • Every dark fill trades fill probability against adverse selection: judge venues by markouts, not fill rates. Leakage is the hidden cost; regulators have fined dark-pool operators up to $84.3M.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: execution · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How much of an order should go to the close and to non-displayed liquidity, and how do I get those fills without being picked off? Inputs → Outputs parent order, auction volume forecast, imbalance feed, venue fill rates and markouts → MOC/LOC and offset orders, dark child orders Used by strategies Auctions and closing liquidity · Flow-driven · ETF and index arbitrage · Event-driven · Cross-sectional alpha · Factor investing · Fundamental signals Latency / compute regime seconds for close decisions (imbalance updates about every second); milliseconds for dark routing Key parameters auction cap 10–20% of forecast print; close share of parent 10–30% (100% if close-benchmarked); minimum fill 1–5% of order; markouts 1 s–5 min Main failure modes imbalance on your side; no NYSE cancels after 3:58 p.m.; pinging; stale midpoints; overfills Lab Lab 17

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Large orders want liquidity without advertising it. The close is a scheduled call auction: one price, huge volume, and the official benchmark for index funds and NAVs (mechanics in order types and auctions). Dark pools are continuous, non-displayed books, usually crossing at the midpoint. Both hide your order from the lit book. Both carry a selection problem: the fills you get are not a random sample of the fills you wanted.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Forecast auction volume: median of recent closing prints, scaled up on rebalance days.
  2. Size: the benchmark sets the close fraction (everything for a close-benchmarked trade; the close's slice of the volume curve for VWAP). Cap it at 10–20% of the forecast print [Lore]; trade the rest earlier. Submit MOC, or LOC to bound price, before the cutoff.
  3. React: if the imbalance opposes you, add offsetting LOC, Nasdaq imbalance-only or NYSE closing-offset orders. If it is on your side, you cannot add.
  4. Dark: score venues by fill rate and post-fill markout; rest midpoint pegs with minimum fill sizes, and conditionals at block venues, firming up only if still needed. Cap total resting size to bound overfills.
import numpy as np

def size_close_order(remaining, side, close_frac, auction_hist,
                     rebalance_day=False, max_auction_pct=0.15):
    """Signed shares to send MOC/LOC before the cutoff (NYSE 3:50, Nasdaq 3:55 pm ET).
    side: +1 buy, -1 sell. auction_hist: recent closing-auction volumes."""
    forecast = np.median(auction_hist) * (2.5 if rebalance_day else 1.0)
    want = close_frac * remaining                         # what the benchmark asks for
    return side * min(want, max_auction_pct * forecast)   # never dominate the print

def react_to_imbalance(side, unfilled, imbalance, max_offset_pct=0.25):
    """After the cutoff only orders that OFFSET the imbalance are accepted.
    imbalance: signed shares (+ = buy imbalance). Returns extra LOC shares."""
    if np.sign(imbalance) == -side:                       # other side is crowded:
        return side * min(unfilled, max_offset_pct * abs(imbalance))  # supply it
    return 0                                              # our side: cannot add

def allocate_dark(remaining, venues, max_dark_pct=0.5, min_fill_frac=0.02):
    """Split resting midpoint and conditional orders across dark venues.
    venues: dicts with name, fill_rate, half_spread_bps, block flag, and
    markout_bps (signed, + = price moved our way after our fills)."""
    edge = np.array([v["half_spread_bps"] + v["markout_bps"] for v in venues])
    score = np.maximum(edge, 0.0) * np.array([v["fill_rate"] for v in venues])
    if score.sum() == 0:
        return {}                                         # nothing worth resting dark
    budget = max_dark_pct * remaining                     # caps worst-case overfill
    min_qty = int(min_fill_frac * remaining)              # small fills leak information
    alloc = {}
    for v, s in zip(venues, score):
        qty = int(budget * s / score.sum())
        if qty >= min_qty:
            alloc[v["name"]] = dict(qty=qty, min_qty=min_qty,
                                    conditional=v.get("block", False))
    return alloc

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Buy 400,000 shares of a $40 stock, 30% meant for the close; the median closing print is 360,000 shares.

Close. Want 0.30 × 400,000 = 120,000; cap 0.15 × 360,000 = 54,000 MOC; the other 66,000 join the afternoon schedule. At 3:50 p.m. NYSE shows a 500,000-share sell imbalance with 80,000 shares still unfilled. Offset: min(80,000, 0.25 × 500,000) = 80,000 LOC. The close prints $39.90, 10¢ under the last sale, saving $13,400 on 134,000 shares. A buy imbalance would have pushed the MOC fill up, with nothing to add.

Dark. Midday, 200,000 shares left; spread 2¢ (5 bps), so a midpoint fill saves 2.5 bps.

Venue Fill rate Markout Net edge Allocation A (midpoint pool) 0.10 −1.0 bps +1.5 bps 78,947 B (midpoint pool) 0.30 −4.0 bps −1.5 bps 0 C (block, conditional) 0.02 −0.5 bps +2.0 bps 21,052

Budget 100,000; minimum fill 4,000. Venue B fills most and is dropped: its fills are followed by a 4 bps adverse move, more than the spread saved.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Auction cap: lower in crowded rebalance names, higher for close-benchmarked flow [Lore].
  • LOC limits: a few bps through the 3:50 price cap the damage from late swings.
  • Minimum fill: higher blocks probing but lowers fill odds; block venues set it per order [Verified] (Cboe BIDS).
  • Markout horizon: seconds catch latency arbitrage, minutes informed flow (M5).

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Scale of the close: record 9.44% of notional in Q2 2024; about 20% on rebalance and expiry days [Reported].
  • Pecking order: midpoint dark pools first (cheap, slow), other dark next, lit last; urgency moves traders down the order [Verified] (Menkveld, Yueshen & Zhu).
  • Dark selection: in Zhu's model, informed traders crowd one side, so they fill less in the dark, and dark pools attract the less informed [Verified].
  • Venue defenses: Nasdaq's M-ELO midpoint order must rest before trading, 500 ms at launch and 10 ms from May 2020, a cut Nasdaq estimated cost 0.10 bps of markout [Verified].
  • Block venues: Cboe BIDS takes firm or conditional orders with minimum sizes and counterparty scorecards [Verified].
  • Leakage is real: Barclays ($70M) and Credit Suisse ($84.3M) settled SEC and New York charges over dark-pool representations in 2016; ITG paid $20.3M in 2015 for a secret desk using subscribers' order information [Verified].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Close: slippage vs the official close; your share of the print; overnight reversion of the close (large = you moved it).
  • Dark: per-venue fill rate vs markout, refreshed weekly.
  • Leakage: drift after order start vs comparable orders not shown dark.
  • Lab 17 builds the volume curve whose closing slice is sized here.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Late imbalance swings, with NYSE cancels barred after 3:58 p.m. [Verified].
  • Pinging: small IOC probes find resting orders.
  • Stale midpoints: a lagging NBBO view gets you filled at an old midpoint.
  • Overfills and missed firm-ups that downgrade your scorecard.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're 12% of the expected print." → auction participation.
  • "The imbalance flipped at 3:57." → late swing in the closing book.
  • "That pool's markouts are ugly at one second." → latency-sensitive counterparties.
  • "Send conditionals, firm up on invites." → block-venue workflow.
  • "We got paid to supply the imbalance." → offset order filled at a concession.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. How do you forecast closing volume on rebalance days?
  2. What share of the print will you be?
  3. Do you rank dark venues by fill rate, markout, or both?
  4. How do you detect pinging?
  5. 🔒 What markout cut-off removes a venue?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: when to rest dark, and why fills are adversely selected

Rest dark one interval (fill probability \(p\), half-spread \(h\), markout given a fill \(m_f\), drift cost \(d\) if unfilled) or cross now:

\[ \mathbb{E}[\text{dark}] = p\,(h + m_f) - (1-p)\,d \quad\text{vs}\quad \mathbb{E}[\text{lit}] = -h . \]

The trap: \(m_f = \mathbb{E}[m \mid \text{fill}] < \mathbb{E}[m]\), because you fill most when someone better informed wants the other side. Estimate \(m_f\) from your own fills by venue.

The auction uncross maximizes matched volume \(\min(B(p), S(p))\) over price \(p\), so an imbalance moves the price until offsetting supply covers it.

docs.title: Execution algorithms: overview
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • An execution algo turns one parent order into thousands of child orders through three layers: a scheduler (how much by when), placement (post or take, size, price) and a smart order router (where).
  • Families differ mainly in the benchmark they chase: TWAP, VWAP, POV, implementation shortfall (arrival), target close, liquidity-seeking, pegged.
  • Choose by size (% of ADV), urgency (alpha decay, risk) and benchmark; the benchmark can make a bad choice look good.
  • Lab 17 (synthetic, 10% of ADV in a day): expected cost 12.8–17.9 bps by schedule, against a shortfall SD of about 120 bps.
  • About 40% of US buy-side equity flow runs through algos; 36% of desks use algo wheels (2025) [Reported].

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: execution · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which algorithm, benchmark and settings should a parent order get? Inputs → Outputs parent order, % of ADV, volatility, alpha half-life, benchmark, limits → algo, parameters, child orders Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Stat arb · Factor-residual · Momentum · Factor investing · Value, quality, low vol · Fundamental signals · Event-driven · Flow-driven · Trend following Latency / compute regime schedule re-planned every 1–5 min; placement seconds to ms; routing µs to ms Key parameters urgency; maximum participation 5–30% of volume [Lore]; start and end time; limit price; dark and auction allowances; randomization Main failure modes wrong benchmark; leakage; over-constrained orders; small-sample broker rankings Lab Lab 17

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: The portfolio manager decides what to buy; execution decides how. An agency algo is a contractor: it takes a parent order and instructions and bills you in slippage. It fights three costs at once. Going fast pays market impact; going slow carries price risk and lets alpha decay; being predictable leaks information that others trade against. Each family is a different compromise between them.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Pre-trade: estimate cost and risk (P5).
  2. Choose family and benchmark (table below).
  3. Schedule (E2, E3), place (post or cross, dark: E5), route (E4).
  4. Adapt to fills, volume and price; measure (E6).
import numpy as np

def choose_algo(pct_adv, alpha_half_life_days, benchmark, urgency="medium"):
    """First-pass algo choice. Not in the lab; thresholds are rules of thumb [Lore]."""
    if benchmark == "close":
        return "target_close"                    # E5: index funds, NAV-benchmarked flow
    if urgency == "high" or alpha_half_life_days < 0.5:
        return "is_arrival_high"                 # E3: front-load, accept impact
    if pct_adv > 0.20:
        return "multi_day_pov_plus_dark"         # E5 blocks; spread risk over days
    if benchmark == "vwap" or alpha_half_life_days > 5:
        return "vwap"                            # E2: passive, follows the volume curve
    return "is_arrival_medium"

def run_parent_order(order, algo, market):
    """Three layers per bin: scheduler -> placement -> router (all names illustrative)."""
    plan = vwap_schedule(market.volume_curve, order.qty)  # Lab 17; TWAP = flat curve
    filled = 0.0
    for t in market.bins():
        if algo == "pov":                                # Lab 17: printed volume only
            want = pov_child_order(order.rate, market.others_volume_so_far(t),
                                   filled, order.qty - filled)
        else:
            want = plan[: t + 1].sum() - filled          # catch up to the schedule
        if order.limit_px is not None and market.mid(t) > order.limit_px:
            continue                                     # buy limit: pause, risk non-completion
        want = min(want, order.max_pct * market.expected_volume(t))   # participation cap
        child = place(want, market.book(t), passive_share=0.6,
                      size_jitter=0.3)                   # post vs cross; randomize sizes
        filled += sum(f.qty for f in smart_order_route(child, market.venues(t)))  # E4
    return filled
Family Slices by Typical use Main weakness Used by (2025) TWAP the clock illiquid names overtrades midday 38% VWAP forecast volume curve low urgency benchmark absorbs own impact 81% POV live volume (participation rate) size matters more than time chases spikes; may not finish 74% IS / arrival urgency, front-loaded alpha-driven orders pays impact for speed 51% Target close ramp into the auction index funds moves the close 56% Liquidity-seeking contra-side blocks, dark large % of ADV adverse selection 74% Pegged resting at bid or midpoint patient, small non-fill n/a

Share of long-only desks using each type: The TRADE 2025 survey, mostly European respondents [Reported].

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. $50 stock, ADV 5M shares, volatility 2% (200 bps) a day; square-root impact, Y = 0.5, average fill 2/3 of peak (P5); risk SD ≈ σ√(T/3) over T days (E6).

Order Choice Why 25,000 shares (0.5% ADV), 2-hour alpha IS high urgency small; decay beats impact 500,000 (10%), index add target close, auction slice capped the close is the benchmark 2,000,000 (40%), slow value signal multi-day POV plus dark too big for one day

For the 40% order:

  • One day: peak impact 0.5 × 200 × √0.40 = 63 bps; average 42 bps ($420,000 on $100M). Risk SD 200 × √(1/3) = 115 bps.
  • Four days at 10%: peak 0.5 × 200 × √0.10 = 31.6 bps, average 21 bps if impact fades overnight (optimistic). Risk SD 200 × √(4/3) = 231 bps.

Spreading halves expected cost and doubles risk: the Almgren-Chriss trade-off (E3).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Urgency maps to a risk-aversion setting [Verified] (IBKR).
  • Participation cap: IBKR's POV and VWAP accept up to 50% [Verified]; institutions run 5–20% [Lore].
  • Limit price bounds damage but risks non-completion; dark and auction allowances: E5.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Benchmarks: early cost studies used VWAP (1988); implementation shortfall was defined the same year [Verified].
  • Layering: scheduling, then tactical placement, then routing is the textbook architecture [Reported] (Lehalle and Laruelle).
  • Broker suites: a few branded strategies on a shared engine; IBKR's include VWAP, TWAP, POV, Arrival Price, Close Price and Dark Ice [Verified]. Large clients get custom variants [Lore].
  • Adoption: nearly 40% of North American buy-side flow runs through algos; algo wheels are used by 36% of desks, up 4 points [Reported] (Coalition Greenwich, 2026-01).
  • Algo wheels: orders in a bucket (say, VWAP, 1–5% of ADV) go to brokers at random under preset weights; TCA compares like with like and reweights quarterly [Lore].
  • Leakage: high-frequency traders first lean against large institutional orders, then trade with the most informed ones [Verified] (van Kervel and Menkveld 2019); hence randomized sizes and timing [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Shortfall vs arrival and vs the pre-trade estimate, by algo and size bucket; completion; information leakage (drift beyond modeled impact).
  • Synthetic lab result (Lab 17, 500 days, buy 10% of ADV): expected cost TWAP 14.0, VWAP 12.8, POV 13.1, close-heavy 17.9 bps; shortfall SD about 120 bps; POV finished on only 61% of days. Real orders this size cost nearer 20 bps [Estimate] (square-root law), with per-order SDs of 50–150 bps (E6).
  • Telling VWAP from TWAP (1.3 bps) across unrelated orders takes about 77,000 orders.

Lab 17, synthetic: vs arrival (left) all four drown in noise; vs interval VWAP (middle) they look tight; costs by component (right).

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Wrong benchmark: a target-close order scored 0.0 ± 48 bps against the close but cost the most vs arrival in Lab 17.
  • Over-constraint: tight limits and low caps leave shares unfilled.
  • Predictability: fixed slices on a fixed clock are easy to detect.
  • Conflicts: routing to the broker's own pool; see the dark-pool settlements in E5.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Put it in VWAP, 15% max." → volume-curve schedule with a participation cap.
  • "It's a 40% of ADV name, take three days." → spread size over days.
  • "Arrival, high urgency, the signal is fast." → IS algo, front-loaded.
  • "We're on the wheel for anything under 5% of ADV." → randomized broker allocation.
  • "We got footprinted." → leakage: someone read the pattern.
  • "Beat VWAP, lost to arrival." → the benchmark flattered the trade.

docs.text:

  2. How do you map signal half-life to urgency?
  3. How do you check dark fills aren't leaking?
  4. How many orders before you trust a wheel's ranking?
  5. Broker algos or your own?
  6. 🔒 What does in-house execution save?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the cost-risk trade-off and why benchmarks need large samples

For \(Q\) shares over \(T\) days with square-root impact and a steady schedule:

\[ \mathbb{E}[\text{cost}] \approx \tfrac{2}{3} Y\sigma\sqrt{\frac{Q}{V\,T}}, \qquad \mathrm{SD} \approx \sigma\sqrt{T/3} , \]

assuming impact decays between days. Slower is cheaper but riskier; urgency picks the point. To detect a gap \(\delta\) between algos with per-order SDs \(s_1, s_2\) at two standard errors with unpaired orders:

\[ n \approx \left(\frac{2\sqrt{s_1^2 + s_2^2}}{\delta}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{2 \times 175}{1.26}\right)^2 \approx 77{,}000 . \]

docs.title: Implementation shortfall and Almgren-Chriss
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Implementation shortfall (Perold 1988) charges execution against the decision price, unfilled shares included. IS algos minimize it.
  • Almgren-Chriss minimizes E[IS] + λ·Var[IS]: impact punishes speed, risk punishes waiting. Holdings decay like sinh; λ = 0 is TWAP.
  • Lab 16, $500M at 50% of a $1B ADV over 5 days (synthetic): TWAP expects 46 bps, SD 254; a risk-averse schedule 96 bps, SD 110.
  • Real IS algos expose urgency, cap participation, adapt to prices and route dark and lit.
  • Under square-root impact the fastest schedule costs 84 bps, not the linear model's 242. On single orders TWAP beats the risk-averse schedule 61% of the time.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: execution · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How fast should a large order be worked when speed costs impact and delay costs risk? Inputs → Outputs shares X, horizon T, ADV, σ, spread, impact η and γ, urgency λ, cap → holdings per interval, expected cost and SD, the frontier Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Factor-residual · Stat arb · Pairs · Momentum · Factor investing · Value, quality, low vol · Fundamental signals · Revisions · Event-driven · Flow-driven · Trend following Latency / compute regime milliseconds: closed form at arrival, re-solved every few minutes; impact refit monthly Key parameters λ 1e-9 to 1e-6 per $ (Lab 16: half-lives 4.8 to 0.15 days); participation cap 10–30% of volume; horizon hours to days; 10–80 intervals Main failure modes linear impact at speed; arbitrary λ; ignored alpha and overnight gaps; leakage; judging single orders Lab Lab 16

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Implementation shortfall compares the real portfolio with a paper one filled at the decision price; TCA splits it afterwards. Beforehand, the question is speed. Sell fast and you pay market impact. Sell slowly and the unsold block is an unhedged position. The Almgren-Chriss model prices both in dollars: one schedule per risk aversion λ, tracing a frontier of expected cost vs standard deviation. The client picks a point.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Benchmark: record the decision price.
  2. Calibrate: daily σ in $/share, temporary impact η (cost per unit of trading speed), permanent impact γ (lasting price move per share). Lab 16 anchors them to the square-root law: 20 bps at 10% of ADV, and 50 bps of permanent impact once the whole order is done.
  3. Pick λ from the client's urgency.
  4. Schedule: urgency κ ≈ √(λσ²/η); holdings x(t) = X·sinh(κ(T−t))/sinh(κT); trade n_k = x_{k−1} − x_k per interval.
  5. Report E and SD against TWAP's; check peak participation against the cap.
  6. Execute and re-solve on the remaining shares each interval.
import numpy as np

# Units: shares, $, trading days. Sell program; a buy is the mirror image.
# Execution price = S - epsilon - eta * (shares per day); S falls gamma per share sold.
def ac_trajectory(X, T, n, sigma, eta, gamma, lam):
    """Lab 16: Almgren-Chriss holdings x_0..x_n for selling X shares in n intervals."""
    tau = T / n
    t = np.arange(n + 1) * tau
    eta_tilde = eta - 0.5 * gamma * tau          # discrete-time correction from the paper
    if lam <= 0:
        return X * (1.0 - t / T)                 # risk-neutral: straight line = TWAP
    kappa_tilde_sq = lam * sigma**2 / eta_tilde
    kappa = np.arccosh(0.5 * kappa_tilde_sq * tau**2 + 1.0) / tau   # urgency, 1/day
    return X * np.sinh(kappa * (T - t)) / np.sinh(kappa * T)

def ac_cost_variance(holdings, T, sigma, eta, gamma, epsilon=0.0):
    """Lab 16: expected shortfall E ($) and variance V ($^2) of ANY sell schedule."""
    x = np.asarray(holdings, dtype=float)
    tau = T / (len(x) - 1)
    trades = -np.diff(x)                         # n_k: shares sold in interval k
    eta_tilde = eta - 0.5 * gamma * tau
    expected = (0.5 * gamma * x[0] ** 2          # permanent: identical for every schedule
                + epsilon * np.abs(trades).sum() # half-spread
                + eta_tilde / tau * np.sum(trades**2))   # temporary: punishes speed
    variance = sigma**2 * tau * np.sum(x[1:] ** 2)       # risk: punishes waiting
    return expected, variance

def pre_trade_report(X, T, n, S0, sigma, eta, gamma, epsilon, lam, adv, cap=0.25):
    """Not in the lab: the numbers an IS algo shows before it starts."""
    hold = ac_trajectory(X, T, n, sigma, eta, gamma, lam)
    E, V = ac_cost_variance(hold, T, sigma, eta, gamma, epsilon)
    peak = np.max(-np.diff(hold)) / (T / n) / adv    # first-interval rate, share of ADV
    bps = 1e4 / (X * S0)
    return dict(cost_bps=E * bps, sd_bps=np.sqrt(V) * bps,
                peak_pct_adv=100 * peak, breaches_cap=peak > cap)

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Lab 16's calibration (synthetic): sell X = 10M shares at $50 ($500M, 1 bp = $50,000), ADV 20M shares, T = 5 days in 50 intervals (τ = 0.1 day), σ = $1.00 per √day (2%), half-spread ε = $0.0075, η = 5×10⁻⁸, γ = 2.5×10⁻⁸.

TWAP by hand (200,000 shares per interval):

  • Permanent: ½γX² = 0.5 × 2.5×10⁻⁸ × 10¹⁴ = $1.25M = 25.0 bps.
  • Temporary: η̃ = η − ½γτ = 4.875×10⁻⁸; (η̃/τ) × Σn² = 4.875×10⁻⁷ × 50 × (2×10⁵)² = $0.975M = 19.5 bps.
  • Spread: εX = $75,000 = 1.5 bps. Total 46.0 bps, $2.3M.
  • Risk: σ²τΣx² = 0.1 × 10¹⁴ × 16.17 → SD $12.7M = 254 bps, dwarfing the impact.

Risk-averse, λ = 10⁻⁷. κ ≈ √(10⁻⁷ × 1 / 5×10⁻⁸) = 1.41 per day (1.43 with the discrete formula), a half-life of ln 2 ÷ 1.43 = 0.48 days. About 1 − e^(−1.43) = 76% is sold on day 1, and the first interval runs at 67% of ADV.

Schedule (Lab 16) E[IS] SD 95th pct E[IS], square-root impact Peak rate TWAP 46 bps ($2.3M) 254 bps 465 bps 47 bps 10% ADV AC λ = 10⁻⁸ 51 bps 197 bps 377 bps 49 bps 23% AC λ = 10⁻⁷ 96 bps ($4.8M) 110 bps 277 bps 61 bps 67% AC λ = 10⁻⁶ 242 bps ($12.1M) 52 bps 328 bps 84 bps 181% Front-loaded, 50% day 1 57 bps 186 bps 365 bps 50 bps 25%

λ = 10⁻⁷ pays $2.5M more expected cost to cut the standard deviation by $7.2M. Whether that is worth it is the client's call, not the model's.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• λ is unobservable: desks map urgency labels to half-lives, or pick the frontier point that fits a dollar risk budget [Lore].
  • η and γ: fit on your own fills (P5). The paper's rule of thumb (10% of daily volume moves price one spread) gives far less permanent impact at today's spreads than square-root fits [Reported].
  • Participation cap: 10–30% of volume [Lore]; binds first in fast schedules.
  • Horizon: alpha decay and the close; multi-day orders carry overnight gaps.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Benchmark: Perold (1988) defined paper-vs-real shortfall [Verified].
  • Model: Almgren & Chriss (2000) solved the mean-variance schedule with linear impact [Verified]. Almgren (2003) extended it to power-law impact [Verified]; measured exponents are about 0.6 [Verified] (Almgren et al. 2005, per Tóth et al. 2011).
  • Products: arrival-price algos take an urgency level (Passive to Get Done), a maximum share of ADV (1–50%) and start and end times [Verified] (Interactive Brokers).
  • Adaptive: the mean-variance-optimal dynamic schedule is "aggressive in the money": it speeds up after favorable moves [Reported] (Lorenz & Almgren 2011). Desks also offer the reverse, slowing down on favorable moves [Lore].
  • Microstructure: slices post first, take dark midpoint fills (E5) and route via E4 [Lore]. Transient impact changes the optimum [Verified] (Obizhaeva & Wang 2013).

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Realized ÷ predicted cost and SD ≈ 1 by urgency bucket, over hundreds of orders.
  • Frontier: Lab 16's 40,000 simulated orders match the closed form within 0.87 standard errors; the front-loaded heuristic sits 3.4 bps above the frontier (synthetic lab result).
  • Noise: TWAP beat AC λ = 10⁻⁷ on 61% of single orders (synthetic lab result).

Lab 16, synthetic: higher λ sells faster; λ = 0 is TWAP's straight line.

Lab 16, synthetic: open circles show the same schedules under square-root impact, far below the linear frontier at high urgency.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Impact misspecification: linear impact overprices speed; fitted at one rate, it misleads at others.
  • Impossible schedules: λ = 10⁻⁶ demands 181% of ADV in its first interval.
  • Alpha ignored: an expected drift against you argues for front-loading whatever λ is.
  • Leakage: a smooth, predictable schedule invites front-running.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Run it at medium urgency, 15% max." → λ via a label, plus a participation cap.
  • "We were 40 bps behind arrival." → implementation shortfall.
  • "Front-load it, there's a leak." → drift beats risk aversion.
  • "The model says 240 bps; nobody pays that." → linear impact overprices speed.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. How do urgency settings map to λ or half-life?
  2. Is your temporary impact linear or square-root?
  3. Does the algo adapt to price moves, and in which direction?
  4. 🔒 How much of realized shortfall is your own leakage?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the Almgren-Chriss solution

Holdings \(x(t)\), speed \(v = -\dot x\), temporary cost \(\eta v\), permanent drift \(-\gamma v\):

\[ E = \tfrac12 \gamma X^2 + \eta \int_0^T v^2\,dt, \qquad V = \sigma^2 \int_0^T x^2\,dt . \]

Minimizing \(E + \lambda V\) gives \(\ddot x = \kappa^2 x\) with \(\kappa^2 = \lambda\sigma^2/\eta\):

\[ x(t) = X\,\frac{\sinh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)} . \]

Discretely, \(\tilde\eta = \eta - \gamma\tau/2\) and \(\cosh(\kappa\tau) = 1 + \tfrac12 \tilde\kappa^2 \tau^2\) with \(\tilde\kappa^2 = \lambda\sigma^2/\tilde\eta\). Sweeping \(\lambda\) traces the frontier. Cost: O(n).

docs.title: Smart order routing
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A smart order router (SOR) decides venue, order type, size and sequence for each child order, minimizing all-in cost: spread + fees − rebates + markout + non-fill cleanup.
  • Aggressive orders ping dark midpoint pools, then sweep every protected quote at once with intermarket sweep orders (ISOs). Passive orders go where fill odds, rebate and toxicity net out best.
  • Venue quality must be learned and forgotten. High fill rates often signal toxicity: in Lab 18 a fill-chasing router cost 2.83 bps vs 1.48 for a markout-aware bandit (synthetic).
  • Rules in flux (2026-11): Rule 611's repeal was proposed in June 2026; the $0.0010 access-fee cap is deferred to November 2027.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: execution · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Where, how and in what order should each child order go to get the best all-in price? Inputs → Outputs child order, protected quotes and depth, fees, latencies, learned fill rates and markouts → venue, order type and size per slice; updated venue statistics Used by strategies Fee-driven · Equity MM · ETF MM · Latency arbitrage · ETF arbitrage · Internalization · ML short-horizon · Reversal · Cross-sectional alpha Latency / compute regime microseconds to milliseconds per decision; sweep slices land within microseconds; statistics refreshed intraday Key parameters markout horizons 1 s–5 min; memory about 1,000 fills per venue; prior weight about 5; ping minimum size Main failure modes fill-chasing; stale statistics; rebate conflicts; ping leakage; quote fade Lab Lab 18

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: A US stock trades on 18 exchanges, about 33 alternative trading systems and wholesalers [Reported]. The same displayed price is not the same price: fees, fill odds and what happens after the fill differ. Routing is procurement: unit price (quote ± fee), delivery risk (fill probability), defect rate (markout). And under Regulation NMS you may not ignore a better protected quote.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Venue view: protected quotes, depth, fees, latency, learned fill rate and markout per venue and order type.
  2. Aggressive: ping dark midpoint pools with minimum-size IOCs, then send ISOs to every protected quote inside the limit, timed to arrive together. Re-route or post the rest.
  3. Passive: post where expected all-in cost is lowest.
  4. Learn: update fill rate and markout with capped memory; explore by Thompson sampling (route to the cheapest plausible venue).
  5. Comply: no trade-throughs except via ISOs, no locked quotes, regular best-execution reviews (FINRA Rule 5310).
import math
import numpy as np

def expected_all_in_cost(venue, mode, fill_prob, markout_bps, price=50.0,
                         half_spread_bps=1.0, fallback_bps=None):
    """Lab 18: expected cost (bps, + = cost) of one child order at `venue`.
    venue: {"kind": "lit" or "mid", "make", "take"} in $/share; + = fee, - = rebate."""
    fee_bps = (venue["make"] if mode == "passive" else venue["take"]) / price * 1e4
    spread_bps = 0.0 if venue["kind"] == "mid" else (   # midpoint: no spread
        -half_spread_bps if mode == "passive" else half_spread_bps)
    if fallback_bps is None:                  # finish elsewhere if we miss
        fallback_bps = {"passive": 2.6, "aggressive": 2.1}[mode]
    return fill_prob * (spread_bps + fee_bps + markout_bps) + (1 - fill_prob) * fallback_bps

def route(order, venues, stats, policy="net_of_toxicity", rng=None, markout_sd_bps=5.0):
    """Lab 18: pick a venue index; with an rng, explore by Thompson sampling."""
    mode = order["mode"]
    if policy == "fee_greedy":
        return int(np.argmin([v["make"] if mode == "passive" else v["take"] for v in venues]))
    best, best_cost = 0, math.inf
    for i, v in enumerate(venues):
        n_sent, n_fill = stats["sent"][i] + stats["prior_n"], stats["fills"][i] + stats["prior_n"]
        fill, markout = stats["fill_rate"][i], stats["markout"][i]
        if rng is not None:                   # plausible draws, wide when evidence is thin
            fill = rng.beta(1 + fill * n_sent, 1 + (1 - fill) * n_sent)
            markout = rng.normal(markout, markout_sd_bps / math.sqrt(n_fill))
        if policy == "fill_weighted":
            markout = 0.0                     # the blind spot: toxicity not priced
        cost = expected_all_in_cost(v, mode, fill, markout)
        if cost < best_cost:
            best, best_cost = i, cost
    return best

def update_stats(stats, venue, filled, markout_bps, memory=1_000):
    """Lab 18 (run with memory=1,000): running means, counts capped -> an EWMA."""
    stats["sent"][venue] = min(stats["sent"][venue] + 1, memory)
    w = 1.0 / (stats["sent"][venue] + stats["prior_n"])
    stats["fill_rate"][venue] += w * (float(filled) - stats["fill_rate"][venue])
    if filled:
        stats["fills"][venue] = min(stats["fills"][venue] + 1, memory)
        w = 1.0 / (stats["fills"][venue] + stats["prior_n"])
        stats["markout"][venue] += w * (markout_bps - stats["markout"][venue])

An aggressive buy, as step 2 runs it (illustrative):

  participant D as Dark pool
  participant X as Exchange X
  participant Z as Exchange Z
  S->>D: IOC midpoint 50.005, min 500
  D-->>S: filled 600
  S->>X: ISO buy 1,000 at 50.01
  S->>Z: ISO buy 1,400 at 50.02
  Note over S,Z: Sent together so both land before quotes fade
  X-->>S: filled 1,000
  Z-->>S: filled 1,100, 300 faded
  S->>X: Post remaining 300 at 50.01

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Lab 18's true parameters for passive orders (synthetic): $50 stock, half-spread 1 bp, cleanup 2.6 bps if unfilled. Fees: $0.0025 ÷ $50 = 0.5 bp.

Venue Fee (+) or rebate (−) Fill rate Markout True all-in What a fill-chaser sees A: maker-taker, high rebate −0.50 0.30 1.5 1.82 1.37 B: maker-taker, standard rebate −0.32 0.40 0.6 1.27 1.03 D: low-fee lit 0.00 0.35 0.5 1.52 1.34 F: toxic dark midpoint pool +0.10 0.70 3.0 2.95 0.85

Venue B by hand: 0.40 × (−1.00 − 0.32 + 0.60) + 0.60 × 2.6 = −0.29 + 1.56 = 1.27 bps.

  • Fee-greedy picks A (biggest rebate): 1.82 bps.
  • Fill-chasing ignores markouts, so F looks cheapest (0.85) and costs 2.95.
  • Net-of-toxicity picks B. If B's markout jumps to 2.4, B costs 0.40 × 1.08 + 1.56 = 1.99 and D (1.52) wins.

The lab's 0.40 bp saving over fee-greedy is about $1,980 per million shares.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Markout horizon: about 1 s exposes latency-driven counterparties; minutes expose informed flow (M5).
  • Memory: long enough to separate venues, short enough to notice change. Telling venues 0.5 bp apart takes about 770 fills each (Lab 18).
  • Ping size: larger minimums resist probing but fill less (E5).
  • Fee tiers: rebates depend on monthly volume, so the marginal share can be worth more than the average one [Lore].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Order protection: Rule 611 makes trading centers prevent trade-throughs of protected quotes, except for ISOs whose sender takes every better quote simultaneously [Verified] (17 CFR 242.611). ISOs were 46% of trades and 41% of volume in one sample [Verified] (Chakravarty et al. 2012).
  • Rule change: on 2026-06-11 the SEC proposed rescinding Rule 611 and the locked/crossed ban (Release 34-105655; comments closed 2026-08-17) [Verified]. The $0.0010 access-fee cap is deferred to the first business day of November 2027 (Release 34-105656) [Verified]. Without Rule 611, fill odds and markouts would weigh more [Estimate].
  • Learning: dark-pool allocation as censored-exploration bandit, tested on broker data [Verified] (Ganchev et al. 2010); stochastic split algorithms [Verified] (Laruelle, Lehalle & Pagès 2011).
  • Synchronized sweeps: RBC's THOR staggers sends so slices land together [Reported] (company claim).
  • Agency vs principal: agency routers owe best execution and publish Rule 606 reports; routing client limit orders for rebates worsens fills [Verified] (Battalio, Corwin & Jennings 2016). Principal routers optimize the firm's own markouts, latency and tiers [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Venue scorecards: fill rate, fade rate and markouts at 1 s, 10 s, 1 min by venue and order type.
  • Lab 18 (synthetic lab result), passive / aggressive bps: fee-greedy 1.87 / 1.71; fill-weighted 2.83 / 1.97; bandit 1.48 / 1.44; oracle 1.41 / 1.40. After B turned toxic, the memory-capped bandit cost 1.65 bps (2,800 more orders to B); the never-forgetting one 1.97 bps (16,210).

Lab 18, synthetic: pricing markouts beats both fee-greedy and fill-chasing routing.

Lab 18, synthetic: the bandit shifts flow from B to D after the break.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Fill-chasing: Lab 18's fill-weighted router sent 94% of passive orders to the toxic pool.
  • Quote fade: size vanishes mid-sweep (latency arbitrage).
  • Leakage: pings and sprayed orders reveal the parent.
  • Stale NBBO: midpoint pegs priced off a slow feed get picked off (NBBO and market data).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Sweep it with ISOs." → take every protected quote at once.
  • "That pool fills everything, which is the problem." → toxic counterparties.
  • "Ping dark before you go lit." → midpoint IOCs first.
  • "We're routing for the tier." → chasing a monthly rebate threshold.
  • "Our scorecard dropped them at one-second markouts." → latency-driven flow.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. How do you rank venues: fees, fill rate or markouts?
  2. How quickly does the router forget a venue's history?
  3. How do you time a multi-venue sweep?
  4. What changes if Rule 611 goes?
  5. 🔒 Which venues have you cut on markouts?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: all-in cost, Thompson sampling and sample size

Venue \(v\), fill probability \(p_v\), spread \(s_v\), fee \(f_v\), markout \(m_v\), cleanup \(c\):

\[ C_v = p_v\,(s_v + f_v + m_v) + (1 - p_v)\,c . \]

Thompson sampling draws \(\tilde p_v \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1 + p_v n_v,\ 1 + (1-p_v) n_v)\), \(\tilde m_v \sim N(m_v, \sigma_m^2/k_v)\) and routes to \(\arg\min_v C_v\). Separating markouts \(\delta\) apart needs

\[ k \approx \Big(\frac{1.96\,\sigma_m \sqrt{2}}{\delta}\Big)^2 = \Big(\frac{1.96 \times 5 \times 1.414}{0.5}\Big)^2 \approx 770 \]

fills per venue.

docs.title: Transaction cost analysis
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Transaction cost analysis (TCA) is variance analysis for trading: pre-trade forecasts cost and picks the strategy; post-trade measures, attributes and recalibrates.
  • The benchmark decides the verdict. Implementation shortfall vs the decision price (Perold 1988) captures everything; VWAP is easy to beat by trading with the market and can hide large costs.
  • Decompose shortfall into delay, spread, market move, impact and timing, opportunity cost and fees, each with an owner.
  • One order is mostly noise: per-order standard deviations of 50–150 bps against broker differences of a few bps mean hundreds to thousands of orders per comparison. Randomize allocation (algo wheels) and market-adjust.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: execution · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) What did execution cost, against which benchmark, why, and which broker or algo does it better? Inputs → Outputs parent orders, timestamped fills with venues, mids, VWAPs, closes, index returns, fees → shortfall components, benchmark slippages, markouts, league tables with error bars Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Factor-residual · Reversal · ML short-horizon · Stat arb · Momentum · Factor investing · Fundamental signals · Flow-driven · Event-driven · Trend following Latency / compute regime overnight batch (seconds per day of fills); live dashboards for orders in flight Key parameters benchmark (arrival mid at order receipt); market adjustment β × index; markout horizons 1 s–1 day; 300–3,000 orders per comparison; participation-weighted price at 10–20% Main failure modes benchmark gaming; ignoring unfilled shares; bad timestamps; small samples; hard orders routed to the best broker Lab Lab 17

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Budget vs actual: the cost model estimate is the budget; post-trade TCA is the variance bridge. Perold compares the paper portfolio (every share at the decision price, no costs) with the real one. The gap is the implementation shortfall; TCA splits it and asks: skill, market or noise?

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Stamp decision, arrival (order reaches the algo), every fill (time, price, size, venue, mid) and the end.
  2. Shortfall = paper minus real P&L, split into delay, spread, drift, opportunity and fees.
  3. Market-adjust the drift: subtract β × index return over the order's life.
  4. Benchmarks: also report slippage vs interval VWAP, the close and a participation-weighted price (VWAP over the window a 15% participation rate would need; Kissell 2014).
  5. Markouts per fill at 1 s, 1 min, 5 min and the close, by venue and order type.
  6. Aggregate notional-weighted by broker, algo, urgency and size bucket, with standard errors, and compare to the pre-trade estimate.
import numpy as np

def is_decomposition(side, order_qty, decision_px, arrival_px, fills, end_px,
                     fees=0.0, beta=1.0, index_ret=0.0):
    """Implementation shortfall of one parent order (Perold 1988), bps of decision notional.
    side: +1 buy, -1 sell. fills: list of (qty > 0, fill_px, mid_at_fill).
    end_px: values unfilled shares (close or cancel time). index_ret: market
    return from arrival to the last fill. Positive numbers are costs."""
    q, px, mid = (np.array(col, float) for col in zip(*fills))
    filled = q.sum()
    delay = side * filled * (arrival_px - decision_px)       # waited before starting
    spread = side * (q * (px - mid)).sum()                   # paid vs mid at each fill
    drift = side * (q * (mid - arrival_px)).sum()            # mid moved while we traded
    market = side * filled * arrival_px * beta * index_ret   # drift the market explains
    parts = dict(delay=delay, spread=spread, market=market,
                 impact_timing=drift - market,               # our impact plus timing/alpha
                 opportunity=side * (order_qty - filled) * (end_px - decision_px),
                 fees=fees)
    bps = {k: 1e4 * v / (order_qty * decision_px) for k, v in parts.items()}
    bps["total"] = sum(bps.values())                         # = paper P&L - real P&L
    return bps

def vwap_slippage_bps(side, fills, interval_vwap):
    """Slippage vs interval VWAP of the filled part: easy to look good on."""
    q, px, _ = (np.array(col, float) for col in zip(*fills))
    return 1e4 * side * ((q * px).sum() / q.sum() - interval_vwap) / interval_vwap

def orders_needed(sd_bps=60.0, diff_bps=5.0, z_alpha=1.96, z_power=0.84):
    """Orders per arm to detect a mean cost difference (two-sample test)."""
    return int(np.ceil(2 * (z_alpha + z_power) ** 2 * (sd_bps / diff_bps) ** 2))
