docs.text:
Illustrative. The PM decides to buy 100,000 shares at yesterday's close, $50.00 ($5M; 1 bp = $500). The algo starts at $50.10, fills 80,000 at an average $50.25 when the mid averaged $50.23, and stops at a participation cap. The close is $50.60. Commissions are $800. The market (β = 1) rose 0.10% while the order worked.

Component Calculation $ bps Delay 80,000 × (50.10 − 50.00) 8,000 16.0 Spread 80,000 × (50.25 − 50.23) 1,600 3.2 Market 80,000 × 50.10 × 0.10% 4,008 8.0 Impact and timing 80,000 × 0.13 − 4,008 6,392 12.8 Opportunity 20,000 × (50.60 − 50.00) 12,000 24.0 Fees 800 1.6 Total 32,800 65.6

Check: paper P&L = 100,000 × 0.60 = $60,000; real = 80,000 × 0.35 − 800 = $27,200; gap $32,800.

Interval VWAP was $50.28, so a VWAP report says the algo beat its benchmark by 6 bps. Shortfall says 65.6 bps went missing, most of it from not finishing. Owners: the desk (delay), the algo (spread and impact, 16 bps), the participation cap (opportunity).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Benchmark: arrival mid for alpha-driven orders; the close for index funds; VWAP only for genuinely passive orders.
  • Market adjustment: β × index or sector ETF return; cuts noise without bias.
  • Sample size: per-order standard deviation σ, difference δ: n ≈ 2(1.96 + 0.84)²(σ/δ)² per arm. At σ = 60 bps, δ = 5 bps: about 2,260 orders each; at δ = 10 bps, about 570 [Estimate].
  • Peer universes: other managers' orders of similar size and liquidity. ANcerno (formerly Abel Noser) data underpin academic studies [Verified] (Bucci et al.), but peers' urgency differs.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: Perold's shortfall [Verified] (Perold 1988).
  • Practice: brokers lead with VWAP slippage; buy-side quants anchor on market-adjusted arrival [Lore].
  • Noise: in Lab 16, TWAP beat a risk-averse schedule on 61% of single orders even though the risk-averse schedule had far lower risk (synthetic lab result).
  • Algo wheels randomize orders across brokers within a bucket, so "best broker gets the hardest orders" stops biasing the league table [Lore].
  • US rules: FINRA Rule 5310 requires firms without order-by-order review to run "regular and rigorous" reviews, at least quarterly, by security and order type [Verified]. Amended Rule 605 reports add realized spreads; compliance began 2026-08-01 [Verified].
  • EU comparison: MiFID II's firm-level "top five venues" reports (RTS 28) were deleted in the 2024 review as hardly read; ESMA told national regulators to deprioritize them in February 2024, as it had for venue reports (RTS 27) after February 2023 [Verified]. The UK dropped RTS 28 from December 2021 [Reported].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Realized ÷ pre-trade estimate ≈ 1 per bucket, with error bars.
  • Components sum to the books (zero residual).
  • Rankings that survive a bootstrap and a second period.
  • Markouts on passive fills not systematically negative at 1 minute.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Benchmark gaming: VWAP algos look good by trading with the market.
  • Dropping cancelled shares removes opportunity cost, often the biggest line.
  • Timestamps: decision time recorded late hides delay cost.
  • Selection bias: urgent orders go to trusted brokers, who then look expensive.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We beat VWAP but lost to arrival." → traded with the market, paid for it.
  • "Delay ate 15 bps before the algo started." → the desk, not the broker.
  • "What's the standard error on that league table?" → probably noise.
  • "Put it on the wheel." → randomized broker allocation.
  • "Five-minute markouts are negative." → passive fills are adversely selected.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Which benchmark is official, and who chose it?
  2. How do you charge unfilled shares?
  3. How many orders before you trust a broker comparison?
  4. Do you market-adjust?
  5. 🔒 How do realized costs feed back into your cost model and alpha haircuts?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the shortfall identity and why single orders are noise

For a buy of \(X\) shares decided at \(P_d\), fills \(q_j\) at \(p_j\) with mids \(m_j\), arrival \(P_0\), unfilled shares valued at \(P_e\), fees \(F\):

\[ IS = \sum_j q_j (p_j - P_d) + (X - \textstyle\sum_j q_j)(P_e - P_d) + F , \] \[ \sum_j q_j (p_j - P_d) = \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_j q_j (p_j - m_j)}_{\text{spread}} + \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_j q_j (m_j - P_0)}_{\text{drift}} + \underbrace{(\textstyle\sum_j q_j)(P_0 - P_d)}_{\text{delay}} . \]

Price noise for a steady schedule over \(T\) days: \(\mathrm{sd}(IS) \approx \sigma\sqrt{T/3}\), about 115 bps for a full day at 2% daily volatility, 64 bps for two hours. Detecting a difference \(\delta\) needs \(n \approx 2(z_{\alpha/2} + z_\beta)^2\,\mathrm{sd}^2/\delta^2\) orders per arm.

docs.title: VWAP, TWAP and POV
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Three answers to "how much now?" for a low-urgency order: TWAP slices by the clock, VWAP by a forecast volume curve, POV by live volume.
  • US volume is U-shaped by time of day; the closing auction alone took a record 9.4% of notional in Q2 2024 [Reported]. A VWAP engine is mostly a volume forecaster.
  • Lab 17 (synthetic, 10% of ADV in a day): expected cost VWAP 12.8 bps, POV 13.1, TWAP 14.0.
  • The VWAP benchmark is easy to hit and hides about a third of the true cost. POV finished the order on only 61% of days.
  • Production versions add limit prices, participation caps, passive posting and intraday curve updates.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: execution · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) How many shares should a non-urgent order trade in each interval of the day? Inputs → Outputs quantity, start and end, 20–60 days of intraday volume, live volume, limits → shares per bin, fills, slippage vs interval VWAP and arrival Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Factor investing · Value, quality, low vol · Momentum · Fundamental signals · Revisions · Flow-driven · Intraday patterns · Trend following Latency / compute regime curve built overnight; schedule checked every bin (1 min); POV reacts each bin Key parameters curve lookback 20–60 days; POV rate 5–20% [Lore]; participation cap (brokers allow up to 50%) [Verified]; limit price; auction slice Main failure modes event days off the curve; POV chasing news volume; non-completion; self-flattering benchmark; predictable slices Lab Lab 17

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Budgeting analogy: TWAP spreads the order straight-line over the day; VWAP follows last year's seasonality (the average intraday volume curve); POV spends a fixed share of whatever revenue (volume) actually comes in. Trading in proportion to volume keeps your participation rate, and so your impact per share, roughly constant. Under concave impact that is the cheapest way to fill a fixed quantity in a fixed window when you have no view on price.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Forecast the curve: average each past day's normalized volume profile, closing auction as the last bin.
  2. VWAP: shares per bin proportional to the curve; TWAP is a flat curve with nothing in the auction.
  3. POV: each bin, buy enough that ours ÷ (others + ours) = target rate, using only volume already printed.
  4. Constrain: limit price, participation cap, minimum and maximum child size.
  5. Measure: slippage vs interval VWAP and arrival; completion.
import numpy as np

def volume_curve(hist_volumes):
    """Lab 17: mean normalized profile; days x 391 bins (390 minutes + closing auction)."""
    return (hist_volumes / hist_volumes.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)).mean(axis=0)

def vwap_schedule(volume_curve, qty):
    """Lab 17: shares per bin proportional to the forecast curve. TWAP = flat curve."""
    w = np.asarray(volume_curve, dtype=float)
    cum_target = np.round(qty * np.cumsum(w) / w.sum())   # rounding keeps the total exact
    return np.diff(np.concatenate([[0.0], cum_target]))

def pov_child_order(target_rate, market_volume_so_far, executed_so_far, remaining):
    """Lab 17: ours / (others + ours) = rate  =>  ours = rate / (1 - rate) * others.
    Uses only printed volume, so POV lags volume and cannot promise to finish."""
    target = target_rate / (1.0 - target_rate) * market_volume_so_far
    return float(np.clip(target - executed_so_far, 0.0, remaining))

def child_order_costs_bps(qty, market_volume, half_spread_bps, bought_before, adv, daily_vol,
                          eta=0.15, gamma=0.30, exponent=0.6):
    """Lab 17 stylized costs for a buy (bps): spread, temporary, permanent impact."""
    participation = np.divide(qty, market_volume, out=np.zeros_like(qty, dtype=float),
                              where=market_volume > 0)       # ours per share of others
    temporary = 1e4 * eta * daily_vol * participation ** exponent
    permanent = 1e4 * gamma * daily_vol * bought_before / adv  # lifts all later prices
    spread = np.where(qty > 0, half_spread_bps, 0.0)           # no spread in the auction
    return spread, temporary, permanent

# Not in the lab: a production-style limit price. Bins where the mid is above the
# limit get zero shares; the shortfall rolls forward and may never fill.
def apply_limit(schedule, mids, limit_px):
    return np.where(mids <= limit_px, schedule, 0.0)

# Usage: twap = vwap_schedule(np.r_[np.ones(390), 0.0], qty)   # flat, no auction

docs.text:
Illustrative, Lab 17's stock. Buy 500,000 shares (10% of a 5M-share ADV) of a $50 stock, daily volatility 2%, quoted spread 3 bps.

Half hour Others trade VWAP buys (q/v) TWAP buys (q/v) 9:30–10:00 (11% of day) 550,000 55,000 (0.100) 38,462 (0.070) 12:00–12:30 (4.5%) 225,000 22,500 (0.100) 38,462 (0.171)

TWAP's 1,282 shares a minute is 6.5% participation at the open and 14.6% at lunch; VWAP holds 9.1%.

Temporary impact is 0.15 × 200 bps × (q/v)^0.6, with q/v our shares per share others trade:

  • VWAP: 30 × 0.10^0.6 = 30 × 0.251 = 7.5 bps.
  • TWAP: 6.1 bps at the open, 10.4 at lunch: 8.25 bps across the two.
  • Plus 1.5 bps half-spread and, after 250,000 shares, 0.30 × 200 × 0.05 = 3 bps permanent impact.

POV 10%: others print 12,000 shares, so buy 0.10 ÷ 0.90 × 12,000 = 1,333. On a day 25% light (3.75M), POV gets 0.111 × 3.75M = 417,000 shares: 83% filled.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Curve: 20–60-day profiles by stock or liquidity bucket, special curves for expiries, index rebalances and half-days [Lore].
  • POV rate: 5–20% [Lore]; above 20% impact dominates.
  • Caps: maximum participation on VWAP (IBKR allows 10–50%) [Verified].
  • Limit price and the auction slice (see E5).

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Benchmark: VWAP became a cost yardstick in Berkowitz, Logue and Noser (1988) [Verified]; Kissell (2014) is the standard practitioner text.
  • Shape: hourly NYSE volume is U-shaped (Jain and Joh 1988), and discretionary traders cluster (Admati and Pfleiderer 1988) [Reported]. The closing auction: record 9.4% of notional in Q2 2024 (NYSE), about 5–10% of monthly share volume in 2025 [Reported].
  • Slicing theory: Konishi (2002) derives the optimal static slice under volume uncertainty; dynamic intraday volume forecasts beat static curves (Białkowski et al. 2008; Humphery-Jenner 2011) [Reported].
  • Products: IBKR's best-efforts VWAP can avoid taking liquidity and then may not fill; its guaranteed VWAP is discontinued [Verified] (IBKR). VWAP is used by 81% of long-only desks, POV 74%, TWAP 38% [Reported] (The TRADE 2025).
  • Practice: child orders mostly post passively and step up when behind schedule [Lore]; Lab 17 crosses the spread every time.

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Tracking error vs interval VWAP (curve error vs execution); participation by time of day; completion; slippage vs arrival.
Lab 17 (synthetic, 500 days) Expected cost vs interval VWAP Shortfall SD Completion TWAP 14.0 bps 9.7 ± 11.2 125 100% VWAP (20-day curve) 12.8 8.2 ± 3.0 122 100% VWAP (perfect foresight) 12.3 7.7 ± 0.8 123 100% POV 10% 13.1 9.1 ± 3.2 123 93.8% (61% of days)

Synthetic lab result: stylized impact, every child crosses, volume independent of price. Real 10%-of-ADV days cost nearer 20 bps [Estimate] (square-root law).

Lab 17, synthetic: cumulative fills vs market volume on one day (left); TWAP's participation swings from 5% to 14%, VWAP and POV hold near 10% (right).

Lab 17, synthetic: vs interval VWAP every schedule looks tight; vs arrival all are noise-dominated.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Self-flattering benchmark: interval VWAP includes your own prints and impact; VWAP showed 8.2 bps against a true 12.8.
  • Event days: expiries and rebalances break the curve.
  • POV chases volume: news lifts volume and price together, so POV buys most when it is dearest. On below-median-volume days it filled 88%.
  • Predictability: identical slices on a fixed clock invite front-running.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Work it VWAP to the close, 15% cap." → curve schedule with a participation limit.
  • "Go 10% of volume, limit 50.25." → POV with a price limit.
  • "We were 3 bps behind VWAP, all curve error." → volume forecast missed.
  • "Don't VWAP a fast signal." → low urgency only.
  • "POV left 80k on the table." → non-completion on a light day.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. How do you forecast the curve on expiry and rebalance days?
  2. Do you update the curve intraday?
  3. Is VWAP slippage measured against the full day or only your interval?
  4. What happens to POV's leftovers at the close?
  5. 🔒 How much of your VWAP tracking error is curve error?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: why VWAP is cost-optimal under power-law impact, and POV's rule

Fill \(Q\) over bins with others' volume \(v_i\) and temporary cost per share \(\eta\,(q_i/v_i)^{\beta}\):

\[ \min_{q}\ \sum_i \eta\, q_i \left(\frac{q_i}{v_i}\right)^{\beta} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_i q_i = Q . \]

The first-order condition \((1+\beta)\,\eta\,(q_i/v_i)^{\beta} = \mu\) makes \(q_i/v_i\) constant: trade in proportion to volume. With known volume and no price view, VWAP is optimal; risk aversion or alpha pull toward front-loading (E3). POV keeps \(q/(q+v) = r\), so \(q = \tfrac{r}{1-r}v\): one share per nine at 10%.

docs.title: Adverse selection and markouts
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Adverse selection: whoever chooses to hit your quote knows more, on average. In Glosten-Milgrom the uninformed pay the spread that covers losses to the informed.
  • A markout marks a fill forward: side × (mid at t+h − fill price). At h = 0 it is the spread captured; the fall after that is adverse selection.
  • In Lab 04 (synthetic) informed flow looks profitable at 1 s but ends at −1.46 bps at 60 s; noise ends at +2.13.
  • Segment markouts set spreads and choose flow and venues; Rule 605's realized spread is the public version.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which fills made money after the price moved, and which flow is toxic? Inputs → Outputs own fills with segment tags, a mid or fair-value series → markout curves with standard errors, segment spreads, venue rankings Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Options market making · Retail flow internalization · Auctions and closing liquidity · Fee-driven strategies · Latency arbitrage Latency / compute regime warm path: per-fill markouts at 100 ms–60 s; segment curves in an overnight batch Key parameters horizons 50 ms–5 min; mid or microprice reference; per-share weights; 5–30 min cluster blocks Main failure modes horizon too short; per-fill averaging; naive standard errors; fees omitted; only fills observed Lab Lab 04

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Glosten and Milgrom (1985): a dealer cannot tell informed from uninformed takers. Every buy is partly news that value is higher, so the ask is set at expected value given a buy; losses to the informed are recovered from the uninformed. Kyle (1985) adds that informed traders hide in noise, moving price in proportion to flow (order-book signals).

A market maker cannot see who is informed, only what the price did after each fill. A segment whose markouts end below zero knows more than the spread charges.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Record each passive fill: time, price, side (+1 if our bid was hit), size, segment tags.
  2. Markout at horizon h, in bps: side × (mid(t+h) − price) / price × 10⁴; at h = 0, the mid just before the fill.
  3. Average per share by segment; cluster standard errors by time block.
  4. Read: markout₀ − markout_h is adverse selection; markout_h plus rebates minus fees is what you keep.
  5. Act: widen, skew or stop quoting toxic segments; reweight venues.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
HORIZONS_S = [0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 300]   # 0 = mid just BEFORE the fill

def markouts(fills, mid_series, horizons=HORIZONS_S):
    # Lab 04: markout_h = side * (mid(t_fill + h) - fill_price) / fill_price * 1e4 (bps)
    # side = +1 our bid was hit (we bought), -1 our offer was lifted. + = we made money.
    t_book = mid_series.index.to_numpy()
    mid = mid_series.ffill().to_numpy()
    t_fill, price, side = (fills[c].to_numpy() for c in ("time", "price", "side"))
    out = {}
    for h in horizons:
        if h == 0:
            j = np.searchsorted(t_book, t_fill, side="left") - 1      # last mid before fill
        else:
            j = np.searchsorted(t_book, t_fill + h, side="right") - 1  # last mid at/before t+h
        out[h] = side * (mid[j] - price) / price * 1e4
    return pd.DataFrame(out, index=fills.index)       # markout_0 = spread captured

def markout_curve(mo, weights, blocks):
    # Share-weighted mean per horizon; standard error clustered by time block
    w = np.asarray(weights, float)
    mean = mo.mul(w, axis=0).sum() / w.sum()
    resid = (mo - mean).mul(w, axis=0)
    by_block = resid.groupby(np.asarray(blocks)).sum()  # fills in a block share one path
    se = np.sqrt((by_block ** 2).sum()) / w.sum()
    return mean, se

def segment_half_spread_bps(curves, horizon=60, fees_bps=0.0, margin_bps=0.2):
    # Not in the lab: break-even half-spread per segment = adverse selection + costs
    return {seg: max(m[0] - m[horizon], 0.0) + fees_bps + margin_bps
            for seg, m in curves.items()}

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
One fill (illustrative). Our bid at 50.00 is hit for 1,000 shares; the mid just before is 50.005.

Horizon Mid Markout, $/share bps $ on 1,000 shares 0 s 50.005 +0.005 +1.0 +5 10 s 49.995 −0.005 −1.0 −5 60 s 49.985 −0.015 −3.0 −15

Spread captured $5, adverse selection $20, net −$15: this seller knew something. In Rule 605 terms the seller's effective spread is 2 × 0.5¢ = 1.0¢, the 60-second realized spread is −3.0¢ (twice our markout), and price impact is the 4.0¢ difference.

Lab 04's liquidity providers, synthetic lab result in $ per day: spread captured +77,818; adverse selection at 60 s −49,723; net +28,096, so they keep 36%. Informed takers cost them 18,106 net; uninformed takers pay them 46,202.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Horizon. Long enough for informed flow to finish: Lab 04's informed curve crosses zero near 5 s. Amended Rule 605 reports 50 ms, 1 s, 15 s, 1 min and 5 min [Reported].
  • Reference price. The mid is standard; a microprice cuts short-horizon noise but bakes in your model.
  • Weighting. Per share: Lab 04's 60-second markout is +0.99 bps per fill, +0.82 per share.
  • Segments. Broker, venue, size, time of day, queue position; thin segments are shrunk toward pooled estimates [Lore]. Add rebates and fees per share.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Many speeds. The models have one informed type; real information decays over milliseconds (latency arbitrage) to hours (sliced parent orders), so desks read whole curves [Lore].
  • Who is toxic. HFTs' passive trades are adversely selected while their aggressive trades predict seconds ahead (Brogaard, Hendershott and Riordan 2014) [Verified]. A large HFT market maker lost on inventory and earned on the spread (Menkveld 2013) [Verified].
  • Retail versus institutional. Retail flow is benign over seconds, which is what wholesalers pay for, but mildly informed over a week (Boehmer et al. 2021) [Verified]; wholesalers price identical orders by broker (Schwarz et al. 2025) [Verified].
  • Venues. Euronext's quants found markouts rise almost linearly with the spread and differ by 0.4–0.8 bps across venues [Reported] (exchange research with a commercial interest).

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
Curves should be stable across days, and markout plus inventory P&L plus fees should reconcile to booked P&L (live monitoring).

Lab 04, synthetic lab result (136,488 passive fills), bps:

Segment Volume share 0 s 1 s 60 s Informed takers (ground truth) 36% +2.53 +1.13 −1.46 Uninformed takers 64% +2.14 +1.54 +2.13 Taker orders of 800+ shares 21% +3.03 +1.25 −0.45

The toy flatters the method: its informed flag is ground truth (desks see only proxies), informed traders send single large orders (real ones slice), and there are no fees or latency. In real liquid large caps adverse selection typically eats most of the gross half-spread [Lore].

Lab 04, synthetic. Informed flow (orange) looks profitable at 1 s, then settles near −1.4 bps.

Lab 04, synthetic. Order size proxies toxicity; spread state here does not.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Short horizons hide toxicity, as Lab 04's informed flow shows at 1 s.
  • Naive standard errors: 0.012 versus 0.026 bps clustered at 10 s in Lab 04; clustering per Petersen (2009) [Verified].
  • Selection: you see only fills, and changing quotes changes who fills you.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "That broker marks out flat at a minute." → Benign flow, worth paying for.
  • "We're getting run over at five seconds." → Informed flow is hitting the quotes.
  • "Mark it to micro, not mid." → Less noise at sub-second horizons.
  • "One day, one client: cluster it." → Small samples overstate significance.
  • "Net of rebate we're flat." → Spread plus rebate just covers adverse selection.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: Which horizons do you mark out at?
  2. Basic: Mid or fair value as the reference?
  3. Informed: How do you separate pick-offs from ordinary adverse selection?
  4. Informed: Do you average per share or per fill?
  5. Sharp: Which segment did you stop quoting last year? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: the Glosten-Milgrom spread and spread decompositions

Value is \(V_H\) or \(V_L\) with equal odds, \(\Delta = V_H - V_L\), and a share \(\pi\) of takers know it. Bayes on a buy gives

\[ \text{ask} = \mathbb{E}[V \mid \text{buy}] = \frac{V_H + V_L}{2} + \pi\,\frac{\Delta}{2}. \]

Selling at the ask, the dealer marks out \(-(1-\pi)\Delta/2\) against the informed and \(+\pi\Delta/2\) against the uninformed: zero on average, very different by segment.

For a trade at \(P\) with sign \(q\) (+1 buyer-initiated) and mids \(M_t\), \(M_{t+h}\):

\[ \underbrace{2q(P - M_t)}_{\text{effective}} = \underbrace{2q(P - M_{t+h})}_{\text{realized}} + \underbrace{2q(M_{t+h} - M_t)}_{\text{price impact}}. \]

docs.title: Algorithmic risk controls
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Controls come in layers (strategy, firm or broker gateway, exchange port, market-wide), each assuming the one before has failed.
  • SEC Rule 15c3-5 (2010) makes broker-dealers with market access automatically reject orders that breach pre-set credit or capital thresholds or price and size limits, or that look duplicative [Verified].
  • Knight Capital, 1 August 2012: 212 retail orders became over 4 million executions in 154 stocks in 45 minutes, and a loss of over $460 million [Verified].
  • Good controls are strict on the way in and generous on the way out: cancels and risk-reducing orders always pass.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) May this order go out now, and should this strategy still be trading at all? Inputs → Outputs order, positions, open orders, P&L, market state, limits → accept, reject, throttle, reduce-only or kill; audit log Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Options market making · Retail flow internalization · Auctions and closing liquidity · Latency arbitrage · Lead-lag arbitrage · ETF and index arbitrage · Fee-driven strategies · ML short-horizon alpha Latency / compute regime inline, ns–µs per order; P&L and staleness checks every ms–s; surveillance end of day Key parameters collar 1–5% from reference [Lore]; max order size (Cboe default 25,000 shares [Verified]); message rate (Cboe default 5,000/s per port [Verified]); position, notional and loss limits Main failure modes limits that only alert; account-level instead of firm-wide limits; false kills; a kill that strands hedges Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: This is SOX for orders: pre-trade checks are preventive controls, monitors and surveillance detective, the kill switch corrective, and the CEO certifies them annually. The difference is speed: a runaway algorithm can lose the firm's capital before anyone picks up a phone, so controls must be automatic, inline and independent of the strategy code.

For a market maker that is its own broker-dealer, the first two gates are one.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Regulatory: restricted list, halts, short-sale rules.
  2. Data sanity: a stale reference price means no order.
  3. Price collar: reject a buy more than x% above the reference (NBBO mid or own fair value), or a sell that far below; respect the LULD bands.
  4. Size ("fat finger"): maximum shares and notional per order.
  5. Duplicates and rate: repeated identical orders; a token-bucket message limit.
  6. Exposure: worst case if every open order on that side fills; gross notional against a capital threshold.
  7. Modes: a loss stop switches to reduce-only; a kill cancels everything. Cancels never pass through the gate.
def pre_trade_check(order, state, limits):
    """Return (ok, reason). Runs inline before every new or replace; cancels skip it.
    order.side: +1 buy, -1 sell. M1's pre_trade_ok(o, s.limits) wraps this. Illustrative."""
    sym, side, qty, px = order.symbol, order.side, order.qty, order.px
    if state.mode == "killed":
        return False, "kill switch"
    if sym in limits.restricted or state.halted.get(sym, False):
        return False, "restricted or halted"                # regulatory, 15c3-5(c)(2)
    ref = state.ref_price(sym)                               # NBBO mid or own fair value
    if ref is None or state.now - state.last_md_time[sym] > limits.max_md_age_s:
        return False, "stale market data"
    if side * (px - ref) / ref > limits.collar_pct:          # buy far above or sell far below ref
        return False, "price collar"                         # erroneous order, 15c3-5(c)(1)(ii)
    lo, hi = state.luld_band(sym)
    if not lo <= px <= hi:
        return False, "outside LULD band"
    if qty > limits.max_order_qty or qty * px > limits.max_order_notional:
        return False, "fat finger"
    if state.recent_identical(order, window_s=1.0) >= limits.max_duplicates:
        return False, "duplicative orders"
    if not state.rate_bucket.take(1):                        # token bucket, messages per second
        return False, "message rate"
    pos = state.position[sym]
    reduces = abs(pos + side * qty) < abs(pos)
    if state.daily_pnl < -limits.max_daily_loss:
        state.mode = "reduce_only"                           # loss stop: no new risk
    if state.mode == "reduce_only" and not reduces:
        return False, "reduce-only mode"
    worst = pos + side * (qty + state.open_qty(sym, side))  # if every open order this side fills
    if abs(worst) > limits.max_position[sym] and not reduces:
        return False, "position limit"
    gross = state.gross_notional + state.open_notional() + qty * px
    if gross > limits.max_gross_notional and not reduces:
        return False, "capital threshold"                    # credit or capital, 15c3-5(c)(1)(i)
    return True, "ok"

docs.text:
Illustrative: XYZ quoted $50.00 × $50.02 (reference $50.01); collar 2%; maximum 5,000 shares or $250,000 per order; position limit ±10,000; position +8,000 with 3,000 shares of open buys; 5% LULD bands around $50.00, so $47.50–$52.50.

Order Check Result Buy 1,000 @ 50.01 worst case 8,000 + 3,000 + 1,000 = 12,000 > 10,000 reject: position Sell 2,000 @ 50.02 position falls to 6,000 accept, even in reduce-only Buy 500 @ 51.50 (51.50 − 50.01) ÷ 50.01 = 2.98% > 2% reject: collar (inside LULD, so the market would accept it) Buy 50,000 @ 50.01 50,000 > 5,000 shares; $2.5M > $250k reject: fat finger

Knight's arithmetic [Estimate]. Final positions of $3.5 billion long and $3.15 billion short are $6.65 billion gross built in 2,700 seconds, about $2.5 million a second. A $50 million firm-wide gross cap would have tripped after about 20 seconds (50 ÷ 2.46). The loss was about $1.16 per share traded ($460M ÷ 397M shares).

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Normal
  Normal --> Throttled: message rate near cap
  Throttled --> Normal: rate falls
  Normal --> ReduceOnly: loss stop or limit breach
  ReduceOnly --> Normal: risk manager re-enables
  Normal --> Killed: kill switch, stale feed or lost heartbeat
  ReduceOnly --> Killed: further breach
  Killed --> ReduceOnly: manual restart after review

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Nesting: strategy limits sit inside desk, firm, broker and exchange limits, so the innermost fires first [Lore].
  • Calibration: normal usage plus headroom; warn near 80%, stop at 100% [Lore].
  • Collars: wider for cheap or volatile names, and checked against own fair value because the NBBO can be stale.
  • Loss stop: at 3 daily standard deviations it fires falsely on Φ(−3) ≈ 0.13% of days, about once in three years [Estimate].
  • Repeat executions: FIA recommends disabling a strategy after a set number of automatic fill-and-re-enter cycles [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• The rule: 15c3-5 also requires pre-order regulatory checks, authorized-only access, immediate post-trade reports to surveillance, direct and exclusive broker control, and a CEO-certified annual review [Verified].
  • Knight's findings: the SEC's first market-access case found no check comparing orders leaving the router with those entering it, an account limit not linked to any automated firm-wide control, and reliance on people instead of automated alerts; penalty $12 million [Verified]. A repurposed flag had woken dead code on one of eight servers missed in a deployment [Verified].
  • Exchange ports: Cboe offers fat-finger rejection through the NBBO, notional cutoffs, duplicate-order protection, cancel-on-disconnect and self-trade prevention [Verified].
  • Market-wide: LULD bands are 5% for Tier 1 stocks above $3 (10% for Tier 2); a 15-second limit state becomes a 5-minute pause [Verified]. Circuit breakers halt everything for 15 minutes on S&P 500 falls of 7% or 13% before 3:25 p.m., and for the day at 20%; Level 1 fired four times in March 2020 [Verified]. Regular-hours trades inside the bands are generally not bustable as clearly erroneous, so a firm keeps its mistakes [Verified].
  • Surveillance: spoofing and layering post orders meant to be cancelled to push the price, then trade the other way. FINRA Rule 5210 bans them [Verified]; in 2019 a jury found Avalon FA liable for layering and cross-market manipulation that made over $25 million [Verified]. Intent is invisible pre-trade, so detection is post-trade [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Rejects by reason: low but not zero; zero means limits never bind [Lore].
  • Kill-switch drills, timed from trigger to confirmed cancels.
  • Drop-copy reconciliation with zero breaks (FIA) [Verified].

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Alert-only limits: Knight's 97 pre-open warning emails went unread [Verified].
  • Kills that strand hedges: half-hedged books; hence reduce-only mode.
  • Stale references: collars block everything, or pass junk.
  • Bypass paths: a "temporary" manual tool that skips the gate.
  • Self-surveillance: a market maker's heavy cancelling can resemble layering.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're reduce-only on that book." → it may only shrink positions.
  • "The collar's bouncing everything." → the reference price broke.
  • "Hit the big red button." → kill switch.
  • "COD saved us when the line dropped." → cancel-on-disconnect pulled resting orders.
  • "We tripped the gross cap." → the firm-wide notional limit fired.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: Which checks run before every order, and where?
  2. Basic: What happens to resting orders if a connection drops?
  3. Informed: Are limits firm-wide or per account?
  4. Sharp: How does a kill avoid leaving you half-hedged?
  5. Sharp: What are your actual collar and loss-stop levels? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Worst-case exposure, rate limits and false-kill odds

Worst-case position on side \(s = \pm 1\), with open quantity \(Q_s\) and new order \(x\):

\[ q^{\text{wc}} = q + s\,(Q_s + x). \]

A token bucket of capacity \(b\) and refill rate \(r\) allows bursts of \(b\) messages and a sustained \(r\) per second. A loss stop at \(k\) daily standard deviations fires falsely once every \(1/\Phi(-k)\) days.

docs.title: Anatomy of an HFT trading loop
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A market maker's system is one event loop: packet in, book update, fair value, quote decision, risk check, order out. Acks and fills return later and update inventory and hedges.
  • Tick-to-trade is about 2.5 µs in very good software and tens of nanoseconds on FPGAs [Verified]. Rank in a microsecond race matters more than absolute speed.
  • Models are fit offline and pushed in as parameters; the hot path only does arithmetic and lookups.
  • The core is built single-threaded and deterministic, so a recorded day replays to identical orders.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) What happens between a packet arriving and an order leaving, and how fast? Inputs → Outputs binary exchange feeds, own acks and fills, offline parameters, limits → order messages, hedges, positions, a replayable event log Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Options market making · Retail flow internalization · Latency arbitrage · Lead-lag arbitrage · ETF and index arbitrage · Fee-driven strategies Latency / compute regime ns–µs per event; exchange round trip tens of µs Key parameters per-stage budget at p50 and p99; requote hysteresis of about a tick [Lore]; venue message caps (Cboe default 5,000/s per port [Verified]) Main failure modes tail latency in bursts; stale book after packet loss; unacked order state; runaway loops; research ≠ production code Lab Lab 01

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Think of a spinal reflex: the hand leaves the stove before the brain hears about it, because the brain set the reflex in advance. Research is the brain, fitting weights and limits offline; the live loop is the reflex. Speed matters because quoting is a race: when news moves fair value, the market maker's cancel competes with rivals' orders to hit its stale quote. In London Stock Exchange data the modal race was won by 5–10 µs [Verified], so a loop 3 µs slower than a rival's leaks its edge.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Feed handler. Exchanges multicast binary, order-by-order feeds: Nasdaq TotalView-ITCH 5.0 (nanosecond timestamps, a 36-byte Add Order message) or Cboe PITCH [Verified]. Each is sent on lines A and B; keep whichever copy of each sequence number arrives first. If both miss a packet, the book is stale until recovered by retransmission or snapshot [Verified]; quotes are pulled meanwhile.
  2. Book build. Apply adds, executions and cancels to a per-venue order book; order-level detail makes queue position trackable.
  3. Fair value. Microprice plus flow and lead-lag terms (M2, M3).
  4. Quote. Skew a reservation price against inventory (M4); requote only past a threshold, to keep queue priority.
  5. Risk gate (M9), then order entry in the venue's binary protocol (Nasdaq OUCH, Cboe BOE) or FIX.
  6. Acks and fills advance each order's state machine. Inventory changes on fills, never on sends; hedges follow.
  7. Log everything with hardware timestamps for markouts, P&L and refits.
# One symbol, one thread, one pinned core. Production is C++ or FPGA logic: no locks, no heap
# allocation, no system calls. Same names as pipeline 1 in "There is no single algorithm".
def on_packet(pkt, s):                             # lines A and B deliver identical sequenced copies
    if pkt.seq < s.next_seq:
        return                                     # duplicate from the slower line: drop it
    if pkt.seq > s.next_seq:                       # gap (after a brief wait for the other line)
        s.book_stale = True
        s.gateway.cancel_all(s.symbol)             # pull quotes first, recover second
        s.recovery.request(s.next_seq, pkt.seq)    # retransmission or snapshot (cold path)
        return
    s.next_seq = pkt.seq + 1
    for msg in decode(pkt):                        # fixed byte offsets, no text parsing
        on_market_data(msg, s)

def on_market_data(msg, s):
    book = s.book.apply(msg)                       # 1. add / execute / cancel / replace
    if s.book_stale or s.halted:
        return
    fv = microprice(book) + s.signals.predict_ticks(book, msg) * s.tick   # 2. fair value (M2, M3)
    r = fv - s.inventory * s.gamma * s.sigma**2 * s.horizon              # 3. inventory skew (M4)
    half = max(s.min_half_spread, s.half_spread(book, s.toxicity))
    targets = (("buy", floor_to_tick(r - half, s.tick)), ("sell", ceil_to_tick(r + half, s.tick)))
    for side, px in targets:
        live = s.live[side]
        if live is not None and abs(live.px - px) < s.requote_ticks * s.tick:
            continue                               # small move: keep the order and its queue spot (M6)
        o = Order(side, px, size=s.clip_for(side, s.inventory))
        if pre_trade_ok(o, s.limits):              # 4. inline risk gate (M9)
            s.gateway.replace(live, o)             # 5. binary OUCH / BOE message out
        s.log.record(msg, o, s.clock.hw_now())     # warm path: copied to a logger thread

def on_ack(ack, s):
    s.orders.transition(ack.order_id, ack.state)   # pending -> live -> pending-cancel -> done

def on_fill(fill, s):
    s.inventory += fill.signed_qty                 # 6. position first
    s.markouts.track(fill, horizons_s=[0.1, 1, 10])     # adverse selection (M5), warm path
    h = s.hedger.order_for(fill, s.inventory)      # 7. e.g. offset an ETF fill with futures (M7)
    if h is not None and pre_trade_ok(h, s.limits):
        s.gateway.send(h)

Lab 01 builds the matching engine and book this loop assumes.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Latency budget (illustrative, colocated; stage splits [Estimate], totals sourced):

Stage Very good software FPGA Wire to user space, decode 0.5–1 µs a few to tens of ns Book, fair value, quote, risk 0.3–1 µs ns (precomputed lookup) Encode, back to the wire 0.5–1 µs a few to tens of ns Tick-to-trade ~2.5 µs (Cook 2017) [Verified] 13.9 ns, 2024 STAC-T0, network I/O only [Verified] Exchange round trip sub-40 µs (Nasdaq's older claim) [Verified] same

Every firm pays the exchange round trip, so it rarely decides who is first. Physics counts: a 100-byte frame takes 80 ns to serialize at 10 Gb/s.

Burst (illustrative). An E-mini tick moves fair value in 500 correlated symbols. At 1 µs per symbol on one core, the 500th quote updates 500 µs later, long after rivals hit it. Across 16 cores (about 31 symbols each) the last update leaves after about 31 µs. Hence sharding, largest-exposure-first requoting, and measuring the tail rather than the average.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Requote threshold: too small burns messages and queue spots; too large leaves stale quotes. Tuned on markouts [Lore].
  • Gap policy: Optiver's Carl Cook: if anything looks wrong, pull all orders, then ask questions [Verified].
  • Sharding: an ETF and its hedges on one core, so one thread sees both books [Lore].
  • Message budget: above a port's per-second cap, Cboe rejects new orders [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: Avellaneda-Stoikov quoting assumes instant, continuous reaction. Practice: discrete events, queues and a race.
  • Hot path: Cook (2017) says it runs about 0.01% of the time; a frequent dummy pass through the whole system keeps caches and branch predictors warm [Verified].
  • Slow models, fast triggers: a 2026 Optiver deep dive describes slow models arming fast triggers, and some loops living on one FPGA or ASIC with precomputed responses [Reported].
  • Determinism: LMAX runs its trading platform's business logic on one thread at about 6 million orders per second and rebuilds state by replaying its input journal [Verified]. Trading firms use the same pattern [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Switch-timestamped tick-to-trade at p50, p99 and p99.9, especially at the open.
  • Cancels rejected as "already filled" count lost races [Lore]; markouts price them.
  • Yesterday's captured packets replay to production's orders byte for byte.
  • Gap counts per line; order state reconciled to the exchange drop copy.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Tail latency (page faults, interrupts, noisy neighbours) loses races when markets are busiest.
  • Stale book after packet loss: quoting prices that no longer exist.
  • In-flight state: mishandled unacked orders cause double hedges.
  • Runaway loops: Knight Capital's 2012 router sent child orders without counting fills (M9).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "What's our wire-to-wire at p99 on the open?" → tail latency in the busiest minutes.
  • "B line's flapping; we're on A alone." → one multicast copy drops packets; no redundancy.
  • "We gapped on EDGX and pulled." → a missed sequence number triggered cancels.
  • "Replay doesn't match prod." → something nondeterministic leaked into the logic.
  • "We lose the ES trigger by two micros." → a rival reacts faster to futures.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: Which stages run in software and which in hardware?
  2. Basic: What happens when you miss a packet?
  3. Informed: Can you replay a day and get byte-identical orders?
  4. Sharp: What is your p99 tick-to-trade at the open? 🔒
  5. Sharp: On which triggers are you first, and how do you know? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Latency arithmetic and burst queueing

Serialization takes \(t = 8B/R\) for \(B\) bytes at rate \(R\). With \(N\) symbols to requote, work \(w\) each and \(k\) cores, the last update leaves after

\[ T_{\text{last}} \approx \lceil N/k \rceil \, w . \]

With utilization \(\rho = \lambda w\), an M/M/1 queue's mean time in system is

\[ \frac{w}{1-\rho}, \]

ten times the service time at \(\rho = 0.9\), which is why systems are sized for bursts.

docs.title: Fair value and microprice
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Fair value is what a market maker quotes around: the mid adjusted for imbalance, flow and related instruments, over a few price changes.
  • The weighted mid leans toward the thin side by imbalance × half-spread; Stoikov's (2018) microprice learns how much of that lean comes true.
  • In Lab 02 (synthetic) the microprice cuts next-move forecast error only 3.5% versus the mid; the weighted mid is 41% worse. Past ~5 seconds nothing book-based beats the mid.
  • The book is not the information: real fair values add flow and futures or ETF leads, each shrunk.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Where is the price really, over the next few price changes? Inputs → Outputs top of book, trades, leaders (ES, sector ETF, basket), offline tables → fair value for quoting, taking, hedging and markouts Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Options market making · Retail flow internalization · Latency arbitrage · Lead-lag arbitrage · ETF and index arbitrage · Fee-driven strategies Latency / compute regime µs: one table lookup per book update; tables refit overnight (seconds of batch) Key parameters imbalance buckets 5–20 (Lab 02: 11); spreads 1–3 ticks; horizon 1–3 mid changes; leader shrinkage 0.3–0.7 [Lore] Main failure modes wide-spread over-reaction; transient moves; stale leaders; wrong horizon; bait size Lab Lab 02

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
With 4,500 shares bid at 50.00 and 500 offered at 50.01, the next tick is more likely up: 500 shares get eaten faster (the limit order book). How far above the mid is fair? The weighted mid answers mechanically, in proportion to order-book imbalance. The microprice answers empirically: from this state, where did the mid go? Stoikov defines it as the limit of expected future mids, a martingale by construction [Verified].

When E-mini futures tick up, every S&P 500 name's fair value moves before its book does (lead-lag). Quotes then sit at fair value ∓ a half-spread, skewed for inventory (M4).

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Per book update: imbalance \(I = (Q_b - Q_a)/(Q_b + Q_a)\) and spread; discretize into a state.
  2. Offline, in event time, count transitions: \(Q\) (mid unchanged), \(R\) (mid moved), \(r\) (mean move). Sum the expected change over the next mid move and every later one, \(g^* = \sum_i B^i G^1\), mirroring each book so it converges.
  3. Online: fair value = mid + \(g^*\)[state] × tick + flow and leader terms, weighted by regression at the consumer's horizon.
import numpy as np
N_IMB, MAX_SPREAD_TICKS = 11, 3     # Lab 02: 11 imbalance buckets x spreads of 1-3 ticks

def weighted_mid(bid, ask, bid_size, ask_size):
    # = mid + imbalance * spread / 2: leans toward the side with LESS size
    return (bid * ask_size + ask * bid_size) / (bid_size + ask_size)

def book_state(imbalance, spread_ticks, n_imb=N_IMB, max_spread_ticks=MAX_SPREAD_TICKS):
    half = (n_imb - 1) // 2                  # imbalance = (Qb - Qa) / (Qb + Qa), in [-1, 1]
    bucket = np.rint(np.asarray(imbalance) * half).astype(int) + half
    spread = np.rint(np.asarray(spread_ticks)).astype(int)
    ok = (spread >= 1) & (spread <= max_spread_ticks)
    return np.where(ok, (spread - 1) * n_imb + bucket, -1)      # -1: fall back to the mid

def estimate_microprice_adjustment(state, mid_ticks, n_imb=N_IMB,
                                   max_spread_ticks=MAX_SPREAD_TICKS, max_iter=200, tol=1e-6):
    # Offline, event time: consecutive book updates are transitions (Stoikov 2018)
    s, s_next, dm = state[:-1], state[1:], np.diff(mid_ticks)
    mirror = lambda x: (x // n_imb) * n_imb + (n_imb - 1 - x % n_imb)   # flip imbalance
    s, s_next, dm = np.r_[s, mirror(s)], np.r_[s_next, mirror(s_next)], np.r_[dm, -dm]
    n = n_imb * max_spread_ticks
    count = np.maximum(np.bincount(s, minlength=n), 1).astype(float)
    moved = dm != 0
    Q, R = np.zeros((n, n)), np.zeros((n, n))
    np.add.at(Q, (s[~moved], s_next[~moved]), 1.0)   # book changed, mid did not
    np.add.at(R, (s[moved], s_next[moved]), 1.0)     # mid moved; s_next = state after it
    Q, R = Q / count[:, None], R / count[:, None]
    r = np.bincount(s, weights=dm, minlength=n) / count     # mean mid move per update
    inv = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(n) - Q)
    G1, B = inv @ r, inv @ R      # change up to the next mid move; state right after it
    g, term = G1.copy(), G1.copy()
    for _ in range(max_iter - 1):              # g* = G1 + B G1 + B^2 G1 + ...
        term = B @ term
        g += term
        if np.max(np.abs(term)) < tol:
            break
    return g.reshape(max_spread_ticks, n_imb)  # ticks; row = spread - 1, col = bucket

def fair_value(mid, state, g_star, tick, extra_ticks=0.0):
    # Online. extra_ticks = flow (M3) and leader terms, each pre-shrunk. Not in the lab.
    adj = g_star.ravel()[state] if state >= 0 else 0.0
    return mid + (adj + extra_ticks) * tick

Lab 02, synthetic. At 2 ticks wide the weighted mid (dashed) leans 2.6 times further than the microprice (blue); realized moves are smaller still.

docs.text:
Illustrative book, 1-cent tick; \(g^*\) from Lab 02's fitted table (synthetic).

1-tick spread 2-tick spread Bid / ask (sizes) 50.00 / 50.01 (4,500 / 500) 50.00 / 50.02 (4,500 / 500) Imbalance \(I\) 4,000 / 5,000 = 0.8 0.8 Weighted mid 50.005 + 0.8 × 0.005 = 50.0090 50.010 + 0.8 × 0.010 = 50.0180 Microprice 50.005 + 0.432 × 0.01 = 50.0093 50.010 + 0.309 × 0.01 = 50.0131

At two ticks a weighted-mid desk thinks a new 50.01 bid is 0.8 ticks cheap; the microprice says 0.31. Lab 02's test days realized 0.16 ticks by the next change: a fivefold overstatement.

Adding a leader (illustrative). ES ticks up 0.25 points at 6,000 (+4.17 bps). With beta 1.2 shrunk by 0.5, fair value rises 0.5 × 1.2 × 4.17 = 2.5 bps = $0.0125, to 50.0218: through the 50.01 offer. The engine cancels its own offer and may lift rivals' stale ones (latency arbitrage).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Tick regime. Queue imbalance predicts much better in large-tick stocks than small-tick ones (Gould and Bonart 2016) [Verified]; see tick-constrained stocks.
  • Horizon. Fit weights at the consumer's horizon: one second ahead, Lab 02's microprice is worse than the mid (+0.5% MSE).

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Reference price. Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008) quote around a Brownian mid [Verified]; desks substitute their own fair value ("theo") [Lore].
  • Inputs. On 115 Nasdaq stocks, models fed order flow beat models fed raw book states, with an effective horizon of about two price changes (Kolm, Turiel and Westray 2023) [Verified].
  • Futures lead. E-mini futures carry most S&P 500 price discovery (Hasbrouck 2003) [Verified]; lagged cross-asset flow also helps, briefly (Cont, Cucuringu and Zhang 2023) [Verified].
  • ETF basket. The public iNAV is slow and not required by Rule 6c-11 [Verified]; desks value baskets themselves (ETF, futures and options linkages).

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
Score against the future mid at the consumer's horizon, check calibration (realized on predicted move; slope 1 = unbiased) and markouts of fills it called cheap.

Lab 02, synthetic lab result (46,558 test snapshots), MSE change versus the mid:

Horizon Weighted mid Microprice Best book-state forecast Next mid change +41.2% −3.5% −5.6% 10 s +6.6% +0.7% −0.1% 60 s +0.9% +0.1% +0.1%

Calibration falls from 0.63 at the next move to 0.12 after 20. Why so modest:

  • Weak by design. Real large-tick books carry a stronger imbalance signal than the toy.
  • Not Markov. Simulated liquidity providers refill depleted queues toward a slow hidden belief, so moves partly revert.
  • Information is elsewhere. The latent value's correlation with the microprice adjustment is +0.0006; informed traders reveal it through trades (M3).

Lab 02, synthetic. Left: MSE change versus the mid by horizon. Right: calibration slope.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Wide spreads: Lab 02's weighted mid is 61% worse than the mid at 2 ticks.
  • Broken leaders: stale feeds, halts, single-stock news.
  • Bait size: spoofed size tilts imbalance; desks discount size that rarely trades [Lore].

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We quote off micro, not mid." → Fair value includes the imbalance adjustment.
  • "Weighted mid is fine one tick wide, dangerous at three." → It over-reacts at wide spreads.
  • "Theo's through the offer, lift it." → Fair value is above the ask: take.
  • "Shrink the ES term at the open." → The leader beta is unstable then.
  • "What horizon is that theo for?" → Fair value only means something at a horizon.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: Do you quote around the mid or your own fair value?
  2. Basic: Which input moves it most: book, trades or futures?
  3. Informed: Is your horizon in clock time or price changes?
  4. Informed: How do you value a basket with halted names?
  5. Sharp: How much markout improvement came from fair value rather than quoting? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: weighted mid, microprice recursion, horizon decay

With bid \(P_b\), ask \(P_a\), sizes \(Q_b, Q_a\), mid \(M\), spread \(S\):

\[ W = \frac{P_b Q_a + P_a Q_b}{Q_a + Q_b} = M + I\,\frac{S}{2}. \]

With \(\tau_k\) the time of the \(k\)-th mid change:

\[ P^{\text{micro}}_t = \lim_{k\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\big[M_{\tau_k} \mid I_t, S_t\big] = M_t + g^*(I_t, S_t), \qquad G^{k+1} = G^1 + B\,G^k . \]

Estimation inverts a 33 × 33 matrix; online cost is one lookup.

Horizon decay [Estimate]: Lab 02's best book forecast removes 5.6% × 0.375 ≈ 0.021 ticks² at the next mid change; the mid's 60-second MSE is 23.9 ticks², so the same gain is under 0.1%.

docs.title: Hedging algorithms
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Hedging buys lower P&L variance with trading costs. More frequent rebalancing shrinks hedge-error variance but, before costs, not expected P&L.
  • Timing rules: a clock, a band on net delta, or a utility-optimal band (Whalley–Wilmott).
  • Net across books, then hedge in the cheapest correlated instrument at a minimum-variance ratio; only options hedge gamma and vega.
  • Lab 06 (synthetic): residual sd ∝ rebalances^−0.56; 15-minute hedging costs more than the quoted edge.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which risk do I lay off, in what instrument, how much and when, given that hedging costs money? Inputs → Outputs net Greeks and inventory, betas, instrument costs, limits → hedge orders; residual-risk and cost reports Used by strategies Options market making · Equity market making · ETF market making · Retail flow internalization · Auctions and closing liquidity · Lead-lag and cross-asset arbitrage · ETF and index arbitrage · Volatility risk premium and vol arb · Dispersion and correlation trading · Pairs trading Latency / compute regime µs–ms auto-hedging on fills and ticks; hedge ratios and vega rebalancing overnight Key parameters delta band ±0.02–0.10 per share [Lore]; clock 15 min–1 day; cost 0.2–2 bp per trade; beta lookback 60–250 days Main failure modes costs above edge; gaps; basis risk; stale ratios; hedging gross instead of net Lab Lab 06

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
In accounting terms, hedging is a cost center: costs are a recurring expense, residual risk is earnings volatility. A delta-hedged short option earns theta and pays gamma, ½ΓS²(σ²_implied − σ²_realized) per unit time: the variance risk premium bet (Bakshi & Kapadia 2003). Hedging strips out direction and leaves that bet. The stale hedge between rebalances leaves a mean-zero residual whose sd falls like 1/√N in N rebalances (Boyle & Emanuel 1980); costs grow like √N. With a thin edge, costs win early.

A clock trades when nothing happened; a band trades when delta has drifted. For an equity or ETF market maker, inventory is the delta, a future or ETF the hedge, and the band how much to warehouse (M4).

docs.title: Where it sits in the pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  fills["Fills from M4 quoting"] --> pos["Positions and inventory"]
  greeks["M8 theo and Greeks"] --> pos
  pos --> net["Net across books<br/>beta-map to index dollars"]
  cov["P2 betas and covariances"] --> hedge

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Net across books: delta per underlying, beta-weighted index dollars, vega by expiry.
  2. Map each exposure to the cheapest instrument per unit of variance removed; size proxies at the minimum-variance hedge ratio.
  3. When: on a clock, or when net delta leaves ±band.
  4. How much: back to zero (Lab 06) or only to the band edge, optimal with proportional costs (Whalley & Wilmott 1999).
  5. Execute and attribute: passive when there is time; compare cost with variance removed.
flowchart TD
  r["Net exposure after netting"] --> q{"Which risk?"}
  q -->|"index or beta delta"| fut["Index future or ETF"]
  q -->|"single-name delta"| stk["The stock, or a correlated name<br/>at a min-variance ratio"]
  q -->|"gamma or vega"| opt["Other options<br/>buy wings, sell near-dated"]
  fut --> b["Residual: basis risk"]
  stk --> b
  opt --> s["Residual: smile and term risk"]
import numpy as np

def delta_hedge_pnl(spot, position_delta, rebalance_every=1, band=None, cost_bps=1.0,
                    to_edge=False):
    """Lab 06's hedger on one path (the lab vectorizes over trades). spot, position_delta:
    arrays on one grid (n + 1 points); delta in shares per share of underlying.
    Time-based: rebalance every k steps. Move-based: only when |net delta| > band.
    to_edge (not in the lab): trade only back to the band edge (Whalley & Wilmott);
    the lab, like most simple hedgers, trades back to zero net delta."""
    n = len(spot) - 1
    held, traded_usd, n_reb = 0.0, 0.0, 0
    shares = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n):
        net = held + position_delta[i]                  # stock hedge + option delta
        if band is None:
            rebalance = i % rebalance_every == 0
        else:
            rebalance = abs(net) > band or i == 0
        if rebalance:
            target = -position_delta[i]                 # flatten net delta
            if to_edge and band is not None and i > 0:
                target += np.sign(net) * band           # ...or stop at the band edge
            traded_usd += abs(target - held) * spot[i]
            held, n_reb = target, n_reb + 1
        shares[i] = held                                # shares held over step i
    traded_usd += abs(held) * spot[n]                   # unwind at expiry
    return {"shares": shares, "hedge_pnl": np.sum(shares * np.diff(spot)),
            "costs": traded_usd * cost_bps / 1e4, "n_rebalances": n_reb}

def ww_half_band(gamma, spot, cost_frac, risk_aversion, tau=0.0, r=0.0):
    """Whalley-Wilmott (1997) half-width of the no-trade band around the BS delta."""
    return (1.5 * np.exp(-r * tau) * cost_frac * spot * gamma ** 2 / risk_aversion) ** (1 / 3)

def min_variance_ratio(r_asset, r_hedge):
    """Hedge units per unit of asset (Ederington 1979): slope of asset on hedge returns."""
    c = np.cov(r_asset, r_hedge)
    return c[0, 1] / c[1, 1]

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
A. What each rebalance buys (Lab 06, synthetic lab result, $ per short straddle contract):

Change Extra hedging cost Change in P&L sd Daily → hourly 7.90 − 3.60 = +$4.30 134.6 → 114.1: −$20.5 Hourly → every 15 min 14.86 − 7.90 = +$6.96 114.1 → 113.7: −$0.4 Hourly → ±0.10 band 5.85 − 7.90 = −$2.05 114.1 → 116.8: +$2.7

The first $4.30 removes $4.8 of sd per dollar; the next $6.96, 6 cents per dollar. The band saves 16% of the $13.06 edge for $2.7 of sd.

B. Cross-hedge (illustrative). An ETF market maker, long $10M of a sector ETF (vol 25%), hedges with E-mini S&P 500 futures (vol 18%, correlation 0.85).

  • Ratio = 0.85 × 25 / 18 = 1.18: short $11.8M of futures, 39 contracts at $300,000 each (6,000 × $50).
  • Residual vol = 25% × √(1 − 0.85²) = 13.2%; one-day sd falls from $157,000 to $83,000.
  • Cost: half the 0.25-point tick is 0.21 bp, about $246, against $1,500 to sell the basket at 1.5 bp.

The 13.2% left is basis risk: sector moves the future does not carry.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Band width: tuned on the cost–variance frontier by replay [Lore]. Whalley–Wilmott scale it as cost^(1/3) × Γ^(2/3): doubling cost widens it 26%.
  • Backstop: bands plus a daily flatten [Lore].
  • Hedge ratios: 60–250 days, exponentially weighted, shrunk toward 1 [Lore].
  • Instrument: cheapest all-in cost per unit of variance removed; E-minis trade nearly 23 hours [Verified].
  • Gamma and vega: limits by expiry; when they bind, trade options [Lore].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: continuous, costless hedging. Practice: discrete hedging error (Boyle & Emanuel 1980) and cost-adjusted vol (Leland 1985) [Verified].
  • Utility bands: Whalley & Wilmott (1997) give the band in closed form; their 1999 sequel trades to an interior point when costs are fixed [Verified]. Desks often set bands by judgment [Lore].
  • Machine learning: Deep hedging learns cost-aware hedges [Verified]; a 2026 preprint finds the Whalley–Wilmott band too narrow at large costs [Reported].
  • Netting: wholesalers net opposite retail flow before hedging [Lore] (retail flow).
  • Minimum variance: the ratio is a regression slope (Ederington 1979) [Verified].
  • Feedback: whether dealer gamma hedging amplifies moves is contested (linkages) [Reported].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• P&L attribution (L1): residual mean near zero, costs below edge, small "unexplained".
  • Hedge effectiveness, 1 − Var(hedged)/Var(unhedged), near ρ².

Lab 06 (synthetic lab result, mean $ per contract): theta +262.6 and gamma −210.8 net to +51.8, dollar-gamma-weighted implied minus realized variance. Hedging every 15 minutes costs $14.9, more than the $13.1 edge (total +$40.5); daily hedging costs $3.6 but leaves a residual with sd $58 (total +$47.4). Residual sd scales with rebalances^−0.56 (theory −0.5); total sd floors near $114, vol risk no delta hedge removes.

The lab is cleaner than reality: no jumps, a flat 1 bp cost, marks from the true model. Even so, 35% of daily-hedged trades lose. Real index hedges cost nearer 0.2 bp [Estimate]; real short-gamma books lose most in a few gap days [Lore].

Lab 06, synthetic: Greeks attribution (top); hedge frequency moves P&L sd, not the mean (bottom left); P&L tracks dollar-gamma-weighted implied minus realized variance, R² 0.82 (bottom right).

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Overhedging: costs exceed edge.
  • Gaps: earnings and overnight moves; no frequency helps.
  • Basis: proxies decorrelate in stress.
  • Stale ratios: betas fitted in calm fail in crises.
  • Gross, not net: paying the spread twice.
  • Pin risk: near expiry, delta flips at the strike.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Hedge to the edge, not the middle." → trade back only to the band.
  • "Long $12M of beta; sell 40 minis." → beta-weighted delta into E-minis.
  • "Don't chase gamma on a chop day." → widen the band.
  • "The hedge ate the edge." → costs exceeded quoted edge.
  • "Basis blew out." → the proxy hedge failed.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Clock or band?
  2. Back to zero, or to the edge?
  3. Futures, ETF or basket for index delta?
  4. How do you net across desks?
  5. When do you hedge gamma and vega with options?
  6. 🔒 What does hedging cost as a share of edge, by product?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: discrete hedging, costs, bands and hedge ratios

Theta plus gamma per step (\(r = 0\), position gamma \(\Gamma\)):

\[ \tfrac12\,\Gamma S^2\left(\left(\tfrac{dS}{S}\right)^2 - \sigma_{\text{impl}}^2\,dt\right). \]

Residual \(\sum (h + \Delta)\,dS\), with \(h + \Delta \approx \Gamma\,(S_t - S_{\text{last}})\): mean zero, sd \(\propto N^{-1/2}\). Each rebalance trades about \(|\Gamma|\,\sigma S\sqrt{T/N}\) shares, so costs grow like \(\sqrt N\).

Whalley–Wilmott half-band, cost fraction \(\lambda\), risk aversion \(\gamma\):

\[ h = \left(\frac{3\,e^{-r(T-t)}\,\lambda\,S\,\Gamma^2}{2\gamma}\right)^{1/3}. \]

docs.title: Options pricing and vol surfaces for market making
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Black–Scholes is the quoting language, not the model: prices become implied volatility, one scale for every strike and expiry.
  • The model is the volatility surface: a smooth smile per expiry (SVI, spline, SABR) fitted to filtered quotes and checked for static arbitrage.
  • Two speeds: refit every second to minute; reprice thousands of series on every underlying tick, under a sticky-strike or sticky-delta rule.
  • In Lab 06 (synthetic), a parabola misses the wings by 1.25 vol points, SVI by 0.12.

Level: Deep dive · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) What is every listed option worth now, consistently across the chain, and how does that move with spot? Inputs → Outputs option quotes, underlying fair value, rates, dividends, borrow → forward and smile per expiry; theo, vol and Greeks per series Used by strategies Options market making · Volatility risk premium and vol arb · Dispersion and correlation trading Latency / compute regime refit every 1–60 s (ms per expiry); theo updates per underlying tick (µs) Key parameters SVI (5 per expiry) or spline (9–15 nodes); vega or 1/spread weights; quote filters; refit cadence; spot-vol rule Main failure modes wrong forward; wing extrapolation; stale quotes; arbitrage; wrong smile dynamics Lab Lab 06

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
$2.29 for a 30-day call is cheap or rich only relative to strike, expiry and spot. Implied vol compares across the chain, converts to risk through vega, and is how traders quote ("I'll pay 20.1").

Equity smiles slope down: since 1987, out-of-the-money index puts carry higher vols than calls (Derman 1999). Vols also vary by expiry: the term structure. A market maker needs an arbitrage-free value for every series, including strikes with no usable quote. So it fits a surface σ(k, T) in log-moneyness k = ln(K/F) and sets theo = Black–Scholes(F, K, T, σ(k, T)). Quoting skews around theo.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Forward. Put-call parity near the money gives F = K + e^{rT}(C − P), absorbing dividends and borrow. American single-stock prices are first converted to European with a tree or the Barone-Adesi–Whaley approximation [Lore].
  2. Filter. Out-of-the-money options only; drop crossed, stale, small or very wide quotes.
  3. Fit each expiry in total variance w = σ²T. SVI's wings are linear in k, as Lee's (2004) moment formula requires. Weight by vega or 1/spread.
  4. Check calendar (w non-decreasing in T) and butterfly (non-negative density) arbitrage.
  5. Move. Between refits, slide smiles with spot; reprice everything.
import numpy as np

def svi_total_variance(p, k):
    """Raw SVI (Gatheral 2004): total implied variance w = sigma^2 T at log-moneyness k."""
    a, b, rho, m, s = p
    return a + b * (rho * (k - m) + np.sqrt((k - m) ** 2 + s ** 2))

def fit_smile(log_moneyness, implied_vol, T, method="svi", weights=None):
    """Lab 06's fit_smile: returns k -> implied vol for one expiry.
    weights (e.g. vega / bid-ask spread) are an addition; the lab fits unweighted."""
    k, iv = np.asarray(log_moneyness, float), np.asarray(implied_vol, float)
    ok = np.isfinite(iv)                                  # no time value -> no vol
    k, iv = k[ok], iv[ok]
    wt = np.ones_like(iv) if weights is None else np.asarray(weights, float)[ok]
    if method == "quadratic":                             # local fit: fine ATM, wrong wings
        c2, c1, c0 = np.polyfit(k, iv, 2, w=np.sqrt(wt))
        return lambda x: c0 + c1 * x + c2 * x ** 2
    q2, q1, q0 = np.polyfit(k, iv ** 2 * T, 2)            # start: parabola in total variance
    b0 = max(0.2 * q2, abs(q1) / 0.9, 1e-4)               # with m = 0, s = 0.1
    x0 = [q0 - 0.1 * b0, b0, np.clip(q1 / b0, -0.9, 0.9), 0.0, 0.1]
    bounds = ([-1.0, 0.0, -0.999, -1.0, 1e-3], [1.0, 5.0, 0.999, 1.0, 2.0])  # b >= 0, |rho| < 1
    def resid(p):                                         # fit in vol space
        w = np.maximum(svi_total_variance(p, k), 1e-10)
        return np.sqrt(wt) * (np.sqrt(w / T) - iv)
    p = least_squares(resid, x0, bounds=bounds).x         # scipy.optimize, as in the lab
    return lambda x: np.sqrt(np.maximum(svi_total_variance(p, x), 1e-10) / T)

def calendar_arbitrage(w_near, w_far):
    """Same k grid, two expiries: total variance must not fall with maturity."""
    return np.any(w_far < w_near - 1e-12)

def theo_vol(K, F_now, F_fit, smile, rule="sticky_strike"):
    """Vol for strike K after the forward moves from F_fit (last refit) to F_now."""
    if rule == "sticky_strike":                           # vol pinned to the strike
        return smile(np.log(K / F_fit))
    return smile(np.log(K / F_now))                       # sticky delta: smile slides with spot

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Spot = forward = $100, zero rates, 30 days (T = 0.0822). Smile: σ(K) = 20% − 0.40 × ln(K/F).

Step Calculation Result 100-strike call at 20% Black–Scholes $2.287; vega $11.43 per vol point per contract Spot to $98, sticky strike vol stays 20.00% theo $1.403 Spot to $98, sticky delta 2.02% out of the money: 20 − 0.4 × 2.02 = 19.19% theo $1.318 Gap $0.086 × 100 shares $8.57 per contract

That 0.8-vol-point gap exceeds a 0.5-point edge ($5.30 at the new vega). The hedge moves too: under sticky delta the strike's vol rises 0.40/S = 0.004 per $1, so delta is 0.511 + 11.43 × 0.004 = 0.557 (vega per share per unit of vol is also 11.43). On 1,000 contracts: 4,573 shares, about $457,000 (hedging algorithms).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Model. SVI or SSVI for indices [Lore]; one vendor platform fits splines with separate put and call wing slopes [Verified]; SABR in rates.
  • Filters. The same guide drops strikes quoted wider than 2.5–3 times the at-the-money width and republishes at most once a second, at least once a minute [Verified].
  • Spot-vol rule. Sticky strike in range-bound markets, sticky delta in trending ones (Derman 1999) [Verified]; Bergomi's skew stickiness ratio spans both [Reported].
  • Events. Earnings variance is carved out as a one-day jump [Lore].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: one model prices the chain. Practice: a surface fitted slice by slice; models for exotics and sanity checks [Lore]. SVI came from Merrill Lynch (Gatheral 2004) [Verified]; Gatheral's book (2006) is the reference.
  • Arbitrage-free? Not automatically: Gatheral & Jacquier (2014) give conditions for SVI surfaces; Martini & Mingone characterize butterfly-free slices [Verified].
  • Dynamics. Hagan et al. (2002) built SABR because local vol moves the smile the wrong way with spot [Verified].
  • Scale. 15.2 billion US option contracts traded in 2025 [Verified]; OPRA plans for 13.6 million messages per 100 ms by July 2026 [Verified]. Traders who time fills against fair value pay effective spreads under 40% of conventional measures (Muravyev & Pearson 2020) [Verified].
  • American exercise. Many holders skip optimal pre-dividend call exercise; professionals capture the value (Pool, Stoll & Whaley 2008) [Reported].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Fitted vols inside bid-ask on liquid strikes; residuals in vega dollars; stable parameters; no arbitrage flags.
  • Markouts of fills against theo (M5); small "unexplained" in Greeks attribution (L1).

Lab 06, synthetic lab result (fit on strikes 0.85–1.15 of spot, predict 0.80 and 1.20):

Fit In-sample RMSE Wing error, mean abs Wing error, max Quadratic 0.50 vol pts 1.25 4.7 Raw SVI 0.035 0.12 0.35

Quotes come from the generating Heston model, without bid-ask or stale prints, so fits look far cleaner than live ones; what transfers is that a parabola is local. Implied ran 1.9 points above realized (20.3% vs 18.4%); the real VIX has averaged about 4 points above realized since 1990 [Reported].

Lab 06, synthetic: implied vs subsequently realized vol (top); SVI and a parabola extrapolated to the shaded wings (bottom left); implied minus realized (bottom right).

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Wrong forward: a stale dividend or borrow squeeze looks like skew.
  • Wings: parabolas bend the wrong way.
  • Garbage quotes at the open and in fast markets.
  • Wrong dynamics: leaves hidden vanna.
  • 0DTE and events: 0DTE was a record ~66% of SPX volume in July 2026 [Reported].

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Puts are a vol over the fit." → market vol 1 point above the surface.
  • "We're sticky strike; it's chopping." → strike vols unchanged as spot moves.
  • "Parity forward's 20 cents under our div model." → market implies more dividend or costlier borrow.
  • "Take earnings out first." → strip event variance.
  • "Theo ticks with the future." → two-speed loop.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Do you fit in vol or price, and how do you weight strikes?
  2. Dividend-model forward or parity forward?
  3. How often do you refit, and what moves theos in between?
  4. Which spot-vol rule do your deltas assume, and how do you test it?
  5. 🔒 What is your wing model?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: SVI, static arbitrage, smile-adjusted delta

Raw SVI with wing slopes \(b(1 \pm \rho)\), bounded by Lee: \(\limsup_{|k|\to\infty} w/|k| \le 2\).

\[ w(k) = a + b\left(\rho (k-m) + \sqrt{(k-m)^2 + s^2}\right) \]

No butterfly arbitrage iff (Durrleman)

\[ g(k) = \left(1 - \frac{k\,w'}{2w}\right)^2 - \frac{w'^2}{4}\left(\frac{1}{w} + \frac{1}{4}\right) + \frac{w''}{2} \ge 0; \]

no calendar arbitrage iff \(\partial_T w \ge 0\). Smile-adjusted delta, vega \(\mathcal{V}\):

\[ \Delta = \Delta_{BS} + \mathcal{V}\,\partial \sigma(K; S)/\partial S, \]

zero under sticky strike; \(-f'(k)/S\) times vega under sticky moneyness \(\sigma = f(\ln(K/S))\). Between refits, \(\text{theo} + \Delta\,dS + \tfrac12\Gamma\,dS^2\) costs a few multiply-adds per series.

docs.title: Order-book and trade-flow signals
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Four families: queue imbalance, order-flow imbalance (OFI), trade imbalance and cross-asset flow. VPIN is a contested toxicity gauge.
  • Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov (2014): over 10-second intervals the mid change ≈ OFI ÷ (2 × depth). In 50 NYSE stocks OFI explained 65% of price variance, trade imbalance 32% [Verified].
  • Explaining is not predicting: in Lab 03 (synthetic) OFI explains 70% of the same 10-second move but 4.5% of the next one.
  • Takers rarely monetize it: Lab 03's taker loses 1.44 ticks per round trip. Market makers use it free, to skew and cancel.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which way is the next tick, and is the flow hitting me informed? Inputs → Outputs book updates, signed trades, depth, leaders' flow → OFI, queue and trade imbalance, impact slopes for fair value, skew and cancels Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Retail flow internalization · Latency arbitrage · Lead-lag arbitrage · Fee-driven strategies · Intraday patterns · ML short-horizon alpha Latency / compute regime ns–µs running sums per event; windows 100 ms–60 s; coefficients refit daily Key parameters window or half-life 1–10 s (CKS: 10 s); book levels 1–5; depth normalization; trade-sign rule Main failure modes same-interval fit taken as a forecast; overlapping-window t-stats; spoofed or hidden size; taker costs Lab Lab 03

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: The mid moves when a queue at the touch runs out; a new bid, a cancelled offer or a market buy all push it up. Order-flow imbalance (OFI) is that bookkeeping. A thin book moves more per share, so impact scales with 1/depth: Kyle's lambda at the touch. Trades are only part of the flow; most quote changes are limit orders and cancels that never trade, which is why OFI beats trade imbalance on real data.
