docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Per top-of-book update, the CKS contribution: at an unchanged bid, the change in bid size; if the bid ticks up, the whole new queue; if down, minus the old one. The ask mirrors, sign flipped.
  2. Sum over intervals (or decay) to get OFI; record average depth.
  3. Trade imbalance (buyer- minus seller-initiated volume) and end-of-interval queue imbalance.
  4. Explain: regress the mid change on OFI. Predict: regress the next interval's change and score on held-out days.
import numpy as np
# Lab 03 sign convention: positive OFI = net buying pressure at the touch

def ofi_contributions(bid, ask, bid_size, ask_size):
    # CKS (2014) e_n of each top-of-book update n vs n-1, in shares
    b0, b1, a0, a1 = bid[:-1], bid[1:], ask[:-1], ask[1:]
    qb0, qb1, qa0, qa1 = bid_size[:-1], bid_size[1:], ask_size[:-1], ask_size[1:]
    e = (b1 >= b0) * qb1 - (b1 <= b0) * qb0 - (a1 <= a0) * qa1 + (a1 >= a0) * qa0
    return np.concatenate([[0.0], e])             # first update has no predecessor

def compute_ofi(time, bid, ask, bid_size, ask_size, mid, interval=10.0, tick=0.01):
    # Lab 03 takes a quotes DataFrame; plain arrays here, one row per book update
    e = ofi_contributions(bid, ask, bid_size, ask_size)
    n = int(np.ceil(time[-1] / interval))
    k = np.minimum((time // interval).astype(int), n - 1)        # interval of each update
    ofi = np.bincount(k, weights=e, minlength=n)
    depth = np.bincount(k, weights=0.5 * (bid_size + ask_size), minlength=n)
    depth /= np.maximum(np.bincount(k, minlength=n), 1)          # CKS average depth
    last = np.searchsorted(time, np.arange(n + 1) * interval, side="right") - 1
    mid_change = np.diff(mid[np.maximum(last, 0)] / tick)         # ticks
    return ofi, mid_change, depth

def trade_imbalance(trade_time, size, side, interval, n_intervals):
    # Lab 03 takes a trades DataFrame; side +1 buyer-, -1 seller-initiated
    k = np.minimum((trade_time // interval).astype(int), n_intervals - 1)
    return np.bincount(k, weights=size * side, minlength=n_intervals)

def fit_and_forecast(X_train, y_next_train, X_test):
    # Predictive use: NEXT interval's mid change on [ofi, trade_imb, queue_imb] (OLS)
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X_train)), X_train])
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y_next_train, rcond=None)
    return np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X_test)), X_test]) @ coef

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Start: bid 50.00 × 800, ask 50.01 × 600.

Event Contribution (shares) New 300-share bid at 50.00 +300 (bid size 800 → 1,100) Market buy for 600 clears the ask; next ask 50.02 × 900 +600 (old ask queue gone) 400 bid shares cancelled −400 New 200-share bid at 50.01 (bid ticks up) +200 (whole new queue) OFI +700

Trade imbalance is only +600. With average depth near 700, CKS predicts 700 ÷ (2 × 700) = 0.5 ticks (Lab 03's fitted constant gives 0.41). The mid actually rose a full tick: single intervals are noisy.

Can a taker trade it? Lab 03's 10-second forecast earns +0.32 ticks mid to mid. Crossing the 0.88-tick half-spread to enter leaves −0.56 ticks; crossing again to exit, −1.44 ticks per round trip (synthetic lab result).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Window. CKS used 10-second intervals; desks typically use event-time decayed sums matched to the forecast horizon [Lore].
  • Levels. Adding deeper levels improves fit (Xu, Gould and Howison 2018) [Verified].
  • Trade sign. Use the feed's aggressor flag; otherwise the Lee and Ready (1991) quote and tick rules [Verified].

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Linear impact. CKS find the OFI relation linear, depth-scaled and stable across stocks; the volume relation is noisier [Verified]. Desks feed OFI to nonlinear models [Lore]; in research, order-flow inputs beat raw book states, over about two price changes (Kolm, Turiel and Westray 2023) [Verified].
  • Trade flow. Kyle (1985) prices impact per unit of signed volume [Verified]. Order signs are long-memory because large orders are sliced (Lillo and Farmer 2004) [Verified], so trade imbalance persists.
  • Cross-asset. Lagged cross-asset OFI helps briefly (Cont, Cucuringu and Zhang 2023) [Verified]; HFT trade direction tracks book imbalance and predicts seconds ahead (Brogaard, Hendershott and Riordan 2014) [Verified].
  • VPIN (contested). Easley, López de Prado and O'Hara (2012) proposed volume-bucketed imbalance as a toxicity gauge [Verified]. Andersen and Bondarenko (2014) found it a poor volatility predictor that peaked after, not before, the Flash Crash, its power mostly a mechanical link to trading intensity [Verified]; the authors' rejoinder disputes this [Verified]. Desks lean on their own markouts [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
Keep explanatory and predictive R² apart; judge a maker's signal by markouts.

Lab 03, synthetic lab result (three simulated days):

Interval R², same interval (OFI) Out-of-sample R², next interval (all three signals) 1 s 25% 6.3% 5 s 57% 10.4% 10 s 70% 4.7% 30 s 82% 0.1%

The depth law holds: across 39 half-hours the slope of log impact on log depth is −1.01 (s.e. 0.18; model −1). The toy exaggerates twice: trade imbalance matches OFI (CKS found 32% versus 65%) because simulated liquidity providers requote after every market order, and the 5-second predictability peak comes from their 20-second belief lag. Real predictability is shorter and weaker after fees and latency. Same-interval fit is partly mechanical: CKS's R² fell to 35–60% without price-changing events [Verified].

Lab 03, synthetic. 10-second mid changes against OFI (with the CKS line) and trade imbalance.

Lab 03, synthetic. Note the different y-scales: explaining is easy, predicting is not.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Look-ahead: "forecasting" interval t with interval t's own OFI.
  • Overlapping windows inflate t-stats.
  • Spoofed, hidden and odd-lot size distort imbalance.
  • Fragmentation: per-venue and consolidated OFI disagree.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "OFI's ripping; lean the offer." → Skew quotes on flow rather than take.
  • "Great R², but it's contemporaneous." → It explains, it cannot be traded.
  • "The signal's real; it just doesn't pay the spread." → Predicted move < half-spread.
  • "VPIN spiked." "Check volume first." → VPIN largely tracks trading intensity.
  • "Normalize by depth or the betas won't travel." → Impact per share scales with 1/depth.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: Per venue or consolidated book?
  2. Basic: Book imbalance or trades: which matters more?
  3. Informed: What is your flow signal's half-life in price changes?
  4. Informed: How do you guard against spoofed size?
  5. Sharp: Do you ever take on flow, or only skew? 🔒

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: OFI, the depth law, Kyle's lambda and VPIN

CKS contribution of update \(n\) (bid \(P^B\), size \(q^B\); ask \(P^A\), size \(q^A\)):

\[ e_n = \mathbb{1}\{P^B_n \ge P^B_{n-1}\} q^B_n - \mathbb{1}\{P^B_n \le P^B_{n-1}\} q^B_{n-1} - \mathbb{1}\{P^A_n \le P^A_{n-1}\} q^A_n + \mathbb{1}\{P^A_n \ge P^A_{n-1}\} q^A_{n-1} \]

If every level holds \(D\) shares, removing \(D\) moves one side a tick and the mid half a tick, so \(\Delta \text{mid} \approx \mathrm{OFI}/(2D)\) ticks.

Kyle: price moves \(\lambda(x+u)\) with \(\lambda = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\Sigma_0}/\sigma_u\).

VPIN over \(n\) volume buckets of size \(V\), with bulk classification \(V^B_\tau = V\,\Phi(\Delta P_\tau/\sigma_{\Delta P})\):

\[ \mathrm{VPIN} = \frac{\sum_{\tau=1}^{n} \lvert V^S_\tau - V^B_\tau \rvert}{nV}. \]

docs.title: Queue position and order placement
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A resting order is worth P(fill) × (half-spread + rebate + markout). Both terms worsen with every share queued ahead of you.
  • In large-tick stocks priority is worth about half a tick: $0.56 per 100 shares in Lab 01 (synthetic), above a market maker's net margin.
  • Position is estimated: exact with order-level feeds, a guess about cancels with level-only feeds.
  • Placement compares expected values: stay, join elsewhere, improve, step back, take, or pay an inverted venue for priority.

Level: Deep dive · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Where am I in the queue, what is my order worth, and should I keep it, move it or take? Inputs → Outputs order-level (MBO) or level (MBP) feeds, own acks, fees, fill and markout history → shares ahead, P(fill), order value, placement action Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Options market making · Fee- and microstructure-driven · ML short-horizon · Reversal Latency / compute regime microseconds per book event at your price; fill and markout curves refit overnight Key parameters fill horizon 1–60 s; cancel model f (zero, log, identity); markout horizon 1–30 s; replace hysteresis 0.01–0.05 ticks Main failure modes optimistic cancel attribution; hidden size ahead; ack latency; amending away priority; stale fill curves Lab Lab 01

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: A resting limit order is an option written to the market. Flow that reaches the back of a long queue is disproportionately informed: it had to chew through everyone ahead first. In tick-constrained names the price cannot improve, so firms compete on queue position, speed and fees. In small-tick names, with spreads several ticks wide, you buy priority by improving the price instead. The limit order book shows the arithmetic; this card is the machinery.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Seed. Order-level feeds (Nasdaq TotalView-ITCH tags every add, execution and cancel with an order number) give the displayed shares ahead exactly. Level-only feeds: start from the level's size at the ack.
  2. Update. Trades come off the front. With level data, assign a fraction p of each cancel to the queue ahead (Rigtorp 2013).
  3. Fill probability from your own history, by shares ahead.
  4. Value = P(fill) × (markout + rebate), with the markout measured from fill price to the mid h seconds later, half-spread included.
  5. Place. Move (another venue, a better price in small-tick names, one level back, or take) only if the gain beats lost priority.
import numpy as np

def on_fill(fill, v):
    """Lab 01's queue rule with order-level data. v: our order {side: +1 buy / -1 sell,
    price, size, ahead_ids (orders resting ahead when we joined), traded, filled}."""
    hits_my_side = fill.taker_side == -v["side"]          # sells hit bids, buys lift asks
    at_or_through = fill.price <= v["price"] if v["side"] == 1 else fill.price >= v["price"]
    if hits_my_side and at_or_through and fill.maker_id not in v["ahead_ids"]:
        v["traded"] += fill.size        # everything ahead is gone: this volume reaches us
        if v["traded"] >= v["size"]:
            v["filled"], v["fill_time"] = True, fill.time

def update_shares_ahead(ahead, level_size, my_size, dq, is_trade, f=np.log1p):
    """Level-only (MBP) feeds; not in the lab (Rigtorp 2013). dq < 0: level shrank.
    f = identity: cancels pro rata; f = np.log1p: tilted to the back;
    f = np.zeros_like: risk-averse, every cancel is behind us."""
    if is_trade:
        return max(ahead + dq, 0.0)     # trades always come off the front
    behind = max(level_size - my_size - ahead, 0.0)
    denom = f(ahead) + f(behind)
    p_ahead = f(ahead) / denom if denom > 0 else 0.0
    return max(ahead + p_ahead * dq, 0.0)

def order_value_ticks(p_fill, markout_ticks, rebate_ticks=0.0):
    """Lab 01: value = P(fill) x mean markout of fills; unfilled orders earn 0.
    markout = side x (mid(t_fill + h) - fill price) / tick, half-spread included.
    Rebate (+) or maker fee (-) per fill is added here; the lab has no fees."""
    return p_fill * (markout_ticks + rebate_ticks)

def place(options, hysteresis_ticks=0.02):
    """options: {action: (p_fill, markout_ticks, rebate_ticks)}, including "stay"."""
    ev = {a: order_value_ticks(*o) for a, o in options.items()}
    best = max(ev, key=ev.get)
    if best != "stay" and ev[best] - ev["stay"] < hysteresis_ticks:
        return "stay", ev               # any move resets priority: demand a margin
    return best, ev

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. You join a $19.99 bid with 500 shares behind 4,000; 1,500 join behind you. A 1,000-share sell prints, leaving 3,000 ahead. Then the level shrinks by 1,200 with no print: cancels.

Cancel model Share of the 1,200 assumed ahead Shares ahead after Risk-averse, f = 0 0% 3,000 Log, f = ln(1 + x): 8.01 ÷ (8.01 + 7.31) 52% 2,373 Pro rata, f = x: 3,000 ÷ 4,500 67% 2,200

On Lab 01's curve: 10-second fill probability about 43% vs 33% (synthetic).

Buying priority. Lab 01's quartile results plus illustrative fees: a 0.29¢ maker rebate, or a 0.15¢ maker fee on an inverted venue, which takers sweep first because it pays them.

Per share posted (ticks) Back of the queue, maker-taker Front of the queue, inverted P(fill within 60 s) 0.82 0.94 Markout at 30 s, half-spread included −0.35 +0.29 Rebate (+) or fee (−) per fill +0.29 −0.15 Expected value 0.82 × (−0.06) = −0.05 0.94 × 0.14 = +0.13

A 0.44-tick fee swing buys 0.64 ticks of markout: +0.18 ticks net.

Why half a cent matters. The market maker's income statement in fees, rebates and ticks nets 0.16¢ a share; a 0.56¢ priority gap is 3.5 times that. Posting 20M shares a day from the back instead of the front costs about $112,000 a day [Estimate] (illustrative volume).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Cancel model f: fit on your own orders, matching predicted to realized fills [Reported] (Rigtorp). Backtesters default to risk-averse [Verified] (hftbacktest).
  • Horizons: fill horizon near the signal's half-life; markouts long enough to catch informed sweeps (10–30 s in Lab 01).
  • Hysteresis: repricing or adding size resets priority; reducing size keeps it.
  • Tick regime: Lab 01's spread sat at one tick 54% of the time (synthetic), a large-tick name.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: Poisson queues make fill probability a first-passage problem [Verified] (Cont, Stoikov & Talreja 2010). Moallemi and Yuan value large-tick queue positions, adverse selection included, at the order of the spread [Reported] (per Huang et al.).
  • Speed buys the queue: when the tick binds, providers compete on speed ("queue rationing") [Verified] (Yao & Ye 2018). Desks race to be first on a new level [Lore].
  • Inverted venues sell priority around binding ticks [Verified] (Comerton-Forde, Grégoire & Zhong 2019); their share in the 2016 Tick Size Pilot's trade-at group rose from 15% to 28% [Reported].
  • Pro-rata markets (some options and futures) reward size, not speed [Lore].
  • Regulation: a half-penny tick, deferred to November 2027 [Verified], would shorten queues [Estimate].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Calibration: predicted vs realized fills by shares-ahead bucket. Backtest fills above live fills mean an optimistic cancel model.
  • Markouts by position: if back-of-queue fills do not look worse, the position estimate is noise.
  • Lab 01 (synthetic lab result), 14,004 probes: 10-second fill rate 86% (front quartile) vs 47% (back); 10-second markouts +0.28 vs −0.23 ticks; front vs back of the same queue +0.56 vs +0.08 ticks.

Lab 01, synthetic: fill probability falls as shares ahead rise.

Lab 01, synthetic: back-of-queue fills give back the half-spread within about 10 s.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Invisible size: odd lots and reserve refills distort the count.
  • Ack latency: the level grows while your order travels.
  • Self-inflicted resets: a "refresh" cancel-and-replace sends you to the back.
  • Stationarity: fill curves shift around news, the open and the close.
  • Message limits: constant re-placement breaches order-to-trade limits.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We're 3k deep on BYX, 40k on the maker venue." → shares ahead, by venue.
  • "Back-of-queue fills are toxic." → they come just before the level breaks.
  • "Don't refresh it, you'll lose your spot." → amending resets priority.
  • "Pay the inverted fee to jump the line." → buying priority with the maker fee.
  • "The sim assumes pro-rata cancels; live looks risk-averse." → backtest overstates fills.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Which venues give you order-level data?
  2. How do you attribute cancels on level-only feeds?
  3. How much worse are back-of-queue markouts?
  4. When is an inverted venue's fee worth paying?
  5. 🔒 What priority value do you assign per venue?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: fill probability, order value and cancel attribution

With \(A\) shares ahead, size \(q\), traded volume \(N(t)\) and cancels ahead \(C(t)\):

\[ P_{\text{fill}}(h) = \Pr\big[N(h) + C(h) \ge A + q\big]. \]

For a buy with half-spread \(s/2\) and rebate \(r\):

\[ V = P_{\text{fill}}(h)\,\Big(\tfrac{s}{2} + r + \mathbb{E}\big[m_{t+h} - m_t \mid \text{fill}, A\big]\Big), \]

Queue value is \(V(0) - V(A)\). Level-only feeds, cancel \(\Delta Q < 0\), \(B\) shares behind:

\[ \hat A \leftarrow \max\!\Big(\hat A + \frac{f(\hat A)}{f(\hat A) + f(B)}\,\Delta Q,\ 0\Big). \]

Cost: O(1) per event per order.

docs.title: Quoting and inventory control
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A market maker earns the distance between its quotes and fair value on each fill and loses when leftover inventory moves against it. Quoting control sets where quotes are centered and how wide they are.
  • Avellaneda & Stoikov (2008): center on a reservation price \(r = s - q\gamma\sigma^2(T-t)\) that leans against inventory \(q\).
  • Guéant, Lehalle & Fernandez-Tapia (2013): closed-form, clock-free quotes with inventory limits, leaning a constant amount per lot.
  • Lab 05 (synthetic): GLFT earns what naive quoting earns ($95 vs $94 an hour) at a fifth of the risk. Adverse selection cuts it to $42; cancelling stale quotes faster recovers $68; widening barely helps.
  • Practice: fair value and an adverse-selection floor matter more than the formula [Lore].

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: market making · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Given fair value, inventory and fill rates, where should I bid and offer now? Inputs → Outputs fair value (M2), volatility σ, fill parameters A and k, inventory and limits, expected markout (M5), tick, fees → bid and ask (or none) and sizes Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Options market making · Retail flow internalization · Auctions and closing liquidity · Fee- and microstructure-driven strategies Latency / compute regime microseconds per requote (a lookup table by inventory); parameters refit intraday or overnight Key parameters γ from a target inventory half-life of seconds to minutes [Lore]; σ per second; A, k from own fills; per-name limit of hundreds to thousands of shares [Lore]; floor = markout + fees Main failure modes bad A and k; literal AS with a long horizon; skew lagging informed flow; sub-tick leans; per-name skew on factor risk Lab Lab 05

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Tight quotes fill often, but every fill leaves the dealer long or short, and inventory risk is an unhedged bet on the next move. A shop overstocked on umbrellas marks them down and offers suppliers less. A market maker long 3,000 shares lowers both quotes, so its offer is lifted more and its bid hit less: that lean is skew. Width sets how much each fill earns versus how often it happens. The lean grows with inventory × variance × expected holding time.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Center on fair value: the mid in the models, a microprice plus signals in practice (M2).
  2. Fill model: a quote \(\delta\) from fair value fills at Poisson rate \(\lambda(\delta) = A e^{-k\delta}\).
  3. Quote. Avellaneda-Stoikov: reservation price plus total spread. GLFT: a distance per side, with no bid at \(+q_{max}\) and no ask at \(-q_{max}\).
  4. Practitioner layer (not in the lab): floor at markout plus fees, snap to the tick, requote only on about a tick of change to keep queue position (M6).
  5. On fills: update \(q\), book the income-statement lines, send factor exposure to the hedger (M7).
import numpy as np
# Lab 05 units: prices in cents/share, q in lots of 100 shares, gamma in 1/$, k in 1/cent, A in fills/s.
# The lab clips distances at 0 (quotes never cross the mid) and applies a hard limit to every rule.

def as_quotes(mid, q, t, gamma, sigma, k, T):
    """Avellaneda & Stoikov (2008): lean the center against inventory, widen with risk."""
    tau = T - t
    reservation = mid - q * gamma * sigma**2 * tau                        # long (q > 0) -> both quotes lower
    spread = gamma * sigma**2 * tau + (2.0 / gamma) * np.log1p(gamma / k)
    return reservation - spread / 2, reservation + spread / 2            # bid, ask

def glft_quotes(q, gamma, sigma, A, k, q_max=np.inf):
    """Gueant, Lehalle & Fernandez-Tapia (2013): stationary distances from the mid."""
    base = np.log1p(gamma / k) / gamma                                     # fill-rate term
    c = np.sqrt(sigma**2 * gamma / (2 * k * A) * np.exp((1 + k / gamma) * np.log1p(gamma / k)))
    d_bid = base + (2 * q + 1) / 2 * c                                     # lean c per lot of inventory
    d_ask = base - (2 * q - 1) / 2 * c
    return np.where(q >= q_max, np.inf, d_bid), np.where(q <= -q_max, np.inf, d_ask)  # inf = no quote

def step_pnl(q_before, bought, sold, d_bid, d_ask, jump, diffusion):
    """Income-statement lines for one step ($): fills first, then the mid moves."""
    spread = bought * d_bid + sold * d_ask                                 # distance from mid earned
    adverse = (bought - sold) * jump                                       # move right after the fill
    inventory = q_before * jump + (q_before + bought - sold) * diffusion   # holding inventory
    return spread, adverse, inventory

# Practitioner wrapper: NOT in the lab (it has no tick, fees or markout floor). Illustrative.
def quote(fair, q, p, tick=1.0):
    d_bid, d_ask = glft_quotes(q, p.gamma, p.sigma, p.A, p.k, p.q_max)
    floor = p.exp_markout + p.fee_net_of_rebate                            # never quote inside expected toxicity
    d_bid, d_ask = np.maximum(d_bid, floor), np.maximum(d_ask, floor)
    bid = np.floor((fair - d_bid) / tick) * tick                            # snap outward to the grid
    ask = np.ceil((fair + d_ask) / tick) * tick
    return bid, ask

Lab 05, synthetic. Naive inventory wanders to the limit. GLFT leans a constant 0.25 cents per lot; AS leans 0.92 at the open and 0.08 at minute 55, so its inventory drifts late.

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Lab 05's illustrative parameters: $50 stock, σ = 0.654 cents/√s (σ² = 0.4274), A = 0.06/s, k = 1.5 per cent, γ = 0.01 per $; 1 cent × 1 lot (100 shares) = $1.

Step Calculation Result Fill-rate term (1/γ) ln(1 + γ/k) = 100 × ln(1.00667) 0.664 cents Lean per lot c √(0.4274 × 0.01 ÷ 0.18 × 1.00667^151) = √(0.02374 × 2.727) 0.254 cents Flat: each side 0.664 + c/2; fills 0.06 e^(−1.19) 0.792 cents; 66 an hour Long 3 lots: bid 0.664 + 3.5c; fills 0.06 e^(−2.33) 1.555 cents ($49.9845); one per 172 s Long 3 lots: ask 0.664 − 2.5c; fills 0.06 e^(−0.04) 0.028 cents ($50.0003); one per 17 s

Long 300 shares, the center sits 3c = 0.76 cents below the mid and the dealer sells ten times as fast as it buys. Width stays 2 × 0.664 + c = 1.58 cents at any inventory: GLFT skews, it does not widen. Flat spread income is 2 × 0.0183 × 0.792 = $0.029 a second, about $104 an hour (the simulation captured $96).

AS with the same γ and an hour left leans γσ²(T − t) = 0.01 × 0.4274 × 3,600 = 15.4 cents per lot, 60 times more. AS equals GLFT only at T − t = c/(γσ²) = 59.5 s.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• γ. Nobody knows their utility. Desks pick γ to hit an inventory half-life (say 30–120 s) or an inventory standard-deviation cap [Lore].
  • A, k. Bucket time quoted by distance from fair value, count fills, fit by Poisson regression (Go deeper). Refit by time of day and volatility. Your quotes choose which fills you see; in one-tick names queue position beats distance (M6).
  • σ. Per-second realized volatility of the microprice; a spike raises lean and width together.
  • Limits and floor. Inventory caps are enforced again in M9; the floor comes from markouts (M5).
  • Horizon. With AS, roll a horizon of tens of seconds to minutes, never the time to the close.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Lineage. Ho & Stoll (1981) is the classic dealer model of prices shading with inventory [Verified]. AS moved it to the limit order book [Verified]; GLFT bounded inventory and found the stationary solution [Verified]; Guéant (2017) extends it to several assets [Verified]. Cartea, Jaimungal & Penalva (2015), chapter 10, is the textbook, including quoting at the touch and adverse selection [Verified].
  • Fair value, not mid. Desks center on a microprice (Stoikov 2018) or a forecast [Verified]; Cartea, Jaimungal & Ricci (2014) put alpha and adverse selection into the quoting problem [Verified]. The forecast often moves quotes more than inventory does [Lore].
  • Linear skew in ticks: fair value − β·q, β a fraction of a tick per 100 shares scaled by volatility, then a floor and the grid [Lore]. GLFT justifies the linear, clock-free form.
  • Ticks bind. In tick-constrained names skew becomes which side you show and how much size [Lore].
  • Offload and hedge. Menkveld's HFT market maker was passive on 78% of trades yet offloaded positions on the incumbent exchange [Verified]. Factor exposure goes to futures and ETFs, leaving skew for stock-specific inventory [Lore].
  • Real intermediaries lean. NYSE specialist price pressure averaged 0.49% with a 0.92-day half-life (Hendershott & Menkveld 2014) [Verified]; spreads widened when specialists held large positions or lost money (Comerton-Forde et al. 2010) [Verified].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Inventory P&L averaging near zero; persistently negative means the lean is too slow or fair value lags.
  • Inventory half-life, time at the limit, end-of-day inventory.
  • Inventory-increasing fills should not mark out worse than inventory-reducing ones.

Lab 05, synthetic lab result (2,000 one-hour sessions, one stock, no ticks, fees or rivals):

Rule Mean $/hour Sd $/hour Sharpe-like (per hour) Fills/hour Inventory sd (lots) Naive, 0.67-cent half-spread 94 217 0.43 151 5.5 AS, γ = 0.0006 (matched risk) 86 46 1.88 131 1.2 GLFT, γ = 0.01 95 46 2.06 143 1.1 GLFT with adverse selection 42 53 0.78 180 1.2 … widened 0.25 cents (best widening) 44 53 0.83 130 1.2 … cancelling half of stale quotes 68 52 1.32 161 1.2

Naive's mean has a $5 standard error, so the means tie; the risk ranking holds across seeds. Do not annualize: a dealer with no rivals, fees or latency flatters every ratio. Real Sharpe ratios are measured daily on capital (equity market making).

Lab 05, synthetic. Left: model sessions cluster near $90; naive ones range from −$400 to +$600. Right: GLFT beats AS at every risk level; adverse selection (dashed) halves everyone.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Literal AS, long horizon: with γ = 0.01 it quotes about 17 cents wide, fills 19 times an hour and earns $16 (Lab 05).
  • Bad fill model: lean scales as \(1/\sqrt{kA}\); overstate A fourfold and you lean half as hard.
  • Inventory is information: repeated bid fills often mean fair value is falling; inventory-only skew reacts late.
  • Widening is blunt: widening by the measured 0.44-cent markout earned $40.5 vs $41.7 (Lab 05); speed helps more.
  • One factor, many names: long 200 stocks into a sell-off is one bet.
  • Sub-tick leans do nothing unless expressed through size or side.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "We lean a quarter tick per hundred." → center moves 0.25 tick per 100 shares.
  • "We're full; pull the bid." → at the long limit, stop bidding.
  • "Skew, don't widen." → move the center for inventory; keep width for toxicity.
  • "What's the half-life on inventory?" → seconds until a position halves.
  • "Our floor is markout plus fees." → minimum distance from fair value.
  • "Hedge the beta, skew the residual." → futures take factor risk; quotes lean on stock-specific inventory.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: Do you skew on price, size, or by dropping a side?
  2. Basic: How do you set risk aversion?
  3. Informed: How do you fit fill intensity when your quotes decide which fills you see?
  4. Informed: When do you hedge instead of skewing?
  5. Sharp: Do inventory-increasing fills mark out worse?
  6. Sharp: 🔒 Your skew per 100 shares and inventory half-life by liquidity bucket?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: AS and GLFT formulas, and fitting A and k

Mid \(dS_t = \sigma\,dW_t\); quotes \(S_t \mp \delta\) fill at rate \(A e^{-k\delta}\); the dealer maximizes \(\mathbb{E}[-\exp(-\gamma(X_T + q_T S_T))]\). AS obtain

\[ r_t = S_t - q\gamma\sigma^2(T-t), \qquad \delta^a + \delta^b = \gamma\sigma^2(T-t) + \frac{2}{\gamma}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\right). \]

The second term tends to \(2/k\) as \(\gamma \to 0\): the risk-neutral \(1/k\) per side. GLFT bound \(|q| \le Q\), reduce the HJB equation to linear ODEs, and far from \(T\) get

\[ \delta^{b,a}(q) \approx \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\right) \pm \frac{2q \pm 1}{2}\,c, \qquad c = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2\gamma}{2kA}\left(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\right)^{1+k/\gamma}}, \]

(upper signs for the bid), that is, AS with \(T-t\) fixed at \(\tau^* = c/(\gamma\sigma^2)\). AS motivate the exponential intensity from power-law order sizes with log price impact. To fit it, with \(T_j\) seconds quoted at distance \(\delta_j\) and \(N_j\) fills, maximize

\[ \ell(A,k) = \sum_j \big[N_j(\ln A - k\delta_j) - T_j A e^{-k\delta_j}\big]. \]

docs.title: Alpha decay detection and model retirement
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Alphas decay through publication, crowding, capacity and market-structure change. Across 97 published predictors, returns fell ~26% out of sample and ~58% after publication (McLean & Pontiff 2016).
  • Telling decay from bad luck is slow: SE(Sharpe) ≈ \(\sqrt{(1 + SR^2/2)/T}\) with SR and \(T\) in the same units, about \(1/\sqrt{\text{years}}\) for daily data. Separating Sharpe 1.0 from 0 at two standard errors takes about four years.
  • Monitors stack weak evidence: rolling IC t-stats, a CUSUM alarm on signal P&L, a Bayesian Sharpe posterior, crowding and capacity checks.
  • Retirement is staged (watch, down-weight, freeze, retire), and alarms trigger a human review, not an automatic kill.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: live · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Has this signal stopped working or is it having a bad run, and how much capital should it keep? Inputs → Outputs daily signal P&L and IC, backtest prior, ex-ante risk, crowding and cost data → alarm state, posterior Sharpe, weight multiplier, review ticket Used by strategies Cross-sectional alpha · Fundamental quant signals · Analyst revisions · Alternative data · NLP and LLM signals · ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Short-term reversal · Momentum · Factor timing and crowding Latency / compute regime overnight batch after attribution; milliseconds per signal, minutes for thousands of signals Key parameters backtest haircut 30–60%; prior SD 0.3–0.7 Sharpe; IC window 63–252 days; CUSUM slack \(k\) = half the shift to detect, threshold \(h\) for a 3–5 year false-alarm interval Main failure modes killing good signals at drawdown lows; detecting too late; false alarms across many signals; cost or data errors mistaken for decay Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Think of a goodwill impairment test. A signal was booked at its backtested value; each period, live evidence tests whether the carrying value is impaired. The catch: the evidence is so noisy that one bad year is weak proof, yet waiting for proof means funding a dead signal for years. Good monitors balance the two errors explicitly, like a credit watch list.

docs.text:
flowchart LR

  bt["Backtest prior, haircut"] --> mon

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Each night take the signal's standalone P&L and its information coefficient from attribution.
  2. Rolling IC t-stat over 63–252 days: mean IC ÷ (SD of IC ÷ √n). Below 2 is not significant; persistently below 1 puts the signal on watch.
  3. CUSUM (Page 1954) on standardized P&L shortfall: \(S_t = \max(0, S_{t-1} - z_t - k)\); alarm when \(S_t > h\). It accumulates only persistent underperformance and forgets isolated bad days.
  4. Bayesian Sharpe: shrink the live Sharpe ratio toward a haircut prior, weighting each by its precision.
  5. Diagnose the cause: crowding, capacity (costs rising with AUM), or publication.
  6. Act: posterior ÷ prior scales the weight the combiner gives the signal; alarms open a review.
import numpy as np

def decay_monitor(daily_pnl, daily_ic, vol_daily, sr_prior=1.0, prior_sd=0.5,
                  shift_sr=1.0, h=25.0, ic_window=126):
    """Nightly decay monitor for one signal (arrays, one entry per day).
    daily_pnl: standalone signal P&L from attribution; vol_daily: ex-ante daily P&L sigma
    sr_prior: annual Sharpe believed at launch, already haircut from the backtest
    shift_sr: Sharpe drop we want to catch (1.0 = alpha gone)
    h: CUSUM threshold in daily-sigma units (25 ~ one false alarm per 5 years)"""
    mu0 = sr_prior * vol_daily / np.sqrt(252)        # expected daily P&L if alpha is intact
    k = 0.5 * shift_sr / np.sqrt(252)                # slack = half the shift, in sigma units
    S, rows = 0.0, []
    for t in range(len(daily_pnl)):
        z = (daily_pnl[t] - mu0) / vol_daily         # standardized surprise vs expectation
        S = max(0.0, S - z - k)                      # lower CUSUM: grows on persistent shortfall
        alarm = S > h

        ic = daily_ic[max(0, t - ic_window + 1): t + 1]
        ic_t = ic.mean() / (ic.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(ic))) if len(ic) > 20 else np.nan

        n = t + 1                                    # Bayesian update of the annual Sharpe
        sr_hat = np.mean(daily_pnl[:n]) / vol_daily * np.sqrt(252)
        se2 = (1 + (sr_hat / np.sqrt(252)) ** 2 / 2) * 252 / n   # Lo (2002), iid, annualized
        w = (1 / prior_sd**2) / (1 / prior_sd**2 + 1 / se2)       # weight on the prior
        sr_post = w * sr_prior + (1 - w) * sr_hat

        weight_mult = float(np.clip(sr_post / sr_prior, 0.0, 1.0))  # sent to the combiner
        rows.append((t, S, alarm, ic_t, sr_post, weight_mult))
        if alarm:
            S = 0.0                                  # human review opens; restart the count
    return rows

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
How long until a drop is statistically visible? With daily data, SE(annual Sharpe) ≈ \(\sqrt{1/T}\) for \(T\) years. A two-standard-error gap needs \(T = (2/\Delta SR)^2\):

Sharpe before → after Drop Years to a 2-SE gap 1.0 → 0 1.0 (2/1)² = 4.0 3.0 → 1.5 1.5 (2/1.5)² = 1.8 8.0 → 4.0 4.0 (2/4)² = 0.25 (≈ 3 months)

The absolute drop is what matters, so a high-Sharpe market maker sees decay in weeks while a monthly factor book needs years.

Bayesian update (illustrative). Prior N(1.0, 0.5²), so prior precision 4. One live year at Sharpe −0.2 has variance ≈ 1/1 (precision 1): posterior = (4 × 1.0 + 1 × −0.2) ÷ 5 = 0.76. Two such years (precision 2): (4 − 0.4) ÷ 6 = 0.60. Three: (4 − 0.6) ÷ 7 = 0.49. The weight multiplier falls to 0.76, 0.60, 0.49.

CUSUM, \(k\) = 0.5/√252 = 0.0315, \(h\) = 25. A −1.5σ day adds 1.5 + 0.063 − 0.0315 ≈ 1.53 to \(S\). In 300 simulated Gaussian paths per case [Estimate]: mean time to a false alarm with Sharpe intact ≈ 5.1 years; mean time to alarm after Sharpe falls to 0 ≈ 1.6 years, to −0.5 ≈ 1.2 years, to 0.5 ≈ 2.7 years.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Prior haircut: start from a backtest Sharpe cut by 30–60%, in line with the out-of-sample evidence below [Estimate].
  • Threshold \(h\): set from the false-alarm interval you can afford. With 200 signals and one false alarm per signal per 5 years, expect ~40 reviews a year [Estimate], which is why alarms open reviews instead of killing signals.
  • Stages (illustrative): watch on alarm or IC t-stat below 1; down-weight by posterior ÷ prior; freeze capital below 0.5; retire after a review finds no economic story.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Live
  Live --> Watch: CUSUM alarm or IC t below 1
  Watch --> Live: review finds noise
  Watch --> DownWeighted: posterior below prior
  DownWeighted --> Frozen: posterior below half of prior
  Frozen --> Retired: no economic story
  Frozen --> Live: new evidence, re-validated
  Retired --> [*]

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Publication decay: McLean & Pontiff (2016) find returns of 97 predictors fall ~26% out of sample (an upper bound on data mining) and ~58% post-publication, so at least ~32% (58 − 26) reflects publication-informed trading [Verified].
  • Out-of-sample decay: Falck, Rej & Thesmar (2022) find 72 published strategies keep about half their in-sample performance; publication year alone explains about 30% of the variance in decay across strategies, and overfitting proxies add roughly 15% [Verified].
  • Crowding: Lou & Polk's comomentum (excess return correlation among momentum stocks) flags crowding; when high, momentum returns tend to revert [Verified]. Desks also watch short interest in the short leg and holdings overlap [Lore].
  • Capacity decay is yours alone: gross alpha holds, net falls as impact rises with size (cost models) [Estimate]. Plot gross and net bps against AUM.
  • Textbook: test "Sharpe = 0". Practice: tests lack power, so firms shrink and down-weight gradually [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Realized false-alarm rate matches the designed interval.
  • Retired signals, paper-traded afterwards, earn about zero; if they keep earning, the monitor is too trigger-happy [Lore].
  • Posterior Sharpe predicts next year's realized Sharpe better than the backtest does.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Pro-cyclical retirement: killing a factor at the bottom of a crowding drawdown locks in the loss (quant winters).
  • Regime vs decay: a signal dormant in one regime looks dead.
  • Autocorrelated P&L (overlapping holding periods) shrinks the true sample; use effective \(T\).
  • Re-launching variants of a retired idea is multiple testing in disguise (V4).

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "It's in the penalty box." → down-weighted pending review.
  • "Is that decay or a drawdown?" → structural loss or bad luck?
  • "CUSUM tripped on the revisions sleeve." → persistent shortfall alarm fired.
  • "Comomentum is spiking." → crowded trade; unwind risk rising.
  • "The alpha's fine; we're too big for it." → capacity decay.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. What haircut do you apply to backtest Sharpe before going live?
  2. How many years of live data before you trust a signal's Sharpe?
  3. Do alarms trigger automatic de-risking or a review?
  4. How do you separate capacity decay from alpha decay?
  5. 🔒 Which crowding indicators actually led your drawdowns?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: Sharpe standard error, Bayesian update, CUSUM run lengths

For iid returns, per-period Sharpe \(s\), \(n\) periods (Lo 2002):

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat s) \approx \frac{1 + s^2/2}{n}. \]

With \(q\) periods a year (\(n = qT\)): \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{SR}) \approx (1 + SR^2/2q)/T\); for daily data the \(SR^2\) term is negligible. Fat tails and autocorrelation raise it (Bailey & López de Prado 2012).

Prior \(N(\mu_0, \tau^2)\), estimate variance \(\sigma^2/T\):

\[ \mu_{\text{post}} = \frac{\mu_0/\tau^2 + \widehat{SR}\,T/\sigma^2}{1/\tau^2 + T/\sigma^2}. \]

A standard approximation for Gaussian CUSUM (\(b = h + 1.166\)) gives mean run length \((e^{2kb} - 2kb - 1)/2k^2\) ≈ 1,285 days here, matching the simulation.

docs.title: Live monitoring and P&L attribution
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Attribution splits P&L into lines with an owner and an expected value: factor vs specific (alpha), holding vs trading, cost vs the cost model, and each alpha sleeve's share.
  • Quant equity book: P&L = Σ (dollar factor exposure × factor return) + specific P&L + trading P&L. Alpha should appear in the specific line.
  • Market maker: the same idea as an income statement: spread capture + rebates − adverse selection ± inventory − hedging costs − fees.
  • Monitoring adds exposures, limits, fill rates, latency and drift, wired to alerts someone acts on.

Level: Core · Pipeline stage: live · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Did the book make money for the reasons the model says, and is anything drifting or about to break? Inputs → Outputs positions, fills, prices, risk-model exposures and factor returns, cost forecasts, sleeve targets → P&L by factor, specific, trading, cost and sleeve; dashboards and alerts Used by strategies Equity market making · ETF market making · Options market making · Retail flow internalization · Cross-sectional alpha · Factor-residual mean reversion · ML-driven short-horizon alpha · Stat arb overview Latency / compute regime real time for marks and limits (sub-second at a market maker); end-of-day batch attribution (seconds for 3,000 names × 60–80 factors) Key parameters risk model (≈ 10 styles + 50–70 industries); markout horizons 1 s–5 min; alert bands (P&L beyond 3σ of ex-ante risk, slippage > 1.5–2× model, limit usage > 80%) Main failure modes bad marks; attribution model ≠ optimizer's; naive sleeve splits; ignored alerts Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Think segment reporting plus budget-vs-actual variance analysis. Each line has a budget: specific return P&L should be positive on average (the alpha), factor P&L near zero in a neutral book, costs close to the cost model. The variance says where to look: beta, a style tilt, stock picks or the trading itself.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Reconcile. P&L from positions and cash must match the books to the dollar; a residual is a data problem.
  2. Holding P&L = prior-close dollars × today's return: the no-trade P&L.
  3. Factor split. With \(r_i = \sum_k X_{ik} f_k + u_i\) from the risk model, dollar factor exposure \(E_k = \sum_i h_i X_{ik}\) earns \(E_k f_k\); the rest, \(\sum_i h_i u_i\), is specific P&L.
  4. Trading P&L = total − holding. Split into slippage vs arrival (implementation shortfall) and post-arrival drift; compare slippage with the model.
  5. Per-alpha. Run each sleeve's paper portfolio through steps 2–4; the gap to the real book is a netting line.
  6. Link days so monthly lines still sum; alert on lines outside their bands.
import numpy as np

def factor_attribution(h_start, h_end, px_prev, px_close, fills, X, f, model_cost_bps):
    """One day's attribution for an equity book; all money in $.
    h_start, h_end: shares at prior close / today's close, shape (N,)
    fills: list of (i, signed_shares, fill_px, arrival_px)
    X: (N, K) risk-model exposures; f: (K,) today's factor returns
    model_cost_bps: (N,) pre-trade cost forecast. Fees, rebates, borrow booked separately."""
    r = px_close / px_prev - 1.0                     # total stock returns
    dollars = h_start * px_prev                      # $ held at the start of the day
    holding_pnl = dollars * r                        # P&L had we not traded

    exposure = X.T @ dollars                         # $ exposure per factor, (K,)
    factor_pnl = exposure * f                        # P&L per factor, (K,)
    u = r - X @ f                                    # specific (residual) returns
    specific_pnl = dollars * u                       # per-stock alpha P&L, (N,)

    trading, slip, slip_model = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for i, q, fill_px, arrival_px in fills:
        trading += q * (px_close[i] - fill_px)       # fill marked to the close
        slip += -q * (fill_px - arrival_px)          # vs arrival; negative = cost
        slip_model += -abs(q) * arrival_px * model_cost_bps[i] / 1e4

    total = holding_pnl.sum() + trading
    cash_spent = sum(q * p for _, q, p, _ in fills)
    books = h_end @ px_close - h_start @ px_prev - cash_spent
    assert abs(total - books) < 1e-6 * max(1.0, abs(books)), "unexplained P&L: fix data"
    return {
        "factor": factor_pnl,                        # should be ~0 on average if neutral
        "specific": specific_pnl.sum(),              # the alpha line
        "trading": trading,
        "slippage_vs_arrival": slip,
        "slippage_vs_model": slip - slip_model,      # > 0: cheaper than the model said
        "after_arrival_drift": trading - slip,       # timing, not execution quality
        "total": total,
    }

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. One factor (beta). Long $10M of A (beta 1.2), short $10M of B (beta 0.8). Factor return −2.0%; A returns −1.5%, B −3.0%.

  • Dollar beta 10 × 1.2 − 10 × 0.8 = +$4M → factor P&L = −$80,000.
  • \(u_A\) = −1.5% + 2.4% = +0.9% → +$90,000; \(u_B\) = −3.0% + 1.6% = −1.4%, short earns +$140,000 → specific +$230,000.
  • Holding: −$150,000 + $300,000 = +$150,000 = −80,000 + 230,000 ✓.

The book also bought 50,000 A: arrival $99.80, average fill $99.86, close $98.50.

  • Trading P&L = 50,000 × (98.50 − 99.86) = −$68,000.
  • Slippage vs arrival = −50,000 × 0.06 = −$3,000 (6 bps); the model said 8 bps (−$3,992), so execution beat it by $992.
  • The other −$65,000 is A falling after arrival: a timing question, not execution.

Total +$82,000. The alpha made $230,000; an unintended beta tilt cost $80,000. Fix the hedge, not the alpha.

A market maker's day as an income statement:

Line $ (illustrative) Measured as Spread capture +120,000 signed qty × (mid at fill − fill price) Rebates net of take fees +35,000 fee schedule × volume Adverse selection −85,000 markout: qty × (mid +1 min − mid at fill) Inventory P&L −10,000 drift beyond the markout horizon Hedging costs −15,000 hedge slippage and fees Clearing and regulatory fees −8,000 per share and notional Net trading income +37,000

Watch adverse selection ÷ spread capture (here 71%).

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Risk model: use the optimizer's, or "factor P&L" stops meaning "risk we chose or failed to hedge".
  • Markout horizons: 1 s, 10 s, 1 min, 5 min; the curve's shape matters more than one point (M5).
  • Alert bands: scale to ex-ante risk; warn near 80% of a limit, hard stop at 100% [Lore].
  • Dashboards: factor and sector exposures, limit usage, fill rates, order-to-ack latency (p50/p99), live vs training forecast distribution (drift), each with an owner.

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Textbook: Brinson sector attribution vs a benchmark. Practice: factor attribution off the risk model; vendor tools report factor contributions, specific return and trading impact [Verified] (MSCI).
  • Holding vs trading is Perold's paper-vs-real portfolio gap (1988) [Verified].
  • Linking: daily lines do not sum to compounded returns; Menchero (2004) finds one linking method meets all his criteria [Verified].
  • Market makers: Menkveld's study of one HFT market maker found ≈ €1.55 per trade from the spread against ≈ €0.68 of positioning losses, ≈ €0.88 overall [Verified] (working-paper figures).
  • Monitoring: before Knight Capital's 2012 loss, 97 automated emails flagged an error pre-open, but were not designed as alerts and went unread; the SEC's first market access rule case followed ($12M penalty) [Verified].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• Reconciliation residual is zero daily.
  • Factor P&L averages near zero in a neutral book; a persistent sign is an unhedged bet.
  • Realized ÷ forecast slippage ≈ 1.0 over 20 days (TCA).
  • Daily P&L ÷ ex-ante σ has standard deviation 0.8–1.2 [Estimate]; otherwise suspect the risk model.
  • Specific-P&L Sharpe tracks the haircut backtest; slides go to alpha decay detection.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Bad marks: stale closes or missed splits book phantom specific P&L.
  • Leakage: an alpha with a momentum tilt shows as factor P&L; hedging it away hedges away alpha.
  • Pro-rata sleeves: sleeves wanting +$6M and −$2M; pro-rating the +$4M net misstates both.
  • Alert fatigue: amber lights train people to ignore red ones.

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "Specific was +2.3 bps; we gave it back on beta." → the alpha worked, the hedge didn't.
  • "What's the unexplained?" → reconciliation residual; nonzero means bad data.
  • "Slippage ran 1.4× model." → costs above forecast.
  • "Markouts go negative at ten seconds." → informed flow is picking us off.
  • "Momentum ate us on the attribution." → a style factor dominated.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Is your attribution model the optimizer's risk model?
  2. What share of P&L variance is factor vs specific?
  3. How do you split P&L across alphas in a netted book?
  4. Which alert last fired, and what changed afterwards?
  5. 🔒 What markout horizon defines "toxic" for you?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: factor attribution and the market-maker identity

Holdings \(h\) (dollars), exposures \(X\), regression factor returns \(f\):

\[ h^\top r = (X^\top h)^\top f + h^\top u . \]

One fill of signed size \(q\) at price \(p\); mid \(m_t\) at fill, \(m_{t+\tau}\) at the markout horizon, \(m_T\) at the close:

\[ q(m_T - p) = \underbrace{q(m_t - p)}_{\text{spread}} + \underbrace{q(m_{t+\tau} - m_t)}_{\text{adverse sel.}} + \underbrace{q(m_T - m_{t+\tau})}_{\text{inventory}} . \]

Cost is \(O(NK)\) per day.

docs.title: Reinforcement learning in trading
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Reinforcement learning (RL) learns a policy (state → action) that maximizes cumulative reward when today's action changes tomorrow's state. Execution, market making and hedging fit because inventory carries over.
  • Key evidence: Nevmyvaka, Feng & Kearns (2006) on execution, Spooner et al. (2018) on market making, Buehler et al. (2019) on deep hedging. Most results beat simple baselines, not production algos.
  • Hard because markets are non-stationary, simulators cannot show how the market reacts to you, agents exploit simulator flaws, and there is one history to learn from.
  • Reported production use is mainly bank execution (J.P. Morgan's LOXM, 2017); deep hedging was co-developed by J.P. Morgan researchers. RL as a quant-fund profit engine is lore.

Level: Deep dive · Pipeline stage: live · Last verified: 2026-11

Field Value Purpose (the question it answers) Which actions (trade size, quote placement, hedge size) maximize reward when each action changes the next state? Inputs → Outputs state features (time left, inventory, spread, imbalance), a simulator or replay, a reward → a policy (table or network), tested against model-based baselines Used by strategies Equity market making · Options market making · ML-driven short-horizon alpha Latency / compute regime training offline (CPU-hours to GPU-days); inference µs–ms (table lookup or small network); decisions every 1–60 s for execution Key parameters discount γ 1.0 (finite-horizon execution) to 0.99–0.999 (market making); learning rate 0.01–0.1; exploration ε 0.05–0.2, decaying; 5–20 buckets per state variable; inventory or risk penalty; 10⁴–10⁷ episodes Main failure modes overfitting the simulator; reward hacking; regime change; costly live exploration; opaque policies Lab —

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Supervised learning predicts; RL decides. A price forecast does not say how fast to sell 10,000 shares, because selling moves the price and what you still hold shapes the next choice. That is dynamic programming, as in real-options valuation, except RL learns the transitions by trial and error. The problem is framed as a Markov decision process:

Problem State Action Reward Baseline to beat Execution time left, shares left, spread, imbalance child size or limit-price offset −slippage vs arrival mid × shares; penalty for leftovers TWAP, Almgren-Chriss Market making inventory, spread, microprice signal, volatility bid and ask offsets, size spread P&L + inventory mark − inventory penalty Avellaneda-Stoikov quotes Hedging position Greeks, time to expiry, cost hedge trade size −risk measure of hedging error − costs delta hedge with bands

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
Tabular Q-learning for a toy liquidation:

  1. Discretize state: step \(t\) and lots left.
  2. Keep a table \(Q(s, a)\): total reward expected from action \(a\) in state \(s\), then acting well.
  3. Each step, mostly take the best-looking action, sometimes a random one (ε-greedy exploration).
  4. Observe reward \(r\) and next state \(s'\); nudge \(Q(s,a)\) toward \(r + \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\).
  5. Repeat for many episodes; the greedy policy is the argmax of each row.
import numpy as np

def q_learning_execution(n_lots=10, lot=1_000, T=5, max_sell=4, half_spread=0.01,
                         eta=1e-6, sigma=0.10, risk_aversion=2e-5,
                         alpha=0.1, eps=0.1, n_episodes=50_000, seed=0):
    """Tabular Q-learning: sell n_lots * lot shares within T steps.
    State = (step t, lots left); action = lots to sell now (0..max_sell).
    Reward = -(half-spread + linear temporary impact) - variance penalty on unsold shares.
    Simplified: price noise enters only via the risk penalty, so rewards are
    deterministic; a real study replays historical order books instead."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Q = np.zeros((T + 1, n_lots + 1, max_sell + 1))   # Q[t, lots_left, action]

    def step(t, inv, a):
        a = inv if t == T - 1 else min(a, inv)        # last step: must sell what is left
        q = a * lot                                   # shares sold now
        cost = q * (half_spread + eta * q)            # spread + impact ($)
        risk = risk_aversion * ((inv - a) * lot * sigma) ** 2   # $ penalty for holding risk
        return -(cost + risk), inv - a

    for _ in range(n_episodes):
        inv = n_lots
        for t in range(T):
            if inv == 0:
                break
            explore = rng.random() < eps              # epsilon-greedy exploration
            a = int(rng.integers(max_sell + 1)) if explore else int(Q[t, inv].argmax())
            r, nxt = step(t, inv, a)
            target = r + (Q[t + 1, nxt].max() if nxt > 0 else 0.0)  # gamma = 1
            Q[t, inv, a] += alpha * (target - Q[t, inv, a])         # TD update
            inv = nxt
    return Q, Q.argmax(axis=2)                        # policy: lots to sell per (t, lots_left)

docs.title: Worked example with numbers
docs.text:
Illustrative. Sell 10,000 shares in 5 steps; half-spread $0.01; impact $0.001 per 1,000 shares sold in a step; σ = $0.10 per share per step; risk aversion 2 × 10⁻⁵ per dollar.

  • All at once: 10,000 × (0.01 + 0.01) = $200, no risk penalty.
  • TWAP (2,000 per step): cost 5 × 2,000 × 0.012 = $120; risk 2 × 10⁻⁵ × (800² + 600² + 400² + 200²) = $24; total $144.
  • Learned 4-2-2-1-1 (thousands): cost 56 + 24 + 24 + 11 + 11 = $126; risk 2 × 10⁻⁵ × (600² + 400² + 200² + 100²) = $11.4; total $137.4, the brute-force optimum.

One update by hand: from \(Q = 0\), selling 4 lots at \(t=0\) gives \(r\) = −(56 + 2 × 10⁻⁵ × 600²) = −63.2; next-state values are still 0, so \(Q\) ← 0 + 0.1 × (−63.2 − 0) = −6.32. After convergence that entry reaches −137.4, the full cost-to-go.

The toy front-loads, as Almgren-Chriss does in closed form. RL earns its keep only when the state carries information the closed form ignores, such as spread and imbalance.

docs.title: Key parameters and how practitioners tune them
docs.text:
• Reward design matters most: raw P&L teaches the agent to gamble on inventory; add inventory and leftover penalties.
  • State size: 10 variables × 10 buckets is 10¹⁰ cells, so real work uses function approximation (tile coding, neural networks).
  • Data split by time, with the test period after training, as in time-series cross-validation.
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Agent
  participant M as Market or simulator
  A->>M: action (sell 4 lots)
  M-->>A: reward (minus cost and risk)
  M-->>A: next state (t=1, 6 lots left)
  A->>A: update Q toward reward plus best next value

docs.title: Textbook version vs what firms actually do
docs.text:
• Execution: Nevmyvaka, Feng & Kearns used 1.5 years of millisecond NASDAQ order-book data (12 months train, 6 test); state was time and inventory left plus market variables, action the limit price; they report substantial gains over baselines [Verified], roughly 27–36% over submit-and-leave per a course summary [Reported]. Ning, Lin & Jaimungal's double deep Q-network beat TWAP on most of nine stocks [Verified].
  • Market making: Spooner et al.'s temporal-difference agent, trained in a limit-order-book simulator with a reward shaped to control inventory risk, beat simple benchmarks and an online-learning method [Verified].
  • Hedging: Buehler et al.'s deep hedging minimizes a convex risk measure and beat the complete-market hedge under transaction costs in a Heston model; two authors were at J.P. Morgan [Verified].
  • Production: the FT reported in 2017 that J.P. Morgan's LOXM used deep RL trained on historic and simulated trades in European equity algos, constrained while it learned; performance claims are the bank's [Reported]. RL quoting at HFT firms has no public evidence [Lore].

docs.title: How to tell if it's working
docs.text:
• It beats the model-based baseline out of sample, after costs, with confidence intervals.
  • The policy is sane: sells faster with more inventory and less time; skews quotes against inventory.
  • Simulated fill rates and slippage match shadow trading; a gap means the simulator is being gamed.

docs.title: Failure modes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Simulator fidelity: replayed history cannot react to your orders. Agent-based simulators such as ABIDES try to [Verified], but calibration is hard.
  • Reward hacking: agents find simulator artifacts, e.g. assuming a fill whenever price touches the order [Lore].
  • Non-stationarity: tick sizes, fees and competitors change; old policies degrade (alpha decay).
  • Sample efficiency: one history; a daily policy sees 252 decisions a year, and live exploration costs real money.

For the wider literature, see the survey by Hambly, Xu & Yang (2023) [Verified].

docs.title: How practitioners talk about it
docs.text:
• "It's just DP with a learned model." → RL as approximate dynamic programming.
  • "What's the reward?" → the first question; most bugs live there.
  • "It learned the simulator, not the market." → overfit to simulator artifacts.
  • "Does it beat Almgren-Chriss net of costs?" → the right baseline.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Which baseline does it beat, by how many bps out of sample?
  2. Replay or agent-based simulation? How is impact modeled?
  3. Did the agent ever game the reward?
  4. What triggers retraining?
  5. 🔒 Which decisions in your stack are learned policies vs closed-form rules?

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
Math: Bellman equation, Q-learning, deep hedging objective

Optimal action values satisfy

\[ Q^*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}\left[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \mid s, a\right], \]

which Q-learning approximates stochastically; tabular memory is \(O(|S||A|)\).

Deep hedging chooses hedge ratios \(\delta_t\) from a network to minimize a convex risk measure \(\rho\) of the hedged payoff \(Z\):

\[ \min_{\delta} \; \rho\left(-Z + \sum_t \delta_t (S_{t+1} - S_t) - C_T(\delta)\right), \]

with \(C_T\) the transaction costs.

docs.title: Walkthrough: a day at an ETF market maker
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • One simulated day for the market maker and authorized participant of a 50-stock US equity ETF: quote around fair value, hedge fills with futures, create whole units at the close.
  • The quote is hedge cost plus expected adverse selection plus a lean. The lean comes from the risk left after the futures hedge: 0.10 bp per creation unit, against 0.70 bp unhedged.
  • Net trading income was $10,284, or 2.35 bps of $43.8M of ETF traded (synthetic lab result). Spread earned $14,142; pick-offs, hedging, the basket and fees took most of it back; a lucky $4,292 basis gain made up the rest.
  • The raw markout on a hedged block is mostly market noise: +20 bps at 60 s, −34 bps by the close. Measured against the futures hedge it stays near +8 to +11 bps, close to the spread charged.
  • Creating 4 units cost 6.1 bps each, against about 7.6 bps to buy back from rivals. A pure-arbitrage check at the closing premium of 0.45 bp adds nothing: arbitrage starts at 7.45 bps.

Level: Core · Read time: ~13 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Cast and setup
docs.text:
The firm is the lead market maker and an authorized participant (AP) in Lab 07's synthetic fund: the 50 largest names of a simulated 200-stock market, 50,000 ETF shares per creation unit. It quotes on exchange, answers a block request for quote (RFQ), hedges with an index future and settles its net position through creation and redemption.

The day is day 316 of Lab 07's five-year world (seed 7): the first day after day 300 that was calm, rose modestly (index +26.6 bps) and had an ETF-versus-index basis move under 5 bps, so the income statement shows the business rather than one basis swing. Intraday paths are Brownian, bridged to the simulator's closes, with market-wide news jumps about once a minute.

Assumption (illustrative) Value ETF NAV at yesterday's close; unit value $43.92; $2.20M Hedges future on all 200 names ($50 × 6,000, 0.25-point tick, $1 a contract); peer ETF on the top 100 Client flow 500-share Poisson fills at 0.07·e^(−0.67·δ) per second per side (δ in bps); buys 1.2×, sells 0.8× Fast arbitrageurs hit a stale quote for 2,000 shares when news jumps through it; we cancel half in time RFQ block client buys 250,000 shares (5 units) at 11:00 Fees maker rebate $0.0020 and closing-auction fee $0.0010 a share [Estimate]; SEC Section 31 fee $20.60 per million sold [Verified]

The script labs/walkthroughs/etf-market-maker.py (deterministic, about 1 s) chains the labs' core functions and writes etf-market-maker.json: nav, no_arbitrage_band and arb_decision from Lab 07; glft_quotes and step_pnl from Lab 05; markouts from Lab 04; the microprice table of Lab 02. Every dollar figure is a synthetic lab result for one stylized fund with no competing quoters: it shows mechanisms and proportions, not a real desk's profit.

flowchart LR
    pre["Pre-open<br/>basket file, band, limits"] --> fv["Fair value<br/>NAV of live basket"]
    fut["Index future and peer ETF"] --> fv
    fv --> q["Quotes<br/>GLFT lean, cost floor, band cap"]
    q --> fills["Fills<br/>clients, fast arbs, RFQ block"]
    fills --> inv["Inventory"]
    inv --> hedge["Futures hedge"]
    inv --> q
    hedge --> close["Close<br/>MOC basket, create units"]
    inv --> close
    fills --> mo["Markouts by counterparty"]
    close --> pnl["Income statement"]
    mo --> pnl

docs.title: Pre-open: basket, creation unit, borrow and limits
docs.text:
Before 9:30 the desk loads the basket file: shares of each stock per unit plus a $1,823 cash component; the top ten names are 36.5% of the fund. From yesterday's closing data, Lab 07's no_arbitrage_band prices the band:

Cost of creating one unit bps ETF half-spread 1.49 Basket half-spreads, cap-weighted 1.73 Basket impact (square-root law) 1.95 Creation fee ($500 per order) 2.28 Create bound (the redeem bound adds 0.07 bp of borrow) 7.45 (7.52)

That is close to Lab 07's five-year average of 7.38 bps; in stress the band reached 14.86 bps (synthetic lab result). The fee is Lab 07's stylized $500. SPY's real fee is the lower of $3,000 or 10 bps of a unit, per participant per day [Verified].

Borrow. Bona fide market making is exempt from the Reg SHO locate requirement [Verified], so the desk can sell ETF shares it does not own (shorting and settlement). Overnight shorts pay an assumed 30 bps a year; redemptions borrow the basket at Lab 07's 25 bps.

Limits (M9 risk controls): ±10 units of ETF ($22M, Lab 07's balance-sheet cap), 100 futures, ±$500k of residual delta after hedging, 1 unit carried overnight, and a loss stop to reduce-only. Peak use today: 5.67 units, 43 contracts, $150k.

timeline
    title The simulated day, day 316
    Pre-open : Load basket file : Price the band at 7.45 bps : Set limits
    09.30 to 11.00 : Quote around NAV : Clients net buyers, short 0.62 units by 10.30
    11.00 : RFQ block sells 5 units at fair value plus 8.53 bps : Hedge up to 43 futures within a second
    11.00 to 15.50 : Skewed quotes attract sellers : Short falls to 4.46 units
    15.50 MOC cutoff : Basket MOC order for 4 units
    16.00 Close : Create 4 units : Sell 30 futures : Carry 0.36 units hedged

docs.title: Fair value from the basket, futures and a peer ETF
docs.text:
Fair value is Lab 07's nav() on live constituent prices each second: $43.924 at the open, $44.040 at the close (+26.4 bps). Two outside instruments show where the basket is heading and what can hedge it, with hedge ratios from the previous 250 days:

Daily, last 250 days Beta to ETF Correlation Residual vol (bps/day) Index future (all 200 names) 1.034 0.989 18.7 Peer ETF (top 100 names) 1.022 0.995 12.2 ETF alone, unhedged 126.5

The peer ETF tracks the fund better because it holds the same big names; the future is far cheaper to trade. One-minute correlations during the day were similar (0.983 and 0.993).

The order book adds little at the basket level. In Lab 02's fitted table, a name at a one-tick spread with imbalance +0.6 has a microprice 0.299 ticks above its mid. If all 50 names showed that at once, NAV would rise 0.60 bp; with random imbalances the errors diversify to 0.11 bp. Lab 02's microprice beat the mid by only 3.55% on next-move error (synthetic lab result).

What matters is speed. The day had 410 news jumps, averaging 1.52 bps of fair value and reaching 11.5 bps. In real markets news usually shows up in the future first (linkages); in the toy it moves everything at once. Either way, any quote not yet moved is a free option for latency arbitrage. M2 covers blending leads into one number.

fv = nav(px_basket_now, basket_shares, cash_per_unit)        # Lab 07 nav(): $ per ETF share
g = g_table[book_state(imbalance, spread_ticks)]             # Lab 02 microprice, ticks per name
fv_micro = nav(px_basket_now + g * 0.01, basket_shares, cash_per_unit)   # about +0.1 bp

docs.title: Quoting: width from hedge cost, skew from inventory
docs.text:
The desk quotes with Lab 05's glft_quotes, in bps of fair value, with 500-share lots (M4). Fill parameters A = 0.07 per second and k = 0.67 per bp give a half-spread of 1.49 bps when flat, which is Lab 07's assumed ETF half-spread of 1.5 bps.

The key choice is σ, because the lean per lot scales with it. This desk hedges every fill, so its inventory risk is the leftover basis: 18.7 bps a day, 0.12 bp per √second. With γ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ per bp-lot the lean is 0.10 bp per unit. With the ETF's full 126.5 bps it would be 0.70 bp, and a five-unit block would push quotes 3.5 bps off NAV for no reason. Hedge first, then skew what is left.

Two clamps sit on the formula. A floor of 0.98 bp (0.48 bp for futures in and out plus 0.5 bp of expected adverse selection) stops quoting inside costs. A cap at the band: nobody pays more than the create cost, because rival APs would create and undercut.

d_bid, d_ask = glft_quotes(q_lots, gamma=2.5e-6, sigma=0.1225, A=0.07, k=0.67, q_max=1000)  # Lab 05
d_bid = min(max(d_bid, 0.48 + 0.5), redeem_cost_bps)     # floor: hedge cost + expected markout
d_ask = min(max(d_ask, 0.48 + 0.5), create_cost_bps)     # cap: the creation band (7.45 bps)
bid, ask = fv * (1 - d_bid / 1e4), fv * (1 + d_ask / 1e4)

The RFQ at 11:00 is priced from costs: futures in and out 0.48 bp, plus the basket and fee for five units from no_arbitrage_band(n_units=5) (1.73 half-spreads, 4.36 impact, 0.46 fee), plus a 1.5 bp margin: fair value + 8.53 bps. The ETF market making dossier's example used 8 bps.

docs.title: Fills and inventory
docs.text:
Counterparty Fills Shares Net, from our side Uninformed clients 1,158 587,000 we sold 2,000 Fast arbitrageurs 81 162,000 we bought 34,000 RFQ block 1 250,000 we sold 250,000 Time 10:30 11:00, after block 13:00 15:00 15:50 16:00 ETF inventory (units) −0.62 −5.67 −5.50 −4.49 −4.46 −4.36 Futures held 5 43 42 34 34 3 after close

After the block the quotes sat about 0.55 bp above fair value, so sellers came to the desk and buyers went to rivals. That worked off 1.3 units by the close for nothing beyond the screen spread. The ETF's quoted mid stayed 0.45–0.55 bp above NAV all afternoon, well inside the band. Lab 07 leaves this intraday quoting out: with only end-of-day arbitrage its closing premium has a 6.7 bp standard deviation, against 45.7 bps with none (synthetic lab result).

Lab 07, synthetic data: end-of-day arbitrage pins the premium to the band edges. Intraday quoting, as in this walkthrough, keeps it well inside.

docs.title: Hedging: futures vs basket vs peer ETF
docs.text:
For the block, the desk compares three hedges held five hours to the close: round-trip cost plus the leftover basis risk, charged at the quotes' γ, about 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ per dollar (M7):

Hedge for $11.0M short Cost (bps) Cost ($) Basis sd to close ($) Cost + ½γ·sd² ($) Index future 0.48 531 18,051 716 Peer ETF 1.60 1,757 11,758 1,836 Basket now 6.09 6,687 0 6,687

Futures win; a desk roughly 11 times as risk-averse would pick the peer ETF. The basket is the hedge of last resort, bought only to create. Rebalancing whenever the hedge was a whole contract off target took 119 trades and 185 contracts. The short ETF lost $41,492 in the rally and the futures made $45,784: a $4,292 basis gain, well inside the $18,051 standard deviation. Luck, not skill.

docs.title: The create/redeem decision at the close
docs.text:
MOC orders must be in by 3:50 p.m. on NYSE and 3:55 p.m. on Nasdaq [Verified] (E5). At the cutoff the desk was short 4.46 units. Units are whole, and each has three possible exits:

Option, per unit Cost Create: buy the basket MOC, pay the fee (4 units) 1.78 half-spread + 3.75 impact + 0.57 fee = 6.09 bps Buy back on screen: rivals price size off their own band ~7.62 bps [Estimate] Carry overnight, futures-hedged 0.08 bp of borrow a day, plus overnight basis and gap risk; capped at 1 unit

The desk creates 4 units and carries 0.36 unit (18,000 shares) hedged with 3 futures. Lab 07's arb_decision then asks whether the premium alone justifies extra units: at 0.45 bp, far inside the 7.45 bp bound, it does not.

extra = arb_decision(premium_bps=0.45, create_cost_bps=7.45, redeem_cost_bps=7.52,
                     impact_bps_per_unit=2.0, max_units=10)       # Lab 07 -> 0 units
n_create = int(np.floor(units_short))                             # 4.36 -> 4 whole units
create_cost = no_arbitrage_band(w, hs, vol, adv, unit_value, n_units=4,
                                etf_half_spread_bps=0.0)[0]       # ETF already sold: 6.09 bps

Lab 07's curve shows why the arbitrage trigger sits at the band. A fixed trigger at 0 bps loses $0.53M a year. The best fixed trigger, 7 bps, earns $0.18M, and the cost-aware rule earns $0.21M, 2.8 bps per unit (synthetic lab result). See ETF and index arbitrage.

Lab 07, synthetic data: arbitraging inside your own cost band loses money; P&L peaks near the one-unit cost.

docs.title: Markouts: adverse selection by counterparty
docs.text:
Lab 04's markouts marks every fill forward against fair value (a markout). The table covers fills with a full 300 s ahead, in bps, weighted by shares (M5):

Segment Shares 0 s 1 s 60 s 300 s s.e. at 60 s Uninformed clients 576,500 +1.48 +1.47 +1.60 +2.12 0.16 Fast arbitrageurs 158,000 +1.39 −1.80 −1.97 −1.96 0.53 All screen fills 734,500 +1.46 +0.77 +0.84 +1.24 0.20

The arbitrageurs were 22% of screen volume. Their markouts turn negative within a second and stay there, like Lab 04's informed flow (−1.46 bps at 60 s); Lab 05 showed faster cancels beat widening against adverse selection. Skew has a hidden cost: the side you lean toward sits closer to fair value and gets picked off more (arbitrageurs sold the desk a net 34,000 shares).

Mark a hedged trade against its hedge. The block's raw markout was +8.5 bps at once, +20.5 at 60 s, +31.8 at 300 s and −33.7 by the close: the ETF fell, then rallied 42 bps. Net of 1.034 × the future's move it reads +8.8, +8.1 and +10.8 bps: the desk kept the spread, and the flow showed no information. One block is one draw, so it says little about that client.

Lab 04, synthetic data: informed flow looks profitable at 1 s and loses by 10 s; uninformed flow stays positive.

docs.title: The closing auction
docs.text:
The desk sends a market-on-close (MOC) order for 4 units of basket: 176,040 shares, $8.80M across 50 names. If each closing auction trades 10% of daily volume, that is 1.8% of auction volume cap-weighted and 4.5% at most, too small to set the print. It sells 30 futures at the close; CME's Basis Trade at Index Close (BTIC) prices futures at the official index close plus an agreed basis, matching the MOC prints [Verified].

sequenceDiagram
    participant D as ETF desk
    participant X as Stock exchanges
    participant F as Futures market
    participant I as ETF issuer
    D->>X: 15.50 MOC buy, 176,040 basket shares
    X->>D: Fills at the closing prints
    D->>F: Sell 30 futures at the close or via BTIC
    D->>I: Creation order for 4 units before the cutoff
    I->>D: 200,000 new ETF shares, T+1
    D->>D: Deliver them against the short, carry 18,000 shares

docs.title: P&L / cost attribution
docs.text:
Lab 05's step_pnl splits the ETF leg into spread, adverse-selection and inventory lines every second. The script checks that all lines sum exactly to cash plus positions marked at the closing NAV and futures price (L1, P&L attribution).

Line (synthetic lab result) $ bps of $43.83M ETF traded Spread capture, screen +4,792 +1.09 Spread capture, RFQ block +9,350 +2.13 Rebates net of fees (rebates +1,498; futures −185, MOC −176, Section 31 −550) +587 +0.13 Adverse selection (moves right after fills) −2,208 −0.50 Inventory P&L net of hedge (ETF −41,492; futures +45,784) +4,292 +0.98 Hedge slippage (futures half-ticks) −1,156 −0.26 Basket execution at the close −4,866 −1.11 Creation fee −500 −0.11 Financing and borrow −7 −0.00 Net trading income +10,284 +2.35 
flowchart TD
    s["Spread capture<br/>+14,142"] --> r["Rebates net of fees<br/>+587"]
    r --> a["Adverse selection<br/>-2,208"]
    a --> h["Hedge slippage<br/>-1,156"]
    h --> b["Basket, creation fee, borrow<br/>-5,373"]
    b --> c["Core result<br/>+5,992, 1.37 bps"]
    c --> i["Inventory and basis luck<br/>+4,292"]
    i --> n["Net trading income<br/>+10,284, 2.35 bps"]

Excluding basis luck, the desk kept 1.37 bps of ETF traded, about 1 bp of the $108M traded across all legs. Flow Traders' 2025 net trading income was about 2.5 bps of its €1,940bn of ETP value traded [Reported]. Any match is coincidence: the toy has no rival quoters, a known closing print and Brownian basis. One client's block produced two thirds of spread revenue and paid for the basket: one ticket and one creation instead of 500 screen fills.

docs.title: What would be different in real life
docs.text:
• Competition. Here the desk is the only quoter and RFQ dealer. Real RFQs go to several dealers, and winning margins are thinner [Lore].
  • One risk book. Real desks quote thousands of ETFs and net factor risk before hedging (equity market making).
  • Ticks. At $44 a one-cent tick is 2.3 bps, so a 1.49 bp half-spread is not quotable: join a queue or improve a full tick.
  • Harder fair values. Bond and international baskets are stale or shut and small caps illiquid; such funds' premiums are far wider (Petajisto 2017) [Verified].
  • Tails. Basis here is Brownian. On 24 August 2015 there were 1,278 LULD halts, 1,058 in 327 ETPs [Verified], and desks could not price baskets [Reported] (failure gallery).
  • The print. The toy knows the close. Real MOC orders face imbalances and prints that move against the hedge; the auction charges impact, not Lab 07's half-spread.
  • Fund terms. Fees, order cutoffs, cash or custom baskets (Rule 6c-11) and settlement fails differ by fund [Verified].
  • Below the line. Capital, clearing, data and staff are missing; in the dossier's illustrative split they take about 60% of net trading income.

docs.title: Walkthrough: executing a $500M buy order
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A $500M buy is half a day's volume in a $1B-ADV large cap. The square-root law and Lab 16 agree on about 46–47 bps ($2.3M) of expected cost over five even days. The price risk is five times larger: a 254 bps ($12.7M) standard deviation.
  • An Almgren-Chriss schedule with λ = 10⁻⁸ buys 37% on day 1. It costs 5.3 bps ($263K) more and cuts the standard deviation by $2.9M. Faster schedules break a 25% participation cap.
  • Each day's quota follows the volume curve as thousands of child orders. A markout-aware router pays 1.44–1.48 bps all-in, against 1.71–1.87 for fee-greedy routing (Lab 18). The close is capped at 15% of the expected print.
  • In a 75th-percentile simulated week the order cost 178.8 bps ($8.9M) against the decision price, 132 bps of it timing. The same fills "beat" VWAP by 43 bps and the close by 131 bps.
  • Every basis point is someone's revenue: market makers, liquidity providers, venues, the broker. The 25 bps of permanent impact goes to whoever sold after the rise.

Level: Core · Read time: ~13 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Cast and setup
docs.text:
Scenario (illustrative). A US public pension fund raises its weight in one US large cap by $500M: a parent order for 10M shares at $50. The stock trades 20M shares ($1B) a day, so the order is 50% of ADV. Volatility is 2% a day; the quoted spread averages 3 bps.

Where the numbers come from. The calibration is Lab 16's: temporary impact η = 5×10⁻⁸, permanent impact γ = 2.5×10⁻⁸, half-spread 1.5 bps, five days in 50 intervals of about 39 minutes. Lab 16 simulates a sell; this page mirrors it for a buy: fills at S + ε + η·rate, and each share bought lifts the price by γ. Expected cost and variance are unchanged; a buy on price path z costs what the lab's sell costs on −z. The helper script labs/walkthroughs/institutional-execution.py (seed 7, under 1 s) asserts this, reuses Lab 16's functions and price paths, and computes every derived number below. Lab 17 supplies intraday schedule costs and Lab 18 venue costs. Costs are in bps of the order (1 bp = $50,000); + = cost. All are synthetic lab results.
